:question/problem: What are the critical points of the function $f(x)=\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+4}?$
:question/worked-solution:
A critical point of $f(x)$ is a point $x=c$ in the domain of $f$ such that either ${f}^{′}(c)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(c)$ does not exist.

Differentiating $f(x),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+4}) \\  & =\frac{(x)^{′}\cdot ({x}^{2}+4)-x\cdot ({x}^{2}+4)^{′}}{({x}^{2}+4)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+4)-x\cdot 2x}{({x}^{2}+4)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4-{x}^{2}}{({x}^{2}+4)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

- First, we compute the points where ${f}^{′}(c)=0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4-{x}^{2}}{({x}^{2}+4)^{2}} & =0 \\ 4-{x}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2} & =4 \\ x & =\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has stationary points at $x=-2$ and $x=2.$

- Second, we note that ${f}^{′}(x)$ exists for all values of $x$ in the domain of $f(x).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, we conclude that the critical points of $f(x)$ are $x=-2$ and $x=2.$

Evaluate the geometric series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{3}\frac{1}{{5}^{n-1}}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Notice that we can rewrite the series as follows:

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{3}\frac{1}{{5}^{n-1}}={\sum }_{n=1}^{3}{(\frac{1}{5})}^{n-1}
$$

Since the above series is in the form ${\sum }_{n=1}^{N}{a}_{1}{r}^{n-1},$ it is a geometric series.

To determine the sum, we use the formula for the sum ${S}_{N}$ of a geometric series.

$$
{S}_{N}={a}_{1}\frac{(1-{r}^{N})}{1-r}
$$

In this case, ${a}_{1}=1,$ $r=\frac{1}{5}$ and $N=3.$ If we substitute these values into the above formula, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{3}\frac{1}{{5}^{n-1}} & =1\cdot \frac{[1-{(\frac{1}{5})}^{3}]}{(1-\frac{1}{5})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{124}{125})}{(\frac{4}{5})} \\  & =\frac{31}{25}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Determine the value of the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{4}\frac{1}{{6}^{n}}$  rounded to $3$ decimal places.

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{4}\frac{1}{{6}^{n}}={\sum }_{n=1}^{4}{(\frac{1}{6})}^{n}
$$

Since the above series is in the form ${\sum }_{n=1}^{N}a{r}^{n},$ it is a geometric series. 

To determine the sum, we use the formula for the sum ${S}_{N}$ of a geometric series.

$$
{S}_{N}={a}_{1}\frac{(1-{r}^{N})}{1-r}
$$

In this case, $r=\frac{1}{6}$ and $N=4.$ We need to figure out ${a}_{1}.$

The formula for the $n$th term of the series is

$$
{a}_{n}={(\frac{1}{6})}^{n},
$$

and therefore the first term of the series is

$$
{a}_{1}={(\frac{1}{6})}^{1}=\frac{1}{6}.
$$

If we substitute ${a}_{1}=\frac{1}{6},r=\frac{1}{6}$ and $N=4$ into the formula for ${S}_{N}$, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{4}{(\frac{1}{6})}^{n} & =\frac{1}{6}\cdot \frac{[1-{(\frac{1}{6})}^{4}]}{(1-\frac{1}{6})} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot [1-{(\frac{1}{6})}^{4}] \\  & ≈0.200\end{aligned}

:question/problem: Determine the value of the geometric series ${\sum }_{n=0}^{7}8{(\frac{3}{5})}^{n-1}$ rounded to $3$ decimal places.

Since the given series is in the form $\sum a{r}^{n-1},$ it is a geometric series. Notice that the index starts from $n=0$ instead of $n=1.$

To determine the sum, we use the formula for the sum ${S}_{N}$ of a geometric series.

$$
{S}_{N}={a}_{0}\frac{(1-{r}^{N})}{1-r}
$$

In this case, $r=\frac{3}{5}.$ Also, note that $N=8,$ since there are $8$ terms in total.

The formula for the $n$th term of the series is

$$
{a}_{n}=8{(\frac{3}{5})}^{n-1},
$$

and so the first term ${a}_{0}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =8{(\frac{3}{5})}^{0-1} \\  & =8{(\frac{3}{5})}^{-1} \\  & =8(\frac{5}{3}) \\  & =\frac{40}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

If we substitute ${a}_{0}=\frac{40}{3}\,,r=\frac{3}{5}$ and $N=8$ into the formula for ${S}_{N}$, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{8} & =\frac{40}{3}\cdot \frac{[1-{(\frac{3}{5})}^{8}]}{(1-\frac{3}{5})} \\  & =\frac{40}{3}\cdot \frac{[1-{(\frac{3}{5})}^{8}]}{(\frac{2}{5})} \\  & =\frac{100}{3}\cdot [1-{(\frac{3}{5})}^{8}] \\  & ≈32.773\end{aligned}

:question/problem: Consider the positive infinite geometric sequence that has a first term equal to $18$ and a third term equal to $2.$ What is the sum to infinity of the terms of this sequence?
:question/worked-solution:
The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

From the question statement we have ${a}_{1}=18$ and ${a}_{3}=2.$ We can find the common ratio using the following formula:

$$
{r}^{n-m}=\frac{{a}_{n}}{{a}_{m}}
$$

Substituting in the known information into the above gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{3-1} & =\frac{2}{18} \\ {r}^{2} & =\frac{1}{9} \\ r & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{9}} \\ r & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we have taken the positive square root since we're told that the sequence is positive.

So, using the formula, we find that the sum to infinity is

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{\infty } & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{18}{(1-\frac{1}{3})} \\  & =\frac{18}{(\frac{2}{3})} \\  & =27.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The position vector $r$ of a particle $P$ (relative to a fixed origin $O$) at time $t$ is given by

$$
r=⟨\frac{{t}^{2}}{2},\,3t+7⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the speed of the particle at time $t=4.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate the velocity vector $v.$ Differentiating the position vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t+7)⟩ \\  & =⟨t,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the velocity when $t=4,$ we substitute in the above:

$$
v=⟨4,3⟩
$$

To find the speed at $t=4$ we calculate the magnitude of $v(4),$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|v(4)| & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16+9} \\  & =\sqrt{25} \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the speed when $t=4$ is $5.$

$$
\text{E}[X]={\sum }_{x\in S}x\cdot f(x).
$$

We're given the frequencies of the children's ages, so we can start by computing the corresponding probabilities. The total number of children is $2+4+4=10,$ so the corresponding probabilities are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=10)=f(10) & =\frac{2}{10}=\frac{1}{5} \\ P(X=11)=f(11) & =\frac{4}{10}=\frac{2}{5} \\ P(X=12)=f(12) & =\frac{4}{10}=\frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

We organize these results in the table below.

| $x$ | $10$ | $11$ | $12$ |

:question/problem: In a class, $\frac{1}{3}$ of the students are boys, and $\frac{2}{3}$ are girls. Of the boys, $\frac{1}{6}$ of them play soccer, and of the girls, $\frac{1}{4}$ of them play soccer. What is the probability that a randomly selected student plays soccer?
:question/worked-solution:
Let $S$ be the event that the chosen student plays soccer, and let $B$ be the event that the student is a boy. Then ${B}^{′}$ is the event that the student is a girl.

To calculate the probability that a randomly selected student plays soccer, we can use the law of total probability:

$$
P(S)=P(S|B)P(B)+P(S|{B}^{′})P({B}^{′})
$$

Let's go through the problem statement and translate each bit of information into mathematical notation.

- Since $\frac{1}{3}$ of the students are boys and $\frac{2}{3}$ are girls, we have

$$
P(B)=\frac{1}{3},\,P({B}^{′})=\frac{2}{3}.
$$

- Since $\frac{1}{6}$ of the boys play soccer and $\frac{1}{4}$ of the girls play soccer, we have

$$
P(S|B)=\frac{1}{6},\,P(S|{B}^{′})=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

Substituting the above information into the law of total probability, the probability that a randomly selected student plays soccer is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(S) & =P(S|B)P(B)+P(S|{B}^{′})P({B}^{′}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{6})(\frac{1}{3})+(\frac{1}{4})(\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{18}+\frac{1}{6} \\  & =\frac{1+3}{18} \\  & =\frac{2}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: In a class, $\frac{3}{5}$ of the students are boys, and $\frac{2}{5}$ are girls. Of the boys, $\frac{1}{12}$ of them play basketball. The probability that a randomly selected student plays basketball is $\frac{1}{15}.$ If a girl is selected at random, what is the probability that she plays basketball?
:question/worked-solution:
Let $A$ be the event that the chosen student plays basketball, and let $B$ be the event that the student is a boy. Then ${B}^{′}$ is the event that the student is a girl.

To calculate the probability that a randomly selected student plays basketball, we can use the law of total probability:

$$
P(A)=P(A|B)P(B)+P(A|{B}^{′})P({B}^{′})
$$

Let's go through the problem statement and translate each bit of information into mathematical notation.

- Since $\frac{3}{5}$ of the students are boys and $\frac{2}{5}$ are girls, we have

$$
P(B)=\frac{3}{5},\,P({B}^{′})=\frac{2}{5}.
$$

- Since $\frac{1}{12}$ of the boys play basketball, we have

$$
P(A|B)=\frac{1}{12}.
$$

- Since the probability that a randomly selected student plays basketball is $\frac{1}{15},$ we have

$$
P(A)=\frac{1}{15}.
$$

Substituting the above information into the law of total probability and solving for $P(A|{B}^{′}),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A) & =P(A|B)P(B)+P(A|{B}^{′})P({B}^{′}) \\ \frac{1}{15} & =(\frac{1}{12})(\frac{3}{5})+P(A|{B}^{′})(\frac{2}{5}) \\ \frac{1}{15} & =\frac{1}{20}+\frac{2}{5}P(A|{B}^{′}) \\ 60\cdot (\frac{1}{15}) & =60\cdot (\frac{1}{20}+\frac{2}{5}P(A|{B}^{′}))​ \\ 4 & =3+24P(A|{B}^{′}) \\ 1 & =24P(A|{B}^{′}) \\ P(A|{B}^{′}) & =\frac{1}{24}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability that a randomly selected girl plays basketball is $\frac{1}{24}.$

:question/problem:
In a factory, soda cans are filled with a mean volume of $12$ ounces of soda. However, $1%$ of cans contain no more than $11.5$ ounces of soda. Assuming that the volume of soda in each can is normally distributed, find the standard deviation of the volume of soda in a can, rounded to $2$ decimal places.

*Hint: A table of values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p$ is given below, where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $p$ | $\,0.900\,$ | $\,0.950\,$ | $\,0.975\,$ | $\,0.990\,$ | $\,0.995\,$ | $\,0.999\,$ | $\,0.9995\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\,1.2816\,$ | $\,1.6449\,$ | $\,1.9600\,$ | $\,2.3263\,$ | $\,2.5758\,$ | $\,3.0902\,$ | $\,3.2905\,$ |
:question/worked-solution:
Let $X$ represent the volume (in ounces) of soda in a can. Then we have $X∼N(12,{\sigma }^{2}),$ and we want to find the standard deviation $\sigma .$ 

We know that $P(X\le 11.5)=0.01.$ Converting $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 11.5) & =0.01 \\ P(Z\le \frac{11.5-12}{\sigma }) & =0.01 \\ Φ(-\frac{0.5}{\sigma }) & =0.01 \\ -\frac{0.5}{\sigma } & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.01).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, 

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(0.99)=2.3263,
$$

and therefore by symmetry, we have

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(1-0.99)={Φ}^{-1}(0.01)=-2.3263.
$$

Finally then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{0.5}{\sigma } & =-2.3263 \\ \frac{1}{\sigma } & =4.6524 \\ \sigma  & =\frac{1}{4.6524} \\  & ≈0.21.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
In a factory, cookies contain $15$ grams of sugar on average. However, $10%$ of cookies contain more than $17$ grams of sugar. | ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\,1.2816\,$ | $\,1.6449\,$ | $\,1.9600\,$ | $\,2.3263\,$ | $\,2.5758\,$ | $\,3.0902\,$ | $\,3.2905\,$ |

$$

$$

*In addition, you're given the following table of values for $p=Φ(z)$*.

| $\,-1.7\,$ | $\,0.0446\,$ | $\,0.0436\,$ | $\,0.0427\,$ |
:question/worked-solution:
Let $X$ represent the number of grams of sugar in a cookie. Then we have $X∼N(15,{\sigma }^{2}),$ and we want to find $P(X<12).$ But first, we need to find the standard deviation $\sigma .$ 

We know that $P(X>17)=0.1.$ First, we convert this to a cumulative probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 17) & =1-P(X>17) \\  & =1-0.1 \\  & =0.9\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 17) & =0.9 \\ P(Z\le \frac{17-15}{\sigma }) & =0.9 \\ Φ(\frac{2}{\sigma }) & =0.9 \\ \frac{2}{\sigma } & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.9)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, 

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(0.9)≈1.2816.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sigma } & =1.2816 \\ \frac{1}{\sigma } & =0.6408 \\ \sigma  & =\frac{1}{0.6408} \\  & ≈1.5605.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve for $P(X<12)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<12) & =P(X\le 12) \\  & =P(Z\le \frac{12-15}{1.5605}) \\  & ≈P(Z\le -1.92) \\  & =Φ(-1.92) \\  & =0.0274 \\  & ≈2.7%\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, approximately $2.7%$ of cookies contain less than $12$ grams of sugar.

:question/problem: Write $y = 7x+\dfrac{2}{5}$ in standard form.
:question/worked-solution:
Our goal is to write the equation in the form $ax+by = c,$ where $a,b,$ and $c$ are integers with no common factors, and $a\geq 0.$

We begin by moving all of the variables to the left-hand side and all of the constants to the right-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =7x+\frac{2}{5} \\ y-7x & =\frac{2}{5} \\ -7x+y & =\frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Now the equation is in the form $ax+by=c.$ However, it violates the rule $a \geq 0.$ We can fix this by multiplying the equation by $-1$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-7x+y & =\frac{2}{5} \\ (-1)\cdot (-7x+y) & =(-1)\cdot (\frac{2}{5}) \\ 7x-y & =-\frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

However, $c$ is a fraction, not an integer. To fix this, we multiply by $5$ to get rid of the fraction:

$$
\begin{aligned}7x-y & =-\frac{2}{5} \\ 5\cdot (7x-y) & =5\cdot (-\frac{2}{5}) \\ 35x-5y & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, $a,b,$ and $c$ are integers with no common factors, and $a\geq 0.$ So we are done!

The standard form of the line is $35x-5y=-2.$

:question/problem:
Use the transformation $y = vx$  (where $v=v(x)$) to rewrite the given first-order homogeneous ODE 

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x}    =   \cos \left( \frac {y} {x} \right)
$$

as a separable ODE in $v$ and $x.$
:question/worked-solution:
With $y = vx$ (where $v = v(x)$), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging that into the differential equation and separating variables, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{y}{x}) \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(v) \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(v)-v \\ (\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(v)-v})\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Which of the following differential equations are homogeneous?

- $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac{y}{x}$

- $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac{y}{x^2}$

- $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac{y}{2x}\sin{\left(\dfrac{x^2}{y^2}\right)}$
:question/worked-solution:
A first-order ordinary differential equation that is written in the form

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x}
    =
    f(x, y)
$$

is said to be homogeneous if $f(x,y)$ is a homogeneous function of degree zero, meaning that it satisfies

$$
f(tx, ty) = f(x, y).
$$

With that in mind, let's take a look at the right-hand side function in each differential equation.

- The function $f(x,y) = \dfrac{y}{x}$ is a homogeneous function of degree zero:
 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty) & =\frac{(ty)}{(tx)} \\  & =\text{ }\frac{t\cdot y}{t\cdot x} \\  & =\frac{y}{x} \\  & =f(x,y)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, equation I is a homogenous differential equation.

- The function $f(x,y) = \dfrac{y}{x^2}$ is *not* a homogeneous function of degree $0.$ Rather, it is a homogeneous function of degree $-1\mathbin{:}$
 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty) & =\frac{(ty)}{(tx)^{2}} \\  & =\text{ }\frac{t\cdot y}{{t}^{2}\cdot {x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{t}\cdot \frac{y}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{t}\cdot f(x,y) \\  & ={t}^{-1}f(x,y)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, equation II is *not* a homogenous differential equation.

- The function $f(x,y) = \dfrac{y}{2x}\sin{\left(\dfrac{x^2}{y^2}\right)}$ is a homogeneous function of degree zero:
 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty) & =\frac{ty}{2(tx)}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{(tx)^{2}}{(ty)^{2}}) \\  & =\text{ }\frac{t\cdot y}{t\cdot 2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{{t}^{2}{x}^{2}}{{t}^{2}{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{y}{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =f(x,y)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, equation III is a homogenous differential equation.

In conclusion, the correct answer is "I and III only."

:question/problem: Given that $\sin{\theta}=\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{2}< \theta < \pi$, what is the value of $\sin2\theta$?
:question/worked-solution:
To find the value of $\sin2\theta$, we use the double-angle formula for sine:

$$
\sin2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta
$$

First, we need to find the value of $\cos{\theta}$. From the Pythagorean identity, we have

$$
\cos \theta = \pm \sqrt{1 - \sin^2 \theta}
$$

Substituting

$$
\sin{\theta} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}
$$

into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
\cos θ &= ± \sqrt{1 - (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})^{2}} \\
&= ± \sqrt{1 - \frac{2}{4}} \\
&= ± \sqrt{1 - \frac{1}{2}} \\
&= ± \sqrt{\frac{1}{2}} \\
&= ± \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\
&= ± \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\theta$ lies in the second quadrant. Therefore, $\cos\theta \lt 0$, and we take the *negative* square root in the above expression. Hence,

$$
\cos x = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}
$$

Finally, substituting our values for sine and cosine into the double-angle formula for sine, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sin 2θ &= 2\sin θ\cos θ \\
&= 2 \cdot (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\
&=-\frac{2 \cdot \sqrt{2} \cdot \sqrt{2}}{2 \cdot 2} \\
&=-\frac{2 \cdot 2}{2 \cdot 2} \\
&=-1
\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the exact value of $\csc{2\theta}$ if $\cos{\theta}=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$ and $\theta$ lies in the fourth quadrant.
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that

$$
\csc{2\theta} = \dfrac{1}{\sin{2\theta}}
$$

So, we need to find the value of $\sin{2\theta}$ and then compute its reciprocal.

To find the value of $\sin2\theta$, we use the double-angle formula for sine:

$$
\sin2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta
$$

First, let's find the value of $\sin{\theta}$. From the Pythagorean identity, we have

$$
\sin \theta = \pm \sqrt{1 - \cos^2 \theta}
$$

Substituting

$$
\cos \theta = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}
$$

into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sin θ &= ± \sqrt{1 - \cos^{2} θ} \\
&= ± \sqrt{1 - (\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})^{2}} \\
&= ± \sqrt{1 - \frac{1}{3}} \\
&= ± \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \\
&= ± \frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}}
\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\theta$ lies in the fourth quadrant. Therefore, $\sin\theta \lt 0$, and we take the *negative* root in the above expression. Hence,

$$
\sin{\theta} = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt 3}
$$

Now, substituting our values for sine and cosine into the double-angle formula for sine, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sin 2θ &= 2\sin θ\cos θ \\
&= 2 \cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}}) \cdot (\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}) \\
&=-\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\csc 2θ &= \frac{1}{\sin 2θ} = (1)/((-\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3})) =-\frac{3}{2\sqrt{2}} =-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}
\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $\cos{\theta} = \dfrac{1}{3}$ and $0^\circ < \theta < 90^{\circ}$, what is the value of $\sin{2\theta}$?
:question/worked-solution:
To find the value of $\sin2\theta$, we use the double-angle formula for sine:

$$
\sin2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta
$$

First, we need to find the value of $\sin{\theta}$. From the Pythagorean identity, we have

$$
\sin \theta = \pm \sqrt{1 - \cos^2 \theta}
$$

Substituting

$$
\cos{\theta} = \dfrac{1}{3}
$$

into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sin θ &= ± \sqrt{1 - (\frac{1}{3})^{2}} \\
&= ± \sqrt{1 - \frac{1}{9}} \\
&= ± \sqrt{\frac{8}{9}} \\
&= ± \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\theta$ lies in the first quadrant. Therefore, $\sin\theta > 0$, and we take the *positive* square root in the above expression. Hence,

$$
\sin\theta = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}
$$

Finally, substituting our values for sine and cosine into the double-angle formula for sine, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sin 2θ &= 2\sin θ\cos θ \\
&= 2 \cdot (\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}) \cdot (\frac{1}{3}) \\
&= \frac{4\sqrt{2}}{9}
\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Express $\cos^2{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{24}\right)} - \sin^2{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{24}\right)}$ as a single trigonometric ratio.

:question/problem: Express $\dfrac{2\tan \left(\dfrac{\pi}{5}\right)}{\tan^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{5}\right) - 1}$ as a single trigonometric ratio.
:question/worked-solution:
First, we multiply the numerator and denominator of the given expression by $(-1)$ and rewrite it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(2\tan (\frac{π}{5}))/(\tan^{2} (\frac{π}{5}) - 1) &= (-2\tan (\frac{π}{5}))/(1 - \tan^{2} (\frac{π}{5})) \\
&= - (2\tan (\frac{π}{5}))/(1 - \tan^{2} (\frac{π}{5}))
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's recall the double-angle formula for tangent:

$$
\tan 2x = \dfrac{2\tan x}{1-\tan^2 x}
$$

Substituting

$$
x=\dfrac{\pi}{5}
$$

into the above, we get

$$
\tan\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\right) = \dfrac{2\tan \left(\dfrac{\pi}{5}\right)}{1 - \tan^2 \left(\dfrac{\pi}{5}\right)}
$$

Therefore,

$$
-\dfrac{2\tan \left(\dfrac{\pi}{5}\right)}{1-\tan^2 \left(\dfrac{\pi}{5}\right)} = -\tan \left(\dfrac{2\pi}{5} \right)
$$

:question/problem: Simplify the expression $\dfrac{5\tan{2x}}{\cot{x}-\tan{x}}$.
:question/worked-solution:
Substituting

$$
\cot{x}=\dfrac{1}{\tan{x}}
$$

into our expression and then simplifying, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{5\tan 2x}{\cot x - \tan x} &= (5\tan 2x)/((\frac{1}{\tan x} - \tan x)) \\
&= \frac{5\tan 2x \cdot \tan x}{1 - \tan^{2} x} \\
&= 5\tan 2x \cdot (\frac{\tan x}{1 - \tan^{2} x})
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's recall the double-angle formula for tangent:

$$
\tan {2x} = \dfrac {2\tan x}{1-\tan^2 x}
$$

Writing our expression in terms of $\tan2x$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
5\tan 2x \cdot (\frac{\tan x}{1 - \tan^{2} x}) &= \frac{5}{2}\tan 2x \cdot (\frac{2\tan x}{1 - \tan^{2} x}) \\
&= \frac{5}{2}\tan 2x \cdot (\tan 2x) \\
&= \frac{5}{2}\tan^{2} 2x
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{5\tan{2x}}{\cot{x}-\tan{x}} = \dfrac{5}{2} \tan^2 {2x}
$$

:question/problem: Simplify $\dfrac{8\tan{2\theta}}{1-\tan^2{2\theta}}$.
:question/worked-solution:
First, let's recall the double-angle formula for tangent:

$$
\tan 2x = \dfrac{2\tan x}{1-\tan^2 x}
$$

Substituting $x=2\theta$ into the above, we get

$$
\tan 4θ = \frac{2\tan 2θ}{1 - \tan^{2} 2θ}
$$

Writing our expression in terms of $\tan 2\theta$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{8\tan 2θ}{1 - \tan^{2} 2θ} &= 4 \cdot (\frac{2\tan 2θ}{1 - \tan^{2} 2θ}) = 4\tan 4θ
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{8\tan{2\theta}}{1-\tan^2{2\theta}} = 4\tan{4\theta}
$$

:question/problem: Express $z=-5+12\textrm{i}$ in the form $r(\cos\theta + \textrm{i}\sin\theta).$ Round $\theta$ to three decimal places.
:question/worked-solution:
In polar form, $r$ represents the magnitude $|z|.$ For a complex number $z=x+y\textrm{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z| = \sqrt{x^2+y^2} .
$$

So, for $z = -5+12\textrm{i},$ the magnitude is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{(-5)}^{2}+{(12)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25+144} \\  & =\sqrt{169} \\  & =13.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar form, $\theta$  represents the argument $\arg(z).$ Since $x = -5$ is negative and $y = 12$ is positive, $z$ lies in the second quadrant. So, we can find $\theta$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{12}{-5}| \\  & =\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{12}{5}) \\  & ≈1.966,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places. 

Finally, we write the complex number $z = -5 + 12\textrm{i}$ in polar form:

$$
z = 13(\cos(1.966)+\textrm{i}\sin(1.966))
$$

:question/problem: Express $z=4\left(\cos\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)+\textrm{i}\sin\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)\right)$ in the form $z=x+\textrm{i}y.$
:question/worked-solution:
We will simplify the right-hand side. Since $\cos\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and $\sin\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =4(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6})+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6})) \\  & =4(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}+\text{i}\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-2\sqrt{3}+2\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Express $z=\dfrac{3}{2-\textrm{i}}$ in the form $r(\cos\theta+\textrm{i}\sin\theta).$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we express the given complex number in the form $z=x+y\textrm{i}.$ To do this, we remove $\textrm{i}$ from the denominator by multiplying the numerator and denominator of $z$ by the complex conjugate of the denominator, which is $2+\textrm{i}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{3}{2-\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{3(2+\text{i})}{(2-\text{i})(2+\text{i})} \\  & =\frac{3(2+\text{i})}{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3}{5}(2+\text{i}) \\  & =\frac{6}{5}+\frac{3}{5}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

In polar form, $r$ represents the magnitude $|z|.$ For a complex number $z=x+y\textrm{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z| = \sqrt{x^2+y^2} .
$$

So, for $z= \dfrac{6}{5} +\dfrac{3}{5}\textrm{i},$ the magnitude is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{(\frac{6}{5})}^{2}+{(\frac{3}{5})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{36+9}{25}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{45}{25}} \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar form, $\theta$  represents the argument $\arg(z).$ Since $x = \dfrac{6}{5}$ and $y = \dfrac{3}{5}$ are both positive, $z$ lies in the first quadrant. So, we can find $\theta$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{(\frac{3}{5})}{(\frac{6}{5})}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =0.464,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places. 

Finally, we write the complex number $z$ in polar form:

$$
z = \dfrac{3\sqrt{5}}{5} \left (\cos(0.464)+ \textrm{i} \sin(0.464) \right)
$$

:question/problem: Write the complex number $z=4+4\textrm{i}$ in exponential form.
:question/worked-solution:
To write our complex number in the form $z = r\textrm{e}^{\textrm{i}\theta},$ where $r=|z|$ and $\theta = \arg(z),$ we first calculate $r\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $z$ lies in the first quadrant of the complex plane, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $r=4\sqrt{2}$ and $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ into $z=re^{\textrm{i}\theta},$ we get

$$
z = 4\sqrt{2}\,\textrm{e}^{\pi\textrm{i}/4}.
$$

:question/problem: Find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola with the parametric equations $x = 6\sec{t},\, y = 4 \sqrt{2}\tan{t}.$
:question/worked-solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola, we need to eliminate the parameter $t.$ We can do this using the secant-tangent identity.

- Isolating the $\sec t$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =6\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{x}{6} & =\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ {(\frac{x}{6})}^{2} & ={(\operatorname{sec}⁡t)}^{2} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{6}^{2}} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{36} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

- Isolating the $\tan{t}$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =4\sqrt{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{y}{4\sqrt{2}} & =\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ {(\frac{y}{4\sqrt{2}})}^{2} & ={(\operatorname{tan}⁡t)}^{2} \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{(4\sqrt{2})}^{2}} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{32} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the two equations into the identity $\tan^2{t} + 1 = \sec^2{t}$ and rearranging, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{tan}^{2}⁡t+1 & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{32}+1 & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{36} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{36}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{32} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: A curve is defined parametrically by the equations $x=\dfrac{1}{t}, y=\sqrt{(t-2)(3t-1)}$. What are the coordinates of the $x$-intercepts of the curve?
:question/worked-solution:
To find the coordinates of the $x$-intercepts, we set $y=0$ and solve for $t$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
y &= \sqrt{(t - 2)(3t - 1)} \\
0 &= \sqrt{(t - 2)(3t - 1)} \\
0 &= (t - 2)(3t - 1)
\end{aligned}
$$

The right-hand side equals zero if one of the factors is zero.

- For the factor $(t-2)$, we have
$(t - 2)|= 0; t|= 2$.
- For the factor $(3t-1)$, we get
$(3t - 1)|= 0; 3t|= 1; t|= \frac{1}{3}$.

Then, we substitute our solutions for $t$ into the equation

$$
x=\dfrac 1t
$$

- Substituting $t=2$ gives
$x|= \frac{1}{t}; = \frac{1}{2}$.
- Substituting $t=\dfrac{1}{3}$ gives
$x|= \frac{1}{t}; = (1)/((\frac{1}{3})); = 3$.

Therefore, the $x$-intercepts are

$$
\left(\dfrac{1}{2},0\right)
$$

and $(3,0)$.

:question/problem: Determine if $(4-3x)$ is a factor of $p(x)=-6x^2+11x-4.$
:question/worked-solution:
According to the factor theorem, $(ax-b)$ is a factor of $p(x)$ if the root $x = \dfrac{b}{a}$ is also a root of $p(x).$ 

Here, we are considering $(4-3x).$ The root of this expression can be found by setting the expression equal to $0$ and solving:

$$
\begin{aligned}4-3x & =0 \\ 4 & =3x \\ x & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

According to the factor theorem, then, $(4-3x)$ is a factor of $p(x)$ if the root $x=\dfrac{4}{3}$ is also a root of $p(x).$

So, we just need to check if $x=\dfrac{4}{3}$ is a root of $p(x).$ In other words, we need to check if $p\left( \dfrac{4}{3} \right) =0\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\frac{4}{3}) & =-6{(\frac{4}{3})}^{2}+11(\frac{4}{3})-4 \\  & =-6\cdot \frac{16}{9}+\frac{44}{3}-4 \\  & =\frac{-32+44-12}{3} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Indeed, $p \left( \dfrac{4}{3} \right)=0,$ so $x=\dfrac{4}{3}$ is a root of the polynomial. Consequently, by the factor theorem, we conclude that $(4-3x)$ is indeed a factor of $p(x).$

:question/problem: Determine the horizontal asymptote of $f(x) = \dfrac{2x^3}{x^2-1}.$
:question/worked-solution:
To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to\infty.$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is $x^2.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by $x^2,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}-1} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}})}{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & =\frac{2x}{(1-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the term $\dfrac{1}{x^2}$ becomes very small. Therefore, as $x\to\infty,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{2x}{(1-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & ≈\frac{2x}{1-0} \\  & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

This is not a constant, which means that $y = f(x)$ does not have a horizontal asymptote.

:question/problem: Find, in radians to two decimal places, the argument of $z=-\sqrt{3}-\textrm{i}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Let's plot $z$ in the complex plane.

![](images/00/0095750158d9a296c9950c2d753ffe820735298c96cdf4de23aef0747862658d.png)

The complex number $z$ lies in the third quadrant of the complex plane. Therefore $\pi<        \arg(z)<        \dfrac{3\pi}{2}.$ If $\alpha$ is the angle that $z$ makes with the negative real axis, then

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})=\frac{\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta=\arg(z) = \pi +\dfrac\pi 6 = \dfrac{7\pi}{6}.
$$

:question/problem:
What set of parametric equations, defined for $t\in(-\infty, \infty),$ generate the parabola shown below?

![](images/0a/0ae3d46a511cfe74b489eec33e6f6fec0adcb5be7d955a1880f979963b0e01f6.png)
:question/worked-solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at $(0,0),$ and passes through the point $(4,8).$

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola  that has its vertex at $(0,0)$ are

$$
x = 2pt, \qquad y = pt^2,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Since the parabola passes through $(4,8),$ we can substitute $x=4$ and $y=8$ into the standard parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4 &=2pt \\ 8 &=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =2pt \\ 2 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{2}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}8 & =p{(\frac{2}{p})}^{2} \\ 8 & =p\cdot \frac{4}{{p}^{2}} \\ 8 & =\frac{4}{p} \\ p & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x = 2\left(\dfrac 12 \right)t, \qquad y = \left(\dfrac 12 \right)t^2 ,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x = t, \qquad y = \dfrac 12 t^2 .
$$

:question/problem: Find the first three non-zero terms of the expansion of $f(x) = \ln{\left(\dfrac{1+2x}{1+x}\right)}.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, using the laws of logarithms, we observe that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1+2x}{1+x}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+2x)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+x)\,.\end{aligned}
$$

For the expansion of $\ln(1+x),$ we use the standard result

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+x) & =x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}-⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

To obtain the expansion of $\ln{(1+2x)},$ we replace $x$ with $2x$ in the standard expansion:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+2x) & =2x-\frac{1}{2}(2x)^{2}+\frac{1}{3}(2x)^{3}-⋯ \\  & =2x-2{x}^{2}+\frac{8}{3}{x}^{3}-⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we subtract the two series to give the desired result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1+2x}{1+x}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+2x)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+x) \\  & =(2x-2{x}^{2}+\frac{8}{3}{x}^{3}-⋯)-(x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}-⋯) \\  & =x-\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{7}{3}{x}^{3}-⋯\end{aligned}
$$

For the series $\ln(1+2x),$ the radius of convergence is given by

$$
-1 < 2x \leq 1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x\in \left(-\dfrac12,\dfrac12\right].
$$

The series $\ln(1+x)$ has a radius of convergence of $x\in(-1,1].$ Therefore, the radius of convergence of $f(x)$ is

$$
x\in \left(-\dfrac12,\dfrac12\right] \cap (-1,1] = \left(-\dfrac12,\dfrac12\right] .
$$

:question/problem: What is the sum of the series $1+\dfrac{2}{3} + \dfrac{4}{9} + \dfrac{8}{27} + \cdots + \dfrac{2^n}{3^n}+\cdots\,?$
:question/worked-solution:
The first thing we notice is that we can rewrite the terms of the series as powers of $\dfrac{2}{3}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}1+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{4}{9}+\frac{8}{27}+⋯+\frac{{2}^{n}}{{3}^{n}}+⋯ & =1+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{2}^{3}}{{3}^{3}}+⋯+\frac{{2}^{n}}{{3}^{n}}+⋯ \\  & =1+\frac{2}{3}+{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2}+{(\frac{2}{3})}^{3}+⋯+{(\frac{2}{3})}^{n}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we recognize that the series looks similar to the Maclaurin expansion for $f({\color{blue}x}) = \dfrac{1}{1-{\color{blue}x}}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{1-x} & =1+x+{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}+⋯+{x}^{n}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x={\color{blue}\dfrac{2}{3}}$ into our Maclaurin expansion gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{(1-\frac{2}{3})} & =1+\frac{2}{3}+{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2}+{(\frac{2}{3})}^{3}+⋯+{(\frac{2}{3})}^{n}+⋯ \\ 3 & =1+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{4}{9}+\frac{8}{27}+⋯+\frac{{2}^{n}}{{3}^{n}}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the sum of the series is $3.$

Notice that we can rewrite the given sum as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}-\frac{(2/3)^{2}}{2}+\frac{(2/3)^{3}}{3}+⋯+\frac{(-1)^{n+1}(2/3)^{n}}{n}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we recognize that the series looks similar to the Maclaurin expansion for $f(x) = \ln(1+x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+x) & =x-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x={\color{blue}\dfrac{2}{3}}$ into our Maclaurin expansion gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+\frac{2}{3}) & =\frac{2}{3}-\frac{(2/3)^{2}}{2}+\frac{(2/3)^{3}}{3}+⋯+\frac{(-1)^{n+1}(2/3)^{n}}{n}+⋯ \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{5}{3}) & =\frac{2}{3}-\frac{(2/3)^{2}}{2}+\frac{(2/3)^{3}}{3}+⋯+\frac{(-1)^{n+1}(2/3)^{n}}{n}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the sum of the series is $\ln\left(\dfrac{5}{3}\right).$

:question/problem: Given that $\csc \theta = 2$ and $\theta$ lies in the first quadrant, what is the value of $\sin 2\theta$?
:question/worked-solution:
To find the value of $\sin2\theta$, we use the double-angle formula for sine:

$$
\sin2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta
$$

First, recall that

$$
\sin{\theta} = \dfrac{1}{\csc{\theta}}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\sin \theta = \dfrac{1}{\csc \theta} = \dfrac{1}{2}
$$

Now, we need to find the value of $\cos{\theta}$. From the Pythagorean identity, we have

$$
\cos \theta = \pm \sqrt{1 - \sin^2 \theta}
$$

Substituting

$$
\sin\theta = \dfrac12
$$

into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
\cos θ &= ± \sqrt{1 - \sin^{2} θ} \\
&= ± \sqrt{1 - (\frac{1}{2})^{2}} \\
&= ± \sqrt{1 - \frac{1}{4}} \\
&= ± \sqrt{\frac{3}{4}} \\
&= ± \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\theta$ lies in the first quadrant. Therefore, $\cos\theta \gt 0$, and we take the *positive* square root in the above expression. Hence,

$$
\cos{\theta} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}
$$

Finally, substituting our values for sine and cosine into the double-angle formula for sine, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sin 2θ &= 2\sin θ\cos θ \\
&= 2 \cdot (\frac{1}{2}) \cdot (\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\
&= \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3{y}^{3}}{x{y}^{2}+y{x}^{2}}.
$$

If the transformation $y=v(x)x$ is applied to the differential equation, what is the resulting equation?
:question/worked-solution:
Using the transformation $y=vx$ (where $v=v(x)$), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) \\  & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given differential equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{3{y}^{3}}{x{y}^{2}+y{x}^{2}} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{3(vx)^{3}}{x(vx)^{2}+(vx){x}^{2}} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{3{v}^{3}{x}^{3}}{v{x}^{3}(v+1)} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{3{v}^{3}\cancel{{x}^{3}}}{v\cancel{{x}^{3}}(v+1)} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{3{v}^{2}}{v+1}-v \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{3{v}^{2}}{v+1}-\frac{v(v+1)}{v+1} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{3{v}^{2}-{v}^{2}-v}{v+1} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2{v}^{2}-v}{v+1} \\ (\frac{v+1}{2{v}^{2}-v})\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/d7/d7eb4042a5422d631c867cba1c1fa9c52b400d0061fd5fe7d2fa380d721dbac5.png)

Write the complex number $z$, shown on the Argand diagram above, in the form $r{e}^{\text{i}\theta },$ giving $\theta $ in radians to three decimal places.
:question/worked-solution:
The complex number shown in the Argand diagram can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =x+\text{i}y \\  & =4+3\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

To write it in the form $z=r{\text{e}}^{\text{i}\theta },$ where $r=|z|$ and $\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z),$ we first calculate $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $z$ lies in the first quadrant, we can find the angle $\theta $ as

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{3}{4}) \\  & ≈0.644.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $r=5$ and $\theta =0.644$ into $z=r{e}^{\text{i}\theta },$ we get 

$$
z=5\,{\text{e}}^{0.644\,\text{i}}.
$$

:question/problem: Write the complex number $z=-1+2\text{i}$ in the form $r{e}^{\text{i}\theta },$ giving $\theta $ in radians to $3$ decimal places.
:question/worked-solution:
To write our complex number in the form $z=r{\text{e}}^{\text{i}\theta },$ where $r=|z|$ and $\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z),$ we first calculate $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $z$ lies in the second quadrant of the complex plane, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\pi -|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})| \\  & =\pi -|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{2}{-1})| \\  & =\pi -|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-2)| \\  & ≈2.034.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $r=\sqrt{5}$ and $\theta =2.034$ into $z=r{e}^{\text{i}\theta },$ we get

$$
z=\sqrt{5}\,{\text{e}}^{2.034\,\text{i}}\,.
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the following first-order linear ODE for the function $y = y(x)$:
$\frac{dy}{dx} + y = \cos x$
Write the equation in the form $\frac{d}{dx}(yI(x)) = I(x)Q(x)$, where $I(x)$ is an integrating factor.
Find the first two non-zero terms of the Maclaurin expansion of $\sin (2x) + \sin (\frac{x}{2})$.

:question/worked-solution:
Our goal is to write the equation in the form $ax+by=c,$ where $a,b,$ and $c$ are integers with no common factors and $a\ge 0.$

We begin by moving all of the variables to the left-hand side and all of the constants to the right-hand side. This gives

$$
\frac{1}{5}x+y=\frac{1}{2}
$$

Now, we multiply both sides of the equation by $10:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}x+y & =\frac{1}{2} \\ 10\cdot (\frac{1}{5}x+y) & =10\cdot (\frac{1}{2}) \\ 2x+10y & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, $a,b,$ and $c$ are integers with no common factors, and $a\ge 0.$ So we are done!

The standard form of the line is 

$$
2x+10y=5.
$$

:question/problem: Express ${cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4})-{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4})$ as a single trigonometric ratio.
:question/worked-solution:
First, let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x
$$

Substituting $x=\frac{3\pi }{4}$ into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4})-{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{3\pi }{4}) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Express $2{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3})-1$ as a single trigonometric ratio.
:question/worked-solution:
First, let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
2{cos}^{2}⁡x-1=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x
$$

Substituting $x=\frac{5\pi }{3}$ into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3})-1 & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{5\pi }{3}) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{10\pi }{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the exact value of ${cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{12})-{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{12}).$
:question/worked-solution:
First, let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x
$$

Substituting $x=\frac{\pi }{12}$ into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{12})-{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{12}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{12}) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

What is the equation of the ellipse given above?

:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

Here, the horizontal radius has length $a=\frac{3}{2}$ and the vertical radius has length $b=\frac{9}{2}.$ Therefore, the equation of the ellipse is

$$

:question/problem: Given the curve $y=5x-4{x}^{2}$, calculate ${y}^{′}(x)$ using the definition of the derivative.
:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=5x-4{x}^{2}.$ The definition of ${y}^{′}(x)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x)={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying this to $f(x)=5x-4{x}^{2}$, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{(5(x+h)-4(x+h)^{2})-(5x-4{x}^{2})}{h}) \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{5x+5h-4{x}^{2}-8xh-4{h}^{2}-5x+4{x}^{2}}{h}) \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{h(5-8x-4h)}{h}) \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(5-8x-4h) \\  & =5-8x-4(0) \\  & =5-8x.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $-4{e}^{z}+7=5,$ then $z=$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange our equation into a form that is more convenient for logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{e}^{z}+7 & =5 \\ -4{e}^{z} & =-2 \\ {e}^{z} & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we find the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation and solve for $z:$

$$

$$

Therefore, the solution is $z=-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2).$

To write it in the form $z=r{\text{e}}^{\text{i}\theta },$ where $r=|z|$ and $\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z),$ we first calculate $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{(\sqrt{3})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2\end{aligned}

Now, since $z$ lies in the second quadrant, we can find the angle $\theta $ as

$$

Finally, substituting $r=2$ and $\theta =\frac{2\pi }{3}$ into $z=r{e}^{\text{i}\theta },$ we get

$$
z=2\,{\text{e}}^{2\pi \text{i}/3}.
$$

:question/worked-solution:
To determine which of the following differential equations is a first-order linear ordinary differential equation, we attempt to write each option in the standard form.

A first-order linear ODE is in standard form if it is written as

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x).
$$

Note that the option

\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2xy=6{x}^{2}

:question/problem: Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(0,0)$ and which passes through the point $(-3,-3)?$
:question/worked-solution:
The parametric equations of a vertical parabola  that has its vertex at $(0,0)$ are

$$
x=2pt,\,y=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Since the parabola passes through $(-3,-3),$ we can substitute $x=-3$ and $y=-3$ into the standard parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-3 &=2pt \\ -3 &=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-3 & =2pt \\ t & =-\frac{3}{2p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-3 & =p{(-\frac{3}{2p})}^{2} \\ -3 & =p\cdot \frac{9}{4{p}^{2}} \\ -3 & =\frac{9}{4p} \\ 4p & =-3 \\ p & =-\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x=2(-\frac{3}{4})t,\,y=(-\frac{3}{4}){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x=-\frac{3}{2}t,\,y=-\frac{3}{4}{t}^{2}.
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Since the parabola passes through $(3,-6),$ we can substitute $x=3$ and $y=-6$ into the standard parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3 &=p{t}^{2} \\ -6 &=2pt.\end{aligned}\right.

Solving the second equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-6 & =2pt \\ -3 & =pt \\ t & =-\frac{3}{p}.\end{aligned}

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x=(3){t}^{2},\,y=2(3)t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x=3{t}^{2},\,y=6t.
$$
