:question/problem:
Which of the following vector-valued functions are differentiable with respect to $t$ on $t\in (0,\pi )?$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)⟩ \\ g(t) & =⟨1+{t}^{2},\,-t+2,\,\sqrt{t}⟩ \\ h(t) & =⟨\frac{1}{t},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
All of these vector-valued functions are defined for all $t\in (0,\pi ).$ 

A function is differentiable on the interval $(0,\pi )$ if and only if each of 
 its component functions are differentiable on that interval.

Let's now consider the functions one-by-one.

- We differentiate $f(t)$ to find ${f}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))⟩ \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since each component of ${f}^{′}(t)$ is defined for all  $t\in (0,\pi )$, we conclude that $f(t)$ is differentiable on this interval.

- Next, we differentiate $g(t)$  to find ${g}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-t+2),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,-1,\,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since each component of ${g}^{′}(t)$ is defined for all $(0,\pi )$, we have that   $g(t)$ is also differentiable on this interval.

- Finally, we differentiate $h(t)$ to find ${h}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{tan}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},\,{sec}^{2}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second component of this vector, $\operatorname{sec}⁡t$, is undefined at $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$,  we conclude that the function $h(t)$ is not differentiable on $(0,\pi ).$

Therefore, the answer is:

$\,$ $f(t)$ and $g(t)$ only

:question/problem:
Find ${lim}_{t\to 0}[3f(t)-g(t)]$ given that
$f(t)$ and $g(t)$ are defined as:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,{t}^{2}-2,\frac{t-3}{{t}^{2}+1}⟩ \\ g(t) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\sqrt{t}+\sqrt{2},2⟩\end{aligned}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the limit of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}f(t) & =⟨{lim}_{t\to 0}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,{lim}_{t\to 0}({t}^{2}-2),\,{lim}_{t\to 0}(\frac{t-3}{{t}^{2}+1})⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡0,{0}^{2}-2,\frac{0-3}{{0}^{2}+1}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,-2,-3⟩ \\ {lim}_{t\to 0}g(t) & =⟨{lim}_{t\to 0}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,{lim}_{t\to 0}(\sqrt{t}+\sqrt{2}),\,{lim}_{t\to 0}(2)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡0,\sqrt{0}+\sqrt{2},2⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\sqrt{2},2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use properties of limits to calculate the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}[3f(t)-g(t)] & ={lim}_{t\to 0}3f(t)-{lim}_{t\to 0}g(t) \\  & =3{lim}_{t\to 0}f(t)-{lim}_{t\to 0}g(t) \\  & =3⟨1,-2,-3⟩-⟨0,\sqrt{2},2⟩ \\  & =⟨3,-6,-9⟩-⟨0,\sqrt{2},2⟩ \\  & =⟨3-0,-6-\sqrt{2},-9-2⟩ \\  & =⟨3,-6-\sqrt{2},-11⟩\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
A tank initially holds $120\,\text{gal}$ of a brine (salt-water) solution containing $20\,\text{lb}$ of salt.
Fresh water is poured into the tank at a rate of $4\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed brine leaves the tank at a rate of $4\,\text{gal/min}.$
Find an equation for the amount of salt $Q(t),$ in pounds, in the tank $t$ minutes after the fresh water is first added.

$Q(t)=$
{{field-1}}
:question/worked-solution:
Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which salt enters the tank minus the rate at which salt leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which salt enters the tank.

First, note that fresh water (i.e., a brine solution containing $0\,\text{lb/gal}$ of salt) enters the tank at a rate of $4\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *salt* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (4\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (4\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which salt exits the tank.

Note that the rate of flow in equals the rate of flow out, so the volume of water in the tank remains $120\,\text{gal}.$
Then, since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the tank, the *concentration* of the brine at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{120}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed brine leaves at a rate of $4\,\text{gal/min},$ *salt* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(4\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{120}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(4\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{120}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{4Q}{120}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{Q}{30}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\ \frac{dQ}{dt} & =0-\frac{Q}{30} \\ \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{1}{30}\,Q.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{1}{30} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\int (-\frac{1}{30})\,dt \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \,dQ & =-\frac{1}{30}\int \,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-\frac{t}{30}+C \\ |Q| & ={e}^{-t/30+C} \\ Q(t) & =A{e}^{-t/30},\end{aligned}
$$

where $A=\pm {e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the tank initially contains $20\,\text{lb}$ of salt. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=20,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =20 \\ A{e}^{-0/30} & =20 \\ A & =20\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
Q(t)=20{e}^{-t/30}
$$

:question/problem:
A wastewater holding basin initially holds $450\,\text{L}$ of water containing $9\,\text{kg}$ of dissolved contaminants.
Clean water is pumped into the basin at a rate of $20\,\text{L/min},$ while the completely mixed liquid leaves the basin at a rate of $25\,\text{L/min}.$
Find, rounded to two decimal places, the amount of contaminants in the basin $12$ minutes after the clean water pumping begins.
:question/worked-solution:
Let $Q$ be the amount of contaminants in the basin at time $t.$ Then, the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which contaminants enter the basin minus the rate at which contaminants leave the basin.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which contaminants enter the basin.

Note that clean water (i.e., water containing $0\,\text{kg/L}$ of contaminants) enters the basin at a rate of $20\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *contaminants* enter the basin is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (20\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (20\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which contaminants exit the basin.

To find the rate at which contaminants leave the basin, we first determine the volume of wastewater in the basin at time $t.$

The basin initially contains $450\,\text{L}$ of wastewater; water enters at $20\,\text{L/min}$ and drains out at $25\,\text{L/min}.$
As a result, the amount of wastewater in the basin after $t$ minutes is 

$$
450+20t-25t=(450-5t)\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the amount of contaminants in the basin, the *concentration* of the wastewater at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{450-5t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of $25\,\text{L/min},$ *contaminants* leave at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(25\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{450-5t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(25\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{450-5t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{25Q}{450-5t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{5Q}{90-t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0-\frac{5Q}{90-t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}=-\frac{5}{90-t}\,Q.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{5}{90-t} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\int (-\frac{5}{90-t})\,dt \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \,dQ & =-5\int \frac{1}{90-t}\,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-5(-\operatorname{ln}⁡|90-t|)+C \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(90-t)^{5}|+C \\ |Q| & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|(90-t)^{5}|+C} \\ Q(t) & =A(90-t)^{5},\end{aligned}
$$

where $A=\pm {e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the basin initially contains $9\,\text{kg}$ of contaminants. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=9,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =9 \\ A(90-0)^{5} & =9 \\ A & =\frac{9}{{90}^{5}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =\frac{9}{{90}^{5}}(90-t)^{5} \\  & =9{(\frac{90-t}{90})}^{5} \\  & =9{(1-\frac{t}{90})}^{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the amount of contaminants in the basin $12$ minutes after the clean water is first pumped in is

$$
Q(12)=9{(1-\frac{12}{90})}^{5}≈4.40\,\text{kg},
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

:question/problem: A $9\,000\,\text{mL}$-capacity tank initially holds $6\,000\,\text{mL}$ of a brine (salt-water) solution containing $180\,\text{g}$ of salt. Fresh water begins to flow into the tank at a rate of $90\,\text{mL/s},$ while the completely mixed brine flows out at a rate of $60\,\text{mL/s}.$ Find the amount of salt in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow.
:question/worked-solution:
Let $Q$ be the amount of salt in the tank at time $t.$ Then, the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in seconds. This is equal to the rate at which salt enters the tank minus the rate at which salt leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{g}/\text{s}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which salt enters the tank.

First, note that fresh water (i.e., a brine solution containing $0\,\text{g/mL}$ of salt) enters the tank at a rate of $90\,\text{mL/s}.$ So, the rate at which the *salt* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{mL}})\cdot (90\,\frac{\text{mL}}{\text{s}}) \\  & =(0\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{mL}}})\cdot (90\,\frac{\cancel{\text{mL}}}{\text{s}}) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{s}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which salt exits the tank.

To find the rate at which salt leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of brine in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $6\,000\,\text{mL}$ of brine; fresh water enters at $90\,\text{mL/s},$ and mixed brine leaves at $60\,\text{mL/s}.$
As a result, the amount of brine in the tank after $t$ seconds is 

$$
V(t)=6\,000+90t-60t=30(200+t)\,\text{mL}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the tank, the concentration of the brine at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{30(200+t)}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{mL}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed brine leaves at a rate of $60\,\text{mL/s},$ *salt* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(60\,\frac{\text{mL}}{\text{s}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{30(200+t)}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{mL}}) \\  & =(60\,\frac{\cancel{\text{mL}}}{\text{s}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{30(200+t)}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{mL}}}) \\  & =\frac{2Q}{200+t}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{s}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0-\frac{2Q}{200+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}=-\frac{2}{200+t}\,Q.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{2}{200+t} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\int (-\frac{2}{200+t})\,dt \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \,dQ & =-2\int \frac{1}{200+t}\,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-2(\operatorname{ln}⁡|200+t|)+C \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(200+t)^{-2}|+C \\ |Q| & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|(200+t)^{-2}|+C} \\ Q(t) & =\frac{A}{(200+t)^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $A=\pm {e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the tank initially contains $180\,\text{g}$ of salt. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=180,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =180 \\ \frac{A}{(200+0)^{2}} & =180 \\ A & =180(200)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =\frac{180(200)^{2}}{(200+t)^{2}} \\  & =180{(\frac{200}{200+t})}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $9\,000\,\text{mL},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=9\,000$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =9\,000 \\ 30(200+{t}_{o}) & =9\,000 \\ 200+{t}_{o} & =300 \\ {t}_{o} & =100\,\text{s}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the amount of salt in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(100) & =180{(\frac{200}{200+100})}^{2} \\  & =180{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2} \\  & =80\,\text{g}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: A $9\,800\,\text{mL}$-capacity tank initially holds $7\,000\,\text{mL}$ of a brine (salt-water) solution containing $196\,\text{g}$ of salt. Fresh water begins to flow into the tank at a rate of $105\,\text{mL/s},$ while the completely mixed brine flows out at a rate of $70\,\text{mL/s}.$ Find the amount of salt in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow.
:question/worked-solution:
Let $Q$ be the amount of salt in the tank at time $t.$ Then, the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in seconds. This is equal to the rate at which salt enters the tank minus the rate at which salt leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{g}/\text{s}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which salt enters the tank.

First, note that fresh water (i.e., a brine solution containing $0\,\text{g/mL}$ of salt) enters the tank at a rate of $105\,\text{mL/s}.$ So, the rate at which the *salt* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{mL}})\cdot (105\,\frac{\text{mL}}{\text{s}}) \\  & =(0\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{mL}}})\cdot (105\,\frac{\cancel{\text{mL}}}{\text{s}}) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{s}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which salt exits the tank.

To find the rate at which salt leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of brine in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $7\,000\,\text{mL}$ of brine; fresh water enters at $105\,\text{mL/s},$ and mixed brine leaves at $70\,\text{mL/s}.$
As a result, the amount of brine in the tank after $t$ seconds is 

$$
V(t)=7\,000+105t-70t=35(200+t)\,\text{mL}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the tank, the concentration of the brine at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{35(200+t)}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{mL}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed brine leaves at a rate of $70\,\text{mL/s},$ *salt* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(70\,\frac{\text{mL}}{\text{s}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{35(200+t)}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{mL}}) \\  & =(70\,\frac{\cancel{\text{mL}}}{\text{s}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{35(200+t)}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{mL}}}) \\  & =\frac{2Q}{200+t}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{s}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0-\frac{2Q}{200+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}=-\frac{2}{200+t}\,Q.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{2}{200+t} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\int (-\frac{2}{200+t})\,dt \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \,dQ & =-2\int \frac{1}{200+t}\,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-2(\operatorname{ln}⁡|200+t|)+C \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(200+t)^{-2}|+C \\ |Q| & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|(200+t)^{-2}|+C} \\ Q(t) & =\frac{A}{(200+t)^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $A=\pm {e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the tank initially contains $196\,\text{g}$ of salt. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=196,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =196 \\ \frac{A}{(200+0)^{2}} & =196 \\ A & =196(200)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =\frac{196(200)^{2}}{(200+t)^{2}} \\  & =196{(\frac{200}{200+t})}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $9\,800\,\text{mL},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=9\,800$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =9\,800 \\ 35(200+{t}_{o}) & =9\,800 \\ 200+{t}_{o} & =280 \\ {t}_{o} & =80\,\text{s}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the amount of salt in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(80) & =196{(\frac{200}{200+80})}^{2} \\  & =196{(\frac{5}{7})}^{2} \\  & =100\,\text{g}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find a parametrization of the tangent line to the curve $\mathbf r(t)=\left\langle \cos{t}, \: \sin{t},\: 4t^2\right\rangle$ at the point where $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Let  $P$ be the point at the tip of the vector $\mathbf r\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right ).$  At this point,  the vector $\mathbf r'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right )$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

$$
\mathbf R(u)=\mathbf r\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right )+u \, \mathbf r'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right ), \qquad u \in (-\infty, \infty).
$$

 

First, we find $\mathbf r\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,4{(\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}⟩=⟨0,1,{\pi }^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now,  we calculate $\mathbf r'(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,8t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,8(\frac{\pi }{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,0,4\pi ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the given curve at the point $P$ where $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(u)=⟨0,1,{\pi }^{2}⟩+u⟨-1,0,4\pi ⟩,\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Simplify $\sqrt{\dfrac{9}{64}}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that if $a\geq 0,$ then 

$$
\sqrt{a^2} = a.
$$

First, notice that $9$ and $64$ are both perfect squares, where

$$
9=3^2,
$$

and

$$
64 = 8^2.
$$

So, to work out $\sqrt{\dfrac{9}{64}},$ we express $\dfrac{9}{64}$ as a perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{9}{64}} &= \sqrt{\frac{{3}^{2}}{{8}^{2}}} \\ &= \sqrt{\frac{3\cdot 3}{8\cdot 8}} \\ &= \sqrt{\frac{3}{8}\cdot \frac{3}{8}} \\ &= \sqrt{{(\frac{3}{8})}^{2}} \\ &= \frac{3}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Calculate the value of $\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{1}{64}}.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, notice that the numbers $1$ and $64$ are both perfect cubes. 

So, to determine the value of $\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{1}{64}},$ we express $\dfrac{1}{64}$ as a perfect cube:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[3]{\frac{1}{64}} &= \sqrt[3]{\frac{{1}^{3}}{{4}^{3}}} \\ &= \sqrt[3]{\frac{1\cdot 1\cdot 1}{4\cdot 4\cdot 4}} \\ &= \sqrt[3]{\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{1}{4}} \\ &= \sqrt[3]{{(\frac{1}{4})}^{3}} \\ &= \frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The unit tangent vector to a curve at an arbitrary point is given by

$$
\mathbf T(t) =\sin{t} \,\mathbf i -\cos{t}\,\mathbf j.
$$

Find the principal normal vector at the point where $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Remember that in general, the principal normal vector is given by

$$
\mathbf N(t)= \dfrac{\mathbf T'(t)}{\|\mathbf T'(t)\|}.
$$

First, we calculate $\mathbf T'(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j \\ {T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,j \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,i+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,j \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we find the magnitude of $\mathbf T'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖ & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}‖i+j‖ \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\sqrt{{(1)}^{2}+{(1)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\sqrt{2} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $\mathbf T'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ and obtain the principal normal vector to the curve at the point where $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}N(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})}{‖{T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖}=\frac{\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i+j)}{1}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,i+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

To check our result, we can verify that $\mathbf T$ and $\mathbf N$ are perpendicular by computing their dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\frac{\pi }{4})\cdot N(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,i-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,j)\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,i+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,j) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given  the curve $\mathbf r(t)=\left\langle \sqrt 3 t , \:  \cos t, \: \sin{t}\right\rangle,$ find the principal normal vector $\mathbf N(t)$ at an arbitrary point on the curve.
:question/worked-solution:
Remember that in general, the principal normal vector is given by

$$
\mathbf N(t)= \dfrac{\mathbf T'(t)}{\|\mathbf T'(t)\|}.
$$

First, we find the unit tangent vector $\mathbf T(t).$ To do this, we calculate $\mathbf r'(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{3}t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\sqrt{3},\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{3+{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the unit tangent vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}⟨\sqrt{3},\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\,-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{2},\,\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal normal $\mathbf{N}(t).$ To do this, we calculate $\mathbf T'(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{2}⟨0,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $\mathbf T'(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{\frac{1}{2}⟨0,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩}{(\frac{1}{2})}=⟨0,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

To check our result, we can verify that $\mathbf T$ and $\mathbf N$ are perpendicular by computing their dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t)\cdot N(t) & =⟨\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\,-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{2},\,\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{2}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot 0+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{2}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{2} \\  & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The unit tangent vector to a curve at an arbitrary point is given by

$$
\mathbf T(t) = \sin{t} \cdot \mathbf q(t).
$$

Find the principal normal vector at the point where $t = \dfrac{\pi}{4},$ if 

$$
\begin{aligned}q(\frac{\pi }{4})=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,i-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,j+k,\,{q}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})=-2\,k.\end{aligned}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
Remember that in general, the principal normal vector is given by

$$
\mathbf N(t)= \dfrac{\mathbf T'(t)}{\|\mathbf T'(t)\|}.
$$

First, we calculate $\mathbf T'(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot q(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot q(t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(q(t)) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot q(t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot {q}^{′}(t) \\  \\ {T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\cdot q(\frac{\pi }{4})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\cdot {q}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,i-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,j+k)+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(-2\,k) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\,i-\frac{1}{2}\,j-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we find the magnitude of $\mathbf T'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖ & =\sqrt{{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{2}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $\mathbf T'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve at the point where $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}N(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})}{‖{T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖} \\  & =\frac{-\frac{1}{2}\,i-\frac{1}{2}\,j-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,k}{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\,i-\frac{1}{2}\,j-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the orthogonal trajectories of the family of curves $y = \dfrac{C}{x^2},$ where $C\neq0$ is a parameter.
:question/worked-solution:
Orthogonal trajectories are families of curves that intersect another given family of curves at right angles. In other words, the tangent lines of curves from each family are perpendicular at every intersection point.

Let's determine the slope of the family of curves given by $y = \dfrac{C}{x^2}.$ First, we implicitly differentiate with respect to $x$ and solve for the derivative of $y{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dx}(y) & =\frac{d}{dx}\,(\frac{C}{{x}^{2}}) \\ {y}^{′} & =-\frac{2C}{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must eliminate $C.$ From the original family of curves equation, we have

$$
y = \dfrac{C}{x^2}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
C = x^2y.
$$

Substituting this into our slope equation, we get

$$
y' = -\dfrac{2C}{x^3} = -\dfrac{2x^2y}{x^3}
= -\dfrac{2y}{x}.
$$

For a curve to intersect this family orthogonally, its slope $y'_\perp$ must be the negative reciprocal of the slope $y'$ above. Hence,

$$
y'_\perp = -\dfrac{1}{y'} = -\dfrac{1}{\left(-\dfrac{2y}{x}\right)}
= \dfrac{x}{2y}.
$$

Hence, the orthogonal trajectories must satisfy

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}= \dfrac{x}{2y}.
$$

To find the general solution, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2y\cdot \frac{dy}{dx} & =x \\ \int 2y\cdot \frac{dy}{dx}\,dx & =\int x\,dx \\ \int 2y\,dy & =\int x\,dx \\ {y}^{2} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+K \\ 2{y}^{2}-{x}^{2} & =K\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K$ is a constant of integration.

Therefore, the orthogonal trajectories of the family of curves $y = \dfrac{C}{x^2},$ where $C$ is a parameter, are given by

$$
2y^2 - x^2 = K,
$$

where $K$ is a parameter. Some curves from each family for specific parameter values are given in the diagram below.

**Note**: Since $C\neq0,$ we have $y\neq0$ on every curve in the family, so slopes $y'$ and $'_\perp$ are well-defined.

:question/problem:
![](images/46/46e9f26846b088dfe225b36b889c788ed847c08376295f02dc2c9fbaf72a1645.png)

Find the shortest distance between the origin and the osculating plane for the curve $\mathbf r(t)$ at the point where $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4},$ given that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡6t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡6t,\,8t⟩ \\ T(t) & =\frac{1}{5}⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡6t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡6t,\,4⟩ \\ N(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡6t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡6t,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $\mathbf T$ and $\mathbf N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the Cartesian equation of the osculating plane, we need to compute the position vector $\mathbf p$ and a vector $\mathbf n$ that is perpendicular to the osculating plane. 

The position vector of the point where $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ is

$$
\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{r}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \left\langle \sin{\left(6\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)} , \:  -\cos{\left(6\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)}, \: 8\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \right\rangle  = \left\langle -1, 0, 2\pi \right\rangle.
$$

To compute the perpendicular vector, we need to compute the unit tangent $\mathbf T \left( \dfrac{\pi}{4} \right)$ and the principal normal $\mathbf N \left( \dfrac{\pi}{4} \right) \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\frac{1}{5}⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}),\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}),\,4⟩=\frac{1}{5}⟨0,-3,4⟩ \\ N(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}),\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}),\,0⟩=⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we take the cross product of these two vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =T(\frac{\pi }{4})\times N(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨0,-3,4⟩\times ⟨1,0,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot \left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & -3 & 4 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}0 & -3 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(4\,j+3\,k) \\  & =⟨0,\frac{4}{5},\frac{3}{5}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since we are interested only in the direction of the vector above, we can multiply it by a constant to yield a simpler vector that points in the same direction:

$$
\mathbf{n} = 5\cdot \left\langle 0 , \dfrac{4}{5} , \dfrac{3}{5} \right\rangle = \langle 0, 4, 3  \rangle
$$

Finally, the shortest distance between our plane and the origin is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\frac{|(p-0)\cdot n|}{‖n‖} \\  & =\frac{|p\cdot n|}{‖n‖} \\  & =\frac{|⟨-1,0,2\pi ⟩\cdot ⟨0,4,3⟩|}{‖⟨0,4,3⟩‖} \\  & =\frac{6\pi }{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{3}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{6\pi }{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Consider the curve  $\mathbf r(t)=\left\langle 2t-1 ,\: 8t+2 ,\: -2t \right\rangle, \, t \geq 0,$ for which the arc length $s$ from $\mathbf{r}(0)$ to $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is given by $s=6\sqrt{2}t.$ Find $\mathbf R(s),$ the parametrization of the curve by its arc length $s.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, since  $s=6\sqrt{2}t,$ we have that

$$

:question/problem: Given the curve  $\mathbf r(t)=\cos{t}\,\mathbf i - \sin{t}\,\mathbf j+\sqrt{3}t\,\mathbf k, \, t \geq 0,$ for which the arc length $s$ from $\mathbf r(0)$ to $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by $s=2t,$ find the corresponding unit tangent $\mathbf{T}(s),$ parametrized by $s.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, since $s=2t,$ we have that $t=\dfrac{s}{2}.$

Therefore, the vector function $\mathbf R(s)$ that parametrizes $\mathbf r(t)$ by its arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r(\frac{s}{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{s}{2})\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{s}{2})\,j+\sqrt{3}\cdot \frac{s}{2}k \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{s}{2})\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{s}{2})\,j+\frac{\sqrt{3}s}{2}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, since the curve is parametrized by its arc length $s,$ the unit tangent can be found as

$$
\mathbf T(s) = \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}s}\mathbf R(s).
$$

So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}T(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}R(s) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{s}{2}))\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{s}{2}))j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{\sqrt{3}s}{2})k \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{s}{2})\,i-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{s}{2})\,j+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{s}{2})\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{s}{2})\,j+\sqrt{3}\,k).\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the curve $\mathbf r(s)$ parametrized by arc length $s.$ Find the curvature at the point where $s=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ if the unit tangent vector of the curve is given by

$$
\mathbf T(s) = -\dfrac{4}{5}\sin{s}\,\mathbf i+\dfrac{3}{5} \sin{s}\, \mathbf j + \cos{s}\,\mathbf k.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
Since we are given that $\mathbf{r}(s)$ and its unit tangent vector $\mathbf T(s)$ are both parametrized by the arc length $s,$ we will use the following formula for the curvature:

$$
\kappa(s) = \| \mathbf T'(s) \|
$$

Now, we differentiate $\mathbf T(s)$ with respect to $s$ and evaluate it at $s=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(-\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡s)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡s)j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\operatorname{cos}⁡s)k \\  & =-\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡s\,i+\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡s\,j-\operatorname{sin}⁡s\,k \\ {T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})\,i+\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})\,j-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})\,k \\  & =0\,i+0\,j-k \\  & =-k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain the curvature at the point where $s=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =‖{T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})‖=‖-k‖=\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=1\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider a curve $\mathbf r(s)$ parametrized by its arc length $s.$ Find the radius of curvature of $\mathbf r(s)$ at an arbitrary point knowing that  its  unit tangent vector $\mathbf T(s)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}T(s) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{s}{3})\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{s}{3})\,j\,.\end{aligned}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
Since the curve $\mathbf{r}(s)$ and its unit tangent vector $\mathbf T(s)$ are both parametrized by arc length $s,$ we will use the following formula for the radius of curvature:

$$
R(s) = \dfrac{1}{\kappa(s)} = \dfrac{1}{\|\mathbf T'(s)\|}
$$

We differentiate $\mathbf T(s)$ with respect to $s$ and calculate its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{s}{3}))i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{s}{3}))\,j \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{s}{3})\,i-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{s}{3})\,j \\ ‖{T}^{′}(s)‖ & =\sqrt{(-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{s}{3}))^{2}+(-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{s}{3}))^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{9}({cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{s}{3})+{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{s}{3}))} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the radius of curvature is

$$
R(s) = \dfrac{1}{\|\mathbf T'(s)\|} = \dfrac{1}{\:\dfrac{1}{3}\:} = 3\,.
$$

:question/problem: Find the radius of curvature for the curve  $\mathbf r(t) =  t \, \mathbf i + \sin t\, \mathbf j$ at $t = \dfrac \pi 2.$
:question/worked-solution:
The curvature $\kappa(t)$ of a plane curve $\mathbf r(t) = x(t) \, \mathbf i + y(t)\,\mathbf j$ is given by

$$
\kappa (t) = \dfrac {|x'(t) y''(t) - y'(t) x''(t)|} {\big([x'(t)]^2 + [y'(t)]^2\big)^{3/2}}.
$$

The radius of curvature $R$ is defined as
$R(t) = \dfrac 1 {\kappa(t)}.$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t) = t, \qquad y(t) = \sin t.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =1,\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =0,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|1\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 0|}{{({1}^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|\operatorname{sin}⁡t|}{{(1+{cos}^{2}⁡t)}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t = \dfrac{\pi}2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\frac{|\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})|}{{(1+{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{(1+{0}^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the radius of curvature at $t = \dfrac{\pi}2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\frac{1}{κ(\frac{\pi }{2})}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

that lies in the range $[0,2\pi)$.

$$
-\dfrac{7\pi} 4 + 2\pi = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\tan\left(-\dfrac{7\pi} 4\right) = \tan \left(\dfrac{\pi} {4}\right)

Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

:question/worked-solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 8 & 0 \\ 5 & 11 & -6 \\ 0 & -4 & 16\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{5}{4}){R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\frac{5}{4} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{{E}_{1}}\cdot A \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}4 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -6 \\ 0 & -4 & 16\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+4{R}_{2} & ⟺ & \,\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{{E}_{2}}\cdot {E}_{1}\cdot A \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}4 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & -8\end{bmatrix} \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since $E_2E_1A=U,$ we can invert $E_2$ and $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ {E}_{1}A & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ A & ={\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\frac{5}{4} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}U \\ A & =(\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ \frac{5}{4} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -4 & 1\end{bmatrix})U \\ A & =\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ \frac{5}{4} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -4 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{L}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}4 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & -8\end{bmatrix}}_{U}\end{aligned}

:question/problem: Determine if the vector $\mathbf{u}$ lies on the plane $\;\Pi \,:\, \mathbf{r}=s \mathbf{b} + t \mathbf{c}, \, t,s \in \mathbb{R},$ where  $\mathbf{b}=\langle 1, 4, 5 \rangle, \mathbf{c} = \langle 2, 4, 6 \rangle$ and  $\mathbf{u}= \langle 2, 10, 12 \rangle.$
:question/worked-solution:
By definition, $\mathbf{u} \in \Pi$ if there exist $t$ and $s$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}sb+tc & =u \\ s\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 4 \\ 6\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 10 \\ 12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}s+2t &=2 \\ 4s+4t &=10 \\ 5s+6t &=12\end{aligned}\right.
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 2 \\ 4 & 4 & 10 \\ 5 & 6 & 12\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -4 & 2 \\ 5 & 6 & 12\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-5{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -4 & 2 \\ 0 & -4 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -4 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}s+2t &=2 \\ -4t &=2 \\ 0 &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second equation, we get

$$
-4t = 2 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad t = -\dfrac{1}{2}.
$$

Substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}s+2t & =2 \\ s+2(-\frac{1}{2}) & =2 \\ s-1 & =2 \\ s & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we found a solution $s=3, \, t=-\dfrac{1}{2},$ we conclude that $\mathbf{u}$ does indeed lie on the plane $\Pi.$ In fact, we have

$$
\mathbf{u}=3\mathbf{b} - \dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{c}.
$$

:question/problem:
Given  the curve $r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,4t⟩$, find the principal normal vector $N(t)$ at an arbitrary point on the curve.

$N(t)=⟨\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$
{{field-1}}$,0\,⟩$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the unit tangent vector $T(t).$ To do this, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(4)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)+16} \\  & =\sqrt{25} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the unit tangent vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\frac{4}{5}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal normal $N(t).$ To do this, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{5})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0⟩ \\  & =-\frac{3}{5}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{25}({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${T}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{-\frac{3}{5}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0⟩}{(\frac{3}{5})}=⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

If $x=2\sqrt{y}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{y}},$ find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at the point $(5,9).$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we differentiate $x(y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(2\sqrt{y}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{y}}) \\  & =2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\sqrt{y})-3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}) \\  & =2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{1/2})-3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{-1/2}) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}-3\cdot (-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-3/2}) \\  & ={y}^{-1/2}+\frac{3}{2}{y}^{-3/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}+\frac{3}{2\sqrt{{y}^{3}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}+\frac{3}{2y\sqrt{y}} \\  & =\frac{2y+3}{2y\sqrt{y}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, taking the reciprocal of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y},$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{-1}=\frac{2y\sqrt{y}}{2y+3}.
$$

Finally, substituting the point $(5,9),$ we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{(x,y)=(5,9)} & =\frac{2(9)\sqrt{9}}{2(9)+3}=\frac{18}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given a curve $x=\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}-{y}^{2},$ what is the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point $(9,3)?$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we differentiate $x(y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}-{y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{3})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot 3{y}^{2}-2y \\  & =2{y}^{2}-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, taking the reciprocal of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y},$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2{y}^{2}-2y}.
$$

The slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $(9,3)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{(x,y)=(9,3)} \\  & =\frac{1}{2(3)^{2}-2(3)} \\  & =\frac{1}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the point-slope formula for a tangent line, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-3 & =\frac{1}{12}(x-9) \\ y & =\frac{x}{12}-\frac{3}{4}+3 \\ y & =\frac{x}{12}+\frac{9}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, taking the reciprocal of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y},$ we get

:question/problem:
The equations of a curve $r(t)$ and its corresponding unit tangent vector $T(t)$ at an arbitrary point are given below. Find the principal normal vector to that curve at the point $P(0,3,4).$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k,\,t\in [0,2\pi ) \\ T(t) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k,\,t\in [0,2\pi )\end{aligned}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to the point $P(0,3,4)$ on the given curve. We know that:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨0,3,4⟩ \\ 5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k & =0\text{ }i+3\text{ }j+4\text{ }k\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components of $i$, $j$, and $k$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}5\operatorname{cos}⁡t &=0 \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡t &=3 \\ 4\operatorname{sin}⁡t &=4\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equality, $t=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(0,3,4)$ is at the tip of the vector $r(\frac{\pi }{2}).$ 

Now, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\frac{\pi }{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,k \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j-\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k \\ {T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}\,i-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}\,j-\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}\,k \\  & =-\frac{3}{5}\,j-\frac{4}{5}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the magnitude of ${T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})‖ & =\sqrt{(0)^{2}+{(-\frac{3}{5})}^{2}+{(-\frac{4}{5})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{25}+\frac{16}{25}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve $r(t)$ at the point $P(0,3,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})}{‖{T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})‖}=\frac{-\frac{3}{5}\,j-\frac{4}{5}\,k}{1}=-\frac{3}{5}\,j-\frac{4}{5}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Note that when we find the scalar product of $T$ and $N$ at the point where at $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\frac{\pi }{2})\cdot N(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =(-i)\cdot (-\frac{3}{5}\,j-\frac{4}{5}\,k) \\  & =\frac{3}{5}(i\cdot j)+\frac{4}{5}(i\cdot k) \\  & =0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The unit tangent vector to a curve at an arbitrary point is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+2}⟨-2,\,2t,\,{t}^{2}⟩.
