:question/problem:
The point $P$ is located in the second quadrant and lies on the unit circle. 
The $y$-coordinate of $P$ is $\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}.$ What is the $x$-coordinate of $P?$
:question/worked-solution:
Since the point $P$ lies on the unit circle, it must satisfy the Pythagorean theorem: 

$$
x^2+y^2=1 .
$$

Substituting $y=\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}$ into the above and solving for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =1-\frac{1}{2} \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ x & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{1}{2}} \\ x & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we select the negative answer since $x$ is negative in the second quadrant. Therefore, $x = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.$

:question/problem:
![](images/22/2262bdc869d10cef3cc7a779365f5afa0eb712676a397e39d248c813b305cbf0.png)

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that $\sin\theta=-\dfrac{3}{4},$ what is the value of $\cos \theta?$
:question/worked-solution:
We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\cos\theta\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\sin\theta = -\dfrac{3}{4}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(-\frac{3}{4})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{9}{16}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{7}{16}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{7}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the negative answer since $\cos\theta$ is negative in the third quadrant. So, $\cos\theta = -\dfrac {\sqrt {7}}{4}.$

:question/problem:
![](images/0c/0c29b3961f3e1178f0c82680ca3f67904e57b6fe2cc8b887f09926fcf6c2149a.png)

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that $\sin\theta=-\dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2},$ what is the value of $\tan\theta?$
:question/worked-solution:
We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\cos\theta\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\sin\theta = -\dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{3}{4}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{1}{4}} \\  & =\pm \frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the positive answer since $\cos\theta$ is positive in the fourth quadrant. So, $\cos\theta = \dfrac 1 2.$

Finally, knowing that $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta},$ we have

$$
\tan\theta = \dfrac{\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)} =-\sqrt 3.
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/0e/0e88dc5962fc5bd128c0de5502e8dcd1edf34353de1d31c2d8a21ac672633644.png)

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that the $x$-coordinate of the point $P$ is $-\dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2},$ what is $\csc\theta?$
:question/worked-solution:
We're given that $x=-\dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\cos\theta = -\dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2}.
$$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\sin\theta\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ sin⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\cos\theta = -\dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}sin⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{3}{4}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{1}{4}} \\  & =\pm \frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the negative answer since $\sin\theta$ is negative in the third quadrant. So, $\sin\theta = -\dfrac 1 2.$

Finally, knowing that $\csc\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta},$ we have

$$
\csc\theta = \dfrac{1}{\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)} =-2.
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the repeated integral $\displaystyle \int_{2}^{4}  \int_{0}^{2} \dfrac{x^3}{y^2} \, \textrm{d}x  \, \textrm{d}y.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:    

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{4}[{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{{x}^{3}}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y & ={\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}(\frac{{2}^{4}}{4}-\frac{{0}^{4}}{4})\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{4}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =4{\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y & =4{[-\frac{1}{y}]}_{2}^{4} \\  & =4(-\frac{1}{4}-(-\frac{1}{2})) \\  & =4\cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the double integral $\displaystyle \iint \limits_{D} \dfrac y{x^2} \, \textrm d A$, where 
$D=\left\{ (x,y) \: : \:2 \leq x \leq 4,\: 0 \leq y \leq 3\right\}.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we express our double integral as a repeated integral:    

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[-\frac{y}{x}]}_{2}^{4}\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(-\frac{y}{4}-(-\frac{y}{2}))\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{y}{4}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{y}{4}\,\text{d}y & ={[\frac{{y}^{2}}{8}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{{3}^{2}}{8}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{8} \\  & =\frac{9}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: The point $P$ has cylindrical polar coordinates $\left(4, \dfrac{\pi}{6}, -8 \right).$ Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P.$
:question/worked-solution:
If $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x = r\cos\theta, \qquad
y = r\sin\theta, \qquad 
z = z.
$$

Calculating $x$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =4\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating $y$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =4\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are $(2\sqrt3, 2, -8).$

:question/problem: The point $Q$ has spherical coordinates $\left(2\sqrt3, \pi, \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \right).$ Find the Cartesian coordinates of $Q.$
:question/worked-solution:
If $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x = \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad
y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad 
z = \rho\cos\phi.
$$

Calculating $x,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ \\  & =2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6}) \\  & =2\sqrt{3}\cdot (-1)\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =-\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ \\  & =2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6}) \\  & =2\sqrt{3}\cdot 0\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\  & =2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6}) \\  & =2\sqrt{3}\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $Q$ are $(-\sqrt3, 0, -3).$

:question/problem: The point $P$ has Cartesian coordinates $(-\sqrt2,0,\sqrt2).$ What are the spherical polar coordinates of  $P?$
:question/worked-solution:
If $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x = \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad 
y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad 
z = \rho\cos\phi.
$$

From the above equations, we can express $\rho$, $\theta$, and $\phi$ in terms of $x$, $y$, and $z$ as follows:

$$
\rho = \sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}, \qquad
\tan\theta = \dfrac{y}{x}, \qquad
\cos\phi = \dfrac{z}{\rho}.
$$

First, we find $\rho\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\sqrt{2})^{2}+{0}^{2}+{(\sqrt{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2+0+2} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, $(x,y) = (-\sqrt2,0)$ lies on the negative $x$-axis, so

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, for $\phi,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}ϕ & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{z}{\rho }) \\  & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the spherical coordinates of $P$ are $\left(2, \pi,  \dfrac{\pi}4 \right).$

:question/problem:
Using the change of variables 

$$
u =3x-2y, \quad v=x+y,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the curve $(3x-2y)^2 - y - x = 0$ and the line $x+y=4.$
:question/worked-solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y.
$$

Let's define a transformation $\mathbf T$ as follows: 

![](images/1e/1efa09fa657f5c016d251adfd8db31d473bf901b07efea0c0f40c4ef161cc8f3.svg)

This transformation maps some region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right|  \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v
$$

where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u = 3x-2y, \qquad v=x+y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function $\mathbf T^{-1},$ that is

![](images/e1/e1236dd6d81a7cb3217fa4b64989220dcfde67d04a5252eef02f2f3ce0b33c20.svg)

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $\Delta,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ 

Substituting $3x-2y = u$ and $x+y = v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(3x-2y)^{2}-y-x=0\,⟹\,{u}^{2}-v=0\,⟹\,v={u}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting $x + y = v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y+x=4\,⟹\,v=4.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}v &={u}^{2} \\ v &=4\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}u &=\pm 2 \\ v &=4.\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm 2, 4).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: -2 \leq u \leq 2, \, u^2 \leq v \leq 4\big\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/0a/0a3d0211dfbe18e5737b62e8b61cf9308af2735ef827d14bae7b5dbfffaa4faa.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}{:}$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 1 & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{aligned}| \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T{:}$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T$ is

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} \right)^{-1} = (5)^{-1} = \dfrac 15.
$$

Note that $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \neq 0$ everywhere inside $\Delta.$  In other words, $\mathbf T$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-2}^{2}[{\int }_{{u}^{2}}^{4}\,dv]du \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-2}^{2}[v]_{{u}^{2}}^{4}\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-2}^{2}(4-{u}^{2})\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot 2{\int }_{0}^{2}(4-{u}^{2})\,du \\  & =\frac{2}{5}{[4u-\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}(8-\frac{8}{3}) \\  & =\frac{2}{5}(\frac{16}{3}) \\  & =\frac{32}{15}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate $\displaystyle \int_{0}^{\pi/8} \int_0^{\sin2\theta} r \, \textrm d r\,\textrm d \theta.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we integrate with respect to $r,$ treating $\theta$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{[{r}^{2}]}_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{sin}^{2}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the double-angle formula

$$
\cos{2x} = 1-2\sin^2 x.
$$

Substituting $x=2\theta$ and rearranging, we get

$$
\sin^22\theta = \dfrac12\left(1-\cos4\theta\right).
$$

 

Finally, we can finish our integral by integrating with respect to $\theta,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{sin}^{2}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}1-\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{[\theta -\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta ]}_{0}^{\pi /8} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[(\frac{\pi }{8}-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))-(0-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\frac{\pi }{8}-\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\frac{\pi }{8}-\frac{2}{8}) \\  & =\frac{1}{32}(\pi -2)\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Integrate the function $f(x, y) = 15xy^2$ over the portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at the origin, where $x \geq 0,y \geq 0.$
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D\mathbin{:}$

![](images/05/051cfbbf3fd37f01ff7e4442fccdc5ec4ce506e3c452b68bfa2ed5ae6e5cf6b9.png)

In polar coordinates $(r, \theta),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 2, \:0\leq \theta \leq  \dfrac{\pi}{2} \right\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}15x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}15r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot (r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}15{r}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}5{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,{[{r}^{5}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta ({2}^{5}-0)\text{d}\theta  \\  & =32{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =32{[{sin}^{3}⁡\theta ]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =32({sin}^{3}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-{sin}^{3}⁡(0)) \\  & =32(1-0) \\  & =32.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Consider the arc of the curve $y=e^x$ that lies between the lines $x=0$ and $x=2.$ What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis?
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S = \int 2\pi y\,\textrm d s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y = f(x),$ we have 

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}\right)^2}\,\textrm d x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{x_1}^{x_2} y \sqrt{1+ \left( \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \right)^2} \: \textrm{d}x.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from $x_1=0$ to $x_2={2}.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{x})={e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{x}\sqrt{1+({e}^{x})^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{x}\sqrt{1+{e}^{2x}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Consider the arc of the curve $y=\sqrt{x-2}$ that lies between the lines $x=2$ and $x=4.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis.
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S = \int 2\pi y\,\textrm d s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y = f(x),$ we have 

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}\right)^2}\,\textrm d x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{x_1}^{x_2} y \sqrt{1+ \left( \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \right)^2} \: \textrm{d}x.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from $x_1=2$ to $x_2=4.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{x-2})=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x-2}}\,⇒\,{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}=\frac{1}{4(x-2)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{2}^{4}\sqrt{x-2}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4(x-2)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{2}^{4}\sqrt{x-2}\sqrt{\frac{4x-7}{4(x-2)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{2}^{4}\sqrt{x-2}(\frac{\sqrt{4x-7}}{2\sqrt{x-2}})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{4}\sqrt{4x-7}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the substitution 

$$
u=4x-7 \quad \Rightarrow\quad \textrm du = 4\,\textrm dx,
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{4}\sqrt{4x-7}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{9}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{\sqrt{{u}^{3}}\,|}_{1}^{9} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(27-1) \\  & =\frac{13\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the arc of the curve $x=y^3-y$ that lies in the second quadrant between its $y$-intercepts. What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis?

![](images/1b/1bdbe21cbb517645dfe9362f3313c2d85118acfea1d839fe33ae9b9ac6c3ed50.png)
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S = \int 2\pi y\,\textrm d s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x = f(y),$ we have 

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d y}\right)^2}\,\textrm d y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{y_1}^{y_2} y \sqrt{1+ \left( \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} \right)^2} \: \textrm{d}y.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{3}-y & =0 \\ y({y}^{2}-1) & =0 \\ y & =0,\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=1.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{3}-y)=3{y}^{2}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y\sqrt{1+{(3{y}^{2}-1)}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y\sqrt{2-6{y}^{2}+9{y}^{4}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the general solution to the difference equation $a_n + 100a_{n-2} =0$.
:question/worked-solution:
Let

$$
a_n=\lambda^n
$$

Then, we have

$$
a_{n-1} = \lambda^{n-1}, \qquad a_{n-2} = \lambda^{n-2}
$$

Substituting the above into our difference equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
λ^{n} + 100λ^{n - 2} &= 0 \\
λ^{n - 2}(λ^{2} + 100) &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

The characteristic equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}
λ^{2} + 100 &= 0 \\
λ^{2} &= -100 \\
λ &= ± 10\textrm{i}
\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\lambda_1 = 10\textrm i
$$

and

$$
\lambda_2 = -10\textrm i
$$

Expressing our solutions in polar form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
λ_{1} &= 10(\cos (\frac{π}{2}) + \textrm{i}\sin (\frac{π}{2})), \\
λ_{2} &= 10(\cos (\frac{π}{2}) - \textrm{i}\sin (\frac{π}{2}))
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using De Moivre's theorem, we can write the general solution to the difference equation as

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{n} &= Cλ_{1}^{n} + Dλ_{2}^{n} \\
&= C[10(\cos (\frac{π}{2}) + \textrm{i}\sin (\frac{π}{2}))]^{n} + D[10(\cos (\frac{π}{2}) - \textrm{i}\sin (\frac{π}{2}))]^{n} \\
&= C[10^{n}(\cos (\frac{nπ}{2}) + \textrm{i}\sin (\frac{nπ}{2}))] + D[10^{n}(\cos (\frac{nπ}{2}) - \textrm{i}\sin (\frac{nπ}{2}))] \\
&= 10^{n}(A\cos (\frac{nπ}{2}) + B\sin (\frac{nπ}{2}))
\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
A = C+D, \qquad B = \textrm i(C-D)
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the recurrence relation
$a_n = -6a_{n-1} - 12a_{n-2}, \quad a_0 =-1, \quad a_1=3+\sqrt{3}$.
Given that the solution takes the form
$a_n = \big(2\sqrt{3}\big)^n \left(A\cos\left(\dfrac{5n\pi}{6}\right) + B\sin\left(\dfrac{5n\pi}{6}\right) \right)$,
find the value of $A + B$.
:question/worked-solution:
The general solution to the recurrence relation is

$$
a_n = \big(2\sqrt{3}\big)^n \left(A\cos\left(\dfrac{5n\pi}{6}\right) + B\sin\left(\dfrac{5n\pi}{6}\right) \right)
$$

We find the constants $A$ and $B$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $a_0 = -1$ into the general solution gives
$(2\sqrt{3})^{0}(A\cos (\frac{0 \cdot 5π}{6}) + B\sin (\frac{0 \cdot 5π}{6}))|=-1; 1 \cdot (A \cdot 1 + B \cdot 0)|=-1; A|=-1$.
- Substituting $a_1=3+\sqrt{3}$ and $A=-1$ into the general solution gives
$(2\sqrt{3})^{1}(-1 \cdot \cos (\frac{1 \cdot 5π}{6}) + B\sin (\frac{1 \cdot 5π}{6}))|= 3 + \sqrt{3}; 2\sqrt{3}(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + B \cdot \frac{1}{2})|= 3 + \sqrt{3}; 3 + \sqrt{3}B|= 3 + \sqrt{3}; B|= 1$.

Therefore,

$$
A + B = -1 + 1 = 0
$$

Finally, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{n} &= (2\sqrt{3})^{n}(\sin (\frac{5nπ}{6}) - \cos (\frac{5nπ}{6}))
\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Solve the recurrence relation
$a_n =2a_{n-1} - 2a_{n-2}, \quad a_0=2, \quad a_1=5$.
:question/worked-solution:
Moving all terms of our recurrence relation to the left-hand side, we obtain

$$
a_n - 2a_{n-1} + 2a_{n-2} = 0
$$

First, we find the roots of the characteristic equation:

$$
\lambda^2 - 2\lambda + 2 = 0
$$

This equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}
λ^{2} - 2λ + 2 &= 0 \\
(λ^{2} - 2λ + 1) - 1 + 2 &= 0 \\
(λ - 1)^{2} + 1 &= 0 \\
(λ - 1)^{2} &= -1 \\
λ - 1 &= ± \textrm{i} \\
λ &= 1 ± \textrm{i}
\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\lambda_1 = 1 + \textrm{i}, \qquad \lambda_2 = 1 - \textrm{i}
$$

Expressing our solutions in polar form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
λ_{1} &= \sqrt{2}(\cos (\frac{π}{4}) + \textrm{i}\sin (\frac{π}{4})), \\
λ_{2} &= \sqrt{2}(\cos (\frac{π}{4}) - \textrm{i}\sin (\frac{π}{4}))
\end{aligned}
$$

So, the general solution to the recurrence relation is

$$
a_n = \big(\sqrt{2}\big)^n \left(A\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi}{4}\right) + B\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi}{4}\right)\right)
$$

We now find the constants $A$ and $B$ using the initial conditions:

- Substituting $a_0 = 2$ into the general solution gives
$(\sqrt{2})^{0}(A\cos (\frac{0 \cdot π}{4}) + B\sin (\frac{0 \cdot π}{4}))|= 2; 1 \cdot (A \cdot 1 + B \cdot 0)|= 2; A|= 2$.
- Substituting $a_1=5$ and $A=2$ into the general solution gives
$(\sqrt{2})^{1}(2 \cdot \cos (\frac{1 \cdot π}{4}) + B\sin (\frac{1 \cdot π}{4}))|= 5; \sqrt{2} \cdot (\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{2} + B \cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})|= 5; 2 + B|= 5; B|= 3$.

Therefore, the solution is

$$
a_n = \big(\sqrt{2}\big)^n \left(2\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi}{4}\right) + 3\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi}{4}\right)\right)
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x = t-\sin t, \quad y = 1-\cos t, \quad t\in \left[0,\pi\right].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis?
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S = \int 2\pi y\,\textrm d s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{t_1}^{t_2} y \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from $t_1=0$ to $t_2=\pi.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the identity $\sin^2 t +\cos^2 t= 1,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{2(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{3}}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x = \sin t, \quad y = e^t, \quad t\in \left[0,1\right].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis?
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S = \int 2\pi x\,\textrm d s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{t_1}^{t_2} x \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from $t_1=0$ to $t_2=1.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{({e}^{t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t+{e}^{2t}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x = 1+3t, \quad y = 2t^{3/2}, \quad t\in \left[0,1\right].
$$

Calculate the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis.
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S = \int 2\pi x\,\textrm d s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{t_1}^{t_2} x \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from $t_1=0$ to $t_2=1.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+3t)=3 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3/2})=3{t}^{1/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(1+3t)\sqrt{{(3)}^{2}+{(3{t}^{1/2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(1+3t)\sqrt{9+9t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(1+3t)\sqrt{9(1+t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(1+3t)\cdot 3\sqrt{1+t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =6\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(1+3t)\sqrt{1+t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u = 1+t.$ Then, $1+3t=3u-2$ and $\textrm{d}u = \textrm d t.$ We also need to compute new limits, given below.

| **$t$** | $0$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $2$ |

Therefore, we get

$$

:question/problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=3t-{t}^{3},\,y=3{t}^{2},\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Calculate the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis.
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=1.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t-{t}^{3})=3-3{t}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2})=6t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}3{t}^{2}\sqrt{{(3-3{t}^{2})}^{2}+{(6t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}3{t}^{2}\sqrt{9-18{t}^{2}+9{t}^{4}+36{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}3{t}^{2}\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+18{t}^{2}+9}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, factoring the expression $9{t}^{4}+18{t}^{2}+9,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}3{t}^{2}\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+18{t}^{2}+9}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}3{t}^{2}\sqrt{9({t}^{4}+2{t}^{2}+1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}3{t}^{2}\cdot 3\sqrt{{t}^{4}+2{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =18\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\sqrt{({t}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =18\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\cdot |{t}^{2}+1|\,\text{d}t \\  & =18\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}({t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =18\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{4}+{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =18\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{4}+{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =18\pi \cdot {[\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}+\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =18\pi [(\frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{3})-(\frac{0}{5}+\frac{0}{3})] \\  & =18\pi \cdot \frac{8}{15} \\  & =\frac{48\pi }{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

:question/problem:
Using the change of variables 

$$
u=y-2x,\,v=y+x,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the lines

$$
y=2x-1,\,y=2x+1,\,y=1-x,\,y=2-x.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=y-2x,\,v=y+x
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u=y-2x$ into the equations of the first and second lines:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=2x-1 & ⟹\, & y-2x=-1 & ⟹\, & u=-1 \\  & y=2x+1 & ⟹\, & y-2x=1 & ⟹\, & u=1\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v=y+x$ into the equations of the third and fourth lines:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=1-x & ⟹\, & y+x=1 & ⟹\, & v=1 \\  & y=2-x & ⟹\, & y+x=2 & ⟹\, & v=2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 1,\,1\le v\le 2\}
$$

![](images/21/2116f558e3712a08c13d49238054336dcb60efc7d9602bed220be8115d392be7.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{3}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|-\frac{1}{3}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{∬}_{Δ}\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \text{Area}(Δ) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot 2\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Use a change of variables to calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the following lines.

$$
3y=5x+2,\,3y=5x-2,\,2x=y,\,4x=2y+3
$$
:question/worked-solution:

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

We'll assume this transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv,
$$

  

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required area, we proceed in five steps:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

Notice that we can rewrite the equations of our curves as follows:

$$
5x-3y=-2,\,5x-3y=2,\,4x-2y=0,\,4x-2y=3
$$

This suggests the following change of variables:

$$
u=5x-3y,\,v=4x-2y
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u=5x-3y$ into the equations of the first and second curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 5x-3y=-2\,⟹\,u=-2 \\  & 5x-3y=2\,⟹\,u=2\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v=4x-2y$ into the equations of the third and fourth curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 4x-2y=0\,⟹\,v=0 \\  & 4x-2y=3\,⟹\,v=3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$

$$

![](images/46/46b808722b24d467ba1015214268658e601779801ca54e8892b92b527ef9ee1d.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}5 & -3 \\ 4 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-10+12 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{∬}_{Δ}\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}\,\text{d}u{\int }_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (2-(-2))\cdot (3-0) \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/0a/0a85b0be5f8e5db2cf4d1716e4afe4a2780c500d94a1ce282a9d0044f93ba084.png)

Consider the plate that occupies the region $D$ enclosed by the polar circles $r=1$ and $r=\sqrt{3}$ and the polar rays $\theta =\frac{\pi }{6}$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{3}$ in the first quadrant, as shown above. The mass density function of the plate is given by $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{6}{x}.$ Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $y$-axis.
:question/worked-solution:
For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (r,\theta ),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, note that the region $D$ in polar coordinates can be expressed as

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le \sqrt{3},\,\,\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}\}.
$$

Also, the mass density function in polar coordinates is 

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{6}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }=\frac{6}{r}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}(\frac{6}{r}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta ){r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}6{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}6{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =2{r}^{3}{|}_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {|}_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3} \\  & =2(3\sqrt{3}-1)\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{3}-1}{2}) \\  & =(3\sqrt{3}-1)\cdot (\sqrt{3}-1) \\  & =10-4\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
A rectangular plate of mass $\frac{4}{5}\,\text{kg}$ and uniform mass density occupies the region
$D={(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 1,\,-2\le y\le 2},$
where $x$ and $y$ are measured in meters. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about a line perpendicular to $D$ at a distance of $\sqrt{2}\,\text{m}$ from a parallel line passing through its center of mass.
:question/worked-solution:
For a plane lamina of mass $M$ and a line ${l}_{M}$ perpendicular to the lamina passing through its center of mass, the parallel axis theorem states that the moment of inertia of the lamina about a line $l$ parallel to ${l}_{M}$ is given by

$$
{I}_{l}={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M,
$$

where $d$ is the distance between the lines, and ${I}_{M}$ and ${I}_{l}$ are the moments of inertia about the lines ${l}_{M}$ and $l,$ respectively.

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=2\cdot 4=8\,{\text{m}}^{2}.$
Since the plate has a uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{(\frac{4}{5})}{8}=\frac{1}{10}\,\text{kg}/{\text{m}}^{2},
$$

and its center of mass is its centroid:

$$
(\overset{¯}{x},\overset{¯}{y})=(\frac{-1+1}{2},\frac{-2+2}{2})=(0,0)
$$

Since the center of mass is at the origin, the moment of inertia about the perpendicular line through the center of mass is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{M} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-2}^{2}\frac{1}{10}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{10}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{[{x}^{2}y+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{y=-2}^{y=2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{10}{\int }_{-1}^{1}4{x}^{2}+\frac{16}{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{10}{[\frac{4}{3}{x}^{3}+\frac{16}{3}x]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{10}(\frac{8}{3}+\frac{32}{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{10}(\frac{40}{3}) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia about a line $\sqrt{2}\,\text{m}$ from the center of mass is

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M \\  & =\frac{4}{3}+(\sqrt{2})^{2}\cdot \frac{4}{5} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}+\frac{8}{5} \\  & =\frac{44}{15}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: The point $P$ is located in the third quadrant and lies on the unit circle. The $x$-coordinate of $P$ is $-\frac{2}{5}.$ What is the $y$-coordinate of $P?$
:question/worked-solution:
Since the point $P$ lies on the unit circle, it must satisfy the Pythagorean theorem: 

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1
$$

Substituting $x=-\frac{2}{5}$ into the above and solving for $y$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {(-\frac{2}{5})}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ (\frac{4}{25})+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {y}^{2} & =1-\frac{4}{25} \\ {y}^{2} & =\frac{21}{25} \\ y & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{21}{25}} \\ y & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{21}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we select the negative answer since $y$ is negative in the third quadrant. So our final answer is $y=-\frac{\sqrt{21}}{5}.$

:question/problem:
![](images/c2/c2644fc906d4588bc39aa92d887836ff8942f5eb4b28de1baf3dc1030d2dca67.png)

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that $sin⁡\theta =\frac{1}{3},$ what is the value of $cos⁡\theta ?$
:question/worked-solution:
![](images/49/4942cec8983dd2bddddd0ba2f8f9332b1b82f3999a44adb138b905457d39c633.png)

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $cos⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $sin⁡\theta =\frac{1}{3}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{1}{9}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{8}{9}} \\  & =\pm \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the negative answer since $cos⁡\theta $ is negative in the second quadrant. So, $cos⁡\theta =-\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}.$

:question/problem: Which of the following expressions gives all of the vertical asymptotes of the function $f(x) = \cot (\frac{x}{2}) + 1$? Assume that $n$ is an integer.
Consider the surface $\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{x}^{3}+yz)=3.$ Given that $n=⟨a,b,c⟩$ is a non-zero normal vector to the surface at the point $(e,{e}^{2},-e),$ what is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$
:question/worked-solution:
Let's define  $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{x}^{3}+yz).$ Then, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=3.$  

Now, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(e,{e}^{2},-e):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{x}^{3}+yz))i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{x}^{3}+yz))j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{x}^{3}+yz))k \\  & =(\frac{1}{2{x}^{3}+yz}\cdot 6{x}^{2})i+(\frac{1}{2{x}^{3}+yz}\cdot z)j+(\frac{1}{2{x}^{3}+yz}\cdot y)k \\  & =\frac{6{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{3}+yz}\text{ }i+\frac{z}{2{x}^{3}+yz}\text{ }j+\frac{y}{2{x}^{3}+yz}\text{ }k \\ ∇f(e,{e}^{2},-e) & =\frac{6{e}^{2}}{2{e}^{3}+{e}^{2}(-e)}\text{ }i+\frac{(-e)}{2{e}^{3}+{e}^{2}(-e)}\text{ }j+\frac{{e}^{2}}{2{e}^{3}+{e}^{2}(-e)}\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{6}{e}\text{ }i-\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}\text{ }j+\frac{1}{e}\text{ }k \\  & =⟨\frac{6}{e},\,-\frac{1}{{e}^{2}},\,\frac{1}{e}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩=⟨\frac{6}{e},\,-\frac{1}{{e}^{2}},\,\frac{1}{e}⟩.$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{(\frac{6}{e})}{(-\frac{1}{{e}^{2}})}=-6e.$

:question/problem: A metal plate occupies the region $D={(x,y):-1\le y\le 1,\,0\le x\le {y}^{2}}.$ The charge density of the plate is given by $\rho (x,y)=x{y}^{2}.$ Find the total charge $Q$ of the plate.
:question/worked-solution:
The total charge $Q$ of a plate that occupies the region $D$ with charge density $\rho (x,y)=x{y}^{2}$ is given by

$$
Q={∬}_{D}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.
$$

Let's sketch our region.

![](images/1c/1cbe96aa4bf517302a2329db9f8eb2e9c56873e4d5a18cd5f1cd676543e97086.png)

Notice that $D$ is a type II region. So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
{∬}_{D}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{y}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}x\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{y}^{2}{[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{{y}^{2}}\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{y}^{2}(\frac{{y}^{4}}{2}-0)\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{y}^{6}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{y}^{6}\,\text{d}y & =\frac{1}{2}{[\frac{{y}^{7}}{7}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{{1}^{7}}{7}-(-\frac{{1}^{7}}{7})) \\  & =\frac{1}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the total charge of the plate is $Q=\frac{1}{7}.$

:question/problem:
Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{x} \\ \sqrt{y}+z \\ {y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $x\ne 0$ and $y>0.$*
:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{x},\,y(x,y,z)=\sqrt{y}+z,\,z(x,y,z)={y}^{2}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =1 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =2y & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} & 1 \\ 0 & 2y & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\begin{vmatrix}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} & 1 \\ 2y & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}} & =(\frac{1}{x})^{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{{y}^{2}} \\  & ={u}^{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{w} \\  & =2{u}^{2}\sqrt{w}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2{u}^{2}\sqrt{w}}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the largest interval of continuity for the function $f(x) = \log_{5} (\frac{x + 7}{x^{2} + 4})$.

Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)),$ given that 

$$
u=2x+y,\,v=-x+3y-2z,\,w=3y+4z.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =2 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =3 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =-2 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =3 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\begin{vmatrix}3 & -2 \\ 3 & 4\end{vmatrix}-1\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -2 \\ 0 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2(12+6)-1(-4-0) \\  & =40.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{40}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the largest union of intervals on which the function $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3}{{x}^{2}-1})$ is continuous.
:question/worked-solution:
The function is a composition of two functions, a rational function, and a sine function.

The sine is continuous at all points in its domain, and its domain consists of all real numbers. So, we focus on the rational function.

Likewise, the rational function $\frac{3}{{x}^{2}-1}$ is continuous at all points in its domain. To find its domain, we start by factoring the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{3}{{x}^{2}-1} \\  & =\frac{3}{(x-1)(x+1)}\end{aligned}
$$

This function is continuous everywhere except at the excluded points $x=-1$ and $x=1.$

Therefore, the domain our original function consists of the union of the intervals $(-\infty ,-1),$ $(-1,1),$ and $(1,\infty ),$ namely

$$
(-\infty ,-1)\cup (-1,1)\cup (1,\infty )
$$

and the function is also continuous on these intervals.

:question/problem:
![](images/91/919b9e8f2a9493fd0dda3e0d7bf66de9af054fc4ed9c0fcf7a68329fdbbaffdd.png)

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that $sin⁡\theta =\frac{1}{2},$ what is the value of $tan⁡\theta ?$
:question/worked-solution:
![](images/94/948610f67267e6ec1b845d2b4e1bc4030b81a1080bcb9a44d9f974ff78c3f7b0.png)

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $cos⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $sin⁡\theta =\frac{1}{2}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{1}{4}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{3}{4}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the negative answer since $cos⁡\theta $ is negative in the second quadrant. So, $cos⁡\theta =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.$

Finally, knowing that $tan⁡\theta =\frac{sin⁡\theta }{cos⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
tan⁡\theta =\frac{(\frac{1}{2})}{(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.
$$

:question/problem: Calculate the period of the function $f(x)=\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5x}{3}-\frac{\pi }{2}).$
:question/worked-solution:
Given a function in the form $f(x)=A\operatorname{sin}⁡(Bx+C)+D,$ the period $T$ is given by $\frac{2\pi }{B}.$

In our case, we have that $B=\frac{5}{3}.$ Therefore, the period is $\frac{2\pi }{(\frac{5}{3})}=\frac{6\pi }{5}.$

A metal rod is heated to $212^{∘}F$ and then allowed to cool to a room temperature of $70^{∘}F$. The function $T(t)$ denotes the temperature of the rod $t$ minutes after being allowed to cool. The graph of $T(t)$ is shown above. Which of the following expressions could be the function $T(t)$?
What is $(9 \cdot \frac{2}{5})^{6}$?
What is $(\frac{3}{7} \cdot \frac{1}{2})^{4}$?
What is $(-7 \cdot 3)^{5}$?

:question/worked-solution:
To raise the product of two numbers to the power of $6$, we can raise each number to the power of $6,$ and then multiply:

$$

:question/problem: The point $P$ has cylindrical polar coordinates $(4,\frac{\pi }{6},-2).$ Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P.$
:question/worked-solution:
If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z
$$

Calculating $x$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =4\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating $y$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =4\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are $(2\sqrt{3},2,-2).$

:question/problem: The point $A$ has Cartesian coordinates $(1,-1,\sqrt{2}).$ What are the spherical polar coordinates of $A?$
:question/worked-solution:
If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

From the above equations, we can express $\rho $, $\theta $, and $ϕ$ in terms of $x$, $y$, and $z$ as follows:

$$
\rho =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{y}{x},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=\frac{z}{\rho }
$$

First, we find $\rho :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(\sqrt{2})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1+2} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, $(x,y)=(1,-1)$ lies in the fourth quadrant. So to find $\theta ,$ we first need to find the reference angle ${\theta }_{R}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{-1}{1}| \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we subtract the reference angle from $2\pi $ to get $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =2\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & =2\pi -\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, for $ϕ$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}ϕ & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{z}{\rho }) \\  & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the spherical coordinates of $A$ are $(2,\frac{7\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{4}).$

:question/problem: The point $B$ has Cartesian coordinates $(-1,2,-\sqrt{3}).$ What are the spherical polar coordinates $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ of $B?$ Express $\theta $ and $ϕ$ in radians rounded to three decimal places.
:question/worked-solution:
If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

From the above equations, we can express $\rho $, $\theta $, and $ϕ$ in terms of $x$, $y$, and $z$ as follows:

$$
\rho =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{y}{x},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=\frac{z}{\rho }
$$

First, we find $\rho :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+4+3} \\  & =\sqrt{8} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, $(x,y)=(-1,2)$ lies in the second quadrant. So to find $\theta $, we first need to find the reference angle ${\theta }_{R}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{2}{-1}| \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2) \\  & ≈1.107\,149\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we subtract the reference angle from $\pi $ to get $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & ≈\pi -1.107\,149 \\  & ≈2.034\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, for $ϕ$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}ϕ & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{z}{\rho }) \\  & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{-\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{2}}) \\  & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(-\sqrt{\frac{3}{8}}) \\  & ≈2.230.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the spherical coordinates of $B$ are $(\sqrt{5},2.034,2.230).$

:question/problem:
Using the change of variables 

$$
u=x+y,\,v=x-y,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the curve $(x+y)^{4}-x+y=0$ and  the line $y=0.$
:question/worked-solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=x+y,\,v=x-y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Substituting $x+y=u$ and $x-y=v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+y)^{4}-x+y=0\,⟹\,(x+y)^{4}-(x-y)=0\,⟹\,v={u}^{4},\end{aligned}
$$

Now, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y &=u \\ x-y &=v\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,y=\frac{u-v}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this value into the equation of the given line yields:

$$
\begin{aligned}y=0\, & ⟹\,\frac{u-v}{2}=0\,⟹\,v=u\end{aligned}
$$

 

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}v &={u}^{4} \\ v &=u\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{u}^{3}(u-1) &=0 \\ v &=u.\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the intersection points are $(0,0)$ and $(1,1).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,{u}^{4}\le v\le u\}.
$$

![](images/1e/1ed905e319e689d3fc7955a30f58e0f3ae2e7a751c27b80201d2b43f58b4206c.png)

 

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=(-2)^{-1}=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|-\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{{u}^{4}}^{u}\,dv]du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}[v]_{{u}^{4}}^{u}\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(u-{u}^{4})du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[\frac{{u}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{u}^{5}}{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{5}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{3}{10}) \\  & =\frac{3}{20}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Given that the discrete random variable $Y$ has the cumulative distribution function $F(y)$ shown in the table below, compute $P(\frac{1}{2}\le Y\le \frac{3}{2}).$

| $y$ | $0$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $1$ | $\frac{3}{2}$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $F(y)$ | $0.1$ | $0.2$ | $0.4$ | $0.8$ | $1.0$ |
:question/worked-solution:
The cumulative distribution function of a discrete random variable $Y$ is a function $F(y)$ such that

$$
F(y)=P(Y\le y).
$$

To compute the probability of a random variable $Y$ over an interval, we can use the rule

$$
P(a<Y\le b)=F(b)-F(a).
$$

Here, we want to compute $P(\frac{1}{2}\le Y\le \frac{3}{2}).$ However, this interval is stated in the form $a\le Y\le b,$ not $a<Y\le b.$

So first, we must convert the interval $\frac{1}{2}\le Y\le \frac{3}{2}$ to the form $a<Y\le b.$ Looking at the given possible values of $Y,$ we see that $\frac{1}{2}\le Y$ is equivalent to $0<Y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\frac{1}{2}\le Y\le \frac{3}{2}) & =P(0<Y\le \frac{3}{2}) \\  & =F(\frac{3}{2})-F(0) \\  & =0.8-0.1 \\  & =0.7.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/fd/fd1a5a140c3a2d430312d6f6ceeb21d6b7282119c8ec53365553ff845d8c64d5.png)

Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{D}x\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A,$ where the region $D$ is the semicircle shown above.
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $\frac{1}{2}$ centered at 
$(0,-\frac{1}{2}).$

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ y &=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta\end{aligned}\right.
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the $x=\sqrt{-{y}^{2}-y}$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\sqrt{-{y}^{2}-y} \\ {x}^{2} & =-{y}^{2}-y \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =-y \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) & =-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2} & =-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}+r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

Therefore, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 0\}.
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}x\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta [\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]_{0}^{-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ((-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{4}-{0}^{4})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{4}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{[\frac{{sin}^{5}⁡\theta }{5}]}_{-\pi /2}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{20}({sin}^{5}⁡0-{sin}^{5}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{20}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the mixed integral

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_D \left[ \int_{0}^{z} \dfrac{\cos (2y)}{1-y} \,\textrm{d}x \right] \textrm{d}A
$$

where the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane is given by

$$
D = \left\{ (y,z) \, : \, 0 \leq y \leq \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \: 0 \leq z \leq 2\sqrt{1-y} \right\}.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{z}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}[x]_{x=0}^{x=z}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}(z-0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{z\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the double integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{z\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}{\int }_{0}^{2\sqrt{1-y}}\frac{z\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}{[\frac{{z}^{2}}{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=2\sqrt{1-y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}(\frac{4(1-y)}{2}-0)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =[\operatorname{sin}⁡(2y)]_{y=0}^{y=\pi /6} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Which of the following numbers are surds?

$$
\sqrt[3]{2},\qquad \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{1}{27}},\qquad \sqrt[3]{11}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
A surd is a number containing a radical symbol $\sqrt{\phantom{0}}$ that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

Surds can be square roots $\sqrt{\phantom{0}}$, cube roots $\sqrt[3]{\phantom{0}},$ or higher roots such as $\sqrt[4]{\phantom{0}}, \sqrt[5]{\phantom{0}},\ldots,$ etc.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

- $\sqrt[3]{2}$ is a surd. Using a calculator, we find that $\sqrt[3]{2} = 1.259\,921\,\ldots$

- $\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{1}{27}}$ is **NOT** a surd. Since $1$ and $27$ are perfect cubes, we can get rid of the cube root symbol $(\sqrt[3]{\phantom{0}})$ and obtain a regular fraction.

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[3]{\frac{1}{27}} & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{{1}^{3}}{{3}^{3}}} \\  & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{1\cdot 1\cdot 1}{3\cdot 3\cdot 3}} \\  & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{3}} \\  & =\sqrt[3]{{(\frac{1}{3})}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

- $\sqrt[3]{11}$ is a surd. Using a calculator, we find that $\sqrt[3]{11} = 2.223\,980\,\ldots$

Therefore, the correct answer is: $\sqrt[3]{2}$ and $\sqrt[3]{11}$ only.

:question/problem: Find the value of $\dfrac{3}{5}$ cubed.
:question/worked-solution:
To work out $\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)^3,$ we multiply $\dfrac{3}{5}$ by itself and then multiply the result by $\dfrac{3}{5}$ again:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{3}{5})}^{3} & =\frac{3}{5}\cdot \frac{3}{5}\cdot \frac{3}{5} \\  & =\frac{3\cdot 3\cdot 3}{5\cdot 5\cdot 5} \\  & =\frac{27}{125}\end{aligned}
$$

- $\sqrt{\dfrac{64}{81}}$ is **NOT** a surd. Since $64$ and $81$ are perfect squares, we can get rid of the square root symbol $(\sqrt{\phantom{0}})$ and obtain a regular fraction.

:question/problem: The formula for the $n$th term of a geometric sequence is $f(n) =\dfrac{6}{(-2)^n}$ for $n\geq 1.$  What is the recursive formula for this sequence?
:question/worked-solution:
The recursive formula for a geometric sequence is

$$
f(n+1) = r \cdot f(n).
$$

To complete the formula, we must determine the common ratio $r$ and state the first term $a_1.$ The first two terms are

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1) & =\frac{6}{(-2)^{1}}=\frac{6}{(-2)}=-3, \\ f(2) & =\frac{6}{(-2)^{2}}=\frac{6}{4}=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the common ratio is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{f(2)}{f(1)}=\frac{(\frac{3}{2})}{(-3)}=-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the recursive formula for the geometric sequence is

$$
f(n+1) = -\dfrac{1}{2} f(n), \qquad f(1) = -3, \qquad n \geq 1.
$$

:question/problem:
What is the explicit formula for the $n$th term of the sequence

$$
f(n+1) =-\dfrac{f(n)}{3},\, \quad f(1) = {\color{blue}9},\, \quad n\geq 1?
$$
:question/worked-solution:
First, let's rewrite our recursive formula as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(n+1)=-\frac{f(n)}{3}=-\frac{1}{3}f(n)\end{aligned}
$$

The explicit formula for the $n$th term of a geometric sequence is

$$
f(n) =f(1) \cdot r^{n-1}, \quad n \geq 1.
$$

So, we must determine the first term $f(1)$ and the common ratio $r.$

We are given that the first term is $f(1)=9.$ To find the common ratio, we compare the given sequence with the general recursive formula for a geometric sequence:

$$
f(n+1) = {\color{red}r} \cdot f(n)
$$

 

From the above, we see that $r = -\dfrac{1}{3}.$

Substituting $f(1) = 9$ and $r = -\dfrac{1}{3}$ into the formula for the $n$th term, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(n) &= f(1) \cdot r^{n-1}	\\[5pt]
&= 9 \cdot \left( -\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{n-1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

We can simplify further by manipulating the exponents as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(n) & =9\cdot {(-\frac{1}{3})}^{n-1} \\  & =9\cdot {(-\frac{1}{3})}^{-1}\cdot {(-\frac{1}{3})}^{n} \\  & =9\cdot (-\frac{3}{1})\cdot {(-\frac{1}{3})}^{n} \\  & =-27\cdot \frac{1}{(-3)^{n}} \\  & =-\frac{27}{(-3)^{n}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the formula for the $n$th term is

$$
f(n)=-\dfrac{27}{(-3)^n} ,\quad n\geq 1.
$$

:question/problem:
The polar curve $r=7$ and the ray $\theta=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ intersect at the point $P,$ as shown above. What are the Cartesian coordinates of $P?$

:question/problem:
For the vector ![](images/c3/c32c8627f43b93123b110207a136416c9b498a9b0fbab9adc671e039839f098c.svg) which of the following statements are true?

- $\mathbf{u}$ is orthogonal to the set ![](images/5e/5e3fe028385135bd1e744ae7ee0e0d6ed319bf5fc145ae70bee0b30991008964.svg)
:question/worked-solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $H$ and $V$ as $\{\mathbf{h}_1,\mathbf{h}_2\}$ and $\{\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2\}$ respectively.  

Now, we have to compute the dot product between $\mathbf{u}$ and the vectors in each set.

So $\mathbf u \perp \mathbf h_1$ but $\mathbf u \not\perp \mathbf h_2.$ Because $\mathbf u$ is not orthogonal to every vector in $H,$ we have $\mathbf{u}\not \perp H.$

:question/problem:
Consider the vector $\mathbf{x}$ and the subspace $S=\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2 \},$ where
![](images/36/3693f5fe916109a80a0d7782f7d21781953a7f854cedf82568d353d7e9d23681.svg)

Find the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace $S$ given that the set $\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\}$ is orthogonal.
:question/worked-solution:
Since the set $\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x} 
= \textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{a}_1}\mathbf{x} + \textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{a}_2}\mathbf{x}.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $\mathbf{x}$ onto $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1\}$ and $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_2\}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{2\cdot 1+3\cdot 1+(-2)\cdot 1}{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{1}=1\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{2\cdot (-2)+3\cdot 1+(-2)\cdot 1}{(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{2}=-\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+(-\frac{1}{2})\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ \frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Verify whether the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3$ are linearly independent, and find the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace spanned by the vectors $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3 \},$ where

$$

$$

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$

$$

In our case, we have
![](images/78/7885074c85f490a410f26a1b4d7836134b13a36923b99d31e3b670b8c1dd75f5.svg)

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot {(\begin{bmatrix}4 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}4 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot {\begin{bmatrix}26 & 8 \\ 8 & 3\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}18 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{14}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -8 \\ -8 & 26\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}18 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

:question/problem:
Consider the following vectors:
