Suppose that $V = \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf a_1, \mathbf a_2, \mathbf a_3\}.$ Given that $\mathcal B = \{\mathbf a_1, \mathbf a_2, \mathbf b\}$ is an orthogonal basis for $V, \mathbf{a}_1 \perp \mathbf{a}_2,$ and that $\mathcal B$ is derived from $V$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $\dfrac{c}{a}?$
:question/worked-solution:
Since the first two vectors are already orthogonal, we proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows:

**Step 1**: We set ![](images/ea/ea56a2ffc9a7f267e5de0cace94d505050e7df7ade72986b0b8e5ae6c91e7385.png)

**Step 2**: We set ![](images/a8/a87589c86b41d3fd44e6346b300a103c16301bb6cde410084a794b5430b3599a.png)

**Step 3**. Next, we find $\mathbf{v}_3$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{3} & ={a}_{3}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}\,{a}_{3}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{2}}\,{a}_{3} \\  & ={a}_{3}-\frac{{a}_{3}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}-\frac{{a}_{3}\cdot {v}_{2}}{{v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}}{v}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for $\mathbf{v}_3$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{3} & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-(-\frac{2}{4})\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-\frac{0}{4}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-0\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2} \\ -\frac{3}{2} \\ \frac{3}{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $a=-\dfrac 1 2,$ $c=-\dfrac 3 2,$ and $\dfrac{c}{a} = \dfrac{\left(-\dfrac 3 2\right)}{\left(-\dfrac 1 2\right)} = 3.$

:question/problem:
![](images/1e/1e6a41f2d6f834b7f9b8c937d19a4f47d45ee6bf2705d783e9a254e8478df15d.png)

Suppose that $V = \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf a_1, \mathbf a_2, \mathbf a_3\}.$ Given that $\mathcal B$ is an orthogonal basis for $V,$ and that $\mathcal B$ is derived from $V$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $\dfrac{b}{c}?$
:question/worked-solution:
We find an orthogonal basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows:

**Step 1.** We set ![](images/3f/3f7fd351c90e195ff46d0fdec20b2bda8a5a784c17a97700238fab0b19ebe836.png)

**Step 2.** We find the vector $\mathbf{v}_2$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}\{\mathbf{v}_1\}$ using the usual formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{3}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** We find the vector $\mathbf{v}_3$ orthogonal to $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2 \}$ using the usual formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{3} & ={a}_{3}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}\,{a}_{3}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{2}}\,{a}_{3} \\  & ={a}_{3}-\frac{{a}_{3}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}-\frac{{a}_{3}\cdot {v}_{2}}{{v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}}{v}_{2} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}-(-\frac{3}{3})\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{6}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}+2\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ \frac{3}{2} \\ -\frac{3}{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $b=\dfrac 3 2,$ $c=-\dfrac 3 2,$ and $\dfrac{b}{c} = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac 3 2\right)}{\left(-\dfrac 3 2\right)}=-1.$

:question/problem: Evaluate the line integral of $f(x,y,z) = \dfrac{x}{yz}$ along the curve parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t) = t^2\, \mathbf{i} + t \,\mathbf{j} + 1 \,\mathbf{k}$ for $t \in [0,\sqrt 2].$
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

Since $\mathbf{r}(t) =t^2\, \mathbf{i} + t \,\mathbf{j} + 1 \,\mathbf{k},$ then along the curve we have $x = t^2,$ $y = t,$ and $z=1.$  

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)\,k \\  & =2t\,i+1\,j+0\,k \\  & =2t\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y,z) = \dfrac{x}{yz},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{{t}^{2}}{t\cdot 1}=t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}t\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u= 4t^2+1,$ $\textrm d u=8t\,\textrm d t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}t\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{1}^{9}\frac{1}{8}{u}^{1/2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}{|}_{1}^{9} \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[{9}^{3/2}-{1}^{3/2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[27-1] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\cdot 26 \\  & =\frac{13}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find an integral that is equivalent to $\displaystyle\int\limits_C xy^3 \, \textrm{d}s,$ where $C$ is the curve parametrized by $\mathbf r(t)= \left \langle \cos t, \sin t \right\rangle$ for $t \in \left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right).$
:question/worked-solution:
![](images/f5/f53d78debfec5f8c50e0f3a5947d2a36126e18c073d7b0cc4c59d506753059b3.png)

The path of integration is shown above. We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

Here, we have $f(x,y) =  xy^3$. Along the path, we have $x=\cos t$ and $y=\sin t,$ and so we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =f(\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{3} \\  & ={sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{y}^{3}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 1\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we conclude that

$$
\int\limits_C xy^3 \, \textrm{d}s = \int^{\pi/2}_{0} \sin^3 t \cos t \, \textrm{d}t .
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral $\displaystyle\int\limits_{C}xy\,\textrm{d}s,$ where $C$ is the curve parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t) = 3t\,\mathbf{i}+4t\,\mathbf{j}\,$ for $0\leq t\leq 1.$
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

Since $\mathbf{r}(t) = 3t\,\mathbf{i}+4t\,\mathbf{j},$ then along the curve we have $x=3t$ and $y=4t.$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t)j \\  & =3\,i+4\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{5}^{2}} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, if $f(x,y) =xy,$ then we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3t\cdot 4t \\  & =12{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}12{t}^{2}\cdot 5\,\text{d}t \\  & =60{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =60{[\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =20{[{t}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =20.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Let $V=\mathcal{C}\left[0,2\pi\right]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $\left[0,2\pi\right],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
\langle f(t),g(t) \rangle = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{2\pi} f(t) g(t) \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

Given the functions $f(t) = \cos t$ and $g(t)=\sin 2t,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. $\langle f(t), g(t) \rangle = 0$

II. $\langle f(t), g(t) \rangle = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

III. $f(t) \perp g(t)$ with respect to the inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ in $V$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the identity* $\sin\alpha\cos\beta=\dfrac12(\sin(\alpha-\beta)+\sin(\alpha+\beta)).$
:question/worked-solution:
We need to evaluate

$$
\langle f(t), g(t) \rangle  =  \int_{0}^{2\pi}\cos{t} \sin2t \,\textrm{d}t.
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the given identity, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡3t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡3t}{3}){|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi )}{3}]-\frac{1}{2}[-\operatorname{cos}⁡0-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡0}{3}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[-1-\frac{1}{3}]-\frac{1}{2}[-1-\frac{1}{3}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-\frac{4}{3})-\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-\frac{4}{3}) \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now examine the statements:

- Statement I is true, while statement II is false.

- Statement III is true. Since the inner product is zero, our vectors are orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

:question/problem:
Evaluate $\displaystyle \int_C \left(x^2 + y^2\right)\,\textrm d y,$ where $C$ is the path along the upper-right quarter of the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 4,$ traversed from the point $(2,0)$ to the point $(0,2),$ as shown below.

![](images/8f/8fc3a36829c9780c34e13f253d607c3849bfd3ef1399a77a79a3dd3d30ef7140.png)
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}y = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a quarter of a circle of radius $2$ centered at $O.$ It can be parameterized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \big\langle 2\cos{t}, \: 2\sin{t} \big\rangle, \qquad 0 \le t \le \dfrac{\pi}{2}.
$$

Computing $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =4({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-8\operatorname{sin}⁡0 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/84/8417d2d62e9213ec3f92108495107fc982dc399e52cca8982e01516457f5692a.png)

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}\frac{2y}{x}\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the upper-right quarter of the ellipse $9{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=36,$ traversed from the point $(2,0)$ to the point $(0,3),$ as shown above.
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $2$ and $3,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{2y}{x}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{2\cdot 3\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =3\operatorname{tan}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(3\operatorname{tan}⁡t)\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}9\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-9\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =(-9\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))-(-9\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/6b/6bda5a10df8a1ec081db97e7aa52755796f1d50be5447e3e64f55986116ada6e.png)

Calculate 
${∮}_{∂D}x{y}^{2}\,dx+({x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})\,dy,$
where $D$ is the region shown above.
:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=x{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2xy+{y}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}x{y}^{2}\,dx+({x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2xy+{y}^{2})-2xy\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be represented in Cartesian coordinates as ${Δ}_{1}∖{Δ}_{2},$ where

- ${Δ}_{1}=\{(x,y)\,:\,-4\le x\le 4,-3\le y\le 3\}$ is the region enclosed by the outer curve, and

- ${Δ}_{2}=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,-1\le y\le 2\}$ is the region enclosed by the inner curve.

Therefore, our double integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{{Δ}_{1}}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A-{∬}_{{Δ}_{2}}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{3}{\int }_{-4}^{4}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-4}^{4}\,\text{d}x{\int }_{-3}^{3}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}x{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =x\,{|}_{-4}^{4}\cdot \frac{{y}^{3}}{3}\,{|}_{-3}^{3}-x\,{|}_{0}^{2}\cdot \frac{{y}^{3}}{3}{|}_{-1}^{2} \\  & =(4-(-4))\cdot (9-(-9))-(2-0)\cdot (\frac{8}{3}-(-\frac{1}{3})) \\  & =8\cdot 18-2\cdot 3 \\  & =138.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Let $S$ be the boundary of the rectangular prism enclosed by the planes $x=0,$ $x=2,$ $y=0,$ $y=1,$ $z=0,$ $z=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Given that the surface $S$ is positively (outward) oriented and $F={x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡z\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,j+(x+y)\,k,$ find the flux of $F$ across $S.$
:question/worked-solution:
Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∭}_{R}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $F,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡z)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡z)+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x+y) \\  & =2x\operatorname{cos}⁡z+0+0 \\  & =2x\operatorname{cos}⁡z.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $R$ be the solid region enclosed by $S.$ Then, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS & ={∭}_{R}2x\operatorname{cos}⁡z\,\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2x\operatorname{cos}⁡z\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2x\,\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}\text{d}y\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡z\,\text{d}z \\  & =[{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=2}\cdot (1-0)\cdot [\operatorname{sin}⁡z]_{z=0}^{z=\pi /2} \\  & =({2}^{2}-{0}^{2})\cdot 1\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =4\cdot 1\cdot 1 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Calculate ${∬}_{D}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,dA,\,$ where $D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le y\le x}.$
:question/worked-solution:
The integral is defined over the type I region $D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le y\le x}.$ 

So, we can express the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,dy\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[{\int }_{0}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,dy]\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)]_{0}^{x}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,dx & ={[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡x]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi +\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-0 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Calculate ${\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{\pi /2}}{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡{y}^{3}\,dx\,dy.$
:question/worked-solution:
The integral is defined over a type II region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{\pi /2}}{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡{y}^{3}\,dx\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{\pi /2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡{y}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}dx]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{\pi /2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡{y}^{3}[x]_{0}^{{y}^{2}}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{\pi /2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡{y}^{3}({y}^{2}-0)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{\pi /2}}{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡{y}^{3}\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{\pi /2}}{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡{y}^{3}\,dy & ={[-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{\pi /2}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}(0-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: If $u=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -3 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\,,$ $v=\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ -1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\,,$ and $u\cdot u=15,$ then $\frac{u\cdot (\frac{1}{2}u)}{u\cdot (\frac{3}{4}v)}=$
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the fact that the dot product is linear.

To quickly compute the numerator $u\cdot (\frac{1}{2}u),$ we multiply $u\cdot u$ by $\frac{1}{2}.$ Doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot (\frac{1}{2}u) & =\frac{1}{2}(u\cdot u) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 15 \\  & =\frac{15}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

To quickly compute the denominator $u\cdot (\frac{3}{4}v),$ we compute $u\cdot v$ first and then multiply the result by $\frac{3}{4}.$ Doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot (\frac{3}{4}v) & =\frac{3}{4}(u\cdot v) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}({u}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}+{u}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}+{u}_{3}\cdot {v}_{3}+{u}_{4}\cdot {v}_{4}) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}((-1)\cdot (-3)+(-3)\cdot (-1)+(-2)\cdot (-2)+1\cdot 2) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}(3+3+4+2) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\cdot 12 \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{u\cdot (\frac{1}{2}u)}{u\cdot (\frac{3}{4}v)} & =\frac{(\frac{15}{2})}{9}=\frac{5}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},\,{a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix},\,\,x=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the acute angle between $x$ and the subspace $S$ given that the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal.   Round the answer to $2$ decimal places.
:question/worked-solution:
Since the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{{a}_{1}}$ and $\text{Span}{{a}_{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{1\cdot 0+1\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot (-1)}{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{(-1)}^{2}}{a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{1\cdot 1+1\cdot 2+(-1)\cdot 2}{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{1}{9}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{9}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}(\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 9 \\ -9\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}) \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 11 \\ -7\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x$ or any other non-zero vector that is parallel to ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ So, to make calculations easier, we can find the angle between the vectors

$\,$ $x=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}\,$ and $\,9\,{\text{proj}}_{S}x=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 11 \\ -7\end{bmatrix}.$

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{1\cdot 1+1\cdot 11+(-1)\cdot (-7)}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{11}^{2}+(-7)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{19}{\sqrt{3}\sqrt{171}} \\  & =\frac{19}{\sqrt{3}\cdot 3\sqrt{19}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{57}}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{57}}{9})≈{32.98}^{∘},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

:question/problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s,$ where $f(x,y)=\sqrt{2}(x-y)$ and the curve $C$ is parametrized 
 by $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}+t,\,{t}^{2}-t⟩$ for $t\in [0,\sqrt{2}]?$
:question/worked-solution:
Since $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}+t,\,{t}^{2}-t⟩,$ then along the curve we have $x={t}^{2}+t,$ and $y={t}^{2}-t.$ 

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)j \\  & =(2t+1)\,i+(2t-1)\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2t+1)^{2}+(2t-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+4t+1+4{t}^{2}-4t+1} \\  & =\sqrt{8{t}^{2}+2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, since $f(x,y)=\sqrt{2}(x-y)$, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\sqrt{2}[({t}^{2}+t)-({t}^{2}-t)] \\  & =2\sqrt{2}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}2\sqrt{2}t\cdot \sqrt{2}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}t\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the acute angle between the vectors $v=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -\sqrt{5} \\ 7 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ and $w=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 5 \\ \sqrt{5}\end{bmatrix}.$

Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{v,w\},$ where

$$
v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,w=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},\,\,x=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the acute angle between $x$ and the subspace $S$ given that the set $\{v,w\}$ is orthogonal.
:question/worked-solution:
Since the set $\{v,w\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{v}x+{\text{proj}}_{w}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{v\}$ and $\text{Span}\{w\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{v}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot v}{v\cdot v}v=\frac{3\cdot 1+3\cdot 1+0\cdot 1}{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}v=2\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\ {\text{proj}}_{w}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot w}{w\cdot w}w=\frac{3\cdot 2+3\cdot (-1)+0\cdot (-1)}{{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}w=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x$ or any other non-zero vector that is parallel to ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ So, to make calculations easier, we can find the angle between the vectors

$\,$ $x=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,$ and $\,\frac{2}{3}{\text{proj}}_{S}x=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{3\cdot 2+3\cdot 1+0\cdot 1}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{3}^{2}+{0}^{2}}\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{9}{\sqrt{18}\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\frac{9}{6\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})=\frac{\pi }{6},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

:question/problem:
$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix},\,B=\{\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}\}
$$

Consider the subspace $\text{Col}(A)$ and an orthogonal basis $B$ of $\text{Col}(A),$ where $A$ and $B$ are given above. Given that $B$ is derived from $\text{Col}(A)$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $\frac{b}{a}?$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that $\text{Col}(A)$ is the span of the columns of $A.$ 

First, let's denote

$\,$ ${a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,$ and $\,{a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$ 

We proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows.

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 2**: Next, we find ${v}_{2}$, by using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{2}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{2\cdot 3+1\cdot (-1)+2\cdot 0}{{3}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{3}{2} \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $B=\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\}=\{\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{3}{2} \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\}$ is an orthogonal basis for $\text{Col}(A).$

Finally, $a=\frac{1}{2},$ $b=\frac{3}{2},$ and  

$$
\frac{b}{a}=\frac{(\frac{3}{2})}{(\frac{1}{2})}=3.
$$

:question/problem:
$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix},\,B={\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c \\ d\end{bmatrix}}
$$

Consider the subspace $V=\text{Col}(A)$ spanned by the columns ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ of the matrix $A$ and an orthogonal basis $B$ of $\text{Col}(A),$ shown above. Given that ${a}_{1}⊥{a}_{2},$ and that $B$ is derived from $V$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $\frac{a}{d}?$
:question/worked-solution:
Since the first two vectors are already orthogonal, we proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows:

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 2**: We set ${v}_{2}={a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 3**. Next, we find ${v}_{3}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{3} & ={a}_{3}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}\,{a}_{3}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{2}}\,{a}_{3} \\  & ={a}_{3}-\frac{{a}_{3}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}-\frac{{a}_{3}\cdot {v}_{2}}{{v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}}{v}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{3}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{3} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-(-\frac{6}{4})\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{12}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+\frac{3}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(6\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+9\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} \\ 0 \\ \frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
\frac{a}{d}=\frac{(\frac{1}{3})}{(-\frac{2}{3})}=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

:question/problem:
$$
{a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},\,{a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -3 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},\,{a}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix},\,B={\begin{bmatrix}| \\ \frac{{a}_{1}}{‖{a}_{1}‖} \\ |\end{bmatrix}\,,\begin{bmatrix}| \\ \frac{{a}_{2}}{‖{a}_{2}‖} \\ |\end{bmatrix}\,,\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c \\ d\end{bmatrix}}
$$

Suppose that $V=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}.$ Given that $B$ is an **orthonormal** basis for $V,{a}_{1}⊥{a}_{2},$ and that $B$ is derived from $V$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $|\,c\,|?$
:question/worked-solution:
Since the first two vectors are already orthogonal, we proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows:

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 2**: We set ${v}_{2}={a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -3 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 3**. Next, we find ${v}_{3}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{3} & ={a}_{3}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}\,{a}_{3}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{2}}\,{a}_{3} \\  & ={a}_{3}-\frac{{a}_{3}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}-\frac{{a}_{3}\cdot {v}_{2}}{{v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}}{v}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{3}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{3} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-(-\frac{4}{4})\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-(-\frac{8}{12})\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -3 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}+\frac{2}{3}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -3 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(3\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}+3\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}+2\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -3 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize ${v}_{3}$ dividing it by $‖{v}_{3}‖=\frac{\sqrt{6}}{3}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{3} & =\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{(\frac{\sqrt{6}}{3})}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\sqrt{6}}{6} \\ 0 \\ \frac{\sqrt{6}}{3} \\ \frac{\sqrt{6}}{6}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $|\,c\,|=\frac{\sqrt{6}}{3}.$

:question/problem:
$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 & -4 \\ -2 & 1 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 & 4 \\ 2 & 0 & -2\end{bmatrix},\,B={\begin{bmatrix}| \\ \frac{{a}_{1}}{‖{a}_{1}‖} \\ |\end{bmatrix}\,,\begin{bmatrix}| \\ \frac{{a}_{2}}{‖{a}_{2}‖} \\ |\end{bmatrix}\,,\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c \\ d\end{bmatrix}}
$$

Consider the subspace $V=\text{Col}(A)$ spanned by the columns ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ of the matrix $A,$ and an **orthonormal** basis $B$ of $\text{Col}(A),$ shown above. Given that ${a}_{1}⊥{a}_{2},$ and that $B$ is derived from $V$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $|\,c\,|?$
:question/worked-solution:
Since the first two vectors are already orthogonal, we proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process.

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 2**: We set ${v}_{2}={a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 3**. Next, we find ${v}_{3}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{3} & ={a}_{3}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}\,{a}_{3}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{2}}\,{a}_{3} \\  & ={a}_{3}-\frac{{a}_{3}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}-\frac{{a}_{3}\cdot {v}_{2}}{{v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}}{v}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{3}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{3} & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ -2 \\ 4 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}-(-\frac{16}{16})\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-(-\frac{6}{6})\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ -2 \\ 4 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -3 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize ${v}_{3}$ dividing it by $‖{v}_{3}‖=3\sqrt{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{3} & =\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -3 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $|\,c\,|=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.$

:question/problem:
$$
\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 3 \\ 1 & -3 \\ 2 & -3\end{bmatrix}}^{A}=\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}{q}_{11} & {q}_{12} \\ {q}_{21} & {q}_{22} \\ {q}_{31} & {q}_{32}\end{bmatrix}}^{Q}\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}{r}_{11} & {r}_{12} \\ 0 & {r}_{22}\end{bmatrix}}^{R}.
$$

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. Given that the columns ${q}_{1},{q}_{2}$ of $Q$ were obtained from the columns of $A$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, find  the value of ${q}_{22}\cdot {r}_{12}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Let ${a}_{1},{a}_{2}$ be the columns of $A.$

First, we find an orthonormal basis of $\text{Col}(A)=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process.

**Step 1**. We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 2**. We find the vector ${v}_{2}$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}\{{v}_{1}\}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -3 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}-(-\frac{12}{6})\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -3 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}+2\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we normalize ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\ {q}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute $R:$

$$
\begin{aligned}R & ={Q}^{T}\,A \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 3 \\ 1 & -3 \\ 2 & -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{6} & -2\sqrt{6} \\ 0 & \sqrt{3}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following QR factorization of $A:$

$$
\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 3 \\ 1 & -3 \\ 2 & -3\end{bmatrix}}^{A}=\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{bmatrix}}^{Q}\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{6} & -2\sqrt{6} \\ 0 & \sqrt{3}\end{bmatrix}}^{R}.
$$

Finally, ${q}_{22}\cdot {r}_{12}=(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})\cdot (-2\sqrt{6})=2\sqrt{2}.$

Consider the following vectors:

$$

Suppose that $V=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}.$ Given that $B={{a}_{1},{a}_{2},b}$ is an orthogonal basis for $V,{a}_{1}⊥{a}_{2},$ and that $B$ is derived from $V$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $\frac{a}{c}?$
:question/worked-solution:
Since the first two vectors are already orthogonal, we proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows:

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 2**: We set ${v}_{2}={a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -3 \\ -1 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 3**. Next, we find ${v}_{3}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{3} & ={a}_{3}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}\,{a}_{3}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{2}}\,{a}_{3} \\  & ={a}_{3}-\frac{{a}_{3}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}-\frac{{a}_{3}\cdot {v}_{2}}{{v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}}{v}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{3}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{3} & =\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 5 \\ 5 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}-(\frac{0}{4})\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-(-\frac{40}{20})\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -3 \\ -1 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 5 \\ 5 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}-0\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}+2\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -3 \\ -1 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $a=3,$ $c=3,$ and $\frac{a}{c}=\frac{3}{3}=1.$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{3} & ={a}_{3}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}\,{a}_{3}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{2}}\,{a}_{3} \\  & ={a}_{3}-\frac{{a}_{3}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}-\frac{{a}_{3}\cdot {v}_{2}}{{v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}}{v}_{2} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -1 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-\frac{10}{20}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -1 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -1 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-2\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} \\ -\frac{3}{2} \\ -\frac{1}{2} \\ -\frac{3}{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

:question/problem:
Let $V=C[\pi ,2\pi ]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[\pi ,2\pi ],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Calculate the norm of the vector $f(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$
:question/worked-solution:
The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨f(t),f(t)⟩}.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),f(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(f(t))^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }\,{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{t}{2}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}{4}){|}_{\pi }^{2\pi } \\  & =(\frac{2\pi }{2}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡4\pi }{4})-(\frac{\pi }{2}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi }{4}) \\  & =(\pi +0)-(\frac{\pi }{2}+0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we made use of the trigonometric identity 

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡t=\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2}.
$$

Finally then,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖f(t)‖ & =\sqrt{\frac{\pi }{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{12x}{y-1}$ along the curve parametrized by $r(t)={t}^{2}\,i+(t+1)\,j\,$ for $t\in [\sqrt{2},\sqrt{6}].$
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $r(t)={t}^{2}\,i+(t+1)\,j$, then along the curve we have $x={t}^{2}$ and $y=t+1.$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)\,j \\  & =2t\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{12x}{y-1}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{12{t}^{2}}{(t+1)-1} \\  & =\frac{12{t}^{2}}{t} \\  & =12t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{6}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{6}}12t\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=4{t}^{2}+1,$ $\text{d}u=8t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{6}}12t\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{9}^{25}\frac{3}{2}{u}^{1/2}\text{d}u \\  & ={u}^{3/2}{|}_{9}^{25} \\  & ={25}^{3/2}-{9}^{3/2} \\  & =125-27 \\  & =98\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the following set of functions:

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{f}_{2}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,{f}_{3}(t)=t
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $C[0,\pi ]$ of continuous functions over $[0,\pi ]$ is defined as 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement “${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product” is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the identity $\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)){|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi ))-\frac{1}{2}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{4}{3}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-\frac{4}{3}) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement “${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product” is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,t⟩={\int }_{0}^{\pi }t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's use integration by parts. We denote

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⟹ & {u}^{′}=1, \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡t & ⟹ & v=\int {v}^{′}\,\text{d}t=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, applying the integration by parts formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =uv{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{u}^{′}v\,\text{d}t \\  & =(t\operatorname{sin}⁡t){|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\pi \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(0))+\operatorname{cos}⁡t{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =0+(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =-2\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement “$S=\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)\}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product” is false. Since ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true."

:question/problem:
Consider the curve $C,$ defined parametrically as

$$
r(t)=⟨t+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi t}{2}),t+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi t}{2})⟩,\,0\le t\le 1.
$$

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ for $F=x{y}^{2}\,i+{x}^{2}y\,j.$ 

*Hint: You may wish to use the fact that $F$ is conservative.*
:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

To apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we must first find a potential function $f$ such that $F=∇f.$ Since we're given that $F$ is conservative, we know that such a function exists. Therefore, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =x{y}^{2}, \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & ={x}^{2}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Reconstructing the function $f$ from its gradient in the usual way, we get

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}.
$$

Note that we set $C=0$ for the arbitrary constant since we can use any function $f$ that satisfies $∇f=F.$

We're now ready to apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals. The position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,1⟩, \\ r(1) & =⟨2,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(0,1)$ and $(2,1).$

Finally, applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =f(2,1)-f(0,1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {2}^{2}\cdot {1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot {0}^{2}\cdot {1}^{2} \\  & =2-0 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Let $f(x,y,z)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+y\operatorname{cos}⁡z.$ Given that $C$ is the path along the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,t,2t⟩$ for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}],$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r.$
:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

In our case, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,0,0⟩ \\ r(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨1,\frac{\pi }{2},\pi ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(0,0,0)$ and $(1,\frac{\pi }{2},\pi ).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(r(\pi ))-f(r(0)) \\  & =f(1,\frac{\pi }{2},\pi )-f(0,0,0) \\  & =(1\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi )-(0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡0+0\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =(1+\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot (-1))-0 \\  & =1-\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Simplify $\dfrac{1}{3}k +1 + \dfrac{4}{3}k - 3.$
:question/worked-solution:
We collect and combine the like terms, simplifying the coefficients as much as possible.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}k+1+\frac{4}{3}k-3 &= (\frac{1}{3}k+\frac{4}{3}k)+(1-3) \\ &= (\frac{1+4}{3})k+(-2) \\ &= \frac{5}{3}k-2\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Simplify $\dfrac{1}{2}(p-4q).$
:question/worked-solution:
Applying the distributive law and simplifying, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(p-4q) &= (\frac{1}{2})\cdot p-(\frac{1}{2})\cdot 4q \\ &= \frac{1}{2}p-\frac{4q}{2} \\ &= \frac{1}{2}p-2q\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Simplify the expression $-\dfrac{1}{2}u  + \dfrac{7}{8}u.$
:question/worked-solution:
We combine the like terms by adding the coefficients.

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}u+\frac{7}{8}u &= (-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{7}{8})u\end{aligned}
$$

In order to add the coefficients, we have to convert them to have the same denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}(-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{7}{8})u &= (-\frac{4}{8}+\frac{7}{8})u \\ &= (\frac{-4+7}{8})u \\ &= \frac{3}{8}u\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the expression simplifies to $\dfrac{3}{8}u.$

:question/problem: Simplify $\dfrac{1}{3}(3a+6b)+2a.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we apply the distributive law.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}(3a+6b)+2a &= (\frac{1}{3})\cdot 3a+(\frac{1}{3})\cdot 6b+2a \\ &= \frac{3a}{3}+\frac{6b}{3}+2a \\ &= a+2b+2a\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we collect and combine the like terms, simplifying the coefficients as much as possible.

$$
\begin{aligned}a+2b+2a &= a+2a+2b \\ &= 3a+2b\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: What is $3.4 \,\textrm{cm}^2$ measured in $\textrm{mm}^2$?
:question/worked-solution:
There are $10\,\textrm{mm}$ per $\textrm{cm}$, which we can write as follows:

$$
\dfrac{10\,\textrm{mm}}{\textrm{cm}}
$$

We need to convert this into area units. So, by squaring this quantity and applying the rules of exponents, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
(\frac{10mm}{cm})^{2} &= \frac{10^{2}mm^{2}}{cm^{2}} \\
&= \frac{100mm^{2}}{cm^{2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

This is our conversion factor.

Now, multiplying $3.4 \, \textrm{cm}^2$ by our conversion factor, we get

$$
{\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle 3.4 \hspace{0.167em} {\text{cm}}^{2} & \displaystyle  = 3.4 \hspace{0.167em} {\text{cm}}^{2} \cdot  {\displaystyle \frac{100 \hspace{0.167em} {\text{mm}}^{2}}{ {\text{cm}}^{2}}} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 3.4 \hspace{0.167em} \cancel{ {\text{cm}}^{2}} \cdot  {\displaystyle \frac{100 \hspace{0.167em} {\text{mm}}^{2}}{\cancel{ {\text{cm}}^{2}}}} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 3.4 \cdot  100 \hspace{0.167em} {\text{mm}}^{2} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 340 \hspace{0.167em} {\text{mm}}^{2} .\end{array}}
$$

Therefore, $3.4\,\textrm{cm}^2$ is equivalent to $340\,\textrm{mm}^2$.

&= \frac{1000000m^{2}}{km^{2}}

This is our conversion factor.

Now, multiplying $0.053\,\textrm{km}^2$ by our conversion factor, we get

$$
{\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle 0.053 \hspace{0.167em} {\text{km}}^{2} & \displaystyle  = 0.053 \hspace{0.167em} {\text{km}}^{2} \cdot  {\displaystyle \frac{1 \hspace{0.167em} 000 \hspace{0.167em} 000 \hspace{0.167em} {\text{m}}^{2}}{ {\text{km}}^{2}}} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 0.053 \hspace{0.167em} \cancel{ {\text{km}}^{2}} \cdot  {\displaystyle \frac{1 \hspace{0.167em} 000 \hspace{0.167em} 000 \hspace{0.167em} {\text{m}}^{2}}{\cancel{ {\text{km}}^{2}}}} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 0.053 \cdot  1 \hspace{0.167em} 000 \hspace{0.167em} 000 \hspace{0.167em} {\text{m}}^{2} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 53 \hspace{0.167em} 000 \hspace{0.167em} {\text{m}}^{2} .\end{array}}

:question/problem: If $y$ varies inversely with $x$ and $y=15$ when $x=\dfrac{3}{5}$, find the value of $y$ when $x=3.$
:question/worked-solution:
Since $y$ varies inversely with $x,$ we use the equation

$$
y=\dfrac{k}{x}.
$$

We are told that $y=15$ when $x=\dfrac{3}{5}.$ We substitute this data into the equation to find $k\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}15 & =\frac{k}{(\frac{3}{5})} \\ 15\cdot (\frac{3}{5}) & =k \\ \frac{45}{5} & =k \\ 9 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the inverse variation is given by 

$$
y = \dfrac{9}{x}.
$$

Finally, substituting the value of $x=3$ into this equation gives

$$
y=\dfrac{9}{3} = 3.
$$

:question/problem:
The frequency of a wave is given by the formula

$$
f = \dfrac{v}{l},
$$

where $v$ represents the velocity of the wave in $\dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}},$ while $l$ represents the length of the wave in meters. Find an appropriate measurement unit for frequency.
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the unit of frequency by substituting the given units of velocity and length into the formula and simplifying. 

$$
\begin{aligned}f & =\frac{v}{l} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}})}{\text{m}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\text{m}}\cdot (\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{m}}{\text{m}\cdot \text{s}} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{\text{m}}}{\cancel{\text{m}}\cdot \text{s}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\text{s}}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the unit of frequency is $\dfrac{1}{\textrm{s}}.$

:question/problem: The third term of a geometric sequence is $80$ and its fifth term is $20.$  Find the common ratio $r$ of this sequence given that $r$ is positive.
:question/worked-solution:
To find the common ratio $r$ of a geometric sequence given two terms $a_m$ and $a_n,$ we use the formula

$$
r^{n-m} = \dfrac{a_n}{a_m}.
$$

In this case, we're given $a_5 = 20$ and $a_3 = 80.$ Substituting $n=5$ and $m=3$ into the formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{5-3} & =\frac{{a}_{5}}{{a}_{3}} \\ {r}^{2} & =\frac{20}{80} \\ {r}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, solving the equation for $r$ and considering that $r$ is positive, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {r}^{2} & ={(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\ r & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Use the Laplace transform of $f(t) = e^{kt}$ to find the Laplace transform of $\sinh(3t).$
:question/worked-solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
\mathcal L\{\alpha f(t) + \beta g(t)\} = \alpha\cdot \mathcal L\{f(t)\} + \beta\cdot \mathcal L \{g(t)\},
$$

where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are constants.

First, recall that, by definition

$$
\sinh(3t) = \dfrac{e^{3t} - e^{-3t}}{2}.
$$

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t)} & =L{\frac{{e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{3t}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{-3t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{3t}}{2}}-L{\frac{{e}^{-3t}}{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{3t}}-\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-3t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall that 

$$
\mathcal L\left\{e^{kt}\right\} = \dfrac{1}{s-k}, \qquad s > k.
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{3t}} & =\frac{1}{s-3},\,s>3 \\ L{{e}^{-3t}} & =\frac{1}{s+3},\,s>-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $\sinh(3t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t)} & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{3t}}-\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-3t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s-3}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s+3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{s-3}-\frac{1}{s+3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{(s+3)-(s-3)}{(s-3)(s+3)}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{6}{{s}^{2}-9}) \\  & =\frac{3}{{s}^{2}-9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $\mathcal L\{e^{3t}\}$ is defined for $s\in (3,\infty)$ and $\mathcal L \{e^{-3t}\}$ is defined for $s\in (-3,\infty),$ we have that $\mathcal L\{\sinh(3t)\}$ is defined for

$$
(3,\infty) \cap (-3,\infty) = (3,\infty),
$$

that is, $s > 3.$

:question/problem: Find the degree of the homogeneous function $g(x,y) = \dfrac{1}{x}\cos\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right).$
:question/worked-solution:
A function $g(x,y)$ is homogeneous of degree $n$ if it satisfies the property

$$
g(tx,ty) = t^ng(x,y).
$$

So first, we compute $g(tx,ty),$ and then we simplify by writing it as $t^n g(x,y)$ for some $n\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(tx,ty) & =\frac{1}{tx}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{ty}{tx}) \\  & =\frac{1}{tx}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{y}{x}) \\  & =\frac{1}{t}\cdot \frac{1}{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{y}{x}) \\  & ={t}^{-1}\cdot \frac{1}{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{y}{x}) \\  & ={t}^{-1}g(x,y)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
g(tx,ty) = t^{-1} g(x,y)
$$

and so the degree of the homogeneous function $g(x,y)$ is $-1.$

:question/problem:
Which symbols could replace the empty box below to make the statement true?
$\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^2 \,\,\square\,\, \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^1$

1. $>$
2. $<$
3. $=$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate

$$
\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^2
$$

We have

$$
\begin{aligned}
(\frac{1}{3})^{2} &= \underbrace{\frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{1}{3}}_{{{\color{blue}2} }\text{ times}} \\
&= \frac{1 \cdot 1}{3 \cdot 3} \\
&= \frac{1}{9}
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, for

$$
\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^1
$$

we have

$$
(\frac{1}{4})^{1} = \frac{1}{4}
$$

Because

$$
\dfrac{1}{9} < \dfrac{1}{4}
$$

the correct statement must be

$$
\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^2 < \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^1 \,
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
y'' + 9y = 6\cos x.
$$

The corresponding homogeneous equation has the fundamental solutions $y_1(x) = \cos(3x)$ and $y_2 = \sin(3x).$ 

According to the method of variation of parameters, we should seek a particular solution 

$$
y_p(x) = u_1(x) y_1 + u_2(x) y_2
$$

that satisfies the following constraints:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}^{′} &=6\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $\displaystyle u_2(x) = \int g(x)\,\textrm d x,$ find the function $g.$
:question/worked-solution:
We notice that the forcing term is $f(x) = 6\cos x.$ Additionally, we're given the fundamental solutions

$$
y_1(x) = \cos(3x), \qquad y_2(x) = \sin(3x).
$$

First, let's verify that the fundamental solutions $y_1$ and $y_2$ are independent by computing the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{1}^{′}{y}_{2} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))^{′}-(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))^{′}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)) \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))(3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))-(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)) \\  & =3{cos}^{2}⁡(3x)+3{sin}^{2}⁡(3x) \\  & =3\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions $y_1(x)$ and $y_2(x)$ are linearly independent. 

Now, we have the following constraints:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))}^{′} &=6\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x) &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-3{u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x) &=6\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x) &=0\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

We wish to find an integral expression for $u_2.$ We start by eliminating $u_1'$ from the second equation:

$$
u_1' = -\dfrac{u_2'\sin(3x)}{\cos(3x)}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-3{u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x) & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ -3(-\frac{{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)})\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x) & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ 3{u}_{2}^{′}\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡(3x)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}+3{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x) & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ 3{u}_{2}^{′}\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡(3x)+{cos}^{2}⁡(3x)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)} & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ 3{u}_{2}^{′}\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)} & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {u}_{2}^{′} & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x).\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}_{2}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\ {u}_{2} & =\int 2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that $g(x) = 2\cos x \cos(3x).$

:question/problem:
Find the Laplace transform $\mathcal{L}\left\{f''(t) \right\}$ for $s > 0,$ given that the function $f(t)$ is continuous on $[0,\infty),$ $f'(0)=2,$ $f(0)=-1,$ and

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\} =   \dfrac{2 - s}{s^2+4}, \quad s>0.
$$

Assume that $f'$ is continuous and $f''$ piecewise continuous on $[0,\infty).$
:question/worked-solution:
Suppose $F(s) = \mathcal L \{f(t)\}$ where $f(t)$ is a continuous function of exponential order $a$ on $[0,\infty).$ If $f'(t)$ is continuous and $f''(t)$ is piecewise continuous on $[0,\infty),$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{f}^{″}(t)} & ={s}^{2}L{f(t)}-sf(0)-{f}^{′}(0).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the Laplace transform of $f''(t)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{f}^{″}(t)} & ={s}^{2}L{f(t)}-sf(0)-{f}^{′}(0) \\  & ={s}^{2}\cdot \frac{2-s}{{s}^{2}+4}-s\cdot (-1)-2 \\  & =\frac{{s}^{2}(2-s)}{{s}^{2}+4}+s-2 \\  & =-\frac{{s}^{2}(s-2)}{{s}^{2}+4}+(s-2) \\  & =(s-2)(-\frac{{s}^{2}}{{s}^{2}+4}+1) \\  & =(s-2)(\frac{4}{{s}^{2}+4}) \\  & =\frac{4(s-2)}{{s}^{2}+4}\end{aligned}
$$

valid for $s > 0.$

:question/problem:
Find $y(t)$ if the Laplace transform of the initial value problem

$$
y'' +  6y = 2\sin {2t}, \quad y(0) = 0, \quad y'(0) = 2
$$

is given by

$$
s^2Y(s) - 2 +6 Y(s)  =  2\left(\dfrac{2}{s^2 + 4}\right).
$$
:question/worked-solution:
Using the transformed equation, we can solve for $Y(s)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}^{2}Y(s)-2+6Y(s) & =2(\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4}), \\ ({s}^{2}+6)Y(s) & =2+\frac{4}{{s}^{2}+4} \\ ({s}^{2}+6)Y(s) & =\frac{2{s}^{2}+12}{{s}^{2}+4} \\ ({s}^{2}+6)Y(s) & =\frac{2({s}^{2}+6)}{{s}^{2}+4} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4}\end{aligned}
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}=\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, taking the inverse Laplace transform, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{Y(s)} & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4}} \\ y(t) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y(t) =  \sin {2t}$ is the solution of the original differential equation.

Use the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{\text{i}\omega t}$ to find the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).$$\,L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)}=$ {{field-1}},
defined for {{field-2}}.
:question/worked-solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

First, recall that the sine function can be defined in terms of complex exponentials as follows: 

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)=\frac{{e}^{3\text{i}t}-{e}^{-3\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}
$$

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)} & =L{\frac{{e}^{3\text{i}t}-{e}^{-3\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{3\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}-\frac{{e}^{-3\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{3\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}}-L{\frac{{e}^{-3\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}L{{e}^{3\text{i}t}}-\frac{1}{2\text{i}}L{{e}^{-3\text{i}t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall that 

$$
L{{e}^{\text{i}\omega t}}=\frac{1}{s-\text{i}\omega },\,s>0.
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{3\text{i}t}} & =\frac{1}{s-3\text{i}},\,s>0 \\ L{{e}^{-3\text{i}t}} & =\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}},\,s>0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)} & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}L{{e}^{3\text{i}t}}-\frac{1}{2\text{i}}L{{e}^{-3\text{i}t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}\cdot \frac{1}{s-3\text{i}}-\frac{1}{2\text{i}}\cdot \frac{1}{s+3\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}(\frac{1}{s-3\text{i}}-\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}(\frac{(s+3\text{i})-(s-3\text{i})}{(s-3\text{i})(s+3\text{i})}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}(\frac{6\text{i}}{{s}^{2}+9}) \\  & =\frac{3}{{s}^{2}+9},\end{aligned}
$$

defined for $s>0.$

:question/problem:
Find $y(t)$ given that the Laplace transform of the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}(t)-y(t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=1
$$

is given by

$$
{s}^{2}Y(s)-1-Y(s)=-2(\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1}).
$$

{{field-1}}

Using the transformed equation, we can solve for $Y(s)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}^{2}Y(s)-1-Y(s) & =-2(\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1}) \\ ({s}^{2}-1)Y(s) & =1-\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+1} \\ ({s}^{2}-1)Y(s) & =\frac{{s}^{2}-1}{{s}^{2}+1} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}

Now, taking the inverse Laplace transform, we get
