The continuous random variable $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{3{x}^{2}+4}{5},\,0<x<1
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{11}{20},$ compute $\text{E}[2X-{X}^{3}+1].$

*Hint: You may assume that $\text{E}[aX+bY]=a\text{E}[X]+b\text{E}[Y]$ for any random variables $X$ and $Y$ and constants $a$ and $b.$*
:question/worked-solution:
First, we simplify using the hint and the properties of expected value:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[2X-{X}^{3}+1] & =2\text{E}[X]-\text{E}[{X}^{3}]+\text{E}[1] \\  & =2\text{E}[X]-\text{E}[{X}^{3}]+1\end{aligned}
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We already know $\text{E}[X].$ So, we compute the third raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{3}] & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}\cdot (\frac{3{x}^{2}+4}{5})\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{3}{5}{x}^{5}+\frac{4}{5}{x}^{3})\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{1}{10}{x}^{6}+\frac{1}{5}{x}^{4})|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{5} \\  & =\frac{3}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\text{E}[X]=\frac{11}{20}$ and $\text{E}[{X}^{3}]=\frac{3}{10}$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[2X-{X}^{3}+1] & =2\text{E}[X]-\text{E}[{X}^{3}]+1 \\  & =2\cdot \frac{11}{20}-\frac{3}{10}+1 \\  & =\frac{11}{10}-\frac{3}{10}+1 \\  & =\frac{9}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Let ${J}_{n}(\lambda )$ denote an $n\times n$ Jordan block with $\lambda $ on the main diagonal. Fill in the missing entries in the matrix below.

|  |  | $6$ | {{field-1}} | $-3$ | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\operatorname{sin}⁡({J}_{4}(\frac{\pi }{6}))=\frac{1}{12}\,\,$ |  | $0$ | $6$ | {{field-3}} | $-3$ |  |
|  | $0$ | $0$ | $6$ | {{field-4}} |  |  |
|  |  | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $6$ |  |
:question/worked-solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=\begin{bmatrix}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In this case, we have $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ $n=4,$ and $\lambda =\frac{\pi }{6}.$

Since $n=4,$ we need to compute the first $4-1=3$ derivatives of $f:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{4}(\frac{\pi }{6})) & =\begin{bmatrix}f(\frac{\pi }{6}) & {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6}) & \frac{1}{2!}{f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{6}) & \frac{1}{3!}{f}^{‴}(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\ 0 & f(\frac{\pi }{6}) & {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6}) & \frac{1}{2!}{f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\ 0 & 0 & f(\frac{\pi }{6}) & {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & f(\frac{\pi }{6})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) & -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) & -\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\ 0 & \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) & -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\ 0 & 0 & \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & -\frac{1}{4} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{12} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & -\frac{1}{4} \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{2}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\begin{bmatrix}6 & 6\sqrt{3} & -3 & -\sqrt{3} \\ 0 & 6 & 6\sqrt{3} & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 6 & 6\sqrt{3} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Let ${J}_{n}(\lambda )$ denote an $n\times n$ Jordan block with $\lambda $ on the main diagonal. Fill in the missing entries in the matrix below.

|  |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} | {{field-3}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3})\,⊕\,{J}_{2}(\frac{\pi }{4}))=\,\,$ |  | $0$ | {{field-4}} | {{field-5}} |  |
|  |  | $0$ | $0$ | {{field-6}} |  |
:question/worked-solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=\begin{bmatrix}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3})\,⊕\,{J}_{2}(\frac{\pi }{4})) & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\begin{bmatrix}{J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3}) & 0 \\ 0 & {J}_{2}(\frac{\pi }{4})\end{bmatrix}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3})) & 0 \\ 0 & \operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{2}(\frac{\pi }{4}))\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3}))\,⊕\,\operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{2}(\frac{\pi }{4})).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we compute the function of each Jordan block separately.

- For ${J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3}),$ we have $n=1$ and $\lambda =\frac{\pi }{3}.$ Since $n=1,$ we don't need any derivatives. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3})) & =\begin{bmatrix}f(\frac{\pi }{3})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{3}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For ${J}_{2}(\frac{\pi }{4}),$ we have $n=2$ and $\lambda =\frac{\pi }{4}.$ Since $n=2,$ we need to compute the first derivative of $f$ only:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & ={sec}^{2}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{2}(\frac{\pi }{4})) & =\begin{bmatrix}f(\frac{\pi }{4}) & {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ 0 & f(\frac{\pi }{4})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) & {sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ 0 & \operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3})\,⊕\,{J}_{2}(\frac{\pi }{4})) & =\operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3}))\,⊕\,\operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{2}(\frac{\pi }{4})) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{3} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Isolating the exponential term, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}2\cdot {8}^{2x} & <\frac{1}{3} \\ {8}^{2x} & <\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, taking the logarithm to base $8$ of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{8}⁡({8}^{2x}) & <{log}_{8}⁡(\frac{1}{6}) \\ 2x & <{log}_{8}⁡({6}^{-1}) \\ 2x & <-{log}_{8}⁡(6) \\ x & <-\frac{1}{2}{log}_{8}⁡(6).\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the following statement. 

If $f(x)=3{e}^{2x}+2x,$ then $f=O({e}^{2x})$ as $x\to \infty .$

A proof of the statement is given below

 $\text{L1}:\,f=O(3{e}^{2x}+2x)$

$\text{L2}:\,{lim}_{x\to \infty }(\frac{2x}{3{e}^{2x}})=0$

$\text{L3}:\,2x=O(3{e}^{2x})$ 

$\text{L4}:\,f=O(3{e}^{2x})$  

$\text{L5}:\,f=O({e}^{2x})$ 

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L1}$ follows from {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from lines 
{{field-2}} and 
{{field-3}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from line {{field-4}}  and 
{{field-5}}.
:question/worked-solution:
Suppose $f(x),g(x),h(x)$ and $k(x)$ are functions and $c$ is a nonzero constant. Then, we have the following properties of Big-O notation. 

- The sum and product properties. If

$$
f=O(h)\,\text{and}\,g=O(k)\,\text{as}\,x\to a
$$

 
then

$$
f+g=O(h+k)\,\text{and}\,fg=O(hk)\,\text{as}\,x\to a.
$$

- The constant multiple property. If 

$$
f=O(cg)\,\text{as}\,x\to a
$$

 
then

$$
f=O(g)\,\text{as}\,x\to a.
$$

- The reflexive property. 

$$
f=O(f)\,\text{as}\,x\to a
$$

- The transitive property. If 

$$
f=O(g)\,\text{and}\,g=O(h)\,\text{as}\,x\to a
$$

then

$$
f=O(h)\,\text{as}\,x\to a.
$$

- The absorption property. If

$$
f=O(g+h)\,\text{and}\,g=O(h)\,\text{as}\,x\to a
$$

 
then 

$$
f=O(h)\,\text{as}\,x\to a.
$$

With that in mind, let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider line $\text{L1},$ which states that

$$
f=O(\underbrace{3{e}^{2x}+2x}_{f})
$$

and this is true by $\text{the reflexive property}.$

- Next, we consider line $\text{L4}.$ From line $\text{L1},$ we have

$$
f=O(3{e}^{2x}+2x)
$$

and from line $\text{L3},$ we have

$$
2x=O(3{e}^{2x}).
$$

Thus, by lines $\text{L1 and L3}$ and the $\text{absorption property},$ we have 

$$
f=O(3{e}^{2x}+2x)=O(3{e}^{2x}).
$$

- Finally, we consider line $\text{L5}.$ From line $\text{L4},$ we have

$$
f=O(3{e}^{2x})
$$

and by the $\text{constant multiple property}$ with $c=3,$ we have

$$
f=O({e}^{2x}).
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2y=4\operatorname{cosh}⁡2x.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below. 

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-2{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{2x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{2x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{2x})}^{′}-2(u{e}^{2x}) & =4\operatorname{cosh}⁡2x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{2x}+2u{e}^{2x}-2u{e}^{2x} & =4\operatorname{cosh}⁡2x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{2x}+\cancel{2u{e}^{2x}}-\cancel{2u{e}^{2x}} & =4\operatorname{cosh}⁡2x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{2x} & =4\operatorname{cosh}⁡2x \\ {u}^{′} & =4{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cosh}⁡2x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\operatorname{cosh}⁡2x=\frac{{e}^{2x}+{e}^{-2x}}{2}
$$

our equation for $u$ becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =4{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cosh}⁡2x \\  & =4{e}^{-2x}(\frac{{e}^{2x}+{e}^{-2x}}{2}) \\  & =2{e}^{-2x}({e}^{2x}+{e}^{-2x}) \\  & =2+2{e}^{-4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =2+2{e}^{-4x} \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2+2{e}^{-4x}\,\text{d}x \\ u & =2x-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{2x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{2x} \\  & =2x{e}^{2x}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(1,-2)$ and which passes through the point $(-3,6)?$
:question/worked-solution:
The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(1,-2),$ and so we have

$$
x-1=2pt,\,y+2=p{t}^{2}.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(-3,6),$ we can substitute $x=-3$ and $y=6$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-4 &=2pt \\ 8 &=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-4 & =2pt \\ t & =-\frac{2}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}8 & =p{(-\frac{2}{p})}^{2} \\ 8 & =p\cdot \frac{4}{{p}^{2}} \\ 8 & =\frac{4}{p} \\ p & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-1=2(\frac{1}{2})t,\,y-(-2)=(\frac{1}{2}){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-1=t,\,y+2=\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}.
$$

:question/problem: Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the horizontal parabola given by the Cartesian equation $(y-1)^{2}=-5(x-1)?$
:question/worked-solution:
The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h)$ that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=p{t}^{2},\,y-k=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h),$ we see that the parabola has its vertex at $(h,k)=(1,1).$ So we have

$$
x-1=p{t}^{2},\,y-1=2pt.
$$

Now, comparing the right-hand sides of the given Cartesian equation and the general case, then solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4p(x-h) & =-5(x-1) \\ 4p(x-1) & =-5(x-1) \\ 4p & =-5 \\ p & =-\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-1=(-\frac{5}{4}){t}^{2},\,y-1=2(-\frac{5}{4})t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-1=-\frac{5}{4}{t}^{2},\,y-1=-\frac{5}{2}t.
$$

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the parabola shown above?

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},

where $p$ is constant.

x+2=2pt,\,y-4=p{t}^{2}.

Since the parabola passes through $(2,2),$ we can substitute $x=2$ and $y=2$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4 &=2pt \\ -2 &=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}\right.

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =2pt \\ 2 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{2}{p}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

:question/problem:
![](images/75/75df54dd30da590814e89153396ac7cf8a713fc9a6e04d14786780147ba57cfe.png)

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the parabola shown above?
:question/worked-solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola is horizontal, has its vertex at $(5,-1),$ and passes through the point $(17,11).$

The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=p{t}^{2},\,y-k=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(5,-1),$ and so we have

$$
x-5=p{t}^{2},\,y+1=2pt.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(17,11),$ we can substitute $x=17$ and $y=11$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}12 &=p{t}^{2} \\ 12 &=2pt.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the second equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}12 & =2pt \\ 6 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{6}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the first equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}12 & =p{(\frac{6}{p})}^{2} \\ 12 & =p\cdot \frac{36}{{p}^{2}} \\ 12 & =\frac{36}{p} \\ p & =\frac{36}{12} \\ p & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-5=(3){t}^{2},\,y+1=2(3)t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-5=3{t}^{2},\,y+1=6t.
$$

:question/problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the parabola defined by the parametric equations

$$
x-6=3t,\,y-3=\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2},\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$
:question/worked-solution:
First, let's make $t$ the subject of the parametric equations. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}t & =\frac{x-6}{3},\,{t}^{2}=\frac{2(y-3)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring both sides of the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & ={(\frac{x-6}{3})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{(x-6)^{2}}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now eliminate the parameter $t$ by substituting the above into the equation ${t}^{2}=\frac{2(y-3)}{3}$ and rearranging to find the Cartesian equation of the parabola, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-6)^{2}}{9} & =\frac{2(y-3)}{3} \\ (x-6)^{2} & =9\cdot (\frac{2(y-3)}{3}) \\ (x-6)^{2} & =6(y-3).\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the parabola defined by the parametric equations

$$
x-2=3t,\,y+2=\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2},\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$
:question/worked-solution:
First, let's make $t$ the subject of the parametric equations. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}t & =\frac{x-2}{3},\,{t}^{2}=\frac{2(y+2)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring both sides of the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & ={(\frac{x-2}{3})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{(x-2)^{2}}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now eliminate the parameter $t$ by substituting the above into the equation ${t}^{2}=\frac{2(y+2)}{3}$ and rearranging to find the Cartesian equation of the parabola, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-2)^{2}}{9} & =\frac{2(y+2)}{3} \\ (x-2)^{2} & =9\cdot (\frac{2(y+2)}{3}) \\ (x-2)^{2} & =6(y+2).\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Solve the inequality $3{e}^{x}-4<0.$
:question/worked-solution:
Isolating the exponential term, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}3{e}^{x}-4 & <0 \\ 3{e}^{x} & <4 \\ {e}^{x} & <\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x}) & <\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{4}{3}) \\ x & <\operatorname{ln}⁡4-\operatorname{ln}⁡3.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Solve the inequality $3 \cdot (\frac{2}{7})^{x} + 1 \ge 16$.

The function $y=f(x)$ satisfies the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2y+{x}^{2}.
$$

 

Given that the point $P(1,-1)$ lies on the graph of the function, evaluate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}$ at $P.$
:question/worked-solution:
To find an expression for the second derivative, we differentiate the equation with respect to $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2y+{x}^{2}) \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2y)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y)+2x \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the given expression for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ into the above and simplify the resulting expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =2(2y+{x}^{2})+2x \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =4y+2{x}^{2}+2x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute the coordinates of our point into the above expression for the second derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}|}_{(1,-1)} & ={(4y+2{x}^{2}+2x)|}_{(1,-1)} \\  & =4(-1)+2(1)^{2}+2(1) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The function $y=f(x)$ satisfies the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2{x}^{3}-y.
$$

Given that the point $(1,2)$ lies on the graph of $y=f(x),$ which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the value of the first and second derivatives of the function at the given point.

To find the first derivative of $f$ at $(1,2),$ we substitute the coordinates of our point into the differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(1,2)} & ={(2{x}^{3}-y)|}_{(1,2)} \\  & =2(1)^{3}-(2) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

To find the second derivative, we first need to differentiate the equation and then substitute the coordinates of the point:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3}-y) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y) \\  & =6{x}^{2}-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\  & =6{x}^{2}-(2{x}^{3}-y) \\  & =6{x}^{2}-2{x}^{3}+y \\ {\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}|}_{(1,2)} & ={(6{x}^{2}-2{x}^{3}+y)|}_{(1,2)} \\  & =6(1)^{2}-2(1)^{3}+(2) \\  & =6 \\  & >0.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine the statements in turn.

- Statement “$(1,2)$ is a stationary point of the function $f$” is true. Indeed, since 

$$
{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(1,2)}=0,
$$

 we obtain that $(1,2)$ is a stationary point of the function $f.$

- Statement “$(1,2)$ is a local maximum point of the function $f$” is false. There is a critical point at $(1,2).$ So, according to the second derivative test, since 

$$
{\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}|}_{(1,2)}>0,
$$

 we have a local minimum (not a local maximum) at that point.

- Statement “$(1,2)$ is an inflection point of the function $f$” is false. Since the second derivative is not zero, there is no inflection point at $(1,2).$

Therefore, the correct answer is “$(1,2)$ is a stationary point of the function $f$” only.

:question/problem:
The function $y=f(x)$ satisfies the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=y{e}^{x}.
$$

Given that the point $(0,e)$ lies on the graph of $y=f(x),$ which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the value of the first and second derivatives of the function at the given point.

To find the first derivative of $f$ at $(0,e),$ we substitute the coordinates of our point into the differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(0,e)} & ={(y{e}^{x})|}_{(0,e)} \\  & =e\cdot {e}^{0} \\  & =e\end{aligned}
$$

To find the second derivative, we first need to differentiate the equation and then substitute the coordinates of the point:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y)\cdot {e}^{x}+y\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\cdot {e}^{x}+y{e}^{x} \\  & =(y{e}^{x}){e}^{x}+y{e}^{x} \\  & =y{e}^{2x}+y{e}^{x} \\ {\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}|}_{(0,e)} & ={(y{e}^{2x}+y{e}^{x})|}_{(0,e)} \\  & =e\cdot {e}^{2(0)}+e\cdot {e}^{0} \\  & =2e \\  & >0\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine the statements in turn.

- Statement “$(0,e)$ is a stationary point of the function $f$” is false. Indeed, since

$$
{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(0,e)}=e\ne 0,
$$

we obtain that $(0,e)$ is not a stationary point of the function $f.$

- Statement “$(0,e)$ is a local minimum point of the function $f$” is false. There is no critical point at $(0,e),$ therefore we cannot have a local minimum at that point.

- Statement “$(0,e)$ is an inflection point of the function $f$” is false. Since the second derivative is not zero, there is no inflection point at $(0,e).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of those listed."

Therefore, we're required to compute the conditional probability

$$

$$

By the multiplication law for conditional probability, we have

$$
P(X = 2 \,|\, Y = 2) = \dfrac{P(X = 2, Y = 2)}{P(Y = 2)} = \dfrac{f(2,2)}{f_Y(2)}
$$

where $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability mass function of $X$ and $Y,$ and $f_Y(y)$ is the marginal distribution of $Y.$

Recall that the marginal distribution for $Y$ corresponds to the column totals. Thus, 

$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $X$ are shown above. Find the expression for the conditional expected value $\textrm{E}\big[Y \,|\, X=x\big]$ for $0 <     x <     2.$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\textrm E\big[ Y \,|\, X = x \big] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} y \, f_{Y|X}(y \,|\, x) \; \textrm{d}y.
$$

Note that $\textrm E\big[ Y \,|\, X = x \big]$ is a function of $x.$ 

The conditional density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{x+y}{4})}{(\frac{3{x}^{2}}{8})} \\  & =\frac{2(x+y)}{3{x}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0 \leq y \leq x,\; 0 <              x <             2.$ Outside this domain, we have $f_{Y|X} (y \,|\, x) = 0.$ 

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{x}y\cdot \,\frac{2(x+y)}{3{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{3{x}^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{x}(xy+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{3{x}^{2}}{[\frac{x{y}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{x} \\  & =\frac{2}{3{x}^{2}}[\frac{{x}^{3}}{2}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-0] \\  & =\frac{2}{3{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{5{x}^{3}}{6} \\  & =\frac{1}{3{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{5{x}^{2}\cdot x}{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{3\cancel{{x}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{5\cancel{{x}^{2}}\cdot x}{3} \\  & =\frac{5x}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/9c/9cf18d64c3f283c730e1d32ee81e3f193e615bb7b0b936dac009c46328826b3d.svg)

The joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ for the continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is shown above. Given that 

$$
\textrm {E}[X]= \dfrac{3}{4},\qquad
\textrm {E}[Y]= \dfrac{5}{12}, \qquad
\textrm {SD}[X]\approx 0.1936, \qquad
\textrm {SD}[Y]\approx 0.2444,
$$

 
find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\textrm{Cov}[X, Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\textrm {SD}[X]$ and $\textrm {SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}xy\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{x}xy\cdot 2(x+y)\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{x}(2{x}^{2}y+2x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}x{y}^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=x}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{4}+\frac{2}{3}{x}^{4})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{5}{3}{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the covariance and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-(\frac{3}{4})(\frac{5}{12}) \\  & =\frac{1}{48}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & ≈\frac{(\frac{1}{48})}{(0.1936)\cdot (0.2444)} \\  & ≈0.44,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

:question/problem:
Let $X$ be a random variable with the probability density function shown below. What is the mode of $X?$

![](images/a3/a3de8797a3b489ada861edbebb5de935dc5c840dafc509bf2b41ad093d7cc2b4.svg)
:question/worked-solution:
The mode of a random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ is the value of $x$ at the global maximum of $f(x).$

To find the global maximum of $f(x),$ we find the critical points of $f(x)$ and then apply the candidates test.

First, we find the critical points.

- The piece of $f(x)$ defined on $0 \leq x\leq \pi$ is $f(x) = \dfrac{\sin x}{2}.$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and solving $f'(x) = 0,$ we get

$$
\dfrac{\cos x}{2} = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad x= \dfrac{\pi}{2}+k\pi ,
$$

where $k$ is any integer.
Among these critical points, only $x= \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ lies within the interval $\left[0, \pi \right].$

- The derivative doesn't exist at the endpoints $x = 0, \pi.$ So, these are critical points as well.

Now, we evaluate $f(x)$ at the critical points $x=0,\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \pi{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0) & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡0=0 \\ f(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=\frac{1}{2} \\ f(\pi ) & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compare all of the values above. The largest value is

$$
f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the mode of $X$ is $\dfrac{\pi}{2}.$

- Then, we differentiate $F_Y$ to get the probability density function $f_Y.$

Before we start, note that $Y = 1-3X$ is a strictly decreasing function of $X.$  Moreover, for $0 < x < 1,$ we have $-2 \lt y \lt 1 .$

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $-2 \lt y \lt 1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P(1-3X\le y) \\  & =P(-3X\le y-1) \\  & =P(X\ge \frac{1-y}{3}) \\  & =1-{F}_{X}(\frac{1-y}{3})\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {f}_{X}(\frac{1-y}{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot 2\cdot (\frac{1-y}{3}) \\  & =\frac{2}{9}(1-y).\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function
![](images/6e/6efcc38c3e389b9f858b71d089077924d9780b4b3daf771c4682e88098393977.svg)
where $c$ is a positive real number. Find the value of $c.$
:question/worked-solution:
To verify that $f(x,y)$ is a valid joint probability density function, we must check the following conditions:

- $f(x,y) \geq 0$ for all $(x,y)\in \mathbb R^2$

- $\displaystyle \iint_{\mathbb R^2} f(x,y) \;\textrm{d}x\textrm{d}y= 1$

First, let's sketch the region $D = \left\{(x,y) \::\:  0\lt x\lt \dfrac{\pi}{2},0\lt y \lt \dfrac{\pi}{2} \right\}.$

![](images/cc/ccb7cc52f8404dcca5d555d4fd81e6ae03e9689ccdd7c462fccbc2dc611db235.png)

Now, let's check our conditions:

- Since $c > 0,$ we clearly have $f(x,y) \geq 0$ for all $(x,y)\in \mathbb R^2.$ So the first condition is satisfied.

- For the second condition to be satisfied, we must have 

$$
\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\int_{0}^{\pi/2}c\sin (x+y) \;\textrm{d}y\,\textrm{d}x= 1.
$$

We evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating  $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}c\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x & =c{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & =c{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)]_{y=0}^{y=\pi /2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =c{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+\frac{\pi }{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =c{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+\frac{\pi }{2})\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}c{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+\frac{\pi }{2})\,\text{d}x & =c{[\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+\frac{\pi }{2})]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =c[(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )-(\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))] \\  & =c[(1-0)-(0-1)] \\  & =c[1-(-1)] \\  & =2c\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
2c=1 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad c=\dfrac{1}{2}.
$$

:question/problem:
The salaries of a company's employees range from $\[math]30\,000$ to $\[/math]90\,000$ dollars. A company director wishes to carry out a hypothesis test with the following null and alternative hypotheses:

- $H_0:\:$ The salaries are distributed uniformly.
- $H_1:\:$ The salaries are not distributed uniformly.

A random sample of employees is taken, and the frequency distribution of their salaries is shown below. Calculate the expected frequency $E_i$ for each salary category.

| Salary (thousands of $\[math]$) | $30\leq s_i < 42$ | $42\leq s_i < 60$ | $60\leq s_i < 80$ | $80\leq s_i \leq 90$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Observed Frequency $(O_i)$ | $12$ | $10$ | $6$ | $2$ |
| Expected Frequency $(E_i)$ |  |  |  |  |
:question/worked-solution:
Let $X$ be the salary of a randomly selected employee (in thousands of dollars). Under the null hypothesis, we have that $X\sim U[30,90]$. Therefore,

$$
P(a\leq X\lt b)= \dfrac{b-a}{90-30} = \dfrac{b-a}{60}
$$

where $a \lt b$ and $a,b\in [30,90]$.

The sample size is

$$
N = 12+10+6+2 = 30
$$

Therefore, the expected frequencies for each class of observations are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E_{1} &= N \cdot P(30 \le X < 42) \\
&= 30 \cdot (\frac{42 - 30}{60}) \\
&= 6 \\
E_{2} &= N \cdot P(42 \le X < 60) \\
&= 30 \cdot (\frac{60 - 42}{60}) \\
&= 9 \\
E_{3} &= N \cdot P(60 \le X < 80) \\
&= 30 \cdot (\frac{80 - 60}{60}) \\
&= 10 \\
E_{4} &= N \cdot P(80 \le X \le 90) \\
&= 30 \cdot (\frac{90 - 80}{60}) \\
&= 5
\end{aligned}
$$

A table summarizing the observed and corresponding expected frequencies is given below:

| Salary (thousands of $\[math]$) | $30\leq s_i < 42$ | $42\leq s_i < 60$ | $60\leq s_i < 80$ | $80\leq s_i \leq 90$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Observed Frequency $(O_i)$ | $12$ | $10$ | $6$ | $2$ |
| Expected Frequency $(E_i)$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}6}$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}9}$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}10}$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}5}$ |

The salaries of a company's employees range from $\[math]30\,000$ to $\[/math]90\,000$ dollars. A random sample of employees is taken, and the frequency distribution of their salaries is shown below.

| Salary (thousands of $\[math]$) | $30\leq y_i \lt 40$ | $40\leq y_i \lt 60$ | $60\leq y_i \lt 80$ | $80\leq y_i \leq 90$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Observed Frequency $(O_i)$ | $\,27\,$ | $\,49\,$ | $\,27\,$ | $\,17\,$ |

Conduct a chi-squre goodness -of-fit test at the $5\%$ significance level with the following null and alternative hypotheses:

- $H_0:\:$ The salaries are distributed uniformly.
- $H_1:\:$ The salaries are not distributed uniformly.

The table below gives the values of $w$ that satisfy $P(W\geq w) = p$, where $W\sim \chi^2(\nu)$.

| $\nu \setminus p$ | $0.010$ | $0.050$ | $0.100$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $2$ | $\,9.210\,$ | $\,5.991\,$ | $\,4.605\,$ |
| $3$ | $\,11.345\,$ | $\,7.815\,$ | $\,6.251\,$ |
| $4$ | $\,13.277\,$ | $\,9.488\,$ | $\,7.779\,$ |
| $5$ | $\,15.086\,$ | $\,11.070\,$ | $\,9.236\,$ |
:question/worked-solution:
Suppose we have a set of observed frequencies $O_i$ and corresponding expected frequencies $E_i$, as defined by a theoretical model under the null hypothesis. Then, the random variable

$$
X = \sum_{i} \frac{(O_i - E_i)^2}{E_i}
$$

approximately follows a chi-square distribution with $\nu$ degrees of freedom, where

- $O_i$ is the observed frequency for category $i$, and
- $E_i$ is the expected frequency for category $i$, as predicted under the null hypothesis.

This approximation holds when all expected frequencies $E_i$ are sufficiently large (typically

$$
E_i \geq 5
$$

for each category), and the observations are independent.

Let $Y$ be the salary of a randomly selected employee (in thousands of dollars). Under the null hypothesis, we have that $Y\sim U[30,90]$. Therefore,

$$
P(a\leq Y\lt b)= \dfrac{b-a}{90-30} = \dfrac{b-a}{60}
$$

where $a \lt b$ and $a,b\in [30,90]$.

The sample size is

$$
N = 27+49+27+17 = 120
$$

Therefore, the expected frequencies for each class of observation are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E_{1} &= N \cdot P(30 \le Y < 40) \\
&= 120 \cdot (\frac{40 - 30}{60}) \\
&= 20 \\
E_{2} &= N \cdot P(40 \le Y < 60) \\
&= 120 \cdot (\frac{60 - 40}{60}) \\
&= 40 \\
E_{3} &= N \cdot P(60 \le Y < 80) \\
&= 120 \cdot (\frac{80 - 60}{60}) \\
&= 40 \\
E_{4} &= N \cdot P(80 \le Y \le 90) \\
&= 120 \cdot (\frac{90 - 80}{60}) \\
&= 20
\end{aligned}
$$

A table summarizing the observed and corresponding expected frequencies is given below:

| Salary (thousands of $\[math]$) | $30\leq y_i \lt 40$ | $40\leq y_i \lt 60$ | $60\leq y_i \lt 80$ | $80\leq y_i \leq 90$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $O_i$ | $\,27\,$ | $\,49\,$ | $\,27\,$ | $\,17\,$ |
| $E_i$ | $\,20\,$ | $\,40\,$ | $\,40\,$ | $\,20\,$ |
| $\dfrac{(O_i-E_i)^2}{E_i}$ | $\,2.45\,$ | $\,2.025\,$ | $\,4.225\,$ | $\,0.45\,$ |

We compute our test statistic by summing the last row:

$$
\begin{aligned}
∑_(i)((O_{i} - E_{i})^{2})/(E_{i}) &= 2.45 + 2.025 + 4.225 + 0.45 \\
&= 9.15
\end{aligned}
$$

There is only one constraint on our data: the total number of observations must equal $N$. Therefore, the number of degrees of freedom $\nu$ is calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
ν &= number of categories - number of constraints \\
&= 4 - 1 \\
&= 3
\end{aligned}
$$

So, there are

$$
\nu = \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}3}
$$

degrees of freedom.

From the given chi-square table, the critical value for $\nu=3$ at a $5\%$ significance level is

$$
\chi^2_{\textrm{critical}}=7.815
$$

and the critical region is

$$
X\geq 7.815
$$

as shown below.

![](images/62/62ad82a0764f10c5ace9ae36e49c87c10121238f9b94db6062b6b6541352c128.png)

Our test statistic $(9.15)$ lies in the critical region. Therefore, there is $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{sufficient}}$ evidence to reject the null hypothesis.

:question/problem:
Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}4{e}^{-4x},\, & x>0 \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

If $Y=2X,$ then what is the probability density function of $Y?$
:question/worked-solution:
To compute the probability density function of a random variable $Y,$ where $Y=u(X)$ is a continuous, strictly monotonic function of a continuous random variable $X,$ we follow two steps:

- First, we find an expression for ${F}_{Y}$ terms of ${F}_{X},$ where ${F}_{Y}$ and ${F}_{X}$ are the cumulative distribution functions of $Y$ and $X,$ respectively.

- Then, we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ to get the probability density function ${f}_{Y}.$

Before we start, note that $Y=2X$ is a strictly increasing function of $X.$ Moreover, for $x>0,$ we have $y>0.$

![](images/8b/8b2d1487d180db1df306cd8c83088ef0334d29769bd7ef94eed7f75d4e6cedf7.png)

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $y>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P(2X\le y) \\  & =P(X\le \frac{y}{2}) \\  & ={F}_{X}(\frac{y}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the PDF ${f}_{Y}(y)$ for $y>0,$ we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(\frac{y}{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {f}_{X}(\frac{y}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of ${f}_{X},$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {f}_{X}(\frac{y}{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4{e}^{-4\cdot y/2} \\  & =2{e}^{-2y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =\{\begin{aligned}2{e}^{-2y}, & \,y>0 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
You're given that if $X∼Bernoulli(p)$, the moment-generating function (MGF) of $X$ is
$M_{X}(t) = 1 - p + pe^{t}, t ∈ R$.

Let $Y = 2X - 4$, where $X∼Bernoulli(\frac{1}{4})$. What is the MGF of $Y$ for $t ∈ R$?

The probability distribution of the random variable $X$ is given below. Given that $\text{E}[X]=7,$ calculate $\text{Var}[5X].$ 

| $x$ | $5$ | $6$ | $9$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $\frac{1}{5}$ | $\frac{2}{5}$ | $\frac{2}{5}$ |
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that for any random variable $X$ and constant $a,$ we have

$$
\text{Var}[aX]={a}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X].
$$

In our case, $a=5.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[5X] & ={5}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =25\cdot \text{Var}[X].\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the variance of $X$ using the following formula:

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}
$$

Additionally, we're given that $\text{E}[X]=7.$ 

We start by computing $\text{E}[{X}^{2}].$ Summing up the products of each value of ${X}^{2}$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={5}^{2}\cdot f(5)+{6}^{2}\cdot f(6)+{9}^{2}\cdot f(9) \\  & =25(\frac{1}{5})+36(\frac{2}{5})+81(\frac{2}{5}) \\  & =\frac{259}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{259}{5}-{7}^{2} \\  & =\frac{259}{5}-49 \\  & =\frac{14}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[5X] & =25\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =25\cdot \frac{14}{5} \\  & =14\cdot 5 \\  & =70.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}c{x}^{2}y,\, & {x}^{2}\le y<1, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

 
where $c$ is a positive real number. Find the value of $c.$
:question/worked-solution:
To verify that $f(x,y)$ is a valid joint probability density function, we must check the following conditions:

- $f(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}$

- ${∬}_{{R}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y=1$

First, let's sketch the region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}\le y<1\}.$

![](images/b9/b9cfac7f0f82088900ab5e603588a73d4932f08f592321c797a1fd94b8bafb4e.png)

Now, let's check our conditions:

- Since $c>0,$ we clearly have $f(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}.$ So the first condition is satisfied.

- For the second condition to be satisfied, we must have 

$$
{∬}_{{R}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}c{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x=1.
$$

We evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating  $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}c{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{[c{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y={x}^{2}}^{y=1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}c{x}^{2}(\frac{1-{x}^{4}}{2})\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}c{x}^{2}(\frac{1-{x}^{4}}{2})\,\text{d}x & ={[c(\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}-\frac{{x}^{7}}{14})]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{4c}{21}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\frac{4c}{21}=1\,⇒\,c=\frac{21}{4}.
$$

:question/problem:
Find $\text{E}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(X+Y)],$ given that random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{8}{{\pi }^{2}},\, & 0\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le y\le x, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are continuous random variables, and $f(x,y)$ is their joint probability density function. If $r:{R}^{2}\to R$ is a function of two variables, then the rule of the lazy statistician states that

$$
\text{E}[r(X,Y)]={∬}_{{R}^{2}}r(x,y)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
r(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y).
$$

Now, let's sketch the region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le y\le x\},$ where $f(x)$ is nonzero.

![](images/a4/a4f7e4e3f5e6a46fdc1b61a40986aec7b47fe75b37c8f042497aa0f3a0969f30.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(X+Y)] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{D}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\cdot \frac{8}{{\pi }^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{8}{{\pi }^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{8}{{\pi }^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)]_{y=0}^{y=x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{8}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)]\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{8}{{\pi }^{2}}{[\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)]}_{x=0}^{x=\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{8}{{\pi }^{2}}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )]-0 \\  & =\frac{8}{{\pi }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ 4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ -5\end{bmatrix},\,W=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

 

Consider the matrices $A$ and $W,$ and the vector $b$ shown above. If the general solution for the weighted least-squares problem $W\,Ax=Wb$ is 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}b \\ c\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of  $9a+\frac{b}{c}?$
:question/worked-solution:
To get the normal equation corresponding to $W\,Ax=Wb,$ we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by $(W\,A)^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(W\,A)^{T}\cdot W\,Ax & =(W\,A)^{T}\cdot Wb \\ {A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)Ax & ={A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)b\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since

$$
{W}^{T}W=\begin{bmatrix}{1}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {1}^{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

our normal equation can be written, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 4 & -2 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ 4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 4 & -2 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ -5\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-2 & 4 & -2 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ 16 & -8 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 4 & -2 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 4 \\ -5\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}72 & -36 \\ -36 & 18\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}20 \\ -10\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}72 & -36 & 20 \\ -36 & 18 & -10\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}72 & -36 & 20 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{5}{18}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{18}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{18} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
9a+\frac{b}{c}=9\cdot \frac{5}{18}+\frac{(\frac{1}{2})}{1}=3.
$$

:question/problem:
| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ | $Y=6$ |

| $X=1$ | $\frac{1}{18}$ | $\frac{5}{18}$ | $\frac{1}{9}$ | $\frac{2}{9}$ |
