:question/problem:
$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -4 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix},\,J=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},\,P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & a \\ 1 & b\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the matrices above. Given that $A=PJ{P}^{-1}$ is a Jordan canonical decomposition of $A,$ find the value of $a-2b.$
:question/worked-solution:
From the Jordan matrix $J,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=1.
$$

As a result, we obtain that 

- the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ of the eigenvalue $\lambda =1,$

- the second column of $P$ corresponds to the vector ${v}_{2}$ such that $(A-I){v}_{2}={v}_{1}.$

Now, computing $A-I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -4 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -4 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the matrix equation $(A-I){v}_{2}={v}_{1}$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -4 & 2 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{1}{2}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & -4 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=1+2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1+2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get  

$$
{v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, $a-2b=3-2\cdot 1=1.$

:question/problem: Consider the arc of the curve $y=\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3/2}$ that lies between the lines $x=0$ and $x=3.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis.
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3/2})={x}^{1/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}=x.
$$

Then, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}x\sqrt{1+x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=1+x.$ Then, $\text{d}x=\text{d}u.$

We also need to compute new limits:

| **$x$** | $0$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $4$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}x\sqrt{1+x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{4}(u-1)\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{4}({u}^{3/2}-{u}^{1/2})\text{d}u \\  & =2\pi {[\frac{2{u}^{5/2}}{5}-\frac{2{u}^{3/2}}{3}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =2\pi [\frac{2(4)^{5/2}}{5}-\frac{2(4)^{3/2}}{3}-(\frac{2(1)^{5/2}}{5}-\frac{2(1)^{3/2}}{3})] \\  & =2\pi (\frac{64}{5}-\frac{16}{3}-\frac{2}{5}+\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =2\pi (\frac{116}{15}) \\  & =\frac{232\pi }{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/58/5806f57e41eeb5548b0c041533adf3952dd7f35236121f9056c57f03c2854ddc.png)

Consider the arc of the curve $y=\sqrt{1-x}$ that lies in the first quadrant between $x=0$ and its $x$-intercept. What integral gives the area of the surface generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $x$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1-x} & =0 \\ 1-x & =0 \\ x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=1.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{1-x})=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1-x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}x\sqrt{1+{(-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1-x}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}x\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4(1-x)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}x\sqrt{\frac{5-4x}{4(1-x)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}x\sqrt{\frac{4x-5}{x-1}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the surface area of the part of the plane $z=2x+3y$ that is bounded by the constraints $0\le x\le 1$ and $1\le y\le 3.$
:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=2x+3y,\,0\le x\le 1,\,1\le y\le 3.
$$

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+3y)=2, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+3y)=3,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(2)^{2}+(3)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4+9}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{14}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{14}{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{14}\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =\sqrt{14}\cdot (1-0)\cdot (3-1) \\  & =2\sqrt{14}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Consider the portion of the paraboloid $z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ whose projection onto the $xy$-plane is bounded by the lines $y=x,$ $x=1,$ and the $x$-axis. Find a repeated integral expression for the surface area of this surface.
:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2},\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le x\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/0b/0b6de7829e702377d1b20bb1b297d3d28e6fb8bae9672b0137d92b4d53a96c83.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(2x)^{2}+(2y)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the surface area of the part of the surface $z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ that is subject to the constraint ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1.$
:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2},\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/f0/f0faa92e0f89c86248abffad7f61cac5d94a3848a7f7be4464c4b28d3915aa32.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(2x)^{2}+(2y)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region $D$ can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{1}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=1+4{r}^{2},$ we get $\text{d}u=8r\,\text{d}r.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & 0 & 1 \\ u & 1 & 5\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r & =2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{8}{\int }_{1}^{5}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{5}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{5} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{5} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}[{5}^{3/2}-1] \\  & =\frac{\pi (5\sqrt{5}-1)}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate $lim_(x → ∞)(\frac{x + 3}{x + 2})^{4x + 8}$.
Express $\frac{9}{4}$ as a base raised to a negative exponent.
:question/worked-solution:
First, we write $\frac{9}{4}$ as a base raised to a power:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{4} & =\frac{3\times 3}{2\times 2} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\times \frac{3}{2} \\  & ={(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the reciprocal of the base $(\frac{3}{2}),$ and then raise that reciprocal to the same power but with the *opposite* sign $(-2),$ as follows:

$$
{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}={(\frac{2}{3})}^{-2}
$$

:question/problem:
Find the radius of convergence $R$ and interval of convergence $I$ for the series

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(x-1)^{2n-1}}{2n-1}\,.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
To apply the ratio test, we define ${a}_{n}=\frac{(x-1)^{2n-1}}{2n-1}.$ Then, we calculate the ratio of two successive terms and take the limit as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{(x-1)^{2(n+1)-1}}{2(n+1)-1}\cdot \frac{2n-1}{(x-1)^{2n-1}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{(x-1)^{2n+1}}{2n+1}\cdot \frac{2n-1}{(x-1)^{2n-1}}| \\  & =|x-1{|}^{2}{lim}_{n\to \infty }(\frac{2n-1}{2n+1}) \\  & =|x-1{|}^{2}{lim}_{n\to \infty }(\frac{(2-\frac{1}{n})}{(2+\frac{1}{n})}) \\  & =|x-1{|}^{2}\cdot \frac{2}{2} \\  & =|x-1{|}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

The series converges if $L<1.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}|x-1{|}^{2} & <1 \\ |x-1| & <1 \\ -1<x-1 & <1 \\ 0<x & <2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the radius of convergence is $R=1,$ and the series converges for any $x$ that lies in the open interval $(0,2).$

The ratio test gives no conclusion about the convergence of the series when $L=1.$ So, when $|x-1|=1,$ we do not know if the series converges. This means that the endpoints $x=0$ and $x=2$ need to be investigated separately using another test for convergence.

- When $x=0$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(x-1)^{2n-1}}{2n-1} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{((0)-1)^{2n-1}}{2n-1} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{2n-1}}{2n-1} \\  & =-1-\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{5}-⋯ \\  & =-(1+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{5}+⋯)\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing the above series in parentheses with ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{n},$ we see that the series is divergent by the limit comparison test.

- When $x=2$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(x-1)^{2n-1}}{2n-1} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{((2)-1)^{2n-1}}{2n-1} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(1)^{2n-1}}{2n-1} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2n-1} \\  & =1+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{5}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing the above series with ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{n},$ we see that the series is divergent by the limit comparison test.

So the interval of convergence is $I=(0,2).$

:question/problem:
Suppose ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{16}$ is an I.I.D random sample with ${X}_{i}∼Po(\theta )$ and unknown rate parameter $\theta .$ For a particular sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{16},$ you're given that 

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{16}{x}_{i}=18,\,{\prod }_{i=1}^{16}({x}_{i})!=6.
$$

Find the likelihood function of the sample.

*Hint: The probability mass function for a Poisson distribution is given by* 

$$
f(x)=\frac{{\theta }^{x}{e}^{-\theta }}{x!},\,x=0,1,2,…
$$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
L(\theta )={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\theta ).
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=16$ independent Poisson random variables with unknown parameter $\theta ,$ for which the probability mass function is

$$
f(x;\theta )=\frac{{\theta }^{x}{e}^{-\theta }}{x!},\,x=0,1,2,…\,.
$$

We can calculate the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\theta ) \\  & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}\frac{{\theta }^{{x}_{i}}{e}^{-\theta }}{{x}_{i}!} \\  & =(\frac{{\theta }^{{x}_{1}}{e}^{-\theta }}{{x}_{1}!})\cdot (\frac{{\theta }^{{x}_{2}}{e}^{-\theta }}{{x}_{2}!})⋯(\frac{{\theta }^{{x}_{n}}{e}^{-\theta }}{{x}_{n}!}) \\  & ={\theta }^{\sum {x}_{i}}\cdot {e}^{-\sum \theta }\cdot {\prod }_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{({x}_{i})!} \\  & ={\theta }^{\sum {x}_{i}}\cdot {e}^{-n\theta }\cdot \frac{1}{{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i})!} \\  & =\frac{1}{C}\,{\theta }^{S}\,{e}^{-n\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

where $C={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i})!$ is a constant and $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}.$

We are told that $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}=18,$ $C={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i})!=6,$ and $n=16.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & =\frac{1}{6}\,{\theta }^{18}\,{e}^{-16\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the surface area of the part of the paraboloid $x=5+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}$ that is subject to the constraint ${y}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 3.$
:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $x=f(y,z)$ with $(y,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
x=5+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2},\,(y,z)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 3},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/66/66b05919a7644818eea7265ff3ae8fc3ced4ac7d1d6d30352f612649393c876a.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(5+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})=2y, \\ \frac{∂x}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(5+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})=2z,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(2y)^{2}+(2z)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4({y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region $D$ can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le \sqrt{3},\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4({y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=1+4{r}^{2},$ we get $\text{d}u=8r\,\text{d}r.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & 0 & \sqrt{3} \\ u & 1 & 13\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r & =2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{8}{\int }_{1}^{13}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{13}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{13} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{13} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}[(13)^{3/2}-1] \\  & =\frac{\pi (13\sqrt{13}-1)}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=3-3{t}^{2},$ where $t⩾0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=2\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=2\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time whan the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
:question/worked-solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 3-3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ 3(1-t)(1+t) & =0 \\ t & =\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t⩾0$, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t=1\,\text{s}.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}(t) & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3-3{t}^{2}) \\  & =-6t \\ {v}^{″}(1) & =-6(1) \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(1)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=1\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (3-3{t}^{2})\text{d}t \\  & =3t-{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(2)=2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3(2)-{2}^{3}+C & =2 \\ 6-8+C & =2\,⟹\,C=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=4+3t-{t}^{3}.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(1)=4+3(1)-{1}^{3}=6\,\text{m}/\text{s}
$$

We recognize that the series looks similar to the Maclaurin expansion for $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =x-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}+\frac{{x}^{5}}{5!}-⋯+\frac{(-1)^{n}{x}^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$ into our Maclaurin expansion gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\frac{\pi }{4}-\frac{(\pi /4)^{3}}{3!}+\frac{(\pi /4)^{5}}{5!}-\frac{(\pi /4)^{7}}{7!}+⋯+\frac{(-1)^{n}(\pi /4)^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!}+⋯ \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & =\frac{\pi }{4}-\frac{(\pi /4)^{3}}{3!}+\frac{(\pi /4)^{5}}{5!}-\frac{(\pi /4)^{7}}{7!}+⋯+\frac{(-1)^{n}(\pi /4)^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the sum of the series is $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.$

:question/problem:
A particle $P$ is traveling along the $x$-axis with displacement $s(t)$ from a fixed origin $O$ given by

$$
s(t)={t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(t),\,t\ge 0.
$$

Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and find the value of the velocity at this moment.
:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)) \\  & =2t\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+t\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+2t\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+3\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we put $a=0$ to find the time when the acceleration is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+3 \\ 2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t) & =-3 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(t) & =-\frac{3}{2} \\ t & ={e}^{-3/2}\end{aligned}
$$

So the acceleration is zero when $t={e}^{-3/2}.$ To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into $v(t)$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}v({e}^{-3/2}) & =2({e}^{-3/2})\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-3/2})+{e}^{-3/2} \\  & =2{e}^{-3/2}(-\frac{3}{2})+{e}^{-3/2} \\  & =-2{e}^{-3/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Solve the inequality $\dfrac{3x-2k}{5} \ge -1$ for the variable $x$.
:question/worked-solution:
We solve the inequality using the addition and multiplication principles, treating $k$ like any other number.

First, we multiply both sides of the inequality by $5$ to eliminate the fraction:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3x - 2k}{5} & \ge - 1 \\ 5 \cdot (\frac{3x - 2k}{5}) & \ge 5 \cdot (-1) \\ 3x - 2k & \ge - 5\end{bmatrix}
$$

Now, we apply the addition principle, adding $2k$ to both sides of the inequality:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}3x - 2k & \ge - 5 \\ 3x - 2k + 2k & \ge - 5 + 2k \\ 3x & \ge - 5 + 2k \\ 3x & \ge 2k - 5\end{bmatrix}
$$

Finally, we apply the multiplication principle, dividing both sides of the inequality by $3{:}$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}3x & \ge 2k - 5 \\ \frac{3x}{3} & \ge \frac{2k - 5}{3} \\ x & \ge \frac{2k - 5}{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $k< 0$, solve the inequality $\dfrac{kx +3}3 \geq 2k$ for the variable $x$.
:question/worked-solution:
We solve the inequality using the addition and multiplication principles, treating $k$ like any other number.

First, we multiply both sides of the inequality by $3$ to eliminate the fraction:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{kx + 3}{3} & \ge 2k \\ 3 \cdot (\frac{kx + 3}{3}) & \ge 3 \cdot 2k \\ kx + 3 & \ge 6k\end{bmatrix}
$$

Now, we apply the addition principle, subtracting $3$ from both sides of the inequality:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}kx + 3 & \ge 6k \\ kx & \ge 6k - 3\end{bmatrix}
$$

Then, we divide by $k$. Since $k < 0$, we need to flip the inequality:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}kx & \ge 6k - 3 \\ \frac{kx}{k} & \le \frac{6k - 3}{k} \\ x & \le \frac{6k - 3}{k}\end{bmatrix}
$$

:question/problem:
Which of the following is the graph of the function $y = \dfrac{5}{x^2+4x-5}$?

*(Note: Figures not drawn to scale)*

![](images/a0/a0936b30d28e001a20d8a7ef1415cd75a4893f8579437f4e188a0b1c51a638eb.png)
:question/worked-solution:
First, we denote

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{5}{x^2+4x-5}
$$

To determine the correct graph, we follow four steps:

- **Step 1:** We find the $y$-intercept. To do this, we evaluate $f(0)$:
$f(x)|= \frac{5}{x^{2} + 4x - 5}; f(0)|= (5)/((0)^{2} + 4(0) - 5); f(0)|= \frac{5}{-5}; f(0)|=-1$
So, the $y$-intercept is $(0,-1)$.
- **Step 2:** We find the $x$-intercepts. To do this, we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for $x$.In this case, the numerator is a constant, and so there are no $x$-intercepts.
- **Step 3:** We find the vertical asymptotes. To do this, we need to set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x$:
$x^{2} + 4x - 5|= 0; (x + 5)(x - 1)|= 0$
Therefore, the vertical asymptotes are $x=-5$ and $x=1$.
- **Step 4:** We find the horizontal asymptotes. To do this, we divide numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, which is $x^2$ in this case:
$f(x)|= \frac{5}{x^{2} + 4x - 5}; = ((\frac{5}{x^{2}}))/((1 + \frac{4}{x} - \frac{5}{x^{2}}))$
Now, as $\mid x \mid$ gets very large, $\dfrac{5}{x^2}$ and $\dfrac{4}{x}$ become very small. Therefore, as $\mid x \mid \to\infty$, we have
$f(x) \mid \approx \frac{0}{1 + 0 - 0} = 0$.
So, the horizontal asymptote is $y = 0$.

Finally, among the options given, only graph I satisfies the above conditions:

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y) = e^{x+y}$ along the line segment from $(0,3)$ to $(2,3).$
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_{t_a}^{t_b}  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(0,3)$ to $(2,3).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $\mathbf{a}=3\,\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{b}=2\,\mathbf{i}+3\,\mathbf{j}.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =3\,j+t[(2\,i+3\,j)-3\,j] \\  & =3\,j+t(2\,i) \\  & =2t\,i+3\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0 \le t \le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=2t$ and $y=3$ along the segment.

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3)j \\  & =2\,i \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = e^{x+y},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & ={e}^{2t+3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{e}^{x+y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{2t+3}\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{2t+3}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=2t+3,$ $\textrm d u=2\,\textrm d t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{2t+3}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{3}^{5}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={e}^{u}\,{|}_{3}^{5} \\  & ={e}^{5}-{e}^{3} \\  & ={e}^{3}({e}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find, as a definite integral, an expression for the line integral of the function $f(x,y) = 2x+y^2$ along the quarter-circle $x^2+y^2=4,$ traversed from the point $(0,2)$ to the point $(-2,0)$ in the second quadrant.
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a quarter-circle of radius $2$ centered at $O,$ shown below. 

![](images/d0/d0ae53dd5d0932cbf834a166e851c227f75cb546b591a9fd43930ec06f0e9ddf.png)

The curve $C$ can be parametrized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \big\langle 2\cos{t}, \: 2\sin{t} \big\rangle, \qquad \dfrac{\pi}{2} \le t \le \pi.
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = 2x+y^2,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =4(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(2x+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }4(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: The half-life of bismuth-210 is $5.012$ days. How long does it take for a $1\,280\,\textrm g$ sample of bismuth-210 to reduce to $5\,\textrm g?$
:question/worked-solution:
The mass $M(t)$ of a radioactive substance at time $t$ can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
M'(t) = -kM(t), \qquad M(0) = M_0.
$$

The general solution to this equation is

$$
M(t) = M_0e^{-kt}.
$$

The half-life $t_{1/2}$ is the time taken for the mass of the substance to reduce by one half and is given by

$$
t_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{k}.
$$

There are two methods that we can use to solve this problem. We describe each of them below.

**Method 1**

Since we know that $t_{1/2} = 5.012$ days we have

$$
5.012 = \dfrac{\ln 2}{k}\quad\Rightarrow\quad k = \dfrac{\ln 2}{5.012}
$$

Also, since $M_0 = 1\,280\,\textrm g,$ we have the particular solution

$$
M(t) = 1\,280 e^{-t\ln 2/5.012}.
$$

We wish to calculate the time $t$ such that $M(t) = 5\,\textrm g.$ So, we set up our equation as follows:

$$
5 = 1\,280 e^{-t\ln 2/5.012}
$$

Solving this equation for $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5 & =1\,280{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/5.012} \\ \frac{5}{1\,280} & ={e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/5.012} \\ \frac{1}{256} & ={e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/5.012} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{256}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/5.012}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡256 & =-\frac{t\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{5.012} \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡256 & =-\frac{t\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{5.012} \\ t & =\frac{5.012\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡256}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ t & ≈40.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that it takes approximately $40$ days for the mass of the substance to reduce to $5\,\textrm g.$

**Method 2**

We wish to calculate the time $t$ such that $M(t) = 5\,\textrm g.$ Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{M(t)}{M(0)} & =\frac{5\,\text{g}}{1\,280\,\text{g}} \\  & =\frac{1}{256} \\  & ={(\frac{1}{2})}^{8},\end{aligned}
$$

or equivalently

$$
M(t) =  \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^8\cdot M(0).
$$

From this equation, we see that $8$ half-lives must have occurred for the mass to reduce from $1\,280\,\textrm g$ to $5\,\textrm g.$ Hence,

$$
t = 8\cdot t_{1/2} =8 \cdot 5.012 \approx 40.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that it takes approximately $40$ days for the mass of the substance to reduce to $5\,\textrm g.$

:question/problem: Find the real solution to the equation $96x^5=3.$
:question/worked-solution:
We can solve this equation by isolating the $x^5$ term and then taking the $5$th root of each side.

First, let's isolate the $x^5$ term on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}96{x}^{5} & =3 \\ {x}^{5} & =\frac{1}{32}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we take the $5$th root of each side and solve for $x.$ Since $n=5$ is odd, there is only one real solution to this equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{5} & =\frac{1}{32} \\ \sqrt[5]{{x}^{5}} & =\sqrt[5]{\frac{1}{32}} \\ x & =\sqrt[5]{{(\frac{1}{2})}^{5}} \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=\dfrac12.$

:question/problem: Find the expression for the general term $a_n$ for $n\geq 0$ of the sequence with the generating function $\dfrac{6}{5-4x}$.
:question/worked-solution:
Let's rewrite the expression and expand it as a geometric series:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{6}{5 - 4x} &= \frac{6}{5} \cdot (1)/(1 - (\frac{4}{5}x)) \\
&= \frac{6}{5}[1 + (\frac{4}{5}x) + (\frac{4}{5}x)^{2} + (\frac{4}{5}x)^{3} + ⋯] \\
&= \frac{6}{5} + \frac{6}{5}(\frac{4}{5})x + \frac{6}{5}(\frac{4}{5})^{2}x^{2} + \frac{6}{5}(\frac{4}{5})^{3}x^{3} + ⋯
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general term $a_n$ of our sequence is

$$
a_n = \dfrac{6}{5}\left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)^n
$$

:question/problem: Given that $\mathbf F(x,y) = \left\langle \dfrac 1x, xy \right \rangle$ and $f(x,y) = \dfrac 1{x},$ calculate $\nabla \cdot (f\,\mathbf F).$
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the following identity:

$$
\nabla \cdot (f\,\mathbf F) = f\, \nabla \cdot \mathbf {F}+  \mathbf F \cdot \nabla f
$$

First, we compute $\nabla \cdot \mathbf {F}$ and $\nabla f.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}},0⟩, \\ ∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{x})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy)=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}+x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot (f\,F) & =f\,∇\cdot F+F\cdot ∇f \\  & =\frac{1}{x}(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}+x)+⟨\frac{1}{x},xy⟩\cdot ⟨-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}},0⟩ \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}+1-\frac{1}{{x}^{3}} \\  & =1-\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Monica pays $\[math]3\,500$ into an investment account at the beginning of every year. She earns an annual interest of $2\%$, paid at the end of the year. To the nearest dollar, how much money will be in her investment account by the end of the $9$th year?
:question/worked-solution:
Let $S_n$ be the value of Monica's investment at the end of the $n$th year.

- At the end of the year $1$, Monica's investment will be worth
$S_1 = \[math]3\,500\cdot (1.02)$.
- To calculate the value of the investment at the end of year $2$, we need to add $\[/math]3\,500$ to the balance at the end of year $1$, and then increase the entire amount by $2 \%$. Therefore, at the end of the year $2$, Monica's investment will be worth
$S_{2}|= (S_{1} + \[math]3500) \cdot (1.02); = (\[/math]3500 \cdot (1.02) + \[math]3500) \cdot (1.02); = \[/math]3500 \cdot (1.02)^{2} + \[math]3500 \cdot (1.02)$.
- Similarly, at the end of the year $3$, Monica's investment will be worth
$S_{3}|= (S_{2} + \[/math]3500) \cdot (1.02); = [(\[math]3500 \cdot (1.02)^{2} + \[/math]3500 \cdot (1.02)) + \[math]3500] \cdot (1.02); = \[/math]3500 \cdot (1.02)^{3} + \[math]3500 \cdot (1.02)^{2} + \[/math]3500 \cdot (1.02)$.
- $\quad \vdots$
- Continuing this process, we may deduce that by the end of the year $9$, Monica's investment will be worth
$S_{9}|= \[math]3500 \cdot (1.02)^{9} + \[/math]3500 \cdot (1.02)^{8} + ⋯ + \[math]3500 \cdot (1.02); = \[/math]3500 \cdot (1.02) \cdot [(1.02)^{8} + (1.03)^{7} + ⋯ + 1]$.

Notice that the expression inside the square brackets is a geometric series with $a_1 = 1$, $r = 1.02$, and $N = 9$. Thus, after $9$ years, Monica's investment will be worth

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_{9} &= \[math]3500 \cdot (1.02) \cdot ((a_{1}(1 - r^{N}))/(1 - r)) \\
&= \[/math]3570 \cdot ((1 \cdot (1 - 1.02^{9}))/(1 - 1.02)) \\
&= \[math]3570 \cdot (\frac{1 - 1.02^{9}}{1 - 1.02}) \\
&\approx \[math]34824
\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest dollar.

:question/problem: Harold pays $\[math]2\,500$ into an investment account at the beginning of every year. He earns an annual interest of $4\%$, compounded continuously. To the nearest dollar, how much money will be in his investment account by the end of the $10$th year?
:question/worked-solution:
Let $S_n$ be the value of Harold's investment at the end of the $n$th year.

- The interest rate is $4\%$ per year, compounded continuously. Therefore, at the end of year $1$, Harold's investment will be worth
$S_1 = \[math]2\,500e^{0.04}$
- To calculate the value of the investment at the end of year $2$, we need to add $\[/math]2\,500$ to the balance at the end of year $1$, and then increase the entire amount by $4\%$, compounded continuously. Therefore, at the end of year $2$, Harold's investment will be worth
$S_{2}|= (S_{1} + [math]2500)e^{0.04}; = (\[/math]2500 \cdot e^{0.04} + \[math]2500) \cdot e^{0.04}; = \[/math]2500 \cdot [e^{0.04}]^{2} + \[math]2500 \cdot e^{0.04}$.
- $\quad \vdots$
- Continuing this process, we may deduce that by the end of year $10$, Harold's investment will be worth
$S_{10}|= \[/math]2500 \cdot [e^{0.04}]^{10} + \[math]2500 \cdot [e^{0.04}]^{9} + ⋯ + \[/math]2500 \cdot e^{0.04}; = \[math]2500 \cdot e^{0.04} \cdot {[e^{0.04}]^{9} + [e^{0.03}]^{8} + ⋯ + [e^{0.04}] + 1}$

Notice that the expression inside the curly braces is a geometric series with $a_1=1$, $r=e^{0.04}$, and $N=10$. Thus, after $10$ years, Harold's investment will be worth

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_{10} &= \[/math]2500 \cdot e^{0.04} \cdot ((a_{1}(1 - r^{N}))/(1 - r)) \\
&= \[math]2500 \cdot e^{0.04} \cdot ((1 \cdot (1 - [e^{0.04}]^{10}))/(1 - e^{0.04})) \\
&= \[/math]2500 \cdot e^{0.04} \cdot (\frac{1 - [e^{0.04}]^{10}}{1 - e^{0.04}}) \\
&\approx \[math]31358
\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest dollar.

:question/problem:
![](images/69/69447f99f5d726fb86ec1eb34c7acea36be929a3d109280e1b46730c8837f4a3.png)

Which of the following could be the equation of the graph shown above?

*(Note: Figure not drawn to scale)*

1. $y = \dfrac{x^2-2x}{(x^2-x)(x-2)}$
2. $y = \dfrac{2(x^2-x)}{x^2-1}$
3. $y = \dfrac{x^2-2x}{x^2-x}$
4. $y = \dfrac{x^3-2x^2}{x(x-1)(x-2)}$
:question/worked-solution:
From the graph of the function, we note the following:

- The function has only one vertical asymptote, $x = 1$. Therefore, the function's denominator must be zero at $x=1$, but the numerator should not be zero at this point. This allows us to discard the following option:
$y = \dfrac{2(x^2-x)}{x^2-1}$
- The function has two open circles, at $x = 0$ and $x=2$. This means that $x = 0$ and $x=2$ are holes, and so the numerator and denominator are both zero at $x = 0$ and $x=2$. This allows us to discard the following option:
$y = \dfrac{x^2-2x}{x^2-x}$So, we're left with the following options:
$y = \dfrac{x^3-2x^2}{x(x-1)(x-2)}, \qquad y = \dfrac{x^2-2x}{(x^2-x)(x-2)}$
- The function has a horizontal asymptote at $y = 0$. This means that $y \to 0$ as $\mid x \mid \to \infty$. Note that for large $\mid x \mid$, we have
$(x^{3} - 2x^{2})/(x(x - 1)(x - 2))|= (x^{2}(x - 2))/(x(x - 1)(x - 2)); = \frac{x}{x - 1}; = ((\frac{x}{x}))/((\frac{x}{x} - \frac{1}{x})); = (1)/((1 - \frac{1}{x})); \approx 1$.
So, we can discard the following option:
$y = \dfrac{x^3-2x^2}{x(x-1)(x-2)}$

Therefore, among the given options, the only one that satisfies the above conditions is

$$
y = \dfrac{x^2-2x}{(x^2-x)(x-2)}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/2e/2e4e808d8264685f9b88c5b0052870174d8be3ed2a7195149d45552118186a49.png)

By setting $y = t$ where $t$ is a parameter, find a definite integral with respect to $t$ that is equivalent to the integral $\displaystyle \int \limits_{C} \dfrac{x}{y} \, \textrm ds,$ where $C$ is the arc of the parabola $x = y^2$ traversed between the points $(1,1)$ and $(9 , 3),$ as shown above.
:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $x = x(y).$ Therefore, by setting $y = t,$ we have 

$$
x = x(t) = t^2.
$$

 

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle t^2 , \: t \right\rangle, \qquad 1 \leq t \leq 3
$$

Note that the domain $1 \leq t \leq 3$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the endpoints on the path.

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =2t\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(2t)}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y) = \dfrac{x}{y},$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{{t}^{2}}{t} \\  & =t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{x}{y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{3}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}t\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find, as a definite integral, an expression for the line integral of the function $f(x,y) = x^2-1,$ traversed once along the circle $C$ with equation $x^2 + y^2 = 1.$
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a circle of radius $1$ centered at $O.$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \big\langle \cos{t}, \: \sin{t} \big\rangle, \qquad 0 \le t \lt 2\pi.
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = x^2-1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}-1 \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡t-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({cos}^{2}⁡t-1)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡t-1\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/fd/fda8bfb0533b86dc4050d1b8e309e332996b26263b1052d3e251bf0a5c98e816.png)

Evaluate the line integral $\displaystyle\int_\limits{C}12xy\:\textrm{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is the quarter-ellipse $4x^2+y^2=4$ traversed from the point $(0,2)$ to the point $(-1,0),$ as shown above.
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
x^2 + \dfrac{y^2}{2^2}  = 1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $1$ and $2,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \big\langle \cos{t}, \: 2\sin{t} \big\rangle, \qquad \dfrac{\pi}{2} \le t \le \pi.
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{3{cos}^{2}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{1+3{cos}^{2}⁡t}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = 12xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =12\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t=24\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}12xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }24\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{1+3{cos}^{2}⁡t}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =24{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{1+3{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=1+3\cos^2 {t},$ $\textrm d u=-6\sin t\cos 
 t\,\textrm d t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}24{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{1+3{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t & =-4{\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-4\cdot \frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}{|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =-\frac{8}{3}({4}^{3/2}-{1}^{3/2}) \\  & =-\frac{8}{3}(8-1) \\  & =-\frac{56}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: What expression is equivalent to $\displaystyle \int_\limits{C} \dfrac{x}{y} \: \textrm{d}s,$ where $C$ is the ellipse $x^2 + 16y^2 = 16,$ traversed once in the counterclockwise direction?
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{4^2} + \dfrac{y^2}{1^2} = 1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $4$ and $1,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle 4\cos{t}, \: \sin{t} \right\rangle, \qquad 0 \le t \lt 2\pi.
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{15{sin}^{2}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{15{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = \dfrac{x}{y},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}=4\operatorname{cot}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{x}{y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4\operatorname{cot}⁡t\sqrt{15{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cot}⁡t\sqrt{15{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y) =x^2-2$ along the circle $C$ with equation $x^2 + y^2 = 4.$
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a circle of radius $2$ centered at $O.$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \big\langle 2\cos{t}, \: 2\sin{t} \big\rangle, \qquad 0 \le t \le 2\pi.
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = x^2-2,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}-2 \\  & =4{cos}^{2}⁡t-2 \\  & =2(2{cos}^{2}⁡t-1) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=2t,$ $\textrm d u=2\,\textrm d t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,\text{d}t & =2{\int }_{0}^{4\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡u{|}_{0}^{4\pi } \\  & =2(0-0) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/d0/d0cebdd804ff244d037e14df6ec33efb86b522644f7b4addc688e27fd6a57e95.png)

Evaluate the line integral
$\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} y^3e^{-x} \: \textrm{d}s,$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $x = \ln{y}$ from $(0, 1)$ to $\left(\dfrac32\ln 2 , 2\sqrt{2}\right),$ as shown above.
:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $x = x(y).$ Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have

$$
x = x(t) = \ln{t}.
$$

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle \ln{t}, \: t \right\rangle, \qquad 1 \leq t \leq 2\sqrt{2}
$$

Note that the domain $1 \leq t \leq 2\sqrt{2}$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the endpoints on the path.

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{1}{t}\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{t})}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{t}^{2}+1}{{t}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}}{|t|} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}}{t}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y) = y^3e^{-x},$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & ={t}^{3}{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡t} \\  & ={t}^{3}\cdot \frac{1}{t} \\  & ={t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{y}^{3}{e}^{-x}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{2\sqrt{2}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2\sqrt{2}}{t}^{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}}{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2\sqrt{2}}t\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u = t^2 + 1,$ $\textrm{d}u = 2t \, \textrm{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2\sqrt{2}}t\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{2}^{9}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{3}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}\,{|}_{2}^{9} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\sqrt{{9}^{3}}-\sqrt{{2}^{3}}] \\  & =\frac{27-2\sqrt{2}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find a definite integral that is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y) = x+\sin{y},$ traversed along the line segment from $(1,0)$ to $(1,1).$
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  =  \int\limits_{t_a}^{t_b}  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(1,0)$ to $(1,1).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =i+t[(i+j)-i] \\  & =i+t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0 \le t \le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=1$ and $y=t$ along the segment.

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =0\,i+j \\  & =j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = x+\sin{y}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =1+\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the line integral of the function $f(x,y,z) = x^2+y-z,$ traversed along the line segment from $(0,1,-3)$ to $(-1,2,-2)?$
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}s  =  \int\limits_{t_a}^{t_b}  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(0,1,-3)$ to $(-1,2,-2).$

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{j}-3\mathbf{k}$ and $\mathbf{b}=-\,\mathbf{i}+2\,\mathbf{j}-2\,\mathbf{k}.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(j-3k)+t[(-\,i+2\,j-2\,k)-(j-3k)] \\  & =(j-3k)+t(-i+\,j+k) \\  & =-t\,i+(t+1)\,j+(t-3)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

where $0 \le t \le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=-t, y=t+1,$ and $z=t-3$ along the segment.

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-3)k \\  & =-i+j+k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = x^2+y-z$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(-t)^{2}+(t+1)-(t-3) \\  & ={t}^{2}+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}+4)\cdot \sqrt{3}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}+4)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/71/71df4fc7bd52fe5dd97c7e01502dec2ad68ae31fdf224cccd812c6b7318c70b7.png)

Find, as a definite integral, an expression for the line integral of the function $\displaystyle\int_\limits{C} 2xy \:\textrm{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is the right half of the ellipse $9x^2 + 4y^2 = 36,$ shown above.
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{2^2} + \dfrac{y^2}{3^2} = 1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $2$ and $3,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle 2\cos{t}, \: 3\sin{t} \right\rangle, \qquad -\dfrac{\pi}{2} \le t \le \dfrac{\pi}{2}.
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t+9{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{5{cos}^{2}⁡t+4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{5{cos}^{2}⁡t+4}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = 2xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =12\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}2xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}12\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{5{cos}^{2}⁡t+4}\,\text{d}t \\  & =12{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{5{cos}^{2}⁡t+4}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/6e/6eebbc5ae9f548f5b00de9a12d454fa788884bf73ad46a1065eab0d26330a921.png)

The curve $C$ is given by $y = \dfrac14x^2$ from the point $\left(0,0\right)$ to the point $\left(4,4\right).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = -2\,\mathbf{i} + x\,\mathbf{j}$ through $C,$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ *must* be a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $\mathbf T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = t, \qquad
y = \dfrac{t^2}{4},
\qquad
t\in \left[0,4\right].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(0,0)$ to the point $(4,4).$ Therefore, $\mathbf n$ is indeed a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of $\mathbf T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](images/2b/2b94e24344f600fc02ec5ecac6c1e0ee4c6a5450132753a0a5ac5fceaa9aa1fc.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =-2, \\ Q(x,y) & =x=t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{t}^{2}}{4})=\frac{t}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(-2)\cdot (\frac{t}{2})-(t)\cdot (1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}-2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{t}^{2}{|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =-16-0 \\  & =-16\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Calculate $\lim_\limits{\theta \to 0} \:\dfrac{\tan 2\theta}{\theta}$.
:question/worked-solution:
First, we can simplify the limit using trigonometric identities, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
lim_(θ → 0)\frac{\tan 2θ}{θ} &= lim_(θ → 0)((\frac{\sin 2θ}{\cos 2θ}))/(θ) \\
&= lim_(θ → 0)(\frac{\sin 2θ}{θ} \cdot \frac{1}{\cos 2θ}) \\
&= lim_(θ → 0)\frac{\sin 2θ}{θ} \cdot lim_(θ → 0)\frac{1}{\cos 2θ}
\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now evaluate the limits separately:

- Consider the first limit. Notice that as $\theta \to 0$, both numerator and denominator approach $0$. So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get
$\lim_\limits{\theta \to 0}\: \dfrac{\sin 2\theta}{\theta} = \dfrac{0}{0}$,
which is an indeterminate form. Instead, let's recall the following special limit:
$\lim_\limits{x \to 0}\: \dfrac{\sin x}{x} =1$We rewrite the given limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:
$lim_(θ → 0)\frac{\sin 2θ}{θ}|= lim_(θ → 0)(2 \cdot \frac{\sin 2θ}{2θ}); = 2 \cdot lim_(θ → 0)\frac{\sin2θ}{2θ}$Let $x = 2\theta$. Then, since $x\to0$ as $\theta \to 0$, we have
$2 \cdot \lim_\limits{\theta \to 0}\: \dfrac{\sin \color{blue}2\theta}{\color{blue}2\theta} = 2 \cdot \lim_\limits{x \to 0}\: \dfrac{\sin \color{blue}x}{\color{blue}x} = 2 \cdot 1 =2$.
- Consider the second limit. Evaluating it directly, we get
$\lim_\limits{\theta \to 0} \: \dfrac{1}{\cos 2\theta} = \dfrac{1}{\cos 0} = \dfrac11 = 1$.

Therefore, we have

$$
lim_(θ → 0)\frac{\sin 2θ}{θ} \cdot lim_(θ → 0)\frac{1}{\cos 2θ} = 2 \cdot 1 = 2
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ along the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16.$
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a circle of radius $4$ centered at $O.$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+16{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{16({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}-(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =16{cos}^{2}⁡t-16{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =16({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =16\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }16\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\cdot 4\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =64{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=2t,$ $\text{d}u=2\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}64{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t & =32{\int }_{0}^{4\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =32\operatorname{sin}⁡u{|}_{0}^{4\pi } \\  & =32(0-0) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=x+{y}^{2},$ traversed once along the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4?$
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a circle of radius $2$ centered at $O.$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x+{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4{sin}^{2}⁡t)\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/3b/3bf746cfb21805587a65c7beeac90e75464f630bab1fbf3453de69ca3e6639eb.png)

Which of the following gives the line integral ${\int }_{C}\frac{4y}{x}\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is the left half of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}=16,$ shown above?
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}+{y}^{2}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $4$ and $1,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{15{sin}^{2}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{15{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{4y}{x},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{4y}{x} \\  & =4\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)} \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{4y}{x}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{tan}⁡t\sqrt{15{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral
${\int }_{C}\frac{24x}{y}\,\text{d}s,$
where $C$ is the arc of the parabola ${y}^{2}=8x$ from $(0,0)$ to $(\frac{9}{8},3).$
:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve can be expressed in the form $x=x(y),$ as follows:

$$
{y}^{2}=8x\,⟹\,x=\frac{{y}^{2}}{8}.
$$

Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have

$$
x=x(t)=\frac{{t}^{2}}{8}.
$$

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨\frac{{t}^{2}}{8},\,t⟩,\,0\le t\le 3
$$

Note that the domain $0\le t\le 3$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{t}^{2}}{8})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{t}{4}\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{t}{4})}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{t}^{2}}{16}+1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{{t}^{2}+16}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=\frac{24x}{y}$, then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{24x}{y} \\  & =\frac{24\cdot (\frac{{t}^{2}}{8})}{t} \\  & =3t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{24x}{y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}3t\cdot \frac{1}{4}\sqrt{{t}^{2}+16}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{\int }_{0}^{3}t\sqrt{{t}^{2}+16}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve this using the substitution $u={t}^{2}+16,$ $\text{d}u=2t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4}{\int }_{0}^{3}t\sqrt{{t}^{2}+16}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{3}{8}{\int }_{16}^{25}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot {u}^{3/2}\,{|}_{16}^{25} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}({25}^{3/2}-{16}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(125-64) \\  & =\frac{61}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}$ along the quarter-circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16,$ traversed from the point $(0,-4)$ to the point $(4,0)$ in the fourth quadrant?
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $4$ centered at $O,$ shown below. 

![](images/0b/0baaafbe9846ccef2c06a3b1a86eccac394344afc2dfd94bba2907ebb1cf2362.png)

The curve $C$ can be parametrized as

$$

:question/problem: Which of the following diagrams represents the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{3}-2{y}^{2}}{4}?$

The gradient vector field of a function $f$ is given by $∇f.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{3}-2{y}^{2}}{4}) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{x}^{2} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{x}^{3}-2{y}^{2}}{4}) \\  & =-y\end{aligned}

So, the gradient vector field of $f(x,y)$ is

$$

Next, we have to sketch the vector field at the points $(-2,2),$ $(2,-3),$ and $(2,1).$

To sketch the vector field at the given points, we substitute their coordinates into the expression for $∇f.$

$$

Now, we draw the vectors starting at the corresponding points and obtain the following diagram:

:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-y,$ traversed along the line segment from $(0,2)$ to $(3,1)?$
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(0,2)$ to $(3,1).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=2\,j$ and $b=3\,i+j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =2\,j+t[(3\,i+j)-2\,j] \\  & =2\,j+t(3\,i-j) \\  & =3t\,i+(2-t)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=3t$ and $y=2-t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-t)j \\  & =3\,i-j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(3t)^{2}-(2-t) \\  & =9{t}^{2}+t-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(9{t}^{2}+t-2)\cdot \sqrt{10}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{10}{\int }_{0}^{1}(9{t}^{2}+t-2)\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/0b/0b0f3ae9a464812957c297c09ff3f65bfe5964bdac70298e72ec3dbde2325e72.png)

Which of the following gives the line integral ${\int }_{C}(6{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is the right half of the ellipse $6{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=6,$ shown above?
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{(\sqrt{6})^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $1$ and $\sqrt{6},$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\sqrt{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{6}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+6{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{5{cos}^{2}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{5{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=6{x}^{2}-{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =6(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}-(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =6{cos}^{2}⁡t-6{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =6({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(6{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\sqrt{5{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =6{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\sqrt{5{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y),$ traversed along the line segment from $(1,3)$ to $(0,3)?$
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(1,3)$ to $(0,3).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=i+3\,j$ and $b=3\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(i+3\,j)+t[3\,j-(i+3\,j)] \\  & =(i+3\,j)-t\,i \\  & =(1-t)\,i+3\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=1-t$ and $y=3$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3)j \\  & =-i \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-t)+3) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(4-t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{ln}⁡(4-t)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{ln}⁡(4-t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: What is the value of $(-10) \div (-\frac{2}{3})$?
Find an expression for the general term $a_{n}$ for $n \ge 0$ of the sequence with the generating function $\frac{1}{x + 2} + \frac{2}{3x - 1}$.

A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $k(1-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ at the origin and has velocity $v=3\,m/s$ when its displacement is $\frac{3}{2}\,m,$ find the maximum velocity of the particle.
:question/worked-solution:
![](images/75/75ef4755be2965b674fc7a5440ff05bb3f37d70507941eb48eeae554fcb2d538.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $k(1-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k(1-x).
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}k(1-x) & =0 \\ 1-x & =0 \\ x & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=1\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,1)$ | $1$ | $(1,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $\frac{1}{2}$ |  | $\frac{3}{2}$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $\frac{k}{2}>0$ | $0$ | $-\frac{k}{2}<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=1\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k(1-x).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int k(1-x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+C.
$$

Now, since $v=\sqrt{6}\,{m/s}^{2}$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}-x)+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{6})^{2} & =k(0-\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2})+C \\ C & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+3.
$$

Also, since $v=3\,{m/s}^{2}$ when $x=\frac{3}{2}\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+3 \\ \frac{1}{2}(3)^{2} & =k(\frac{3}{2}-\frac{1}{2}{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2})+3 \\ \frac{9}{2} & =\frac{3}{8}k+3 \\ \frac{3}{8}k & =\frac{3}{2} \\ k & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =4x-2{x}^{2}+3 \\ {v}^{2} & =8x-4{x}^{2}+6 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{8x-4{x}^{2}+6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{8x-4{x}^{2}+6}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(1)=\sqrt{8(1)-4(1)^{2}+6}=\sqrt{10}\,m/s.
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/cb/cbd92b205693f1056e4dc2d0fc8154843e62b433b66d9b0ba8918d7f5bb3b8bf.png)

Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}$ along the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4,$ traversed from the point $(-2,0)$ to the point $(0,-2),$ as shown above.
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $2$ centered at $O.$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ $\text{d}u=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,\text{d}t & =2{\int }_{0}^{-2}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2{e}^{u}{|}_{0}^{-2} \\  & =2{e}^{-2}-2{e}^{0} \\  & =\frac{2}{{e}^{2}}-2\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/78/78f8ca3e70afb8377748a18d7024ba297e330add59550a41a87025a0145b56bb.png)

Evaluate the line integral ${\int }_{C}9xy\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is the quarter of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=4$  traversed from the point $(2,0)$ to the point $(0,1).$
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+{y}^{2}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $2$ and $1,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{3{sin}^{2}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{1+3{sin}^{2}⁡t}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=9xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =9\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t=18\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}9xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}18\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{1+3{sin}^{2}⁡t}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =18{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{1+3{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=1+3{sin}^{2}⁡t,$ $\text{d}u=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}18{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{1+3{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t & =3{\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\cdot \frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}{|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =2({4}^{3/2}-{1}^{3/2}) \\  & =2(8-1) \\  & =14\end{aligned}
$$
