\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{9}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{″}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation:

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{9}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+16({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}))={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Rearranging the terms to find a common denominator:

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}(16-\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{9})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})
$$

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}(\frac{144-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{9})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Now, equating the sine coefficients:

$$
\frac{{b}_{n}(144-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})}{9}=\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }\,⇒\,{b}_{n}=\frac{9(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi (144-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})}.
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{9(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi (144-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

:question/problem:
Let $f(x)$ be the $4$-periodic extension of the function $F(x)=-\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}$ defined on $[-2,2).$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below, showing the derivation of a series converging to the $4$-periodic extension of 

$$
G(x)=-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{3}={\int }_{0}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from the corresponding Fourier series of $f(x).$

The Fourier series of $f(x)$ is given by

$$
-\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}∼-2+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{24(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{{field-1}}.
$$

Since $f$ is 
{{field-2}} 
on $R,$ we may integrate its Fourier series term-by-term to get

$$
-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{3}∼-2x+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{{field-3}}\cdot {{field-4}}.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
First, notice that $F(x)$ is an even function. So, the Fourier series of its $2L$-periodic extension has the form

$$
\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{L}).
$$

In our case, $L=2$ and we are already given the coefficients for $n\ge 1.$ Thus, the Fourier series of $f(x)$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼-2+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{24(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, notice that the function $F$ is continuous on $(-2,2).$ 
Therefore, the $4$-periodic extension $f$ is $\text{piecewise continuous}$ on $R,$ so we may integrate its Fourier series term-by-term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{x}(-\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t & ∼{\int }_{0}^{x}(-2+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{24(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi t}{2}))\text{d}t \\ {[-\frac{1}{2}{t}^{3}]}_{0}^{x} & ∼[-2t]_{0}^{x}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{24(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}\cdot [\frac{2}{n\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi t}{2})]_{0}^{x} \\ -\frac{1}{2}{x}^{3} & ∼-2x+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{48(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}{\pi }^{3}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation ${y}^{″}+4{\pi }^{2}y=f(x),$ where the $1$-periodic forcing function is given by 

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2n\pi x).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below regarding the resonant component of a particular solution of the equation.

The natural frequency of the system matches the frequency of the {{field-1}} harmonic of the forcing function. 

Consequently, the particular solution contains a resonant term of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}={{field-2}}.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+4{\pi }^{2}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{4{\pi }^{2}}=2\pi .
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $1$-periodic function $(L=\frac{1}{2})$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{(\frac{1}{2})}=2n\pi .
$$

For $n=1$, we have ${\omega }_{1}=2\pi .$ Since ${\omega }_{1}=\omega ,$ the $n=1$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=1$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x)).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{1}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x))+x(-2\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x)+2\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x)) \\ {y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″} & =-4\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x)+4\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x)-4{\pi }^{2}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{1}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+4{\pi }^{2}y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x):$

$$
[-4\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x)+4\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x)-4{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{1}}]+4{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{1}}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x)
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-4\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x)+4\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-4\pi A &=0 \\ 4\pi B &=1\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}A &=0 \\ B &=\frac{1}{4\pi }\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=\frac{x}{4\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x).
$$

:question/problem: The expression $60x^2 + 180x$ is equivalent to $rx(3x + 9)$, where $r$ is a constant. What is the value of $r$?
:question/worked-solution:
We begin with the expression $60x^2 + 180x$ and compare it to the form $rx(3x + 9)$.

First, we factor $x$ from both terms in the original expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}
60x^{2} + 180x &= x(60x + 180)
\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we factor out the greatest common factor from the binomial $60x + 180$. The GCF of $60$ and $180$ is $60$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x(60x + 180) &= x(60)(x + 3) \\
&= 60x(x + 3)
\end{aligned}
$$

We are told the expression is written as $rx(3x + 9)$. Notice that

$$
3x + 9 = 3(x + 3)
$$

so we rewrite the expression as

$$
\begin{aligned}
60x(x + 3) &= (3 \cdot \frac{60}{3})x(x + 3) \\
&= (\frac{60}{3}) \cdot x \cdot 3(x + 3) \\
&= 20x(3x + 9)
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the value of $r$ is $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{20}$.

:question/problem: Two variables, $h$ and $j$, are related such that for each increase of $1$ in the value of $h$, the value of $j$ is multiplied by $\dfrac{3}{2}$. When $h = 0$, $j = 64$. Which equation represents this relationship?
:question/worked-solution:
We are told that the value of $j$ is multiplied by

$$
\dfrac{3}{2}
$$

for each increase of $1$ in $h$. That means the variable $j$ grows exponentially with base

$$
\dfrac{3}{2}
$$

Therefore, $h$ and $j$ are related by the expression

$$
j = a \cdot \left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^h
$$

Now, we know that $j = 64$ when $h = 0$. Hence, we can determine the value of $a$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
j &= a \cdot (\frac{3}{2})^{h} \\
64 &= a \cdot (\frac{3}{2})^{0} \\
64 &= a \cdot 1 \\
a &= 64
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
j = 64 \cdot \left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^h
$$

:question/problem: A machine was purchased in $2015$ for $\[math]32{,}000$. Its value halves every $6$ years. In which year will the value reach $\[/math]2{,}000$?
:question/worked-solution:
We're told that a machine was purchased in $2015$ for $\[math]32{,}000$, and its value halves every $6$ years. We want to find the year when the value will reach $\[/math]2{,}000$.

The formula for exponential decay, in terms of a halving period $d$, is

$$
y = a \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{t/d}
$$

In our case, we have the following:

- $a=32{,}000$ is the initial value in $2015$.
- The value halves every $6$ years. So, the halving period is $d=6$.
- $t$ is the time, in years, after $2015$.

Therefore, the expression for the value $y$ after $t$ years is

$$
y = 32{,}000 \cdot \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{t/6}
$$

Now, we need to find $t$ when

$$
y = 2{,}000
$$

Substituting $y = 2{,}000$ in the last equation and simplifying, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
2,000 &= 32,000 \cdot (\frac{1}{2})^{t/6} \\
\frac{2,000}{32,000} &= (\frac{1}{2})^{t/6} \\
\frac{1}{16} &= (\frac{1}{2})^{t/6}
\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that

$$
\dfrac{1}{16} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^4
$$

Therefore,

$$
\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^4 = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{t/6}
$$

Equating the exponents, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
4 &= \frac{t}{6} \\
t &= 4 \cdot 6 \\
t &= 24
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, it will take $24$ years for the value to reach $\[math]2{,}000$.

Finally, to find the year, we add this to the initial year $2015{:}$

$$
2015 + 24 = 2039
$$

So, the value will reach $\[/math]2{,}000$ in the year ${2039}$.

:question/problem: An exponential function $D$ is defined by $D(x) = 400 \cdot b^x$, where $b$ is a positive constant. If $D(2) = 100$, what is the value of $D(5)$?
:question/worked-solution:
We are told that

$$
D(x) = 400 \cdot b^x
$$

and that $D(2) = 100$.

Substituting $x = 2$ into the function $D$ and solve for $b$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
D(2) &= 400 \cdot b^{2} \\
100 &= 400 \cdot b^{2} \\
b^{2} &= \frac{100}{400} \\
b^{2} &= \frac{1}{4} \\
b &= ± \frac{1}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Taking into account that $b$ is positive, we get

$$
b = \dfrac{1}{2}
$$

Finally, we substitute

$$
b=\dfrac{1}{2}
$$

into the function to calculate $D(5){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
D(5) &= 400 \cdot (\frac{1}{2})^{5} \\
&= 400 \cdot \frac{1}{32} \\
&= 12.5
\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The equation below relates the distinct positive real numbers $a$, $b$, and $z{:}$
$\dfrac{36a}{6b} = 12\sqrt{z + 10}$.
Express $z$ in terms of $a$ and $b$.
:question/worked-solution:
First, notice that we can simplify the fraction left-hand side since $36$ and $6$ have a common factor of $6{:}$

$$
\dfrac{36a}{6b} = \dfrac{6a}{b}
$$

So, the equation becomes

$$
\dfrac{6a}{b} = 12\sqrt{z + 10}
$$

To express our equation in terms of $z$, we first isolate the square root by dividing both sides by $12{:}$

$$
{\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle {\displaystyle \frac{6 a}{b \cdot  12}} & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{12 \sqrt{z + 10}}{12}} \\ \displaystyle {\displaystyle \frac{6 a}{b \cdot  12}} & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{\cancel{12} \sqrt{z + 10}}{\cancel{12}}} \\ \displaystyle {\displaystyle \frac{a}{2 b}} & \displaystyle  = \sqrt{z + 10}\end{array}}
$$

Next, we square both sides:

$$
\left(\dfrac{a}{2b}\right)^2 = z + 10
$$

Finally, we solve for $z$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(\frac{a}{2b})^{2} &= z + 10 \\
(\frac{a}{2b})^{2} - 10 &= z + 10 - 10 \\
(\frac{a}{2b})^{2} - 10 &= z
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is

$$
z = \left(\dfrac{a}{2b}\right)^2 - 10
$$

:question/problem:
${\left\{  \begin{array}{l}y = - 5 {x}^{2} + 10 x - 1 \\ y = 4 x - k\end{array} \right. }$

The graphs of the equations given in the system of equations above, where $k$ is a constant, intersect at exactly one point in the $xy$-plane. Find the point of intersection.
:question/worked-solution:
The line $y=4x - k$ intersects the parabola

$$
y=-5x^2 + 10x - 1
$$

where

$$
-5x^2 + 10x - 1 = 4x - k
$$

We need to determine the value of $k$ such that this equation has one real solution.

A quadratic equation has exactly one real root if the discriminant is zero:

$$
\mathcal{D} = 0
$$

First, rewrite the equation in standard quadratic form:

$$
\begin{aligned}
-5x^{2} + 10x - 1 &= 4x - k \\
- 5x^{2} + 10x - 1 - 4x + k &= 0 \\
- 5x^{2} + 6x + (k - 1) &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

The coefficients of our quadratic equation are the following:

$$
a = -5, \qquad b = 6, \qquad c = k-1
$$

So, computing the discriminant, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
D &= b^{2} - 4ac \\
&= 6^{2} - 4(-5)(k - 1) \\
&= 36 + 20(k - 1) \\
&= 36 + 20k - 20 \\
&= 16 + 20k
\end{aligned}
$$

To have exactly one real solution, we need

$$
\mathcal{D} = 0{:}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
16 + 20k &= 0 \\
20k &= -16 \\
k &= -\frac{16}{20} \\
k &= -\frac{4}{5}
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the equation of the line is

$$
y=4x-\left(-\dfrac{4}{5}\right)=4x+\dfrac{4}{5}
$$

To find the $x$-coordinate, we solve the original quadratic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
-5x^{2} + 6x + (-\frac{4}{5} - 1) &= 0 \\
- 5x^{2} + 6x - \frac{9}{5} &= 0 \\
- 25x^{2} + 30x - 9 &= 0 \\
- (25x^{2} - 30x + 9) &= 0 \\
- (5x - 3)^{2} &= 0 \\
5x - 3 &= 0 \\
x &= \frac{3}{5}
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the $y$-coordinate by substituting

$$
x=\dfrac{3}{5}
$$

into one of the two equations and solving:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y &= 4(\frac{3}{5}) + \frac{4}{5} \\
&= \frac{12}{5} + \frac{4}{5} \\
&= \frac{16}{5}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point of intersection is

$$
\Big(\dfrac{3}{5},\dfrac{16}{5}\Big)
$$

:question/problem:
The function
$P(t) = 775 \cdot (0.95)^{(3/4)t}$
models the population of bacteria in a sealed container $t$ weeks after a chemical is introduced. According to the model, what percentage is the population predicted to decrease by every $2$ days? Round your answer to two decimal places.
:question/worked-solution:
Explanation:

We are given the exponential model

$$
P(t) = 775 \cdot (0.95)^{(3/4)t}
$$

which represents the population $t$ weeks after the chemical is introduced. We want to rewrite this model in terms of days instead of weeks.

Note the following:

- Since there are $7$ days in a week, we substitute $t=\dfrac{d}{7}$ into the original equation.
- We *divide* by $7$ (not multiply) because we want $d=7$ days to correspond to $t=1$ week.

Substituting, we get a model $p(d)$ for the population as a function of time in days $d$ after the chemical is introduced:

$$
\begin{aligned}
p(d) = P(\frac{d}{7}) &= 775 \cdot (0.95)^{(3/4) \cdot (d/7)} \\
&= 775 \cdot (0.95)^{3d/28}
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we want to find the percentage decrease over $2$ days. Inspecting the model in terms of days $p(d)$, we see that the decay factor over $d$ days is
$(0.95)^{3d/28}$.

So, the decay factor over $2$ days is

$$
(0.95)^{3\cdot 2/28} = (0.95)^{3/14} \approx 0.989\,069
$$

This corresponds to a decrease of approximately

$$
1 - 0.989\,069 = 0.010\,931 \approx 1.09\%
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

Therefore, the population is predicted to decrease by $1.09\%$ every $2$ days.

:question/problem: The function is defined by $f(x) = -a^{x} + d$, where $a$ and $d$ are positive constants. The graph of $y = f(x)$ in the $xy$-plane passes through the point $\left(0, \dfrac{5}{2}\right)$, and the product of $a$ and $d$ is $\dfrac{21}{2}$. What is the value of $a$?
:question/worked-solution:
Let's examine the given conditions in turn.

- Since the graph passes through the point $\left(0, \dfrac{5}{2}\right)$, we have that $f(0) = \dfrac{5}{2}$. So, we have the following equation, which we solve for $d{:}$
$f(0)|= \frac{5}{2}; - a^{0} + d|= \frac{5}{2}; - 1 + d|= \frac{5}{2}; - 1 + d + 1|= \frac{5}{2} + 1; d|= \frac{7}{2}$
- Since $ad=\dfrac{21}{2}$, using the fact that $d = \dfrac{7}{2}$, we obtain the following equation, which we solve for $a{:}$
$ad|= \frac{21}{2}; a(\frac{7}{2})|= \frac{21}{2}; \frac{7a}{2}|= \frac{21}{2}; 2 \cdot \frac{7a}{2}|= 2 \cdot \frac{21}{2}; 7a|= 21; \frac{7a}{7}|= \frac{21}{7}; a|= 3$

Therefore, $a=3$.

:question/problem:
The function
$C(t) = 95 \cdot (1.05)^{(5/2)t}$
models the number of data packets processed, in thousands, by a server $t$ minutes after a throughput upgrade. According to the model, in how many seconds is the number of packets expected to increase by $5\%$?
:question/worked-solution:
We are given the exponential model

$$
C(t) = 95 \cdot (1.05)^{(5/2)t}
$$

which represents the number of data packets processed, in thousands, $t$ minutes after the upgrade. We want to rewrite this model in terms of seconds rather than minutes.

Note the following:

- Since there are $60$ seconds in a minute, we substitute $t=\dfrac{s}{60}$ into the original equation.
- We *divide* by $60$ (not multiply) because we want $s=60$ seconds to correspond to $t=1$ minute.

Substituting, we get a model $c(s)$ for the number of packets as a function of time in seconds $s$ after the upgrade:

$$
\begin{aligned}
c(s) = C(\frac{s}{60}) &= 95 \cdot (1.05)^{(5/2) \cdot (s/60)} \\
&= 95 \cdot (1.05)^{s/24}
\end{aligned}
$$

The base $1.05$ means that the number of packets grows by $5\%$ each time the exponent increases by $1$, i.e., once every growth period.

The exponent

$$
\dfrac{s}{24}
$$

shows that for every increase in $s=24$ seconds, the exponent increases by $1$.

Therefore, the number of packets is expected to increase by $5\%$ every ${24}$ seconds.

:question/problem:
The expression $4x - g$ is a factor of $16x^{2} + 12x - 7g$. Which of the following could be the value of $g$?

1. $g=0$ or $g=4$
2. $g=4$ only
3. $g=-1$ or $g=0$
4. $g=0$ only
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that by the factor theorem, if $(sx-r)$ is a factor of a polynomial $p(x)$, then

$$
x=\dfrac{r}{s}
$$

is a root of the polynomial.

Now, since $4x - g$ is a factor of the polynomial

$$
p(x)=16x^{2} + 12x - 7g
$$

we must have

$$
p\left(\dfrac{g}{4}\right) = 0
$$

So, substituting

$$
x=\dfrac{g}{4}
$$

into the expression for $p(x)$, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}
p(\frac{g}{4}) &= 16(\frac{g}{4})^{2} + 12(\frac{g}{4}) - 7g \\
&= g^{2} + 3g - 7g \\
&= g^{2} - 4g \\
&= g(g - 4)
\end{aligned}
$$

Using the zero product rule, we conclude that $g(g - 4)=0$ if

$$
g=0 \qquad\text{or}\qquad g-4=0
$$

which gives $g=0$ or $g=4$.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only"

:question/problem:
Which of the following expressions has a factor of $2x - 5m$, where $m$ is a **negative integer** constant?

1. $4x^{2} + 2x + 18m$
2. $4x^{2} + 2x + 10m$
3. $4x^{2} + 2x + 20m$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that by the factor theorem, if $(sx-r)$ is a factor of a polynomial $p(x)$, then

$$
x=\dfrac{r}{s}
$$

is a root of the polynomial.
Thus, since $2x -5m$ is a factor of our polynomial $p(x)$, we must have

$$
p\left(\dfrac{5m}{2}\right) = 0
$$

With that in mind, let's examine the given options in turn.

- Option I, $p(x) = 4x^{2}+2x+18m$, is not valid. Here, we have
$p(\frac{3c}{2})|= 4(\frac{5m}{2})^{2} + 2(\frac{5m}{2}) + 18m; = 25m^{2} + 5m + 18m; = 25m^{2} + 23m; = m(25m + 23)$.
This equals zero only at $m=0$ or $m=-\dfrac{23}{25}$, neither of which is a negative integer. ${\color{red}\times}$

*Option II,*

$$
p(x)=4x^{2}+2x+10m
$$

is not valid. Here, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
p(\frac{3c}{2}) &= 4(\frac{5m}{2})^{2} + 2(\frac{5m}{2}) + 10m \\
&= 25m^{2} + 5m + 10m \\
&= 25m^{2} + 15m \\
&= 5m(5m + 3)
\end{aligned}
$$

This equals zero only at $m=0$ or

$$
m=-\dfrac{3}{5}
$$

neither of which is a negative integer. ${\color{red}\times}$

*Option III,*

$$
p(x)=4x^{2}+2x+20m
$$

is valid. Indeed,

$$
\begin{aligned}
p(\frac{3c}{2}) &= 4(\frac{5m}{2})^{2} + 2(\frac{5m}{2}) + 20m \\
&= 25m^{2} + 5m + 20m \\
&= 25m^{2} + 25m \\
&= 25m(m + 1)
\end{aligned}
$$

This equals zero only at $m=0$ or $m=-1$, and $m=-1$ is a negative integer. ${\color{darkgreen}\checkmark}$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".

:question/problem:
A rocket is launched upward and after each stage separation it reaches $\dfrac{1}{2}$ the height it reached in the previous stage. The rocket initially reaches a height of $64.0 \, \text{m}$.

What is the maximum height the rocket reaches above the ground between the first and second stage separations?
:question/worked-solution:
We're told that a rocket is launched upward to an initial height of $64.0\,\text{m}$. After each stage separation, it reaches

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}
$$

the height it reached on the previous stage.

This scenario represents exponential decay, where the height is multiplied by a factor of

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}
$$

after each stage. The general form for this type of relationship can be expressed as

$$
H(n) = a \cdot b^n
$$

where $H(n)$ is the height after $n$ stages, $a$ is the initial height, and $b$ is the decay factor.

In our case, we have the following:

- $a=64.0$ is the initial height of the rocket.
- $b = \dfrac{1}{2}$ is the decay factor.
- $n$ represents the number of stage separations.

So, the expression for $H(n)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
H(n) &= 64.0 \cdot (\frac{1}{2})^{n}
\end{aligned}
$$

We are looking for the height between the first and second stage separations. This corresponds to the height after the first separation. Hence, we need to calculate $H(1)$.

Substitute $n=1$ into the formula for $H(n)$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
H(1) &= 64.0 \cdot (\frac{1}{2})^{1} \\
&= 64.0 \cdot \frac{1}{2} \\
&= \frac{64.0}{2} \\
&= 32.0
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the maximum height the rocket reaches above the ground between the first and second stage separations is $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{32.0}\,\text{m}$.

:question/problem:
In a science experiment, Priya heated a metal rod and then left it to cool in a room that maintained a constant temperature of $65^\circ \mathrm{F}$. At $3{:}00$ p.m., the rod’s temperature was $200^\circ \mathrm{F}$. After $5$ minutes, its temperature had dropped to $170^\circ \mathrm{F}$, and after $10$ minutes, it was $146.5^\circ \mathrm{F}$. The rod continued to cool over time.

Write the function that best models the temperature $T(t)$ in degrees Fahrenheit of the rod $t$ minutes after it was removed from the heat.
:question/worked-solution:
The temperature $T(t)$ at time $t$ is modeled by the equation

$$
T(t) = a \cdot b^t + T_r
$$

where

- $T_r = 65^\circ \mathrm{F}$ is the room (ambient) temperature,
- $a$ and $b$ are constants to be determined, and
- $t$ is the time, in minutes.

At $t=0$, the temperature is $T(0) = 200$. Therefore, we can determine the value of $a{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
T(0) &= 200 \\
a \cdot b^{0} + 65 &= 200 \\
a \cdot 1 &= 135 \\
a &= 135
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, our model becomes

$$
T(t) = 135 \cdot b^t + 65
$$

At $t=5$, the temperature is $T(5) = 170$. Hence, we can determine the value of $b{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
T(5) &= 170 \\
135 \cdot b^{5} + 65 &= 170 \\
135 \cdot b^{5} &= 105 \\
b^{5} &= \frac{105}{135} \\
b^{5} &= \frac{7}{9} \\
b &= (\frac{7}{9})^{1/5}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function best models the temperature $T(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
T(t) &= 135 \cdot ((\frac{7}{9})^{1/5})^{t} + 65 \\
&= 135 \cdot (\frac{7}{9})^{t/5} + 65
\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Let $z(w) = \mid 25 - 5w \mid$. For which values of $k$ does $z(k) = 5k$?
:question/worked-solution:
We are given the equation

$$
z(w) = \mid 25 - 5w \mid
$$

and asked to find the value of $k$ for which $z(k) = 5k$. Therefore, we need to solve the equation

$$
\mid 25 - 5k \mid = 5k
$$

We now split into two cases based on the definition of absolute value.

- First, we consider the case where $25 - 5k \ge 0$. Then, we have
$\mid 25 - 5k \mid = 25 - 5k$.
Therefore, our absolute value equation becomes
$25 - 5k = 5k$.
Solving the above equation for $k$, we obtain
$25 - 5k|= 5k; 25|= 10k; k|= \frac{5}{2}$.
Now, we check whether this value of $k$ satisfies the condition for the first case:
$25 - 5(\frac{5}{2})|= 25 - \frac{25}{2}; = \frac{25}{2}; \ge 0✓$
So, $k = \dfrac{5}{2}$ is a valid solution.
- Now, we consider the case where $25 - 5k < 0$. Then, we have
$\mid 25 - 5k \mid = -(25 - 5k)$.
This equation becomes:
$-25 + 5k = 5k \Rightarrow -25 = 0$,
which is not true. Therefore, no solution arises from this case.

Thus, the only value that satisfies the equation $z(k) = 5k$ is

$$
k = \dfrac{5}{2}
$$

:question/problem: The expression $5a^2 - \dfrac{4}{9}b^2$ is equivalent to $5(a - cb)(a + cb)$, where $c$ is a positive constant. What is the value of $c$?
:question/worked-solution:
Since our equivalent expression has a constant factor $5$, we start by factoring $5$ out of our original expression:

$$
5a^2 - \dfrac{4}{9}b^2 = 5\left(a^2 - \dfrac{4}{45}b^2\right)
$$

To write our bracketed expression as a difference of squares, we must write

$$
\dfrac{4}{45}
$$

as a square. Applying the exponent rules, we have

$$
\dfrac{4}{45} = \left(\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{45}}\right)^2 = \left(\dfrac{2}{3\sqrt{5}}\right)^2
$$

Hence, we apply our formula for factoring a difference of squares:

$$
a^2-b^2=(a-b)(a+b)
$$

With $a=a$ and

$$
b=\dfrac{2b}{3\sqrt{5}}
$$

this yields

$$
\begin{aligned}
5(a^{2} - \frac{4}{45}b^{2}) &= 5(a^{2} - (\frac{2}{3\sqrt{5}})^{2}b^{2}) \\
&= 5(a^{2} - (\frac{2b}{3\sqrt{5}})^{2}) \\
&= 5(a - \frac{2b}{3\sqrt{5}})(a + \frac{2b}{3\sqrt{5}}) \\
&= 5(a - \frac{2}{3\sqrt{5}}b)(a + \frac{2}{3\sqrt{5}}b)
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
c = \dfrac{2}{3\sqrt{5}}
$$

A maglev train accelerates at a rate of $5.6 \, \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}^2}$. What is this acceleration rate, in miles per minute squared, rounded to the nearest tenth?

Hint: $1\,\textrm{mi} = 1,609\,\textrm{m}$
:question/worked-solution:
We are given the units

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}^2}
$$

and we want to convert this into

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{mi}}{\textrm{min}^2}
$$

We're converting two units instead of just one, so we're going to have to multiply by two conversion factors:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}^2}\cdot \,\dfrac{?}{?} \cdot \,\dfrac{?}{?} = \dfrac{\textrm{mi}}{\textrm{min}^2}
$$

One of the conversion factors should change $\textrm{m}$ to $\textrm{mi}$.

$$
\dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{m}}}{\textrm{s}^2}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{mi}}{\cancel{\textrm{m}}} \cdot \,\dfrac{?}{?} = \dfrac{\textrm{mi}}{\textrm{min}^2}
$$

The other conversion factor should change $\textrm{s}^2$ into $\textrm{min}^2$.

$$
\dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{m}}}{\cancel{\textrm{s}^2}}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{mi}}{\cancel{\textrm{m}}} \cdot \dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{s}^2}}{\textrm{min}^2} = \dfrac{\textrm{mi}}{\textrm{min}^2}
$$

So, our conversion formula is

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}^2}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{mi}}{\textrm{m}} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{s}^2}{\textrm{min}^2} = \dfrac{\textrm{mi}}{\textrm{min}^2}
$$

Now that we have our conversion formula, we need to determine the correct numbers to use and apply them.

- The acceleration rate given in the problem statement is $5.6 \, \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}^2}$.
- We are given that there are $1,609$ meters per mile. Taking the reciprocal, we find that there are $\dfrac{1}{1,609}$ miles per meter.
- There are $60\,\textrm{s}$ per $\textrm{min}$. We can write this as follows:
$\dfrac{60\,\textrm{s}}{\textrm{min}}$
To determine the number of seconds squared in one minute squared, we square this quantity and apply the rules of exponents, as follows:
$(\frac{60s}{min})^{2}|= \frac{60^{2}s^{2}}{min^{2}}; = \frac{3, 600s^{2}}{min^{2}}$

Now, applying our conversion formula, we have

$$
{\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle 5.6 \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{\text{m}}{ {\text{s}}^{2}}} & \displaystyle  = 5.6 \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{\text{m}}{ {\text{s}}^{2}}} \cdot  {\displaystyle \frac{1}{1 , 609}} \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{\text{mi}}{\text{m}}} \cdot  3 , 600 \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{ {\text{s}}^{2}}{ {\text{min}}^{2}}} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = ( 5.6 \cdot  {\displaystyle \frac{1}{1 , 609}} \cdot  3 , 600 ) \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{\cancel{\text{m}}}{\cancel{ {\text{s}}^{2}}}} \cdot  {\displaystyle \frac{\text{mi}}{\cancel{\text{m}}}} \cdot  {\displaystyle \frac{\cancel{ {\text{s}}^{2}}}{ {\text{min}}^{2}}} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{5.6 \cdot  3 , 600}{1 , 609}} \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{\text{mi}}{ {\text{min}}^{2}}} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{20 , 160}{1 , 609}} \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{\text{mi}}{ {\text{min}}^{2}}} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  \approx  12.5 \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{\text{mi}}{ {\text{min}}^{2}}} ,\end{array}}
$$

rounded to the nearest tenth.

Therefore, the maglev train is accelerating at a speed of approximately

$$
12.5\,\dfrac{\textrm{mi}}{\textrm{min}^2}
$$

:question/problem:
A professional sports complex covers $3,872,000 \, \textrm{yd}^2$. What is the area of the complex in square miles? Round your answer to two decimal places.

Hint: $1\,\textrm{mi} = 1,760\,\textrm{yd}$
:question/worked-solution:
We want to convert the area from square yards to square miles.

We are given that there are $1,760$ yards per mile, which we can write as follows:

$$
\dfrac{1,760 \, \textrm{yd}}{\textrm{mi}}
$$

We need to convert this into area units. So, by squaring this quantity and applying the rules of exponents, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
(\frac{1, 760yd}{mi})^{2} &= \frac{1, 760^{2}yd^{2}}{mi^{2}} \\
&= \frac{3, 097, 600yd^{2}}{mi^{2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

However, since we're converting from a smaller unit of area $(\textrm{yd})^2$ to a larger one $(\textrm{mi})^2$, we need to multiply $3,872,000 \, \textrm{yd}^2$ by the reciprocal of the above:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{mi}^2}{3,097,600 \, \textrm{yd}^2}
$$

This is our conversion factor.

Now, multiplying $3,872,000 \, \textrm{yd}^2$ by our conversion factor, we get

$$
{\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle 3 , 872 , 000 \hspace{0.167em} {\text{yd}}^{2} & \displaystyle  = 3 , 872 , 000 \hspace{0.167em} {\text{yd}}^{2} \cdot  {\displaystyle \frac{ {\text{mi}}^{2}}{3 , 097 , 600 \hspace{0.167em} {\text{yd}}^{2}}} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 3 , 872 , 000 \cancel{ {\text{yd}}^{2}} \cdot  {\displaystyle \frac{ {\text{mi}}^{2}}{3 , 097 , 600 \cancel{ {\text{yd}}^{2}}}} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{3 , 872 , 000}{3 , 097 , 600}} \hspace{0.167em} {\text{mi}}^{2} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 1.25 \hspace{0.167em} {\text{mi}}^{2} ,\end{array}}
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

Therefore, the area is approximately $1.25\,\textrm{mi}^2$.

An archaeological site spans $1.1\,\textrm{mi}^2$. What is the total area of the site in square yards?

Hint: $1\,\textrm{mi} = 1,760\,\textrm{yd}$
:question/worked-solution:
We want to convert the area of the site from square miles to square yards.

$$
\dfrac{1,760\,\textrm{yd}}{\textrm{mi}}
$$

We need to convert this into area units. So, by squaring this quantity and applying the rules of exponents, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
(\frac{1, 760yd}{mi})^{2} &= \frac{1, 760^{2}yd^{2}}{mi^{2}} \\
&= \frac{3, 097, 600yd^{2}}{mi^{2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

This is our conversion factor.

Now, multiplying $1.1\,\textrm{mi}^2$ by our conversion factor, we get

$$
{\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle 1.1 \hspace{0.167em} {\text{mi}}^{2} & \displaystyle  = 1.1 \hspace{0.167em} {\text{mi}}^{2} \cdot  {\displaystyle \frac{3 , 097 , 600 \hspace{0.167em} {\text{yd}}^{2}}{ {\text{mi}}^{2}}} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 1.1 \hspace{0.167em} \cancel{ {\text{mi}}^{2}} \cdot  {\displaystyle \frac{3 , 097 , 600 \hspace{0.167em} {\text{yd}}^{2}}{\cancel{ {\text{mi}}^{2}}}} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 1.1 \cdot  3 , 097 , 600 \hspace{0.167em} {\text{yd}}^{2} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 3 , 407 , 360 \hspace{0.167em} {\text{yd}}^{2} .\end{array}}

:question/problem: Simplify the expression $\dfrac{7}{8}\left(2^{-s}\right) - \left(2^{-s}\right)$.
:question/worked-solution:
We need to write the expression

$$
\dfrac{7}{8}\left(2^{-s}\right) - \left(2^{-s}\right)
$$

in the form

$$
k\left(2^{-s}\right)
$$

Factoring out the common factor of

$$
\left(2^{-s}\right)
$$

in the expression, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{7}{8}(2^{-s}) - (2^{-s}) &= \frac{7}{8} \cdot (2^{-s}) - 1 \cdot (2^{-s}) \\
&= (\frac{7}{8} - 1) \cdot (2^{-s}) \\
&= (\frac{7}{8} - \frac{8}{8}) \cdot (2^{-s}) \\
&= (-\frac{1}{8}) \cdot (2^{-s}) \\
&=-\frac{1}{8}(2^{-s})
\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Express $\dfrac{64}{27}\left(\dfrac43\right)^t$ as a power of $\dfrac43$ only.
:question/worked-solution:
Let's recall the rules of exponents:

- Negative exponents: $x^{-n} = \dfrac{1}{x^n}$
- Radicals as fractional exponents: $\sqrt[n]{x} = x^{1/n}$
- The product rule: $a^n \cdot a^m = a^{n+m}$
- The quotient rule: $\dfrac{a^n}{a^m} = a^{n-m}$
- The power rule: $\left(a^m \right)^n = a^{mn}$
- The power of product rule: $(ab)^n = a^nb^n$
- The power of quotient rule: $\left(\dfrac a b \right)^n = \dfrac{a^n}{b^n}$

Now, our expression

$$
\dfrac{64}{27}\left(\dfrac43\right)^t
$$

has an additional factor of

$$
\dfrac{64}{27}
$$

However, notice that

$$
64=4^3 \qquad\text{and}\qquad 27=3^3
$$

are both perfect cubes. Therefore, we can write our expression as

$$
\dfrac{4^3}{3^3}\left(\dfrac43\right)^t
$$

By the power of the quotient rule, we have

$$
\left(\dfrac43\right)^3\left(\dfrac43\right)^t
$$

Finally, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(\frac{4}{3})^{3}(\frac{4}{3})^{t} &= (\frac{4}{3})^{t + 3}
\end{aligned}
$$

The scatter plot above shows an approximate trend line for the relationship between two variables $x$ and $y$ in a dataset $R$.

A new dataset $S$ is formed by multiplying the $x$-coordinate of every data point of $R$ by $2$. Which of the following could be an equation of a trend line for dataset $S$?

2. $y=0.75x+2$
3. $y=0.75x+\dfrac 2 3$

:question/worked-solution:
First, we find an approximate trend line for $R$ from the plot.

![](images/9a/9a21a7f3d6768769f0884dd4a2c712f05cd6e62002569abe9ab593fa5f1b9c30.png)

It seems that the trend line passes through the points

$$
(x_1,y_1) \approx (4,8)
$$

and

$$
(x_2,y_2) \approx (12,20)
$$

So, an estimate of the slope $m$ of the line is

$$
m \mid \approx \frac{y_{2} - y_{1}}{x_{2} - x_{1}}; = \frac{20 - 8}{12 - 4}; = \frac{12}{8}; = 1.5
$$

So, an approximate trend line, in slope-intercept form, is

$$
y=1.5x+b
$$

where $b$ is the $y$-intercept to be estimated. We do this by substituting in the coordinates of a point on the line, say $(4,8){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
y &= 1.5x + b \\
8 &= 1.5(4) + b \\
8 &= 6 + b \\
2 &= b
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the trend line for dataset $R$ is

$$
y=1.5x+2
$$

We're told that dataset $S$ is formed by multiplying the $x$-coordinate of every data point of $R$ by $2$.

Let $x_R$ be a $x$-value in $R$ and $x_S$ be the corresponding $x$-value in $S$. Then, we have

$$
x_S = 2 x_R
$$

Subsituting

$$
x_R = \dfrac {x_S} 2
$$

into the equation for $R{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
y_{S} &= 1.5(\frac{x_{S}}{2}) + 2 \\
&= 0.75x + 2
\end{aligned}
$$

So, a suitable line of best fit for $S$ is

$$
y=0.75x+2
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is **only II.**

:question/problem:
Consider the d’Alembert differential equation

$$
y = x\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}-1\right)^2 + 2\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}\right).
$$

If $y'(x) = t,$ then general solution can be expressed in parametric form $(x(t), y(t)),$ where

$$
y(t) = \left( \dfrac{2\ln|t| - t^2+C}{2(t-1)^2} \right) f(t) + g(t)
$$

and $C$ is an arbitrary constant. Find $f(t)+g(t).$

*Hint: Under the given transformation, we have*

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} + \dfrac{2x}{t-1} = \frac{1+t}{t(1-t)}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
A differential equation is a d'Alembert differential equation if it can be expressed in the form

$$
y = xf(y') + g(y'),
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are differentiable functions of $y'.$ 

We're told that, under the substitution $y'(x) = t,$ our d’Alembert differential equation transforms to the first-order linear equation

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} + \dfrac{2x}{t-1} = \frac{1+t}{t(1-t)}.
$$

We'll solve this equation using the method of integrating factors. Since this equation is already of the form

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} + P(t)x = Q(t)
$$

we compute our integrating factor as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int P(t)\,\text{d}t} \\  & ={e}^{\int 2/(t-1)\,\text{d}t} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|t-1|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(t-1)^{2}} \\  & =(t-1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying our differential equation by $I(t)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(t-1)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+2(t-1)x & =(t-1)^{2}\frac{1+t}{t(1-t)} \\ (t-1)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+2(t-1)x & =\frac{1-{t}^{2}}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Rewriting the left-hand side as an exact derivative, and integrating both sides of the equation with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x(t-1)^{2}) & =\frac{1-{t}^{2}}{t} \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x(t-1)^{2})\,\text{d}t & =\int \frac{1-{t}^{2}}{t}\,\text{d}t \\ x(t-1)^{2} & =\int \frac{1}{t}-t\,\text{d}t \\ x(t-1)^{2} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+C \\ x & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|-{t}^{2}+C}{2(t-1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
x(t) = \dfrac{2\ln|t| - t^2+C}{2(t-1)^2}.
$$

To recover $y$, we substitute $x$ into

$$
y = x(t-1)^2 + 2t,
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|-{t}^{2}+C}{2(t-1)^{2}})(t-1)^{2}+2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that $f(t)=(t-1)^2,\ g(t)=2t,$ and

$$
f(t)+g(t) = t^2 +1.
$$

:question/problem: Consider a spherical planet with radius $(8\times10^5)\,\textrm{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g = 16\,\textrm{m/s}^2.$ Which equation best models the velocity $v$ of an object projected radially outward from the planet's surface with an initial velocity of $(9\times10^{4})\,\textrm{m/s},$ where $r$ is the distance from the planet's center to the object. Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.
:question/worked-solution:
Let $R$ be the planet's radius and $g$ be the planet's surface gravitational acceleration.

According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the planet is

$$
F_\text{in} = G\,\dfrac{mM}{r^2},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, and $M$ is the planet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-F_\textrm{in}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, 

$$
a=-\dfrac{k}{r^2},
$$

 with constant of proportionality $k=GM > 0.$

When at the surface, $r=R,$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-g.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k{:}$

$$
-g = -\dfrac{k}{R^2} 
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
k = gR^2
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a = -\dfrac{gR^2}{r^2}.
$$

Now, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}r} = -\dfrac{gR^2}{r^2}
$$

Solving using separation of variables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int v\frac{dv}{dr}\,dr & =\int (-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}})\,dr \\ \int v\,dv & =-g{R}^{2}\int \frac{1}{{r}^{2}}\,dr \\ \frac{{v}^{2}}{2} & =-g{R}^{2}(-\frac{1}{r})+{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{r}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C=2C_1$ is a constant of integration.

Let $v_0$ be the initial velocity of the object. Applying the initial condition $v(R) = v_0,$ we can solve for $C{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(R)^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{R}+C \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =2gR+C \\ C & ={v}_{0}^{2}-2gR\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation for the velocity of the object is

$$
v^2 = \dfrac{2gR^2}{r} + v_0^2 - 2gR.
$$

Finally, substituting in the values
$R=(8\times10^5),$
$g=16,$ and
$v_0=(9\times10^{4}),$
we conclude that the equation for the velocity is

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2\cdot 16\cdot (8\times {10}^{5})^{2}}{r}+(9\times {10}^{4})^{2}-2\cdot 16\cdot (8\times {10}^{5}) \\  & =\frac{2048\times {10}^{10}}{r}+(81\times {10}^{8})-(256\times {10}^{5}) \\  & =\frac{2.048\times {10}^{13}}{r}+(8.1\times {10}^{9})-(0.0256\times {10}^{9}) \\  & =\frac{2.048\times {10}^{13}}{r}+((8.1-0.0256)\times {10}^{9}) \\  & =\frac{2.048\times {10}^{13}}{r}+(8.0744\times {10}^{9}).\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider a planet with radius $(1.2\times10^{8})\,\textrm{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g = 18.9\,\textrm{m/s}^2.$
What is the escape velocity of an object launched radially outward from the planet's surface? Assume only the force due to gravity acts on the object, 

Express your answer in scientific notation, rounding to **three significant figures** where appropriate.
:question/worked-solution:
Escape velocity is the minimum launch speed from a planet’s surface required to escape its gravity and reach infinity, neglecting all forces except gravity.

Let $R$ be the planet's radius and $g$ be the planet's surface gravitational acceleration.

According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the planet is

$$
F_\text{in} = G\,\dfrac{mM}{r^2},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, $M$ is the planet's mass, and $r$ is the distance from the planet's center to the object.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-F_\textrm{in}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, 

$$
a=-\dfrac{k}{r^2},
$$

 with constant of proportionality $k=GM > 0.$

When at the surface, $r=R,$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-g.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k{:}$

$$
-g = -\dfrac{k}{R^2} 
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
k = gR^2
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a = -\dfrac{gR^2}{r^2}.
$$

Now, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}r} = -\dfrac{gR^2}{r^2}
$$

Solving using separation of variables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int v\frac{dv}{dr}\,dr & =\int (-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}})\,dr \\ \int v\,dv & =-g{R}^{2}\int \frac{1}{{r}^{2}}\,dr \\ \frac{{v}^{2}}{2} & =-g{R}^{2}(-\frac{1}{r})+{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{r}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C=2C_1$ is a constant of integration.

Let $v_0$ be the initial velocity of the object. Applying the initial condition $v(R) = v_0,$ we can solve for $C{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(R)^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{R}+C \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =2gR+C \\ C & ={v}_{0}^{2}-2gR\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation for the velocity of the object is

$$
v^2 = \dfrac{2gR^2}{r} + v_0^2 - 2gR.
$$

For the object to escape the planet's gravity, we require a positive initial velocity, and for the velocity to never equal zero.

Notice in our velocity equation that as $r \to \infty,$ the expression $\dfrac{2gR^2}{r}$ approaches zero. So, for the velocity to never vanish, we must have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{0}^{2}-2gR & \ge 0 \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & \ge 2gR \\ {v}_{0} & \ge \sqrt{2gR}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the minimum velocity of the object to escape the surface of the planet is

$$
v_e = \sqrt{2gR}.
$$

Finally, substituting in the values $R=(1.2\times10^{8})$ and $g=18.9,$ we conclude that the escape velocity is

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{e} & =\sqrt{2\cdot (1.2\times {10}^{8})\cdot 18.9} \\  & =\sqrt{(2\cdot 1.2\cdot 18.9)\times {10}^{8}} \\  & =\sqrt{45.36}\times \sqrt{{10}^{8}} \\  & ≈(6.73\times {10}^{4})\,\text{m/s},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three significant figures.

:question/problem:
A water-treatment holding tank initially holds $700\,\textrm{L}$ of liquid containing $12\,\textrm{kg}$ of dissolved coagulant.
A feed solution containing $0.05\,\textrm{kg/L}$ of the coagulant is pumped into the tank at a rate of $30\,\textrm{L/min},$ while the completely mixed liquid is drained out at a rate of $20\,\textrm{L/min}.$
Find, rounded to two decimal places, the amount of coagulant in the tank $8$ minutes after pumping begins.
:question/worked-solution:
Let $Q$ be the amount of coagulant in the tank at time $t,$ in minutes. Then, the derivative 

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t.$ This is equal to the rate at which coagulant enters the tank minus the rate at which coagulant leaves the tank.

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = Q'_{\textrm{in}} - Q'_{\textrm{out}}
$$

Note that the units of $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t}, Q'_{\textrm{in}}$ and $Q'_{\textrm{out}}$ are $\textrm{kg}/\textrm{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which coagulant enters the tank.

Note that a feed solution containing $0.05\,\textrm{kg/L}$ of the coagulant enters the tank at a rate of $30\,\textrm{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *coagulant* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.05\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (30\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.05\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (30\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =1.5\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which coagulant exits the tank.

To find the rate at which coagulant leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $700\,\textrm{L}$ of liquid; a solution enters at $30\,\textrm{L/min}$ and leaves at $20\,\textrm{L/min}.$
As a result, the volume of liquid in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
700 + 30t - 20t = (700+10t)\,\textrm{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the amount of coagulant in the tank, the *concentration* of the mixed solution at time $t$ is

$$
\dfrac{Q}{700+10t}\,\textrm{kg/L}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of $20\,\textrm{L/min},$ *coagulant* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(20\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{700+10t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(20\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{700+10t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{20Q}{700+10t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{70+t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =1.5-\frac{2Q}{70+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{70+t}Q=1.5.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(70+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|70+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(70+t)^{2}} \\  & =(70+t)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t) = (70+t)^2$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(70+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{70+t}Q) & =(70+t)^{2}\cdot 1.5 \\ (70+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(70+t)Q & =1.5(70+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(70+t)^{2}) & =1.5(70+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(70+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 1.5(70+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(70+t)^{2} & =1.5\cdot \frac{1}{3}(70+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =0.5(70+t)+\frac{C}{(70+t)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the tank initially contains $12\,\textrm{kg}$ of coagulant. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0) = 12,$ and solve for $C{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =12 \\ 0.5(70+0)+\frac{C}{(70+0)^{2}} & =12 \\ 35+\frac{C}{{70}^{2}} & =12 \\ \frac{C}{{70}^{2}} & =-23 \\ C & =-23(70)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =0.5(70+t)-\frac{23(70)^{2}}{(70+t)^{2}} \\  & =0.5(70+t)-23{(\frac{70}{70+t})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,  the amount of coagulant in the tank $8$ minutes after pumping begins is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(8) & =0.5(70+8)-23{(\frac{70}{70+8})}^{2} \\  & =39-23{(\frac{70}{78})}^{2} \\  & ≈20.48\,\text{kg},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

:question/problem: A syrup mixing tank in a confectionery factory can hold up to $240\,\textrm{gal}$ of liquid. Initially, it contains $96\,\textrm{gal}$ of syrup solution with $32\,\textrm{lb}$ of dissolved sugar. A more concentrated syrup with concentration $1.5\,\textrm{lb/gal}$ flows into the tank at a rate of $24\,\textrm{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed solution drains out at a rate of $16\,\textrm{gal/min}.$ Rounded to one decimal place, find the amount of sugar in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow.
:question/worked-solution:
Since $Q$ is the amount of sugar in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which sugar enters the tank minus the rate at which sugar leaves the tank.

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = Q'_{\textrm{in}} - Q'_{\textrm{out}}
$$

Note that the units of $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t}, Q'_{\textrm{in}}$ and $Q'_{\textrm{out}}$ are $\textrm{lb}/\textrm{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which sugar enters the tank.

First, note that a solution containing $1.5\,\textrm{lb/gal}$ of sugar enters the tank at a rate of $24\,\textrm{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *sugar* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(1.5\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (24\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(1.5\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (24\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =36\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which sugar exits the tank.

To find the rate at which sugar leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of solution in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $96\,\textrm{gal}$ of solution; solution enters at $24\,\textrm{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $16\,\textrm{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t) = 96 + 24t - 16t = 8(12+t)\,\textrm{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of sugar in the tank, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\dfrac{Q}{8(12 + t)}\,\textrm{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $16\,\textrm{gal/min},$ *sugar* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(16\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{8(12+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(16\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{8(12+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{16Q}{8(12+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{12+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =36-\frac{2Q}{12+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} + \dfrac{2}{12 + t}\,Q = 36.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(12+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|12+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(12+t)^{2}} \\  & =(12+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t) = (12+t)^2$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(12+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{12+t}\,Q) & =(12+t)^{2}\cdot 36 \\ (12+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(12+t)Q & =36(12+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(12+t)^{2}) & =36(12+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(12+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 36(12+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(12+t)^{2} & =36\cdot \frac{1}{3}(12+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =12(12+t)+\frac{C}{(12+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the tank initially contains $32\,\textrm{lb}$ of sugar. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0) = 32,$ and solve for $C{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =32 \\ 12(12+0)+\frac{C}{(12+0)^{2}} & =32 \\ 12\cdot 12+\frac{C}{(12)^{2}} & =32 \\ 144+\frac{C}{{12}^{2}} & =32 \\ \frac{C}{{12}^{2}} & =-112 \\ C & =-112(12)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =12(12+t)-\frac{112(12)^{2}}{(12+t)^{2}} \\  & =12(12+t)-112{(\frac{12}{12+t})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let $t_o$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $240\,\textrm{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V(t_o) = 240$ to solve for $t_o{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =240 \\ 96+24{t}_{o}-16{t}_{o} & =240 \\ 96+8{t}_{o} & =240 \\ 8{t}_{o} & =144 \\ {t}_{o} & =18\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of sugar in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(18) & =12(12+18)-112{(\frac{12}{12+18})}^{2} \\  & =360-112{(\frac{12}{30})}^{2} \\  & ≈342.1\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Use the definition of Laplace transforms to calculate $F(s) = \mathcal L\{f(t)\},$ where $f(t)$ is given by 
![](images/e7/e70e54b6a70cebd480b86baf9d0e1d90bde0b3d9277c982d5d5e77218d0d2f5d.png)
:question/worked-solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

So, for the piecewise function 
![](images/48/48965cee8a09df4f637b4d997fdb9c90673e69a90ea1320434f9b471a2fed280.png)

we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{2t}\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{3}^{\infty }1\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{2t-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{3}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{(2-s)t}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{3}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the improper integral diverges if $s \leq 0.$

For $s > 0,$ we calculate our Laplace transform as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{(2-s)t}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{3}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2-s}{[{e}^{(2-s)t}]}_{0}^{3}+{\int }_{3}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3(2-s)}-1}{2-s}+{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{3}^{a}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3(2-s)}-1}{2-s}+{lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{-{e}^{-st}}{s})|}_{3}^{a} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3(2-s)}-1}{2-s}-\frac{1}{s}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }({e}^{-as}-{e}^{-3s}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3(2-s)}-1}{2-s}-\frac{1}{s}\cdot (0-{e}^{-3s}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3(2-s)}-1}{2-s}+\frac{{e}^{-3s}}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

valid for $s > 0.$

:question/problem: Use the definition of Laplace transforms to calculate $F(s) = \mathcal L\{f(t)\}$ for $f(t) = u(t - 2) + u(t-6),$ where $u$ is the unit step function.
:question/worked-solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the unit step function is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t)={\begin{aligned}0,\, & t<0 \\ 1,\, & t\ge 0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, for the piecewise functions $u(t-2)$ and $u(t-6),$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t-2) & ={\begin{aligned}0,\, & t<2 \\ 1,\, & t\ge 2\end{aligned} \\ u(t-6) & ={\begin{aligned}0,\, & t<6 \\ 1,\, & t\ge 6.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

![](images/6d/6ddb2983dec1f3221778a336bb6ef3cce3138476b67d64334ab6660184a79f95.png)

So, for our Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}0\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{2}^{6}1\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{6}^{\infty }2\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{6}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{6}^{\infty }2{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the second integral diverges for $s \leq 0.$

For $s > 0,$ we calculate our Laplace transform as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{2}^{6}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{6}^{\infty }2{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{6}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+2{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{6}^{a}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[-\frac{{e}^{-st}}{s}]}_{2}^{6}+2{lim}_{a\to \infty }{(-\frac{{e}^{-st}}{s})|}_{6}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-6s}}{s}+\frac{{e}^{-2s}}{s}-\frac{2}{s}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }({e}^{-sa}-{e}^{-6s}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-2s}}{s}-\frac{{e}^{-6s}}{s}-\frac{2}{s}(0-{e}^{-6s}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-2s}}{s}-\frac{{e}^{-6s}}{s}+\frac{2{e}^{-6s}}{s} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-2s}}{s}+\frac{{e}^{-6s}}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\} =\dfrac{e^{-2s}}{s} +\dfrac{e^{-6s}}{s}, 
\qquad 
s > 0.
$$

To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation with constant coefficients on the left-hand side, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
3\frac{\text{d}{y}_{c}}{\text{d}x}-6{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{2x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x).$ So, we assume the particular solution to be 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
3(-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))-6(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))=4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
(-6\alpha +6\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+(-6\alpha -6\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x).
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-6\alpha +6\beta &=4\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)) \\ -6\alpha -6\beta &=0\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{1}{3},\beta =\frac{1}{3}.$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{2x}+(-\frac{1}{3})\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+(\frac{1}{3})\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

:question/problem: Consider a spherical planet with radius $(2.5\times {10}^{8})\,\text{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g=18.4\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Which equation best models the velocity $v$ of an object projected radially outward from the planet's surface with an initial velocity of $(9.6\times {10}^{4})\,\text{m/s},$ where $r$ is the distance from the planet's center to the object. Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.
:question/worked-solution:
Let $R$ be the planet's radius and $g$ be the planet's surface gravitational acceleration.

According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the planet is

$$
{F}_{\text{in}}=G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, and $M$ is the planet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-{F}_{\text{in}}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, 

$$
a=-\frac{k}{{r}^{2}},
$$

 with constant of proportionality $k=GM>0.$

When at the surface, $r=R,$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-g.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k:$

$$
-g=-\frac{k}{{R}^{2}}\,\,\,⟹\,k=g{R}^{2}
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a=-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}}.
$$

Now, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\frac{dv}{dr}=-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}}
$$

Solving using separation of variables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int v\frac{dv}{dr}\,dr & =\int (-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}})\,dr \\ \int v\,dv & =-g{R}^{2}\int \frac{1}{{r}^{2}}\,dr \\ \frac{{v}^{2}}{2} & =-g{R}^{2}(-\frac{1}{r})+{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{r}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C=2{C}_{1}$ is a constant of integration.

Let ${v}_{0}$ be the initial velocity of the object. Applying the initial condition $v(R)={v}_{0},$ we can solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(R)^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{R}+C \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =2gR+C \\ C & ={v}_{0}^{2}-2gR\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation for the velocity of the object is

$$
{v}^{2}=\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{r}+{v}_{0}^{2}-2gR.
$$

Finally, substituting in the values
$R=(2.5\times {10}^{8}),$
$g=18.4,$ and
${v}_{0}=(9.6\times {10}^{4}),$
we conclude that the equation for the velocity is

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2\cdot 18.4\cdot (2.5\times {10}^{8})^{2}}{r}+(9.6\times {10}^{4})^{2}-2\cdot 18.4\cdot (2.5\times {10}^{8}) \\  & =\frac{230\times {10}^{16}}{r}+(92.16\times {10}^{8})-(92\times {10}^{8}) \\  & =\frac{2.3\times {10}^{18}}{r}+((92.16-92)\times {10}^{8}) \\  & =\frac{2.3\times {10}^{18}}{r}+(0.16\times {10}^{8}) \\  & =\frac{2.3\times {10}^{18}}{r}+(1.6\times {10}^{7}).\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
A de-icing salt reservoir can hold up to $300\,\text{gal}$ of liquid. Initially, it contains $180\,\text{gal}$ of brine with $54\,\text{lb}$ of dissolved salt. A stronger brine with concentration $0.8\,\text{lb/gal}$ flows into the reservoir at a rate of $6\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed brine drains out at a rate of $4\,\text{gal/min}.$
Find the amount of salt in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow.
:question/worked-solution:
Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which minerals enter the tank minus the rate at which minerals leave the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which minerals enter the tank.

First, note that a brine solution containing $0.8\,\text{lb/gal}$ of salt enters the reservoir at a rate of $6\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *salt* enters the reservoir is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.8\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (6\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.8\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (6\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =4.8\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which minerals exit the tank.

To find the rate at which salt leaves the reservoir, we must first determine the volume of brine in the reservoir at time $t.$

The reservoir initially contains $180\,\text{gal}$ of brine; brine enters at $6\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed brine leaves at $4\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of brine in the reservoir after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=180+6t-4t=2(90+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the reservoir is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the reservoir, the concentration of the brine at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{2(90+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed brine leaves at a rate of $4\,\text{gal/min},$ *salt* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(4\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{2(90+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(4\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{2(90+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{4Q}{2(90+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{90+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =4.8-\frac{2Q}{90+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{90+t}\,Q=4.8.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(90+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|90+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(90+t)^{2}} \\  & =(90+t)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(90+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(90+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{90+t}\,Q) & =(90+t)^{2}\cdot 4.8 \\ (90+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(90+t)Q & =4.8(90+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(90+t)^{2}) & =4.8(90+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(90+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 4.8(90+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(90+t)^{2} & =4.8\cdot \frac{1}{3}(90+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =1.6(90+t)+\frac{C}{(90+t)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the reservoir initially contains $54\,\text{lb}$ of salt. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=54,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =54 \\ 1.6(90+0)+\frac{C}{(90+0)^{2}} & =54 \\ 144+\frac{C}{(90)^{2}} & =54 \\ C & =-90(90)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =1.6(90+t)-\frac{90(90)^{2}}{(90+t)^{2}} \\  & =1.6(90+t)-90{(\frac{90}{90+t})}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the reservoir begins to overflow. The reservoir has a capacity of $300\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=300$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =300 \\ 2(90+{t}_{o}) & =300 \\ 90+{t}_{o} & =150 \\ {t}_{o} & =60\,\text{min}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the amount of salt in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(60) & =1.6(90+60)-90{(\frac{90}{90+60})}^{2} \\  & =240-90{(\frac{9}{15})}^{2} \\  & =207.6\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
A storage tank initially holds $600\,\text{L}$ of liquid containing $5\,\text{kg}$ of dissolved stabilizer.
A feed solution containing $0.04\,\text{kg/L}$ of the stabilizer is pumped into the tank at a rate of $15\,\text{L/min},$ while the completely mixed liquid is drained out at a rate of $10\,\text{L/min}.$
Find, rounded to two decimal places, the amount of stabilizer in the tank $10$ minutes after pumping begins.
:question/worked-solution:
Let $Q$ be the amount of stabilizer in the tank at time $t,$ in minutes. Then, the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t.$ This is equal to the rate at which stabilizer enters the tank minus the rate at which stabilizer leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which stabilizer enters the tank.

Note that a feed solution containing $0.04\,\text{kg/L}$ of the stabilizer enters the tank at a rate of $15\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *stabilizer* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.04\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (15\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.04\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (15\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0.6\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which stabilizer exits the tank.

To find the rate at which stabilizer leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $600\,\text{L}$ of liquid; a solution enters at $15\,\text{L/min}$ and leaves at $10\,\text{L/min}.$
As a result, the volume of liquid in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
600+15t-10t=(600+5t)\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the amount of stabilizer in the tank, the *concentration* of the mixed solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{600+5t}\,\text{kg/L}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of $10\,\text{L/min},$ *stabilizer* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(10\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{600+5t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(10\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{600+5t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{10Q}{600+5t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{120+t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0.6-\frac{2Q}{120+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{120+t}Q=0.6.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(120+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|120+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(120+t)^{2}} \\  & =(120+t)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(120+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(120+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{120+t}Q) & =(120+t)^{2}\cdot 0.6 \\ (120+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(120+t)Q & =0.6(120+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(120+t)^{2}) & =0.6(120+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(120+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 0.6(120+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(120+t)^{2} & =0.6\cdot \frac{1}{3}(120+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =0.2(120+t)+\frac{C}{(120+t)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the tank initially contains $5\,\text{kg}$ of stabilizer. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=5,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =5 \\ 0.2(120+0)+\frac{C}{(120+0)^{2}} & =5 \\ 24+\frac{C}{{120}^{2}} & =5 \\ \frac{C}{{120}^{2}} & =-19 \\ C & =-19(120)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =0.2(120+t)-\frac{19(120)^{2}}{(120+t)^{2}} \\  & =0.2(120+t)-19{(\frac{120}{120+t})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,  the amount of stabilizer in the tank $10$ minutes after pumping begins is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(10) & =0.2(120+10)-19{(\frac{120}{120+10})}^{2} \\  & =26-19{(\frac{12}{13})}^{2} \\  & ≈9.81\,\text{kg},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

:question/problem:
Consider the d’Alembert differential equation
$y = x(\frac{dy}{dx})^{2} + \frac{dy}{dx}$.
Using the substitution $t = \frac{dy}{dx}$, the equation can be transformed to a first-order linear equation of the form
$\frac{dx}{dt} + P(t)x = Q(t)$.
Find the functions $P$ and $Q$.$P(t) =$
{{field-1}}
$, Q(t) =$
{{field-2}}

Consider the d’Alembert differential equation

$$
y=x(1+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}.
$$

If ${y}^{′}(x)=t,$ then general solution can be expressed in parametric form $(x(t),y(t)),$ where

$$
x(t)=C{e}^{-t}+f(t)
$$

and $C$ is an arbitrary constant. Find the function $f(t).$

*Hint: Under the given transformation, we have*

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x=-2t.
$$

*You may also wish to make use of the following result (constants omitted):*

$$
\int t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t=(t-1){e}^{t}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
A differential equation is a d'Alembert differential equation if it can be expressed in the form

$$
y=xf({y}^{′})+g({y}^{′}),
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are differentiable functions of ${y}^{′}.$ 

We're told that, under the substitution ${y}^{′}(x)=t,$ our d’Alembert differential equation transforms to the first-order linear equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x=-2t.
$$

We'll solve this equation using the method of integrating factors. Since this equation is already of the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+P(t)x=Q(t)
$$

we compute our integrating factor as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int P(t)\,\text{d}t}={e}^{\int 1\,\text{d}t}={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying our differential equation by $I(t)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{t}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x{e}^{t} & =-2t{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Rewriting the left-hand side as an exact derivative, and integrating both sides of the equation with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x{e}^{t}) & =-2t{e}^{t} \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x{e}^{t})\,\text{d}t & =-2\int t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\ x{e}^{t} & =-2\int t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\ x{e}^{t} & =-2(t-1){e}^{t}+C \\ x & =-2(t-1)+C{e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
x(t)=C{e}^{-t}+2-2t
$$

and finally, $f(t)=2-2t.$

:question/problem:
Consider the d’Alembert differential equation

$$
y=x{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}+(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}).
$$

If ${y}^{′}(x)=t,$ then general solution can be expressed in parametric form $(x(t),y(t)),$ where

$$
y(t)=(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|-t+C}{(1-t)^{2}})f(t)+g(t)
$$

and $C$ is an arbitrary constant. Find $f(t)+g(t).$

*Hint: Under the given transformation, we have*

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{2x}{t-1}=\frac{1}{t(1-t)}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
A differential equation is a d'Alembert differential equation if it can be expressed in the form

$$
y=xf({y}^{′})+g({y}^{′}),
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are differentiable functions of ${y}^{′}.$ 

We're told that, under the substitution ${y}^{′}(x)=t,$ our d’Alembert differential equation transforms to the first-order linear equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{2x}{t-1}=\frac{1}{t(1-t)}
$$

We'll solve this equation using the method of integrating factors. Since this equation is already of the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+P(t)x=Q(t)
$$

we compute our integrating factor as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int P(t)\,\text{d}t} \\  & ={e}^{\int 2/(t-1)\,\text{d}t} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|t-1|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(t-1)^{2}} \\  & =(t-1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying our differential equation by $I(t)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(t-1)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(t-1)^{2}\frac{2x}{t-1}=(t-1)^{2}\frac{1}{t(1-t)} \\ (t-1)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+2(t-1)x=-(t-1)^{2}\frac{1}{t(t-1)} \\ (t-1)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+2(t-1)x=-\frac{t-1}{t} \\ (t-1)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+2(t-1)x=\frac{1-t}{t}\end{aligned}
$$

Rewriting the left-hand side as an exact derivative, and integrating both sides of the equation with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x(t-1)^{2}) & =\frac{1-t}{t} \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x(t-1)^{2})\,\text{d}t & =\int \frac{1-t}{t}\,\text{d}t \\ x(t-1)^{2} & =\int \frac{1}{t}-1\,\text{d}t \\ x(t-1)^{2} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|-t+C \\ x & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|-t+C}{(t-1)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
x(t)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|-t+C}{(t-1)^{2}}.
$$

To recover $y$, we substitute $x$ into

$$
y=x{t}^{2}+t,
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|-t+C}{(t-1)^{2}}){t}^{2}+t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that $f(t)={t}^{2},g(t)=t,$ and

$$
f(t)+g(t)={t}^{2}+t.
$$
