:question/problem: Calculate the integral $\int ({log}_{4}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
We need to use integration by parts.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=({log}_{4}⁡x)^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2{log}_{4}⁡x}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡4} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \,\text{d}x=x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({log}_{4}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={({log}_{4}⁡x)}^{2}(x)-\int (x)(\frac{2{log}_{4}⁡x}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡4})\,\text{d}x \\  & =x{({log}_{4}⁡x)}^{2}-\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\int {log}_{4}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate  $\int {log}_{4}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{4}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡4} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \,\text{d}x=x.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {log}_{4}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({log}_{4}⁡(x))(x)-\int (x)(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡4})\,\text{d}x \\  & =x{log}_{4}⁡(x)-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\int \,\text{d}x \\  & =x{log}_{4}⁡(x)-\frac{x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({log}_{4}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =x{({log}_{4}⁡x)}^{2}-\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}(x{log}_{4}⁡(x)-\frac{x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+D) \\  & =x{({log}_{4}⁡x)}^{2}-\frac{2x{log}_{4}⁡(x)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+\frac{2x}{{ln}^{2}⁡4}-\frac{2D}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4} \\  & =x({({log}_{4}⁡x)}^{2}-\frac{2{log}_{4}⁡(x)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+\frac{2}{{ln}^{2}⁡4})+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-\frac{2D}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}.$

We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u={ln}^{2}⁡({x}^{3})\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{6\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \,\text{d}x=x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {ln}^{2}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({ln}^{2}⁡({x}^{3}))(x)-\int (x)(\frac{6\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =x{ln}^{2}⁡({x}^{3})-6\int \operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int \operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \,\text{d}x=x.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}))(x)-\int (x)(\frac{3}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})-3\int \text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})-3x+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is a constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {ln}^{2}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x & =x{ln}^{2}⁡({x}^{3})-6(x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})-3x+D) \\  & =x{ln}^{2}⁡({x}^{3})-6x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})+18x+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-6D.$ 

Finally then, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}{ln}^{2}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x & ={[x{ln}^{2}⁡({x}^{3})-6x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})+18x]}_{1}^{e} \\  & =[e{ln}^{2}⁡({e}^{3})-6e\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{3})+18e]-[(1){ln}^{2}⁡({1}^{3})-6(1)\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{3})+18(1)] \\  & =9e-18e+18e-18 \\  & =9e-18.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we pull out the factor of $2$ from the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{3x-4}{2x+3}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{3x-4}{2(x+\frac{3}{2})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{3x-4}{(x+\frac{3}{2})}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.

$$
\begin{aligned} & x & {x}^{0} \\ -\frac{3}{2} & 3 & -4 \\  & ↓ & -\frac{9}{2} \\  & 3 & -\frac{17}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3x-4}{(x+\frac{3}{2})} & =3-\frac{(\frac{17}{2})}{(x+\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =3-\frac{17}{2(x+\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =3-\frac{17}{2x+3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{3x-4}{2x+3}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(3-\frac{17}{2x+3})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[3{\int }_{0}^{2}\text{d}x-17{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2x+3}\,\text{d}x] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[3x-\frac{17}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+3|]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[3(2-0)-\frac{17}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡|2(2)+3|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|2(0)+3|)] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[6-\frac{17}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡7-\operatorname{ln}⁡3)] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[6-\frac{17}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{7}{3})] \\  & =3-\frac{17}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{7}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

First, we pull out the factor of $3$ from the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{0}\frac{2x+5}{3x-1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}\frac{2x+5}{3(x-\frac{1}{3})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{-1}^{0}\frac{2x+5}{(x-\frac{1}{3})}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.

$$
\begin{aligned} & x & {x}^{0} \\ \frac{1}{3} & 2 & 5 \\  & ↓ & \frac{2}{3} \\  & 2 & \frac{17}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2x+5}{(x-\frac{1}{3})} & =2+\frac{(\frac{17}{3})}{(x-\frac{1}{3})} \\  & =2+\frac{17}{3(x-\frac{1}{3})} \\  & =2+\frac{17}{3x-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{0}\frac{2x+5}{3x-1}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{-1}^{0}(2+\frac{17}{3x-1})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[2{\int }_{-1}^{0}\text{d}x+17{\int }_{-1}^{0}\frac{1}{3x-1}\,\text{d}x] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{[2x+\frac{17}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|3x-1|]}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[2(0-(-1))+\frac{17}{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡|3(0)-1|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|3(-1)-1|)] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[2(1)+\frac{17}{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡4)] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[2-\frac{17}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{2})] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[2-\frac{34}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡2] \\  & =\frac{2}{9}[3-17\operatorname{ln}⁡2].\end{aligned}
$$

First, we pull out the factor of $6$ from the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1/12}^{0}\frac{2x+1}{6x+1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-1/12}^{0}\frac{2x+1}{6(x+\frac{1}{6})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{-1/12}^{0}\frac{2x+1}{(x+\frac{1}{6})}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.

$$
\begin{aligned} & x & {x}^{0} \\ -\frac{1}{6} & 2 & 1 \\  & ↓ & -\frac{1}{3} \\  & 2 & \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2x+1}{(x+\frac{1}{6})} & =2+\frac{(\frac{2}{3})}{(x+\frac{1}{6})} \\  & =2+\frac{4}{6x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1/12}^{0}\frac{2x+1}{6x+1}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{-1/12}^{0}(2+\frac{4}{6x+1})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[2{\int }_{-1/12}^{0}\text{d}x+4{\int }_{-1/12}^{0}\frac{1}{6x+1}\,\text{d}x] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{[2x+\frac{4}{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡|6x+1|]}_{-1/12}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{[2x+\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|6x+1|]}_{-1/12}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[2(0-(-\frac{1}{12}))+\frac{2}{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡|6(0)+1|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|6(-\frac{1}{12})+1|)] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[2(\frac{1}{12})+\frac{2}{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2}))] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[\frac{1}{6}+\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡2] \\  & =\frac{1}{36}(1+4\operatorname{ln}⁡2).\end{aligned}
$$

First, we pull out the factor of $4$ from the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1/8}^{0}\frac{8x+1}{4x-1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-1/8}^{0}\frac{8x+1}{4(x-\frac{1}{4})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-1/8}^{0}\frac{8x+1}{(x-\frac{1}{4})}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.

$$
\begin{aligned} & x & {x}^{0} \\ \frac{1}{4} & 8 & 1 \\  & ↓ & 2 \\  & 8 & 3\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{8x+1}{(x-\frac{1}{4})} & =8+\frac{3}{(x-\frac{1}{4})} \\  & =8+\frac{12}{4x-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1/8}^{0}\frac{8x+1}{4x-1}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-1/8}^{0}(8+\frac{12}{4x-1})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[8{\int }_{-1/8}^{0}\text{d}x+12{\int }_{-1/8}^{0}\frac{1}{4x-1}\,\text{d}x] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[8x+3\operatorname{ln}⁡|4x-1|]_{-1/8}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[8(0-(-\frac{1}{8}))+3(\operatorname{ln}⁡|4(0)-1|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|4(-\frac{1}{8})-1|)] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[8(\frac{1}{8})+3(\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{2}))] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[1-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{2})].\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{1}^{e}4x({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2{log}_{3}⁡x}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=4x\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int 4x\,\text{d}x=2{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4x({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={({log}_{3}⁡x)}^{2}(2{x}^{2})-\int (2{x}^{2})(\frac{2{log}_{3}⁡x}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{x}^{2}({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}-\frac{4}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\int x{log}_{3}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int x{log}_{3}⁡(x)\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{3}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=x\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int x\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{log}_{3}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({log}_{3}⁡x)(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})-\int (\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}{log}_{3}⁡x}{2}-\frac{1}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\int x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}{log}_{3}⁡x}{2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is a constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4x({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =2{x}^{2}({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}-\frac{4}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}(\frac{{x}^{2}{log}_{3}⁡x}{2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+D) \\  & =2{x}^{2}({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}-\frac{2{x}^{2}{log}_{3}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}+C \\  & =\frac{2{x}^{2}{ln}^{2}⁡x}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}-\frac{2{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}(2{ln}^{2}⁡x-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-\frac{4D}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}.$ 

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{3}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}.$

Finally then, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}4x({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}(2{ln}^{2}⁡x-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1)]}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}(2{ln}^{2}⁡e-2\operatorname{ln}⁡e+1)-\frac{{1}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}(2{ln}^{2}⁡1-2\operatorname{ln}⁡1+1) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}(2-2+1)-\frac{1}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}(0-0+1) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}-1}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we complete the square in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-6x+18 & ={x}^{2}-2\cdot 3x+({3}^{2}-{3}^{2})+18 \\  & =({x}^{2}-2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2})-9+18 \\  & =(x-3)^{2}+9\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}-6x+18}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{(x-3)^{2}+9}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+((x-3)/3)^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent:

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $(\frac{x-3}{3}).$

So, let's perform the substitution

$$
u=\frac{x-3}{3}.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=3\,\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}-6x+18}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+((x-3)/3)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot 3\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x-3}{3})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{4-(6x+1)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{4(1-(6x+1)^{2}/4)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{4}\cdot \sqrt{1-(6x+1)^{2}/4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{2\sqrt{1-(6x+1)^{2}/4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(6x+1)^{2}/4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-((6x+1)/2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse sine:

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $(\frac{6x+1}{2}).$

So, let's perform the substitution 

$$
u=\frac{6x+1}{2}.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{4-(6x+1)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-((6x+1)/2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{6x+1}{2})+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{|x-3|\sqrt{(x-3)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{|x-3|\sqrt{(x-3)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse secant:

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $(x-3).$

So, let's perform the substitution 

$$
u=x-3.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{|x-3|\sqrt{(x-3)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{|x-3|\sqrt{(x-3)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\,\text{arcsec}(u)+C \\  & =2\,\text{arcsec}(x-3)+C\end{aligned}
$$

First, we complete the square for the expression inside the square root:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-8x+15 & ={x}^{2}-2\cdot 4x+({4}^{2}-{4}^{2})+15 \\  & =({x}^{2}-8x+16)-16+15 \\  & =(x-4)^{2}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above in the given integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{|x-4|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-8x+15}}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{|x-4|\sqrt{(x-4)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse secant:

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}\,u+C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $x-4.$

So, let's perform the substitution 

$$
u=x-4.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{|x-4|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-8x+15}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{|x-4|\sqrt{(x-4)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\text{arcsec}\,u+C \\  & =\text{arcsec}(x-4)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we complete the square for the expression inside the square root:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+4x+3 & ={x}^{2}+2\cdot 2x+({2}^{2}-{2}^{2})+3 \\  & =({x}^{2}+4x+4)-4+3 \\  & =(x+2)^{2}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above in the given integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{|x+2|\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4x+3}}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{|x+2|\sqrt{(x+2)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse secant:

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}\,u+C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $x+2.$

So, let's perform the substitution 

$$
u=x+2.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{|x+2|\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4x+3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{|x+2|\sqrt{(x+2)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\text{arcsec}\,u+C \\  & =\text{arcsec}(x+2)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=({log}_{2}⁡x)^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2{log}_{2}⁡x}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=9{x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int 9{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=3{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 9{x}^{2}({log}_{2}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={({log}_{2}⁡x)}^{2}(3{x}^{3})-\int (3{x}^{3})(\frac{2{log}_{2}⁡x}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{x}^{3}{({log}_{2}⁡x)}^{2}-\frac{6}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int {x}^{2}{log}_{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate  $\int {x}^{2}{log}_{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{2}⁡x\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{log}_{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({log}_{2}⁡x)(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})-\int (\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}{log}_{2}⁡x}{3}-\frac{1}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}{log}_{2}⁡x}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 9{x}^{2}({log}_{2}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =3{x}^{3}{({log}_{2}⁡x)}^{2}-\frac{6}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(\frac{{x}^{3}{log}_{2}⁡x}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+D) \\  & =3{x}^{3}{({log}_{2}⁡x)}^{2}-\frac{2{x}^{3}{log}_{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3{ln}^{2}⁡2}+C \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{3}{ln}^{2}⁡x}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}-\frac{2{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}+\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3{ln}^{2}⁡2}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}(3{ln}^{2}⁡x-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\frac{2}{3})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-\frac{6D}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{2}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$

Finally then, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}9{x}^{2}({log}_{2}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & ={[\frac{{x}^{3}}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}(3{ln}^{2}⁡x-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\frac{2}{3})]}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3}}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}(3{ln}^{2}⁡e-2\operatorname{ln}⁡e+\frac{2}{3})-\frac{{1}^{3}}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}(3{ln}^{2}⁡1-2\operatorname{ln}⁡1+\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3}}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}(3-2+\frac{2}{3})-\frac{1}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}(0-0+\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =\frac{5{e}^{3}}{3{ln}^{2}⁡2}-\frac{2}{3{ln}^{2}⁡2} \\  & =\frac{5{e}^{3}-2}{3{ln}^{2}⁡2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u={({log}_{3}⁡({x}^{2}))}^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{4{log}_{3}⁡({x}^{2})}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \,\text{d}x=x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {({log}_{3}⁡({x}^{2}))}^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x{({log}_{3}⁡({x}^{2}))}^{2}-\int (x)(\frac{4{log}_{3}⁡({x}^{2})}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =x{({log}_{3}⁡({x}^{2}))}^{2}-\frac{4}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\int {log}_{3}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate  $\int {log}_{3}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{3}⁡({x}^{2})\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \,\text{d}x=x.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {log}_{3}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({log}_{3}⁡({x}^{2}))(x)-\int (x)(\frac{2}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =x{log}_{3}⁡({x}^{2})-\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\int \,\text{d}x \\  & =x{log}_{3}⁡({x}^{2})-\frac{2x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {({log}_{3}⁡({x}^{2}))}^{2}\,\text{d}x & =x{({log}_{3}⁡({x}^{2}))}^{2}-\frac{4}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}(x{log}_{3}⁡({x}^{2})-\frac{2x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+D) \\  & =x{({log}_{3}⁡({x}^{2}))}^{2}-\frac{4x{log}_{3}⁡({x}^{2})}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+\frac{8x}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}+C \\  & =\frac{x{ln}^{2}⁡({x}^{2})}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}-\frac{4x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}+\frac{8x}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}+C \\  & =\frac{x}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}({ln}^{2}⁡({x}^{2})-4\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})+8)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-\frac{4D}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}.$

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{3}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}.$

Finally then, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}{({log}_{3}⁡({x}^{2}))}^{2}\,\text{d}x & ={[\frac{x}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}({ln}^{2}⁡({x}^{2})-4\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})+8)]}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{e}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}({ln}^{2}⁡({e}^{2})-4\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2})+8)-\frac{1}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}({ln}^{2}⁡({1}^{2})-4\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{2})+8) \\  & =\frac{e}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}(4-8+8)-\frac{1}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}(0-0+8) \\  & =\frac{4e-8}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{1}^{e}25{x}^{4}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2} & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=25{x}^{4} & \,⟹\,v=\int 25{x}^{4}\text{d}x=5{x}^{5}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 25{x}^{4}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & ={(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}(5{x}^{5})-\int (5{x}^{5})(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x})\text{d}x \\  & =5{x}^{5}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-10\int {x}^{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int {x}^{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡x & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={x}^{4} & \,⟹\,v=\int {x}^{4}\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x(\frac{{x}^{5}}{5})-\int (\frac{{x}^{5}}{5})(\frac{1}{x})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{5}-\frac{1}{5}\int {x}^{4}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{5}-\frac{{x}^{5}}{25}+D\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 25{x}^{4}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\text{d}x & =5{x}^{5}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-10\int {x}^{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\text{d}x \\  & =5{x}^{5}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-10(\frac{{x}^{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{5}-\frac{{x}^{5}}{25}+D) \\  & =5{x}^{5}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-2{x}^{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\frac{2{x}^{5}}{5}-10D \\  & ={x}^{5}(5{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\frac{2}{5})+C\,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-10D.$ Finally then, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}25{x}^{4}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\text{d}x & ={[{x}^{5}(5{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\frac{2}{5})]}_{1}^{e} \\  & =[{e}^{5}(5{(\operatorname{ln}⁡e)}^{2}-2\operatorname{ln}⁡e+\frac{2}{5})]-[{1}^{5}(5{(\operatorname{ln}⁡1)}^{2}-2\operatorname{ln}⁡1+\frac{2}{5})] \\  & =[{e}^{5}(5-2+\frac{2}{5})]-\frac{2}{5} \\  & =\frac{17{e}^{5}-2}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Calculate $\int \frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x$ using integration by parts.
:question/worked-solution:
First, we let

$$
I=\int \frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={ln}^{2}⁡x & \,⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4x} & \,⇒\,v=\int \frac{1}{4x}\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int \frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={ln}^{2}⁡x(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4})(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{3}⁡x}{4}-2\int \frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{3}⁡x}{4}-2I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $I,$ remembering to add a constant of integration $C$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\frac{{ln}^{3}⁡x}{4}-2I \\ 3I & =\frac{{ln}^{3}⁡x}{4} \\ I & =\frac{{ln}^{3}⁡x}{12}+C\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{{ln}^{6}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x$ using integration by parts.
:question/worked-solution:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I=\int \frac{{ln}^{6}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={ln}^{6}⁡x & \,⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{6{ln}^{5}⁡x}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x} & \,⇒\,v=\int \frac{1}{x}\text{d}x=\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int \frac{{ln}^{6}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({ln}^{6}⁡x)(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)(\frac{6{ln}^{5}⁡x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={ln}^{7}⁡x-6\int \frac{{ln}^{6}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={ln}^{7}⁡x-6I.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $I.$ We can ignore the constant of integration in this case, because it is insignificant for further evaluation of the definite integral.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={ln}^{7}⁡x-6I \\ 7I & ={ln}^{7}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{ln}^{7}⁡x}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{{ln}^{6}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{7}({ln}^{7}⁡x){|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{1}{7}({ln}^{7}⁡(e)-{ln}^{7}⁡(1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{{ln}^{9}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x$ using integration by parts.
:question/worked-solution:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I=\int \frac{{ln}^{9}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={ln}^{9}⁡x & \,⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{9{ln}^{8}⁡x}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4x} & \,⇒\,v=\int \frac{1}{4x}\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int \frac{{ln}^{9}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({ln}^{9}⁡x)(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4})(\frac{9{ln}^{8}⁡x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{10}⁡x}{4}-9\int \frac{{ln}^{9}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{10}⁡x}{4}-9I.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $I.$ We can ignore the constant of integration in this case, because it is insignificant for further evaluation of the definite integral.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\frac{{ln}^{10}⁡x}{4}-9I \\ 10I & =\frac{{ln}^{10}⁡x}{4} \\ I & =\frac{{ln}^{10}⁡x}{40}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{{ln}^{9}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{40}({ln}^{10}⁡x){|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{1}{40}({ln}^{10}⁡(e)-{ln}^{10}⁡(1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{40}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Solve the inequality $\frac{1}{3}{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x+1}\le \frac{1}{9}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Isolating the exponential term, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x+1} & \le \frac{1}{9} \\ {(\frac{1}{2})}^{x+1} & \le \frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡[{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x+1}] & \le \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{3}) \\ (x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2}) & \le \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{3}) \\ (x+1)(\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & \le \operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ (x+1)(-\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & \le -\operatorname{ln}⁡3.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, note that $-\operatorname{ln}⁡2$ is a negative quantity, so when we divide both sides by it, we need to flip the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & \ge \frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{-\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ x & \ge \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-1\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Solve the inequality ${(\frac{3}{4})}^{x+6}+1\ge 2.$
:question/worked-solution:
Isolating the exponential term, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{3}{4})}^{x+6}+1 & \ge 2 \\ {(\frac{3}{4})}^{x+6} & \ge 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡[{(\frac{3}{4})}^{x+6}] & \ge \operatorname{ln}⁡1 \\ (x+6)\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{4}) & \ge 0 \\ (x+6)(\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\operatorname{ln}⁡4) & \ge 0 \\ (x+6)(\operatorname{ln}⁡3-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & \ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, note that $\operatorname{ln}⁡3-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2$ is a negative quantity, so when we divide both sides by it, we need to flip the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+6) & \le \frac{0}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ x+6 & \le 0 \\ x & \le -6\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Solve the inequality $2{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2x+7}+1<-5.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we isolate the exponential term:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2x+7}+1 & <-5 \\ 2{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2x+7} & <-6 \\ {(\frac{1}{3})}^{2x+7} & <-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, recall that a positive number raised to any real power is always positive. Since $\frac{1}{3}>0,$ we have

$$
{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2x+7}>0
$$

for every real value of $x.$

Therefore, ${(\frac{1}{3})}^{2x+7}$ cannot be less than $-3.$ Hence, the inequality

$$
{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2x+7}<-3
$$

has no solutions.

:question/problem: Solve the inequality ${5}^{x-1}<{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2-x}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{x-1} & <{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2-x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({5}^{x-1}) & <\operatorname{ln}⁡[{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2-x}] \\ (x-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡5 & <(2-x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2}) \\ (x-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡5 & <(2-x)(\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\ (x-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡5 & <(2-x)(0-\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\ (x-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡5 & <(x-2)\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡5-\operatorname{ln}⁡5 & <x\operatorname{ln}⁡2-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡5-x\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & <\operatorname{ln}⁡5-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ x(\operatorname{ln}⁡5-\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & <\operatorname{ln}⁡5-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ x & <\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡5-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Calculate $\int \frac{4x-10}{(x-2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\frac{4x-10}{(x-2)^{2}}=\frac{A}{(x-2)}+\frac{B}{(x-2)^{2}}
$$

To determine the coefficients $A,$ and $B,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $(x-2)^{2}$ and get

$$
4x-10=A(x-2)+B.
$$

Plugging in $x=2,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4(2)-10 & =A(2-2)+B \\ -2 & =0+B \\ B & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, plugging in $x=0$ and substituting the known value of $B,$ we can solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4(0)-10 & =A(0-2)+B \\ -10 & =-2A-2 \\ -2A & =-8 \\ A & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integrand as the partial sum

$$
\frac{4x-10}{(x-2)^{2}}=\frac{4}{(x-2)}-\frac{2}{(x-2)^{2}}.
$$

Finally, we integrate this expression term by term to get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4x-10}{(x-2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{4}{(x-2)}-\frac{2}{(x-2)^{2}})\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\int \frac{1}{x-2}\,\text{d}x-2\int \frac{1}{(x-2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-2|-2(-\frac{1}{x-2})+C \\  & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-2|+\frac{2}{x-2}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

What is the equation of the parabola shown above?

$$

:question/problem: Evaluate ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡4x}{x}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\operatorname{ln}⁡4x=\infty $ and ${lim}_{x\to \infty }x=\infty ,$ respectively, so we have the case $\frac{\infty }{\infty }.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡4x}{x} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{[\operatorname{ln}⁡4x]^{′}}{{[x]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{1}{x})}{1} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{1}{x} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{(\frac{1}{x})}{\operatorname{cot}⁡x}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{1}{x}=\infty $ and ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\infty ,$ respectively, so we have the case $\frac{\infty }{\infty }.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{(\frac{1}{x})}{\operatorname{cot}⁡x} & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{{[\frac{1}{x}]}^{′}}{{[\operatorname{cot}⁡x]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})}{-{csc}^{2}⁡x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})}{(\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x}{{x}^{2}} \\  & ={({lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{(\frac{1}{x})}{\operatorname{cot}⁡x} & ={({lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x})}^{2} \\  & ={({lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{[\operatorname{sin}⁡x]^{′}}{[x]^{′}})}^{2} \\  & ={({lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{1})}^{2} \\  & ={(\operatorname{cos}⁡0)}^{2} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate ${lim}_{x\to {\frac{\pi }{2}}^{-}}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)}.$

Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are ${lim}_{x\to {\frac{\pi }{2}}^{-}}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)=-\infty $ and ${lim}_{x\to {\frac{\pi }{2}}^{-}}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)=\infty ,$ respectively, so we have the case $\frac{-\infty }{\infty }.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {\frac{\pi }{2}}^{-}}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)} & ={lim}_{x\to {\frac{\pi }{2}}^{-}}\frac{[\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)]^{′}}{{[\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {\frac{\pi }{2}}^{-}}\frac{(-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x})}{(\frac{{sec}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x})} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to {\frac{\pi }{2}}^{-}}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x}{{sec}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to {\frac{\pi }{2}}^{-}}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x})}{(\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x})\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to {\frac{\pi }{2}}^{-}}\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x}{(\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}){cos}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to {\frac{\pi }{2}}^{-}}{sin}^{2}⁡x \\  & =-{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt{x}}{{ln}^{2}⁡x}.$

Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\sqrt{x}=\infty $ and ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{ln}^{2}⁡x=\infty ,$ respectively, so we have the case $\frac{\infty }{\infty }.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt{x}}{{ln}^{2}⁡x} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{[\sqrt{x}]^{′}}{{[{ln}^{2}⁡x]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}})}{(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{x}{4\sqrt{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt{x}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x}.\end{aligned}
$$

The resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{\infty }{\infty }.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt{x}}{{ln}^{2}⁡x} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt{x}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{[\sqrt{x}]^{′}}{[4\operatorname{ln}⁡x]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}})}{(\frac{4}{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{x}{8\sqrt{x}} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\sqrt{x} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Let $f$ be a function such that ${f}^{′}(x)=2{e}^{2x}x(x+1)$ and $f(1)={e}^{2}.$ Use the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=1$ to estimate the value of $f(\frac{3}{4}).$
:question/worked-solution:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(1)+{f}^{′}(1)(x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $f(1)={e}^{2},$ and since ${f}^{′}(x)=2{e}^{2x}x(x+1),$ then ${f}^{′}(1)=2{e}^{2\cdot 1}\cdot 1(1+1)=4{e}^{2}.$ So, the tangent line approximation is given by

$$
L(x)={e}^{2}+4{e}^{2}(x-1).
$$

Now, we can approximate $f(\frac{3}{4})$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=\frac{3}{4}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{3}{4}) & ≈L(\frac{3}{4}) \\  & ={e}^{2}+4{e}^{2}(\frac{3}{4}-1) \\  & ={e}^{2}+4{e}^{2}(-\frac{1}{4}) \\  & ={e}^{2}-{e}^{2} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

To determine the coefficients $A,B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $(3x+1)^{3}$ and get

$$

and substituting back into $A+B=-1,$ we get

:question/problem:
Given that 

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}+5x-2}{(x+1)({x}^{2}+5)}=\frac{2x+B}{{x}^{2}+5}-\frac{1}{x+1},
$$

where $B$ is a constant to be found, calculate $\int \frac{{x}^{2}+5x-2}{(x+1)({x}^{2}+5)}\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the constant $B.$ Multiplying both sides of the given equality by $(x+1)({x}^{2}+5)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+5x-2 & =(2x+B)(x+1)-({x}^{2}+5).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=0$  into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{0}^{2}+5(0)-2 & =(2(0)+B)(0+1)-({0}^{2}+5) \\ -2 & =B-5 \\ B & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

 

We now integrate this function term by term, adding the constant of integration at the very end.

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}+5x-2}{(x+1)({x}^{2}+5)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{2x+3}{{x}^{2}+5}-\frac{1}{x+1})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+5}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{3}{{x}^{2}+5}\,\text{d}x-\int \frac{1}{x+1}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

For the first integral, we use the substitution ${x}^{2}+5=u.$ Then, $2x\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u,$ and we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+5}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u| \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+5).\end{aligned}
$$

For the second integral, we use the fact that $\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{a}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{a}),$ which results in

$$
\begin{aligned}3\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+5}\,\text{d}x & =3\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+(\sqrt{5})^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{5}}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{\sqrt{5}}) \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{5}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{5}x}{5}).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, for the third integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{x+1}\text{d}x=\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+1|.
$$

So, we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}+5x-2}{(x+1)({x}^{2}+5)}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+5)+\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{5}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{5}x}{5})-\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+1|+C\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Substituting $x=0$  into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4(0)^{2}+20 & =(0-2)(0+2)+D({0}^{2}+8) \\ 20 & =-4+8D \\ 24 & =8D \\ D & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

 

We now integrate this function term by term, adding the constant of integration at the very end.

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4{x}^{2}+20}{(x+2)({x}^{2}+8)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{x-2}{{x}^{2}+8}+\frac{3}{x+2})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{x}{{x}^{2}+8}\,\text{d}x-2\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+8}\,\text{d}x+3\int \frac{1}{x+2}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}2\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+8}\,\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+(2\sqrt{2})^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\cdot \operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{2\sqrt{2}}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{2}x}{4}).\end{aligned}

$$

So, we get the following result:

$$

\begin{aligned}{0}^{2}-5(0)-27 & =(2(0)+B)(0+1)-({0}^{2}+20) \\ -27 & =B-20 \\ B & =-7.\end{aligned}
$$

 

We now integrate this function term by term, adding the constant of integration at the very end.

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}-5x-27}{(x+1)({x}^{2}+20)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{2x-7}{{x}^{2}+20}-\frac{1}{x+1})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+20}\,\text{d}x-7\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+20}\,\text{d}x-\int \frac{1}{x+1}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

For the first integral, we use the substitution ${x}^{2}+20=u.$ Then, $2x\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u,$ and we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+20}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u| \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+20).\end{aligned}
$$

For the second integral, we use the fact that $\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{a}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{a}),$ which results in

$$
\begin{aligned}7\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+20}\,\text{d}x & =7\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+(2\sqrt{5})^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =7\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{2\sqrt{5}}) \\  & =\frac{7\sqrt{5}}{10}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{5}x}{10}).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, for the third integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{x+1}\text{d}x=\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+1|.
$$

So, we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}-5x-27}{(x+1)({x}^{2}+20)}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+20)-\frac{7\sqrt{5}}{10}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{5}x}{10})-\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+1|+C\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Calculate the integral of $\frac{3{x}^{2}-9x+5}{({x}^{2}+1)(x-4)}.$
:question/worked-solution:
The quadratic factor ${x}^{2}+1$ is irreducible, so we proceed with the following partial fraction decomposition:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3{x}^{2}-9x+5}{({x}^{2}+1)(x-4)} & =\frac{Ax+B}{{x}^{2}+1}+\frac{C}{x-4}\end{aligned}
$$

To determine the coefficients $A,B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $({x}^{2}+1)(x-4),$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-9x+5 & =(Ax+B)(x-4)+C({x}^{2}+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for the unknown constants using the usual methods, we get $A=2,B=-1,$ and $C=1.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3{x}^{2}-9x+5}{({x}^{2}+1)(x-4)} & =\frac{2x-1}{{x}^{2}+1}+\frac{1}{x-4}\end{aligned}
$$

We now integrate this function term by term, adding the constant of integration at the very end.

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3{x}^{2}-9x+5}{({x}^{2}+1)(x-4)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{2x-1}{{x}^{2}+1}+\frac{1}{x-4})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x-\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{x-4}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

For the first integral, we use the substitution $u={x}^{2}+3.$ Then $\text{d}u=2x\,\text{d}x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{u}\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u| \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|{x}^{2}+1| \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1).\end{aligned}
$$

For the second integral, we use the fact that $\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{a}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{a}),$ which results in

$$
\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x).
$$

Finally, for the third integral, we have

$$
\int \frac{1}{x-4}\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-4|.
$$

So, we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3{x}^{2}-9x+5}{({x}^{2}+1)(x-4)}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x-\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{x-4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-4|+K\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the integral of $\frac{-{x}^{2}-7x}{({x}^{2}+6)(x-3)}.$
:question/worked-solution:
The quadratic factor ${x}^{2}+6$ is irreducible, so we proceed with the following partial fraction decomposition:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{-{x}^{2}-7x}{({x}^{2}+6)(x-3)} & =\frac{Ax+B}{{x}^{2}+6}+\frac{C}{x-3}\end{aligned}
$$

To determine the coefficients $A,B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $({x}^{2}+6)(x-3),$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}-7x & =(Ax+B)(x-3)+C({x}^{2}+6).\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for the unknown constants using the usual methods, we get $A=1,B=-4,$ and $C=-2.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{-{x}^{2}-7x}{({x}^{2}+6)(x-3)} & =\frac{x-4}{{x}^{2}+6}-\frac{2}{x-3}\end{aligned}
$$

We now integrate this function term by term, adding the constant of integration at the very end.

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{-{x}^{2}-7x}{({x}^{2}+6)(x-3)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{x-4}{{x}^{2}+6}-\frac{2}{x-3})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+6}\,\text{d}x-4\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+6}\,\text{d}x-2\int \frac{1}{x-3}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

For the first integral, we use the substitution $u={x}^{2}+6.$ Then $\text{d}u=2x\,\text{d}x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+6}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u| \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|{x}^{2}+6| \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+6).\end{aligned}
$$

For the second integral, we use the fact that $\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{a}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{a}),$ which results in

$$
\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+6}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{\sqrt{6}}).
$$

Finally, for the third integral, we have

$$
\int \frac{1}{x-3}\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-3|.
$$

So, we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{-{x}^{2}-7x}{({x}^{2}+6)(x-3)}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+6}\,\text{d}x-4\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+6}\,\text{d}x-2\int \frac{1}{x-3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+6)-\frac{4}{\sqrt{6}}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{\sqrt{6}})-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-3|+K\end{aligned}
$$

The quadratic factor ${x}^{2}+3$ is irreducible, so we proceed with the following partial fraction decomposition:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3{x}^{2}+5x-9}{({x}^{2}+3)(x+4)} & =\frac{Ax+B}{{x}^{2}+3}+\frac{C}{x+4}\end{aligned}
$$

To determine the coefficients $A,B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $({x}^{2}+3)(x+4),$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}+5x-9 & =(Ax+B)(x+4)+C({x}^{2}+3).\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for the unknown constants using the usual methods, we get $A=2,B=-3,$ and $C=1.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3{x}^{2}+5x-9}{({x}^{2}+3)(x+4)} & =\frac{2x-3}{{x}^{2}+3}+\frac{1}{x+4}\end{aligned}
$$

We now integrate this function term by term, adding the constant of integration at the very end.

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3{x}^{2}+5x-9}{({x}^{2}+3)(x+4)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{2x-3}{{x}^{2}+3}+\frac{1}{x+4})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+3}\,\text{d}x-3\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+3}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{x+4}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

For the first integral, we use the substitution $u={x}^{2}+3.$ Then $\text{d}u=2x\,\text{d}x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+3}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{u}\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u| \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|{x}^{2}+3| \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+3).\end{aligned}
$$

For the second integral, we use the fact that $\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{a}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{a}),$ which results in

$$
\begin{aligned}3\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+3}\,\text{d}x & =3\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot \operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}) \\  & =\sqrt{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}x}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, for the third integral, we have

$$
\int \frac{1}{x+4}\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+4|.
$$

So, we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3{x}^{2}+5x-9}{({x}^{2}+3)(x+4)}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+3}\,\text{d}x-3\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+3}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{x+4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+3)-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}x}{3})+\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+4|+K\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral  $\int \frac{4{x}^{2}+12x-12}{x({x}^{2}+4x-6)}\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the quadratic factor in the denominator has a discriminant that is not a perfect square:

$$
D=(4)^{2}-4(1)(-6)=40
$$

We have that $\sqrt{40}$ is not a rational number, which implies that the quadratic factor doesn't factor over the rational numbers.

So, we proceed with the following partial fraction decomposition:

$$
\frac{4{x}^{2}+12x-12}{x({x}^{2}+4x-6)}=\frac{A}{x}+\frac{Bx+C}{{x}^{2}+4x-6}
$$

To determine the coefficients $A,B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $x({x}^{2}+4x-6),$ and we get

$$
4{x}^{2}+12x-12=A({x}^{2}+4x-6)+(Bx+C)x
$$

Solving for the unknown constants using the usual methods, we get $A=2,B=2$, and $C=4.$ Therefore,

$$
\frac{4{x}^{2}+12x-12}{x({x}^{2}+4x-6)}=\frac{2}{x}+\frac{2x+4}{{x}^{2}+4x-6}.
$$

We now integrate this function term by term, adding the constant of integration at the very end.

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4{x}^{2}+12x-12}{x({x}^{2}+4x-6)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{2}{x}+\frac{2x+4}{{x}^{2}+4x-6})\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{2x+4}{{x}^{2}+4x-6}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

For the first integral, we have

$$
\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|.
$$

For the second integral, we use the substitution $u={x}^{2}+4x-6.$ Then $\text{d}u=(2x+4)\,\text{d}x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x+4}{{x}^{2}+4x-6}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{u})\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u| \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|{x}^{2}+4x-6|\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4{x}^{2}+12x-12}{x({x}^{2}+4x-6)}\,\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{2x+4}{{x}^{2}+4x-6}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|{x}^{2}+4x-6|+K.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral  $\int \frac{12-5x}{x(2{x}^{2}+5x-6)}\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the quadratic factor in the denominator has a discriminant that is not a perfect square:

$$
D=(5)^{2}-4(2)(-6)=73
$$

We have that $\sqrt{73}$ is not a rational number, which implies that the quadratic factor doesn't factor over the rational numbers.

So, we proceed with the following partial fraction decomposition:

$$
\frac{12-5x}{x(2{x}^{2}+5x-6)}=\frac{A}{x}+\frac{Bx+C}{2{x}^{2}+5x-6}
$$

To determine the coefficients $A,B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $x(2{x}^{2}+5x-6),$ and we get

$$
12-5x=A(2{x}^{2}+5x-6)+(Bx+C)x
$$

Solving for the unknown constants using the usual methods, we get $A=-2,B=4$, and $C=5.$ Therefore,

$$
\frac{12-5x}{x(2{x}^{2}+5x-6)}=-\frac{2}{x}+\frac{4x+5}{2{x}^{2}+5x-6}.
$$

We now integrate this function term by term, adding the constant of integration at the very end.

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{12-5x}{x(2{x}^{2}+5x-6)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (-\frac{2}{x}+\frac{4x+5}{2{x}^{2}+5x-6})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-2\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{4x+5}{2{x}^{2}+5x-6}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

For the first integral, we have

$$
\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|.
$$

For the second integral, we use the substitution $u=2{x}^{2}+5x-6.$ Then $\text{d}u=(4x+5)\,\text{d}x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4x+5}{2{x}^{2}+5x-6}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{u})\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u| \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|2{x}^{2}+5x-6|\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{12-5x}{x(2{x}^{2}+5x-6)}\,\text{d}x & =-2\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{4x+5}{2{x}^{2}+5x-6}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|2{x}^{2}+5x-6|+K.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $r=\theta +6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ for $\theta =\theta (t),$ and that $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}=7$ at the point where $\theta =\frac{7\pi }{6},$ find $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\theta +6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(r) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\theta +6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\theta +6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot (1-6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}=7$ and $\theta =\frac{7\pi }{6},$ and solve for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot (1-6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =7\cdot (1-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{6})) \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =7\cdot 4 \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =28.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $r=-24\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta $ for $\theta =\theta (t),$ and that $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=12$ at the point where $\theta =\frac{5\pi }{3},$ find $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =-24\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(r) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-24\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(-24\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot (24\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta \operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=12$ and $\theta =\frac{5\pi }{3},$ and solve for $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot 24\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta \operatorname{cot}⁡\theta  \\ 12 & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot (24\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3})\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3})) \\ 12 & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot (24\cdot (-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}})\cdot (-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})) \\ \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} & =\frac{12}{16} \\ \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Solve for $m$ where $\frac{3m-1}{{m}^{3}}+\frac{m+2}{{m}^{3}}=\frac{2m+3}{{m}^{3}}.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we note that $m=0$ is an excluded solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

We multiply both sides of the equation by ${m}^{3},$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3m-1}{{m}^{3}}+\frac{m+2}{{m}^{3}} & =\frac{2m+3}{{m}^{3}} \\ {m}^{3}\cdot (\frac{3m-1}{{m}^{3}}+\frac{m+2}{{m}^{3}}) & ={m}^{3}\cdot (\frac{2m+3}{{m}^{3}}) \\ {m}^{3}\cdot \frac{3m-1}{{m}^{3}}+{m}^{3}\cdot \frac{m+2}{{m}^{3}} & ={m}^{3}\cdot \frac{2m+3}{{m}^{3}} \\ \cancel{{m}^{3}}\cdot \frac{3m-1}{\cancel{{m}^{3}}}+\cancel{{m}^{3}}\cdot \frac{m+2}{\cancel{{m}^{3}}} & =\cancel{{m}^{3}}\cdot \frac{2m+3}{\cancel{{m}^{3}}} \\ 3m-1+m+2 & =2m+3\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $m,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}3m-1+m+2 & =2m+3 \\ 4m+1 & =2m+3 \\ 4m-2m & =3-1 \\ 2m & =2 \\ m & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $m=0$ as a solution. But since $m=1\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $m=1.$

:question/problem: Solve for $z$ where $\frac{z+1}{2z}=2-\frac{2z+1}{2z}.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we note that $z=0$ is an excluded solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

We multiply both sides of the equation by $2z,$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{z+1}{2z} & =2-\frac{2z+1}{2z} \\ 2z\cdot (\frac{z+1}{2z}) & =2z\cdot (2-\frac{2z+1}{2z}) \\ 2z\cdot \frac{z+1}{2z} & =2z\cdot 2-2z\cdot \frac{2z+1}{2z} \\ \cancel{2z}\cdot \frac{z+1}{\cancel{2z}} & =2z\cdot 2-\cancel{2z}\cdot \frac{2z+1}{\cancel{2z}} \\ z+1 & =4z-(2z+1) \\ z+1 & =4z-2z-1\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $z,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}z+1 & =4z-2z-1 \\ z+1 & =2z-1 \\ -z & =-2 \\ z & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $z=0$ as a solution. But since $z=2\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $z=2.$

:question/problem: Solve for $w$ where $1-\frac{2w-3}{3w}=\frac{w+5}{3w}.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we note that $w=0$ is an excluded solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

We multiply both sides of the equation by $3w,$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}1-\frac{2w-3}{3w} & =\frac{w+5}{3w} \\ 3w\cdot (1-\frac{2w-3}{3w}) & =3w\cdot (\frac{w+5}{3w}) \\ 3w\cdot 1-3w\cdot \frac{2w-3}{3w} & =3w\cdot \frac{w+5}{3w} \\ 3w-\cancel{3w}\cdot \frac{2w-3}{\cancel{3w}} & =\cancel{3w}\cdot \frac{w+5}{\cancel{3w}} \\ 3w-(2w-3) & =w+5 \\ 3w-2w+3 & =w+5\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $w,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}3w-2w+3 & =w+5 \\ w+3 & =w+5 \\ w-w & =5-3 \\ 0 & =2,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a false statement. Therefore, we conclude that there is no solution.

:question/problem: Which value of $z$ satisfies the equation $\frac{2z-1}{6z}=\frac{3z-1}{3z}+\frac{z-1}{6z}?$
:question/worked-solution:
We note that $z=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

The equation has the denominators $3z$ and $6z.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}(3z,6z)=6z.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $6z,$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2z-1}{6z}=\frac{3z-1}{3z}+\frac{z-1}{6z} \\ 6z\cdot (\frac{2z-1}{6z}) & =6z\cdot (\frac{3z-1}{3z}+\frac{z-1}{6z}) \\ 6z\cdot (\frac{2z-1}{6z}) & =6z\cdot (\frac{3z-1}{3z})+6z\cdot (\frac{z-1}{6z}) \\ \cancel{6z}\cdot (\frac{2z-1}{\cancel{6z}}) & =2\cdot \cancel{3z}\cdot (\frac{3z-1}{\cancel{3z}})+\cancel{6z}\cdot (\frac{z-1}{\cancel{6z}}) \\ 2z-1 & =2\cdot (3z-1)+z-1\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $z,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}2z-1 & =2(3z-1)+z-1 \\ 2z-1 & =6z-2+z-1 \\ 2z-1 & =7z-3 \\ 2z-7z & =-3+1 \\ -5z & =-2 \\ z & =\frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $z=0$ as a solution. But since $z=\frac{2}{5}\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $z=\frac{2}{5}.$

:question/problem: What are the coordinates of the vertex of the parabola ${x}^{2}=6y?$
:question/worked-solution:
The standard equation of an upward- or downward-opening parabola that has its vertex at the origin is

$$
{x}^{2}=4py,
$$

where $p$ is a constant.

We can rewrite the given equation as 

$$
{x}^{2}=4(\frac{3}{2})y.
$$

It is now clear that our equation is of the standard type with $p=\frac{3}{2}.$ Therefore, our parabola has its vertex at $(0,0).$

:question/problem: What are the coordinates of the vertex of the parabola ${y}^{2}=2x?$
:question/worked-solution:
The standard equation of a left- or right-opening parabola that has its vertex at the origin is

$$
{y}^{2}=4px,
$$

where $p$ is a constant.

We can rewrite the given equation as 

$$
{y}^{2}=4(\frac{1}{2})x.
$$

It is now clear that our equation is of the standard type with $p=\frac{1}{2}.$ Therefore, our parabola has its vertex at $(0,0).$

:question/problem: What are the coordinates of the vertex of the parabola $(y-1)^{2}=5(x+7)?$
:question/worked-solution:
The standard equation of a left- or right-opening parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ is

$$
(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h),
$$

where $p$ is constant.

We can rewrite the given equation as 

$$
(y-1)^{2}=4(\frac{5}{4})(x+7).
$$

It is now clear that our equation is of the standard type with $p=\frac{5}{4}.$ 

Comparing our equation with the standard equation, we can see that we have $h=-7$ and $k=1.$ Therefore, the coordinates of the vertex of the parabola are $(-7,1).$

:question/problem: The radius of a circle is increasing. At a particular moment, the rate of increase of the area of the circle is numerically equal to three-fifths of the rate of increase of the diameter. Determine the radius of the circle at that moment.
:question/worked-solution:
Let $r$  be the radius, $A$ the area, and $D$ the diameter of the circle. We wish to find $r$ at the moment when $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=\frac{3}{5}\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}.$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the area $A$ and the diameter $D$ of the circle. Since $D=2r$ and $A=\pi {r}^{2},$ the relationship between $A$ and $D$ is

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}=\pi {(\frac{D}{2})}^{2}=\frac{\pi {D}^{2}}{4}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\pi {D}^{2}}{4}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}D}(\frac{\pi {D}^{2}}{4}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\pi D}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=\frac{3}{5}\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5}\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\pi D}{2} \\ \frac{3}{5} & =\frac{\pi D}{2} \\ D & =\frac{6}{5\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, since $D=2r,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2r & =\frac{6}{5\pi } \\ r & =\frac{3}{5\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Which value of $x$ satisfies the equation $\frac{3x-1}{{x}^{2}}=\frac{2}{x}-\frac{x-3}{{x}^{2}}?$
:question/worked-solution:
We note that $x=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

The equation has the denominators $x$ and ${x}^{2}.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}(x,{x}^{2})={x}^{2}.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by ${x}^{2},$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3x-1}{{x}^{2}}=\frac{2}{x}-\frac{x-3}{{x}^{2}} \\ {x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{3x-1}{{x}^{2}}) & ={x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{2}{x}-\frac{x-3}{{x}^{2}}) \\ {x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{3x-1}{{x}^{2}}) & ={x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{2}{x})-{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{x-3}{{x}^{2}}) \\ \cancel{{x}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{3x-1}{\cancel{{x}^{2}}}) & =x\cdot \cancel{x}\cdot (\frac{2}{\cancel{x}})-\cancel{{x}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{x-3}{\cancel{{x}^{2}}}) \\ (3x-1) & =x\cdot 2-(x-3) \\ (3x-1) & =2x-(x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $x,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}(3x-1) & =2x-(x-3) \\ 3x-1 & =2x-x+3 \\ 3x-1 & =x+3 \\ 3x-x & =3+1 \\ 2x & =4 \\ x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $x=0$ as a solution. But since $x=2\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $x=2.$

:question/problem: Which value of $m$ satisfies the equation $\frac{3}{m}-\frac{3m+4}{2{m}^{2}}=\frac{1}{{m}^{2}}?$
:question/worked-solution:
We note that $m=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

The equation has the denominators $2{m}^{2},$ ${m}^{2}$ and $m.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}(m,{m}^{2},2{m}^{2})=2{m}^{2}.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $2{m}^{2},$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{m}-\frac{3m+4}{2{m}^{2}} & =\frac{1}{{m}^{2}} \\ 2{m}^{2}\cdot (\frac{3}{m}-\frac{3m+4}{2{m}^{2}}) & =2{m}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{{m}^{2}}) \\ 2{m}^{2}\cdot (\frac{3}{m})-2{m}^{2}\cdot (\frac{3m+4}{2{m}^{2}}) & =2{m}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{{m}^{2}}) \\ 2m\cdot \cancel{m}\cdot (\frac{3}{\cancel{m}})-\cancel{2{m}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{3m+4}{\cancel{2{m}^{2}}}) & =2\cdot \cancel{{m}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{1}{\cancel{{m}^{2}}}) \\ 2m\cdot 3-(3m+4) & =2\cdot 1 \\ 6m-(3m+4) & =2\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $m,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}6m-(3m+4) & =2 \\ 6m-3m-4 & =2 \\ 3m & =6 \\ m & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $m=0$ as a solution. But since $m=2\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $m=2.$

:question/problem:
![](images/4f/4fa141d5af6f23e2eaa1d416def8f84e21e48f775b5b195cbc8ed74e4bb64218.png)

A circular iceberg is melting in such a way that the superficial circle is decreasing its area at a rate of $24\pi \,{\text{km}}^{2}\text{/year}.$ Calculate the rate at which the circumference of the iceberg is decreasing at the moment when the radius is  $6\,\text{km}.$
:question/worked-solution:
In this situation, we want to find $\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}$ at the moment when $r=6,$ and we are also told that  $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=-24\pi .$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the area $A$ and the circumference $C$ of the circle. Since $C=2\pi r$ and $A=\pi {r}^{2},$ the relationship between $A$ and $C$ is

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}=\pi {(\frac{C}{2\pi })}^{2}=\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}C}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{C}{2\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

When $r=6\,\text{km},$ $C=2\pi (6)=12\pi \text{ km}.$ Hence, substituting $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=-24\pi $ and $C=12\pi $, and solving for $\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-24\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{12\pi }{2\pi } \\ -24\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot 6 \\ \frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{24\pi }{6} \\ \frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t} & =-4\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the circumference is decreasing at a rate of $4\pi \text{ km/year}.$

:question/problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}=y(x-5)+4,\,y(0)=-1
$$

We wish to approximate the solution using Euler's method. What entry should be placed in the cell indicated in the table below if the step size is $Δx=\frac{1}{3}?$

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,Δy\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $$ | $$ | $$ |
| $\frac{1}{3}$ | $\,?\,$ | $$ | $$ |
:question/worked-solution:
First, because the initial condition is $y(0)=-1,$ we fill $y=-1$ into the table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,Δy\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $-1$ |  |  |

Next, we compute ${y}^{′}$ according to the given rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(x-5)+4 \\  & =(-1)\cdot (0-5)+4 \\  & =9\end{aligned}
$$

So, we add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,Δy\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $-1$ | $9$ |  |

Next, we compute $Δy$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =9\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,Δy\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $-1$ | $9$ | $3$ |

To get the values of $x$ and $y$ in the *next* row, we add $Δx$ to $x$ and $Δy$ to $y,$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx \\  & =0+\frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{3} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\  & =-1+3 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Adding these results to our table gives the following:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,Δy\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $-1$ | $9$ | $3$ |
| $\frac{1}{3}$ | $2$ |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that $y(\frac{1}{3})≈2.$

:question/problem: $2\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})=$

$$
-{90}^{∘}\le \theta \le {90}^{∘}.
$$

![](images/d9/d93c490adbb5cdbc0e9a09b60eea9b82ab93be8e871e334423abc17ddd62955e.png)

From the values on the unit circle, we see that

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡({315}^{∘})=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.
$$

However, ${315}^{∘}$ does not lie within the range of $\theta .$ To get an angle that's coterminal with ${315}^{∘}$ that lies within the range of $\theta ,$ we subtract ${360}^{∘}.$

$$
{315}^{∘}-{360}^{∘}=-{45}^{∘}.
$$

Hence,

$$
\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})=-{45}^{∘}.
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) & =2\cdot (-{45}^{∘}) \\  & =-{90}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the total area of the region between the curve $y=3{x}^{3}+24$ and the $x$-axis from $x=-3$ to $x=-1.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the intersections of the curve with the $x$-axis:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{3}+24 & =0 \\ 3{x}^{3} & =-24 \\ {x}^{3} & =-8 \\ x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Since $-2\in [-3,-1]$, we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-3$ to $x=-2.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-2$ to $x=-1.$

![](images/80/80315b4862adf8ebb1f91f5c4c7606a59dfa5738c40e34179a745e03a0a25693.png)

Notice that the region for $x\in [-3,-2]$ lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-3}^{-2}(3{x}^{3}+24)\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =-{\int }_{-3}^{-2}(3{x}^{3}+24)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-3{\int }_{-3}^{-2}({x}^{3}+8)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-3\cdot {(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}+8x)|}_{-3}^{-2} \\  & =-3\cdot ([4-16]-[\frac{81}{4}-24]) \\  & =-3\cdot (-12+\frac{15}{4}) \\  & =-3\cdot (-\frac{33}{4}) \\  & =\frac{99}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x\in [-2,-1],$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{-1}(3{x}^{3}+24)\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{-2}^{-1}({x}^{3}+8)\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\cdot {(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}+8x)|}_{-2}^{-1} \\  & =3\cdot ([\frac{1}{4}-8]-[4-16]) \\  & =3\cdot (-\frac{31}{4}+12) \\  & =3\cdot \frac{17}{4} \\  & =\frac{51}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}=\frac{99}{4}+\frac{51}{4}=\frac{75}{2}.
$$

:question/problem: Use calculus to find the closest point to $P(6,7)$ that is equidistant to the points $A(0,1)$ and $B(0,6).$
:question/worked-solution:
Let's sketch the situation.

![](images/c4/c4fd419e12879af4910e5d8364426c14342c3dadb970d8bbc43d31213a6ff947.png)

Note the following:

- The dotted line is the *perpendicular bisector* of the segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$

- All the points on this perpendicular bisector are equidistant to $A$ and $B.$

- Our task is to find the point $Q$ on this line that's closest to $P.$

First, we create a function $S$ which represents the *squared* distance between the point $P(6,7)$ and a general point $Q(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x,y) & =(x-6)^{2}+(y-7)^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-12x-14y+85\end{aligned}
$$

The required point $Q(x,y)$ is equidistant to the points $A(0,1)$ and $B(0,6).$ So, by writing down $(QA)^{2}=(QB)^{2},$ we have the following constraint equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\underbrace{(x-0)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}}_{(QA)^{2}} & =\underbrace{(x-0)^{2}+(y-6)^{2}}_{(QB)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

We make $y$ the subject in the constraint equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-0)^{2}+(y-1)^{2} & =(x-0)^{2}+(y-6)^{2} \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2y+1 & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-12y+36 \\ \cancel{{x}^{2}}+\cancel{{y}^{2}}-2y+1 & =\cancel{{x}^{2}}+\cancel{{y}^{2}}-12y+36 \\ 10y & =35 \\ y & =\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our expression for $S(x,y),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x) & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-12x-14y+85 \\  & ={x}^{2}+{(\frac{7}{2})}^{2}-12x-14(\frac{7}{2})+85 \\  & ={x}^{2}-12x+\frac{193}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the first derivative,

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x) & =2x-12,\end{aligned}
$$

and solve ${S}^{′}(x)=0$ to find the stationary point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ 2x-12 & =0 \\ x & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Let's verify that this stationary point is a minimum. Taking the second derivative, we find

$$
{S}^{″}(6)=2>0.
$$

We conclude that the stationary point $x=6$ indeed minimizes the squared distance. 

Finally, the $y$-coordinate is

$$
y=\frac{7}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the required point is $(6,\frac{7}{2}).$

:question/problem: Find the equation of the right-opening parabola that has its vertex at  $(0,0)$ and passes through the point $(8,4).$
:question/worked-solution:
The general standard equation of a parabola whose vertex is $(0,0)$ and whose arms open right or left is given by

$$
{y}^{2}=4px.
$$

Since we know the given parabola passes through the point $(8,4),$ we can substitute $x=8$ and $y=4$ into the standard equation and solve for $p:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2} & =4px \\ {4}^{2} & =4p(8) \\ 16 & =32p \\ p & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equation of the parabola is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2} & =4px \\ {y}^{2} & =4(\frac{1}{2})x \\ {y}^{2} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the area of the closed region between the curve $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2})$, the $y$-axis, and lines  $y=1$ and $y=3.$
:question/worked-solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2}) \\ {e}^{y} & =\frac{x}{2} \\ x & =2{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{1}^{3}2{e}^{y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{\int }_{1}^{3}{e}^{y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{e}^{y}{|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =2({e}^{3}-{e}^{1}) \\  & =2({e}^{3}-e)\end{aligned}

![](images/3d/3dd6c2de764893839a2d3f817ab08faae32e1b2a09e031d4dfb897782917b8af.png)

What is the equation of the parabola shown above?
:question/worked-solution:
We know that for any upward or downward-opening parabola with its vertex at $(h,k),$ the general standard equation is given by

$$
(x-h)^{2}=4p(y-k).
$$

Here, the vertex has coordinates $(h,k)=(4,0).$ Substituting these into the general standard equation, we get

$$
(x-4)^{2}=4py.
$$

We are left to find the value of $p.$ We know that the given parabola also passes through the point $(9,-5),$ so we can substitute $x=9$ and $y=-5$ into the standard equation and solve for $p:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-4)^{2} & =4py \\ (9-4)^{2} & =4p(-5) \\ 25 & =-20p \\ p & =-\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the parabola is 

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-4)^{2} & =4py \\ (x-4)^{2} & =4(-\frac{5}{4})y \\ (x-4)^{2} & =-5y.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The population $y(t)$ of chimpanzees in a Brazilian forest follows the logistic growth model

$$
{y}^{′}=y(1-\frac{y}{500}),\,y(0)=70,
$$

where $t$ is the time, in years, since the observations began. According to this model, what is the maximum possible chimpanzee population?
:question/worked-solution:
A logistic growth equation has the form

$$
{y}^{′}=ky(a-y),
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a>y$ is the carrying capacity. 

The carrying capacity $a$ represents the maximum possible population. A diagram showing a typical logistic growth curve is shown below.

![](images/57/57f4b604c546daed4f1cb3895191fae0ccac33b5c17aac705f203f0a837c7e69.png)

First, let's rewrite the right-hand side of the given equation so that it matches the form above:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(1-\frac{y}{500}) \\  & =y(\frac{500-y}{500}) \\  & =\frac{y}{500}(500-y) \\  & =0.002y(500-y)\end{aligned}
$$

From here, we see that $a=500.$ Hence, the carrying capacity is $500,$ and we conclude that the number of chimpanzees cannot exceed $500.$
