:question/problem: Consider the arc of the curve $x=\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}$ that lies between the lines $y=0$ and $y=\sqrt[4]{3}.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis.
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}) \\  & ={y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}={y}^{4}.
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{3}}\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}\sqrt{1+{y}^{4}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{3}}{y}^{3}\sqrt{1+{y}^{4}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=1+{y}^{4}.$ Then, ${y}^{3}\text{d}y=(\frac{1}{4})\text{d}u.$

We also need to compute new limits:

| **$x$** | $0$ | $\sqrt[4]{3}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $4$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =\frac{2\pi }{3}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{3}}{y}^{3}\sqrt{1+{y}^{4}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}{\int }_{1}^{4}{u}^{1/2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}{[\frac{2{u}^{3/2}}{3}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}[\frac{2(4)^{3/2}}{3}-\frac{2(1)^{3/2}}{3}] \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(\frac{16}{3}-\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(\frac{14}{3}) \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/21/21e8aa9acdca87acf153b2e7ad3f5e51d5708f53b81562e682e16098721d752a.png)

Evaluate ${∮}_{C}({3}^{x}+{x}^{2}y)dx+({2}^{y}+x{y}^{2})\,dy,$ where the path $C$ is shown above.
:question/worked-solution:
Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/92/922ae907661e21ea5510dc0d02f151afc4f4423ad11a572ede6849c623397baa.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y)={3}^{x}+{x}^{2}y,\,Q(x,y)={2}^{y}+x{y}^{2},
$$

 we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}={x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({3}^{x}+{x}^{2}y)dx+({2}^{y}+x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({y}^{2}-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 4,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({y}^{2}-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}({r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}{\int }_{0}^{4}-{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ){\int }_{0}^{4}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ){[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-64{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-64{[\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{2}]}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =-32[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sin}⁡0] \\  & =-16\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: A fair spinner has six sides labeled with the numbers $0,$ $1,$ $2,$ $3,$ $4,$ and $5.$ If the spinner is spun, what is the expected value of the outcome?
:question/worked-solution:
The expected value of a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[X]={\sum }_{x\in S}x\cdot f(x).
$$

Let $X$ be the outcome of the spinner. Then the support is $S=\{0,1,2,3,4,5\},$ and the corresponding probabilities are all $\frac{1}{6}:$

$$
f(0)=f(1)=f(2)=f(3)=f(4)=f(5)=\frac{1}{6}
$$

Summing up the products of each value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =0\cdot f(0)+1\cdot f(1)+2\cdot f(2)+3\cdot f(3)+4\cdot f(5)+5\cdot f(5) \\  & =0(\frac{1}{6})+1(\frac{1}{6})+2(\frac{1}{6})+3(\frac{1}{6})+4(\frac{1}{6})+5(\frac{1}{6}) \\  & =0+\frac{1}{6}+\frac{2}{6}+\frac{3}{6}+\frac{4}{6}+\frac{5}{6} \\  & =\frac{0+1+2+3+4+5}{6} \\  & =\frac{15}{6} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the first three non-zero terms in the Taylor expansion of $\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)$ about the point $x=1.$
:question/worked-solution:
We use Taylor's theorem in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}(a)}{3!}(x-a)^{3}+⋯,
$$

with $f(x)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡x$ and $a=1.$ 

Computing the required derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡x \\ f(1) & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡1=\frac{\pi }{4} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}} \\ {f}^{′}(1) & =\frac{1}{1+1}=\frac{1}{2} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\frac{2x}{(1+{x}^{2})^{2}} \\ {f}^{″}(1) & =-\frac{2(1)}{(1+1)^{2}}=-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{arctan}⁡x & =\frac{\pi }{4}+(\frac{1}{2})(x-1)+\frac{1}{2!}(-\frac{1}{2})(x-1)^{2}+⋯ \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{1}{2}(x-1)-\frac{1}{4}(x-1)^{2}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨1-{t}^{2},3t+4⟩,$ find the point at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $⟨1,1⟩.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t+4)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2t,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $⟨1,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $⟨1,1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨1,1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨1,1⟩\cdot ⟨-2t,3⟩ & =0 \\ 1(-2t)+1(3) & =0 \\ -2t+3 & =0 \\ t & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=\frac{3}{2}.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\frac{3}{2}) & =⟨1-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2},3(\frac{3}{2})+4⟩ \\  & =⟨1-\frac{9}{4},\frac{9}{2}+4⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{5}{4},\frac{17}{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨1,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(-\frac{5}{4},\frac{17}{2}).$

:question/problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨4t-{t}^{2},{t}^{3}⟩,$ find all points at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $⟨2,1⟩.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t-{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨4-2t,3{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c⟨2,1⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c⟨2,1⟩ \\ ⟨4-2t,3{t}^{2}⟩ & =c⟨2,1⟩ \\ ⟨4-2t,3{t}^{2}⟩ & =⟨2c,c⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4-2t &=2c \\ 3{t}^{2} &=c\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equation, we obtain that $c=2-t.$ Substituting in the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{t}^{2} & =2-t \\ 3{t}^{2}+t-2 & =0 \\ (3t-2)(t+1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $⟨2,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the points corresponding to $t=-1,\frac{2}{3}.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1) & =⟨4(-1)-(-1)^{2},(-1)^{3}⟩=⟨-5,-1⟩ \\ r(\frac{2}{3}) & =⟨4(\frac{2}{3})-{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2},{(\frac{2}{3})}^{3}⟩=⟨\frac{20}{9},\frac{8}{27}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨2,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the points $(-5,-1)$ and $(\frac{20}{9},\frac{8}{27}).$

:question/problem: Calculate $\int 5{x}^{2}{e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
We need to use integration by parts.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=5{x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=10x \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={e}^{3x}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int {e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{e}^{3x}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 5{x}^{2}{e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(5{x}^{2})(\frac{{e}^{3x}}{3})-\int (\frac{{e}^{3x}}{3})(10x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5{x}^{2}{e}^{3x}}{3}-\frac{10}{3}\int x{e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int x{e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1 \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={e}^{3x}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int {e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{e}^{3x}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{e}^{3x}\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x(\frac{{e}^{3x}}{3})-\int (\frac{{e}^{3x}}{3})(1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{x{e}^{3x}}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{x{e}^{3x}}{3}-\frac{{e}^{3x}}{9}+D \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3x}}{9}(3x-1)+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 5{x}^{2}{e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{5{x}^{2}{e}^{3x}}{3}-\frac{10}{3}(\frac{{e}^{3x}}{9}(3x-1)+D) \\  & =\frac{5{x}^{2}{e}^{3x}}{3}-\frac{10{e}^{3x}}{27}(3x-1)-\frac{10D}{3} \\  & =\frac{5{e}^{3x}}{27}(9{x}^{2}-6x+2)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-\frac{10D}{3}.$

:question/problem: Calculate the integral $\int ({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
We need to use integration by parts.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2{log}_{3}⁡x}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \,\text{d}x=x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={({log}_{3}⁡x)}^{2}(x)-\int (x)(\frac{2{log}_{3}⁡x}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =x{({log}_{3}⁡x)}^{2}-\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\int {log}_{3}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate  $\int {log}_{3}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{3}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \,\text{d}x=x.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {log}_{3}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({log}_{3}⁡(x))(x)-\int (x)(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =x{log}_{3}⁡(x)-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\int \,\text{d}x \\  & =x{log}_{3}⁡(x)-\frac{x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =x{({log}_{3}⁡x)}^{2}-\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}(x{log}_{3}⁡(x)-\frac{x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+D) \\  & =x{({log}_{3}⁡x)}^{2}-\frac{2x{log}_{3}⁡(x)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+\frac{2x}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}-\frac{2D}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\  & =x({({log}_{3}⁡x)}^{2}-\frac{2{log}_{3}⁡(x)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+\frac{2}{{ln}^{2}⁡3})+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-\frac{2D}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}.$

:question/problem:
![](images/fb/fbfe241043e9014c1b633d163cf7e06234db70702a9052297b5df8b9df3fd82f.png)

Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=x\,i+{y}^{2}\,j$ through the curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\frac{1}{t}\,i+t\,j$ for $t\in [\frac{1}{2},2],$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

In this case, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula. 

![](images/d4/d432857e3350dfcb70a2a00b66ad9b86bc207382edd277c2169be0834c1710e0.png)

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\frac{1}{t},\,y=t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x=\frac{1}{t}, \\ Q(x,y) & ={y}^{2}={t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})=-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}(\frac{1}{t})\cdot (1)-({t}^{2})\cdot (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}\frac{1}{t}+1\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡t+t){|}_{1/2}^{2} \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡2+2)-(\operatorname{ln}⁡\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2+\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the unit tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=\sqrt{t}\,i+(2-t)\,j$ at an arbitrary point where $t\in (0,\infty ).$
:question/worked-solution:
For a curve $r(t)=x(t)i+y(t)j$, the unit tangent vector $T(t)$ at the point $P(x(t),y(t))$ is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-t)\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}\,i-\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}})}^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{4t}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1+4t}{4t}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{1+4t}}{2\sqrt{t}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${r}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the unit tangent vector to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{t}}{\sqrt{1+4t}}(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}i-\,j) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+4t}}(i-2\sqrt{t}\,j)\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=4\,i+2\,j$ through the curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\frac{t}{2}\,i+\frac{1}{2t}\,j$ for $t\in [\frac{1}{2},2],$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
:question/worked-solution:

To apply this formula,

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

In this case, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula. 

![](images/11/11376e6ef18b151a6dd1a02dd09f20b72bce3160c718f4095b4f08b23721ff1f.png)

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\frac{t}{2},\,y=\frac{1}{2t}.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =4, \\ Q(x,y) & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{t}{2})=\frac{1}{2}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{2t})=-\frac{1}{2{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}(4)\cdot (-\frac{1}{2{t}^{2}})-(2)\cdot (\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}-\frac{2}{{t}^{2}}-1\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{2}{t}-t){|}_{1/2}^{2} \\  & =(1-2)-(4-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}

:question/problem:

Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=5{e}^{-x}\,i+4\,j$ through the curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,i+t\,j$ for $t\in [1,e],$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
:question/worked-solution:

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

In this case, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula. 

![](images/55/559bbc20aa7d47eaad47a8975f80c8efb91bd03bc816357bc6047675dc755c9b.png)

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,y=t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =5{e}^{-x}=5{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=\frac{5}{t}, \\ Q(x,y) & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)=\frac{1}{t}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}

The curve $C$ is given by $x=-\operatorname{ln}⁡y$ from the point $(1,\frac{1}{e})$ to the point $(0,1).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=2{y}^{2}\,j$ through $C,$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
:question/worked-solution:

$$
x=-\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,y=t,\,t\in [\frac{1}{e},1].
$$

![](images/08/08fc4561a322b690da7bd28a9e69a91c687256e8a902ec7690dda5e6a1c689a6.png)

Therefore,

:question/problem:
The absolute difference between the outcomes of one roll of two fair tetrahedral dice follows the probability mass function $f(x)$ shown in the table below. What is the expected value of the absolute difference of the outcomes of one roll of the two dice?

| $f(x)$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{3}{8}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |
:question/worked-solution:
The expected value of a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[X]={\sum }_{x\in S}x\cdot f(x).
$$

Summing up the products of each value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =0\cdot f(0)+1\cdot f(1)+2\cdot f(2)+3\cdot f(3) \\  & =0(\frac{1}{4})+1(\frac{3}{8})+2(\frac{1}{4})+3(\frac{1}{8}) \\  & =0+\frac{3}{8}+\frac{2}{4}+\frac{3}{8} \\  & =0+\frac{3}{8}+\frac{4}{8}+\frac{3}{8} \\  & =\frac{0+3+4+3}{8} \\  & =\frac{10}{8} \\  & =\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the unit tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,p(t)$ at the point corresponding to $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$, given that  $p(\frac{\pi }{4})=i-\frac{3}{2}\,j+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\,k\,$ and $\,{p}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})=\sqrt{3}\,k.$
:question/worked-solution:
For a curve $r(t)=x(t)i+y(t)j+z(t)k$, the unit tangent vector $T(t)$ at the point $P(x(t),y(t),z(t))$ is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,p(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{tan}⁡t)\cdot p(t)+\operatorname{tan}⁡t\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(p(t)) \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡t\,p(t)+\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,{p}^{′}(t) \\ {r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & ={sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})p(\frac{\pi }{4})+\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}){p}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =2(i-\frac{3}{2}\,j+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\,k)+(1)(\sqrt{3}\,k) \\  & =(2\,i-3\,j+\sqrt{3}\,k)+\sqrt{3}\,k \\  & =2\,i-3\,j+2\sqrt{3}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖r(\frac{\pi }{4})‖ & =\sqrt{(2)^{2}+(-3)^{2}+(2\sqrt{3})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+9+12} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})}{‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot (2\,i-3\,j+2\sqrt{3}\,k) \\  & =\frac{2}{5}\,i-\frac{3}{5}\,j+\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{5}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the unit tangent vector to the curve at the point that corresponds to $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is
 $T(\frac{\pi }{4})=\frac{2}{5}\,i-\frac{3}{5}\,j+\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{5}\,k.$

:question/problem: Find the unit tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,p(t)$ at the point corresponding to $t=-\frac{\pi }{6}$, given that  $p(-\frac{\pi }{6})=\sqrt{3}\,i+\sqrt{3}\,k$ and $\,{p}^{′}(-\frac{\pi }{6})=-2\,i-8\,j+4\,k.$
:question/worked-solution:
For a curve $r(t)=x(t)i+y(t)j+z(t)k$, the unit tangent vector $T(t)$ at the point $P(x(t),y(t),z(t))$ is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=-\frac{\pi }{6}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,p(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)\cdot p(t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(p(t)) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,p(t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,{p}^{′}(t) \\ {r}^{′}(-\frac{\pi }{6}) & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{3})p(-\frac{\pi }{6})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{3}){p}^{′}(-\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =\sqrt{3}(\sqrt{3}\,i+\sqrt{3}\,k)+\frac{1}{2}(-2\,i-8\,j+4\,k) \\  & =(3\,i+3\,k)+(-\,i-4\,j+2\,k) \\  & =2\,i-4\,j+5\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(-\frac{\pi }{6}):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}^{′}(-\frac{\pi }{6})‖ & =\sqrt{(2)^{2}+(-4)^{2}+(5)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{45} \\  & =3\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${r}^{′}(-\frac{\pi }{6}):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}T(-\frac{\pi }{6}) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(-\frac{\pi }{6})}{‖{r}^{′}(-\frac{\pi }{6})‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{5}}\cdot (2\,i-4\,j+5\,k) \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{15}\,i-\frac{4\sqrt{5}}{15}\,j+\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the unit tangent vector to the curve at the point that corresponds to $t=-\frac{\pi }{6}$ is
 $T(-\frac{\pi }{6})=\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{15}\,i-\frac{4\sqrt{5}}{15}\,j+\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}\,k.$

:question/problem:
Find the shortest distance between the origin and the osculating plane for the curve $r(t)$ at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ given that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨2,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ T(t) & =⟨0,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ N(t) & =⟨0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
:question/worked-solution:
First, notice that the unit tangent and the principal normal at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨0,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})⟩=⟨0,0,1⟩ \\ N(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})⟩=⟨0,-1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, the position vector of the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ is

$$
p=r(\frac{\pi }{2})=⟨2,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})⟩=⟨2,1,0⟩.
$$

Now, we need to find a vector that's perpendicular to the osculating plane. To do that, we use the cross product of the unit tangent $T(\frac{\pi }{2})$ and the principal normal $N(\frac{\pi }{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =T(\frac{\pi }{2})\times N(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =⟨0,0,1⟩\times ⟨0,-1,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =i \\  & =⟨1,0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the shortest distance between our plane and the origin is given by

$$
d=\frac{|(p-0)\cdot n|}{‖n‖}=\frac{|p\cdot n|}{‖n‖}=|p\cdot n|,
$$

since $‖n‖=1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|p\cdot n| \\  & =|⟨2,1,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,0,0⟩| \\  & =|2+0+0| \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨xy-\sqrt{{y}^{2}+1},\,{x}^{3}+y⟩
$$

through the boundary of the triangle with vertices $(0,0),(1,2),$ and $(-1,2).$
:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/00/006d80a7dbe4d03b78cc5fb1a642405e3fdfdd69ec9d80014ee8e0355ad1ae73.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=xy-\sqrt{{y}^{2}+1}$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{3}+y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-\frac{y}{2}\le x\le \frac{y}{2},\,0\le y\le 2\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(y+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-y/2}^{y/2}(y+1)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(y+1)[x]_{-y/2}^{y/2}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(y+1)[\frac{y}{2}-(-\frac{y}{2})]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}({y}^{2}+y)\,dy \\  & ={[\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =(\frac{8}{3}+\frac{4}{2})-0 \\  & =\frac{14}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The unit tangent vector to a curve at an arbitrary point is given by

$$
T(t)=⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩.
$$

Find the principal normal vector at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{6}.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\frac{\pi }{6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩) \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩ \\ {T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6}) & =⟨-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}),\,-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,-\sqrt{3}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we find the magnitude of ${T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6})‖ & =‖⟨-1,-\sqrt{3}⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6})$ and obtain the principal normal vector to the curve at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}N(\frac{\pi }{6}) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6})}{‖{T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6})‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-1,-\sqrt{3}⟩}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}⟨-1,-\sqrt{3}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Note that when we find the scalar product of $N$ and $T$ at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{6},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\frac{\pi }{6})\cdot N(\frac{\pi }{6}) & =⟨-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩\cdot \frac{1}{2}⟨-1,-\sqrt{3}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{4}((-\sqrt{3})(-1)+(1)(-\sqrt{3})) \\  & =0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The unit tangent vector to a curve at an arbitrary point is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+1}\cdot q(t).
$$

Find the principal normal vector at the point where $t=1$, if 

$$
\begin{aligned}q(1)=-i+j+\sqrt{2}\,k,\,{q}^{′}(1)=2\,j+\sqrt{2}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+1}\cdot q(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+1})\cdot q(t)+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+1}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(q(t)) \\  & =-\frac{2t}{({t}^{2}+1)^{2}}\cdot q(t)+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+1}\cdot {q}^{′}(t) \\  \\ {T}^{′}(1) & =-\frac{2(1)}{({1}^{2}+1)^{2}}\cdot q(1)+\frac{1}{{1}^{2}+1}\cdot {q}^{′}(1) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(-i+j+\sqrt{2}\,k)+\frac{1}{2}(2\,j+\sqrt{2}\,k) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we find the magnitude of ${T}^{′}(1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{T}^{′}(1)‖ & =|\frac{1}{2}|\sqrt{(1)^{2}+(1)^{2}+(0)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${T}^{′}(1)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve at the point where $t=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}N(1) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(1)}{‖{T}^{′}(1)‖} \\  & =\frac{\frac{1}{2}(i+j)}{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

Note that when we find the scalar product of $N$ and $T$ at the point where $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(1)\cdot N(1) & =\frac{1}{2}q(1)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i+j) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-i+j+\sqrt{2}\,k)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i+j) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}(-1+1+0) \\  & =0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Find the principal normal vector at the point where $t=2,$ if 

$$
\begin{aligned}q(2)=⟨1,2\sqrt{2}⟩,\,{q}^{′}(2)=⟨0,\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+4t}}\cdot q(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+4t}})\cdot q(t)+\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+4t}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(q(t)) \\  & =-\frac{2}{(1+4t)^{3/2}}\cdot q(t)+\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+4t}}\cdot {q}^{′}(t) \\  \\ {T}^{′}(2) & =-\frac{2}{(1+4(2))^{3/2}}\cdot q(2)+\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+4(2)}}\cdot {q}^{′}(2) \\  & =-\frac{2}{27}⟨1,2\sqrt{2}⟩+\frac{1}{3}⟨0,\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{27}(-2⟨1,2\sqrt{2}⟩+9⟨0,\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩) \\  & =\frac{1}{27}⟨-2,\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{54}⟨-4,\sqrt{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we find the magnitude of ${T}^{′}(2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{T}^{′}(2)‖ & =\frac{1}{54}\sqrt{(-4)^{2}+(\sqrt{2})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{54}\cdot \sqrt{18} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{18}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${T}^{′}(2)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve at the point where $t=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}N(2) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(2)}{‖{T}^{′}(2)‖} \\  & =\frac{\frac{1}{54}⟨-4,\sqrt{2}⟩}{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{18})} \\  & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}⟨-4,\sqrt{2}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨-2\sqrt{2},1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Note that when we find the scalar product of $T$ and $N$ at the point where $t=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(2)\cdot N(2) & =\frac{1}{3}q(2)\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨-2\sqrt{2},1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨1,2\sqrt{2}⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨-2\sqrt{2},1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{9}(1\cdot (-2\sqrt{2})+2\sqrt{2}\cdot 1) \\  & =\frac{1}{9}(-2\sqrt{2}+2\sqrt{2}) \\  & =0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{sin}^{2}⁡t,\,{cos}^{2}⁡t,\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩,$ $t\ge 0,$ for which the arc length $s$ from $r(0)$ to $r(t)$ is given by $s=\sqrt{2}\,t,$ find the corresponding unit tangent $T(s),$ parametrized by $s.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, since $s=\sqrt{2}\,t,$ we have that $t=\frac{s}{\sqrt{2}}.$

Therefore, the vector function $R(s)$ that parametrizes $r(t)$ by its arc length is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r(\frac{s}{\sqrt{2}}) \\  & =⟨{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{s}{\sqrt{2}}),\,{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{s}{\sqrt{2}}),\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{2}})⟩ \\  & =⟨{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{s}{\sqrt{2}}),\,{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{s}{\sqrt{2}}),\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}\,s)⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, since the curve is parametrized by its arc length $s$, the unit tangent can be found as

$$
T(s)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}R(s).
$$

So, we obtain
 

$$
\begin{aligned}T(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}R(s) \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}({sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{s}{\sqrt{2}})),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}({cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{s}{\sqrt{2}})),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}\,s))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{2}}),\,-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{2}}),\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}\,s)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}\,s),\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}\,s),\,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}\,s)⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: What is the parametrization of the curve $r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2,\,1-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,$ $t\ge 0,$ by its arc length $s?$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+9{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{9({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the arc length of the curve from $0$ to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}‖{r}^{′}(u)‖\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}3\,\text{d}u \\  & =3u\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =3t\end{aligned}
$$

Since $s=3t,$ we have that $t=\frac{s}{3}.$

Therefore, the vector function that parametrizes $r(t)$ by its arc length is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r(\frac{s}{3}) \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{s}{3})-2,\,1-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{s}{3})⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Find the value of $(f(t)-3g(t))^{′}$ at $t=0,$ if 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =⟨2\sqrt{t+1},\,{t}^{3},\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)⟩, \\ g(t) & =⟨\frac{1}{3(t+1)},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{tan}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
First, notice that

$$
(f(t)-3g(t))^{′}={f}^{′}(t)-3{g}^{′}(t).
$$

Let's now find the derivatives of each function.

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{t+1}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{t+1}},\,3{t}^{2},\,\frac{1}{t+1}⟩ \\ {g}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{3(t+1)}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{tan}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{3(t+1)^{2}},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{sec}^{2}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(f(0)-3g(0))^{′} & ={f}^{′}(0)-3{g}^{′}(0) \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{0+1}},\,3(0)^{2},\,\frac{1}{0+1}⟩-3⟨-\frac{1}{3(0+1)^{2}},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡0,\,{sec}^{2}⁡0⟩ \\  & =⟨1,0,1⟩-3⟨-\frac{1}{3},1,1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,0,1⟩-⟨-1,3,3⟩ \\  & =⟨2,-3,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Given that $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y,$ find the points $(x,y),$ for $0\le y<\pi ,$ where $∇f(x,y)=0.$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =2x-2\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(x,y)=2(x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,i+2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j.$

Now, we solve $∇f(x,y)=0:$ 

$$
2(x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,i+2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j=0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j
$$

So, by equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j,$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{cases}2(x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)=0 \\ 2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y=0\end{cases}
$$

From the first equation, we get $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡y.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡y & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡2y & =0 \\ y & =0,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y=0,$ we get $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡0=1.$

- For $y=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we get $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=0.$

Therefore, $∇f(x,y)=0,$ for $0\le y<\pi ,$ at two points: $(1,0)$ and $(0,\frac{\pi }{2}).$

:question/problem: Calculate $\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2{e}^{-2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3})(-2{e}^{-2x})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2}{3}\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2}{3}J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2{e}^{-2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})-\int (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})(-2{e}^{-2x})\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{2}{3}\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{2}{3}I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\frac{{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2}{3}J \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2}{3}(-\frac{{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{2}{3}I) \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{2{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{9}-\frac{4}{9}I \\ \frac{13}{9}I & =\frac{3{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-2{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{9} \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-2x}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))}{13}+C\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Calculate $\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{3x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{e}^{3x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3x}(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)}{5})-\int (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)}{5})(3{e}^{3x})\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)}{5}+\frac{3}{5}\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)}{5}+\frac{3}{5}J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{3x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{e}^{3x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3x}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)}{5})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)}{5})(3{e}^{3x})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)}{5}-\frac{3}{5}\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)}{5}-\frac{3}{5}I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-\frac{{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)}{5}+\frac{3}{5}J \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)}{5}+\frac{3}{5}(\frac{{e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)}{5}-\frac{3}{5}I) \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)}{5}+\frac{3{e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)}{25}-\frac{9}{25}I \\ \frac{34}{25}I & =\frac{3{e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)-5{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)}{25} \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{3x}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)-5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x))}{34}+C\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Solve the following system of equations:
    

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=2 \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=-\frac{1}{2} \\ {x}_{3} &=-1\end{aligned}\right.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
The third equation states that ${x}_{3}=-1.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}+(-1)=-\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=-\frac{1}{2}+1=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, we substitute ${x}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}$ and ${x}_{3}=-1$ into the first equation to get

$$
{x}_{1}-2(\frac{1}{2})+(-1)=2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=2+1+1=4.
$$

Therefore, the solution is ${x}_{1}=4$, ${x}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}$, and ${x}_{3}=-1.$ In vector form, the solution can be written as $⟨4,\frac{1}{2},-1⟩.$

:question/problem:
Solve the following system of equations:
    

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-{x}_{3} &=2 \\ {x}_{2}-6{x}_{3} &=3 \\ {x}_{3} &=-\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}\right.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
The third equation states that ${x}_{3}=-\frac{1}{3}.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}-6(-\frac{1}{3})=3\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=3-2=1.
$$

Now, we substitute ${x}_{3}=-\frac{1}{3}$ and ${x}_{2}=1$ into the first equation to get

$$
{x}_{1}+1-(-\frac{1}{3})=2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=2-1-\frac{1}{3}=\frac{2}{3}.
$$

Therefore, the solution is ${x}_{1}=\frac{2}{3}$, ${x}_{2}=1$, and ${x}_{3}=-\frac{1}{3}.$ In vector form, the solution can be written as
$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3} \\ 1 \\ -\frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

:question/problem:
Solve the system of equations represented by the augmented matrix

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{1}{3} & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
The matrix represents a system of three linear equations in three variables, say,  ${x}_{1}$, ${x}_{2}$, and ${x}_{3}.$ We obtain the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=2 \\ {x}_{2}+\frac{{x}_{3}}{3} &=-1 \\ {x}_{3} &=2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The third equation states that ${x}_{3}=2.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}+\frac{2}{3}=-1\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=-1-\frac{2}{3}=-\frac{5}{3}.
$$

Now, we substitute ${x}_{3}=2$ and ${x}_{2}=-\frac{5}{3}$ into the first equation to get

$$
{x}_{1}+3(-\frac{5}{3})+(2)=2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=2+5-2=5.
$$

Therefore, the solution is ${x}_{1}=5$, ${x}_{2}=-\frac{5}{3}$, and ${x}_{3}=2.$ In vector form, the solution can be written as $⟨5,-\frac{5}{3},2⟩.$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant. 

Making a substitution $x+y=u,$ $\text{d}x=\text{d}u,$ we get.

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={\int }_{1}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}[{\int }_{y}^{1+y}\frac{1}{{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{[-\frac{1}{u}]}_{y}^{1+y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(-\frac{1}{y+1}+\frac{1}{y})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}[\frac{1}{y}-\frac{1}{y+1}]\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

 

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}[\frac{1}{y}-\frac{1}{y+1}]\,\text{d}y & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡y-\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+1)]_{1}^{2} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{y}{y+1}){|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{3})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{3})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{3}\cdot 2) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{4}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: ${\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}y\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y=$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}y\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y & ={\int }_{1}^{2}y[{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}y{[-\operatorname{cos}⁡x]}_{0}^{\pi /2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}y[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡0]\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}y\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

 

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}y\,\text{d}y & ={[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =2-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: At which point on the surface $z=3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector  $v=⟨4,-2,-1⟩?$
:question/worked-solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=6x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨6x,\,2y,\,-1⟩.
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨4,-2,-1⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨6x,\,2y,\,-1⟩=⟨4,-2,-1⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}6cx &=4 \\ 2cy &=-2 \\ -c &=-1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
6(1)x=4\,⟹\,x=\frac{2}{3}.
$$

And substituting $c=1$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
2(1)y=-2\,⟹\,y=-1.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=\frac{2}{3}$ and $y=-1$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =3{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2}+(-1)^{2} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}+1 \\  & =\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $v$ at $(\frac{2}{3},-1,\frac{7}{3}).$

:question/problem: The equation $4{z}^{2}+4z=12$ can be written in the form $(z+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $p+q,$ and solve the equation.
:question/worked-solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, divide it by the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}4{z}^{2}+4z & =12 \\ 4({z}^{2}+z) & =12 \\ {z}^{2}+z & =3 \\ {z}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot z & =3 \\ {z}^{2}+2\cdot (\frac{1}{2})\cdot z+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =3 \\ {(z+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(z+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =3 \\ {(z+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-\frac{1}{4} & =\frac{12}{4} \\ {(z+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{13}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=\frac{1}{2},q=\frac{13}{4},$ and $p+q=\frac{15}{4}.$ 

Next, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{(z+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{13}{4}} \\ |z+\frac{1}{2}| & =\frac{\sqrt{13}}{2} \\ z+\frac{1}{2} & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{13}}{2} \\ z & =-\frac{1}{2}\pm \frac{\sqrt{13}}{2} \\ z & =\frac{-1\pm \sqrt{13}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{R}\frac{{y}^{2}+1}{x}\,\text{d}A$ over the rectangle $R=[1,e]\times [0,3].$
:question/worked-solution:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals and then evaluate each of the integrals separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{{y}^{2}+1}{x}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{1}{x})({y}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{0}^{3}({y}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}y) \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡x]_{1}^{e}\cdot [\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}+y]_{0}^{3} \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡e-\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\cdot (\frac{{3}^{3}}{3}+3) \\  & =1\cdot 12 \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{R}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{4+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A$ over the rectangle $R=[0,\pi ]\times [0,2].$

We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals and then evaluate each of the integrals separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{4+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(\frac{1}{4+{y}^{2}})\,\text{d}A \\  & =({\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{4+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =[-\operatorname{cos}⁡x]_{0}^{\pi }\cdot [\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{2})]_{0}^{2} \\  & =-(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡0)\cdot (\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(0)) \\  & =-(-1-1)\cdot (\frac{\pi }{8}-0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x}
$$

Here, we have $X∼B(4,\frac{1}{3}),$ so $X$ has the probability mass function

$$

$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<3) & =P(X\in \{0,1,2\}) \\  & =f(0)+f(1)+f(2) \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{0}){(\frac{1}{3})}^{0}{(\frac{2}{3})}^{4-0}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{1}){(\frac{1}{3})}^{1}{(\frac{2}{3})}^{4-1}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{2}){(\frac{1}{3})}^{2}{(\frac{2}{3})}^{4-2} \\  & =1{(\frac{1}{3})}^{0}{(\frac{2}{3})}^{4}+4{(\frac{1}{3})}^{1}{(\frac{2}{3})}^{3}+6{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2}{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{9}.\end{aligned}

:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation ${x}^{2}{y}^{″}-x{y}^{′}+y=0.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.
:question/worked-solution:
Let's check each statement:

- To determine whether ${y}_{1}(x)$ is a solution to the differential equation, we substitute ${y}_{1}$ and its derivatives into the equation.

First, we find the first and second derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}^{′}(x) & =1 \\ {y}_{1}^{″}(x) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's substitute ${y}_{1}(x)$ and its derivatives into the equation. We get

$$
{x}^{2}(0)-x(1)+x=0.\,✓
$$

So, ${y}_{1}$ is a solution to the equation, and therefore statement “${y}_{1}(x)=x$ is a solution to the equation” is true.

- Similarly, we compute the derivatives of ${y}_{2}$ and substitute to the equation. Computing the derivatives yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′}(x) & =1+\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\ {y}_{2}^{″}(x) & =\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's substitute ${y}_{2}(x)$ and its derivatives into the equation. We get

$$
{x}^{2}(\frac{1}{x})-x(1+\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+x\operatorname{ln}⁡x=0.\,✓
$$

So, ${y}_{2}$ is a solution to the equation, and therefore statement “${y}_{2}(x)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is a solution to the equation” is true.

- So, both ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions of the equation. To check if these functions are linearly independent, we compute the Wronskian.

The Wronskian $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})$ of two functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ is defined as

$$
W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})=|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}|={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{1}^{′}{y}_{2}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =(x)(x\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{′}-(x)^{′}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\  & =x(1+\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-(1)x\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\  & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the  Wronskian is not equal to $0,$ the functions are linearly independent, hence $y=Ax+Bx\operatorname{ln}⁡x$  is the general solution.

Therefore, statement “The general solution of the equation is $y=Ax+Bx\operatorname{ln}⁡x$” is true.

:question/problem:
Which of the following elementary row operations transforms the matrix $A$ into the matrix $B$, where

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 2 & -3 \\ -8 & 0 & 2 \\ 10 & 5 & -5\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
B=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 2 & -3 \\ -8 & 0 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}?
$$
:question/worked-solution:
First, notice that the $1$st and the $2$nd rows are the same in both matrices. The only row that has changed is the $3$rd row. 

By considering the given row operations that modify the $3$rd row, we notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 2 & -3 \\ -8 & 0 & 2 \\ 10 & 5 & -5\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3}:=\frac{1}{5}\cdot {R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}5 & 2 & -3 \\ -8 & 0 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =B.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the required row operation is

$$
{R}_{3}:=\frac{1}{5}\cdot {R}_{3}.
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 & -1 \\ 7 & 7 & 2 \\ -6 & 1 & 6\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=3\cdot {R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 3 & -3 \\ 7 & 7 & 2 \\ -6 & 1 & 6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =D.\end{aligned}

:question/problem:
Which of the following elementary row operations transforms the matrix $E$ into the matrix $F$, where

$$

$$

:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $x\operatorname{cos}⁡y=-y\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(\frac{\pi }{2},0).$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x\operatorname{cos}⁡y & =-y\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{\pi }{2} \\ x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(\frac{\pi }{2},0)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(\frac{\pi }{2},0)={f}_{y}(\frac{\pi }{2},0)i-{f}_{x}(\frac{\pi }{2},0)j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(\frac{\pi }{2},0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x)i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x)j \\  & =(-x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)i-(\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)j \\ t(\frac{\pi }{2},0) & =(-\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡0+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))i-(\operatorname{cos}⁡0+0\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))j \\  & =i-j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $i-j.$

:question/problem: At which point on the curve ${x}^{2}y=-8x-4$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $j?$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}y & =-8x-4 \\ {x}^{2}y+8x & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y+8x,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-4.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y+8x)\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y+8x)\,j \\  & ={x}^{2}\,i-(2xy+8)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $j,$ we must have $t\cdot j=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot j & =0 \\ ({x}^{2}\,i-(2xy+8)\,j)\cdot j & =0 \\ -(2xy+8) & =0 \\ xy+4 & =0 \\ y & =-\frac{4}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=-\frac{4}{x}$ into the equation of our curve gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}y & =-8x-4 \\ {x}^{2}(-\frac{4}{x}) & =-8x-4 \\ -4x & =-8x-4 \\ 4x & =-4 \\ x & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, for $x=-1,$ we get $y=4,$ and the corresponding point is $(-1,4).$

:question/problem: Given $X∼\text{Geom}(\frac{3}{5}),$ compute $P(X\ge 5).$
:question/worked-solution:
If $X∼\text{Geom}(p),$ then $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}(1-p)^{x-1}p, & x=1,2,3,… \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Here, $X∼\text{Geom}(\frac{3}{5}),$ so the distribution of $X$ in this case is

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}{(\frac{2}{5})}^{x-1}(\frac{3}{5}), & x=1,2,3… \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

There are infinitely many values of $X$ such that $X\ge 5.$ However, we can simplify the computation by using the complement instead:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 5) & =1-P(X<5)\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the complement, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<5) & =P(X\in \{1,2,3,4\}) \\  & =P(X=1)+P(X=2)+P(X=3)+P(X=4) \\  & =f(1)+f(2)+f(3)+f(4) \\  & ={(\frac{2}{5})}^{0}(\frac{3}{5})+{(\frac{2}{5})}^{1}(\frac{3}{5})+{(\frac{2}{5})}^{2}(\frac{3}{5})+{(\frac{2}{5})}^{3}(\frac{3}{5}) \\  & =0.9744.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 5) & =1-P(X<5) \\  & =1-0.9744 \\  & =0.0256.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Find the product $AB$, if
$A=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & 0 \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$
and 
$B=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Notice that $B$ is the $2$nd *column* of the identity matrix ${I}_{3}.$

Since we're multiplying the $3\times 3$ matrix $A$ by the $2$nd *column* of the identity matrix ${I}_{3},$ the result must be the $2$nd *column* of $A.$ Therefore,

$$
AB=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Let's check the long way:

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & 0 \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot 0+(\frac{-\sqrt{2}}{2})\cdot 1+0\cdot 0 \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot 0+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot 1+0\cdot 0 \\ 0\cdot 0+0\cdot 1+1\cdot 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:

First, we find the roots of the characteristic polynomial:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+100 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-100 \\ \lambda  & =\pm 10\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =P\operatorname{cos}⁡10x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡10x\end{aligned}
$$

We find the constants $P$ and $Q$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(\frac{\pi }{4})=10$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}Q=10.\end{aligned}
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})=50,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}=-10P\operatorname{sin}⁡10x+10Q\operatorname{cos}⁡10x.
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})=50$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-10P=50\,⟹\,P=-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=-5\operatorname{cos}⁡10x+10\operatorname{sin}⁡10x.
$$

:question/problem: Find the second derivative of $f(t)=2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,i-(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{e}^{t})\,j+(2{t}^{3}+t-2)\,k$ with respect to $t.$
:question/worked-solution:

\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)\,i-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{e}^{t})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3}+t-2)\,k \\  & =\frac{2}{t}\,i-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{e}^{t})\,j+(6{t}^{2}+1)\,k \\  & =\frac{2}{t}\,i+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-{e}^{t})\,j+(6{t}^{2}+1)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

  

Then, we calculate ${f}^{″}(t)$ by differentiating ${f}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2}{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-{e}^{t})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6{t}^{2}+1)\,k \\  & =-\frac{2}{{t}^{2}}\,i+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{t})\,j+12t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: A math exam consists of $10$ questions, with each question containing four possible answers, where only one is the correct answer. Michael takes the exam and, for each question, he randomly chooses one of the four answers. What is the probability that Michael answers at least eight questions correctly? Round your answer to $4$ decimal places.
:question/worked-solution:
Let the random variable $X$ be the number of questions Michael answers correctly.

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=10$ questions on the exam

- the probability of choosing a correct answer is $p=\frac{1}{4}$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(10,\frac{1}{4}).$ 

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{10}{x}){(\frac{1}{4})}^{x}{(1-\frac{1}{4})}^{10-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{10}{x}){(\frac{1}{4})}^{x}{(\frac{3}{4})}^{10-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the probability that Michael answers at least $8$ questions correctly. So, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 8) & =P(X=8)+P(X=9)+P(X=10) \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{10}{8}){(\frac{1}{4})}^{8}{(\frac{3}{4})}^{10-8}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{10}{9}){(\frac{1}{4})}^{9}{(\frac{3}{4})}^{10-9}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{10}{10}){(\frac{1}{4})}^{10}{(\frac{3}{4})}^{10-10} \\  & =45{(\frac{1}{4})}^{8}{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}+10{(\frac{1}{4})}^{9}{(\frac{3}{4})}^{1}+1{(\frac{1}{4})}^{10}{(\frac{3}{4})}^{0} \\  & ≈0.0004\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $4$ decimal places.

:question/problem: Let $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ be square matrices. If $A=B\cdot C,$  $|B|=-15$ and $|{C}^{-1}|=3$, find $|A|.$
:question/worked-solution:
Given two $n\times n$ matrices $M$ and $N,$ we have

$$
det(MN)=det(M)\cdot det(N).
$$

Also, given an invertible $n\times n$ matrix $M,$ we have

$$
det({M}^{-1})=\frac{1}{det(M)}.
$$

Since $|C|=\frac{1}{|{C}^{-1}|}$, we get $|C|=\frac{1}{3}.$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}|A| & =|B|\cdot |C| \\  & =(-15)\cdot (\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: A box of chocolates contains cherry creams and almond little cakes in the ratio of $2:1.$ Four chocolates are selected at random, with replacement. What is the probability of getting at most $2$ cherry creams? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
:question/worked-solution:
Let the random variable $X$ be the number of selected cherry creams.

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=4$ selected chocolates

- since cherry creams and almond little cakes are in the ratio of $2:1,$ the probability of selecting a cherry cream from the box is $p=\frac{2}{3}$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(4,\frac{2}{3}).$ 

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{x}){(\frac{2}{3})}^{x}{(1-\frac{2}{3})}^{4-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{x}){(\frac{2}{3})}^{x}{(\frac{1}{3})}^{4-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the probability of getting at most $2$ cherry creams. So, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 2) & =P(X=0)+P(X=1)+P(X=2) \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{0}){(\frac{2}{3})}^{0}{(\frac{1}{3})}^{4-0}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{1}){(\frac{2}{3})}^{1}{(\frac{1}{3})}^{4-1}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{2}){(\frac{2}{3})}^{2}{(\frac{1}{3})}^{4-2} \\  & =1{(\frac{2}{3})}^{0}{(\frac{1}{3})}^{4}+4{(\frac{2}{3})}^{1}{(\frac{1}{3})}^{3}+6{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2}{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2} \\  & ≈0.407\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

:question/problem: Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface ${z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)={x}^{2}z+y-\frac{\pi }{2}$ at the point $(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1).$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y) & ={x}^{2}z+y-\frac{\pi }{2} \\ {z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}z-y & =-\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}z-y,$ our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=-\frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}z-y)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}z-y)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}z-y)k \\  & =(2xy{z}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}y)-2xz)i+({x}^{2}{z}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}y)-1)j+(2z\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2})k \\ ∇f(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1) & =(2(-1)(\frac{\pi }{2})(1)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡((-1)^{2}\frac{\pi }{2})-2(-1)(1))i+((-1)^{2}(1)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡((-1)^{2}\frac{\pi }{2})-1)j+(2(1)\operatorname{sin}⁡((-1)^{2}\frac{\pi }{2})-(-1)^{2})k \\  & =(-\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+2)i+(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-1)j+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-1)k \\  & =2\,i-j+k \\  & =⟨2,-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1)$ and passes through the point $(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1⟩+t\,∇f(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1)=⟨-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1⟩+t\,⟨2,-1,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

:question/problem: Given that $F=\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,i+\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,j,$ what is $\text{div}\,F?$
:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the divergence of $F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{2xy}{{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}^{2}}-\frac{2xy}{{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{4xy}{{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Find the curvature at an arbitrary point $t>0$ on the curve $r(t)$ given that its derivative ${r}^{′}(t)$ and the derivative of the corresponding unit tangent ${T}^{′}(t)$ are as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)=⟨2t,\,-3{t}^{2}⟩,\,{T}^{′}(t)=-\frac{6}{(9{t}^{2}+4)^{3/2}}⟨3t,\,2⟩,\,t\ge 0\end{aligned}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
Since we are given both the derivative of the curve ${r}^{′}(t)$ and the derivative of the unit tangent ${T}^{′}(t)$, we will use the following formula for the curvature:

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

Now, we find the magnitudes of ${r}^{′}(t)$ and ${T}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{6}{(9{t}^{2}+4)^{3/2}}\cdot \sqrt{{(3t)}^{2}+{(2)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{6}{(9{t}^{2}+4)^{3/2}}\cdot \sqrt{9{t}^{2}+4} \\  & =\frac{6}{9{t}^{2}+4} \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(2t)}^{2}+{(-3{t}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+9{t}^{4}} \\  & =t\sqrt{9{t}^{2}+4}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{6}{9{t}^{2}+4})}{t\sqrt{9{t}^{2}+4}} \\  & =\frac{6}{t(9{t}^{2}+4)^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Find the curvature at an arbitrary point on the curve $r(s)$ parametrized by its arc length $s$, where

$$
r(s)=⟨\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{s}{2}),\,\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{s}{2}),\frac{\sqrt{5}s}{3}⟩,\,0\le s\le 4\pi .
$$
:question/worked-solution:
Let $T(s)$ denote the unit tangent to the given curve as a function of the arc length $s.$ Since we are given the curve $r(s)$ parametrized by the arc length $s$, we will use the following formula for the curvature:

$$
κ(s)=‖{T}^{′}(s)‖=‖{r}^{″}(s)‖
$$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(s)$ and ${r}^{″}(s):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(s) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{s}{2})),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{s}{2})),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{\sqrt{5}s}{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{s}{2}),\,\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{s}{2}),\,\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(s) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{s}{2})),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{s}{2})),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{s}{2}),\,-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{s}{2}),\,0⟩ \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{s}{2}),\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{s}{2}),\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(s) & =‖{r}^{″}(s)‖ \\  & =|-\frac{1}{3}|\cdot \sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{s}{2})+{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{s}{2})+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider a curve $r(s)$ parametrized by its arc length $s.$ Find the radius of curvature of $r(s)$ at an arbitrary point knowing that its unit tangent vector $T(s)$ is given by

$$
T(s)=\frac{1}{2}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡\sqrt{s},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\sqrt{s},\,\sqrt{3}⟩.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
Since the curve $r(s)$ and its unit tangent vector $T(s)$ are both parametrized by arc length $s$, we will use the following formula for the radius of curvature:

$$
R(s)=\frac{1}{κ(s)}=\frac{1}{‖{T}^{′}(s)‖}
$$

We differentiate $T(s)$ with respect to $s$ and calculate its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(s) & =\frac{1}{2}⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\sqrt{s}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\sqrt{s}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\sqrt{3})⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{2}⟨-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\sqrt{s}}{2\sqrt{s}},\,\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\sqrt{s}}{2\sqrt{s}},\,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{4\sqrt{s}}⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡\sqrt{s},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡\sqrt{s},\,0⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(s)‖ & =\frac{1}{4\sqrt{s}}\cdot \sqrt{{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡\sqrt{s})}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\sqrt{s})}^{2}+{(0)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\sqrt{s}}\cdot \sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\sqrt{s}+{cos}^{2}⁡\sqrt{s}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\sqrt{s}}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{4\sqrt{s}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of curvature is

$$
R(s)=\frac{1}{‖{T}^{′}(s)‖}=\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{4\sqrt{s}})}=4\sqrt{s}.
$$

:question/problem: Find the radius of the osculating circle at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ for the curve $r(t)=⟨t,\,\operatorname{ln}⁡\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.$
:question/worked-solution:
Since we are given only the curve $r(t)$, we will use the cross product formula to find the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}),$ and $‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-\operatorname{tan}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =⟨1,-\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})⟩ \\  & =⟨1,-1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖ & =\sqrt{(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{″}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{tan}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-{sec}^{2}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =⟨0,-{sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})$ and ${r}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4})$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})\times {r}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =⟨1,\,-1,\,0⟩\times ⟨0,\,-2,\,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =-2\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})\times {r}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖ & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of curvature at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\frac{{‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})\times {r}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖} \\  & =\frac{(\sqrt{2})^{3}}{2} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the center and radius of the osculating circle to the curve $r(t)$ at the point $P(1,-1)$ where $t=1,$ given that $‖{r}^{′}(1)‖=\sqrt{13},$ and the unit tangent vector $T(t)$ to the curve is

$$

$$
:question/worked-solution:
Since we are given both the value of $‖{r}^{′}(1)‖$ and the unit tangent $T(t)$, we will use the following formula for the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2}{\sqrt{9{t}^{2}+4}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{3t}{\sqrt{9{t}^{2}+4}})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{18t}{\sqrt{{(9{t}^{2}+4)}^{3}}},\,-\frac{12}{\sqrt{{(9{t}^{2}+4)}^{3}}}⟩ \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{{(9{t}^{2}+4)}^{3}}}⟨-3t,\,-2⟩ \\ {T}^{′}(1) & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{{(9({1}^{2})+4)}^{3}}}⟨-3(1),-2⟩ \\  & =\frac{6}{13\sqrt{13}}⟨-3,-2⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(1)‖ & =\frac{6}{13\sqrt{13}}\cdot \sqrt{(-3)^{2}+(-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{6}{13\sqrt{13}}\cdot \sqrt{13} \\  & =\frac{6}{13}\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}R(1) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(1)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(1)‖} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{13}}{(\frac{6}{13})} \\  & =\frac{13\sqrt{13}}{6}.\end{aligned}

:question/problem:
Find the center and radius of the osculating circle to the curve $r(t)$ at the point $P(3,1)$ where $t=0,$ given that $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖=2,$ and the unit tangent vector $T(t)$ to the curve is

$$

$$
:question/worked-solution:
Since we are given both the value of $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖$ and the unit tangent $T(t)$, we will use the following formula for the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

Now, we find ${T}^{′}(t)$, ${T}^{′}(0)$ and $‖{T}^{′}(0)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{\sqrt{{({t}^{2}+1)}^{3}}},\,\frac{t}{\sqrt{{({t}^{2}+1)}^{3}}}⟩ \\ {T}^{′}(0) & =⟨-\frac{1}{\sqrt{{({0}^{2}+1)}^{3}}},\,\frac{0}{\sqrt{{({0}^{2}+1)}^{3}}}⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,0⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(0)‖ & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the radius of curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(0) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(0)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(0)‖} \\  & =\frac{2}{1} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal normal vector at $t=0$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}N(0) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(0)}{‖{T}^{′}(0)‖}=⟨-1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the center of the osculating circle is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0)+R(0)N(0) & =⟨3,1⟩+2⟨-1,0⟩ \\  & =⟨3,1⟩+⟨-2,0⟩ \\  & =⟨1,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$
