:question/problem:
Find the center and radius of the osculating circle to the curve $r(t)$ at the point $P(1,0)$ where $t=0,$ given that $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖=\sqrt{2},$ and the unit tangent vector $T(t)$ to the curve is

$$
T(t)=⟨\frac{{e}^{t}}{\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+1}},\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+1}}⟩.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
Since we are given both the value of $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖$ and the unit tangent $T(t)$, we will use the following formula for the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

Notice that $r(0)=⟨1,0⟩,$ since the point $P(1,0)$ is at the tip of $r(0).$ 

Now, we find ${T}^{′}(t)$, ${T}^{′}(0)$ and $‖{T}^{′}(0)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{e}^{t}}{\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+1}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+1}})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{{e}^{t}}{{({e}^{2t}+1)}^{3/2}},\,-\frac{{e}^{2t}}{{({e}^{2t}+1)}^{3/2}}⟩ \\ {T}^{′}(0) & =⟨\frac{{e}^{0}}{{({e}^{0}+1)}^{3/2}},\,-\frac{{e}^{0}}{{({e}^{0}+1)}^{3/2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}},-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}⟨1,-1⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(0)‖ & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\cdot \sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\cdot \sqrt{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the radius of curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(0) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(0)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(0)‖} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{(\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal normal vector at $t=0$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}N(0) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(0)}{‖{T}^{′}(0)‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨1,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the center of the osculating circle is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0)+R(0)N(0) & =⟨1,0⟩+2\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨1,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,0⟩+2⟨1,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,0⟩+⟨2,-2⟩ \\  & =⟨3,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: ${\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\frac{4}{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}\,dy\,dx=$
:question/worked-solution:
The integral is defined over a type I region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\frac{4}{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}[{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\frac{4}{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}[4\operatorname{arcsin}⁡y]_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}4\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}4x\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}4x\,dx & ={[2{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =2{(\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2} \\  & =2\cdot \frac{{\pi }^{2}}{16} \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The data below is taken from the table of values of the cumulative distribution function $Φ(z)$ for the standard normal distribution. Given that $X∼N(-4,{\sigma }^{2})$ is a normal random variable with $P(-18<X<10)=0.1113,$ find  $\sigma .$

| $z$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,0.0\,$ | $\,0.5080\,$ | $\,0.5120\,$ | $\,0.5160\,$ |
| $\,0.1\,$ | $\,0.5478\,$ | $\,0.5517\,$ | $\,0.5557\,$ |
| $\,0.2\,$ | $\,0.5871\,$ | $\,0.5910\,$ | $\,0.5948\,$ |

*Hint: Note that the interval $-18<X<10$ is symmetric about the mean $\mu =-4.$*
:question/worked-solution:
First, note that the given interval is symmetric about the mean:

$$
P(-18<X<10)=P(-4-14<X<-4+14)
$$

So, we find the cumulative probability using symmetry:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-18<X<10) & =0.1113 \\ 2P(-4<X<10) & =0.1113 \\ P(-4<X<10) & =0.0557 \\ P(X<10)-P(X<-4) & =0.0557 \\ P(X<10)-0.5 & =0.0557 \\ P(X<10) & =0.5557 \\ P(X\le 10) & =0.5557\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 10) & =0.5557 \\ P(Z\le \frac{10-(-4)}{\sigma }) & =0.5557 \\ Φ(\frac{14}{\sigma }) & =0.5557 \\ \frac{14}{\sigma } & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.5557)\end{aligned}
$$

According to the table, we have

$$
Φ(0.14)=0.5557\,⇒\,{Φ}^{-1}(0.5557)=0.14.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{14}{\sigma } & =0.14 \\ \sigma  & =\frac{14}{0.14} \\ \sigma  & =100.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The data below is taken from the table of values of the cumulative distribution function $Φ(z)$ for the standard normal distribution. Given that $X∼N(\mu ,{15}^{2})$ is a normal random variable with $P(-5\mu <X<7\mu )=0.5762,$ determine $\mu .$

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,0.7\,$ | $\,0.7580\,$ | $\,0.7611\,$ | $\,0.7642\,$ |
| $\,0.8\,$ | $\,0.7881\,$ | $\,0.7910\,$ | $\,0.7939\,$ |
| $\,0.9\,$ | $\,0.8159\,$ | $\,0.8186\,$ | $\,0.8212\,$ |

*Hint: Note that the interval $-5\mu <X<7\mu $ is symmetric about the mean $\mu .$*
:question/worked-solution:
Note that we can write the given probability as

$$
P(\mu -6\mu <X<\mu +6\mu )=0.5762,
$$

which tells us that the interval $-5\mu <X<7\mu $ is symmetric about the mean $\mu .$

First, we find the cumulative probability using symmetry:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\mu -6\mu <X<\mu +6\mu ) & =0.5762 \\ 2P(\mu <X<\mu +6\mu ) & =0.5762 \\ P(\mu <X<\mu +6\mu ) & =0.2881 \\ P(X<\mu +6\mu )-P(X<\mu ) & =0.2881 \\ P(X<\mu +6\mu )-0.5 & =0.2881 \\ P(X<\mu +6\mu ) & =0.7881 \\ P(X\le \mu +6\mu ) & =0.7881 \\ P(X\le 7\mu ) & =0.7881\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 7\mu ) & =0.7881 \\ P(Z\le \frac{7\mu -\mu }{15}) & =0.7881 \\ Φ(\frac{6\mu }{15}) & =0.7881 \\ \frac{6\mu }{15} & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.7881) \\ \frac{2\mu }{5} & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.7881)\end{aligned}
$$

 

According to the table, we have

$$
Φ(0.8)=0.7881\,⇒\,{Φ}^{-1}(0.7881)=0.8.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2\mu }{5} & =0.8 \\ 2\mu  & =4 \\ \mu  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: What are the critical points of the function $f(x)=\frac{x-2}{{x}^{2}+6}?$
:question/worked-solution:
A critical point of $f(x)$ is a point $x=c$ in the domain of $f$ such that either ${f}^{′}(c)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(c)$ does not exist.

Differentiating $f(x),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{x-2}{{x}^{2}+6}) \\  & =\frac{(x-2)^{′}\cdot ({x}^{2}+6)-(x-2)\cdot ({x}^{2}+6)^{′}}{({x}^{2}+6)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+6)-(x-2)\cdot 2x}{({x}^{2}+6)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}+6-2{x}^{2}+4x}{({x}^{2}+6)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-{x}^{2}+4x+6}{({x}^{2}+6)^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{{x}^{2}-4x-6}{({x}^{2}+6)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

- First, we compute the points where ${f}^{′}(c)=0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x$ by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{{x}^{2}-4x-6}{({x}^{2}+6)^{2}} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-4x-6 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}-6 & =0 \\ (x-2)^{2}-4-6 & =0 \\ (x-2)^{2}-10 & =0 \\ (x-2)^{2} & =10 \\ x-2 & =\pm \sqrt{10} \\ x & =2\pm \sqrt{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has stationary points at $x=2\pm \sqrt{10}.$

- Second, we note that ${f}^{′}(x)$ exists for all values of $x$ in the domain of $f(x).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, we conclude that the critical points of $f(x)$ are $x=2\pm \sqrt{10}.$

:question/problem:
Find the curvature at an arbitrary point on the curve $r(s)$ parametrized by its arc length $s$, where

$$
r(s)=⟨s-2\operatorname{arctan}⁡s,\,\operatorname{ln}⁡({s}^{2}+1)⟩,\,s\ge 0.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
Let $T(s)$ denote the unit tangent to the given curve as a function of the arc length $s.$ Since we are given the curve $r(s)$ parametrized by the arc length $s$, we will use the following formula for the curvature:

$$
κ(s)=‖{T}^{′}(s)‖=‖{r}^{″}(s)‖
$$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(s)$ and ${r}^{″}(s):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(s) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(s-2\operatorname{arctan}⁡s),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({s}^{2}+1))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{{s}^{2}-1}{{s}^{2}+1},\,\frac{2s}{{s}^{2}+1}⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(s) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{{s}^{2}-1}{{s}^{2}+1}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{2s}{{s}^{2}+1})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{4s}{({s}^{2}+1)^{2}},\,\frac{2(1-{s}^{2})}{({s}^{2}+1)^{2}}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{({s}^{2}+1)^{2}}⟨4s,\,2(1-{s}^{2})⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(s) & =‖{r}^{″}(s)‖ \\  & =\frac{1}{({s}^{2}+1)^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{(4s)^{2}+{(2(1-{s}^{2}))}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{({s}^{2}+1)^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{16{s}^{2}+4{s}^{4}-8{s}^{2}+4} \\  & =\frac{1}{({s}^{2}+1)^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{4{s}^{4}+8{s}^{2}+4} \\  & =\frac{1}{({s}^{2}+1)^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{4({s}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2({s}^{2}+1)}{({s}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Consider the function $f(x)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ If the critical points of $f(x)$ for $x\in (-\pi ,\pi )$ are $x={x}_{1}$ and $x={x}_{2},$ what is the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}?$
:question/worked-solution:
A critical point of $f(x)$ is a point $x=c$ in the domain of $f$ such that either ${f}^{′}(c)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(c)$ does not exist.

Differentiating $f(x),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

- First, we compute the points where ${f}^{′}(c)=0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =0 \\ -3\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ -3\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

The general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})+n\pi  \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{6}+n\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

We set $n=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…,$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain $-\pi <x<\pi .$

- setting $n=0$ gives $x=-\frac{\pi }{6}$

- setting $n=1$ gives $x=\frac{5\pi }{6}$

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain $-\pi <x<\pi .$ So, the solutions to this equation for $x\in (-\pi ,\pi )$ are 

$$
x=-\frac{\pi }{6},\,x=\frac{5\pi }{6}.
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has stationary points at $x=-\frac{\pi }{6}$ and $x=\frac{5\pi }{6}.$

- Second, we note that ${f}^{′}(x)$ exists for all values of $x\in (-\pi ,\pi ).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, we conclude that the critical points of $f(x)$ for $x\in (-\pi ,\pi )$ are ${x}_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{6}$ and ${x}_{2}=\frac{5\pi }{6}.$

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=-\frac{\pi }{6}\cdot \frac{5\pi }{6}=-\frac{5{\pi }^{2}}{36}.
$$

:question/problem: Consider the function $f(x)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡x+7\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ If the critical points of $f(x)$ for $x\in (-\pi ,\pi )$ are $x={x}_{1}$ and $x={x}_{2},$ what is the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}?$ Round your answer to two decimal places.
:question/worked-solution:
A critical point of $f(x)$ is a point $x=c$ in the domain of $f$ such that either ${f}^{′}(c)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(c)$ does not exist.

Differentiating $f(x),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡x+7\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+7\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

- First, we compute the points where ${f}^{′}(c)=0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+7\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡x & =\frac{7}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =\frac{7}{2}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

The general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{7}{2})+n\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

We set $n=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…,$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain $-\pi <x<\pi .$

- setting $n=0$ gives $x≈1.292\,50$ rounded to five decimal places

- setting $n=-1$ gives $x≈-1.849\,10$ rounded to five decimal places

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain $-\pi <x<\pi .$ So, the solutions to this equation for $x\in (-\pi ,\pi )$ are 

$$
x≈1.292\,50,\,x≈-1.849\,10.
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has stationary points at $x≈-1.849\,10$ and $x≈1.292\,50.$

- Second, we note that ${f}^{′}(x)$ exists for all values of $x\in (-\pi ,\pi ).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, we conclude that the critical points of $f(x)$ for $x\in (-\pi ,\pi )$ are ${x}_{1}≈-1.849\,10$ and ${x}_{2}≈1.292\,50.$

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}≈-1.849\,10\cdot 1.292\,50≈-2.39
$$

rounded to two decimal places

:question/problem: A surface $S$ is defined by $z=f(x,y).$ The curve $C$ is the intersection of $S$ with the plane $y=2.$ Given that the point $P$ with $x$-coordinate $-\frac{\pi }{2}$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+xy$, find the slope of the tangent to $C$ at $P.$
:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point where $x=-\frac{\pi }{2}$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(-\frac{\pi }{2},2).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(-\frac{\pi }{2},2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(-\frac{\pi }{2},2) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})+(-\frac{\pi }{2})\cdot 2 \\  & =-1-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=2.$ Given that the point $P(-\frac{\pi }{2},2,2\pi )$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{xy}{\pi }$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(-\frac{\pi }{2},2,2\pi )$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(-\pi /2,2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(-\frac{\pi }{2},2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(-\pi /2,2)} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{(-\frac{\pi }{2})(2)}{\pi } \\  & =-1-1 \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(-\pi /2,2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(-\pi /2,2)}(x-(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\ z-2\pi  & =-2(x+\frac{\pi }{2}) \\ z & =-2x+\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-\frac{\pi }{2},2,2\pi )$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y &=2 \\ z &=-2x+\pi\end{aligned}\right.
$$

:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=2.$ Given that the point $P(2,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(2,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(2,\pi /4)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(2,\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(2,\frac{\pi }{4}) & =4\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =4\cdot 1 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(2,\pi /4)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(2,\pi /4)}(y-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ z-0 & =4(y-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ z & =4y-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(2,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=2 \\ z &=4y-\pi\end{aligned}\right.
$$

:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{z}{\sqrt{x-y}},$ find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ on which $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ exists.
:question/worked-solution:
First, notice that $f(x,y,z)$ is defined only when 

$$
\begin{aligned}x-y & >0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,x-y>0\}.
$$

Now, we compute the partial derivative of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{z}{\sqrt{x-y}}) \\  & =\frac{z}{2\sqrt{(x-y)^{3}}}\end{aligned}
$$

The function ${f}_{y}(x,y,z)$ is defined only for 

$$
\begin{aligned}x-y>0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the domain of ${f}_{y}$ is

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,x-y>0\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ exists on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}} & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,x-y>0\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,x-y>0\} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,x-y>0\}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+z)}{y},$ find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ on which $\frac{∂f}{∂z}$ exists.
:question/worked-solution:
First, notice that $f(x,y,z)$ is defined only when 

$$
\begin{aligned}x+z & >0\,\text{and}\,y\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}={(x,y,z)\,:\,x+z>0\,\,\text{and}\,\,y\ne 0}.
$$

Now, we compute the partial derivative of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+z)}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{1}{x+z} \\  & =\frac{1}{y(x+z)}\end{aligned}
$$

The function ${f}_{z}(x,y,z)$ is defined only for 

$$
\begin{aligned}x+z & \ne 0\,\text{and}\,y\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the domain of ${f}_{z}$ is

$$
{D}_{{f}_{z}}={(x,y,z)\,:\,x+z\ne 0\,\,\text{and}\,\,y\ne 0}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $z$ exists on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={(x,y,z)\,:\,x+z>0\,\,\text{and}\,\,y\ne 0}\cap {(x,y,z)\,:\,x+z\ne 0\,\,\text{and}\,\,y\ne 0} \\  & ={(x,y,z)\,:\,x+z>0\,\,\text{and}\,\,y\ne 0}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)=\frac{\sqrt{x}}{{y}^{2}}?$

Select all that apply.
:question/worked-solution:
First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{\sqrt{x}}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{x}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2{y}^{2}\sqrt{x}} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{\sqrt{x}}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\sqrt{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\sqrt{x}\cdot (-\frac{2}{{y}^{3}}) \\  & =-\frac{2\sqrt{x}}{{y}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement “Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(4,2)$” is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(4,2)$, where we have 

$$
f(4,2)=\frac{\sqrt{4}}{{2}^{2}}=\frac{1}{2},
$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(4,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(4,2) & =\frac{1}{2({2}^{2})\sqrt{4}}=\frac{1}{16} \\ {f}_{y}(4,2) & =-\frac{2\sqrt{4}}{{2}^{3}}=-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “${f}_{x}(0,2)$ is defined” is false. If we substitute $(0,2)$ into ${f}_{x}$, we get

$$
{f}_{x}(0,2)=\frac{1}{2({2}^{2})\sqrt{0}}=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

- Statement “${f}_{y}(0,2)$ is defined” is true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(0,2)$, where we have 

$$
f(0,2)=\frac{\sqrt{0}}{{2}^{2}}=0,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(0,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(0,2)=-\frac{2\sqrt{0}}{{2}^{3}}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is “Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(4,2)$”; “${f}_{y}(0,2)$ is defined” only.

:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y),$ calculate $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y}$ given that $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{2{x}^{2}+y}{{y}^{3}}.$
:question/worked-solution:
To find $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y}$ we differentiate the given first-order partial derivative $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{∂f}{∂y}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-\frac{2{x}^{2}+y}{{y}^{3}}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{{y}^{3}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}+y) \\  & =-\frac{1}{{y}^{3}}(4x) \\  & =-\frac{4x}{{y}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y),$ calculate $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y}$ given that $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{{e}^{y}}{x+y}.$
:question/worked-solution:
To find $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y}$ we differentiate the given first-order partial derivative $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{∂f}{∂y}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{e}^{y}}{x+y}) \\  & ={e}^{y}\cdot (-\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{y}}{(x+y)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
A cinema admission fee is normally distributed with a mean of $\mu $ dollars and a standard deviation of $$0.75.$ Additionally, in $94%$ of cases the admission fee is between $$0.7\mu $ and $$1.3\mu .$ Find the percentage of cases when the admission fee is lower than $$5.$

*Hint: A table of values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p$ is given below, where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $p$ | $\,0.75\,$ | $\,0.80\,$ | $\,0.85\,$ | $\,0.90\,$ | $\,0.95\,$ | $\,0.97\,$ | $\,0.99\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\,0.6745\,$ | $\,0.8416\,$ | $\,1.0364\,$ | $\,1.2816\,$ | $\,1.6449\,$ | $\,1.8808\,$ | $\,2.3263\,$ |

$$

$$

*In addition, you're given the following table of values for $p=Φ(z)$*.

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,0.4\,$ | $\,0.6554\,$ | $\,0.6591\,$ | $\,0.6628\,$ |
| $\,0.5\,$ | $\,0.6915\,$ | $\,0.6950\,$ | $\,0.6985\,$ |
| $\,0.6\,$ | $\,0.7257\,$ | $\,0.7291\,$ | $\,0.7324\,$ |
:question/worked-solution:
Let $X$ represent a randomly selected admission fee. Then we have $X∼N(\mu ,{0.75}^{2}),$ and we want to find $P(X<5).$ But first, we need to find the mean $\mu .$ 

We know that $P(0.7\mu <X<1.3\mu )=0.94.$ First, we convert this to a cumulative probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.7\mu <X<1.3\mu ) & =0.94 \\ 2P(\mu <X<1.3\mu ) & =0.94 \\ P(\mu <X<1.3\mu ) & =0.47 \\ P(X<\mu )+P(\mu <X<1.3\mu ) & =0.5+0.47 \\ P(X<1.3\mu ) & =0.97\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<1.3\mu ) & =0.97 \\ P(Z<\frac{0.3\mu }{0.75}) & =0.97 \\ Φ(\frac{0.3\mu }{0.75}) & =0.97 \\ \frac{0.3\mu }{0.75} & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.97) \\ 0.4\mu  & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.97).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, 

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(0.97)≈1.8808.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}0.4\mu  & =1.8808 \\ \mu  & =\frac{1.8808}{0.4} \\  & ≈4.702.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we can solve for $P(X<5)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<5) & =P(Z<\frac{5-4.702.}{0.75}) \\  & ≈P(Z<0.40) \\  & =Φ(0.40) \\  & =0.6554 \\  & ≈65.5%\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, approximately in $65.5%$ of cases, the admission fee is lower than $$5.$

:question/problem: Find ${g}_{xx}(x,y)-{g}_{yy}(x,y)$ at $(\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3})$ given that ${g}_{x}(x,y)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)$ and ${g}_{y}(x,y)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y).$
:question/worked-solution:
To find ${g}_{xx}(x,y)$ we differentiate the given first-order partial derivative ${g}_{x}(x,y)$ with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{xx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({g}_{x}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)+x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)+x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)\end{aligned}
$$

 

To find ${g}_{yy}(x,y)$ we differentiate the given first-order partial derivative ${g}_{y}(x,y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{yy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({g}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)) \\  & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we evaluate ${g}_{xx}(x,y)$ and ${g}_{yy}(x,y)$ at $(\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{xx}(\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3}) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+\frac{\pi }{3})+\frac{\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+\frac{\pi }{3})=\sqrt{3}-\frac{\pi }{6} \\ {g}_{yy}(\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3}) & =\frac{\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+\frac{\pi }{3})=-\frac{\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
{g}_{xx}(\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3})-{g}_{yy}(\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3})=\sqrt{3}-\frac{\pi }{6}-(-\frac{\pi }{6})=\sqrt{3}.
$$

:question/problem: Find ${g}_{xy}(x,y)+{g}_{yx}(x,y)$ at $(-1,2)$ given that ${g}_{x}(x,y)=\frac{1}{x+2y}$ and ${g}_{y}(x,y)=\frac{2}{x+2y}.$
:question/worked-solution:
To find ${g}_{xy}(x,y)$ we differentiate the given first-order partial derivative ${g}_{x}(x,y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({g}_{x}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{x+2y}) \\  & =-\frac{2}{(x+2y)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

To find ${g}_{yx}(x,y)$ we differentiate the given first-order partial derivative ${g}_{y}(x,y)$ with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({g}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{2}{x+2y}) \\  & =-\frac{2}{(x+2y)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we evaluate ${g}_{xy}(x,y)$ and ${g}_{yx}(x,y)$ at $(-1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{xy}(-1,2) & =-\frac{2}{((-1)+2(2))^{2}}=-\frac{2}{9} \\ {g}_{yx}(-1,2) & =-\frac{2}{((-1)+2(2))^{2}}=-\frac{2}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
{g}_{xy}(-1,2)+{g}_{yx}(-1,2)=-\frac{4}{9}.
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate ${f}_{xyz}(-5,2,3)$ for $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+z).$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the first-order derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+z)) \\  & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${f}_{xy}(x,y,z)$ by differentiating ${f}_{x}(x,y,z)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{x}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+z)) \\  & =2x\cdot \frac{1}{y+z} \\  & =\frac{2x}{y+z}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${f}_{xyz}(x,y,z)$ by differentiating ${f}_{xy}(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xyz}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({f}_{xy}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{2x}{y+z}) \\  & =2x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{1}{y+z}) \\  & =2x\cdot (-\frac{1}{(y+z)^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{2x}{(y+z)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate ${f}_{xyz}(x,y,z)$ at $(-5,2,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xyz}(-5,2,3) & =-\frac{2(-5)}{(2+3)^{2}}=\frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate ${f}_{xxz}(1,\frac{1}{2},\pi )$ for $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz).$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the first-order derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡xyz) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\cdot yz \\  & =yz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${f}_{xx}(x,y,z)$ by differentiating ${f}_{x}(x,y,z)$ with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{x}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(yz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =yz\cdot (-yz\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =-{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${f}_{xxz}(x,y,z)$ by differentiating ${f}_{xx}(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xxz}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({f}_{xx}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(-{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =-{y}^{2}\frac{∂}{∂z}({z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =-{y}^{2}\cdot (2z\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)+xy{z}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =-{y}^{2}z(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)+xyz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz))\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate ${f}_{xxz}(x,y,z)$ at $(1,\frac{1}{2},\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xxz}(1,\frac{1}{2},\pi ) & =-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}\cdot \pi \cdot (2\operatorname{sin}⁡(1\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi )+1\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(1\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi )) \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{4}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

The diameter of the kibble of a particular cat food brand is normally distributed with a mean of $\mu $ and a standard deviation of $0.7\,\text{mm}.$ Additionally, the diameter of $20%$ of kibbles is less than $4.4\,\text{mm}$ in diameter. :question/worked-solution:
Let $X$ represent the diameter of a randomly selected kibble. Then we have $X∼N(\mu ,{0.7}^{2}),$ and we want to find the $P(X<4).$

We know that $P(X<4.4)=0.20.$ First, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<4.4) & =0.20 \\ P(Z<\frac{4.4-\mu }{0.7}) & =0.20 \\ Φ(\frac{4.4-\mu }{0.7}) & =0.20 \\ \frac{4.4-\mu }{0.7} & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.20)\end{aligned}

From the table,

{Φ}^{-1}(0.20)≈-0.8416.

:question/problem: Given that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ evaluate ${f}_{yxy}(6,\frac{\pi }{3})$ if ${f}_{xy}(x,y)=7+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y.$

:question/problem:
Suppose that a function $f(x,y,z)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ and that

$$
\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}=\frac{x{e}^{yz}}{x+y},\,\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂z}=-\frac{z{e}^{yz}}{x+y}.
$$

 

Evaluate the following expression at the point $(1,1,0):$

$$
\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂y∂x∂y}+\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. 

Hence, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂y∂x∂y} & =\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂{y}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x{e}^{yz}}{x+y}) \\  & ={e}^{yz}\cdot (\frac{1\cdot (x+y)-x\cdot 1}{(x+y)^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{y{e}^{yz}}{(x+y)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In addition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂z}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(-\frac{z{e}^{yz}}{x+y}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{x+y}\cdot ({e}^{yz}+yz{e}^{yz}) \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{yz}(1+yz)}{x+y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate both partial derivatives at the point $(1,1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x}{|}_{(1,1,0)} & =\frac{1\cdot {e}^{1\cdot 0}}{(1+1)^{2}}=\frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}{|}_{(1,1,0)} & =-\frac{{e}^{1\cdot 0}(1+1\cdot 0)}{1+1}=-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x}{|}_{(1,1,0)}+\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}{|}_{(1,1,0)} & =\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{2}=-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Replacing $x$ with $-\frac{b}{3}$ and $n$ with $9$ in the above expression, we get

\begin{aligned}\frac{9(9-1)(9-2)(9-3)}{4!}\cdot {(-\frac{b}{3})}^{4} & =\frac{9\cdot 8\cdot 7\cdot 6}{24}\cdot {(-\frac{1}{3})}^{4}\cdot {b}^{4} \\  & =126\cdot \frac{1}{81}{b}^{4} \\  & =\frac{14}{9}{b}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coefficient of ${b}^{4}$ is $\frac{14}{9}.$

:question/problem: If $cot⁡x=\frac{1}{4},$ then $4cot⁡(-x+4\pi )+1=$
:question/worked-solution:
First, let's recall the graph of $y=cot⁡x.$

![](images/6e/6eb672fe024f024f20c7c3c80947d1b47bade8f998e705d6f411ae3f298ecde2.png)

From the graph, we note the following:

- The period of $cot⁡x$ is $\pi .$

- Our graph has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin. This means that $cot⁡x$ is an *odd* function, and we have

$$
cot⁡(-x)=-cot⁡x.
$$

Let's now evaluate our expression:

- Firstly, using the periodicity of $cot⁡x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}cot⁡(-x+4\pi ) & =cot⁡(-x+\pi \cdot 4) \\  & =cot⁡(-x).\end{aligned}
$$

- Secondly, using the oddness of $cot⁡x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}cot⁡(-x) & =-cot⁡x \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}4cot⁡(-x+4\pi )+1 & =4\cdot (-\frac{1}{4})+1 \\  & =-1+1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{\pi /9}^{\pi /6}2{csc}^{2}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
If we let $u=3x,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $\pi /9$ | $\pi /6$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\pi /3$ | $\pi /2$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /9}^{\pi /6}2{csc}^{2}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}2{csc}^{2}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}{csc}^{2}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{cot}⁡u{|}_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}(\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})) \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}(0-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}) \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2} &=-3 \\ {x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} &=1 \\ -5{x}_{1}+10{x}_{2} &=2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}b \\ c\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $2a+\frac{b}{c}?$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -4 \\ 1 & -2 \\ -5 & 10\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & -5 \\ -4 & -2 & 10\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -4 \\ 1 & -2 \\ -5 & 10\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & -5 \\ -4 & -2 & 10\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}30 & -60 \\ -60 & 120\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-15 \\ 30\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ -2 & 4 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}+2{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{2}+2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
2a+\frac{b}{c}=2\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})+\frac{2}{1}=1.
$$

:question/problem:

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}b \\ c\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $4a+\frac{b}{c}?$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3 \\ -2 & 2\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 & -2 \\ -1 & -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3 \\ -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 & -2 \\ -1 & -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}14 & -14 \\ -14 & 14\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}7 \\ -7\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}14 & -14 & 7 \\ -14 & 14 & -7\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}14 & -14 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}+{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2}+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
4a+\frac{b}{c}=4\cdot (\frac{1}{2})+\frac{1}{1}=3.
$$

:question/problem: ${\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}5{e}^{-4x}\,\text{d}x=$
:question/worked-solution:
If we let $u=-4x,$ then, 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-4\,⟹\,-\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u=\text{d}x.
$$

Computing our limits of integration, we get the following:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $-4\operatorname{ln}⁡3$ |

Then, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}5{e}^{-4x}\,\text{d}x & =5{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{e}^{-4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =5{\int }_{0}^{-4\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{e}^{u}(-\frac{1}{4})\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{-4})}{e}^{u}\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}({e}^{u}){|}_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{-4})} \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}({e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{-4})}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}({3}^{-4}-1) \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}(\frac{1}{{3}^{4}}-1) \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}(\frac{1}{81}-1) \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}(-\frac{80}{81}) \\  & =\frac{100}{81}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 \\ -3 & -2\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}16 \\ -3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},\,W=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $W,$ and the vector $b$ shown above. If the general solution for the weighted least-squares problem $W\,Ax=Wb$ is 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}b \\ c\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of  $a+\frac{b}{c}?$
:question/worked-solution:
To get the normal equation corresponding to $W\,Ax=Wb,$ we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by $(W\,A)^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(W\,A)^{T}\cdot W\,Ax & =(W\,A)^{T}\cdot Wb \\ {A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)Ax & ={A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)b\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since

$$
{W}^{T}W=\begin{bmatrix}{1}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {2}^{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix},
$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 & -3 \\ 2 & 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 \\ -3 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 & -3 \\ 2 & 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}16 \\ -3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 & -3 \\ 2 & 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 \\ -12 & -8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 & -3 \\ 2 & 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}16 \\ -12 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}45 & 30 \\ 30 & 20\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}60 \\ 40\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}45 & 30 & 60 \\ 30 & 20 & 40\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-\frac{2}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}45 & 30 & 60 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{4}{3}-\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{3}-\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{3} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{3} \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+\frac{b}{c}=\frac{4}{3}+\frac{(-\frac{2}{3})}{1}=\frac{2}{3}.
$$

:question/problem:
Find the radius of convergence $R$ for the series

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(x-1)^{3n}}{{n}^{n}}=(x-1)^{3}+\frac{(x-1)^{6}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{(x-1)^{9}}{{3}^{3}}+⋯\,.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
To apply the ratio test we define ${a}_{n}=\frac{(x-1)^{3n}}{{n}^{n}}.$ Then, we calculate the ratio of two successive terms and take the limit as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{(x-1)^{3(n+1)}}{(n+1)^{n+1}}\cdot \frac{{n}^{n}}{(x-1)^{3n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{(x-1)^{3}}{(n+1)}\cdot {(\frac{n}{n+1})}^{n}| \\  & =|x-1{|}^{3}{lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{1}{(n+1)}\cdot {(\frac{n}{n+1})}^{n} \\  & =|x-1{|}^{3}\cdot 0\cdot {e}^{-1} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The series converges if $L<1.$ In this case, the convergence condition is satisfied for all $-\infty <x<\infty .$ Therefore, we conclude that the radius of convergence is $R=\infty .$

:question/problem:
A body of mass $5\,\text{kg}$ is moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis under the action of a single force $F,$ measured in Newtons.
At time $t$ seconds, the position of the body is given by $s(t)=t-4\sqrt{t}$ meters.
Find the expression for the force acting on the body at time $t.$
:question/worked-solution:
According to Newton’s second law

$$
F=ma,
$$

 
where $F$ is the force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration.

To find the velocity $v(t),$ we differentiate the displacement $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-4\sqrt{t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-4{t}^{1/2}) \\  & =1-4\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot {t}^{-1/2} \\  & =1-2{t}^{-1/2}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the acceleration $a(t),$ we differentiate the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-2{t}^{-1/2}) \\  & =0-2\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})\cdot {t}^{-3/2} \\  & ={t}^{-3/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{t\sqrt{t}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the force in Newtons is

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\  & =5\cdot (\frac{1}{t\sqrt{t}}) \\  & =\frac{5}{t\sqrt{t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={t}^{2}+1,\,y={t}^{3},\,t\in [0,2].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=2.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+1)=2t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})=3{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{3}\sqrt{{(2t)}^{2}+{(3{t}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{3}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+9{t}^{4}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{3}\sqrt{{t}^{2}(4+9{t}^{2})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{3}\cdot \sqrt{{t}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{(4+9{t}^{2})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{3}\cdot |t|\cdot \sqrt{9{t}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{3}\cdot t\cdot \sqrt{9{t}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{4}\sqrt{9{t}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={e}^{t}-t,\,y=4{e}^{t/2},\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Calculate the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis.
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=1.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}-t)={e}^{t}-1 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{e}^{t/2})=2{e}^{t/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\sqrt{{({e}^{t}-1)}^{2}+{(2{e}^{t/2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\sqrt{{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{t}+1+4{e}^{t}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+2{e}^{t}+1}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, factoring the expression ${e}^{2t}+2{e}^{t}+1,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+2{e}^{t}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\sqrt{({e}^{t}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\cdot |{e}^{t}+1|\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\cdot ({e}^{t}+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{2t}+{e}^{t}-t{e}^{t}-t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi [{\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{2t}+{e}^{t}-t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{1}t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t]\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the integral ${\int }_{0}^{1}t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t$ using integration by parts. We set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⇒ & {u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{t} & ⇒ & v={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}x & =t{e}^{t}-\int {e}^{t}\cdot 1\,\text{d}x \\  & =t{e}^{t}-{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi [{\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{2t}+{e}^{t}-t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{1}t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t] \\  & =2\pi [{(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}+{e}^{t}-\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2})|}_{0}^{1}-{(t{e}^{t}-{e}^{t})|}_{0}^{1}] \\  & =2\pi [(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2}+e-\frac{1}{2})-(\frac{1}{2}+1-0)-(e-e)+(0-1)] \\  & =2\pi [\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2}+e-3] \\  & =({e}^{2}+2e-6)\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=3{t}^{2},\,y=2{t}^{3},\,t\in [0,\sqrt{3}].
$$

Calculate the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis.
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\sqrt{3}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2})=6t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3})=6{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}3{t}^{2}\sqrt{{(6t)}^{2}+{(6{t}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}3{t}^{2}\sqrt{36{t}^{2}+36{t}^{4}}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, factoring the expression $36{t}^{2}+36{t}^{4},$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}3{t}^{2}\sqrt{36{t}^{2}+36{t}^{4}}\,\text{d}t] \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}3{t}^{2}\sqrt{36{t}^{2}(1+{t}^{2})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}3{t}^{2}\cdot |6t|\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}3{t}^{2}\cdot 6t\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =18\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}2{t}^{3}\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=1+{t}^{2}$ Then, ${t}^{2}=u-1$ and $\text{d}u=2t\,\text{d}t.$ We also need to compute new limits, given below.

| **$t$** | $0$ | $\sqrt{3}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $4$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =18\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}2{t}^{3}\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =18\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}2t\cdot {t}^{2}\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =18\pi {\int }_{1}^{4}(u-1)\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =18\pi {\int }_{1}^{4}(u-1){u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =18\pi {\int }_{1}^{4}({u}^{3/2}-{u}^{1/2})\,\text{d}u \\  & =18\pi \cdot {[\frac{2{u}^{5/2}}{5}-\frac{2{u}^{3/2}}{3}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =18\pi [(\frac{2({4}^{5/2})}{5}-\frac{2({4}^{3/2})}{3})-(\frac{2}{5}-\frac{2}{3})] \\  & =18\pi \cdot [(\frac{64}{5}-\frac{16}{3})-(\frac{2}{5}-\frac{2}{3})) \\  & =18\pi \cdot (\frac{62}{5}-\frac{14}{3}) \\  & =18\pi \cdot \frac{116}{15} \\  & =\frac{696\pi }{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=2\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,y=t+\frac{1}{t},\,t\in [1,e].
$$

Calculate the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis.
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=1$ to ${t}_{2}=e.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)=\frac{2}{t} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+\frac{1}{t})=1-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}(t+\frac{1}{t})\sqrt{{(\frac{2}{t})}^{2}+{(1-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}(t+\frac{1}{t})\sqrt{\frac{4}{{t}^{2}}+1-\frac{2}{{t}^{2}}+\frac{1}{{t}^{4}}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}(t+\frac{1}{t})\sqrt{1+\frac{2}{{t}^{2}}+\frac{1}{{t}^{4}}}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, factoring the expression $1+\frac{2}{{t}^{2}}+\frac{1}{{t}^{4}},$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}(t+\frac{1}{t})\sqrt{1+\frac{2}{{t}^{2}}+\frac{1}{{t}^{4}}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}(t+\frac{1}{t})\sqrt{{(1+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})}^{2}} \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}(t+\frac{1}{t})\cdot |1+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}|\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}(t+\frac{1}{t})\cdot (1+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}(\frac{1}{{t}^{3}}+t+\frac{2}{t})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}(\frac{1}{{t}^{3}}+t+\frac{2}{t})\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi \cdot {[-\frac{1}{2{t}^{2}}+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|]}_{1}^{e} \\  & =2\pi [(-\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}}+\frac{{e}^{2}}{2}+2)-(-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}+0)] \\  & =2\pi [\frac{{e}^{4}-1}{2{e}^{2}}+2] \\  & =(\frac{{e}^{4}-1}{{e}^{2}}+4)\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Now, using the identity $\operatorname{sinh}⁡2t=2\operatorname{sinh}⁡t\operatorname{cosh}⁡t,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\sqrt{{sinh}^{2}⁡t+4{sinh}^{2}⁡2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\sqrt{{sinh}^{2}⁡t+4(2\operatorname{sinh}⁡t\operatorname{cosh}⁡t)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\sqrt{{sinh}^{2}⁡t+16{sinh}^{2}⁡t{cosh}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\sqrt{{sinh}^{2}⁡t(1+16{cosh}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{{sinh}^{2}⁡t}\cdot \sqrt{1+16{cosh}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\cdot |\operatorname{sinh}⁡t|\cdot \sqrt{1+16{cosh}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{sinh}⁡t\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\sqrt{1+16{cosh}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Find the acute angle between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix},\,{a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot {(\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot {\begin{bmatrix}5 & 8 \\ 8 & 14\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}14 & -8 \\ -8 & 5\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ Equivalently, it is the acute angle between $x$ and any non-zero vector that is parallel to ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ So, to make calculations easier, we can find the angle between the vectors

$\,$ $x=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\,$ and $\,2\,{\text{proj}}_{S}x=\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{(-1)\cdot (-3)+(-1)\cdot 0+2\cdot 3}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}}\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+{0}^{2}+{3}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{9}{\sqrt{6}\sqrt{18}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})=\frac{\pi }{6},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

:question/problem:
Find the acute angle between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},\,{a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\cdot {(\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\cdot {\begin{bmatrix}9 & 5 \\ 5 & 3\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -5 \\ -5 & 9\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ Equivalently, it is the acute angle between $x$ and any non-zero vector that is parallel to ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ So, to make calculations easier, we can find the angle between the vectors

$\,$ $x=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,$ and $\,2\,{\text{proj}}_{S}x=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{0\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 1+0\cdot 0}{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1}\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})=\frac{\pi }{4},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -3 \\ 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot {(\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 3 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-1 & -3 \\ 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 3 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ -3 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -3 \\ 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot {\begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 \\ 6 & 27\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 18\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -3 \\ 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{18}\begin{bmatrix}27 & -6 \\ -6 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 18\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -3 \\ 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 3 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ Equivalently, it is the acute angle between $x$ and any non-zero vector that is parallel to ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ So, to make calculations easier, we can find the angle between the vectors

$\,$ $x=\begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ -3 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\,$ and $\,2\,{\text{proj}}_{S}x=\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 3 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}.$

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{(-6)\cdot (-3)+(-3)\cdot 3+3\cdot 6}{\sqrt{(-6)^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{3}^{2}}\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+{3}^{2}+{6}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{27}{\sqrt{54}\sqrt{54}} \\  & =\frac{27}{54} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{\pi }{3},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

:question/problem:
Find the acute angle between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix},\,\,x=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Round the answer to $2$ decimal places.
:question/worked-solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot {(\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot {\begin{bmatrix}11 & 8 \\ 8 & 8\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{24}\begin{bmatrix}8 & -8 \\ -8 & 11\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ Equivalently, it is the acute angle between $x$ and any non-zero vector that is parallel to ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ So, to make calculations easier, we can find the angle between the vectors

$\,$ $x=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\,$ and $\,2\,{\text{proj}}_{S}x=\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x\cdot {\text{proj}}_{S}x}{‖x‖‖{\text{proj}}_{S}x‖} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 5+2\cdot 2+1\cdot 1}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{{5}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{15}{\sqrt{9}\sqrt{30}} \\  & =\frac{15}{3\sqrt{30}} \\  & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{30}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{5}{\sqrt{30}})≈{24.09}^{∘},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

:question/problem:

The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

:question/problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-7 & 15 \\ -3 & 7\end{bmatrix},\,D=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix},\,P=\begin{bmatrix}a & 5 \\ b & 3\end{bmatrix}
$$

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$ find the value of  $\frac{a}{b}.$
:question/worked-solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$

So, the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-2.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}=-2.$ Computing $A-(-2)I,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =\begin{bmatrix}-7 & 15 \\ -3 & 7\end{bmatrix}-(-2)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 15 \\ -3 & 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 15 & 0 \\ -3 & 9 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{3}{5}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 15 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

 

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=3{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{3}{1}=3.$

:question/problem: Find matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=B,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix and $B=\begin{bmatrix}7 & -6 \\ 8 & -7\end{bmatrix}.$
:question/worked-solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $B$ using its characteristic equation $det(B-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}7-\lambda  & -6 \\ 8 & -7-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (7-\lambda )(-7-\lambda )-(-6)\cdot 8 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-49+48 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-1 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)(\lambda -1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=1.$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $B.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-1)I & =\begin{bmatrix}7 & -6 \\ 8 & -7\end{bmatrix}-(-1)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & -6 \\ 8 & -6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & -6 & 0 \\ 8 & -6 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}8 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{3}{4}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{4}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=4,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-1I & =\begin{bmatrix}7 & -6 \\ 8 & -7\end{bmatrix}-1\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & -6 \\ 8 & -8\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & -6 & 0 \\ 8 & -8 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+(-\frac{4}{3}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}6 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},\,P=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

:question/problem:
$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 9 & 0 \\ -4 & -8 & 0 \\ -6 & -6 & -4\end{bmatrix}
$$

If the matrix $A$ above is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}5-\lambda  & 9 & 0 \\ -4 & -8-\lambda  & 0 \\ -6 & -6 & -4-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-4-\lambda )\begin{vmatrix}5-\lambda  & 9 \\ -4 & -8-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-4-\lambda )((5-\lambda )(-8-\lambda )+36) & =0 \\ (-4-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda -4) & =0 \\ -(\lambda +4)(\lambda +4)(\lambda -1) & =0 \\ (\lambda +4)^{2}(\lambda -1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ (simple root) and ${\lambda }_{2}=-4$ (double root).

Let's now find the dimension of the eigenspace corresponding to each eigenvalue.

- First, we consider the simple root ${\lambda }_{1}=1.$ Since the root is simple, the dimension of the eigenspace ${V}_{1}$ corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ is

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{1})=1.
$$

- Next, we consider the double root ${\lambda }_{2}=-4.$ Let's find the dimension of the eigenspace ${V}_{-4}$ corresponding to this eigenvalue. To do this, we row-reduce the matrix $A-(-4)I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-4)I & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 9 & 0 \\ -4 & -8 & 0 \\ -6 & -6 & -4\end{bmatrix}-(-4)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}9 & 9 & 0 \\ -4 & -4 & 0 \\ -6 & -6 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{3}+(\frac{4}{9}){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}9 & 9 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -6 & -6 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(\frac{2}{3}){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}9 & 9 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). This implies that we will have $3-1=2$ linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-4.$ So,

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{-4})=2.
$$

Therefore, $A$ is diagonalizable, since

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{1})+\text{dim}({V}_{-4})=1+2=3.\,✓
$$

Finally, a corresponding diagonal matrix is 

$$
D=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

:question/problem: Rewrite $-({x}^{2}+7x+10)$ by completing the square.
:question/worked-solution:
We begin by completing the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
{x}^{2}+7x+10
$$

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with $2$ as a factor:

$$
{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{7}{2}x+10
$$

Then, we *add* and *then subtract* ${(\frac{7}{2})}^{2}$, writing the constant term $10$ last:

$$
\underbrace{{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{7}{2}x+{(\frac{7}{2})}^{2}}-{(\frac{7}{2})}^{2}+10
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
{(x+\frac{7}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{7}{2})}^{2}+10
$$

Evaluating the last two terms, we get

$$
{(x+\frac{7}{2})}^{2}-\frac{9}{4}.
$$

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}-({x}^{2}+7x+10) & =-({(x+\frac{7}{2})}^{2}-\frac{9}{4}) \\  & =-{(x+\frac{7}{2})}^{2}+\frac{9}{4} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}-{(x+\frac{7}{2})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
