Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,0,\,(3-z)\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of a right circular cylinder of height $3$ whose base is a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin, as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
:question/worked-solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $F=⟨0,\,0,\,(3-z)\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral side of $S$ is parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](images/05/05664db64ac6595ff0caec7daeec20cb3508d5c18a5266aa126295e3aa040233.png)

 
Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=3$ for ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1.$ Therefore, for everywhere on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
F(x,y,0)=⟨0,\,0,\,(3-3)\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}⟩=⟨0,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}0\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}0\,\text{d}S \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,(3-z)\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,(3-0)\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-3\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-3\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}S \\  & =-3{∬}_{D}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying a change of variables $(x,y)\to (r,\theta ),\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-3{∬}_{D}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & =-3{∬}_{D}\sqrt{{r}^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-3{∬}_{D}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r \\  & =-3\cdot 2\pi \cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{r}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-6\pi \cdot (\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =-2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =0+(-2\pi ) \\  & =-2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the surface area of the part of the surface $x={y}^{2}+\sqrt{3}z$ whose projection onto the $yz$-plane is bounded by $z=y,$ $y=1,$ and the $y$-axis.
:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $x=f(y,z)$ with $(y,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
x={y}^{2}+\sqrt{3}z,\,(y,z)\in D,
$$

where 

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,0\le z\le y},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/0c/0cf571155f2a4cd78d83c4808326cd8102badb3c22f43e00d95aee2494859f48.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+\sqrt{3}z)=2y, \\ \frac{∂x}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({y}^{2}+\sqrt{3}z)=\sqrt{3},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(2y)^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{4+4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2\sqrt{1+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{y}\sqrt{1+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1+{y}^{2}}\cdot z\,{|}_{z=0}^{z=y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1+{y}^{2}}\cdot y\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=1+{y}^{2},$ we get $\text{d}u=2y\,\text{d}y.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & 0 & 1 \\ u & 1 & 2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1+{y}^{2}}\cdot y\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}\,{|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}({2}^{3/2}-{1}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}(2\sqrt{2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the surface area of the part of the surface $x={e}^{y}-z$ whose projection onto the $yz$-plane is bounded by $z={e}^{2y},$ $y=0,$ $y=\frac{1}{2},$ and the $y$-axis.
:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $x=f(y,z)$ with $(y,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
x={e}^{y}-z,\,(y,z)\in D,
$$

where 

$$
D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le \frac{1}{2},\,0\le z\le {e}^{2y}\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/9c/9cae5b68f77c2d79df8a81d0421146ac2bbe618c6065a457c33c86caceeb1327.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{y}-z)={e}^{y}, \\ \frac{∂x}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{y}-z)=-1,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+({e}^{y})^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{{e}^{2y}+2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}{\int }_{0}^{{e}^{2y}}\sqrt{{e}^{2y}+2}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{{e}^{2y}+2}\cdot z\,{|}_{z=0}^{z={e}^{2y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{{e}^{2y}+2}\cdot {e}^{2y}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u={e}^{2y}+2,$ we get $\text{d}u=2{e}^{2y}\,\text{d}y.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & 0 & 1/2 \\ u & 3 & e+2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{{e}^{2y}+2}\cdot {e}^{2y}\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{3}^{e+2}\frac{1}{2}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{u}^{3/2}\,{|}_{3}^{e+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}((e+2)^{3/2}-{3}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{(e+2)^{3/2}-3\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/9a/9afc7f79f4612ce579e82a6b3c5086922d14051978907bfeb5c133a3f99791c7.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,0,\,x{y}^{2}+z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
:question/worked-solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $F=⟨0,\,0,\,x{y}^{2}+z⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](images/fa/fa4986b1de44fa4ccc75114e64abfd93d0de16618f2f1b29695d9115019b6e3e.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=4$ for $0\le x\le 2$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=4$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,x{y}^{2}+z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,x{y}^{2}+4⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =x{y}^{2}+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}x{y}^{2}+4\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}x{y}^{2}+4\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}x{y}^{2}+4\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+4x]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}+8\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}+8y]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{26}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for $0\le x\le 2$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,0,\,x{y}^{2}+z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,x{y}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-x{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & =-{∬}_{D}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y{\int }_{0}^{2}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{[\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{0}^{1}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot 2 \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{26}{3}+(-\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/01/01902836fd1e91ac829f67a279103a9b3d5732d7b058f03c695b6733a42e673d.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
:question/worked-solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $F=⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+z⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](images/c0/c058465d6ca7855446711ebc44f6b23913ee786d2fd9bb32ae6c671964e1ad32.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=1$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=1$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+1⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & ={x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+1\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+1\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+1\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}+x{y}^{2}+x]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}+\frac{5}{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}+\frac{5}{4}y]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{19}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-({x}^{3}+{y}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-({x}^{3}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}S \\  & =-{∬}_{D}{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}+x{y}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{[\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{4}y]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{7}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{19}{12}+(-\frac{7}{12}) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
$$
{∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A,\,D=\{(y,z)\,:\,\boxed{}\,\}
$$

The integral above gives the surface area of the part of the surface $x={y}^{3}+{e}^{z}$ that lies inside the elliptical cylinder $\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{9}=1.$ From left to right, what are the missing expressions?
:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $x=f(y,z)$ with $(y,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
x={y}^{3}+{e}^{z},\,\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{9}\le 1.
$$

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{3}+{e}^{z})=3{y}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂x}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({y}^{3}+{e}^{z})={e}^{z},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(3{y}^{2})}^{2}+({e}^{z})^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+9{y}^{4}+{e}^{2z}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is

$\,$ $\sqrt{1+9{y}^{4}+{e}^{2z}}\,$ and $\,\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{9}\le 1.$

First, we apply the sum rule and write our repeated integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x-{\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}z\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x
$$

Since the domain of integration $R=[0,4]\times [1,2]\times [0,1]$ is a rectangular box, and each integrand can be expressed as $f(x)\cdot g(y)\cdot h(z),$ we can rewrite our sum of repeated integrals as follows:

$$
{\int }_{0}^{4}x\,\text{d}x{\int }_{1}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,{\int }_{0}^{1}{z}^{3}\,\text{d}z-{\int }_{0}^{4}\text{d}x{\int }_{1}^{2}\text{d}y\,{\int }_{0}^{1}z\,\text{d}z
$$

Let's evaluate each of these separately:

- For the first product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4}x\,\text{d}x{\int }_{1}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,{\int }_{0}^{1}{z}^{3}\,\text{d}z & ={[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{4}\cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{1}^{2}\cdot {[\frac{1}{4}{z}^{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(8-0)(\frac{8}{3}-\frac{1}{3})(\frac{1}{4}-0) \\  & =8(\frac{7}{3})(\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\frac{14}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4}\text{d}x{\int }_{1}^{2}\text{d}y\,{\int }_{0}^{1}z\,\text{d}z & =(4-0)\cdot (2-1)\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{z}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =4\cdot 1\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}-z)\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x=\frac{14}{3}-2=\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨z,\,2,\,-3xy⟩\cdot \text{d}S
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by the equations

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u{v}^{2},\,-1,\,1-2u⟩
$$

for $0\le u\le 1$ and $0\le v\le 1.$
:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u{v}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(-1),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(1-2u)⟩ \\  & =⟨{v}^{2},\,0,\,-2⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u{v}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(-1),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(1-2u)⟩ \\  & =⟨2uv,\,0,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ {v}^{2} & 0 & -2 \\ 2uv & 0 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|,-|\begin{aligned}{v}^{2} & -2 \\ 2uv & 0\end{aligned}|,|\begin{aligned}{v}^{2} & 0 \\ 2uv & 0\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-4uv,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & ={⟨z,\,2,\,-3xy⟩|}_{x=u{v}^{2}\,y=-1\,z=1-2u} \\  & =⟨1-2u,\,2,\,-3(u{v}^{2})(-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨1-2u,\,2,\,3u{v}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨1-2u,\,2,\,3u{v}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,-4uv,\,0⟩ \\  & =(1-2u)\cdot 0+2\cdot (-4uv)+3u{v}^{2}\cdot 0 \\  & =-8uv\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral evaluates to

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨z,\,2,\,-3xy⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-8uv)\,\text{d}A \\  & =-8{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}uv\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u \\  & =-8{\int }_{0}^{1}u\,\text{d}u{\int }_{0}^{1}v\,\text{d}v\, \\  & =-8\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}]}_{0}^{1}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-8(\frac{1}{2})(\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y)=1.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}6y\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}6y\cdot \sqrt{1+{1}^{2}+(1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}6y\cdot \sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{3}{∬}_{D}\,6y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ our domain can be expressed as 

$$

and

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{1+(-1)^{2}+(\sqrt{2})^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{4}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{∬}_{D}\,\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(-{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2})=-2x,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(-{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2})=4y.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(-2x)}^{2}+{(4y)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,{x}^{2}(-{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2})^{2}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}\,({x}^{6}-4{y}^{2}{x}^{4}+4{y}^{4}{x}^{2})\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}}\,\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}

:question/problem: ${\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{z}{\int }_{0}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y+z)\,dx\,dy\,dz=$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{z}{\int }_{0}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y+z)\,dx\,dy\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{z}[{\int }_{0}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y+z)\,dx]dy\,dz \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{z}[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y+z)]_{x=0}^{x=y}\,dy\,dz \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{z}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(y+y+z)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0+y+z)\,dy\,dz \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{z}\operatorname{cos}⁡(y+z)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y+z)\,dy\,dz\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y,$ treating $z$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{z}\operatorname{cos}⁡(y+z)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y+z)\,dy\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[{\int }_{0}^{z}\operatorname{cos}⁡(y+z)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y+z)\,dy]dz \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{[\operatorname{sin}⁡(y+z)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2y+z)]}_{y=0}^{y=z}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(z+z)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2z+z)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0+z)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0+z)\,dz \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2z-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡3z-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,dz\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2z-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡3z-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,dz & ={[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2z+\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{cos}⁡3z+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡z]}_{z=0}^{z=\pi /2} \\  & =[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi +\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})]-[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡0+\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{cos}⁡0+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡0] \\  & =[\frac{1}{2}+0+0]-[-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{6} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{y}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}z}\frac{z}{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{y}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}z}\frac{z}{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,dx]dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{y}{[z\cdot \frac{1}{z}\cdot \operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{z})]}_{x=0}^{x=\sqrt{3}z}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{y}{[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{z})]}_{x=0}^{x=\sqrt{3}z}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{y}\operatorname{arctan}⁡\sqrt{3}-\operatorname{arctan}⁡0\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{y}\frac{\pi }{3}\,dz\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $z,$ treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{y}\frac{\pi }{3}\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{y}\frac{\pi }{3}\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[\frac{\pi }{3}{\int }_{0}^{y}dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{\pi }{3}[z]_{z=0}^{z=y}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{\pi }{3}\cdot y\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{\pi }{3}\,y\,dy & =\frac{\pi }{3}{[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}(2-0) \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:

Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}(x+y)\,\text{d}S,
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=-2x+2y$ and whose domain is the left half-circle of radius $1$ centered at $O$, as shown above.
:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2x+2y)=-2,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2x+2y)=2.
$$

 

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}(x+y)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(x+y)\cdot \sqrt{1+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(x+y)\cdot \sqrt{9}\,\text{d}A \\  & =3{∬}_{D}\,(x+y)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ our domain can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}3{∬}_{D}\,(x+y)\,\text{d}A & =3{∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta  \\  & =3{∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\cdot r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{∬}_{Δ}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ){\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ){[\frac{{r}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =[\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}\frac{xy}{\sqrt{z}}\,\text{d}S
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=\frac{1}{4}+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $-2\le y\le 1.$
:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{4}+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{4}+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\frac{xy}{\sqrt{z}}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{xy}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\sqrt{1+(2x)^{2}+(2y)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{xy}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{2xy}{\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{2xy}{\cancel{\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}}}\cancel{\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,2xy\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-2}^{1}(2xy)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[x{y}^{2}]_{y=-2}^{y=1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[-\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}(1-0) \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}4z\,\text{d}S
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=x+y$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$
:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+y)=1,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y)=1.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}4z\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,4(x+y)\,\sqrt{1+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}4(x+y)\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}{[4xy+2{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}(4x+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{3}{[2{x}^{2}+2x]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =4\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y,$ treating $x$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{{z}^{2}}\frac{x}{z}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{y}{z})\,dy\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[{\int }_{0}^{{z}^{2}}\frac{x}{z}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{y}{z})\,dy]dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{[\frac{x}{z}\cdot z\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{y}{z})]}_{y=0}^{y={z}^{2}}\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}x{[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{y}{z})]}_{y=0}^{y={z}^{2}}\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}x(\operatorname{sin}⁡z-\operatorname{sin}⁡0)\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}x\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,dz\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $z,$ treating $x$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}x\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}[{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}x\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,dz]dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}[-x\operatorname{cos}⁡z]_{z=0}^{z=\pi /2}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}x(-0+1)\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}x\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{0}x\,dx & ={[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{x=-1}^{x=0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(0-1) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}\frac{z-y}{\sqrt{6}y}\,\text{d}S
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=2x+y$ for $1\le x\le 2$ and $1\le y\le e.$
:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+y)=2,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+y)=1.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\frac{z-y}{\sqrt{6}y}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{(2x+y)-y}{\sqrt{6}y}\sqrt{1+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{2x}{y}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{2x}{y}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}2x[\operatorname{ln}⁡y]_{y=1}^{y=e}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =[{x}^{2}]_{1}^{2} \\  & =4-1 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x+8y)=4,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x+8y)=8.

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\frac{z}{36x}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{4x+8y}{36x}\sqrt{1+{4}^{2}+{8}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,9\frac{4(x+2y)}{36x}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{x+2y}{x}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{x}(1+\frac{2y}{x})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{[y+\frac{{y}^{2}}{x}]}_{0}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(x+\frac{{x}^{2}}{x}-0)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =[{x}^{2}]_{1}^{2} \\  & =4-1 \\  & =3\end{aligned}

:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral

where $S$ is defined by $z=1+x+y$ for $0\le x\le \frac{1}{2}$ and $-x\le y\le 0.$
:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(1+x+y)=1,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(1+x+y)=1.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}(1+x+y)^{2}}\sqrt{1+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}{\int }_{-x}^{0}\,\frac{1}{(1+x+y)^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}{[-\frac{1}{1+x+y}]}_{y=-x}^{y=0}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}(-\frac{1}{1+x}+1)\text{d}x \\  & =[-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+x]_{0}^{1/2} \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{2})+\frac{1}{2}-0 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡3+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}

:question/problem:
$$
{∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A,\,D=\{(x,z)\,:\,\boxed{}\,\}
$$

The integral above gives the surface area of the part of the surface $y=\frac{1}{xz}$ that lies inside the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{z}^{2}=2.$ From left to right, what are the missing expressions?
:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $y=f(x,z)$ with $(x,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂y}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
y=\frac{1}{xz},\,{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 2.
$$

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂y}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{xz})=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}z}, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{1}{xz})=-\frac{1}{x{z}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂y}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}z})}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{x{z}^{2}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{{x}^{4}{z}^{2}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}{z}^{4}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}}{{x}^{4}{z}^{4}}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is

$\,$ $\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}}{{x}^{4}{z}^{4}}}\,$ and ${x}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 2.$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
{∭}_{R}16x\,dV
$$

where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,y)\in D,\,0\le z\le x-y},
$$

and $D$ is a finite region in $xy$-plane enclosed between the coordinate axes and the line $y=2x-3$ in the fourth quadrant.
:question/worked-solution:
Writing down our triple integral as a mixed integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}16x\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{x-y}16x\,dz]dA.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z,$ treating $x$ and $y$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{x-y}16x\,dz]dA & ={∬}_{D}[16xz]_{z=0}^{z=x-y}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}16x(x-y)\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

We must now evaluate the double integral above over the region $D$ in the $xy$-plane shown below.

![](images/bd/bddbd1c97fe8cd74f9903dec340495f04401323b8e1236680c57c13b18069eb4.png)

We can evaluate our double integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}16x(x-y)\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{3/2}{\int }_{2x-3}^{0}16x(x-y)\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3/2}16x[{\int }_{2x-3}^{0}(x-y)\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3/2}16x{[xy-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{y=2x-3}^{y=0}dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3/2}16x(0-x(2x-3)+\frac{1}{2}(2x-3)^{2})\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3/2}8x(-4{x}^{2}+6x+4{x}^{2}-12x+9)\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3/2}8x(-6x+9)\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3/2}-48{x}^{2}+72x\,dx \\  & ={[-16{x}^{3}+36{x}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=3/2} \\  & =-16{(\frac{3}{2})}^{3}+36{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2} \\  & =-54+81 \\  & =27\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y,z)=⟨{cos}^{2}⁡(xy),\,{cos}^{2}⁡(xy),\,1⟩,
$$

where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=\operatorname{tan}⁡(xy)$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $-x\le y\le 0.$
:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ given by $z=g(x,y)$ for $(x,y)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡(xy))=\frac{y}{{cos}^{2}⁡(xy)} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{tan}⁡(xy))=\frac{x}{{cos}^{2}⁡(xy)}\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the flux of $F$ through $S$ is given by 

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨{cos}^{2}⁡(xy),\,{cos}^{2}⁡(xy),\,1⟩\cdot \text{d}S
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨{cos}^{2}⁡(xy),\,{cos}^{2}⁡(xy),\,1⟩{|}_{z=\operatorname{tan}⁡(xy)} \\  & =⟨\underbrace{{cos}^{2}⁡(xy)}_{P},\,\underbrace{{cos}^{2}⁡(xy)}_{Q},\,\underbrace{1}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨{cos}^{2}⁡(xy),\,{cos}^{2}⁡(xy),\,1⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-({cos}^{2}⁡(xy))\cdot (\frac{y}{{cos}^{2}⁡(xy)})-({cos}^{2}⁡(xy))\cdot (\frac{x}{{cos}^{2}⁡(xy)})+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-y-x+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-x}^{0}(-y-x+1)\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}-xy+y]}_{y=-x}^{y=0}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-{x}^{2}+x)\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+x)\,dx \\  & ={[-\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the volume of the solid region enclosed by the $xy$-plane, the surface $z=4-{x}^{2},$ and the planes $x=0,$ $x=2,$ $y=0,$ $y=2.$

Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
{∭}_{R}3x\,dV
$$

where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,{x}^{2}\le y\le 4},
$$

and $D$ is a finite region in $xz$-plane enclosed between the $x$-axis, the $z$-axis, and the curve $z+{x}^{2}=4$ in the first quadrant.
:question/worked-solution:
Writing down our triple integral as a mixed integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}3x\,dV={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{4}3x\,dy]dA.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y,$ treating $x$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{4}3x\,dy]dA & ={∬}_{D}3x[y]_{y={x}^{2}}^{y=4}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}3x(4-{x}^{2})\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

We must now evaluate this double integral over the region $D$ in the $xz$-plane shown below.

![](images/bc/bcac3bb634fa04d2ccd4c3897f7b1db891a0b21eacfa96579f672b812fd92c07.png)

 

We can evaluate our double integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}3x(4-{x}^{2})\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{4-{x}^{2}}3x(4-{x}^{2})\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}3x(4-{x}^{2})[z]_{z=0}^{z=4-{x}^{2}}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}3x(4-{x}^{2})(4-{x}^{2})\,dx \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(-2x)(4-{x}^{2})^{2}\,dx \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}{[\frac{(4-{x}^{2})^{3}}{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}(\frac{0-{4}^{3}}{3}) \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}(-\frac{64}{3}) \\  & =32\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the values of $\theta $ at which the curve $x=\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,0\le \theta <2\pi $ intersects the line $\sqrt{3}x+y=0.$
:question/worked-solution:
To find the coordinates of the points of intersection, we take the equation of the line, replace $x$ and $y$ with the parametric formulas, and then solve for $\theta :$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}x+y & =0 \\ \sqrt{3}(\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta } & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta } \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

The principal value of $\theta $ is

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})=-\frac{\pi }{6}.
$$

This value lies outside the domain $0\le \theta <2\pi .$ To get a value that's inside the domain, we add $\pi :$

$$
{\theta }_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{6}+\pi =\frac{5\pi }{6}
$$

To get a second solution, we add $\pi $ to ${\theta }_{1}:$

$$
{\theta }_{2}=\frac{5\pi }{6}+\pi =\frac{11\pi }{6}
$$

Therefore, our solutions are $\frac{5\pi }{6},\,\frac{11\pi }{6}.$

:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)),$ given that 

$$
u=x+y,\,v=z,\,w=4y-2{z}^{2}.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =1 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =4 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =-4z\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 4 & -4z\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 4 & -4z\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(0-4) \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-4)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)),$ given that 

$$
u=z-y,\,v=x+z,\,w=-3x.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =1 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =1 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =1 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =-3 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -3 & 0 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-(-1)\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -3 & 0\end{vmatrix}+1\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(0+3)+1(0-0) \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)),$ given that 

$$
u=y-3z,\,v=x+2z,\,w=3x-y.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =-3 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =1 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =2 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =3 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 3 & -1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-1\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 0\end{vmatrix}-3\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 3 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-1(0-6)-3(-1-0) \\  & =6+3 \\  & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)),$ given that 

$$
u=3x+yz,\,v=z,\,w=-y.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =3 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =z & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =y \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =1 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}3 & z & y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =3\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =3(0+1) \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{x} \\ {e}^{x+y} \\ {e}^{x+y+z}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$
:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)={e}^{x},\,v(x,y,z)={e}^{x+y},\,w(x,y,z)={e}^{x+y+z}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & ={e}^{x} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & ={e}^{x+y} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & ={e}^{x+y} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & ={e}^{x+y+z} & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & ={e}^{x+y+z} & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & ={e}^{x+y+z}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}{e}^{x} & 0 & 0 \\ {e}^{x+y} & {e}^{x+y} & 0 \\ {e}^{x+y+z} & {e}^{x+y+z} & {e}^{x+y+z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{x}\begin{vmatrix}{e}^{x+y} & 0 \\ {e}^{x+y+z} & {e}^{x+y+z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{x}({e}^{2x+2y+z}-0) \\  & ={e}^{3x+2y+z}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{3x+2y+z} & ={e}^{x+(x+y)+(x+y+z)} \\  & ={e}^{x}\cdot {e}^{x+y}\cdot {e}^{x+y+z} \\  & =uvw\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{uvw}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x \\ z-y \\ xy\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $x\ne 0.$*
:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=x,\,v(x,y,z)=z-y,\,w(x,y,z)=xy.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =1 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =y & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =x & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ y & x & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ x & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(0-x) \\  & =-x.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}-x & =-u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-u)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{u}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}xy \\ yz \\ xz\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $x,y,z>0.$*
:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=xy,\,v(x,y,z)=yz,\,w(x,y,z)=xz.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =y & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =x & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =z & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =y \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =z & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}y & x & 0 \\ 0 & z & y \\ z & 0 & x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =y\begin{vmatrix}z & y \\ 0 & x\end{vmatrix}-x\begin{vmatrix}0 & y \\ z & x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =y(xz-0)-x(0-yz) \\  & =xyz+xyz \\  & =2xyz.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2xyz & =2\sqrt{(xyz)^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{xy(yz)(xz)} \\  & =2\sqrt{uvw}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{uvw}}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}y{z}^{2} \\ z{x}^{2} \\ x{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $x,y,z\ne 0.$*
:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=y{z}^{2},\,v(x,y,z)=z{x}^{2},\,w(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & ={z}^{2} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =2yz \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =2xz & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & ={x}^{2} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & ={y}^{2} & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =2xy & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & {z}^{2} & 2yz \\ 2xz & 0 & {x}^{2} \\ {y}^{2} & 2xy & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-{z}^{2}\begin{vmatrix}2xy & {x}^{2} \\ {y}^{2} & 0\end{vmatrix}+2yz\begin{vmatrix}2xz & 0 \\ {y}^{2} & 2xy\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-{z}^{2}(0-{x}^{2}{y}^{2})+2yz(4{x}^{2}yz-0) \\  & ={x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+8{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2} \\  & =9{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2} & =9{({x}^{3}{y}^{3}{z}^{3})}^{2/3} \\  & =9{(y{z}^{2}\cdot z{x}^{2}\cdot x{y}^{2})}^{2/3} \\  & =9(uvw)^{2/3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{9(uvw)^{2/3}}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Which of the following shows the region in the $uv$-plane where the transformation $T,$ given by 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{u}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} \\ u-\frac{1}{3}v\end{bmatrix},
$$

is (locally) orientation-reversing?
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that a transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing at the points where the Jacobian determinant is negative:

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}<0
$$

We have

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{u}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} \\ u-\frac{1}{3}v\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}3{u}^{2} & -v \\ 1 & -\frac{1}{3}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(3{u}^{2})\cdot (-\frac{1}{3})-(1)\cdot (-v) \\  & =v-{u}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the required regions, we solve the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}v-{u}^{2} & <0 \\ v & <{u}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Notice that the equation 

$$
v={u}^{2}
$$

defines a parabola, and the coordinates of, say, $(1,-1)$ satisfy the inequality. 

Therefore, the region where the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing must be the following:
