:question/problem: $\int \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x=$
:question/worked-solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x=2\sqrt{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x(2\sqrt{x})-\int (2\sqrt{x})(\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\sqrt{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)-2\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\sqrt{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)-4\sqrt{x}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

:question/problem: $\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{3\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }=$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we rewrite the expression using the definitions of $\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta $ and $\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta $:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{3\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } & =\frac{\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{3(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta })\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we multiply the numerator and the denominator by $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot (\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta })\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{3(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot {sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta })} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\cdot \frac{1}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }}-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{3(\frac{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\cdot {sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }})} \\  & =\frac{1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use $1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta $ to simplify the expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta } & =\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{\cancel{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }}{3\cancel{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that:

$$
\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{3\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }=\frac{1}{3}
$$

:question/problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\,\,y=3\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$
:question/worked-solution:
First, let's make the trigonometric functions the subject of each equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t=\frac{x}{2} \\ y=3\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{cos}⁡2t=\frac{y}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using double angle formula for cosine and the Pythagorean identity, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t & ={cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =(1-{sin}^{2}⁡t)-{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{sin}⁡t=\frac{x}{2}$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡2t=\frac{y}{3}$ into this formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{3} & =1-2{(\frac{x}{2})}^{2} \\ \frac{y}{3} & =1-2(\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}) \\ \frac{y}{3} & =1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2} \\ y & =3(1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y=3(1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}).$

:question/problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the curve defined parametrically as 

$$

$$
:question/worked-solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t=\frac{x}{4} \\ y=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{cos}⁡2t=\frac{y}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using double angle formula for cosine and the Pythagorean identity, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t & ={cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡t-(1-{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =2{cos}^{2}⁡t-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{cos}⁡t=\frac{x}{4}$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡2t=\frac{y}{2}$ into this formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{2} & =2{(\frac{x}{4})}^{2}-1 \\ \frac{y}{2} & =2(\frac{{x}^{2}}{16})-1 \\ \frac{y}{2} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}-1 \\ y & =2(\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y=2(\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}-1).$

:question/problem: Find ${f}^{′}(x)$ for $f(x)=arccscx\cdot arcsecx$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(arccscx) & =-\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}, \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(arcsecx) & =\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the product rule and the formulae above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =arcsecx\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(arccscx)+arccscx\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(arcsecx) \\  & =arcsecx\cdot (-\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}})+arccscx\cdot (\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}) \\  & =-\frac{arcsecx}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}+\frac{arccscx}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\frac{arccscx-arcsecx}{|x|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: $\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}}}\text{d}x=$
:question/worked-solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{9\cdot (1-{x}^{2}/9)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/9}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/3)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

 

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{3})}^{2}.$  

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{3}.$ Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=3\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/3)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (3\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{x}{3})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: If the $10$th term of an arithmetic series is $-\frac{1}{5}$ and the sum of the first $21$ terms is $0,$ then the first term of the series is ${a}_{1}=${{field-1}}.
:question/worked-solution:
We are given one term of the series. So, to find the first term, we use the formula for the sum of an arithmetic series in the form

$$
{S}_{N}=\frac{N}{2}(2{a}_{1}+(N-1)d),
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term, $d$ is the common difference, and $N$ is the number of terms.

Substituting $N=21$ and ${S}_{N}=0$ into the formula for the sum of an arithmetic series, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{N} & =\frac{N}{2}(2{a}_{1}+(N-1)d) \\ 0 & =\frac{21}{2}(2{a}_{1}+(21-1)d) \\ 0 & =21(2{a}_{1}+20d) \\ 0 & =2{a}_{1}+20d.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we can write an equation for the $10$th term of the arithmetic series and substitute in its known value:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)d \\ {a}_{10} & ={a}_{1}+(10-1)d \\ -\frac{1}{5} & ={a}_{1}+9d\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we obtain the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{5} & \,\,\,=\,{a}_{1}+9d \\ \,0 & \,\,\,=\,2{a}_{1}+20d\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we multiply the first equation by $-2$ and add the result to the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{5} & =-2{a}_{1}-18d \\ 0 & =2{a}_{1}+20d \\ \frac{2}{5} & =2d \\ d & =\frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $d=\frac{1}{5}$ into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{5} & ={a}_{1}+9d \\ -\frac{1}{5} & ={a}_{1}+9(\frac{1}{5}) \\ -\frac{1}{5} & ={a}_{1}+\frac{9}{5} \\ {a}_{1} & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

The first three terms of the binomial expansion for $(1+x)^{n}$ are given by

$$
(1+x)^{n}=1+nx+\frac{n(n-1)}{2!}{x}^{2}+⋯.
$$

By substituting $x=\frac{2b}{7}$ and $n=9$ into the above formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{(1+\frac{2b}{7})}^{9} & =1+9\cdot \frac{2b}{7}+\frac{9(9-1)}{2!}\cdot {(\frac{2b}{7})}^{2}+⋯ \\  & =1+\frac{18b}{7}+\frac{9\cdot 8}{2}\cdot \frac{4{b}^{2}}{49}+⋯ \\  & =1+\frac{18b}{7}+36\cdot \frac{4{b}^{2}}{49}+⋯ \\  & =1+\frac{18}{7}b+\frac{144}{49}{b}^{2}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Find, in ascending powers of $k,$ the **first three terms** of the binomial expansion of ${(1-\frac{k}{5})}^{8}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡(m∠A) & =\frac{BC}{AC} \\ \frac{2}{3} & =\frac{10x-1}{8x+2} \\ 2(8x+2) & =3(10x-1) \\ 16x+4 & =30x-3 \\ 14x & =7 \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}

So, the side lengths are

$$

Therefore, the area of $△ABC$ is

:question/problem: The coefficient of ${k}^{4}$ in the expansion of ${(1-\frac{k}{4})}^{5}$ is{{field-1}}.
:question/worked-solution:
The binomial expansion for $(1+x)^{n}$ is given by

$$
(1+x)^{n}=1+nx+\frac{n(n-1)}{2!}{x}^{2}+⋯.
$$

In particular, the ${x}^{4}$ term is given by

$$
\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)}{4!}{x}^{4}.
$$

Replacing $x$ with $-\frac{k}{4}$ and $n$ with $5$ in the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5(5-1)(5-2)(5-3)}{4!}\cdot {(-\frac{k}{4})}^{4} & =\frac{5\cdot 4\cdot 3\cdot 2}{24}\cdot {(-\frac{1}{4})}^{4}\cdot {k}^{4} \\  & =5\cdot \frac{1}{256}{k}^{4} \\  & =\frac{5}{256}{k}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coefficient of ${k}^{4}$ is $\frac{5}{256}.$

:question/problem: Consider the function $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3x$ and the point $P(\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{3\pi }{2})$ that lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $f(x)$ is invertible in the vicinity of $P,$ calculate ${({f}^{-1})}^{′}(\frac{3\pi }{2}).$
:question/worked-solution:
We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{3\pi }{2}).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =3-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =2\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{3\pi }{2})$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(\frac{3\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2})$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(\frac{3\pi }{2}) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(\frac{3\pi }{2}))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Compute the standard deviation $\sigma $ of the following data set:

$$
15,\,1,\,-10,\,-13,\,-9
$$

Do not round your answer.

$\sigma =$
{{field-1}}
:question/worked-solution:
The standard deviation of a data set ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is the square root of the variance:

$$
\sigma =\sqrt{{\sigma }^{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}}=\sqrt{\,\,\,\overset{―}{{x}^{2}}-{(\overset{―}{x})}^{2}}
$$

First, let's compute $\overset{―}{x}.$ There are $n=5$ points in our data set, so the mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{x} & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot (15+1-10-13-9) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot (-16) \\  & =-\frac{16}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's compute $\overset{―}{{x}^{2}}.$ Computing the mean of the squares of the points in the data set, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{{x}^{2}} & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot [{15}^{2}+{1}^{2}+(-10)^{2}+(-13)^{2}+(-9)^{2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot [225+1+100+169+81] \\  & =\frac{576}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\overset{―}{{x}^{2}}-(\overset{―}{x})^{2} \\  & =\frac{576}{5}-{(-\frac{16}{5})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{576}{5}-\frac{256}{25} \\  & =\frac{2880-256}{25} \\  & =\frac{2624}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the standard deviation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\sigma  & =\sqrt{{\sigma }^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{2624}{25}} \\  & =\frac{8\sqrt{41}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{-1-\sqrt{2}/2}^{-1+\sqrt{2}/2}\frac{14}{\sqrt{1-2x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-2x-{x}^{2} & =1-({x}^{2}+2x) \\  & =1-({x}^{2}+2x+1-1) \\  & =1-((x+1)^{2}-1) \\  & =2-(x+1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1-\sqrt{2}/2}^{-1+\sqrt{2}/2}\frac{14}{\sqrt{1-2x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-1-\sqrt{2}/2}^{-1+\sqrt{2}/2}\frac{14}{\sqrt{2-(x+1)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1-\sqrt{2}/2}^{-1+\sqrt{2}/2}\frac{14}{\sqrt{2(1-(x+1)^{2}/2)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1-\sqrt{2}/2}^{-1+\sqrt{2}/2}\frac{14}{\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{1-(x+1)^{2}/(\sqrt{2})^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{14}{\sqrt{2}}{\int }_{-1-\sqrt{2}/2}^{-1+\sqrt{2}/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-((x+1)/\sqrt{2})^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse sine:

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $(\frac{x+1}{\sqrt{2}})$.

So, let's perform the substitution

$$
u=(\frac{x+1}{\sqrt{2}}).
$$

Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Let's use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u$.

| $x$ | $-1-\sqrt{2}/2$ | $-1+\sqrt{2}/2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $-1/2$ | $1/2$ |

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1-\sqrt{2}/2}^{-1+\sqrt{2}/2}\frac{14}{\sqrt{1-2x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{14}{\sqrt{2}}{\int }_{-1-\sqrt{2}/2}^{-1+\sqrt{2}/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-((x+1)/\sqrt{2})^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{14}{\sqrt{2}}{\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot \sqrt{2}\,\text{d}u. \\  & =14{\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =14\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u\,{|}_{-1/2}^{1/2} \\  & =14(\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{1}{2})-\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(-\frac{1}{2})) \\  & =14(\frac{\pi }{6}-(-\frac{\pi }{6})) \\  & =\frac{14\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{-6-\sqrt{6}}^{-6+\sqrt{6}}\frac{15}{\sqrt{-12-x(x+12)}}\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-12-x(x+12) & =-12-({x}^{2}+12x) \\  & =-12-({x}^{2}+12x+36-36) \\  & =-12-((x+6)^{2}-36) \\  & =24-(x+6)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-6-\sqrt{6}}^{-6+\sqrt{6}}\frac{15}{\sqrt{-12-x(x+12)}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-6-\sqrt{6}}^{-6+\sqrt{6}}\frac{15}{\sqrt{24-(x+6)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-6-\sqrt{6}}^{-6+\sqrt{6}}\frac{15}{\sqrt{24(1-(x+6)^{2}/24)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-6-\sqrt{6}}^{-6+\sqrt{6}}\frac{15}{\sqrt{24}\cdot \sqrt{1-(x+6)^{2}/(2\sqrt{6})^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{15}{2\sqrt{6}}{\int }_{-6-\sqrt{6}}^{-6+\sqrt{6}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-((x+6)/2\sqrt{6})^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse sine:

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $(\frac{x+6}{2\sqrt{6}}).$

So, let's perform the substitution

$$
u=\frac{x+6}{2\sqrt{6}}.
$$

Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{6}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\sqrt{6}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Let's use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $-6-\sqrt{6}$ | $-6+\sqrt{6}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $-\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-6-\sqrt{6}}^{-6+\sqrt{6}}\frac{15}{\sqrt{-12-x(x+12)}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{15}{2\sqrt{6}}{\int }_{-6-\sqrt{6}}^{-6+\sqrt{6}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-((x+6)/2\sqrt{6})^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{15}{2\sqrt{6}}{\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot 2\sqrt{6}\,\text{d}u. \\  & =15{\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =15\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u\,{|}_{-1/2}^{1/2} \\  & =15(\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{1}{2})-\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(-\frac{1}{2})) \\  & =15(\frac{\pi }{6}-(-\frac{\pi }{6})) \\  & =5\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{-5/2}^{-3/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-4x-3}}\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}-4x-3 & =-({x}^{2}+4x+3) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+2\cdot 2x+[{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}]+3) \\  & =-((x+2)^{2}-1) \\  & =1-(x+2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
{\int }_{-5/2}^{-3/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-4x-3}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-5/2}^{-3/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x+2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse sine:

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $x+2.$

So, let's perform the substitution

$$
u=x+2.
$$

Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Let's use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $-5/2$ | $-3/2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $-1/2$ | $1/2$ |

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-5/2}^{-3/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-4x-3}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-5/2}^{-3/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x+2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u\,{|}_{-1/2}^{1/2} \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{1}{2})-\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}+\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the roots of $f(x),$ we must solve $f(x)=0:$

$$
\sqrt[6]{24x+13}-1=0
$$

We solve this equation by making $x$ the subject, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[6]{24x+13}-1 & =0 \\ \sqrt[6]{24x+13} & =1 \\ {(\sqrt[6]{24x+13})}^{6} & ={1}^{6} \\ 24x+13 & =1 \\ 24x & =-12 \\ x & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we must check the answer by substituting it back into the initial equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[6]{24\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})+13}-1 & =0 \\ \sqrt[6]{1}-1 & =0 \\ 0 & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the root of $f(x)$ is $x=-\frac{1}{2}.$

:question/problem:
What is the first term that exceeds  $2\,000$ in the following geometric sequence?

$$
\,\,\,\,10,\,15,\,\frac{45}{2},\,\frac{135}{4},\,…
$$

The first term that exceeds $2\,000$ is the
{{field-1}}th term.
:question/worked-solution:
The first term of the sequence is ${a}_{1}=10$ and the common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{15}{10}=\frac{3}{2}.
$$

So, the $n$th term of the sequence can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =10\cdot {(\frac{3}{2})}^{n-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be greater than $2000.$
Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & >2000 \\ 10\cdot {(\frac{3}{2})}^{n-1} & >2000 \\ {(\frac{3}{2})}^{n-1} & >200 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({(\frac{3}{2})}^{n-1}) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(200) \\ (n-1)\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{2}) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(200) \\ n-1 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(200)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{2})} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(200)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{2})}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

$$
\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(200)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{2})}+1≈14.067.
$$

Therefore, the $15$th term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds $2000.$

:question/problem:
Suppose that for the angles $u$ and $v,$ we have 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡u=\frac{5}{13},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡v=\frac{7}{25},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡v=\frac{24}{25}.
$$

Given that $u$ lies in the first quadrant, then $\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)=${{field-1}}.
:question/worked-solution:
First, we recall the sum formula for cosine:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)=\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v-\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

We know the values of $\operatorname{cos}⁡u,$ $\operatorname{sin}⁡v,$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡v.$ To find the missing value of $\operatorname{sin}⁡u,$ we can use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡u+{cos}^{2}⁡u=1\,⟹\,{sin}^{2}⁡u=1-{cos}^{2}⁡u
$$

Substituting our values into the Pythagorean identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡u & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡u \\  & =1-{(\frac{5}{13})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{{5}^{2}}{{13}^{2}} \\  & =1-\frac{25}{169} \\  & =\frac{169}{169}-\frac{24}{169} \\  & =\frac{144}{169}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+7\operatorname{cos}⁡x=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)+7\operatorname{cos}⁡(x) & =(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Determine a set of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ that generate the above parabola. Express your answer in the form $x=2pt,y=p{t}^{2},$ where $p$ is a constant.

The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at $(0,0),$ and passes through the point $(4,2).$

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola  that has its vertex at $(0,0)$ are

$$
x=2pt,\,y=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Since the parabola passes through $(4,2),$ we can substitute $x=4$ and $y=2$ into the standard parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4 &=2pt \\ 2 &=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =2pt \\ 2 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{2}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =p{(\frac{2}{p})}^{2} \\ 2 & =p\cdot \frac{4}{{p}^{2}} \\ 2 & =\frac{4}{p} \\ p & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x=2(2)t,\,y=(2){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x=4t,\,y=2{t}^{2}.
$$

:question/problem:
A point $P$ has Cartesian coordinates $(\sqrt{3}k,-k),$ where $k$ is a positive real number. Find the polar coordinates of $P$ expressed in terms of $k.$ Give the polar angle in radians and do not round the answer.

Expressed in terms of $k,$ the polar coordinates of $P$ are $(${{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}$).$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we determine $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(\sqrt{3}k)^{2}+(-k)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{3{k}^{2}+{k}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{k}^{2}} \\  & =2k\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute the reference angle ${\theta }_{R}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})| \\  & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{-k}{\sqrt{3}k})| \\  & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})| \\  & =|-\frac{\pi }{6}| \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the point lies in the fourth quadrant, we subtract the reference angle from $2\pi ,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =2\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & =2\pi -\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{11\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the polar coordinates of $P$ are $(2k,\frac{11\pi }{6}).$

:question/problem:
A point $P$ has Cartesian coordinates $(-\sqrt{3},1).$ Find the polar coordinates of $P.$ Give the polar angle in radians and do not round the answer.

The polar coordinates of $P$ are $(${{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}$).$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we determine $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\sqrt{3})^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{3+1} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

For the reference angle, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})| \\  & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{1}{-\sqrt{3}})| \\  & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})| \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the point $P$ lies in the second quadrant, we subtract the reference angle from $\pi $ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi -\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the polar coordinates of $P$ are $(2,\frac{5\pi }{6}).$

:question/problem:
A fair six-sided die is rolled $5$ times. Rounded to $3$ decimal places, what is the probability of getting a $6$ exactly two times?

Rounded to $3$ decimal places, the probability is
{{field-1}}.
:question/worked-solution:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of times that a $6$ is rolled. 

Here, we have the following information:

- There are $n=5$ rolls.

- The probability of getting a $6$ on any roll of the die is

$$
p=\frac{1}{6}.
$$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(5,\frac{1}{6}).$ We want to find the probability of $x=2$ successes.

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for the probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=2) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{2}){(\frac{1}{6})}^{2}{(1-\frac{1}{6})}^{5-2} \\  & =\frac{5!}{2!(5-2)!}{(\frac{1}{6})}^{2}{(\frac{5}{6})}^{3} \\  & =10{(\frac{1}{6})}^{2}{(\frac{5}{6})}^{3} \\  & ≈0.161,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

:question/problem: A fair six-sided die is repeatedly rolled until the number six appears. Rounded to $3$ decimal places, the probability that it will be rolled exactly $2$ times is{{field-1}}.
:question/worked-solution:
A geometric random variable $X$ with probability of success $p$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=(1-p)^{x-1}p
$$

Let $X$ be the number of rolls until a $6$ came on. The probability of getting a $6$ on any roll of the die is

$$
p=\frac{1}{6}.
$$

So, the number of rolls until a $6$ came up can be modeled as a geometric random variable with a probability of success $p=\frac{1}{6}.$

So, $X∼\text{Geom}(\frac{1}{6}).$ In this case, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={(1-\frac{1}{6})}^{x-1}(\frac{1}{6}) \\  & ={(\frac{5}{6})}^{x-1}(\frac{1}{6})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability of getting a $6$ on the $2$nd roll is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=2) & =f(2) \\  & ={(\frac{5}{6})}^{2-1}(\frac{1}{6}) \\  & =(\frac{5}{6})(\frac{1}{6}) \\  & ≈0.139,\end{aligned}
$$

 
rounded to $3$ decimal places.

Let $p$ represent the profit on a single roll of the game. On each roll in the game, there are two possible outcomes:

- If rolling gives an odd number ($1$, $3,$ or $5$), the player loses $$2,$ so we have $p=-2.$

- If rolling gives an even number ($2$ or $4$), the player wins $$10,$ so we have $p=10.$

The probabilities for the outcomes are

$$
P(-2)=\frac{3}{5},\,P(10)=\frac{2}{5}.
$$

Let's summarize this in a table.  If $p$ is the profit (in dollars) on a single game, and $f(p)$ is the probability mass function for $p,$ then we have the following:

| $f(p)$ | $\frac{3}{5}$ | $\frac{2}{5}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $p$ | $-2$ | $10$ |

Therefore, the expected value of $p$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}E[p] & =(-2)\cdot f(-2)+10\cdot f(10) \\  & =(-2)(\frac{3}{5})+10(\frac{2}{5}) \\  & =-\frac{6}{5}+\frac{20}{5} \\  & =\frac{14}{5} \\  & =2.8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the expected profit is $$2.80.$

A laptop's battery life on a single charge is normally distributed with an average of $8$ hours and an unknown standard deviation. Tests show that $20%$ of laptops die after $11$ hours of usage. Assuming a normal model, what percentage of laptops will last less than $6$ hours on a single charge? **Round the answer to $1$ decimal place.**

*Hint: A table of values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p$ is given below, where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $\,p\,$ | $0.75$ | $0.8$ | $0.85$ | $0.9$ | $0.95$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\,0.6745\,$ | $\,0.8416\,$ | $\,1.0364\,$ | $\,1.2816\,$ | $\,1.6449\,$ |

*In addition, you're given the following table of values for $p=Φ(z).$*

| $z$ | $\,0.06\,$ | $\,0.07\,$ | $\,0.08\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,-0.7\,$ | $\,0.2236\,$ | $\,0.2206\,$ | $\,0.2177\,$ |
| $\,-0.6\,$ | $\,0.2546\,$ | $\,0.2514\,$ | $\,0.2483\,$ |
| $\,-0.5\,$ | $\,0.2877\,$ | $\,0.2843\,$ | $\,0.2810\,$ |

Approximately
{{field-1}}$%$ of laptops will last less than $6$ hours on a single charge.
:question/worked-solution:
Let $X$ represent the number of hours of a laptop's battery life. Then we have $X∼N(8,{\sigma }^{2}),$ and we want to find $P(X<6).$ But first, we need to find the standard deviation $\sigma .$ 

We know that $P(X>11)=0.20.$ First, we convert this to a cumulative probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 11) & =1-P(X>11) \\  & =1-0.20 \\  & =0.80\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 11) & =0.80 \\ P(Z\le \frac{11-8}{\sigma }) & =0.80 \\ Φ(\frac{3}{\sigma }) & =0.80 \\ \frac{3}{\sigma } & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.80)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, 

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(0.80)=0.8416.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sigma } & =0.8416 \\ \sigma  & =\frac{3}{0.8416} \\ \sigma  & ≈3.5646.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve for $P(X\le 6)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 6) & =P(Z\le \frac{6-8}{3.5646}) \\  & ≈P(Z\le -0.56) \\  & =Φ(-0.56) \\  & =0.2877 \\  & ≈28.8%\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, approximately $28.8%$ of laptops will last less than $6$ hours on a single charge.

We need to solve the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y &=8x-1 \\ y &=\frac{1}{2x}-1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Setting the equations equal to one another and solving, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}8x-1 & =\frac{1}{2x}-1 \\ 8x & =\frac{1}{2x} \\ 16{x}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{1}{16} \\ x & =\pm \frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the $x$-coordinates of the intersection points are $x=-\frac{1}{4}$ and $x=\frac{1}{4}.$ To find the $y$-coordinates of the intersection points, we plug these values into either curve. Let's choose the second equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =8x-1 \\  & =8(-\frac{1}{4})-1 \\  & =-2-1 \\  & =-3,\end{aligned}
$$

so one point of intersection is $(-\frac{1}{4},-3).$

- Substituting $x=\frac{1}{4},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =8x-1 \\  & =8(\frac{1}{4})-1 \\  & =2-1 \\  & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

so the other point of intersection is $(\frac{1}{4},1).$

First, since $A$ has polar coordinates $(10,{60}^{∘}),$ we must have $r=10.$ Also, since the points $A$ and $B$ both lie on a circle of radius $10,$ the $r$-coordinate of $B$ must also be $10.$

Notice that one must traverse the circle counter-clockwise to move from the point $A$ to point $B.$ Since the $\theta $-coordinate of $A$ is ${60}^{∘},$ the $\theta $-coordinate of $B$ must be

$$
{\theta }_{B}={60}^{∘}+{60}^{∘}={120}^{∘}.
$$

So, the polar coordinates of $B$ are $(10,{120}^{∘})$ 

Now, we convert $B$ to Cartesian coordinates. To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .

$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(-5,5\sqrt{3}).$

:question/problem:
What is the first term that exceeds  $30$ in the following geometric sequence?

$$
2,\,\frac{8}{3},\,\frac{32}{9},\,\frac{128}{27},\,…
$$

The first term that exceeds $30$ is the
{{field-1}}th term.
:question/worked-solution:
The first term of the sequence is ${a}_{1}=2$ and the common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{\frac{8}{3}}{2}=\frac{4}{3}.
$$

So, the $n$th term of the sequence can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =2\cdot {(\frac{4}{3})}^{n-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be greater than $30.$
Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & >30 \\ 2\cdot {(\frac{4}{3})}^{n-1} & >30 \\ {(\frac{4}{3})}^{n-1} & >15 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({(\frac{4}{3})}^{n-1}) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(15) \\ (n-1)\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{4}{3}) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(15) \\ n-1 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(15)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{4}{3})} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(15)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{4}{3})}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

$$
\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(15)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{4}{3})}+1≈10.413.
$$

Therefore, the $11$th term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds $30.$

:question/problem:
What is the first term that is less than $0.000\,31$ in the following geometric sequence?

$$
125,\,25,\,5,\,1,\,…
$$

The first term that is less than $0.000\,31$ is the
{{field-1}}th term.
:question/worked-solution:
The first term of the sequence is ${a}_{1}=125$ and the common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{25}{125}=\frac{1}{5}.
$$

So, the $n$th term of the sequence can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =125\cdot {(\frac{1}{5})}^{n-1} \\  & ={5}^{3}\cdot {5}^{1-n} \\  & ={5}^{4-n}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be less than $0.000\,31.$
Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & <0.000\,31 \\ {5}^{4-n} & <0.000\,31 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({5}^{4-n}) & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,31) \\ (4-n)\operatorname{log}⁡(5) & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,31) \\ 4-n & <\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,31)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(5)} \\ -n & <\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,31)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(5)}-4 \\ n & >4-\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,31)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(5)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

$$
4-\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,31)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(5)}≈9.020.
$$

Therefore, the $10$th term is the first term of the sequence that is less than $0.000\,31.$

:question/problem:
What is the first term that is less than $0.004$ in the following geometric sequence?

$$
20,\,4,\,\frac{4}{5},\,\frac{4}{25},\,…
$$

The first term that is less than $0.004$ is the
{{field-1}}th term.
:question/worked-solution:
The first term of the sequence is ${a}_{1}=20$ and the common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{4}{20}=\frac{1}{5}.
$$

So, the $n$th term of the sequence can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =20{(\frac{1}{5})}^{n-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be less than $0.004.$
Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & <0.004 \\ 20{(\frac{1}{5})}^{n-1} & <0.004 \\ {(\frac{1}{5})}^{n-1} & <\frac{0.004}{20} \\ \operatorname{log}⁡{(\frac{1}{5})}^{n-1} & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,2) \\ (n-1)\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{1}{5}) & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,2) \\ n-1 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,2)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{1}{5})} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,2)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{1}{5})}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we reversed the inequality sign when divided by $\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{1}{5})$ because $\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{1}{5})$ is a negative number. 

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

$$
\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,2)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{1}{5})}+1≈6.292.
$$

Therefore, the $7$th term is the first term of the sequence that is less than $0.004.$

:question/problem: The $5$th term of a geometric sequence is $81$, and the common ratio is $\frac{3}{2}.$ The first term of this sequence to exceed $10\,000$ is the{{field-1}} th term.
:question/worked-solution:
Since we are given that ${a}_{5}=81$ and  $r=\frac{3}{2}$, we can use the $n$th term formula to solve for ${a}_{1}$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\ {a}_{5} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {(\frac{3}{2})}^{5-1} \\ 81 & ={a}_{1}\cdot {(\frac{3}{2})}^{4} \\ 81 & =\frac{81}{16}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{1} & =16\end{aligned}
$$

So, the $n$th term of the geometric sequence is

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =16\cdot {(\frac{3}{2})}^{n-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want $n$th term to be greater than $10\,000.$
Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}16\cdot {(\frac{3}{2})}^{n-1} & >10\,000 \\ {(\frac{3}{2})}^{n-1} & >625 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡{(\frac{3}{2})}^{n-1} & >\operatorname{log}⁡(625) \\ (n-1)\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{2}) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(625) \\ n-1 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(625)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{2})} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(625)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{2})}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

$$
\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(625)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{2})}+1≈16.877.
$$

Therefore, the $17$th term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds $10\,000.$

:question/problem: Which of the following lines is perpendicular to $4x+10y=20?$
:question/worked-solution:
For the two lines to be perpendicular, their slopes must multiply to $-1.$

To find the slope of the given line $4x+10y=20,$ we convert to slope-intercept form:

$$
\begin{aligned}4x+10y & =20 \\ 10y & =-4x+20 \\ y & =-\frac{4}{10}x+\frac{20}{10} \\ y & =-\frac{2}{5}x+2\end{aligned}
$$

In slope-intercept form, the slope is the $x$-coefficient. So, the slope of the given line is $-\frac{2}{5}.$

Looking at the answer choices, the line $y=\frac{5}{2}x-4$ has a slope of $\frac{5}{2}.$

Multiplying the slopes together, we have

$$
(-\frac{2}{5})\cdot \frac{5}{2}=-1.
$$

Since the slopes multiply to $-1,$ we conclude that the line $y=\frac{5}{2}x-4$ is perpendicular to the given line.

Computing the first derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(x) & ={(4{x}^{2}\sqrt{x}-2x+7)}^{′} \\  & ={(4{x}^{5/2}-2x+7)}^{′} \\  & =4(\frac{5}{2}){x}^{3/2}-2+0 \\  & =10{x}^{3/2}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the second derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{″}(x) & ={(10{x}^{3/2}-2)}^{′} \\  & =10(\frac{3}{2}){x}^{1/2}-0 \\  & =15{x}^{1/2} \\  & =15\sqrt{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the second derivative at $x=4$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{″}(4) & =15\sqrt{4} \\  & =15(2) \\  & =30.\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}u}={5}^{u}\operatorname{ln}⁡5,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}v}=\frac{1}{v},\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Applying now the chain rule twice, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}v}\cdot \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={5}^{u}\operatorname{ln}⁡5\cdot (\frac{1}{v})\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & ={5}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\operatorname{ln}⁡5\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x})\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =-{5}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}\operatorname{ln}⁡5\operatorname{tan}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Now we compute ${h}^{′}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(0) & =-{5}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡0)}\operatorname{ln}⁡5\operatorname{tan}⁡0 \\  & =-{5}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡1}\operatorname{ln}⁡5(0) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions to the equation $2\operatorname{sec}⁡x-1=3$ for $0\le x<2\pi ,$ what is ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}?$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, isolating $\operatorname{sec}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sec}⁡x-1 & =3 \\ 2\operatorname{sec}⁡x & =4 \\ \operatorname{sec}⁡x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that $\operatorname{sec}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.$ Therefore, the given equation is equivalent to

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡x=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

First, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\frac{\pi }{3}$ lies inside the required domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}=\frac{\pi }{3}.$

Our first solution lies in the first quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{3}.$ Since $\operatorname{cos}⁡x>0,$ the second solution must lie in the fourth quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{3}.$

![](images/31/318eba038feb091d6e3adb80ddf325de6039bb331a7713cf1e2c02171a6388d4.png)

Since the second solution ${x}_{2}$ lies in the $4$th quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =2\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & =2\pi -\frac{\pi }{3} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are $x=\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{5\pi }{3}.$

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{3}\cdot \frac{5\pi }{3}=\frac{5{\pi }^{2}}{9}.
$$

Our first solution lies in the first quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}={45}^{∘}.$ Since $\operatorname{cos}⁡x>0,$ the second solution must lie in the fouth quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}={45}^{∘}.$

:question/problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions to the equation  $3\operatorname{cot}⁡x=20-\operatorname{cot}⁡x$ for ${0}^{∘}\le x<{360}^{∘},$ what is the numerical value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2},$ rounded to the nearest integer?

:question/problem:
If $p(x)=-5{x}^{2}$ and $q(x)=9{x}^{6},$ then

${lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{{x}^{4}\cdot p(x)}{q(x)}=$
{{field-1}}.

First, let's calculate ${x}^{4}\cdot p(x):$

$$
{x}^{4}\cdot p(x)={x}^{4}\cdot (-5{x}^{2})=-5{x}^{6}
$$

When we divide the two functions ${x}^{4}\cdot p(x)$ and $q(x),$ we get a constant, and the limit of a constant is just the constant itself:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{{x}^{4}\cdot p(x)}{q(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{-5{x}^{6}}{(9{x}^{6})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }(-\frac{5}{9}) \\  & =-\frac{5}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's sketch the graph of $y=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x):$

![](images/fc/fc06a4e63f38a315dd3944f65f871cca2dbdddee26ec268e857f79e5f4ab8848.png)

The domain of $\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)$ is $x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$  

Now, substituting $x=1$ directly into the limit, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,1}\frac{\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)}{\pi x} & =\frac{\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1)}{\pi \cdot (1)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{\pi }{4})}{\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, let's sketch the graph of $y=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x-2):$

![](images/a7/a7e36a5c534a63199ea97985f1301db0c7675adc8fa0d17f33735c61eec9e871.png)

The domain of   $\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x-2)$ is $(-\infty ,\infty ).$  

As $x$ increases to $\infty ,$ the graph tends to $y=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,\infty }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x-2)) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2}{3}\cdot (\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Calculate the integral $\int \frac{{sec}^{2}⁡(1/x)}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
Let $u=\frac{1}{x}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,⟹\,-\text{d}u=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{sec}^{2}⁡(1/x)}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{1}{x})\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡u\cdot (-\text{d}u) \\  & =-\int {sec}^{2}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{tan}⁡u+C \\  & =-\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{1}{x})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $f(x)=\frac{3x+2}{{x}^{2}}.$ Computing the derivative ${f}^{′}(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{3x+2}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{3}{x}+\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{3}{x})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{-1})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{-2}) \\  & =-3{x}^{-2}-4{x}^{-3} \\  & =-\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{4}{{x}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute ${f}^{′}(-1)$, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(-1) & =-\frac{3}{(-1)^{2}}-\frac{4}{(-1)^{3}} \\  & =-3+4 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the point-slope form with $m=1$ and the coordinates of our point $(-1,-1),$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-1) & =1\cdot (x-(-1)) \\ y+1 & =x+1 \\ y & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${86.417}^{∘}$ lies inside the required domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}={86.417}^{∘}.$

Our first solution lies in the first quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}={86.417}^{∘}.$ Since $\operatorname{cos}⁡x>0,$ the second solution must lie in the fourth quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}={86.417}^{∘}.$

:question/problem: $\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x=$
:question/worked-solution:
The difference formula for cosine gives

$$
\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-ϕ) & =R(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) \\  & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡x+R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x=(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ &=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ &=\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Dividing the second equation by the first, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ} & =\frac{(\frac{3}{2})}{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡ϕ & =\sqrt{3} \\ ϕ & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{3}) \\ ϕ & =\frac{\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we find the amplitude $R.$ Squaring the first and the second equations of the system and adding the results together, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)}^{2}+{(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)}^{2} & ={(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}+{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}^{2} \\ {R}^{2}({sin}^{2}⁡ϕ+{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ) & =\frac{9}{4}+\frac{3}{4} \\ {R}^{2} & =3 \\ R & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we only consider the positive root since $R>0.$

Finally, we can write the initial expression in amplitude-phase form as follows:

$$
\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x=\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{3})
$$

:question/problem: Within the interval $[-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}],$ determine the average value of $g(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡3x-\operatorname{cos}⁡3x.$
:question/worked-solution:
Applying the average value formula, we find that the average value of the function is

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{1}{b-a}{\int }_{a}^{b}g(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\frac{\pi }{2}-(-\frac{\pi }{2})}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡3x-\operatorname{cos}⁡3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡3x-\operatorname{cos}⁡3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{1}{\pi }(-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡3x-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡3x)|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3\pi }[(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}))-(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot (-\frac{\pi }{2}))+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot (-\frac{\pi }{2})))] \\  & =-\frac{1}{3\pi }[(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}))-(\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\frac{3\pi }{2})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{3\pi }{2}))] \\  & =-\frac{1}{3\pi }[(0+(-1))-(0+1)] \\  & =-\frac{1}{3\pi }(-2) \\  & =\frac{2}{3\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: A biologist found that the population $P$ of some bacteria in a petri dish can be modeled by the function $P(t)=200+8\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}t),$ where $t$ is the number of hours after $12$ noon. Find the average number of bacteria during the period from $12$ noon to $4$ p.m.
:question/worked-solution:
Since the function is valid starting from $12$ P.M., we can conclude our interval is $[0,4].$

Applying the average value formula, we find that the average value of the function is

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{1}{b-a}{\int }_{a}^{b}P(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{4-0}{\int }_{0}^{4}(200+8\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}t))\text{d}t \\  & ={\frac{1}{4}(200t-\frac{32}{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi \,t}{4}))|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[(200\cdot 4-\frac{32}{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi \cdot 4}{4}))-(200\cdot 0-\frac{32}{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi \cdot 0}{4}))] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[(800-\frac{32}{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ))-(-\frac{32}{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[(800-\frac{32}{\pi }\cdot (-1))+\frac{32}{\pi }\cdot 1] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[800+\frac{32}{\pi }+\frac{32}{\pi }] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(800+\frac{64}{\pi }) \\  & =200+\frac{16}{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}-5{e}^{-2x}\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
If we let $u=-2x,$ then,

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2\,⟹\,-\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=\,\text{d}x.
$$

Computing our limits of integration, we get the following:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $-2\operatorname{ln}⁡4$ |

Then, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}-5{e}^{-2x}\,\text{d}x & =-5{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{e}^{-2x}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-5{\int }_{0}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{e}^{u}(-\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({4}^{-2})}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{5}{2}({e}^{u}){|}_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({4}^{-2})} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}({e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({4}^{-2})}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{5}{2}({4}^{-2}-1) \\  & =\frac{5}{2}(\frac{1}{16}-1) \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\cdot (-\frac{15}{16}) \\  & =-\frac{75}{32}\end{aligned}

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{0}^{1}{3}^{6x}\,\text{d}x.$

If we let $u=6x,$ then

Computing our limits of integration, we get the following:

| $u$ | $0$ | $6$ |

Then, we can write the integral in terms of  $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{3}^{6x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{6}{3}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{0}^{6}{3}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(\frac{{3}^{u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}){|}_{0}^{6} \\  & =\frac{1}{6\operatorname{ln}⁡3}(729-1) \\  & =\frac{728}{6\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\  & =\frac{364}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{6}$ is given by ${f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6}).$

We will calculate ${f}^{′}(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
y=\operatorname{sin}⁡u,\,u=3x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡u)\cdot 3 \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x).\end{aligned}

Evaluating at $x=\frac{\pi }{6},$ we find

$$

Compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{f(x)}{g(x)})$ at $x=5.$

${\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{f(x)}{g(x)})|}_{x=5}=$
{{field-1}}
:question/worked-solution:
Using the quotient rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{f(x)}{g(x)})=\frac{{f}^{′}(x)g(x)-f(x){g}^{′}(x)}{(g(x))^{2}}.
$$

At the point where $x=5$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{f(x)}{g(x)})|}_{x=5} & =\frac{{f}^{′}(5)g(5)-f(5){g}^{′}(5)}{(g(5))^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(-4)(-2)-(3)(6)}{(-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{8-18}{4} \\  & =-\frac{10}{4} \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope at a point, we use implicit differentiation to calculate the derivative of the curve, assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the ${x}^{2}{y}^{3}$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}-4y & =6x \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}{y}^{3}-4y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6x) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}{y}^{3})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6x) \\ [3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2x{y}^{3}]-4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6 \\ 3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2x{y}^{3}-4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6 \\ 3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6-2x{y}^{3} \\ (3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-4)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6-2x{y}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{6-2x{y}^{3}}{3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-4}\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of the tangent at the point $(0,\,0)$ is then given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}_{(0,\,0)} \\  & ={(\frac{6-2x{y}^{3}}{3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-4})}_{(0,\,0)} \\  & =\frac{6-2\cdot 0\cdot {0}^{3}}{3\cdot {0}^{2}\cdot {0}^{2}-4} \\  & =\frac{6}{(-4)} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Given that $y=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{e}^{2x}},$ find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.$

:question/worked-solution:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ and the denominator $v(x)={e}^{2x}.$ 

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{x},\,{v}^{′}(x)=2{e}^{2x}.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $v.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{1}{x})({e}^{2x})-(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)(2{e}^{2x})}{{({e}^{2x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{{e}^{2x}}{x}-2{e}^{2x}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{({e}^{2x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{{e}^{2x}-2x{e}^{2x}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x})}{{({e}^{2x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2x}(1-2x\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{x{({e}^{2x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1-2x\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x{e}^{2x}}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}

:question/problem: Find the slope of $f(x)=\operatorname{cot}⁡(2\pi -3x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$
:question/worked-solution:
The slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ is given by ${f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}).$

We will calculate ${f}^{′}(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f=\operatorname{cot}⁡u,\,u=2\pi -3x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=-{csc}^{2}⁡u\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =-{csc}^{2}⁡u\cdot (-3) \\  & =3{csc}^{2}⁡(2\pi -3x).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =3{csc}^{2}⁡(2\pi -\frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & =3{csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =3\cdot {1}^{2} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ is $3.$

:question/problem: Find the slope of $f(x)=\operatorname{csc}⁡(5x)$ at $x=-\frac{\pi }{2}.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f=\operatorname{csc}⁡u,\,u=5x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=-\operatorname{csc}⁡u\operatorname{cot}⁡u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =-\operatorname{csc}⁡u\operatorname{cot}⁡u\cdot (5) \\  & =-5\operatorname{csc}⁡u\operatorname{cot}⁡u \\  & =-5\operatorname{csc}⁡(5x)\operatorname{cot}⁡(5x).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope $m$ of the tangent line at the point where $x=-\frac{\pi }{2}$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}{|}_{x=-\pi /2} & =-5\operatorname{csc}⁡(5x)\operatorname{cot}⁡(5x){|}_{x=-\pi /2} \\  & =-5\operatorname{csc}⁡(5\cdot (-\frac{\pi }{2}))\operatorname{cot}⁡(5\cdot (-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =-5\operatorname{csc}⁡(-\frac{5\pi }{2})\operatorname{cot}⁡(-\frac{5\pi }{2}) \\  & =-5\cdot (-1)\cdot 0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=-\frac{\pi }{2}$ is $0.$

:question/problem: For the curve $y=\frac{3}{4}{(\frac{1}{5})}^{x}+2,$ find the point of intersection with the $y$-axis.
:question/worked-solution:
**Method 1**

- For the curve $y={(\frac{1}{5})}^{x},$ the point of intersection with the $y$-axis is $(0,1).$

- For the scaled function $\frac{3}{4}{(\frac{1}{5})}^{x},$ the $y$-coordinate becomes

$$
y=\frac{3}{4}\cdot 1=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

- Finally, after a vertical shift of $2$ units up, we get a point with the $y$-coordinate

$$
y=\frac{3}{4}+2=\frac{11}{4}.
$$

**Method 2**

To find the $y$-intercept, we substitute $x=0$ into the equation of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{3}{4}{(\frac{1}{5})}^{0}+2 \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\cdot 1+2 \\  & =\frac{3}{4}+2 \\  & =\frac{11}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $y=\frac{3}{4}{(\frac{1}{5})}^{x}+2$ intercepts the $y$-axis at $(0,\frac{11}{4}).$

Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =5\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(r) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(5\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot (5\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}=-3$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{6},$ and solve for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot (5\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =(-3)\cdot (5\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})) \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =(-3)\cdot 5\cdot (\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}) \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-10.\end{aligned}
$$

We take the derivative of each term and then add them, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-csc⁡x-2{x}^{3}+cos⁡x) \\  & =(-csc⁡xcot⁡x)-2\cdot 3{x}^{2}+(-sin⁡x) \\  & =-csc⁡xcot⁡x-6{x}^{2}-sin⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$ in the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =-csc\,(\frac{\pi }{4})cot\,(\frac{\pi }{4})-6{(\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}-sin\,(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\cdot 1-6\cdot \frac{{\pi }^{2}}{16}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =-\sqrt{2}-\frac{3}{8}{\pi }^{2}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}-\frac{3}{8}{\pi }^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{9})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{9})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (\frac{2x}{9})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (\frac{2y}{9}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting the given information $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=12$ and $x=-5,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}12\cdot (\frac{2(-5)}{9})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (\frac{2y}{9}) & =0 \\ -\frac{120}{9}-\frac{2y}{9}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We also want to substitute for $y,$ but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $x=-5$ into the equation of the hyperbola.

At the point where $x=-5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{(-5)^{2}}{9}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{25}{9}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ 25-{y}^{2} & =9 \\ {y}^{2} & =16 \\ y & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used $y>0$ since we're only interested in the second quadrant.

Finally, substituting $y=4,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{120}{9}-\frac{2(4)}{9}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =0 \\ -\frac{120}{9}-\frac{8}{9}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =0 \\ -\frac{8}{9}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{120}{9} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{120}{8} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =-15.\end{aligned}
$$
