$$

Consider the initial value problem above. By applying the Laplace transform $L$ to both sides of each equation in our system, we get a system with variables ${X}_{1}(s)=L{{x}_{1}(t)}$ and ${X}_{2}(s)=L{{x}_{2}(t)}.$ In terms of the parameter $s,$ the solution of the new system is

${X}_{1}(s)=$ {{field-1}},$\,$
${X}_{2}(s)=\frac{6-s}{s(s-4)}.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we compute the Laplace transforms of both sides of each equation in our system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}L{{x}_{1}^{′}(t)} &=L{-3{x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t)} \\ L{{x}_{2}^{′}(t)} &=L{4{x}_{2}(t)+6}\end{aligned}\right.\,\,
$$

Using the derivative property of the Laplace transform, we obtain the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}sL{{x}_{1}(t)}-{x}_{1}(0) &=-3L{{x}_{1}(t)}+L{{x}_{2}(t)} \\ sL{{x}_{2}(t)}-{x}_{2}(0) &=4L{{x}_{2}(t)}+6L{1}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

which can be simplified to the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)-2 &=-3{X}_{1}(s)+{X}_{2}(s) \\ s{X}_{2}(s)+1 &=4{X}_{2}(s)+\frac{6}{s}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where ${X}_{1}(s)=L{{x}_{1}(t)}$ and ${X}_{2}(s)=L{{x}_{2}(t)},$ and we have used the fact that $L{1}=\frac{1}{s}.$

Now, solving the second equation for ${X}_{2}(s),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}s{X}_{2}(s)+1 & =4{X}_{2}(s)+\frac{6}{s} \\ (s-4){X}_{2}(s) & =-1+\frac{6}{s} \\ (s-4){X}_{2}(s) & =\frac{-s+6}{s} \\ {X}_{2}(s) & =\frac{6-s}{s(s-4)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this in the first equation and solving for ${X}_{1}(s)$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)-2 & =-3{X}_{1}(s)+{X}_{2}(s) \\ (s+3){X}_{1}(s) & =2+{X}_{2}(s) \\ (s+3){X}_{1}(s) & =2+(\frac{6-s}{s(s-4)}) \\ (s+3){X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{2s(s-4)+6-s}{s(s-4)} \\ (s+3){X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{2({s}^{2}-4s)+6-s}{s(s-4)} \\ (s+3){X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{2{s}^{2}-8s+6-s}{s(s-4)} \\ (s+3){X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{2{s}^{2}-9s+6}{s(s-4)} \\ {X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{2{s}^{2}-9s+6}{s(s-4)(s+3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution of the new system in terms of parameter $s$ is 

$$
{X}_{1}(s)=\frac{2{s}^{2}-9s+6}{s(s-4)(s+3)},\,{X}_{2}(s)=\frac{6-s}{s(s-4)}.
$$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)-1 &=4{X}_{1}(s)+{X}_{2}(s) \\ s{X}_{2}(s)-2 &=3{X}_{2}(s)+\frac{1}{s}\end{aligned}\right.

:question/problem:
Find $(f\cdot g)^{′}(t)$, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,i+\frac{1}{t}\,j+t\,k \\ g(t) & =t\,i+\frac{1}{t}\,j+\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,k\end{aligned}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
Using the dot product rule, we can write:

$$
(f\cdot g)^{′}(t)={f}^{′}(t)\cdot g(t)+f(t)\cdot {g}^{′}(t)
$$

Let's now find the derivatives of each function.

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{t}\,i+(-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})\,j+1\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{t}\,i-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,j+k \\ {g}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)\,k \\  & =1\,i+(-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})\,j+\frac{1}{t}\,k \\  & =i-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,j+\frac{1}{t}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}(f\cdot g)^{′}(t) & ={f}^{′}(t)\cdot g(t)+f(t)\cdot {g}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\frac{1}{t}\,i-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,j+k)\cdot (t\,i+\frac{1}{t}\,j+\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,k)+(\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,i+\frac{1}{t}\,j+t\,k)\cdot (i-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,j+\frac{1}{t}\,k) \\  & =(\frac{1}{t}\cdot t-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1}{t}+1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡t)+(\operatorname{ln}⁡t\cdot 1+\frac{1}{t}(-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})+t\cdot \frac{1}{t}) \\  & =1-\frac{1}{{t}^{3}}+\operatorname{ln}⁡t+\operatorname{ln}⁡t-\frac{1}{{t}^{3}}+1 \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡t+2-\frac{2}{{t}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Suppose we wish to approximate the solution to an initial value problem using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy\end{aligned}
$$

If the exact solution is ${y}_{\text{exact}}(x)=\frac{1}{x},$ find an expression for the local truncation error for the step from $x$ to ${x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx.$
:question/worked-solution:
The local truncation error (LTE) is the error made in a single step of a numerical method, when the step begins from an exact value. The LTE of a numerical method at step $n$ from $x$ with exact value ${y}_{\text{exact}}$ to ${x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{τ}_{n} & ={y}_{\text{exact}}({x}_{\text{new}})-{y}_{\text{new}} \\  & ={y}_{\text{exact}}({x}_{\text{new}})-({y}_{\text{exact}}(x)+Δy).\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that the exact solution of the initial value problem is ${y}_{\text{exact}}(x)=\frac{1}{x}.$ Now, let's find the $y$-increment given by the numerical method.

First, the slope at a step starting at $x$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{exact}}^{′}(x)={(\frac{1}{x})}^{′}=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the increment given by the numerical method is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & ={y}_{\text{exact}}^{′}(x)\cdot Δx \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\cdot Δx.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the exact value at ${x}_{\text{new}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{exact}}({x}_{\text{new}}) & =({y}_{\text{exact}}(x)+Δx) \\  & =\frac{1}{x+Δx}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the LTE for step $n$ starting at $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{τ}_{n} & ={y}_{\text{exact}}({x}_{\text{new}})-({y}_{\text{exact}}(x)+Δy) \\  & =\frac{1}{x+Δx}-(\frac{1}{x}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\cdot Δx)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
x{y}^{″}+4y{y}^{′}-3y=3{x}^{2},\,y(1)=1,\,{y}^{′}(1)=0
$$

We wish to approximate the solution using Euler's method by introducing $z={y}^{′}$ and reducing the equation to a system of first-order ODEs. What entries should be placed in the columns for $Δy$ and $Δz$ in the table below if the step size is $Δx=\frac{1}{2}?$

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ |  |  | {{field-1}} |  |  | {{field-2}} |

Therefore, $y(\frac{3}{2})≈$
{{field-3}}.
:question/worked-solution:
For a second-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}=f(x,y,{y}^{′}),\,y(a)=c,\,{y}^{′}(a)=d,
$$

we can use Euler's method to approximate a solution by first reducing the second-order ODE to a system of first-order ODEs,

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} &=z,\, && y(a)=c, \\ {z}^{′} &=f(x,y,z),\, && z(a)=d,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

before applying the update rule component-wise to each equation.

To apply Euler’s method, we first isolate ${y}^{″}$ so it can serve as the derivative of a new variable $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x{y}^{″}+4y{y}^{′}-3y & =3{x}^{2} \\ x{y}^{″} & =3{x}^{2}-4y{y}^{′}+3y \\ {y}^{″} & =\frac{3{x}^{2}-4y{y}^{′}+3y}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute our new variable $z={y}^{′},{z}^{′}={y}^{″}$ in the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{z}^{′}=\frac{3{x}^{2}-4yz+3y}{x}.
$$

Note that the initial value of $z$ is $z(1)={y}^{′}(1)=0.$ So, the initial value problem reduces to the following system of first-order ODEs:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} &=z,\, && y(1)=1, \\ {z}^{′} &=\frac{3{x}^{2}-4yz+3y}{x},\, && z(1)=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, we can proceed with Euler's method by applying the update rule component-wise.

First, because the initial conditions are $y(1)=1$ and $z(1)=0,$ we place $y=1$ and $z=0$ in the table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $1$ |  |  | $0$ |  |  |

Next, we compute both ${y}^{′}$ and ${z}^{′}$ according to the given rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =z=0 \\ {z}^{′} & =\frac{3{x}^{2}-4yz+3y}{x} \\  & =\frac{3\cdot {1}^{2}-4\cdot 1\cdot 0+3\cdot 1}{1} \\  & =\frac{3+0+3}{1} \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

So, we add these to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $1$ | $0$ |  | $0$ | $6$ |  |

Finally, we compute $Δy$ and $Δz$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =0\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =0 \\ Δz & ={z}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =6\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

We add these to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $1$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $6$ | $3$ |

To get the new values of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ in the *next* row, we add $Δx$ to $x,$ $Δy$ to $y,$ and $Δz$ to $z,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=1+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{2} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=1+0=1 \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=0+3=3\end{aligned}
$$

Adding these values to our table in a new row gives the following:

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $1$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $6$ | $3$ |
| $\frac{3}{2}$ | $1$ |  |  | $3$ |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that
$y(\frac{3}{2})≈1.$

:question/problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{″}-x{y}^{′}+{y}^{3}={x}^{3},\,y(0)=1,\,{y}^{′}(0)=1
$$

We wish to approximate the solution using Euler's method by introducing $z={y}^{′}$ and reducing the equation to a system of first-order ODEs. What entries should be placed in the columns for $Δy$ and $Δz$ in the table below if the step size is $Δx=\frac{1}{2}?$

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ |  |  | {{field-1}} |  |  | {{field-2}} |

Therefore, $y(\frac{1}{2})≈$
{{field-3}}.
:question/worked-solution:
For a second-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}=f(x,y,{y}^{′}),\,y(a)=c,\,{y}^{′}(a)=d,
$$

we can use Euler's method to approximate a solution by first reducing the second-order ODE to a system of first-order ODEs,

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} &=z,\, && y(a)=c, \\ {z}^{′} &=f(x,y,z),\, && z(a)=d,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

before applying the update rule component-wise to each equation.

To apply Euler’s method, we first isolate ${y}^{″}$ so it can serve as the derivative of a new variable $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″}-x{y}^{′}+{y}^{3} & ={x}^{3} \\ {y}^{″} & ={x}^{3}+x{y}^{′}-{y}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute our new variable $z={y}^{′},{z}^{′}={y}^{″}$ in the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{z}^{′}={x}^{3}+xz-{y}^{3}.
$$

Note that the initial value of $z$ is $z(0)={y}^{′}(0)=1.$
So, the initial value problem reduces to the following system of first-order ODEs:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} &=z,\, && y(0)=1, \\ {z}^{′} &={x}^{3}+xz-{y}^{3},\, && z(0)=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, we can proceed with Euler's method by applying the update rule component-wise.

First, because the initial conditions are $y(0)=1$ and $z(0)=1,$ we place $y=1$ and $z=1$ in the table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ |  |  | $1$ |  |  |

Next, we compute both ${y}^{′}$ and ${z}^{′}$ according to the given rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =z=1 \\ {z}^{′} & ={x}^{3}+xz-{y}^{3} \\  & ={0}^{3}+0\cdot 1-{1}^{3} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we add these to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $1$ |  | $1$ | $-1$ |  |

Finally, we compute $Δy$ and $Δz$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =1\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2} \\ Δz & ={z}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =(-1)\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We add these to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $1$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $-\frac{1}{2}$ |

To get the new values of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ in the *next* row, we add $Δx$ to $x,$ $Δy$ to $y,$ and $Δz$ to $z,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=0+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=1+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{2} \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=1+(-\frac{1}{2})=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Adding these values to our table in a new row gives the following:

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $1$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $-\frac{1}{2}$ |
| $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{3}{2}$ |  |  | $\frac{1}{2}$ |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
y(\frac{1}{2})≈\frac{3}{2}.
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}=2x-2y-3,\,y(0)=1
$$

To approximate the solution, one step of the Runge-Kutta method has already been computed, resulting in the following estimate:

$$
y(1)≈0
$$

Use the $2$-Step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton Method with one step to approximate $y(2).$

*Hint: The corrector equation of the two-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton method is defined as*

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{′}+8{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx
$$

*where ${y}_{p}$ denotes the predictor at the current step, and ${y}_{-1}^{′}$ is the estimated slope at the previous point.*
:question/worked-solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the $2$-Step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton (ABM $2$-step) Method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Predictor} & : & Δ{y}_{p} & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx, \\ \text{Corrector} & : & Δy & =\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{′}+8{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx,\end{aligned}
$$

where

- ${y}^{′}=f(x,y)$ is the estimated slope at the current point $(x,y),$

- ${y}_{-1}^{′}=f({x}_{-1},{y}_{-1})$ is the estimated slope at the previous point (${x}_{-1},{y}_{-1}),$ and

- ${y}_{p}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p})$ is the estimated slope at the predicted new point $({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p})=(x+Δx,y+Δ{y}_{p}).$

Before we start, let's add the initial condition data and Runge-Kutta step data to a table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ |  | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $0$ |  |  |  |  |  |

Now, since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=2,$ we will use a step size of

$$
Δx=2-1=1.
$$

First, we compute the values of ${y}^{′}$ at each point according to the given rule:

- The slope at the previous point $({x}_{-1},{y}_{-1})=(0,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{-1}^{′} & =2{x}_{-1}-2{y}_{-1}-3 \\  & =2\cdot 0-2\cdot 1-3 \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

- The slope at the current point $(x,y)=(1,0)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =2x-2y-3 \\  & =2\cdot 1-2\cdot 0-3 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

We add these values to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ |  |  |  |  |

Next, we compute $Δ{y}_{p}$ using the predictor equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ{y}_{p} & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3\cdot (-1)-(-5))\cdot 1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $1$ |  |  |  |

So, the coordinates of the predicted new point are

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=1+1=2, \\ {y}_{p} & =y+Δ{y}_{p}=0+1=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's add the second value to the table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $1$ |  |  |

Hence, the slope at this predicted point is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & =2{x}_{\text{new}}-2{y}_{p}-3 \\  & =2\cdot 2-2\cdot 1-3 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-1$ |  |

Finally, we compute $Δy$ using the corrector equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{′}+8{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{12}(5\cdot (-1)+8\cdot (-1)-(-5))\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\cdot (-8) \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $-\frac{2}{3}$ |

The value of $x$ in the next row is ${x}_{\text{new}}=2.$ To get the value of $y$ in the next row, we add $Δy$ to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\  & =0+(-\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Adding these results to our table gives the following:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $-\frac{2}{3}$ |
| $2$ | $-\frac{2}{3}$ |  |  |  |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that $y(2)≈-\frac{2}{3}.$

Now, since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=2,$ we will use a step size of

| $1$ | $2$ | $-11$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $2$ | $-\frac{9}{2}$ | $-\frac{7}{2}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $-\frac{17}{4}$ | $-\frac{11}{4}$ | $-\frac{41}{16}$ |

The value of $x$ in the next row is ${x}_{\text{new}}=3.$ To get the value of $y$ in the next row, we add $Δy$ to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\  & =-\frac{9}{2}+(-\frac{41}{16}) \\  & =-\frac{113}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

Adding these results to our table gives the following:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |

| $1$ | $2$ | $-11$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |

:question/problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}=3x-4y-\frac{1}{2},\,y(0)=0
$$

To approximate the solution, one step of the Runge-Kutta method has already been computed, resulting in the following estimate:

$$
y(1)≈2
$$

Use the $2$-Step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton Method with one step to approximate $y(2).$

*Hint: The corrector equation of the two-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton method is defined as*

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{′}+8{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx
$$

*where ${y}_{p}$ denotes the predictor at the current step, and ${y}_{-1}^{′}$ is the estimated slope at the previous point.*
:question/worked-solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the $2$-Step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton (ABM $2$-step) Method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Predictor} & : & Δ{y}_{p} & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx, \\ \text{Corrector} & : & Δy & =\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{′}+8{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx,\end{aligned}
$$

where

- ${y}^{′}=f(x,y)$ is the estimated slope at the current point $(x,y),$

- ${y}_{-1}^{′}=f({x}_{-1},{y}_{-1})$ is the estimated slope at the previous point (${x}_{-1},{y}_{-1}),$ and

- ${y}_{p}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p})$ is the estimated slope at the predicted new point $({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p})=(x+Δx,y+Δ{y}_{p}).$

Before we start, let's add the initial condition data and Runge-Kutta step data to a table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $0$ |  | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $2$ |  |  |  |  |  |

Now, since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=2,$ we will use a step size of

$$
Δx=2-1=1.
$$

First, we compute the values of ${y}^{′}$ at each point according to the given rule:

- The slope at the previous point $({x}_{-1},{y}_{-1})=(0,0)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{-1}^{′} & =3{x}_{-1}-4{y}_{-1}-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =3\cdot 0-4\cdot 0-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- The slope at the current point $(x,y)=(1,2)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =3x-4y-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =3\cdot 1-4\cdot 2-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =-\frac{11}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We add these values to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $0$ | $-\frac{1}{2}$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $2$ | $-\frac{11}{2}$ |  |  |  |  |

Next, we compute $Δ{y}_{p}$ using the predictor equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ{y}_{p} & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3\cdot (-\frac{11}{2})-(-\frac{1}{2}))\cdot 1 \\  & =-8.\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $0$ | $-\frac{1}{2}$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $2$ | $-\frac{11}{2}$ | $-8$ |  |  |  |

So, the coordinates of the predicted new point are

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=1+1=2, \\ {y}_{p} & =y+Δ{y}_{p}=2+(-8)=-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's add the second value to the table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $0$ | $-\frac{1}{2}$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $2$ | $-\frac{11}{2}$ | $-8$ | $-6$ |  |  |

Hence, the slope at this predicted point is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & =3{x}_{\text{new}}-4{y}_{p}-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =3\cdot 2-4\cdot (-6)-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{59}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $0$ | $-\frac{1}{2}$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $2$ | $-\frac{11}{2}$ | $-8$ | $-6$ | $\frac{59}{2}$ |  |

Finally, we compute $Δy$ using the corrector equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{′}+8{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{12}(5\cdot \frac{59}{2}+8\cdot (-\frac{11}{2})-(-\frac{1}{2}))\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\cdot 104 \\  & =\frac{26}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $0$ | $-\frac{1}{2}$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $2$ | $-\frac{11}{2}$ | $-8$ | $-6$ | $\frac{59}{2}$ | $\frac{26}{3}$ |

The value of $x$ in the next row is ${x}_{\text{new}}=2.$ To get the value of $y$ in the next row, we add $Δy$ to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\  & =2+\frac{26}{3} \\  & =\frac{32}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Adding these results to our table gives the following:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $0$ | $-\frac{1}{2}$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $2$ | $-\frac{11}{2}$ | $-8$ | $-6$ | $\frac{59}{2}$ | $\frac{26}{3}$ |
| $2$ | $\frac{32}{3}$ |  |  |  |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that $y(2)≈\frac{32}{3}.$

:question/problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
x{y}^{″}-3y{y}^{′}=2{x}^{2},\,y(1)=-1,\,{y}^{′}(1)=1
$$

Use Euler's Method with one step to approximate $y(\frac{3}{2})$ and ${y}^{′}(\frac{3}{2}).$

$y(\frac{3}{2})≈$
{{field-1}},
$\,{y}^{′}(\frac{3}{2})≈$
{{field-2}}
:question/worked-solution:
For a second-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}=f(x,y,{y}^{′}),\,y(a)=c,\,{y}^{′}(a)=d,
$$

we can use Euler's method to approximate a solution by first reducing the second-order ODE to a system of first-order ODEs,

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} &=z,\, && y(a)=c, \\ {z}^{′} &=f(x,y,z)\, && z(a)=d,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

before applying the update rule component-wise to each equation.

To apply Euler’s method, we first isolate ${y}^{″}$ so it can serve as the derivative of a new variable $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x{y}^{″}-3y{y}^{′} & =2{x}^{2} \\ x{y}^{″} & =2{x}^{2}+3y{y}^{′} \\ {y}^{″} & =\frac{2{x}^{2}+3y{y}^{′}}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute our new variable $z={y}^{′},{z}^{′}={y}^{″}$ in the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{z}^{′}=\frac{2{x}^{2}+3yz}{x}.
$$

Note that the initial value of $z$ is
$z(1)={y}^{′}(1)=1.$
So, the initial value problem reduces to the following system of first-order ODEs:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} &=z,\, && y(1)=-1, \\ {z}^{′} &=\frac{2{x}^{2}+3yz}{x},\, && z(1)=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, we can proceed with Euler's method by applying the update rule component-wise.

Since we want to find the values of $y$ and ${y}^{′}=z$ at $x=\frac{3}{2},$ we will use a step size of

$$
Δx=\frac{3}{2}-1=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

First, we place the initial condition data in the table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ |  |  | $1$ |  |  |

Next, we compute both ${y}^{′}$ and ${z}^{′}$ according to the given rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =z=1 \\ {z}^{′} & =\frac{2{x}^{2}+3yz}{x} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot {1}^{2}+3\cdot (-1)\cdot 1}{1} \\  & =\frac{2-3}{1} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we add these to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ | $1$ |  | $1$ | $-1$ |  |

Next, we compute $Δy$ and $Δz$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =1\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2} \\ Δz & ={z}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =(-1)\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We add these to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $-\frac{1}{2}$ |

To get the new values of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ in the *next* row, we add $Δx$ to $x,$ $Δy$ to $y,$ and $Δz$ to $z,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=1+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{2} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=-1+\frac{1}{2}=-\frac{1}{2} \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=1+(-\frac{1}{2})=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Adding these values to our table in a new row gives the following:

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $-\frac{1}{2}$ |
| $\frac{3}{2}$ | $-\frac{1}{2}$ |  |  | $\frac{1}{2}$ |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that
$y(\frac{3}{2})≈-\frac{1}{2}$
and
${y}^{′}(\frac{3}{2})=z(\frac{3}{2})≈\frac{1}{2}.$

:question/problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+x{y}^{′}-2y=0,\,y(1)=2,\,{y}^{′}(1)=1
$$

Use Euler's Method with two steps to approximate $y(2)$ and ${y}^{′}(2).$

$$
y(2)≈{{field-1}},\,{y}^{′}(2)≈{{field-2}}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
For a second-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}=f(x,y,{y}^{′}),\,y(a)=c,\,{y}^{′}(a)=d,
$$

we can use Euler's method to approximate a solution by first reducing the second-order ODE to a system of first-order ODEs,

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} &=z,\, && y(a)=c, \\ {z}^{′} &=f(x,y,z)\, && z(a)=d,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

before applying the update rule component-wise to each equation.

To apply Euler’s method, we first isolate ${y}^{″}$ so it can serve as the derivative of a new variable $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+x{y}^{′}-2y & =0 \\ {x}^{2}{y}^{″} & =2y-x{y}^{′} \\ {y}^{″} & =\frac{2y-x{y}^{′}}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute our new variable $z={y}^{′},{z}^{′}={y}^{″}$ in the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{z}^{′}=\frac{2y-xz}{{x}^{2}}.
$$

Note that the initial value of $z$ is $z(1)={y}^{′}(1)=1.$
So, the initial value problem reduces to the following system of first-order ODEs:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} &=z,\, && y(1)=2, \\ {z}^{′} &=\frac{2y-xz}{{x}^{2}},\, && z(1)=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, we can proceed with Euler's method by applying the update rule component-wise.

First, note that we are given the values of $y$ and $z={y}^{′}$ at $x=1$ and asked to find their values at $x=2.$ The distance from $x=1$ to $x=2$ is $1,$ and since we are asked to use two steps of equal size, our step size must be

$$
Δx=\frac{2-1}{2}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, we'll start by creating a table that includes the initial condition data $y(1)=2$ and $z(1)=1.$

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ |  |  | $1$ |  |  |

**Step 1**.

We compute ${y}^{′}$ and $Δy,$ ${z}^{′}$ and $Δz$ (using the values of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ in the first row), and the values of ${x}_{\text{new}},$ ${y}_{\text{new}},$ and ${z}_{\text{new}}$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =z=1 \\ {z}^{′} & =\frac{2y-xz}{{x}^{2}}=\frac{2\cdot 2-1\cdot 1}{{1}^{2}}=3 \\ Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx=1\cdot \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2} \\ Δz & ={z}^{′}\cdot Δx=3\cdot \frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{2} \\ {x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=1+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{2} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=2+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{5}{2} \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=1+\frac{3}{2}=\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We add these values to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ | $1$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $1$ | $3$ | $\frac{3}{2}$ |
| $\frac{3}{2}$ | $\frac{5}{2}$ |  |  | $\frac{5}{2}$ |  |  |

**Step 2**.

We compute ${y}^{′}$ and $Δy,$ ${z}^{′}$ and $Δz$ (using the values of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ in the second row), and the values of ${x}_{\text{new}},$ ${y}_{\text{new}},$ and ${z}_{\text{new}}$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =z=\frac{5}{2} \\ {z}^{′} & =\frac{2y-xz}{{x}^{2}}=\frac{2\cdot \frac{5}{2}-\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{5}{2}}{{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}}=\frac{(\frac{5}{4})}{(\frac{9}{4})}=\frac{5}{9} \\ Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx=\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}=\frac{5}{4} \\ Δz & ={z}^{′}\cdot Δx=\frac{5}{9}\cdot \frac{1}{2}=\frac{5}{18} \\ {x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=2 \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=\frac{5}{2}+\frac{5}{4}=\frac{15}{4} \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=\frac{5}{2}+\frac{5}{18}=\frac{25}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

We add these values to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ | $1$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $1$ | $3$ | $\frac{3}{2}$ |
| $\frac{3}{2}$ | $\frac{5}{2}$ | $\frac{5}{2}$ | $\frac{5}{4}$ | $\frac{5}{2}$ | $\frac{5}{9}$ | $\frac{5}{18}$ |
| $2$ | $\frac{15}{4}$ |  |  | $\frac{25}{9}$ |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that
$y(2)≈\frac{15}{4}$
and
${y}^{′}(2)=z(2)≈\frac{25}{9}.$

:question/problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+4{y}^{′}-y=0,\,y(1)=-1,\,{y}^{′}(1)=2
$$

Use Euler's Method with two steps to approximate $y(2)$ and ${y}^{′}(2).$

$$
y(2)≈{{field-1}},\,{y}^{′}(2)≈{{field-2}}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
For a second-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}=f(x,y,{y}^{′}),\,y(a)=c,\,{y}^{′}(a)=d,
$$

we can use Euler's method to approximate a solution by first reducing the second-order ODE to a system of first-order ODEs,

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} &=z,\, && y(a)=c, \\ {z}^{′} &=f(x,y,z)\, && z(a)=d,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

before applying the update rule component-wise to each equation.

To apply Euler’s method, we first isolate ${y}^{″}$ so it can serve as the derivative of a new variable $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+4{y}^{′}-y & =0 \\ {x}^{2}{y}^{″} & =y-4{y}^{′} \\ {y}^{″} & =\frac{y-4{y}^{′}}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute our new variable $z={y}^{′},{z}^{′}={y}^{″}$ in the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{z}^{′}=\frac{y-4z}{{x}^{2}}.
$$

Note that the initial value of $z$ is $z(1)={y}^{′}(1)=2.$
So, the initial value problem reduces to the following system of first-order ODEs:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} &=z,\, && y(1)=-1, \\ {z}^{′} &=\frac{y-4z}{{x}^{2}},\, && z(1)=2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, we can proceed with Euler's method by applying the update rule component-wise.

First, note that we are given the values of $y$ and $z={y}^{′}$ at $x=1$ and asked to find their values at $x=2.$ The distance from $x=1$ to $x=2$ is $1,$ and since we are asked to use two steps of equal size, our step size must be

$$
Δx=\frac{2-1}{2}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, we'll start by creating a table that includes the initial condition data $y(1)=-1$ and $z(1)=2.$

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ |  |  | $2$ |  |  |

**Step 1**.

We compute ${y}^{′}$ and $Δy,$ ${z}^{′}$ and $Δz$ (using the values of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ in the first row), and the values of ${x}_{\text{new}},$ ${y}_{\text{new}},$ and ${z}_{\text{new}}$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =z=2 \\ {z}^{′} & =\frac{y-4z}{{x}^{2}}=\frac{-1-4\cdot 2}{{1}^{2}}=-9 \\ Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx=2\cdot \frac{1}{2}=1 \\ Δz & ={z}^{′}\cdot Δx=-9\cdot \frac{1}{2}=-\frac{9}{2} \\ {x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=1+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{2} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=-1+1=0 \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=2-\frac{9}{2}=-\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We add these values to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ | $2$ | $1$ | $2$ | $-9$ | $-\frac{9}{2}$ |
| $\frac{3}{2}$ | $0$ |  |  | $-\frac{5}{2}$ |  |  |

**Step 2**.

We compute ${y}^{′}$ and $Δy,$ ${z}^{′}$ and $Δz$ (using the values of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ in the second row), and the values of ${x}_{\text{new}},$ ${y}_{\text{new}},$ and ${z}_{\text{new}}$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =z=-\frac{5}{2} \\ {z}^{′} & =\frac{y-4z}{{x}^{2}}=\frac{0-4(-\frac{5}{2})}{{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}}=\frac{10}{(\frac{9}{4})}=\frac{40}{9} \\ Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx=-\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}=-\frac{5}{4} \\ Δz & ={z}^{′}\cdot Δx=\frac{40}{9}\cdot \frac{1}{2}=\frac{20}{9} \\ {x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=2 \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=0-\frac{5}{4}=-\frac{5}{4} \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=-\frac{5}{2}+\frac{20}{9}=-\frac{5}{18}\end{aligned}
$$

We add these values to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ | $2$ | $1$ | $2$ | $-9$ | $-\frac{9}{2}$ |
| $\frac{3}{2}$ | $0$ | $-\frac{5}{2}$ | $-\frac{5}{4}$ | $-\frac{5}{2}$ | $\frac{40}{9}$ | $\frac{20}{9}$ |
| $2$ | $-\frac{5}{4}$ |  |  | $-\frac{5}{18}$ |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that
$y(2)≈-\frac{5}{4}$
and
${y}^{′}(2)=z(2)≈-\frac{5}{18}.$

:question/problem:
Find the singular solution to the following Clairaut differential equation:

$$
y=x{y}^{′}-({y}^{′})^{4}.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
A Clairaut differential equation has the form

$$
y=x{y}^{′}+g({y}^{′}),
$$

where $g$ is a differentiable function of ${y}^{′}.$

To solve the Clairaut differential equation

$$
y=x{y}^{′}-({y}^{′})^{4},
$$

we start by setting $p={y}^{′}.$

Substituting this into the equation gives

$$
y=xp-{p}^{4}.
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =(xp-{p}^{4})^{′} \\ p & =p+x{p}^{′}-4{p}^{3}{p}^{′} \\ 0 & ={p}^{′}(x-4{p}^{3})\end{aligned}
$$

The product on the right-hand side equals zero, so at least one factor must be zero.

The singular solution of the Clairaut differential equation is obtained if $x-4{p}^{3}=0.$ Then,

$$
x=4{p}^{3}.
$$

Now, let's substitute this into $y=xp-{p}^{4}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =xp-{p}^{4} \\  & =(4{p}^{3})p-{p}^{4} \\  & =4{p}^{4}-{p}^{4} \\  & =3{p}^{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the singular solution is given parametrically by

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=4{p}^{3} \\ y &=3{p}^{4}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

To eliminate $p,$ we first solve the first equation for $p:$

$$
p={(\frac{x}{4})}^{1/3}
$$

Next, let's substitute this expression for $p$ into the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3{p}^{4} \\  & =3{({(\frac{x}{4})}^{1/3})}^{4} \\  & =3{(\frac{x}{4})}^{4/3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the explicit form of the singular solution is

$$
y=3{(\frac{x}{4})}^{4/3}.
$$

:question/problem:
Find the singular solution to the following Clairaut differential equation:

$$
y=x{y}^{′}+\sqrt{{y}^{′}},\,{y}^{′}\ge 0.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
A Clairaut differential equation has the form

$$
y=x{y}^{′}+g({y}^{′}),
$$

where $g$ is a differentiable function of ${y}^{′}.$

To solve the Clairaut differential equation

$$
y=x{y}^{′}+\sqrt{{y}^{′}},
$$

we start by setting
$p={y}^{′}.$

Substituting this into the equation gives

$$
y=xp+\sqrt{p}.
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =(xp+\sqrt{p})^{′} \\ p & =p+x{p}^{′}+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{p}}{p}^{′} \\ 0 & ={p}^{′}(x+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{p}})\end{aligned}
$$

The product on the right-hand side equals zero, so at least one factor must be zero.

The singular solution of the Clairaut differential equation is obtained if $x+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{p}}=0.$ Then,

$$
x=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{p}}.
$$

Now, let's substitute this into $y=xp+\sqrt{p}\,:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =xp+\sqrt{p} \\  & =(-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{p}})p+\sqrt{p} \\  & =-\frac{p}{2\sqrt{p}}+\sqrt{p} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{p}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the singular solution is given parametrically by

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{p}} \\ y &=\frac{\sqrt{p}}{2}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

To eliminate $p,$ we first solve the first equation for $\sqrt{p}\,:$

$$
\sqrt{p}=-\frac{1}{2x}
$$

Since $x=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{p}},$ we must have $x<0.$

Next, let's substitute this expression for $\sqrt{p}$ into the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{\sqrt{p}}{2} \\  & =\frac{(-\frac{1}{2x})}{2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4x}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the explicit form of the singular solution is

$$
y=-\frac{1}{4x},\,x<0.
$$

:question/problem:
Find the singular solution to the following Clairaut differential equation:

$$
y=x{y}^{′}+2({y}^{′})^{2}+3.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
A Clairaut differential equation has the form

$$
y=x{y}^{′}+g({y}^{′}),
$$

where $g$ is a differentiable function of ${y}^{′}.$

To solve the Clairaut differential equation

$$
y=x{y}^{′}+2({y}^{′})^{2}+3,
$$

we start by setting
$p={y}^{′}.$

Substituting this into the equation gives

$$
y=xp+2{p}^{2}+3.
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =(xp+2{p}^{2}+3)^{′} \\ p & =p+x{p}^{′}+4p{p}^{′} \\ 0 & ={p}^{′}(x+4p)\end{aligned}
$$

The product on the right-hand side equals zero, so at least one factor must be zero.

The singular solution of the Clairaut differential equation is obtained if $x+4p=0.$ Then,

$$
x=-4p.
$$

Now, let's substitute this into $y=xp+2{p}^{2}+3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =xp+2{p}^{2}+3 \\  & =(-4p)p+2{p}^{2}+3 \\  & =-4{p}^{2}+2{p}^{2}+3 \\  & =-2{p}^{2}+3\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the singular solution is given parametrically by

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=-4p \\ y &=-2{p}^{2}+3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

To eliminate $p,$ we first solve the first equation for $p:$ 

$$
p=-\frac{x}{4}.
$$

Next, let's substitute this expression for $p$ into the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-2{p}^{2}+3 \\  & =-2{(-\frac{x}{4})}^{2}+3 \\  & =-\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}+3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the explicit form of the singular solution is

$$
y=3-\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}.
$$

By the scalar function multiple rule, we have

$$
(v(t)f(t))^{′}=v(t){f}^{′}(t)+{v}^{′}(t)f(t)
$$

Let's find ${v}^{′}(t)$ and ${f}^{′}(t).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({2}^{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({2}^{t+1}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({2}^{2t}+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨{2}^{t}\operatorname{ln}⁡2,\,{2}^{t+1}\operatorname{ln}⁡2,\,2\cdot {2}^{2t}\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩ \\ {v}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{{2}^{t}})=-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{{2}^{t}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(v(t)f(t))^{′} & =v(t){f}^{′}(t)+{v}^{′}(t)f(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{{2}^{t}}⟨{2}^{t}\operatorname{ln}⁡2,\,{2}^{t+1}\operatorname{ln}⁡2,\,2\cdot {2}^{2t}\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{{2}^{t}}⟨{2}^{t},\,{2}^{t+1},\,{2}^{2t}+1⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{{2}^{t}\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{{2}^{t}},\,\frac{{2}^{t+1}\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{{2}^{t}},\,\frac{2\cdot {2}^{2t}\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{{2}^{t}}⟩-⟨\frac{{2}^{t}\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{{2}^{t}},\,\frac{{2}^{t+1}2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{{2}^{t}},\,\frac{({2}^{2t}+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{{2}^{t}}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,\frac{({2}^{2t}-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{{2}^{t}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+{sin}^{2}t\,k$ at the point corresponding to $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$  valid for all  real values of $u?$
:question/worked-solution:
At the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$,  the vector ${r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

 

$$
R(u)=r(\frac{\pi }{4})+u{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

 

First, we find $r(\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,j+{sin}^{2}(\frac{\pi }{4})\,k \\  & =\,i+\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({sin}^{2}t)\,k \\  & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,j-\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})k \\  & =\,i-\,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point 
 where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is

$$
R(u)=\,i+\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k+u(\,i-\,j+\,k),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the following statement. 

If $f(x)=2{e}^{4x}+x,$ then $f=O({e}^{4x})$ as $x\to \infty .$

A proof of the statement is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,2{e}^{4x}=O(2{e}^{4x})$  

$\text{L2}:\,{lim}_{x\to \infty }(\frac{x}{2{e}^{4x}})=0$  

$\text{L3}:\,x=O(2{e}^{4x})$  

$\text{L4}:\,f=O(4{e}^{4x})$  

$\text{L5}:\,f=O({e}^{4x})$  

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L1}$ follows from  
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from lines  
{{field-2}}  
and  
{{field-3}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from line  
{{field-4}}  
and  
{{field-5}}.
:question/worked-solution:
Suppose $f(x),g(x),h(x)$ and $k(x)$ are functions and $c$ is a nonzero constant. Then, we have the following properties of Big-O notation.

- The sum and product properties. If

$$
f=O(h)\,\text{and}\,g=O(k)\,\text{as}\,x\to a,
$$

then

$$
f+g=O(h+k)\,\text{and}\,fg=O(hk)\,\text{as}\,x\to a.
$$

- The constant multiple property. If

$$
f=O(cg)\,\text{as}\,x\to a,
$$

then

$$
f=O(g)\,\text{as}\,x\to a.
$$

- The reflexive property.

$$
f=O(f)\,\text{as}\,x\to a.
$$

- The transitive property. If

$$
f=O(g)\,\text{and}\,g=O(h)\,\text{as}\,x\to a,
$$

then

$$
f=O(h)\,\text{as}\,x\to a.
$$

- The absorption property. If

$$
f=O(g+h)\,\text{and}\,g=O(h)\,\text{as}\,x\to a,
$$

then

$$
f=O(h)\,\text{as}\,x\to a.
$$

With that in mind, let us justify each selected step.

- We first consider line $\text{L1},$ which states that

$$
2{e}^{4x}=O(2{e}^{4x}),
$$

and this follows by $\text{the reflexive property}.$

- Next, we consider line $\text{L4}.$ From line $\text{L1}$ we have

$$
2{e}^{4x}=O(2{e}^{4x}),
$$

and from line $\text{L3}$ we have

$$
x=O(2{e}^{4x}).
$$

Since $f=2{e}^{4x}+x,$ by lines $\text{L1 and L3}$ and $\text{the sum property},$ we obtain

$$
f=2{e}^{4x}+x=O(2{e}^{4x}+2{e}^{4x})=O(4{e}^{4x}),
$$

which justifies line $\text{L4}.$

- Finally, we consider line $\text{L5}.$ From line $\text{L4}$ we have

$$
f=O(4{e}^{4x}),
$$

and by $\text{the constant multiple property}$ with $c=4,$ we conclude

$$
f=O({e}^{4x}).
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the following initial value problem for the functions $y=y(x),z=z(x):$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} &=xy+z,\, && y(0)=1 \\ {z}^{′} &=x-y+2,\, && z(0)=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use Euler's method with two steps of equal size to approximate $y(1)$ and $z(1).$

$y(1)≈$
{{field-1}},
$\,z(1)≈$
{{field-2}}
:question/worked-solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} &=f(x,y,z),\, && y(a)=c, \\ {z}^{′} &=g(x,y,z),\, && z(a)=d,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Euler's method approximates the solution by applying the update rule component-wise to each equation. More precisely, the increments on $y$ and $z$ are

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}Δy &={y}^{′}\cdot Δx, \\ Δz &={z}^{′}\cdot Δx.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The new values are then given by ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy$ and ${z}_{\text{new}}=z+Δz.$

First, note that we are given the values of $y$ and $z$ at $x=0$ and asked to find their values at $x=1.$ The distance from $x=0$ to $x=1$ is $1,$ and since we are asked to use two steps of equal size, our step size must be

$$
Δx=\frac{1-0}{2}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, let's proceed with Euler's method. We'll start by creating a table that includes the initial condition data $y(0)=1$ and $z(0)=0.$

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ |  |  | $0$ |  |  |

**Step 1**.

We compute ${y}^{′}$ and $Δy,$ ${z}^{′}$ and $Δz$ (using the values of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ in the first row), and the values of ${x}_{\text{new}},$ ${y}_{\text{new}},$ and ${z}_{\text{new}}$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =xy+z=0\cdot 1+0=0 \\ {z}^{′} & =x-y+2=0-1+2=1 \\ Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx=0\cdot \frac{1}{2}=0 \\ Δz & ={z}^{′}\cdot Δx=1\cdot \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2} \\ {x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=0+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=1+0=1 \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=0+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We add these values to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $1$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |
| $\frac{1}{2}$ | $1$ |  |  | $\frac{1}{2}$ |  |  |

**Step 2**.

We compute ${y}^{′}$ and $Δy,$ ${z}^{′}$ and $Δz$ (using the values of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ in the second row), and the values of ${x}_{\text{new}},$ ${y}_{\text{new}},$ and ${z}_{\text{new}}$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =xy+z=(\frac{1}{2})\cdot 1+\frac{1}{2}=1 \\ {z}^{′} & =x-y+2=\frac{1}{2}-1+2=\frac{3}{2} \\ Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx=1\cdot \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2} \\ Δz & ={z}^{′}\cdot Δx=\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{4} \\ {x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=1 \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=1+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{2} \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{3}{4}=\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

We add these values to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $1$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |
| $\frac{1}{2}$ | $1$ | $1$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{3}{2}$ | $\frac{3}{4}$ |
| $1$ | $\frac{3}{2}$ |  |  | $\frac{5}{4}$ |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
y(1)≈\frac{3}{2}\,\text{and}\,z(1)≈\frac{5}{4}.
$$

:question/problem:
The unit tangent vector to a curve at an arbitrary point is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}}⟨1,t⟩.
$$

Find the principal normal vector at the point where $t=1.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}}⟨1,t⟩) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}})⟨1,t⟩+\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}}⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =-\frac{t}{(1+{t}^{2})^{3/2}}⟨1,t⟩+\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}}⟨0,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{(1+{t}^{2})^{3/2}}[-t⟨1,t⟩+(1+{t}^{2})⟨0,1⟩] \\  & =\frac{1}{(1+{t}^{2})^{3/2}}⟨-t,1⟩ \\  \\ {T}^{′}(1) & =\frac{1}{(1+{1}^{2})^{3/2}}⟨-1,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}⟨-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we find the magnitude of ${T}^{′}(1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{T}^{′}(1)‖ & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}‖⟨-1,1⟩‖ \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${T}^{′}(1)$ and obtain the principal normal vector to the curve at the point where $t=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}N(1) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(1)}{‖{T}^{′}(1)‖}=\frac{\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}⟨-1,1⟩}{\frac{1}{2}}=⟨-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Note that when we find the scalar product of $T$ and $N$ at the point where $t=1,$  we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(1)\cdot N(1) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨1,1⟩\cdot ⟨-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the following first-order linear ODE for the function $y=y(x):$

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{1}{2}y={x}^{3}
$$

Write the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yI(x))=I(x)Q(x),$ where $I(x)$ is an integrating factor.
:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=-\frac{1}{2}$ and $Q(x)={x}^{3}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{\int (-1/2)\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{-x/2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={e}^{-x/2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-x/2}\cdot (\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{1}{2}y) & ={e}^{-x/2}\cdot {x}^{3} \\ {e}^{-x/2}\cdot \frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-x/2}\cdot y & ={e}^{-x/2}\cdot {x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x)):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dx}(y{e}^{-x/2}) & ={e}^{-x/2}\cdot {x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
A can of soda is taken out of a refrigerator and left in a room that stays at a constant temperature of $20{\,}^{∘}\text{C}.$ The soda’s temperature $T(t)$ (in degrees Celsius) can be modeled by the differential equation:

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=k(20-T),
$$

where $t\ge 0$ is the time, measured in minutes, and $k>0$ is a constant. The initial temperature of the soda is $8{\,}^{∘}\text{C},$ and after $5$ minutes, the soda has warmed to $12{\,}^{∘}\text{C}.$ To the nearest minute, how long does it take for the soda to reach $16{\,}^{∘}\text{C}?$
:question/worked-solution:
We're told that the temperature of the can is modeled by the inhibited growth equation

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=k(20-T).
$$

We separate variables and integrate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{20-T} & =k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{20-T} & =\int k\,dt \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡|20-T| & =kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited growth equation, we have $20-T>0$ for all $t\ge 0.$ Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}20-T & ={e}^{-kt-C} \\ 20-T & ={e}^{-C}{e}^{-kt} \\ 20-T & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =20-K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{-C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the initial temperature was $8{\,}^{∘}\text{C}.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=8,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}8 & =20-K{e}^{0} \\ 8 & =20-K \\ K & =12\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to our initial value problem is

$$
T(t)=20-12{e}^{-kt}.
$$

We're also told that, after $5$ minutes, the temperature of the soda was $12{\,}^{∘}\text{C}.$ So, applying the condition $T(5)=12,$  we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}12 & =20-12{e}^{-5k} \\ 8 & =12{e}^{-5k} \\ {e}^{-5k} & =\frac{2}{3} \\ -5k & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{3}) \\ k & =-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$  be the time when the soda can reaches $16{\,}^{∘}\text{C}.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T({t}_{1}) & =16 \\ 20-12{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =16 \\ 4 & =12{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} \\ {e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{1}{3} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{3}) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the value of $k,$ we get:

$$
{t}_{1}=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{3})}{-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{3})}=13.547…≈14\text{ }\text{minutes},
$$

rounded to the nearest minute.

:question/problem:
The volume $X(t)$ (in $\text{L}$) of water in a container as it fills toward its maximum capacity can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
\frac{dX}{dt}=0.4(3-X),
$$

where $t\ge 0$ is the time, measured in minutes. If the initial volume is $1.5\,\text{L},$ how long does it take for the container to reach a volume of $2\,\text{L}?$ Round your answer to the nearest integer.
:question/worked-solution:
We're told that the container's volume is modeled by the inhibited growth equation

$$
\frac{dX}{dt}=0.4(3-X).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dX}{3-X} & =0.4\,dt \\ \int \frac{dX}{3-X} & =\int 0.4\,\text{d}t \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡|3-X| & =0.4t+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited growth equation, we have $3-X>0$ for all $t\ge 0.$
Next, we solve for $X(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3-X & ={e}^{-0.4t-C} \\ 3-X & ={e}^{-C}{e}^{-0.4t} \\ 3-X & =K{e}^{-0.4t} \\ X & =3-K{e}^{-0.4t}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{-C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the initial volume was $1.5\,\text{L}.$ So, we apply the initial condition $X(0)=1.5,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}1.5 & =3-K{e}^{0} \\ 1.5 & =3-K \\ K & =1.5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to our initial value problem is

$$
X(t)=3-1.5{e}^{-0.4t}.
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the volume is $2\,\text{L}.$ Then, we have

$$

:question/worked-solution:
Suppose $f(x),g(x),h(x)$ and $k(x)$ are functions and $c$ is a nonzero constant. Then, we have the following properties of Big-O notation. 

- The sum and product properties. If

$$
f=O(h)\,\text{and}\,g=O(k)\,\text{as}\,x\to a
$$

then

$$
f+g=O(h+k)\,\text{and}\,fg=O(hk)\,\text{as}\,x\to a.
$$

- The constant multiple property. If 

$$
f=O(cg)\,\text{as}\,x\to a
$$

then 

$$
f=O(g)\,\text{as}\,x\to a.
$$

- The reflexive property. 

$$
f=O(f)\,\text{as}\,x\to a.
$$

- The transitive property. If 

$$
f=O(g)\,\text{and}\,g=O(h)\,\text{as}\,x\to a
$$

then

$$
f=O(h)\,\text{as}\,x\to a.
$$

- The absorption property. If

$$
f=O(g+h)\,\text{and}\,g=O(h)\,\text{as}\,x\to a
$$

 
then 

$$
f=O(h)\,\text{as}\,x\to a.
$$

With that in mind, let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider line $\text{L1},$ which states that

$$
f=O\,(\frac{1}{x}+\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+1}),
$$

and this is true by $\text{the reflexive property}.$

- Next, we consider line $\text{L3}.$ From line $\text{L1},$ we have

$$
f=O\,(\frac{1}{x}+\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+1})
$$

and from line $\text{L2},$ we have

$$
\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+1}=O\,(\frac{1}{x}).
$$

Thus, by lines $\text{L1 and L2}$ and the $\text{absorption property},$ we have 

$$
f=O\,(\frac{1}{x}).
$$

- Finally, we consider line $\text{L5}.$ From line $\text{L3}$ we have

$$
f=O\,(\frac{1}{x}),
$$

and from line $\text{L4}$ we have

$$
\frac{1}{x}=O(1).
$$

Thus, by lines   $\text{L3 and L4}$ and $\text{the transitive property},$ we obtain

$$
f=O(1).
$$

:question/problem:
Throughout an experiment in a laboratory, a culture contains $1\,200$ bacteria in total (limited by nutrients and space). At the beginning of the experiment, $200$ of the $1\,200$ bacteria are resistant to a new antibiotic. After $4$ hours, the number of resistant bacteria increases to $500.$ To the nearest hour, how long does it take for the number of resistant bacteria to reach $900?$

*Hint: You may assume that the number of resistant bacteria, $P(t),$ increases at a rate that obeys an inhibited growth model, where $t\ge 0$ is the time, in hours.*
:question/worked-solution:
The rate at which the resistant bacteria population, $P(t),$ changes is proportional to the difference between the total bacteria population in the culture and its current resistant population. Therefore, we have the inhibited growth equation

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(a-P),
$$

where $a$ is the total bacteria population the culture can support, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, $a=1\,200$ bacteria, and we have

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(1\,200-P).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dP}{1\,200-P} & =k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dP}{1\,200-P} & =\int k\,dt \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡|1\,200-P| & =kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited growth equation, we have $1\,200-P>0$ for all $t\ge 0.$
Next, we solve for $P(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}1\,200-P & ={e}^{-kt-C} \\ 1\,200-P & ={e}^{-C}{e}^{-kt} \\ 1\,200-P & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ P & =1\,200-K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{-C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial population of resistant bacteria was $200$ cells. So, we apply the initial condition $P(0)=200,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0) & =200 \\ 1\,200-K{e}^{0} & =200 \\ 1\,200-K & =200 \\ K & =1\,000\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $P(t):$

$$
P(t)=1\,200-1\,000{e}^{-kt}
$$

We're also told that, after $4$ hours, the resistant bacteria population was $500$ cells. So, applying the condition $P(4)=500,$ we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(4) & =500 \\ 1\,200-1\,000{e}^{-4k} & =500 \\ 700 & =1\,000{e}^{-4k} \\ {e}^{-4k} & =\frac{700}{1\,000}=\frac{7}{10} \\ -4k & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{7}{10}) \\ k & =-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{7}{10})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when $900$ bacteria are resistant to the antibiotic. Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P({t}_{1}) & =900 \\ 1\,200-1\,000{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =900 \\ 300 & =1\,000{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} \\ {e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{300}{1\,000}=\frac{3}{10} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{10}) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{10}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that $900$ bacteria will be resistant to the antibiotic after

$$
{t}_{1}=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{10})}{-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{7}{10})}=13.502…≈14\,\text{hours},
$$

rounded to the nearest hour.

:question/problem: Find the unit tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩$ at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2}.$
:question/worked-solution:
For a curve $r(t)=⟨x(t),y(t),z(t)⟩$, the unit tangent vector $T(t)$ at the point $P(x(t),y(t),z(t))$ is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\frac{\pi }{2}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2},\,-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2},\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,-2,\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})‖ & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(-2)^{2}+(-2)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+4+4} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})$ and obtain the unit tangent vector to the given curve at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})}{‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨-1,\,-2,\,-2⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{3},\,-\frac{2}{3},\,-\frac{2}{3}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{1}{x}$ and $Q(x)=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x}.$

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)=x$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}y) & =x\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x} \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yx) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yx)\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ yx & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C \\ y & =\frac{-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(\frac{\pi }{2})=1$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\frac{-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+C}{(\frac{\pi }{2})} \\ 1 & =\frac{2C}{\pi } \\ C & =\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\frac{\pi }{2})}{x} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2x}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{x} \\  & =\frac{\pi -2\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
A particle $P$ is traveling along the $x$-axis with displacement $s(t)$ from a fixed origin $O$ given by

$$
s(t)={t}^{2}ln\,({t}^{2}),\,t>0.
$$

Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and find the value of the velocity at this moment.

The acceleration is zero at $t=$
{{field-1}}, and the velocity at this moment is
$v=$
{{field-2}}.
:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
s(t)={t}^{2}ln\,({t}^{2})=2{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\,(2{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)) \\  & =2(2t)\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+2{t}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{t} \\  & =4t\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+2t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+2t) \\  & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+4t\cdot \frac{1}{t}+2 \\  & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+6\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we put $a(t)=0$ to find the time when the acceleration is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}4\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+6 & =0 \\ 4\operatorname{ln}⁡(t) & =-6 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(t) & =-\frac{3}{2} \\ t & ={e}^{-3/2}\end{aligned}
$$

So the acceleration is zero when $t={e}^{-3/2}.$ To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into $v(t)$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}v\,({e}^{-3/2}) & ={e}^{-3/2}(4ln\,({e}^{-3/2})+2) \\  & ={e}^{-3/2}(4\cdot (-\frac{3}{2})+2) \\  & ={e}^{-3/2}(-6+2) \\  & =-4{e}^{-3/2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the acceleration is zero at $t={e}^{-3/2},$ and the velocity at this moment is $v=-4{e}^{-3/2}.$

:question/problem:
![](images/4b/4b304da0cca6e678fd53931c6949ff51546486df844553e79608542a8bf7886d.png)

Find the amplitude of the steady-state current for the RL circuit shown above, rounded to two decimal places.

The amplitude of the steady-state current is approximately
{{field-1}} amperes.
:question/worked-solution:
The diagram shows a series RL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $10\,Ω,$ and an inductor of inductance $2\,\text{H}.$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RL circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=10\,Ω.$

$$
{V}_{R}=10I
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=2\,\text{H}.$

$$
{V}_{L}=2\cdot \frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of current $I$ in the circuit is

$$
6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)=10I+2\cdot \frac{dI}{dt}
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}+5I=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${I}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{I}_{c}}{dt}+5{I}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-5t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $2t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $2t,$ i.e.,

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t), \\ \frac{d{I}_{p}}{dt} & =-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))+5(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ (-2\alpha +5\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+(5\alpha +2\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-2\alpha +5\beta &=3\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\ 5\alpha +2\beta &=0\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{6}{29},$ $\beta =\frac{15}{29}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{6}{29}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{15}{29}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)={I}_{c}(t)+{I}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-5t}-\frac{6}{29}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{15}{29}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-5t}$ is the *transient current*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function ${I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{6}{29}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{15}{29}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)$ is the *steady-state current*. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
I(t)≈{I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{6}{29}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{15}{29}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current is given by

$$
\sqrt{{(-\frac{6}{29})}^{2}+{(\frac{15}{29})}^{2}}≈0.56\,\text{A},
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x)=-\infty $ and ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})=-\infty ,$ respectively, so we have the case $\frac{-\infty }{-\infty }.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})} & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{[\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x)]^{′}}{[\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{(\frac{1}{x})}{(\frac{3}{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{{x}^{-1}}{3{x}^{-1}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the unit tangent vector to the curve   $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,,\,2{cos}^{2}⁡t⟩$  at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{6}.$
:question/worked-solution:
For a curve $r(t)=⟨x(t),y(t),z(t)⟩$, the unit tangent vector $T(t)$ at the point $P(x(t),y(t),z(t))$ is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\frac{\pi }{6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({cos}^{2}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-4\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6}) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{6},\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{6},\,-4\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{6}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{6}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\,-\frac{1}{2},\,-4\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\,-\frac{1}{2},\,-\sqrt{3}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6}):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6})‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+(-\sqrt{3})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+\frac{1}{4}+3} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6})$ and obtain the unit tangent vector to the given curve at the point where $\frac{\pi }{6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\frac{\pi }{6}) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6})}{‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6})‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\text{ }⟨\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\,-\frac{1}{2},\,-\sqrt{3}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4},\,-\frac{1}{4},\,-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}(\frac{3}{{x}^{3}}+1)=\infty $ and ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}(\frac{2}{{x}^{2}})=\infty ,$ respectively, so we have the case $\frac{\infty }{\infty }.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{(\frac{3}{{x}^{3}}+1)}{(\frac{2}{{x}^{2}})} & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{{[\frac{3}{{x}^{3}}+1]}^{′}}{{[\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{(-\frac{9}{{x}^{4}})}{(-\frac{4}{{x}^{3}})} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{{x}^{-4}}{{x}^{-3}} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{1}{x} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\operatorname{csc}⁡(x)=\infty $ and ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\operatorname{cot}⁡(2x)=\infty ,$ respectively, so we have the indeterminate form $\frac{\infty }{\infty }.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\operatorname{csc}⁡(x)}{\operatorname{cot}⁡(2x)} & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{[\operatorname{csc}⁡(x)]^{′}}{[\operatorname{cot}⁡(2x)]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{-\operatorname{csc}⁡(x)\operatorname{cot}⁡(x)}{-2{csc}^{2}⁡(2x)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\operatorname{csc}⁡(x)\operatorname{cot}⁡(x)}{2{csc}^{2}⁡(2x)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{(\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)})(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)})}{2(\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x){sin}^{2}⁡(2x)}{2{sin}^{2}⁡(x)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x){(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x))}^{2}}{2{sin}^{2}⁡(x)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\cdot 4{sin}^{2}⁡(x){cos}^{2}⁡(x)}{2{sin}^{2}⁡(x)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{4{cos}^{3}⁡(x)\cancel{{sin}^{2}⁡(x)}}{2\cancel{{sin}^{2}⁡(x)}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}2{cos}^{3}⁡(x) \\  & =2{cos}^{3}⁡(0) \\  & =2\cdot 1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}{e}^{3/{x}^{2}}=\infty $ and ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})=\infty ,$ respectively, so we have the case $\frac{\infty }{\infty }.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{{e}^{3/{x}^{2}}}{(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})} & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{[{e}^{3/{x}^{2}}]^{′}}{{[\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{{e}^{3/{x}^{2}}(-\frac{6}{{x}^{3}})}{(-\frac{2}{{x}^{3}})} \\  & =3{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{{e}^{3/{x}^{2}}\cancel{(\frac{1}{{x}^{3}})}}{\cancel{(\frac{1}{{x}^{3}})}} \\  & =3{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}{e}^{3/{x}^{2}} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are  ${lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)=-\infty $ and  ${lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}\operatorname{sec}⁡x=\infty ,$ respectively, so we have the case $\frac{-\infty }{\infty }.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x} & ={lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{{[\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)]}^{′}}{{[\operatorname{sec}⁡x]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{-\operatorname{tan}⁡x}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{\cancel{-\operatorname{tan}⁡x}}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x\cancel{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}(-\frac{1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}) \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are ${lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}ln\,(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)=\infty $ and ${lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}ln\,(\operatorname{cot}⁡x)=-\infty ,$ respectively, so we have the case $\frac{\infty }{-\infty }.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{ln\,(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)}{ln\,(\operatorname{cot}⁡x)} & ={lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{{[ln\,(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)]}^{′}}{{[ln\,(\operatorname{cot}⁡x)]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{(\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x})}{(-\frac{{csc}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{cot}⁡x})} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{cot}⁡x}{{csc}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡x\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}}{\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}{sin}^{2}⁡x \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/1a/1a2cc9b62f3eeed4f2c9559c7f8cc5646872bc43b8076bea92bae50c3c6b29a9.png)

Find the amplitude of the steady-state current for the RL circuit shown above, rounded to two decimal places.

The amplitude of the steady-state current is approximately
{{field-1}} amperes.
:question/worked-solution:
The diagram shows a series RL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $12\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $8\,Ω,$ and an inductor of inductance $1\,\text{H}.$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RL circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=8\,Ω.$

$$
{V}_{R}=8I
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=1\,\text{H}.$

$$
{V}_{L}=1\cdot \frac{dI}{dt}=\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of current $I$ in the circuit is

$$
12\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)=8I+\frac{dI}{dt}
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}+8I=12\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${I}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{I}_{c}}{dt}+8{I}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-8t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $4t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $4t,$ i.e.,

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t), \\ \frac{d{I}_{p}}{dt} & =-4\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+4\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-4\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+4\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))+8(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) & =12\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ (-4\alpha +8\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+(8\alpha +4\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & =12\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-4\alpha +8\beta &=12\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) \\ 8\alpha +4\beta &=0\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{3}{5},$ $\beta =\frac{6}{5}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\frac{6}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)={I}_{c}(t)+{I}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-8t}-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\frac{6}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-8t}$ is the *transient current*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function ${I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\frac{6}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$ is the *steady-state current*. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
I(t)≈{I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\frac{6}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current is given by

$$
\sqrt{{(-\frac{3}{5})}^{2}+{(\frac{6}{5})}^{2}}≈1.34\,\text{A},
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

When we divide the two functions, we get a constant, and the limit of a constant is just the constant itself:

$$

$$

The expected value of a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S$ is given by

A function $I(x,y)$ is an integrating factor for the differential equation

$$
P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y=0,
$$

if the following equation is exact:

$$
I(x,y)[P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y]=0.
$$

In our case, we need to check if the following equation is exact:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{y}({x}^{2}\,\text{d}y-{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x) & =0 \\ -y\,\text{d}x+\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}\,\text{d}y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that a differential equation of the form

$$
P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y=0
$$

is exact if it passes the exactness test, i.e.,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}.
$$

For our transformed equation, we have  

$$
P(x,y)=-y,\,Q(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}.

$$

$$

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}\ne \frac{∂Q}{∂x},
$$

Consider the following game featuring an unfair six-sided die. The probability that the die shows an odd number is $\frac{2}{3},$ and the probability that the die shows an even number is $\frac{1}{3}.$ If the roll of a die gives an odd number, the player loses $$4.$ If the roll of a die gives an even number, the player wins $$11.$ What is the expected profit of each roll in this game?

$\text{E}[p]=$${{field-1}}
:question/worked-solution:
Let $p$ represent the profit on a single roll of the game. On each roll in the game, there are two possible outcomes:

- If rolling gives an odd number ($1$, $3,$ or $5$), the player loses $$4,$ so we have $p=-4.$

- If rolling gives an even number ($2$, $4,$ or $6$), the player wins $$11,$ so we have $p=11.$

The probabilities for the outcomes are

$$
P(-4)=\frac{2}{3},\,P(11)=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

Let's summarize this in a table.  If $p$ is the profit (in dollars) on a single game, and $f(p)$ is the probability mass function for $p,$ then we have the following:

| $f(p)$ | $\frac{2}{3}$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $p$ | $-4$ | $11$ |

Therefore, the expected value of $p$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}E[p] & =(-4)\cdot f(-4)+11\cdot f(11) \\  & =(-4)(\frac{2}{3})+11(\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =-\frac{8}{3}+\frac{11}{3} \\  & =\frac{-8+11}{3} \\  & =\frac{3}{3} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the expected profit is $$1.00.$
