\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{3{sin}^{2}⁡x}{2{x}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}(\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot {lim}_{x\to 0}{(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot {[{lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x}]}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot {1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that as $x\to 0,$ both numerator and denominator approach $0.$

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{{sin}^{5}⁡x}{4{x}^{4}}=\frac{0}{0},
$$

which is an indeterminate form.

Instead, let's recall the following special limit:

$$
{lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x}=1
$$

Rewriting the given limit using the algebra of limits and applying our special limit, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{{sin}^{5}⁡x}{4{x}^{4}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}(\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{{sin}^{4}⁡x}{{x}^{4}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot {lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{{sin}^{4}⁡x}{{x}^{4}}\cdot {lim}_{x\to 0}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot {lim}_{x\to 0}{(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x})}^{4}\cdot {lim}_{x\to 0}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot {[{lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x}]}^{4}\cdot {lim}_{x\to 0}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot {1}^{4}\cdot 0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Calculate $\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2})(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2})-\int (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2})(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{1}{2}I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}J \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{1}{2}I) \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{4}-\frac{1}{4}I \\ \frac{5}{4}I & =\frac{2{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{4} \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))}{5}+C\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}=-2x-y,\,y(0)=2
$$

We wish to approximate the solution using the Runge-Kutta (RK4) method. Complete the first row of the table below, given that the step size is $Δx=\frac{1}{2}.$

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{1}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{2}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{3}^{′}\,$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $2$ | $-2$ | $-2$ | $-2$ | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |
| $\,\frac{1}{2}$ | {{field-3}} |  |  |  |  |  |
:question/worked-solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c
$$

the increment in $y$ using the Runge-Kutta (RK4) method with step size $Δx$ is computed as the weighted average of four sample slopes:

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{6}({y}^{′}+2{y}_{1}^{′}+2{y}_{2}^{′}+{y}_{3}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

where

- ${y}^{′}=f(x,y)$ is the estimated slope at the initial point $(x,y),$

- ${y}_{1}^{′}=f({x}_{1},{y}_{1})$ is the estimated slope at $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{′}\cdot Δx),$

- ${y}_{2}^{′}=f({x}_{2},{y}_{2})$ is the estimated slope at $({x}_{2},{y}_{2})=(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}_{1}^{′}\cdot Δx),$

- ${y}_{3}^{′}=f({x}_{3},{y}_{3})$ is the estimated slope at $({x}_{3},{y}_{3})=(x+Δx,\,y+{y}_{2}^{′}\cdot Δx).$

The first three sample slopes, evaluated at the initial point and first intermediate points, are already computed. Now let's find the others.

- The third intermediate point is

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}_{3},{y}_{3}) & =(x+Δx,\,y+{y}_{2}^{′}\cdot Δx) \\  & =(0+\frac{1}{2},\,2+(-2)\cdot \frac{1}{2}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{2},1).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the third intermediate slope is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{3}^{′} & =-2{x}_{3}-{y}_{3} \\  & =-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}-1 \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

We can add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{1}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{2}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{3}^{′}\,$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $2$ | $-2$ | $-2$ | $-2$ | $-2$ |  |

Finally, we compute $Δy$ using the Runge-Kutta Method:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{6}({y}^{′}+2{y}_{1}^{′}+2{y}_{2}^{′}+{y}_{3}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(-2+2\cdot (-2)+2\cdot (-2)+(-2))\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\cdot (-12) \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the completed first row is as given below.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{1}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{2}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{3}^{′}\,$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $2$ | $-2$ | $-2$ | $-2$ | $-2$ | $-1$ |

To get the values of $x$ and $y$ in the *next* row, we add $Δx$ to $x$ and $Δy$ to $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx \\  & =0+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\  & =2+(-1) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Adding these rows to our table gives the following:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{1}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{2}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{3}^{′}\,$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $2$ | $-2$ | $-2$ | $-2$ | $-2$ | $-1$ |
| $\,\frac{1}{2}$ | $1$ |  |  |  |  |  |

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y\,(\frac{1}{2})≈1.\end{aligned}
$$

- The third intermediate point is

\begin{aligned}({x}_{3},{y}_{3}) & =(x+Δx,\,y+{y}_{2}^{′}\cdot Δx) \\  & =(0+1,\,1+\frac{15}{8}\cdot 1) \\  & =(1,\frac{23}{8}).\end{aligned}

So, the third intermediate slope is

Therefore, the completed first row is as given below.

To get the values of $x$ and $y$ in the *next* row, we add $Δx$ to $x$ and $Δy$ to $y,$ as follows:

Adding these rows to our table gives the following:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{1}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{2}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{3}^{′}\,$ | $Δy$ |

$$

$$

Given the curve $r(t)=8t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡6t\,j+\operatorname{sin}⁡6t\,k,$ $t\ge 0,$ for which the arc length $s$ from $r(0)$ to $r(t)$ is given by $s=10t,$ find the corresponding unit tangent $T(s),$ parametrized by $s.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, since $s=10t$, we have that $t=\frac{s}{10}.$

Therefore, the vector function $R(s)$ that parametrizes $r(t)$ by its arc length is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r(\frac{s}{10}) \\  & =8(\frac{s}{10})\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{6s}{10})j+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{6s}{10})k \\  & =\frac{4s}{5}\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3s}{5})j+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3s}{5})k.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, since the curve is parametrized by its arc length $s$, the unit tangent can be found as

$$
T(s)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}R(s).
$$

So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}T(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}R(s) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{4s}{5})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3s}{5}))j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3s}{5}))k \\  & =\frac{4}{5}\,i-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3s}{5})j+\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3s}{5})k.\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the constant out of the integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{5}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =5{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =5\cdot \text{arctan}\,x\,{|}_{1}^{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =5(\text{arctan}(\sqrt{3})-\text{arctan}(1)) \\  & =5(\frac{\pi }{3}-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =5(\frac{\pi }{12}) \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the constant out of the integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{3}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\cdot \operatorname{arcsin}⁡x\,{|}_{0}^{1/2} \\  & =3(arcsin\,(\frac{1}{2})-\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(0)) \\  & =3(\frac{\pi }{6}-0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}=x+2y,\,y(0)=1
$$

Use the trapezoidal method with two steps to approximate $y\,(\frac{1}{2})$ and $y(1),$ rounded to two decimal places.

$$
y\,(\frac{1}{2})≈{{field-1}},\,y(1)≈{{field-2}}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

First, note that we are given $y(0)$ and asked to find $y(1).$ The distance from $x=0$ to $x=1$ is $1,$ and since we are asked to use two steps of equal size, our step size must be

$$
Δx=\frac{1-0}{2}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, let's proceed with the trapezoidal method. In general, $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}((x+2y)+({x}_{\text{new}}+2{y}_{\text{new}}))\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(x+{x}_{\text{new}}+2y)+\frac{1}{2}{y}_{\text{new}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+\frac{1}{4}(x+{x}_{\text{new}}+2y)+\frac{1}{2}{y}_{\text{new}} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{1}{4}(x+{x}_{\text{new}}+6y)+\frac{1}{2}{y}_{\text{new}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we solve for the general formula for ${y}_{\text{new}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{1}{4}(x+{x}_{\text{new}}+6y) \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{1}{2}(x+{x}_{\text{new}}+6y)\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to calculate our approximations of $y\,(\frac{1}{2})$ and $y(1).$

**Step 1**.

From the initial conditions, we have

$$
x=0,\,y=1.
$$

Therefore, the new $x$ value is 

$$
{x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=0+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Hence, the new $y$ value is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{1}{2}(x+{x}_{\text{new}}+6y) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(0+\frac{1}{2}+6\cdot 1) \\  & =\frac{13}{4} \\  & =3.25.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**.

From the previous step, we have

$$
x=\frac{1}{2},\,y=3.25.
$$

Therefore, the new $x$ value is 

$$
{x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=1.
$$

Hence, the new $y$ value is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{1}{2}(x+{x}_{\text{new}}+6y) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{2}+1+6\cdot (3.25)) \\  & =10.50.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
y\,(\frac{1}{2})≈3.25,\,y(1)≈10.50.
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}=x-y,\,y(0)=2
$$

Use the trapezoidal method with two steps to approximate $y\,(\frac{1}{2})$ and $y(1),$ rounded to two decimal places.

$$
y\,(\frac{1}{2})≈{{field-1}},\,y(1)≈{{field-2}}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

First, note that we are given $y(0)$ and asked to find $y(1).$ The distance from $x=0$ to $x=1$ is $1,$ and since we are asked to use two steps of equal size, our step size must be

$$
Δx=\frac{1-0}{2}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, let's proceed with the trapezoidal method. In general, $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}((x-y)+({x}_{\text{new}}-{y}_{\text{new}}))\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(x+{x}_{\text{new}}-y)-\frac{1}{4}{y}_{\text{new}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+\frac{1}{4}(x+{x}_{\text{new}}-y)-\frac{1}{4}{y}_{\text{new}} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{1}{4}(x+{x}_{\text{new}}+3y)-\frac{1}{4}{y}_{\text{new}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we solve for the general formula for ${y}_{\text{new}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{4}{y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{1}{4}(x+{x}_{\text{new}}+3y) \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{1}{5}(x+{x}_{\text{new}}+3y)\end{aligned}

:question/problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$

$$
:question/worked-solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

First, note that we are given $y(1)$ and asked to find $y(2).$ The distance from $x=1$ to $x=2$ is $1,$ and since we are asked to use two steps of equal size, our step size must be

$$
Δx=\frac{2-1}{2}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, let's proceed with the trapezoidal method. In general, $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}((2x+5y)+(2{x}_{\text{new}}+5{y}_{\text{new}}))\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(2x+2{x}_{\text{new}}+5y)+\frac{5}{4}{y}_{\text{new}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+\frac{1}{4}(2x+2{x}_{\text{new}}+5y)+\frac{5}{4}{y}_{\text{new}} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{1}{4}(2x+2{x}_{\text{new}}+9y)+\frac{5}{4}{y}_{\text{new}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we solve for the general formula for ${y}_{\text{new}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{4}{y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{1}{4}(2x+2{x}_{\text{new}}+9y) \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =-(2x+2{x}_{\text{new}}+9y)\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to calculate our approximations of $y(\frac{3}{2})$ and $y(2).$

**Step 1**.

From the initial conditions, we have

$$
x=1,\,y=-2.
$$

Therefore, the new $x$ value is 

$$
{x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=1+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{2}.
$$

Hence, the new $y$ value is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =-(2x+2{x}_{\text{new}}+9y) \\  & =-(2\cdot 1+2\cdot \frac{3}{2}+9\cdot (-2)) \\  & =13.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**.

From the previous step, we have

$$
x=\frac{3}{2},\,y=13.
$$

Therefore, the new $x$ value is 

$$
{x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=2.
$$

Hence, the new $y$ value is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =-(2x+2{x}_{\text{new}}+9y) \\  & =-(2\cdot \frac{3}{2}+2\cdot 2+9\cdot 13) \\  & =-124.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
y(\frac{3}{2})≈13.00,\,y(2)≈-124.00.

Consider the following initial value problem:

$$

$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

First, since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=0,$ we will use a step size of

$$
Δx=0-(-\frac{1}{2})=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, let's proceed with the trapezoidal method. In general, $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(y(2{x}^{3}+3)+{y}_{\text{new}}(2({x}_{\text{new}})^{3}+3))\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}y(2{x}^{3}+3)+\frac{1}{4}{y}_{\text{new}}(2({x}_{\text{new}})^{3}+3).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+\frac{1}{4}y(2{x}^{3}+3)+\frac{1}{4}{y}_{\text{new}}(2({x}_{\text{new}})^{3}+3) \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{1}{4}y(2{x}^{3}+7)+\frac{1}{4}{y}_{\text{new}}(2({x}_{\text{new}})^{3}+3).\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}}-\frac{1}{4}{y}_{\text{new}}(2({x}_{\text{new}})^{3}+3) & =\frac{1}{4}y(2{x}^{3}+7) \\ \frac{1}{4}{y}_{\text{new}}(1-2({x}_{\text{new}})^{3}) & =\frac{1}{4}y(2{x}^{3}+7) \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{y(2{x}^{3}+7)}{1-2({x}_{\text{new}})^{3}}\end{aligned}

$$

Therefore, we conclude that $y(0)≈2.25.$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the following integral.

${\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x=$ {{field-1}}
:question/worked-solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-4x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+4x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))+\frac{1}{10}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(-1-0)+\frac{1}{10}(1-0) \\  & =-\frac{1}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the following integral.

${\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x=$ {{field-1}}

First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the second equation from the first, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-5x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+5x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-\frac{1}{14}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7x)]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))-\frac{1}{14}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(-1-0)-\frac{1}{14}(-1-0) \\  & =-\frac{2}{21}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the following integral.

${\int }_{0}^{3\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x=$ {{field-1}}
:question/worked-solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for sine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(7x+x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(7x-x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(8x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /4}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(8x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{16}\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x)-\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)]}_{0}^{3\pi /4} \\  & =-\frac{1}{16}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))-\frac{1}{12}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{9\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =-\frac{1}{16}(1-1)-\frac{1}{12}(0-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(8x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x-8x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x+8x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(-5x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(11x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(11x)).\end{aligned}

:question/problem:
The rate at which the price of a particular product changes $P(t),$ after $t$ years, is given by the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}P}{\text{d}t}=0.042P.
$$

If the price today is $$120,$ how many years will it take for the price to increase to $$750?$
Round your answer to the nearest year.
:question/worked-solution:
We model the price growth using the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}P}{\text{d}t}=0.042P.
$$

The solution to this equation is

$$
P(t)={P}_{0}\,{e}^{0.042t},
$$

where ${P}_{0}$ is the initial value.

We're told that the price today is $$120,$ so we have ${P}_{0}=120.$

Therefore, the price $P$ of the product after $t$ years is

$$
P(t)=120\,{e}^{0.042t}\,.
$$

To find how many years it takes for the price to grow to $$750,$ we substitute $P(t)=750$ into the equation above and solve for $t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}750 & =120\,{e}^{0.042t} \\ \frac{750}{120} & ={e}^{0.042t} \\ {e}^{0.042t} & =\frac{25}{4} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{0.042t}) & =ln\,(\frac{25}{4}) \\ 0.042t & =ln\,(\frac{25}{4}) \\ t & =\frac{1}{0.042}ln\,(\frac{25}{4}) \\ t & ≈43.633\end{aligned}
$$

Rounding to the nearest integer, we conclude that it takes $44$ years for the price to increase to $$750.$

Complete the arguments in the reasoning below to find the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{t/4}.$First, we apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
L{f(t)}=F(s)={{field-1}}
$$

We now examine the convergence of $F(s)$ for different values of $s:$

$\,$ For {{field-2}}
the integral is convergent.

$\,$ For {{field-3}}
the integral is divergent.

Evaluating our integral in the convergent case, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)t}\,\text{d}t={{field-4}}.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $L{{e}^{t/4}}=\frac{4}{4s-1},$ 
defined for
{{field-5}}.
:question/worked-solution:
For a function $f(t)$ defined on $[0,\infty ),$ the Laplace transform of $f,$ denoted $L{f(t)}$ or $F(s),$ is a function of the variable $s$ defined as

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

provided that this integral exists and is finite. 

For the function $f(t)={e}^{t/4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{t/4}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st+t/4}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(1/4-s)t}\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether $s\ne \frac{1}{4}$ or $s=\frac{1}{4}.$

- If $s\ne \frac{1}{4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(1/4-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{1/4-s}{e}^{(1/4-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{1/4-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-1/4}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-1/4}-\frac{1}{s-1/4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's evaluate the limit. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a}={\begin{aligned}0,\, & s>\frac{1}{4}, \\ \infty ,\, & s<\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $s=\frac{1}{4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(\frac{1}{4}) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(1/4-1/4)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{0t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }t\,{|}_{0}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(a-0) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }a \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- For $s>\frac{1}{4}$ the integral is convergent.

- For $s\le \frac{1}{4}$ the integral is divergent.

Evaluating for $s>\frac{1}{4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s-1/4}-\frac{1}{s-1/4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a} \\  & =\frac{1}{s-1/4}-\frac{1}{s-1/4}\cdot 0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s-1/4} \\  & =\frac{4}{4s-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{t/4}$ is $F(s)=\frac{4}{4s-1},$ defined for $s>\frac{1}{4}.$

:question/problem:
Suppose we wish to calculate the Laplace transform 

$$
L{t\operatorname{cos}⁡4t}.
$$

 
Select the correct options in the reasoning below. You may make use of the following result:

$$
L{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,s>0.
$$

Let $f(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡4t$ and $L{f(t)}=F(s).$ By the smoothness property of Laplace transforms,

$$
L{tf(t)}={{field-1}}.
$$

The Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}={{field-2}},\,s>0.
$$

We have that

$$
{F}^{′}(s)={{field-3}}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
L{t\operatorname{cos}⁡4t}={{field-4}},\,s>0.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
If a function $f(t)$ is piecewise continuous on $[0,\infty )$ and has exponential order $a,$ then its Laplace transform

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}
$$

exists for every real $s>a,$ and $F$ is infinitely differentiable in this region of convergence. Moreover, for each integer $n\ge 0$ and every such $s,$ we have

$$
L{{t}^{n}f(t)}=(-1)^{n}{F}^{(n)}(s).
$$

In particular, for $n=1,$ we have

$$
L{tf(t)}=-{F}^{′}(s).
$$

We have that $f(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡4t.$ Using the given result with $\omega =4,$ the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is 

$$
F(s)=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+16},\,s>0.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $s,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+16}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(s({s}^{2}+16)^{-1}) \\  & =({s}^{2}+16)^{-1}+s(-({s}^{2}+16)^{-2}\cdot 2s) \\  & =\frac{{s}^{2}+16}{({s}^{2}+16)^{2}}-\frac{2{s}^{2}}{({s}^{2}+16)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{16-{s}^{2}}{({s}^{2}+16)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the smoothness property,

$$
\begin{aligned}L{t\operatorname{cos}⁡4t}=-{F}^{′}(s)=\frac{{s}^{2}-16}{({s}^{2}+16)^{2}},\,s>0.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:

:question/worked-solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

First, recall that, by definition

$$
\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)=\frac{{e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t}}{2}.
$$

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)} & =L{\frac{{e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{2t}}{2}+\frac{{e}^{-2t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{2t}}{2}}+L{\frac{{e}^{-2t}}{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{2t}}+\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-2t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall that 

$$
L{{e}^{kt}}=\frac{1}{s-k},\,s>k.
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{2t}} & =\frac{1}{s-2},\,s>2 \\ L{{e}^{-2t}} & =\frac{1}{s+2},\,s>-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)} & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{2t}}+\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-2t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s-2}+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{s-2}+\frac{1}{s+2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{(s+2)+(s-2)}{(s-2)(s+2)}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{2s}{{s}^{2}-4}) \\  & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-4}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
(2,\infty )\cap (-2,\infty )=(2,\infty ),
$$

that is, $s>2.$

:question/problem:
Let $F(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)$ for $x\in R.$ Suppose $f(x)$ is the $\frac{\pi }{2}$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2})$ to $x\in R.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
:question/worked-solution:
Since $f$ is the $\pi /2$-periodic extension of $F,$ we have  

- $f(x+\frac{\pi }{2})=f(x)$ for all $x\in R,$ and

- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}).$

With that in mind, we examine each statement in turn.

- Statement “$f(x+\frac{\pi }{2})=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$” is true. This is exactly the definition of $\frac{\pi }{2}$-periodicity:

$$
f(x+\frac{\pi }{2})=f(x)
$$

for all $x\in R.$

- Statement “$f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in R$” is false. For example, take $x=\frac{3\pi }{4}.$ Using the periodicity of $f(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{3\pi }{4})=f(\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{\pi }{2})=f(\frac{\pi }{4})=F(\frac{\pi }{4})=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})=1,\end{aligned}
$$

while

$$
\begin{aligned}F(\frac{3\pi }{4})=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{3\pi }{4})=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x)\ne F(x)$ for $x=\frac{3\pi }{4}.$

- Statement “$f(x+\frac{\pi }{2})=f(x-\frac{\pi }{2})$ for all $x\in R$” is true. Since $f$ is $\frac{\pi }{2}$-periodic, any shift by a multiple of its period returns the same value:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x+\frac{\pi }{2})=f(x)\,\text{and}\,f(x-\frac{\pi }{2})=f((x-\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{\pi }{2})=f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Since both sides equal $f(x),$ the statement is true for all $x\in R.$

Therefore, the correct answer is “$f(x+\frac{\pi }{2})=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$”; “$f(x+\frac{\pi }{2})=f(x-\frac{\pi }{2})$ for all $x\in R$” only.

:question/problem:
Let $F(x)=cos\,(\frac{x}{2})$ for $x\in R.$ Suppose $f(x)$ is the $2\pi $-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x\in [0,2\pi )$ to $x\in R.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
:question/worked-solution:
Since $f$ is the $2\pi $-periodic extension of $F,$ we have  

- $f(x+2\pi )=f(x)$ for all $x\in R,$ and

- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in [0,2\pi ).$

With that in mind, we examine each statement in turn.

- Statement “$f(x+4\pi )=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$” is true. We have

$$
f(x+4\pi )=f((x+2\pi )+2\pi )=f(x+2\pi )=f(x)
$$

for all $x\in R.$

- Statement “$f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in R$” is false. For example, take $x=2\pi .$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2\pi ) & =f(0+2\pi )=f(0)=F(0)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=1,\end{aligned}
$$

while

$$
F(2\pi )=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )=-1.
$$

Hence, $f(x)\ne F(x)$ for $x=2\pi .$

- Statement “$f(x+2\pi )=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$” is true. This is exactly the definition of $2\pi $-periodicity: 

$$
f(x+2\pi )=f(x)
$$

for all $x\in R.$

Therefore, the correct answer is “$f(x+4\pi )=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$”; “$f(x+2\pi )=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$” only.

:question/problem:
Use the definition of Laplace transforms to calculate $F(s)=L{f(t)},$ where $f(t)=u(t-3)$ and $u$ is the unit step function.

$F(s)=L{f(t)}=$
{{field-1}},
valid for $s\,$
{{field-2}}{{field-3}}.
:question/worked-solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the unit step function is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t)={\begin{aligned}0,\, & t<0 \\ 1,\, & t\ge 0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, for the piecewise function 

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t-3)={\begin{aligned}0,\, & t<3 \\ 1,\, & t\ge 3\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }u(t-3){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}0\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{3}^{\infty }1\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{3}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this improper integral diverges if $s\le 0.$

For $s>0,$ we calculate this integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{3}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{3}^{a}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(-\frac{{e}^{-st}}{s})|}_{3}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{s}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }({e}^{-sa}-{e}^{-3s}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{s}(0-{e}^{-3s}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-3s}}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
L{f(t)}=\frac{{e}^{-3s}}{s},\,s>0.
$$

We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

So, for the piecewise function 

$$
f(t)={\begin{aligned}3,\, & t\le 5 \\ {e}^{3t}\, & t>5\end{aligned}
$$

we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{5}3\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{5}^{\infty }{e}^{3t}\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{5}3\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{5}^{\infty }{e}^{3t-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{5}3{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{5}^{\infty }{e}^{(3-s)t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the improper integral diverges if $s\le 3.$

For $s>3,$ we calculate our Laplace transform as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{5}3{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{5}^{\infty }{e}^{(3-s)t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{3}{s}{[{e}^{-st}]}_{0}^{5}+{\int }_{5}^{\infty }{e}^{(3-s)t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{3}{s}-\frac{3{e}^{-5s}}{s}+{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{5}^{a}{e}^{(3-s)t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{3}{s}-\frac{3{e}^{-5s}}{s}+{lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{{e}^{(3-s)t}}{3-s})|}_{5}^{a} \\  & =\frac{3}{s}-\frac{3{e}^{-5s}}{s}+\frac{1}{3-s}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }({e}^{(3-s)a}-{e}^{5(3-s)}) \\  & =\frac{3}{s}-\frac{3{e}^{-5s}}{s}+\frac{1}{3-s}\cdot (0-{e}^{5(3-s)}) \\  & =\frac{3}{s}-\frac{3{e}^{-5s}}{s}+\frac{{e}^{5(3-s)}}{s-3}\end{aligned}
$$

valid for $s>3.$

:question/worked-solution:
For the Fourier series of a $2L$-periodic function, the constant term is given by

$$
{a}_{0}=\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $L=1$ and $f(x)=6{x}^{2}+5x+1$ for $x\in [-1,1).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(6{x}^{2}+5x+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[2{x}^{3}+\frac{5}{2}{x}^{2}+x]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(2+\frac{5}{2}+1)-((-2)+\frac{5}{2}+(-1)) \\  & =\frac{11}{2}-(-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

The instantaneous rate of change when $x=0$ is given by the value of the derivative ${f}^{′}(x)$ at $x=0.$ 

First, we compute the derivative, using the fact that $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)={sec}^{2}⁡x$ and $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})=2x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡x-{x}^{2}) \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡x-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(0) & ={sec}^{2}⁡(0)-2\cdot 0 \\  & ={(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)})}^{2}-0 \\  & ={(\frac{1}{1})}^{2} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change is $1.$

:question/problem: Determine if the vector $u$ lies on the plane $Π:r=sb+tc,$ $t,s\in R$, where  $b=⟨1,7,-3⟩$, $c=⟨-8,10,-4⟩$, and  $u=⟨6,9,-4⟩.$ In the affirmative case, find the value of $s\cdot t$ from the decomposition $u=sb+tc.$
:question/worked-solution:
By definition, $u\in Π$ if there exist $t$ and $s$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}sb+tc & =u \\ s\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 7 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}-8 \\ 10 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 9 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}s-8t &=6 \\ 7s+10t &=9 \\ -3s-4t &=-4\end{aligned}\right.
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \begin{bmatrix}1 & -8 & 6 \\ 7 & 10 & 9 \\ -3 & -4 & -4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-7{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -8 & 6 \\ 0 & 66 & -33 \\ -3 & -4 & -4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -8 & 6 \\ 0 & 66 & -33 \\ 0 & -28 & 14\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{66}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -8 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & -28 & 14\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+28{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -8 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}s-8t &=6 \\ t &=-\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second equation, we get

$$
t=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}s-8t & =6 \\ s-8(-\frac{1}{2}) & =6 \\ s+4 & =6 \\ s & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we found a solution $s=2,\,t=-\frac{1}{2},$ we conclude that $u$ does indeed lie on the plane $Π.$ In fact, we have

$$
u=2b-\frac{1}{2}c.
$$

Finally, $s\cdot t=2\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})=-1.$

The definition of $\operatorname{cosh}⁡x$ is

$$
\operatorname{cosh}⁡x=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(\frac{1}{3}) & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{1/3}+{e}^{-1/3}).\end{aligned}
$$

The definition of $\operatorname{cosh}⁡x$ is

$$
\operatorname{cosh}⁡x=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(1/3)) & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1/3)}+{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1/3)}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1/3)}+{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{3}+3) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1+9}{3}) \\  & =\frac{10}{6} \\  & =\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope at a point, we use implicit differentiation to calculate the derivative of the curve, assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the ${x}^{2}{y}^{2}$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}2{y}^{3}+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-{x}^{3} & =2 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{y}^{3}+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-{x}^{3}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{y}^{3})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}{y}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2) \\ 6{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+[2x{y}^{2}+2{x}^{2}y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}]-3{x}^{2} & =0 \\ 6{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2x{y}^{2}+2{x}^{2}y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3{x}^{2} & =0 \\ (6{y}^{2}+2{x}^{2}y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}-2x{y}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{3{x}^{2}-2x{y}^{2}}{6{y}^{2}+2{x}^{2}y}\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of the tangent at the point $(1,1)$ is then given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(1,1)} \\  & ={(\frac{3{x}^{2}-2x{y}^{2}}{6{y}^{2}+2{x}^{2}y})|}_{(1,1)} \\  & =\frac{3(1)^{2}-2(1)(1)^{2}}{6(1)^{2}+2(1)^{2}(1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

First of all, we need to find the slope of the normal line at the point $(2,1).$ Remember that the slope of the normal line, ${m}^{′},$ is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line:

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the $xy$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+xy & =6{y}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+xy) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6{y}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xy) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6{y}^{2}) \\ 2x+(y+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}) & =12y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\ 2x+y+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =12y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-12y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x-y \\ (x-12y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x-y \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{-2x-y}{x-12y}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(2,1)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(2,\,1)} \\  & ={(\frac{-2x-y}{x-12y})|}_{(2,\,1)} \\  & =\frac{-2(2)-1}{2-12(1)} \\  & =\frac{(-5)}{(-10)} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{2})}=-2.
$$

We can write the equation of the normal at the point $(2,1)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & ={m}^{′}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-1 & =-2(x-2) \\ y-1 & =-2x+4 \\ y & =-2x+5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this normal line intersects the $y$-axis. At the point $P$ the $x$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $x=0$ and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-2x+5 \\ y & =-2(0)+5 \\ y & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(0,\,5).$

:question/problem:
Find the Laplace transform $Y(s)=L{y(t)}$ for $s>3$ if 

$$

$$

You may make use of the following result:

$$
L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡\omega t}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}},\,s>|\omega |.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the addition and scalar multiplication properties of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{′}+y} & =L{-8\operatorname{cosh}⁡3t} \\ L{{y}^{′}}+L{y} & =-8L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡3t}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate $L{{y}^{′}},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of a derivative and the initial condition $y(0)=1:$

$$
L{{y}^{′}}=sL{y}-y(0)=sY(s)-1
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms, we have the following result:

$$
L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡3t}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-9},\,s>3
$$

Therefore, we can solve for $Y(s):$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{′}}+L{y} & =-8L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡3t} \\ (sY(s)-1)+Y(s) & =-8(\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-9}) \\ sY(s)+Y(s) & =1-\frac{8s}{{s}^{2}-9} \\ (s+1)Y(s) & =\frac{{s}^{2}-8s-9}{{s}^{2}-9} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{{s}^{2}-8s-9}{({s}^{2}-9)(s+1)}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $s>3,$ we simplify as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Y(s) & =\frac{({s}^{2}-8s-9)}{({s}^{2}-9)(s+1)} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{(s-9)(s+1)}{({s}^{2}-9)(s+1)} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{s-9}{{s}^{2}-9}\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of the tangent to $f(x)$ for $x\in [-2,4]$ is $\frac{2}{3}$, hence, ${f}^{′}(1)=\frac{2}{3}.$

The formula for the derivative of the inverse function is 

$$
({f}^{-1})^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(x))}.
$$

Evaluating at $x=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(1) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(1))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{2}{3})} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(1,0).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{x-1}{{x}^{2}+1} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{(x-1)^{′}\cdot ({x}^{2}+1)-(x-1)\cdot {({x}^{2}+1)}^{′}}{{({x}^{2}+1)}^{2}} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1\cdot ({x}^{2}+1)-(x-1)\cdot 2x}{{({x}^{2}+1)}^{2}} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{x}^{2}+1-2{x}^{2}+2x}{{({x}^{2}+1)}^{2}} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1+2x-{x}^{2}}{{({x}^{2}+1)}^{2}} \\ {f}^{′}(1) & =\frac{1+2(1)-{1}^{2}}{{({1}^{2}+1)}^{2}} \\ {f}^{′}(1) & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(1,0)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(0,1)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(0) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(0))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(8,6).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}f(x) & =3\sqrt[3]{x} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =3\cdot \frac{1}{3}{x}^{-2/3} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}} \\ {f}^{′}(8) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{{8}^{2}}} \\ {f}^{′}(8) & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(8,6)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(6,8)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(6) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(6))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(8)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{4})} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Consider the function $f(x)=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{x}$ and the point $P(4,1)$ that lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $f(x)$ is invertible in the vicinity of $P,$ the slope of $y={f}^{-1}(x)$ at the point $(1,4)$ is$\,${{field-1}}.
:question/worked-solution:
We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(4,1).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{x} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{4\sqrt{x}} \\ {f}^{′}(4) & =\frac{1}{4\sqrt{4}} \\ {f}^{′}(4) & =\frac{1}{8}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(4,1)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(1,4)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(1) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(1))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(4)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{8})} \\  & =8.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(\frac{\pi }{4},1).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & ={sec}^{2}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & ={sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =2.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(\frac{\pi }{4},1)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(1,\frac{\pi }{4})$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(1) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(1))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Consider the function $f(x)=\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and the point $P(\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})$ that lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $f(x)$ is invertible in the vicinity of $P,$ the slope of $y={f}^{-1}(x)$ at the point $(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{\pi }{6})$ is$\,${{field-1}}.
:question/worked-solution:
We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}).$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6}) & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\ {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6}) & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6}) & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{\pi }{6})$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6})} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(e,1).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{x} \\ {f}^{′}(e) & =\frac{1}{e}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(e,1)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(1,e)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(1) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(1))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(e)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{e})} \\  & =e.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate $tanh\,(-\frac{3}{4}).$ **Do not round** your answer.

$tanh\,(-\frac{3}{4})=$

| {{field-1}} |
| --- |
| $1+{e}^{3/2}$ |
:question/worked-solution:
The definition of $\operatorname{tanh}⁡x$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tanh}⁡x & =\frac{{e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2x}-1}{{e}^{2x}+1} \\  & =\frac{1-{e}^{-2x}}{1+{e}^{-2x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the third definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}tanh\,(-\frac{3}{4}) & =\frac{1-{e}^{-2(-3/4)}}{1+{e}^{-2(-3/4)}} \\  & =\frac{1-{e}^{3/2}}{1+{e}^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

The definition of $\operatorname{sinh}⁡x$ is 

$$
\operatorname{sinh}⁡x=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡4) & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}-{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4-{4}^{-1}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4-\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{15}{4}) \\  & =\frac{15}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(r) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\,(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }\,(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot (-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{3}$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{3},$ and solve for $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot [-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})] \\ \frac{1}{3} & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot (-2) \\ \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the curve $r(s)$ parametrized by arc length $s.$ Find the curvature at the point where $s=5\pi $, if the unit tangent vector of the curve is given by

 

$$
T(s)=\frac{4}{5}\,i-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3s}{5})\,j+\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3s}{5})\,k.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
Since we are given that the curve $r(s)$ and its unit tangent vector $T(s)$ are parametrized by the arc length $s$, we will use the following formula for the curvature:

$$
κ(s)=‖{T}^{′}(s)‖
$$

Now, we differentiate $T(s)$ with respect to $s$ and evaluate it at $s=5\pi $: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{4}{5})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3s}{5}))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3s}{5}))\,k \\  & =(0)\,i-\frac{9}{25}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3s}{5})\,j-\frac{9}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3s}{5})\,k \\ {T}^{′}(5\pi ) & =-\frac{9}{25}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\cdot (5\pi )}{5})\,j-\frac{9}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\cdot (5\pi )}{5})\,k \\  & =-\frac{9}{25}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi )\,j-\frac{9}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi )\,k \\  & =-\frac{9}{25}\cdot (-1)\,j-\frac{9}{25}\cdot (0)\,k \\  & =\frac{9}{25}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we obtain the curvature:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(5\pi ) & =‖{T}^{′}(5\pi )‖ \\  & =\frac{9}{25}\sqrt{{(0)}^{2}+{(1)}^{2}+{(0)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{9}{25}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: The slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3{x}^{2}+12x}}$ at the point where $x=2$ is{{field-1}}.
:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=3{x}^{2}+12x.$ Then $y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}={u}^{-1/2}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=-\frac{1}{2}{u}^{-3/2}=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{u}^{3}}},
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6x+12.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{u}^{3}}}\cdot (6x+12) \\  & =-\frac{6x+12}{2\sqrt{(3{x}^{2}+12x{)}^{3}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=2} & ={(-\frac{6x+12}{2\sqrt{(3{x}^{2}+12x{)}^{3}}})|}_{x=2} \\  & =-\frac{6(2)+12}{2\sqrt{(3(2{)}^{2}+12(2){)}^{3}}} \\  & =-\frac{24}{2\sqrt{{36}^{3}}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}+2y={u}_{\pi /2}(t)\cdot cos\,(2t-\pi )\,,\,y(0)=-2,
$$

where ${u}_{\pi /2}(t)=u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2})$ is the unit step function.

You're given that the Laplace transform $Y(s)=L{y(t)}$ is

$$
Y(s)=-\frac{2}{s+2}+\frac{s\,{e}^{-\pi s/2}}{({s}^{2}+4)(s+2)}
$$

and that the solution to the initial value problem can be expressed as 

$$
y(t)=-2{e}^{-2t}-\frac{1}{4}u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2})\cdot g(t).
$$

Find the function $g(t).$ 

Hint: You may make use of the following results:

$$
L{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,L{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,s>0.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
To find the function $g(t),$ we need to compute the inverse Laplace transform of the term containing the time delay in $Y(s).$

We focus on the term with the exponential ${e}^{-\pi s/2}$ (which corresponds to the step function in the time domain) and identify the rational function part:

$$
F(s)=\frac{s}{({s}^{2}+4)(s+2)}.
$$

We'll solve this in three steps.

**Step 1.** Partial fraction decomposition

Since the denominator contains a linear factor $(s+2)$ and an irreducible quadratic factor $({s}^{2}+4),$ the decomposition takes the form

$$
\frac{s}{({s}^{2}+4)(s+2)}=\frac{A}{s+2}+\frac{Bs+C}{{s}^{2}+4}.
$$

To find the constants, we clear the denominators:

$$
s=A({s}^{2}+4)+(Bs+C)(s+2).
$$

Now, we find the constants $A,B,$ and $C.$

- Setting $s=-2,$ we have

$$
-2=A((-2)^{2}+4)+0\,⟹\,8A=-2\,⟹\,A=-\frac{1}{4}.
$$

- Comparing the coefficients of ${s}^{2},$ we have

$$
0=A+B\,⟹\,B=-A=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

- Comparing the constant terms, we have

$$
0=4A+2C\,⟹\,0=4\,(-\frac{1}{4})+2C\,⟹\,C=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Thus, we can rewrite $F(s)$ as

$$
F(s)=\frac{1}{4}(-\frac{1}{s+2}+\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4}+\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4}).
$$

**Step 2.** Finding the Inverse of the base function

We find the inverse transform $f(t)={L}^{-1}{F(s)}$ using standard transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =\frac{1}{4}(-{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+2}}+{L}^{-1}{\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4}}+{L}^{-1}{\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(-{e}^{-2t}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Applying the time-shifting property

Finally, we address the ${e}^{-\pi s/2}$ term. By the second shifting theorem, we have

$$
{e}^{-as}\cdot F(s)=L{u(t-a)\cdot f(t-a)}.
$$

Taking the inverse Laplace transform gives

$$
{L}^{-1}{{e}^{-as}F(s)}=u(t-a)\cdot f(t-a).
$$

In our case, $a=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Therefore, we shift $f(t)$ by replacing every instance of $t$ with $(t-\frac{\pi }{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2})f\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2})\cdot \frac{1}{4}[-{e}^{-2(t-\pi /2)}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2}))+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2}))].\end{aligned}
$$

Using the trigonometric identities $cos\,(2\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2}))=-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)$ and $sin\,(2\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2}))=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),$ we simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2})\cdot \frac{1}{4}(-{e}^{-2(t-\pi /2)}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\,u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2})({e}^{-2(t-\pi /2)}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)).\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing this to the second term of the form given in the problem statement $y(t)=-2{e}^{-2t}-\frac{1}{4}u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2})\cdot g(t),$ we identify $g(t)$ as

$$
g(t)={e}^{-2(t-\pi /2)}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

:question/problem:
Find the Laplace transform $Y(s)=L{y(t)}$ for $s>2$ if 

$$
{y}^{′}-2y=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y(0)=1.
$$

You may make use of the following result:

$$
L{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,s>0.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the addition and scalar multiplication properties of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{′}-2y} & =L{-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\ L{{y}^{′}}-2L{y} & =-5L{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate $L{{y}^{′}},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of a derivative and the initial condition $y(0)=1:$

$$
L{{y}^{′}}=sL{y}-y(0)=sY(s)-1
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms, we have the following result:

$$
L{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}=\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1},\,s>0
$$

Therefore, we can solve for $Y(s):$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{′}}-2L{y} & =-5L{\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\ (sY(s)-1)-2Y(s) & =-5(\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1}) \\ sY(s)-2Y(s) & =1-\frac{5}{{s}^{2}+1} \\ (s-2)Y(s) & =\frac{{s}^{2}-4}{{s}^{2}+1} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{{s}^{2}-4}{({s}^{2}+1)(s-2)}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $s>2,$ we simplify as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Y(s) & =\frac{(s-2)(s+2)}{({s}^{2}+1)(s-2)} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{s+2}{{s}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the first derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{6{x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}-8}{2x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{2}+x-4{x}^{-1}) \\  & =6x+1+(-1)(-4{x}^{-2}) \\  & =6x+1+4{x}^{-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6x+1+4{x}^{-2}) \\  & =6+0+(-2)(4{x}^{-3}) \\  & =6-\frac{8}{{x}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the following initial value problem.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+2y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(0)=0
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below to find the solution using Laplace transforms. You may make use of the following results:

$$
L{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,L{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,s>0.
$$

Let $Y(s)=L{y(t)}.$ Taking the Laplace transform of both sides of the equation and solving for $Y,$ we have

$$
Y(s)={{field-1}}.
$$

The partial fraction decomposition of $Y$ is

$$
Y(s)={{field-2}}.
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(t)={{field-3}}.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides of the differential equation. Using the linearity property, we have

$$
L{{y}^{′}}+2L{y}=L{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}+L{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}.
$$

Using the formula for the transform of a derivative $L{{y}^{′}}=sY(s)-y(0)$ and the standard trigonometric transforms

$$
L{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}=\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1},\,L{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+1},
$$

we substitute the known values. Note that $y(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(sY(s)-0)+2Y(s) & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1}+\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+1} \\ (s+2)Y(s) & =\frac{s+1}{{s}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

We rearrange to solve for $Y(s).$ Dividing by $(s+2),$ we obtain

$$
Y(s)=\frac{s+1}{(s+2)({s}^{2}+1)}.
$$

Next, we perform a partial fraction decomposition. Since the denominator has a linear factor $(s+2)$ and an irreducible quadratic factor $({s}^{2}+1),$ we write

$$
\frac{s+1}{(s+2)({s}^{2}+1)}=\frac{A}{s+2}+\frac{Bs+C}{{s}^{2}+1}.
$$

To find the constants, we clear the denominators:

$$
s+1=A({s}^{2}+1)+(Bs+C)(s+2)
$$

- Setting $s=-2,$ we have
 

$$
-2+1=A((-2)^{2}+1)+0\,⟹\,-1=5A\,⟹\,A=-\frac{1}{5}.
$$

- Comparing the coefficients of ${s}^{2},$ we have
  

$$
0=A+B\,⟹\,0=-\frac{1}{5}+B\,⟹\,B=\frac{1}{5}.
$$

- Comparing the constant terms, we have
 

$$
1=A+2C\,⟹\,1=-\frac{1}{5}+2C\,⟹\,C=\frac{3}{5}.
$$

Thus, the decomposition is

$$
Y(s)=\frac{(-\frac{1}{5})}{s+2}+\frac{(\frac{1}{5}s+\frac{3}{5})}{{s}^{2}+1}=-\frac{1}{5(s+2)}+\frac{s+3}{5({s}^{2}+1)}.
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+2}} & ={e}^{-2t} \\ {L}^{-1}{\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+1}} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ {L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1}} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking the inverse Laplace transform of $Y(s),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =-\frac{1}{5}{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+2}}+\frac{1}{5}{L}^{-1}{\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+1}}+\frac{3}{5}{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1}} \\ y(t) & =-\frac{1}{5}{e}^{-2t}+\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Using the formula for the transform of a derivative $L{{y}^{′}}=sY(s)-y(0)$ and the standard trigonometric transforms

we substitute the known values. Note that $y(0)=0:$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Let $Y(s)=L{y(t)}.$ Taking the Laplace transform of both sides of the equation and solving for $Y,$ we have

$$
Y(s)={{field-1}}.
$$

The partial fraction decomposition of $Y$ is

$$
Y(s)={{field-2}}.
$$

$$
y(t)={{field-3}}.
$$

First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides of the differential equation. Using the linearity property, we have

$$
L{{y}^{′}}+3L{y}=2L{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}-3L{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}.
$$

Using the formula for the transform of a derivative $L{{y}^{′}}=sY(s)-y(0)$ and the standard trigonometric transforms

$$
L{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}=\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4},\,L{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4},
$$

we substitute the known values. Note that $y(0)=-2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(sY(s)-(-2))+3Y(s) & =2(\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4})-3(\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4}) \\ (s+3)Y(s)+2 & =\frac{4-3s}{{s}^{2}+4}\end{aligned}
$$

We rearrange to solve for $Y(s).$ First, subtract $2$ from the right-hand side and find a common denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}(s+3)Y(s) & =\frac{4-3s}{{s}^{2}+4}-2 \\ (s+3)Y(s) & =\frac{4-3s}{{s}^{2}+4}-\frac{2({s}^{2}+4)}{{s}^{2}+4} \\ (s+3)Y(s) & =\frac{-2{s}^{2}-3s-4}{{s}^{2}+4}\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing by $(s+3),$ we obtain

$$
Y(s)=\frac{-2{s}^{2}-3s-4}{(s+3)({s}^{2}+4)}.
$$

Next, we perform a partial fraction decomposition. Since the denominator has a linear factor $(s+3)$ and an irreducible quadratic factor $({s}^{2}+4),$ we write

$$
\frac{-2{s}^{2}-3s-4}{(s+3)({s}^{2}+4)}=\frac{A}{s+3}+\frac{Bs+C}{{s}^{2}+4}.
$$

To find the constants, we clear the denominators:

$$
-2{s}^{2}-3s-4=A({s}^{2}+4)+(Bs+C)(s+3)
$$

- Setting $s=-3,$ we have
 

$$
-2(-3)^{2}-3(-3)-4=A((-3)^{2}+4)+0\,⟹\,-13=13A\,⟹\,A=-1.
$$

- Comparing the coefficients of ${s}^{2},$ we have
  

$$
-2=A+B\,⟹\,-2=-1+B\,⟹\,B=-1.
$$

- Comparing the constant terms, we have
 

$$
-4=4A+3C\,⟹\,-4=4(-1)+3C\,⟹\,C=0.
$$

Thus, the decomposition is

$$
Y(s)=-\frac{1}{s+3}+\frac{-s}{{s}^{2}+4}=-\frac{1}{s+3}-\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4}.
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms, we have:

$$

$$

$$

The area of a circle is given by

$$

where $r$ is the radius of the circle.

We know that $C=2\pi r,$ so we can express the area $A$ as a function of the circumference $C$ by substituting $r=\frac{C}{2\pi }$ into the formula above. We get

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}=\pi {(\frac{C}{2\pi })}^{2}=\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }.
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $A(C)$ with respect to $C$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(C) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}C}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\  & =\frac{1}{4\pi }\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}C}({C}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4\pi }(2C) \\  & =\frac{C}{2\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))(x)-(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))(1)}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-3x\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}

$$

A particle of mass $0.8\,\text{kg}$ is attached to a massless spring. An external periodic force $F(t)=2cos\,(\frac{5}{2}t)\,\text{N}$ is applied to the particle.

The position of the particle is $y(t)$ (measured in meters), and $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle moves with forced harmonic motion without damping and the system experiences resonance, what is the spring constant $k?$

$k=$
{{field-1}}${\text{kg/s}}^{2}$
:question/worked-solution:
The equation of motion for a particle of mass $m$ moving with forced harmonic motion without damping under the action of a spring with spring constant $k$ and external force $F(t)$ is given by

$$
m{y}^{″}=-ky+F(t).
$$

Substituting our values for $m$ and $F(t)$ gives

$$
0.8{y}^{″}=-ky+2cos\,(\frac{5}{2}t).
$$

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{5k}{4}y=\frac{5}{2}cos\,(\frac{5}{2}t).
$$

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration, and $\omega $ is the system's internal frequency.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=\frac{5k}{4}\,⟹\,k=\frac{4}{5}{\omega }^{2}.
$$

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency of the external periodic force $f(t)=\frac{5}{2}cos\,(\frac{5}{2}t),$ which is $\frac{5}{2},$ is equal to the frequency of the complementary solution $\omega .$

Therefore,

$$
k=\frac{4}{5}{\omega }^{2}=\frac{4}{5}\cdot {(\frac{5}{2})}^{2}=5\,{\text{kg/s}}^{2}.
$$

:question/problem:
Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{′}-2y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $6$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$

$$

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}∼{{field-1}} & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-3}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Now, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\  & ∼0+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\cdot (-\frac{n\pi }{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}))+{b}_{n}\cdot \frac{n\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & ∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{′}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\  & \,-2(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\  & \,\,=-2+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{4}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned} & -2\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}-2{a}_{n})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & \,\,+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}-2{b}_{n})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & \,\,\,\,=-2+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{4}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, equating the free terms and the coefficients next to sines and cosines, we obtain the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-2\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2} &=-2 \\ \frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}-2{a}_{n} &=\frac{4}{{n}^{2}\pi } \\ -\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}-2{b}_{n} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equation, ${a}_{0}=2,$ which means the constant term is given by

$$
\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=1.
$$

Next, from the third equation, ${b}_{n}=-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{6}.$ Substituting this into the third equation, gives

$$
(-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{6})\frac{n\pi }{3}-2{a}_{n}=\frac{4}{{n}^{2}\pi }\,⇒\,{a}_{n}=-\frac{72}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+36)}.
$$

Therefore, for ${a}_{n}$ with $n\ge 1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{6} \\  & =-\frac{n\pi }{6}\cdot (-\frac{72}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+36)}) \\  & =\frac{12}{n({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+36)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}∼1 & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,-\frac{72}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+36)}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{12}{n({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+36)}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
-4\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}(-\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{4}-4)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})=4+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).

Now, equating the free terms and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-4\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2} &=4 \\ {a}_{n}(-\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{4}-4) &=\frac{2(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{0}}{2} &=-1 \\ {a}_{n} &=\frac{8(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+16)}\end{aligned}\right.

Therefore, our particular solution is
