:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=f(x),$ where the $4$-periodic forcing function is given by 

$$
f(x)∼-2+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below regarding the resonant component of a particular solution of the equation.

The natural frequency of the system matches the frequency of the {{field-1}} harmonic of the forcing function. 

Consequently, the particular solution contains a resonant term of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}={{field-2}}.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}}=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $4$-periodic function $(L=2)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{2}.
$$

For $n=1$, we have ${\omega }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Since ${\omega }_{1}=\omega ,$ the $n=1$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=1$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{1}(x)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{1}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}))+x(-\frac{\pi }{2}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\frac{\pi }{2}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})) \\ {y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″} & =-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{1}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}):$

$$
[-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{1}}]+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{1}}=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-\pi A &=0 \\ \pi B &=6\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}A &=0 \\ B &=\frac{6}{\pi }\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=\frac{6x}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}).
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=f(x),$ where the $6$-periodic forcing function is given by 

$$
f(x)∼-3+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{5}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below regarding the resonant component of a particular solution of the equation.

The natural frequency of the system matches the frequency of the {{field-1}} harmonic of the forcing function. 

Consequently, the particular solution contains a resonant term of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}={{field-2}}.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}}=\frac{2\pi }{3}.
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $6$-periodic function $(L=3)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{3}.
$$

For $n=2$, we have ${\omega }_{2}=\frac{2\pi }{3}.$ Since ${\omega }_{2}=\omega ,$ the $n=2$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=2$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{2}(x)=\frac{5}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{y}_{{p}_{2}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}))+x(-\frac{2\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+\frac{2\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})) \\ \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{y}_{{p}_{2}}^{″} & =-\frac{4\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+\frac{4\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})-\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{2}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{2}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=\frac{5}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}):$

$$
[-\frac{4\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+\frac{4\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})-\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}{y}_{{p}_{2}}]+\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}{y}_{{p}_{2}}=\frac{5}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-\frac{4\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+\frac{4\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})=\frac{5}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{4\pi }{3}A &=\frac{5}{4} \\ \frac{4\pi }{3}B &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}A &=-\frac{15}{16\pi } \\ B &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}=-\frac{15x}{16\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}).
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation ${y}^{″}+{\pi }^{2}y=f(x),$ where the $4$-periodic forcing function is given by 

$$
f(x)∼2+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{4}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below regarding the resonant component of a particular solution of the equation.

The natural frequency of the system matches the frequency of the {{field-1}} harmonic of the forcing function. 

Consequently, the particular solution contains a resonant term of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}={{field-2}}.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+{\pi }^{2}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{{\pi }^{2}}=\pi .
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $4$-periodic function $(L=2)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{2}.
$$

For $n=2$, we have ${\omega }_{2}=\pi .$ Since ${\omega }_{2}=\omega ,$ the $n=2$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=2$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{2}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x))+x(-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)) \\ {y}_{{p}_{2}}^{″} & =-2\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+2\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)-{\pi }^{2}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{2}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{2}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+{\pi }^{2}y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x):$

$$
[-2\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+2\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)-{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{2}}]+{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{2}}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-2\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+2\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-2\pi A &=1 \\ 2\pi B &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}A &=-\frac{1}{2\pi } \\ B &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}=-\frac{x}{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x).
$$

Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{16}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{25} & =1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{16}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{25}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{16})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{25}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{16})+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{25}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (\frac{2x}{16})+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (\frac{2y}{25}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, substituting the given information $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=3$ and $y=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (\frac{2x}{16})+3\cdot (\frac{2(3)}{25}) & =0 \\ \frac{x}{8}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{18}{25} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We also want to substitute for $x,$ but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $y=3$ into the equation of the ellipse.  

At the point where $y=3,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{16}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{25} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{16}+\frac{{3}^{2}}{25} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{16}+\frac{9}{25} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{16} & =\frac{16}{25} \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{256}{25} \\ x & =\frac{16}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used $x>0$ since we're only interested in the first quadrant. 

Finally, substituting $x=\frac{16}{5},$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{8}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{18}{25} & =0 \\ \frac{1}{8}(\frac{16}{5})\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{18}{25} & =0 \\ \frac{2}{5}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{18}{25} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{18}{25}\cdot \frac{5}{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{9}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

In **ascending order**, the $x$-coordinates of the points of inflection for $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)+x$ on the interval $(0,\frac{\pi }{2})$ are

:question/worked-solution:
For continuous, twice-differentiable functions, we can determine possible points of inflection by solving the equation ${f}^{″}(x)=0.$ However, we must be sure to check that the concavity does indeed change at whatever points we find.

First, we calculate the second derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)+1 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-16\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we solve ${f}^{″}(x)=0$ on the interval $(0,\frac{\pi }{2}):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}-16\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x) & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4x) & =0 \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{8},\,\frac{3\pi }{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we need to check if the concavity changes at $x=\frac{\pi }{8}$ and $x=\frac{3\pi }{8}.$ So, we pick points around them, say $x=\frac{\pi }{16},$ $x=\frac{\pi }{4},$ and $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ and compute the sign of ${f}^{″}(x):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{16}) & =-16\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=-16\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})<0 \\ {f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =-16\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )=-16\cdot (-1)>0 \\ {f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-16\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )=-16\cdot (1)<0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, since the concavity changes at $x=\frac{\pi }{8}$ and $x=\frac{3\pi }{8},$ we conclude that, in ascending order, 

$$
x=\frac{\pi }{8}\,\text{and}\,x=\frac{3\pi }{8}
$$

 are indeed points of inflection.

For continuous, twice-differentiable functions, we can determine possible points of inflection by solving the equation ${f}^{″}(x)=0.$ However, we must be sure to check that the concavity does indeed change at whatever points we find. 

First, notice that $f(x)$ is not defined at $x=2,$ so this can't be a point of inflection.

Now, we calculate the second derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =2x+3-\frac{1}{(x-2)^{2}} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =2+\frac{2}{(x-2)^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we solve ${f}^{″}(x)=0,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}2+\frac{2}{(x-2)^{3}} & =0 \\ (x-2)^{3} & =-1 \\ x & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we need to check that the concavity changes at $x=1.$ So, we pick two points around it, say, $x=0$ and $x=\frac{3}{2}$, and compute the sign of ${f}^{″}(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0) & =2+\frac{2}{(0-2)^{3}}=\frac{7}{4}>0 \\ {f}^{″}(\frac{3}{2}) & =2+\frac{2}{{(\frac{3}{2}-2)}^{3}}=-14<0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since the concavity changes at $x=1,$ we conclude that $x=1$ is indeed a point of inflection.

For continuous, twice-differentiable functions, we can determine possible points of inflection by solving the equation ${f}^{″}(x)=0.$ However, we must be sure to check that the concavity does indeed change at whatever points we find. 

First, notice that $f(x)$ is not defined at $x=0,$ so this can't be a point of inflection.

Now, we calculate the second derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =54x+5-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =54+\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we solve ${f}^{″}(x)=0,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}54+\frac{2}{{x}^{3}} & =0 \\ {x}^{3} & =-\frac{1}{27} \\ x & =-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we need to check that the concavity changes at $x=-\frac{1}{3}.$ So, we pick two points around it, say, $x=-1$ and $x=-\frac{1}{6}$, and compute the sign of ${f}^{″}(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(-1) & =54+\frac{2}{(-1)^{3}}=52>0 \\ {f}^{″}(-\frac{1}{6}) & =54+\frac{2}{{(-\frac{1}{6})}^{3}}=-378<0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since the concavity changes at $x=-\frac{1}{3},$ we conclude that $x=-\frac{1}{3}$ is indeed a point of inflection.

$$

:question/problem: The global minimum value of the function $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ on the closed interval $0\le x\le 2\pi $ is{{field-1}}.
:question/worked-solution:
Let's apply the candidates test step by step.

**Step 1**: We find the critical points. Taking the derivative of $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\end{aligned}
$$

and solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =0 \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi \end{aligned}
$$

where $n$ is an integer. We discard all solutions except $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $\frac{3\pi }{2},$ since they are the only values that belongs to the given interval.

So, the critical points are $x=\frac{\pi }{2},\,\frac{3\pi }{2}$ and the endpoints $x=0,2\pi $ (since the derivative is not defined at the endpoints).

**Step 2**: We evaluate $f(x)$ at the critical points.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)=0 \\ f\,(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =sin\,(\frac{\pi }{2})=1 \\ f\,(\frac{3\pi }{2}) & =sin\,(\frac{3\pi }{2})=-1 \\ f(2\pi ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )=0\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: We compare all of the values found in step $2.$

- The greatest value is $f\,(\frac{\pi }{2})=1,$ so the global maximum is $1.$

- The least value is $f\,(\frac{3\pi }{2})=-1,$ so the global minimum is $-1.$

:question/problem: The exact global maximum value of the function $f(x)=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)$ on the closed interval $0\le x\le \pi $ is{{field-1}}.
:question/worked-solution:
Let's apply the candidates test step by step.

**Step 1**: We find the critical points. Taking the derivative of $f(x)=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\end{aligned}
$$

and solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) & =0 \\ 2x & =\pi n \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{2}n,\end{aligned}
$$

where $n$ is an integer. We discard all solutions except $x=0,$ $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ and $x=\pi ,$ since they are the only values that belong to the given interval.

So, the critical points are $x=0,\,\frac{\pi }{2},\,\pi ,$ and the endpoints $x=0,\,\pi $ (since the derivative is not defined at the endpoints).

**Step 2**: We evaluate $f(x)$ at the critical points.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0) & =1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=0 \\ f\,(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )=1-(-1)=2 \\ f(\pi ) & =1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )=0\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: We compare all of the values found in step $2.$

- The greatest value is $f\,(\frac{\pi }{2})=2,$ so the global maximum is $2.$

- The least value is $f(0)=0,$ so the global minimum is $0.$

First, let's compute the *squared* distance $S(x)$ between the two points. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x) & ={((4x)-5)}^{2}+{((-x)-(-1))}^{2} \\  & =(4x-5)^{2}+(-x+1)^{2} \\  & =(16{x}^{2}-40x+25)+({x}^{2}-2x+1) \\  & =17{x}^{2}-42x+26.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want to minimize $S,$ we compute the derivative ${S}^{′}(x).$ This gives

$$
{S}^{′}(x)=34x-42.
$$

The stationary points of $S(x)$ are the points where the derivative ${S}^{′}(x)=0.$ Solving this equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ 34x-42 & =0 \\ x & =\frac{21}{17}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}\,(\frac{21}{17})=34>0.$

So, the squared distance (and therefore the actual distance) reaches a minimum when $x=\frac{21}{17}.$ 

Since $S(x)$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=\frac{21}{17}$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S\,(\frac{21}{17})}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S\,(\frac{21}{17})} \\  & =\sqrt{17{(\frac{21}{17})}^{2}-42(\frac{21}{17})+26} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{441}{17}-\frac{882}{17}+26} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{17}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{17}}{17}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the smallest possible distance between the points $(4x,\,-x)$ and $(5,\,-1)$ is $\frac{\sqrt{17}}{17}.$

$$

$$

Consider the differential equation and the set of fundamental solutions of the corresponding homogeneous equation above. 
Using the method of variation of parameters, the particular solution of the equation can be written in the form

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={u}_{1}(x){e}^{-4x}+{u}_{2}(x){e}^{x}+{u}_{3}(x){e}^{2x}.
$$

What is the function ${u}_{3}(x)?$
:question/worked-solution:
According to the method of variation of parameters, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}={u}_{1}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2}+{u}_{3}{y}_{3},\,{u}_{i}=(-1)^{3-i}\int \frac{g(x){W}_{i}(x)}{W(x)}\,\text{d}x,\,i=1,2,3,
$$

where $g(x)$ is the forcing term, $W(x)$ is the Wronskian of ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},{y}_{3},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}_{1}(x)=|\begin{aligned}{y}_{2} & {y}_{3} \\ {y}_{2}^{′} & {y}_{3}^{′}\end{aligned}|,\,{W}_{2}(x)=|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{3} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{3}^{′}\end{aligned}|,\,{W}_{3}(x)=|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, the forcing term is $g(x)=\frac{6{e}^{3x}}{1+{e}^{2x}}.$ Additionally, we're given the fundamental solutions

$$
{y}_{1}={e}^{-4x},\,{y}_{2}={e}^{x},\,{y}_{3}={e}^{2x}.
$$

First, let's verify that the fundamental solutions ${y}_{1},$ ${y}_{2},$ and ${y}_{3}$ are independent by computing the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W(x) & =W({y}_{1},{y}_{2},{y}_{3}) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{-4x} & {e}^{x} & {e}^{2x} \\ -4{e}^{-4x} & {e}^{x} & 2{e}^{2x} \\ 16{e}^{-4x} & {e}^{x} & 4{e}^{2x}\end{aligned}| \\  & =({e}^{-4x}\cdot {e}^{x}\cdot {e}^{2x})|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ -4 & 1 & 2 \\ 16 & 1 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{-x}[1(4-2)-1(-16-32)+1(-4-16)] \\  & ={e}^{-x}(2-(-48)+(-20)) \\  & =30{e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions ${y}_{1},$ ${y}_{2},$ and ${y}_{3}$ are linearly independent. 

Now, to find ${u}_{3},$ we compute the determinant

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}_{3}(x) & ={W}_{3}({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{-4x} & {e}^{x} \\ -4{e}^{-4x} & {e}^{x}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{-3x}-(-4{e}^{-3x}) \\  & =5{e}^{-3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{3}(x) & =(-1)^{3-3}\int \frac{g(x){W}_{3}(x)}{W(x)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{(\frac{6{e}^{3x}}{1+{e}^{2x}})(5{e}^{-3x})}{30{e}^{-x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{1+{({e}^{x})}^{2}}\cdot {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡({e}^{x}).\end{aligned}
$$

Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(3,3)$ and a general point $P(x,y)$:

$$
S=(x-3)^{2}+(y-3)^{2}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{|x-1|}+3.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x) & =(x-3)^{2}+(y-3)^{2} \\  & =(x-3)^{2}+(\sqrt{|x-1|}+3-3)^{2} \\  & =(x-3)^{2}+(\sqrt{|x-1|})^{2} \\  & =(x-3)^{2}+|x-1|.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x\ge 1,$ we have $|x-1|=x-1,$ so

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x) & =(x-3)^{2}+(x-1) \\  & ={x}^{2}-6x+9+x-1 \\  & ={x}^{2}-5x+8.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=2x-5 & =0 \\ 2x & =5 \\ x & =\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(x)=2>0,$ so $x=\frac{5}{2}$ gives a minimum of $S.$

Since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=\frac{5}{2}$ is given by

$$

$$

$$

In **ascending order**, the critical points of the function  $f(x)=\frac{x+1}{{x}^{2}+8}$ are

$x=$
{{field-1}}

:question/worked-solution:
A critical point of $f(x)$ is a point $x=c$ in the domain of $f$ such that either ${f}^{′}(c)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(c)$ does not exist.

Differentiating $f(x),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{d}{dx}\,(\frac{x+1}{{x}^{2}+8}) \\  & =\frac{(x+1)^{′}\cdot ({x}^{2}+8)-(x+1)\cdot ({x}^{2}+8)^{′}}{({x}^{2}+8)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(1)\cdot ({x}^{2}+8)-(x+1)\cdot (2x)}{({x}^{2}+8)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}+8-(2{x}^{2}+2x)}{({x}^{2}+8)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-{x}^{2}-2x+8}{({x}^{2}+8)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

- First, we compute the points where ${f}^{′}(c)=0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{-{x}^{2}-2x+8}{({x}^{2}+8)^{2}} & =0 \\ -{x}^{2}-2x+8 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+2x-8 & =0 \\ (x+4)(x-2) & =0 \\ x & =-4,\,2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has stationary points at $x=-4$ and $x=2.$

- Second, we note that ${f}^{′}(x)$ exists for all values of $x$ in the domain of $f(x).$ So, $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, in ascending order, the critical points of $f(x)$ are 

$$
x=-4\,\text{and}\,x=2.
$$

$$

The function $f(x)$ is continuous on $[4,9]$ and differentiable on $(4,9),$ hence we can apply the mean value theorem.

$$

Plugging in $a=4$ and $b=9$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(c) & =\frac{f(9)-f(4)}{9-4} \\  & =\frac{(5\sqrt{9}-2)-(5\sqrt{4}-2)}{5} \\  & =\frac{13-8}{5} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}

The charge $q(t)$ on the capacitor, in coulombs, in a series RCL circuit at time $t$ seconds is

$$

The amplitude of the steady-state current is
{{field-1}}
amperes.
:question/worked-solution:
The current $I$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Differentiating the given expression for $q(t),$ we obtain the following expression for $I,$ in amperes:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & =\frac{d}{dt}({e}^{-2t}-3{e}^{-5t}+\frac{3}{10}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\frac{4}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) \\  & =-2{e}^{-2t}+15{e}^{-5t}-\frac{6}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\frac{8}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t).\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${I}_{c}(t)=-2{e}^{-2t}+15{e}^{-5t}$ is the *transient current*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function ${I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{6}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\frac{8}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)$ is the *steady-state current*. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
I(t)≈{I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{6}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\frac{8}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current, in amperes, is given by

$$
\sqrt{{(-\frac{6}{5})}^{2}+{(\frac{8}{5})}^{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{36+64}{25}}=2.
$$

:question/problem:
A series RCL circuit has a source electromotive force (EMF) of $8\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\,\text{V},$ a resistance of $24\,Ω,$ a capacitance of $0.05\,\text{F},$ and an inductance of $L=4\,\text{H}.$ Find the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ (in coulombs) on the capacitor at time $t$ (in seconds).

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
:question/worked-solution:
We have the following circuit diagram.

![](images/64/6494f1905ab90cb3d5655aaa824726255dc7332841ec656dc88c2180b0f93a1c.png)

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=24\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=24I=24\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.05}=20q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=4\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=4\,\frac{dI}{dt}=4\,\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dq}{dt})=4\,\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
8\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)=24\,\frac{dq}{dt}+20q+4\,\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}},
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}+6\,\frac{dq}{dt}+5q=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t).
$$

:question/problem:
A series RCL circuit has a source electromotive force (EMF) of $15\,\text{V},$ a resistance of $30\,Ω,$ a capacitance of $\frac{1}{10}\,\text{F},$ and an inductance of $L=6\,\text{H}.$ Find the steady-state charge for this circuit.

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*

The steady-state charge is
{{field-1}}
coulombs.
:question/worked-solution:
The diagram for our circuit is shown below.

![](images/d7/d7145f4b394e7675b87ed851e344756ecb8441ce737f8664fbfd4b0e426ef36f.png)

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops. In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=30\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=30I=30\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{(1/10)}=10q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=6\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=6\,\frac{dI}{dt}=6\,\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dq}{dt})=6\,\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
6\,\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}+30\,\frac{dq}{dt}+10q=15.
$$

The *steady-state charge* is the value that the charge $q(t)$ approaches as $t\to \infty .$ In a stable RCL circuit with a constant electromotive force, the transient response eventually decays to zero, leaving a constant charge.

When the system reaches steady state, the charge $q$ is constant. Consequently, the first and second derivatives of the charge with respect to time are zero:

$$
\frac{dq}{dt}=0\,\text{and}\,\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}=0.
$$

Substituting these steady-state conditions into the differential equation gives

$$
6(0)+30(0)+10q=15,
$$

which simplifies to

$$
10q=15\,⟹\,q=\frac{15}{10}=\frac{3}{2}.
$$

Physically, this represents the state where the capacitor is fully charged and the current has ceased to flow.

Therefore, the steady-state charge is $\frac{3}{2}$ coulombs.

![](images/7c/7cbcdf7d43a99b9558b1d085d2306c22e1d27134a5b0ea428721ce7bd074b725.png)

Consider the RCL circuit shown above. Given that the charge $q(t)$ of the capacitor at time $t$ seconds is given by

$$
q(t)=A{e}^{-t}+B{e}^{-4t}+\frac{P}{17}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\frac{Q}{17}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)
$$

where $A,$ $B,$ $P,$ and $Q$ are constants, find the value of $P+Q.$

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
:question/worked-solution:
The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $5\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.25\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $1\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=5\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=5I=5\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.25}=4q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=1\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=1\,\frac{dI}{dt}=\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dq}{dt})=\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)=5\,\frac{dq}{dt}+4q+\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}},
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}+5\cdot \frac{dq}{dt}+4q=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}{q}_{c}}{d{t}^{2}}+5\cdot \frac{d{q}_{c}}{dt}+4{q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+B{e}^{-4t},
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a sinusoidal with argument $t,$ i.e.,

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t), \\ \frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt} & =-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(t), \\ \frac{{d}^{2}{q}_{p}}{d{t}^{2}} & =-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t))+5(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(t))\,\,\, &  \\ +4(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t)) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ (3\alpha +5\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+(-5\alpha +3\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3\alpha +5\beta &=0\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)) \\ -5\alpha +3\beta &=2\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{5}{17},$ $\beta =\frac{3}{17}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=-\frac{5}{17}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\frac{3}{17}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t)={q}_{c}(t)+{q}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+B{e}^{-4t}-\frac{5}{17}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\frac{3}{17}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).
$$

Therefore, we have $P=-5,$ $Q=3,$ and

$$
P+Q=-5+3=-2.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.1}=10q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=5\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=5\,\frac{dI}{dt}=5\,\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dq}{dt})=5\,\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
10\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-5\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)=15\,\frac{dq}{dt}+10q+5\,\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}},
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}+3\cdot \frac{dq}{dt}+2q=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}{q}_{c}}{d{t}^{2}}+3\cdot \frac{d{q}_{c}}{dt}+2{q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+B{e}^{-2t},
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a sinusoidal with argument $t,$ i.e.,

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t), \\ \frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt} & =-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(t), \\ \frac{{d}^{2}{q}_{p}}{d{t}^{2}} & =-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t))+3(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(t))\, &  \\ +2(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t)) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ (-3\alpha +\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+(\alpha +3\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-3\alpha +\beta &=2\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)) \\ \alpha +3\beta &=-1\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{7}{10},$ $\beta =-\frac{1}{10}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=-\frac{7}{10}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t)={q}_{c}(t)+{q}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+B{e}^{-2t}-\frac{7}{10}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+B{e}^{-2t}$ is the *transient charge*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function ${q}_{p}(t)=-\frac{7}{10}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)$ is the *steady-state charge*. It governs the charge's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
q(t)≈{q}_{p}(t)=-\frac{7}{10}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state charge, in coulombs, is given by

$$
\sqrt{{(-\frac{7}{10})}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{10})}^{2}}≈0.71,
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

![](images/42/42ab81638355355340008eaa54657a0144612ec9d04e44266350cdb8012051de.png)

Find, in coulombs, the amplitude of the steady state charge for the RCL circuit shown above, rounded to two decimal places.

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
:question/worked-solution:
The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $(8\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-41\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $30\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.05\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $5\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=30\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=30I=30\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.05}=20q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=5\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=5\,\frac{dI}{dt}=5\,\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dq}{dt})=5\,\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
8\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-41\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)=30\,\frac{dq}{dt}+20q+5\,\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}},
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}+6\cdot \frac{dq}{dt}+4q=\frac{8}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{41}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}{q}_{c}}{d{t}^{2}}+6\cdot \frac{d{q}_{c}}{dt}+4{q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{(-3+\sqrt{5})t}+B{e}^{(-3-\sqrt{5})t},
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $3t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a sinusoidal with argument $3t,$ i.e.,

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t), \\ \frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt} & =-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t), \\ \frac{{d}^{2}{q}_{p}}{d{t}^{2}} & =-9\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-9\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,(-9\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-9\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))+6(-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))\, &  \\ +4(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =\frac{8}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{41}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ (-5\alpha +18\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+(-18\alpha -5\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & =\frac{8}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{41}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-5\alpha +18\beta &=\frac{8}{5}\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)) \\ -18\alpha -5\beta &=-\frac{41}{5}\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =\frac{2}{5},$ $\beta =\frac{1}{5}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t)={q}_{c}(t)+{q}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{(-3+\sqrt{5})t}+B{e}^{(-3-\sqrt{5})t}+\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{(-3+\sqrt{5})t}+B{e}^{(-3-\sqrt{5})t}$ is the *transient charge*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function ${q}_{p}(t)=\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$ is the *steady-state charge*. It governs the charge's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
q(t)≈{q}_{p}(t)=\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state charge, in coulombs, is given by

$$
\sqrt{{(\frac{2}{5})}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{5})}^{2}}≈0.45,
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

where $F(t)$ is the force, $m$ is the mass, and $a(t)$ is the acceleration.

To find the acceleration $a(t),$ we differentiate the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2t}{t+1}) \\  & =\frac{(t+1)\cdot (2t)^{′}-2t\cdot (t+1)^{′}}{(t+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2(t+1)-2t(1)}{(t+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(2t+2)-2t}{(t+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{(t+1)^{2}}\end{aligned}

:question/problem:
A body of mass $\sqrt{2}\,\text{kg}$ is moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis under the action of a single force $F,$ measured in Newtons $(\text{N}).$  At time $t$ seconds, the velocity of the body is given by $v(t)=\operatorname{sec}⁡t$ meters per second. 

Calculate the magnitude of the force at time $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ seconds. Do not round the answer.

The magnitude of the force equals
{{field-1}} $\text{N}.$
:question/worked-solution:
According to Newton’s second law,

$$
F(t)=ma(t),
$$

where $F(t)$ is the force, $m$ is the mass, and $a(t)$ is the acceleration.

To find the acceleration $a(t),$ we differentiate the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sec}⁡t) \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, the acceleration at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}\,\text{s}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}a(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the force, in Newtons, is

$$
\begin{aligned}F(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =ma(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the magnitude of the force is

$$
|F(\frac{\pi }{4})|=|2|=2\,\text{N}.
$$

A region is bounded by the curve $y={x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}+3$ and the $x$-axis between $x=-1$ and $x=1$, as shown above. Find the area $A$ of the region. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
:question/worked-solution:
To find the area, we just need to compute the corresponding definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}({x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}+3)\,\text{d}x \\  & =(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}-2\cdot \frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+3x){|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{2}{3}+3)-(\frac{1}{4}+\frac{2}{3}-3) \\  & =\frac{31}{12}-(-\frac{25}{12}) \\  & =\frac{14}{3} \\  & =\frac{14}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

By Newton’s second law,

$$
F(t)=ma(t),
$$

where $F(t)$ is the force, $m$ is the mass, and $a(t)$ is the acceleration.

To find the velocity $v(t),$ we differentiate the displacement $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(t)) \\  & =\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the acceleration $a(t),$ we differentiate the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+1}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[{({t}^{2}+1)}^{-1}] \\  & =-{({t}^{2}+1)}^{-2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+1) \\  & =-\frac{1}{{({t}^{2}+1)}^{2}}\cdot 2t \\  & =-\frac{2t}{{({t}^{2}+1)}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the force, in Newtons, is

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =ma(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot [-\frac{2t}{{({t}^{2}+1)}^{2}}] \\  & =-\frac{t}{{({t}^{2}+1)}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the function $f(x)=\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ In **ascending order**, the **exact values** of the critical points of $f(x)$ for $x\in (-\pi ,\pi )$ are

$x=$
{{field-1}}
$\,$ and $\,x=$
{{field-2}}.
:question/worked-solution:
A critical point of $f(x)$ is a point $x=c$ in the domain of $f$ such that either ${f}^{′}(c)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(c)$ does not exist.

Differentiating $f(x),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-3\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

- First, we compute the points where ${f}^{′}(c)=0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-3\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =0 \\ \sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

The general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =arctan\,(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})+n\pi  \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}+n\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

We set $n=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…,$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain $-\pi <x<\pi .$

- setting $n=-1$ gives $x=-\frac{5\pi }{6},$

- setting $n=0$ gives $x=\frac{\pi }{6}.$

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain $-\pi <x<\pi .$ So, the solutions to this equation for $x\in (-\pi ,\pi )$ are 

$$
x=-\frac{5\pi }{6},\,x=\frac{\pi }{6}.
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has stationary points at $x=-\frac{5\pi }{6}$ and $x=\frac{\pi }{6}.$

- Second, we note that ${f}^{′}(x)$ exists for all values of $x\in (-\pi ,\pi ).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, in ascending order, the critical points of $f(x)$ for $x\in (-\pi ,\pi )$ are 

$$
x=-\frac{5\pi }{6}\,\text{and}\,x=\frac{\pi }{6}.
$$

If we let $u=\frac{\pi x}{4},$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\pi }{4}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{4}{\pi }\,\text{d}u.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\pi /2$ |

Using the above, we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{4})\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot \frac{4}{\pi }\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡u\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{4}{\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{4}{\pi }(1-0) \\  & =\frac{4}{\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

Taking the antiderivative and evaluating the difference at the bounds, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =0-(-1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Taking the antiderivative and evaluating the difference at the bounds, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}(-{csc}^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,{|}_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3} \\  & =cot\,(\frac{\pi }{3})-cot\,(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}-\sqrt{3} \\  & =\frac{1-3}{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Taking the antiderivative and evaluating the difference at the bounds, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(-\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{sec}⁡x\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =-\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-(-\operatorname{sec}⁡(0)) \\  & =-\sqrt{2}+1 \\  & =1-\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Taking the antiderivative and evaluating the difference at the bounds, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\,{|}_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3} \\  & =-\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-(-\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})) \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}-(-2) \\  & =2-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}-2}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Express ${\int }_{0}^{2}({x}^{3}+2x+1)\,\text{d}x$ as the limit of a left Riemann sum.

*Hint: Write down the missing expression in terms of $i$ and $n.$*

${\int }_{0}^{2}({x}^{3}+2x+1)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[(($
{{field-1}}
$)^{3}+2($
{{field-2}}
$)+1)\cdot \frac{2}{n}]$
:question/worked-solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

    

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{0}^{2}({x}^{3}+2x+1)\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)={x}^{3}+2x+1,$ the lower bound is $a=0,$ and the upper bound is $b=2.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{2-0}{n}=\frac{2}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}({x}^{3}+2x+1)\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(0+i\cdot \frac{2}{n})\cdot \frac{2}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(\frac{2i}{n})\cdot \frac{2}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[({(\,\frac{2i}{n}\,)}^{3}+2(\,\frac{2i}{n}\,)+1)\,\cdot \frac{2}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-3}^{6}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{6}^{-3}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{113}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can split up the given integral using the sum rule and factor out the constants. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-3}^{6}(9f(x)+8x)\,\text{d}x & =9{\int }_{-3}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x\,+\,8{\int }_{-3}^{6}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =9(-\frac{113}{9})\,+\,8\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\,{|}_{-3}^{6} \\  & =-113\,+\,8\cdot \frac{{6}^{2}-(-3)^{2}}{2} \\  & =-113\,+\,8\cdot \frac{27}{2} \\  & =-113\,+\,108 \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
What is ${\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{x+1}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?

*Hint: Write down the missing expression in terms of $i$ and $n.$*

${\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{x+1}\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[$
{{field-1}}
$\cdot \frac{3}{n}]$
:question/worked-solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{x+1}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=\sqrt{x+1},$ the lower bound is $a=0$ and the upper bound is $b=3.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{3-0}{n}=\frac{3}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{x+1}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[f(0+i\cdot \frac{3}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[f(\frac{3i}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[\sqrt{(\frac{3i}{n})+1}\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[\,\sqrt{\frac{3i}{n}+1}\cdot \frac{3}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
A contractor has $18\,in$ of trim to mark out a rectangular opening. Find the maximum area ${A}_{\text{max}}$ that can be marked out with the trim. Do not round the answer.

${A}_{\text{max}}=$
{{field-1}} $\,{in}^{2}$
:question/worked-solution:
**Step 1**: Let us call $x$ and $y$ the dimensions of the rectagular area.

![](images/59/59c6b4e09015898c1cd77d96fba2bc0dca037ef7462a15f90765257888e3331d.png)

**Step 2**: We need to find the values of $x$ and $y$ such as the area

$$
A=xy
$$

is the greatest possible value.

**Step 3**: This is subject to the constraint that the perimeter is $18.$ This gives the equation

$$
2x+2y=18.
$$

**Step 4**: We make one of the variables the subject in the constraint equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+2y & =18 \\ y & =9-x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $y=9-x$ in the expression $A=xy$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =x(9-x) \\ A & =9x-{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 5**: We solve the equation ${A}^{′}(x)=0.$ Taking the derivative, we have

$$
{A}^{′}(x)=9-2x,
$$

and solving for the stationary points, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ 9-2x & =0 \\ 2x & =9 \\ x & =\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 6**: We confirm that $x=\frac{9}{2}$ is a maximum using the second derivative test. The second derivative is

$$
{A}^{″}(x)=-2\,⟹\,{A}^{″}(\frac{9}{2})=-2<0.
$$

Since ${A}^{″}(\frac{9}{2})$ is negative, we conclude that $x=\frac{9}{2}$ is indeed a maximum of $A(x).$

Finally, when $x=\frac{9}{2}$, we have 

$$
y=9-\frac{9}{2}=\frac{9}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the dimensions of the rectangle with the largest area are $x=\frac{9}{2}\,in$ and $y=\frac{9}{2}\,in,$ and we conclude that

$$
{A}_{\text{max}}=xy=\frac{9}{2}\cdot \frac{9}{2}=20.25\,{in}^{2}.
$$

:question/problem:
A farmer wants to build a rectangular livestock pen of area $648\,{ft}^{2}.$ One side of the pen is adjacent to a barn, so that side does not require fencing. Find $x+y$ where $x$ and $y$ are the dimensions of the pen that minimize the amount of fencing required.

$x+y=$
{{field-1}} $\text{ft}$
:question/worked-solution:
**Step 1**: We draw a diagram, and introduce variables for the length and width of the fencing.

![](images/83/8377f61340020a602e6226932a14fb56ceb803bc9efff05223682f9cca1cf91e.png)

**Step 2**: We need to find the *minimum* value of the perimeter

$$
P=x+2y.
$$

**Step 3**: The constraint is that the area is exactly $648\,{ft}^{2}.$ This gives the equation

$$
xy=648.
$$

**Step 4**: Solving the above constraint equation for $y$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{648}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into our expression for $P$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x) & =x+2(\frac{648}{x}) \\  & =x+\frac{1296}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 5**: We solve the equation ${P}^{′}(x)=0.$ Taking the derivative, we have

$$
{P}^{′}(x)=1-\frac{1296}{{x}^{2}},
$$

and solving for the stationary points, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ 1-\frac{1296}{{x}^{2}} & =0 \\ {x}^{2} & =1296 \\ x & =36.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 6**: We confirm that $x=36$ is a minimum using the second derivative test. The second derivative is

$$
{P}^{″}(x)=\frac{2592}{{x}^{3}}\,⟹\,{P}^{″}(36)=\frac{2592}{(36)^{3}}=\frac{1}{18}>0\,.
$$

Since ${P}^{″}(36)$ is positive, we conclude that $x=36$ is indeed a local minimum of the function $P(x).$

Finally, when $x=36,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{648}{36}=18.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the dimensions of the lot that has the least perimeter are $x=36\,ft$ and $y=18\,ft,$ and we conclude that 

$$
x+y=36+18=54\,ft.
$$

:question/problem:
The total number of pages of a document printed $t$ minutes after printing begins increases at a rate of $\frac{18}{(t+1)^{2}}.$ If, at $t=0$ minutes, the printer had already produced $40$ pages, how many pages will the printer have produced after $2$ minutes?

After $2$ minutes the printer has produced
{{field-1}} pages.
:question/worked-solution:
Let $a(t)=\frac{18}{(t+1)^{2}}$ be the rate at which the number of pages produced is changing, and let $A(T)$ be the number of pages produced $T$ minutes after printing begins. 

Using our formula for the accumulation of change, we have

$$
A(T)=A(0)+{\int }_{0}^{T}a(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Substituting the known information and carrying out the necessary integration gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A(T) & =A(0)+{\int }_{0}^{T}a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =40+{\int }_{0}^{T}\frac{18}{(t+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =40+(-\frac{18}{t+1}){|}_{0}^{T} \\  & =40+(-\frac{18}{T+1})-(-\frac{18}{1}) \\  & =40-\frac{18}{T+1}+18 \\  & =58-\frac{18}{T+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the number of pages produced $T=2$ minutes after printing begins, we substitute in the above:

$$
A(2)=40-\frac{18}{2+1}+18=52.
$$

Thus, after $2$ minutes, the printer has produced $52$ pages.

$$
x-4=A(x-1)+B.
$$

Plugging in $x=1,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}1-4 & =A(1-1)+B \\ B & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, plugging in $x=0$ and substituting the known value of $B,$ we can solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}0-4 & =A(0-1)+B \\ -4 & =-A-3 \\ A & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integrand as the partial sum:

$$
\frac{x-4}{(x-1)^{2}}=\frac{1}{x-1}-\frac{3}{(x-1)^{2}}.
$$

Finally, we integrate this expression term by term to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{x-4}{(x-1)^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{2}^{4}(\frac{1}{x-1}-\frac{3}{(x-1)^{2}})\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{1}{x-1}\,\text{d}x-3{\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{1}{(x-1)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-1|\,{|}_{2}^{4}+3\cdot \frac{1}{x-1}\,{|}_{2}^{4} \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\operatorname{ln}⁡1)+3(\frac{1}{3}-1) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{1})+3(-\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡3-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Our task is to find $A$ and $B$ such that

$$
\frac{4x+23}{(5-2x)(x+3)}=\frac{A}{5-2x}+\frac{B}{x+3}.
$$

Multiplying both sides by $(5-2x)(x+3)$ gives

$$
4x+23=A(x+3)+B(5-2x).
$$

For $x=-3$, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}4(-3)+23 & =A(-3+3)+B(5-2(-3)) \\ 11 & =11B \\ B & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x=\frac{5}{2},$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}4(\frac{5}{2})+23 & =A(\frac{5}{2}+3)+B(5-2(\frac{5}{2})) \\ 33 & =A(\frac{11}{2}) \\ A & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{4x+23}{(5-2x)(x+3)}=\frac{6}{5-2x}+\frac{1}{x+3}.
$$

:question/problem:
What is the value of $f(t)=\sqrt[3]{{t}^{2}+4}\,i+{3}^{t}\,j+\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi t}{2})\,k$ at $t=2?$

$f(2)=$
{{field-1}} $i\,+\,$

{{field-2}} $j\,+\,$

{{field-3}} $k$
:question/worked-solution:
To evaluate, we substitute $t=2$ into the function, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2) & =\sqrt[3]{{2}^{2}+4}\,i+{3}^{2}\,j+\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{2})\,k \\  & =\sqrt[3]{8}\,i+{3}^{2}\,j+\operatorname{tan}⁡(\pi )\,k \\  & =2\,i+9\,j+0\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Our task is to find $A$, $B$, and $C$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{({x}^{2}+4)(x+2)}=\frac{Ax+B}{{x}^{2}+4}+\frac{C}{x+2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides by $({x}^{2}+4)(x+2)$ gives

$$
5=(Ax+B)(x+2)+C({x}^{2}+4).
$$

For $x=-2$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5 & =C(4+4) \\ 5 & =8C \\ C & =\frac{5}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x=0$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5 & =(A(0)+B)(0+2)+\frac{5}{8}((0)^{2}+4) \\ 5 & =2B+\frac{5}{2} \\ 2B & =\frac{5}{2} \\ B & =\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x=1$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5 & =(A(1)+\frac{5}{4})(1+2)+\frac{5}{8}((1)^{2}+4) \\ 5 & =3A+\frac{15}{4}+\frac{25}{8} \\ 3A & =-\frac{15}{8} \\ A & =-\frac{5}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{({x}^{2}+4)(x+2)} & =\frac{(-\frac{5}{8}x+\frac{5}{4})}{{x}^{2}+4}+\frac{(\frac{5}{8})}{x+2} \\  & =\frac{-5\,x+10}{8({x}^{2}+4)}+\frac{5}{8(x+2)}\end{aligned}
$$

We'll work out the indefinite integral first and then proceed with the definite integral.

First, we convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2x+2}{(x-2)(x+4)} & =\frac{A}{(x-2)}+\frac{B}{(x+4)},\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
2x+2=A(x+4)+B(x-2).
$$

Plugging in $x=-4,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(-4)+2 & =A(-4+4)+B(-4-2) \\ -6 & =-6B \\ B & =1\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, plugging in $x=2,$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(2)+2 & =A(2+4)+B(2-2) \\ 6 & =6A \\ A & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{2x+2}{(x-2)(x+4)}=\frac{1}{x-2}+\frac{1}{x+4}.
$$

Now, we integrate, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x+2}{(x-2)(x+4)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{x-2}+\frac{1}{x+4})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{x-2}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{x+4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-2|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+4|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We can simplify the result using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x+2}{(x-2)(x+4)}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-2|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+4|+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(x-2)(x+4)|+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the definite integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{3}^{6}\frac{2x+2}{(x-2)(x+4)}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(x-2)(x+4)|{|}_{3}^{6} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(40)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(7) \\  & =ln\,(\frac{40}{7}).\end{aligned}
$$

Find $F(t)$ given that

$$

First, let's recall the following result:

:question/problem:
The position vector $r$ of a particle $P$ (relative to a fixed origin $O$) at time $t$ is given by

$$
r=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1),\,\frac{3}{t}⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the speed $|v|$ of the particle at time $t=3.$ Do not round the answer.

The speed at time $t=3$ is
{{field-1}}.
:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate the velocity vector $v.$ Differentiating the position vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{3}{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{t+1},\,-\frac{3}{{t}^{2}}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the velocity when $t=3,$ we substitute in the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(3) & =⟨\frac{1}{3+1},\,-\frac{3}{{3}^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{4},\,-\frac{1}{3}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

To find the speed at $t=3$ we calculate the magnitude of $v(3),$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|v(3)| & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{4})}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{3})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{16}+\frac{1}{9}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{25}{144}} \\  & =\frac{5}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Find the range of values of $k$ for which the series
${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{9}^{kn}}{{3}^{8n}}$
converges. Do not round the answer.

$k$
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}
:question/worked-solution:
First, we rewrite the series so that it's in the form ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }a{r}^{n},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{9}^{kn}}{{3}^{8n}} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{(\frac{{9}^{k}}{{3}^{8}})}^{n} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{(\frac{{9}^{k}}{{9}^{4}})}^{n} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{({9}^{k-4})}^{n}\end{aligned}
$$

We see that this is a geometric series with a common ratio of $r={9}^{k-4}.$ 

For the series to converge, we require $|r|<1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|{9}^{k-4}| & <1 \\ {9}^{k-4} & <1.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we could remove the absolute value bars because ${9}^{k-4}$ is always positive.

The equation ${9}^{k-4}=1$ has the solution $k=4.$ Now, since ${9}^{k-4}$ increases as $k$ increases, the solution to ${9}^{k-4}<1$ must be $k<4.$

:question/problem:
Find the second-degree Taylor polynomial ${P}_{2}(x)$ of $f(x)=\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡(x)$ about $x=\frac{\pi }{4}.$

${P}_{2}(x)=$
{{field-1}}$\,+$
{{field-2}}$(x-\frac{\pi }{4})\,+$
{{field-3}}${(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}$
:question/worked-solution:
To find the second-degree Taylor polynomial about $x=\frac{\pi }{4},$ we plug $a=\frac{\pi }{4}$ into the general formula to give

$$
{P}_{2}(x)=f(\frac{\pi }{4})+{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})(x-\frac{\pi }{4})+\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}){(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}.
$$

So, we need to work out $f(\frac{\pi }{4}),$ ${f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}),$ and ${f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡(x) & ⟹ &  & f(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\frac{3}{2} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡(x)} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =3 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)}{{cos}^{3}⁡(x)} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =6\end{aligned}
$$

We now plug the results for $f(\frac{\pi }{4}),$ ${f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}),$ and ${f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4})$ into our second-degree Taylor polynomial. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(x) & =\frac{3}{2}+3(x-\frac{\pi }{4})+6\cdot \frac{1}{2}{(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}+3(x-\frac{\pi }{4})+3{(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Find the interval of convergence for the following series:

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{x}^{n}}{{4}^{n}(5n-2)}=\frac{x}{4\cdot 3}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{{4}^{2}\cdot 8}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{{4}^{3}\cdot 13}+⋯
$$

The interval of convergence is
{{field-1}}
$\le x$
{{field-2}}{{field-3}}.
:question/worked-solution:
To apply the ratio test, we define ${a}_{n}=\frac{{x}^{n}}{{4}^{n}(5n-2)}.$ Then, we calculate the ratio of two successive terms and take the limit as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{x}^{n+1}}{{4}^{n+1}(5n+3)}\cdot \frac{{4}^{n}(5n-2)}{{x}^{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{x(5n-2)}{4(5n+3)}| \\  & =\frac{|x|}{4}{lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{5n-2}{5n+3} \\  & =\frac{|x|}{4}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{|x|}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

The series converges if $L<1.$ Therefore,

$$
\frac{|x|}{4}<1\,⟹\,|x|<4.
$$

So, the radius of convergence is $4,$ and the series converges for any $x$ that lies in the open interval $(-4,4).$

The ratio test gives no conclusion about the convergence of the series when $L=1.$ So, when $|x|=4,$ we do not know if the series converges. This means that the endpoints $x=-4$ and $x=4$ need to be investigated separately using another test for convergence.

- When $x=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{x}^{n}}{{4}^{n}(5n-2)} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{4}^{n}}{{4}^{n}(5n-2)} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{5n-2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{13}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

To see if this series converges, we use the limit comparison test, with ${a}_{n}=\frac{1}{5n-2}$ and ${b}_{n}=\frac{1}{n}.$ We observe that ${a}_{n}$ and ${b}_{n}$ are positive, and

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{{a}_{n}}{{b}_{n}}={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{1}{5n-2})}{(\frac{1}{n})}={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{n}{5n-2}=\frac{1}{5},
$$

 
which is positive and finite. Hence, the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ and ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}$ either *both* converge or *both* diverge.
Since ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{n}$ is divergent, the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{5n-2}$ is also divergent by the limit comparison test. So, the endpoint $x=4$ is not included in our interval.

- When $x=-4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{x}^{n}}{{4}^{n}(5n-2)} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-4)^{n}}{{4}^{n}(5n-2)} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{5n-2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{8}-\frac{1}{13}+⋯,\end{aligned}
$$

which is convergent by the alternating series test. So, the endpoint $x=-4$ is included in our interval.

Therefore, the interval of convergence is $[-4,4),$ or equivalently, $-4\le x<4.$

:question/problem:
Find the radius of convergence $R$ for the series

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{n}^{3}(x-2)^{n}=(x-2)+{2}^{3}(x-2)^{2}+{3}^{3}(x-2)^{3}+⋯\,.
$$

$R=$
{{field-1}}
:question/worked-solution:
To apply the ratio test, we define ${a}_{n}={n}^{3}(x-2)^{n}.$ Then, we calculate the ratio of two successive terms and take the limit as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{(n+1)^{3}(x-2)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}(x-2)^{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{(n+1)^{3}(x-2)}{{n}^{3}}| \\  & =|x-2|{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{n+1}{n})}^{3} \\  & =|x-2|\cdot 1 \\  & =|x-2|\end{aligned}
$$

The series converges if $L<1.$ In this case, the convergence condition is satisfied if $|x-2|<1.$ Therefore, we conclude that the radius of convergence is $R=1.$

:question/problem:
Find the vector $x$, if $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}},$ and 

$$
{b}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ -\frac{8}{3} \\ 12\end{bmatrix},\,{b}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 10 \\ 18\end{bmatrix},\,[x]_{B}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{2} \\ -3\end{bmatrix}.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
We know that any vector in  $\text{Span}{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ has the form

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ -\frac{8}{3} \\ 12\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 10 \\ 18\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the coordinates relative to the basis $\,B.$ Since we are told that $[x]_{B}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{2} \\ -3\end{bmatrix},$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\underbrace{(\frac{3}{2})}_{{x}_{1}}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ -\frac{8}{3} \\ 12\end{bmatrix}+\underbrace{(-3)}_{{x}_{2}}\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 10 \\ 18\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}12 \\ -4 \\ 18\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-18 \\ -30 \\ -54\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ -34 \\ -36\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

We break up the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{3}{{x}^{2}+25}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{3}{{x}^{2}+25}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{3}{{x}^{2}+25}\,\text{d}x
$$

Evaluating the first of these integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{3}{{x}^{2}+25} & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{3}{{x}^{2}+25}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{25}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{1}{(x/5)^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{25}\cdot 5{lim}_{a\to -\infty }({\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{5})|}_{a}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{3}{5}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\operatorname{arctan}⁡0-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{a}{5})) \\  & =\frac{3}{5}(0-(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand is an **even** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{3}{{x}^{2}+25}\,\text{d}x=\frac{3\pi }{10}.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{3}{{x}^{2}+25}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{3}{{x}^{2}+25}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{3}{{x}^{2}+25}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{10}+\frac{3\pi }{10} \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

We break up the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{8{x}^{7}}{{(5+{x}^{8})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{8{x}^{7}}{{(5+{x}^{8})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{8{x}^{7}}{{(5+{x}^{8})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x
$$

First, we calculate the antiderivative using a substitution. Let  $u=5+{x}^{8}$,  then $\text{d}u=8{x}^{7}\text{d}x.$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{8{x}^{7}}{{(5+{x}^{8})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{u}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{5+{x}^{8}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We now evaluate the first of the improper integrals, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{8{x}^{7}}{{(5+{x}^{8})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{8{x}^{7}}{{(5+{x}^{8})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{(-\frac{1}{5+{x}^{8}})|}_{a}^{0} \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\frac{1}{5+0}-\frac{1}{5+{a}^{8}}) \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\frac{1}{5}-\frac{1}{5+{a}^{8}}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}+0 \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand is an **odd** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{8{x}^{7}}{{(5+{x}^{8})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{5}.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{8{x}^{7}}{{(5+{x}^{8})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{8{x}^{7}}{{(5+{x}^{8})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{8{x}^{7}}{{(5+{x}^{8})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{5} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ and $a=1.$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\sqrt{x}={x}^{1/2} \\ f(1) & ={1}^{1/2}=1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2} \\ {f}^{′}(1) & =\frac{1}{2} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{1}{2}){x}^{-3/2}=-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{-3/2} \\ {f}^{″}(1) & =-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$

The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}\sqrt{{(6{e}^{\theta })}^{2}+{(6{e}^{\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}\sqrt{36{e}^{2\theta }+36{e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}\sqrt{72{e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =6\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{e}^{\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =6\sqrt{2}\,{e}^{\theta }{|}_{0}^{\pi /8} \\  & =6\sqrt{2}({e}^{\pi /8}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =6\sqrt{2}({e}^{\pi /8}-1).\end{aligned}

To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t-(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t-(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length and get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{(t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{t}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡t+{t}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{t}^{2}({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }t\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{2}-0 \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the curve defined parametrically as

$S=$
{{field-1}}
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=1.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t-2{t}^{3})=6-6{t}^{2}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6{t}^{2})=12t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}6{t}^{2}\sqrt{{(6-6{t}^{2})}^{2}+{(12t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}6{t}^{2}\sqrt{36-72{t}^{2}+36{t}^{4}+144{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}6{t}^{2}\sqrt{36{t}^{4}+72{t}^{2}+36}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, factoring the expression $36{t}^{4}+72{t}^{2}+36,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}6{t}^{2}\sqrt{36({t}^{4}+2{t}^{2}+1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}6{t}^{2}\cdot 6\sqrt{{t}^{4}+2{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =72\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\sqrt{({t}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =72\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\cdot |{t}^{2}+1|\,\text{d}t \\  & =72\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}({t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =72\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{4}+{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =72\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{4}+{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =72\pi \cdot {[\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}+\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =72\pi [(\frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{3})-(\frac{0}{5}+\frac{0}{3})] \\  & =72\pi \cdot \frac{8}{15} \\  & =\frac{192\pi }{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡3t.
$$

 

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{6\operatorname{cos}⁡3t}{(-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)} \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡3t}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$ the slope $m$ of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}m=\frac{dy}{dx}\,{|}_{t\,=\,\pi /4} & =-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})} \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4})}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})} \\  & =-\frac{(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-x(x+2) & =-({x}^{2}+2x) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+2\cdot 1x+[{1}^{2}-{1}^{2}]) \\  & =-((x+1)^{2}-1) \\  & =1-(x+1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
{\int }_{-1}^{-1/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{-x(x+2)}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-1}^{-1/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x+1)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse sine:

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $(x+1)$.

So, let's perform the substitution

$$
u=x+1.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Let's use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u$.

| $x$ | $-1$ | $-1/2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $1/2$ |

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{-1/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{-x(x+2)}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u\,{|}_{0}^{1/2} \\  & =\arcsin\,(\frac{1}{2})-\arcsin\,(0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}-0 \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in $x=5,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$

$$
