First, we complete the square in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-8x+20 & ={x}^{2}-2\cdot 4x+({4}^{2}-{4}^{2})+20 \\  & =({x}^{2}-2\cdot 4x+{4}^{2})-16+20 \\  & =(x-4)^{2}+4\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}-8x+20}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{(x-4)^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1+((x-4)/2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent:

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $(\frac{x-4}{2}).$

So, let's perform the substitution

$$
u=\frac{x-4}{2}.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}-8x+20}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1+((x-4)/2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x-4}{2})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}-8x-15 & =-({x}^{2}+8x+15) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+2\cdot 4x+[{4}^{2}-{4}^{2}]+15) \\  & =-((x+4)^{2}-1) \\  & =1-(x+4)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above in the given integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-8x-15}}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x+4)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse sine:

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $(x+4).$

So, let's perform the substitution

$$
u=x+4.
$$

Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-8x-15}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x+4)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(x+4)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the gradient of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(\frac{1}{2},0)$ if $g(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}).$

:question/worked-solution:
Let's first factor the denominator of the integrand:

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}-2x-5}{{x}^{3}-5{x}^{2}}=\frac{{x}^{2}-2x-5}{{x}^{2}(x-5)}
$$

We must convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}-2x-5}{{x}^{2}(x-5)}=\frac{A}{x}+\frac{B}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{C}{(x-5)}.
$$

To determine the coefficients $A,B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by ${x}^{2}(x-5)$ and get

$$
{x}^{2}-2x-5=A(x)(x-5)+B(x-5)+C{x}^{2}.
$$

Plugging in $x=5,$ we can eliminate $A$ and $B$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}({5}^{2})-2(5)-5 & =A(5)(5-5)+B(5-5)+C(5)^{2} \\ 10 & =C(25) \\ C & =\frac{10}{25} \\ C & =\frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, plugging in $x=0,$ we can eliminate $A$ and $C$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(0)^{2}-2(0)-5 & =A(0)(0-5)+B(0-5)+C(0)^{2} \\ -5 & =B(-5) \\ B & =\frac{-5}{-5} \\ B & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, plugging in $x=1$ and substituting the known values of $B$ and $C,$ we can solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}({1}^{2})-2(1)-5 & =A(1)(1-5)+B(1-5)+C(1)^{2} \\ -6 & =-4A-4B+C \\ -6 & =-4A-4(1)+(\frac{2}{5}) \\ 4A & =6-4+\frac{2}{5} \\ 4A & =\frac{10+2}{5} \\ A & =\frac{12}{20} \\ A & =\frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integrand as the partial sum

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}-2x-5}{{x}^{2}(x-5)}=\frac{3}{5x}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{2}{5(x-5)}.
$$

Finally, we integrate this expression term by term to get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}-2x-5}{{x}^{2}(x-5)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{3}{5x}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{2}{5(x-5)})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{5}\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+\frac{2}{5}\int \frac{1}{x-5}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|-\frac{1}{x}+\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-5|+K,\end{aligned}
$$

where $K$ is an integral constant.

:question/problem: Evaluate $\int \frac{{x}^{2}+x-3}{({x}^{2}-2x+3)(x+1)}\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the quadratic factor in the denominator has a negative discriminant:

$$
D=(-2)^{2}-4(1)(3)=-8<0
$$

So, we proceed with the following partial fraction decomposition:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}+x-3}{({x}^{2}-2x+3)(x+1)} & =\frac{Ax+B}{{x}^{2}-2x+3}+\frac{C}{x+1}\end{aligned}
$$

To determine the coefficients $A,$ $B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $({x}^{2}-2x+3)(x+1)$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+x-3 & =(Ax+B)(x+1)+C({x}^{2}-2x+3).\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for the unknown constants using the usual methods, we get  $A=\frac{3}{2},$ $B=-\frac{3}{2},$ and $C=-\frac{1}{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}+x-3}{({x}^{2}-2x+3)(x+1)}=\frac{3x-3}{2({x}^{2}-2x+3)}-\frac{1}{2(x+1)}.
$$

Now we integrate this function term by term, adding the constant of integration only at the very end.

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}+x-3}{({x}^{2}-2x+3)(x+1)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{3x-3}{2({x}^{2}-2x+3)}-\frac{1}{2(x+1)})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\int \frac{x-1}{{x}^{2}-2x+3}\,\text{d}x-\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{x+1}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

For the first integral, we use the substitution $u={x}^{2}-2x+3.$ Then $(2x-2)\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x-1}{{x}^{2}-2x+3}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{u})\frac{\text{d}u}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u| \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|{x}^{2}-2x+3| \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-2x+3).\end{aligned}
$$

For the second integral we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{x+1}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+1|.\end{aligned}
$$

So we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}+x-3}{({x}^{2}-2x+3)(x+1)}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{3}{2}\int \frac{x-1}{{x}^{2}-2x+3}\,\text{d}x-\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{x+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-2x+3)-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡|x+1|+K \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-2x+3)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+1|+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the quadratic factor in the denominator has a discriminant that is not a perfect square:

$$
D={4}^{2}-4(1)(-1)=20
$$

We have that $\sqrt{20}$ is not a rational number, which implies that the quadratic factor doesn't factor over the rational numbers.

So, we proceed with the following partial fraction decomposition:

$$
\frac{3{x}^{2}+9x-4}{(x-1)({x}^{2}+4x-1)}=\frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{Bx+C}{{x}^{2}+4x-1}
$$

To determine the coefficients $A,B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $(x-1)({x}^{2}+4x-1),$ and we get

$$
3{x}^{2}+9x-4=A({x}^{2}+4x-1)+(Bx+C)(x-1)
$$

Solving for the unknown constants using the usual methods, we get $A=2,B=1$ and $C=2.$ Therefore,

$$
\frac{3{x}^{2}+9x-4}{(x-1)({x}^{2}+4x-1)}=\frac{2}{x-1}+\frac{x+2}{{x}^{2}+4x-1}.
$$

We now integrate this function term by term, adding the constant of integration at the very end.

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3{x}^{2}+9x-4}{(x-1)({x}^{2}+4x-1)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{2}{x-1}+\frac{x+2}{{x}^{2}+4x-1})\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\int \frac{1}{x-1}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{x+2}{{x}^{2}+4x-1}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

For the first integral, we have

$$
2\int \frac{1}{x-1}\,\text{d}x=2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-1|.
$$

For the second integral, we use the substitution $u={x}^{2}+4x-1.$ Then $\text{d}u=2(x+2)\,\text{d}x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x+2}{{x}^{2}+4x-1}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{u})\frac{\text{d}u}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u| \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|{x}^{2}+4x-1|.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3{x}^{2}+9x-4}{(x-1)({x}^{2}+4x-1)}\,\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{x-1}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{x+2}{{x}^{2}+4x-1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-1|+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|{x}^{2}+4x-1|+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Recall  ${cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x=1,$ so we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}3{sin}^{2}⁡x+7{cos}^{2}⁡x & =3{sin}^{2}⁡x+3{cos}^{2}⁡x+4{cos}^{2}⁡x \\  & =3({sin}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x)+4{cos}^{2}⁡x \\  & =3+4{cos}^{2}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${cos}^{2}⁡x$ term, given by

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x=2{cos}^{2}⁡x-1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡x=\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1).
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(3+4{cos}^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}[3+\frac{4}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1)]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(5+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)\text{d}x \\  & ={(5x+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =[5\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})]-[5\cdot 0+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot 0)] \\  & =[\frac{5\pi }{4}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})]-[0+\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)] \\  & =[\frac{5\pi }{4}+1]-[0+0] \\  & =\frac{5\pi +4}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

A region in the $xy$-plane is bounded by the curve $y=2{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)+2-x,$ the $x$-axis and the lines $x=0$ and $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$, as shown above. The area of the region is

$A=$
{{field-1}}
:question/worked-solution:
The area of the region is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}A={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(2{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)+2-x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate this integral, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${cos}^{2}⁡x$ term, given by

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x=2{cos}^{2}⁡x-1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡x=\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1).
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(2{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)+2-x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[(\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+1)+2-x]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+3-x)\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡4x+3x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =[\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )+3\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{1}{2}{(\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}]-[\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+3(0)-\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2}] \\  & =[\frac{3\pi }{2}-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{8}]-[0] \\  & =\frac{12\pi -{\pi }^{2}}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{3}+{y}^{2}$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩$ at the point $t=\frac{\pi }{4}.$
:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}+{y}^{2}),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}+{y}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨3{x}^{2},2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ and $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨3{sin}^{2}⁡t,2\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨3{sin}^{2}⁡t,2\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\cdot ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & =3{sin}^{2}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =3{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\frac{\pi }{4}))] & =3{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =3\cdot {(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-2\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}-1 \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}-4}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the identity 

$$
1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x,
$$

we compute the given integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡x(1-{tan}^{2}⁡x)}{1-{tan}^{4}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡x(1-{tan}^{2}⁡x)}{(1-{tan}^{2}⁡x)(1+{tan}^{2}⁡x)}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}{1+{tan}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}{{sec}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /6} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we have to use the identity

$$
1+{cot}^{2}⁡x={csc}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\frac{{cot}^{2}⁡x-1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x(1-{cot}^{4}⁡x)}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\frac{{cot}^{2}⁡x-1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x(1-{cot}^{2}⁡x)(1+{cot}^{2}⁡x)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\frac{1-{cot}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x(1-{cot}^{2}⁡x)(1+{cot}^{2}⁡x)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x(1+{cot}^{2}⁡x)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x{csc}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,{|}_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =0-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\sqrt{2-{x}^{2}},$ $a=0,$ and $b=1.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{2}(2-{x}^{2})^{-1/2}(-2x)=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{2-{x}^{2}}}
$$

Now, let's compute $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}} & =\sqrt{1+{[-\frac{x}{\sqrt{2-{x}^{2}}}]}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2-{x}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{2-{x}^{2}+{x}^{2}}{2-{x}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2-{x}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2-{x}^{2}}}$ to the formula for the arc length, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}))|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[\sqrt{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})]-[\sqrt{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{0}{\sqrt{2}})] \\  & =\sqrt{2}(\frac{\pi }{4})-0 \\  & =\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}+\operatorname{arcsin}⁡x,$ $a=-1,$ and $b=1.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}=\frac{1-x}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}
$$

Now, let's compute $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}} & =\sqrt{1+{(\frac{1-x}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{(1-x)^{2}}{1-{x}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1-{x}^{2}+1-2x+{x}^{2}}{1-{x}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{2-2x}{1-{x}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{2(1-x)}{(1-x)(1+x)}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{2}{1+x}}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{1+x}}$ into the arc length formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{\frac{2}{1+x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{1+x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\sqrt{1+x}\,{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\sqrt{1+1}-2\sqrt{2}\sqrt{1+(-1)} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}(\sqrt{2})-0 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}+\operatorname{arccos}⁡x,$ $a=0,$ and $b=1.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}=-\frac{1+x}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}
$$

Now, let's compute $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}} & =\sqrt{1+{(-\frac{1+x}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{(1+x)^{2}}{1-{x}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1-{x}^{2}+1+2x+{x}^{2}}{1-{x}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{2+2x}{1-{x}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{2(1+x)}{(1-x)(1+x)}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{2}{1-x}}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{1-x}}$ into the arc length formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{\frac{2}{1-x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{1-x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-2\sqrt{2}\sqrt{1-x}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-2\sqrt{2}\sqrt{1-1}-(-2\sqrt{2}\sqrt{1-0}) \\  & =0-(-2\sqrt{2}) \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

If we let $u=-4x,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-4\,⟹\,-\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u=\text{d}x.
$$

Computing our limits of integration, we get the following:

| $x$ | $-1$ | $0$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $4$ | $0$ |

Then, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{0}12{e}^{-4x}\,\text{d}x & =12{\int }_{-1}^{0}{e}^{-4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =12{\int }_{4}^{0}{e}^{u}\cdot (-\frac{1}{4})\,\text{d}u \\  & =-3{\int }_{4}^{0}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-3\cdot {e}^{u}\,{|}_{4}^{0} \\  & =-3({e}^{0}-{e}^{4}) \\  & =-3(1-{e}^{4}) \\  & =3{e}^{4}-3\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we have to use the identity

$$
1+{cot}^{2}⁡x={csc}^{2}⁡x\,⟹\,{cot}^{2}⁡x={csc}^{2}⁡x-1.
$$

Therefore, we have

:question/problem: Solve the inequality $\frac{1}{3}{(\frac{3}{5})}^{x}\le 3\sqrt{3}.$

Isolating the exponential term, we find

$$

Then, taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡[{(\frac{3}{5})}^{x}] & \le \operatorname{ln}⁡(9\sqrt{3}) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{5}) & \le \operatorname{ln}⁡(9\sqrt{3}) \\ x(\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\operatorname{ln}⁡5) & \le \operatorname{ln}⁡(9\sqrt{3}).\end{aligned}

$$

:question/problem:
Consider the d’Alembert differential equation, defined for $t>0:$

$$
y=x{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

Using the substitution $t=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ the equation can be transformed to a first-order linear equation of the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+P(t)x=Q(t).
$$

Find the functions $P$ and $Q.$

$\,\,P(t)=$
{{field-1}}$,\,Q(t)=$
{{field-2}}
:question/worked-solution:
A differential equation is a d'Alembert differential equation if it can be expressed in the form

$$
y=xf({y}^{′})+g({y}^{′}),
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are differentiable functions of ${y}^{′}.$ 

In our case, we wish to transform the equation

$$
y=x{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

into a first-order linear equation for $x=x(t).$ We proceed in three steps:

**Step 1**: Substitute, and differentiate with respect to $x.$

We have the substitution

$$
t=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Substituting this into the equation gives

$$
y=x{t}^{2}+t.
$$

Differentiating both sides with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x{t}^{2}+t).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the sum and product rules and using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x{t}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(t) \\ t & ={t}^{2}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)+x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({t}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(t) \\ t & ={t}^{2}+2xt\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}+\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Isolate the derivative and take its reciprocal.

We isolate $\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}t-{t}^{2} & =2xt\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}+\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x} \\ t(1-t) & =(2xt+1)\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x} \\ \frac{t(1-t)}{2xt+1} & =\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}=\frac{t(1-t)}{2xt+1}.
$$

Therefore, by taking the reciprocal of each side, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\frac{2xt+1}{t(1-t)}.
$$

**Step 3**: Express the derivative as a first-order linear equation.

Finally, we write this in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+P(t)x=Q(t)
$$

as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{2xt+1}{t(1-t)} \\ t(1-t)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =2xt+1 \\ t(1-t)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-2xt & =1 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-\frac{2xt}{t(1-t)} & =\frac{1}{t(1-t)} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-\frac{2x}{1-t} & =\frac{1}{t(1-t)} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{2x}{t-1} & =\frac{1}{t(1-t)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(t)=\frac{2}{t-1},\,Q(t)=\frac{1}{t(1-t)}.
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂y∂z∂z} & =\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂y∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂z}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(3{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz)+3x{y}^{2}z\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz)+3{x}^{2}{z}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)) \\  & =3x{y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz)+3x{y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz)-3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}z\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz)+6{x}^{2}z\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate both partial derivatives at the point $(\pi ,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂y∂y}{|}_{(\pi ,-1,1)} & =6(-1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )+6(\pi )(-1)(1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-3(\pi )^{3}(1)^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )=6\pi  \\ \frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂y∂z∂z}{|}_{(\pi ,-1,1)} & =3(\pi )(-1)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )+3(\pi )(-1)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-3(\pi )^{2}(-1)^{2}(1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )+6(\pi )^{2}(1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\pi )=-6\pi -6{\pi }^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂y∂y}{|}_{(\pi ,-1,1)}+\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂y∂z∂z}{|}_{(\pi ,-1,1)} & =6\pi +(-6\pi -6{\pi }^{2})=-6{\pi }^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
$$
v=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix},\,A=\begin{bmatrix}10 & -7 & -3 \\ 8 & -5 & -3 \\ 10 & -8 & -2\end{bmatrix}
$$

The vector $v$ and the matrix $A$ are given above. 
If $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2,$ then what is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$
:question/worked-solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =2.$ So, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}10 & -7 & -3 \\ 8 & -5 & -3 \\ 10 & -8 & -2\end{bmatrix}-2\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & -7 & -3 \\ 8 & -7 & -3 \\ 10 & -8 & -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}8{x}_{1}-7{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3} &=0 \\ 8{x}_{1}-7{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3} &=0 \\ 10{x}_{1}-8{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & -7 & -3 & 0 \\ 8 & -7 & -3 & 0 \\ 10 & -8 & -4 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{5}{4}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}8 & -7 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{3}{4} & -\frac{1}{4} & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}8 & -7 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{3}{4} & -\frac{1}{4} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=\frac{1}{3}{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{1}{8}(7{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{8}(7(\frac{1}{3}{x}_{3})+3{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{1}{3}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=3,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{2}{1}=2.$

:question/problem:

The vector $v$ and the matrix $A$ are given above. 
If $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3,$ then what is the value of $\frac{b}{c}?$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =3.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 & 2 \\ 9 & -6 & -9 \\ 1 & 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}-3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 9 & -9 & -9 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{3} &=0 \\ 9{x}_{1}-9{x}_{2}-9{x}_{3} &=0 \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{3} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 9 & -9 & -9 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-9){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -9 & -27 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:=(-\frac{1}{9}){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd one). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{3}.$ From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-3{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-2{x}_{3} \\ -3{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{c}=\frac{-3}{1}=-3.$

:question/problem: Calculate ${lim}_{x\to (\pi /3)}({tan}^{2}⁡(x)+3{cot}^{2}⁡(x)).$
:question/worked-solution:
Substituting $x=\frac{\pi }{3}$ directly into the limit, we have

 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (\pi /3)}({tan}^{2}⁡(x)+3{cot}^{2}⁡(x)) & ={tan}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})+3{cot}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & ={(\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}))}^{2}+3{(\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}))}^{2} \\  & ={(\sqrt{3})}^{2}+3{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})}^{2} \\  & =3+3(\frac{3}{9}) \\  & =3+1 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

The vectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2$ of the matrix $A,$ given above. Find the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[a,\,b,\,c]^{T}$ such that the set $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent. What is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find all the eigenvalues of $A$ by solving the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}-1-\lambda  & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 4-\lambda  & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )\begin{vmatrix}-1-\lambda  & 3 \\ 2 & 4-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((-1-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-(3)(2)) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda -10) & =0 \\ -(\lambda -1)(\lambda +2)(\lambda -5) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$ Since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =5.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}-5\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-6{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} &=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=0 \\ -4{x}_{3} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 3 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{5}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{12}{5}){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{5}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{3}=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{1}{2}.$

:question/problem:
$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}
$$

The vectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3$ of the matrix $A,$ given above. Find the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[a,\,b,\,c]^{T}$ such that the set $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent. What is the value of $\frac{a}{c}?$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find all the eigenvalues of $A$ by solving the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}1-\lambda  & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda  & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -2-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-2-\lambda )\begin{vmatrix}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-2-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-(2)(2)) & =0 \\ (-2-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -3) & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)(\lambda +1)(\lambda -3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-2.$ Since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=-2.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =-2.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}-(-2)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 3 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+4{x}_{3} &=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3} &=0 \\ 0 &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 4 & 0 \\ 2 & 3 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-\frac{2}{3}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{5}{3} & -\frac{20}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=4{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{1}{3}(-2{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(-2(4{x}_{3})-4{x}_{3}) \\  & =-4{x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-4{x}_{3} \\ 4{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{c}=\frac{-4}{1}=-4.$

:question/problem: Consider the linear transformation $T:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}-9x-3y+3z \\ -12x-4y+4z \\ 6x+8y+10z\end{bmatrix}.$ Find $\,\text{Ker}(T).$
:question/worked-solution:
Finding the kernel of $T$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $T.$

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=\begin{bmatrix}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ -12 & -4 & 4 \\ 6 & 8 & 10\end{bmatrix}.$

Setting $x=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix},$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we find reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =\begin{bmatrix}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ -12 & -4 & 4 \\ 6 & 8 & 10\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{4}{3}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 6 & 8 & 10\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{2}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 12\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & 6 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$ and $y$, and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$

From the second equation, we get $y=-2z.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}-9x-3y+3z & =0 \\ -9x-3(-2z)+3z & =0 \\ -9x+9z & =0 \\ x & =z\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation $\,T$ is $\{\begin{bmatrix}z \\ -2z \\ z\end{bmatrix}\,:\,z\in R\}.$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the double integral
${∬}_{D}\frac{1}{(1+x+y)^{2}}\,dA,$
where $D$ is the finite region enclosed by the line
$y=1-x$ and the coordinate axes.
:question/worked-solution:
Let's make a sketch of our region.

![](images/95/95ebd0a4eb874972b459e53eecf1d57650f63284698fcad967c09620ac01cd99.png)

Notice that $D$ is a type I region.

- The line $y=1-x$ intercepts the $x$-axis at $x=1.$
So, the $x$-limits are 
$0\le x\le 1.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](images/d0/d048f20f2299722cee598cc1005237627ecdd7643e996b269f26b5a096f01f2f.png)

As a result, the integral is defined over the following type I region: 

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1-x\}
$$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
{∬}_{D}\frac{1}{(1+x+y)^{2}}\,dA={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-x}\frac{1}{(1+x+y)^{2}}\,dy\,dx
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-x}\frac{1}{(1+x+y)^{2}}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{-x+1}\frac{1}{(1+x+y)^{2}}\,dy]\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[-\frac{1}{1+x+y}]}_{0}^{-x+1}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-\frac{1}{1+x+(1-x)}-(-\frac{1}{1+x+0}))\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{1+x})dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{1+x})dx & ={[-\frac{1}{2}x+\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+x)]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-(0+\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/f4/f4fdf6f8d819a4ee043b1cc3b86d795e3166ebfe181e0958246dc084c2f9c6fc.png)

The point $P$ lies on the unit circle. Given that the $x$-coordinate of $P$ is $\frac{3}{7},$ use the Pythagorean Identity to find $sin⁡\theta .$
:question/worked-solution:
![](images/cb/cb569d4b7b76699259d2167b8c930e636e3fb794b14ef25a4d909c224235d7c3.png)

Any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta $ as follows:

$$
x=cos⁡\theta ,\,y=sin⁡\theta 
$$

We're given that $x=\frac{3}{7}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$
cos⁡\theta =\frac{3}{7}.
$$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $sin⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ sin⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $cos⁡\theta =\frac{3}{7}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}sin⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{3}{7})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{9}{49}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{40}{49}} \\  & =\pm \frac{2\sqrt{10}}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we select the positive answer since $sin⁡\theta $ is positive in the first quadrant. So our final answer is $sin⁡\theta =\frac{2\sqrt{10}}{7}$

![](images/6c/6c36dbce847c719accc77fa15f33dfb9a87cfae669691afe30f7693663076d2e.png)

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that the $y$-coordinate of the point $P$ is $\frac{\sqrt{10}}{4},$ use the Pythagorean identity to find $2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .$
:question/worked-solution:
![](images/52/52fe94bb303a001e89f9db221e9730d4ca8c5c284217aa20fb6084ee041dec66.png)

Any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta $ as follows:

$$
x=cos⁡\theta ,\,y=sin⁡\theta 
$$

We're given that $y=\frac{\sqrt{10}}{4}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$
sin⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{10}}{4}.
$$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ 2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =2-2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $sin⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{10}}{4}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =2-2{(\frac{\sqrt{10}}{4})}^{2} \\  & =2-2(\frac{10}{16}) \\  & =2-\frac{20}{16} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

So our final answer is $2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta =\frac{3}{4}.$

:question/problem: If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=\frac{1}{2}$ and ${lim}_{x\to {(1/2)}^{+}}f(x)=4,$ then what is $f(\frac{1}{2})?$
:question/worked-solution:
We're told that $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=\frac{1}{2}.$ According to the definition of continuity, this means that ${lim}_{x\to (1/2)}f(x)$ exists, and

$$
f(\frac{1}{2})={lim}_{x\to (1/2)}f(x)={lim}_{x\to {(1/2)}^{+}}f(x)=4.
$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the repeated integral
${\int }_{-2}^{-1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{{y}^{2}(1+{x}^{2})}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{-1}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{{y}^{2}(1+{x}^{2})}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y & ={\int }_{-2}^{-1}\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{(1+{x}^{2})}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{-1}\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}[\operatorname{arctan}⁡x]_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{-1}\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡\sqrt{3}-\operatorname{arctan}⁡0)\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{-1}\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}(\frac{\pi }{3}-0)\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{-1}\frac{\pi }{3{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{-1}\frac{\pi }{3{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y & ={[-\frac{\pi }{3y}]}_{-2}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{3\cdot (-1)}-(-\frac{\pi }{3\cdot (-2)}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}-\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=x{e}^{-y}.$
:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x{e}^{-y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{x}{{e}^{y}} \\ {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int x\,\text{d}x \\ {e}^{y} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
{e}^{y}=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+C).
$$

:question/problem:
The linear transformation $T$ and the vector $b\in {R}^{4}$ are given below. Determine if there exists a vector $x\in {R}^{4}$ such that $T(x)=b.$
In the affirmative case, find the value of $w-x+y,$ where $w,x,y,z$ are the components of $x.$  

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}w \\ x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}w-3x-2z \\ 2x-2w-4y \\ 3w-y-10x-7z \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we write down the standard matrix of $T:$

$$
T=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 0 & -2 \\ -2 & 2 & -4 & 0 \\ 3 & -10 & -1 & -7 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Since $T$ is the standard matix of $T,$ we have $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Col}(T).$ In order to determine whether $b$ lies in $\text{Im}(T),$ we need to check if the equation $Tx=b$ is consistent. 

So, let's find the row echelon form of the augmented matrix $[T\,|\,b]$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}[T\,|\,b] & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 0 & -2 & 3 \\ -2 & 2 & -4 & 0 & 2 \\ 3 & -10 & -1 & -7 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 0 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & -4 & -4 & -4 & 8 \\ 0 & -1 & -1 & -1 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{1}{4}){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 0 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & -4 & -4 & -4 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -8 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get the false statement $0=-8.$ Therefore, the system is inconsistent, and we conclude that  $b\notin \text{Im}(T).$

:question/problem: Given that $\,A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{bmatrix}\,$ and $\,{A}^{-1}=pI+qA$, find the value $p+q.$
:question/worked-solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & 3 \\ 3 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-9 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +6 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-8A+6I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-8A+6I) & =O \\ A-8I+6{A}^{-1} & =O \\ 6{A}^{-1} & =8I-A \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{4}{3}I-\frac{1}{6}A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{4}{3},$ $q=-\frac{1}{6}$ and

$$
p+q=\frac{4}{3}+(-\frac{1}{6})=\frac{7}{6}.
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ given that $F(x,y)=(y\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\,i+(x+y)\,j$ and $C$ is the path  $r(t)=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡t\,i+2j$ for $t\in [0,\frac{1}{2}].$
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have 

$$
x=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡t,\,y=2.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{arcsin}⁡t)\,i+(\operatorname{arcsin}⁡t+2)\,j \\  & =2t\,i+(\operatorname{arcsin}⁡t+2)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{arcsin}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2)j \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{t}^{2}}}\,i.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(2t\,i+(\operatorname{arcsin}⁡t+2)\,j)\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{t}^{2}}}\,i) \\  & =\frac{2t}{\sqrt{1-{t}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{2t}{\sqrt{1-{t}^{2}}}\,dt \\  & =-2\sqrt{1-{t}^{2}}\,{|}_{0}^{1/2} \\  & =-2(\sqrt{1-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}}-1) \\  & =2-\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
What is the first term that is less than $0.000\,2$ in the following geometric sequence?

$$
18,\,12,\,8,\,\frac{16}{3},\,…
$$
:question/worked-solution:
The first term of the sequence is ${a}_{1}=18$ and the common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{12}{18}=\frac{2}{3}.
$$

So, the $n$th term of the sequence can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =18{(\frac{2}{3})}^{n-1}\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be less than $0.000\,2.$
Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & <0.000\,2 \\ 18{(\frac{2}{3})}^{n-1} & <0.000\,2 \\ {(\frac{2}{3})}^{n-1} & <\frac{0.000\,2}{18} \\ \operatorname{log}⁡{(\frac{2}{3})}^{n-1} & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,011) \\ (n-1)\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{2}{3}) & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,011) \\ n-1 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,011)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{2}{3})} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,011)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{2}{3})}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we reversed the inequality sign when divided by $\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{2}{3})$ because $\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{2}{3})$ is a negative number. 

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get:

$$
\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,011)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{2}{3})}+1≈29.159
$$

Therefore, the $30$th term is the first term of the sequence that is less than $0.000\,2.$

:question/problem:
What is the first term that is less than $0.001$ in the following geometric sequence?

$$
64,\,48,\,36,\,27,\,…
$$
:question/worked-solution:
The first term of the sequence is ${a}_{1}=64$ and the common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{48}{64}=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

So, the $n$th term of the sequence can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =64{(\frac{3}{4})}^{n-1}\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be less than $0.001.$
Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & <0.001 \\ 64{(\frac{3}{4})}^{n-1} & <0.001 \\ {(\frac{3}{4})}^{n-1} & <\frac{0.001}{64} \\ \operatorname{log}⁡{(\frac{3}{4})}^{n-1} & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,016) \\ (n-1)\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{4}) & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,016) \\ n-1 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,016)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{4})} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,016)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{4})}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we reversed the inequality sign when divided by $\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{4})$ because $\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{4})$ is a negative number. 

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get:

$$
\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,016)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{4})}+1≈39.386
$$

Therefore, the $40$th term is the first term of the sequence that is less than $0.001.$

:question/problem:
The $2$nd term of a geometric sequence with a positive common ratio is $\frac{3}{2}$, and the $4$th term is $\frac{2}{3}.$ Given that all terms of the sequence are positive, what is the first term of this sequence to be less than
$0.000\,11?$
:question/worked-solution:
Since we are given that ${a}_{2}=\frac{3}{2}$ and ${a}_{4}=\frac{2}{3}$, we can find the common ratio $r$ of the sequence, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{n-m} & =\frac{{a}_{n}}{{a}_{m}} \\ {r}^{4-2} & =\frac{{a}_{4}}{{a}_{2}} \\ {r}^{2} & =\frac{\frac{2}{3}}{\frac{3}{2}} \\ {r}^{2} & =\frac{4}{9} \\ r & =\pm \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Given that the common ratio is positive, we take the positive value. Now, since ${a}_{4}=\frac{2}{3}$ and  $r=\frac{2}{3}$, we can use the $n$th term formula to solve for ${a}_{1}$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\ {a}_{4} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {(\frac{2}{3})}^{4-1} \\ \frac{2}{3} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {(\frac{2}{3})}^{3} \\ {(\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & ={a}_{1} \\ {a}_{1} & =\frac{9}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the $n$th term of the geometric sequence is

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}\cdot {(\frac{2}{3})}^{n-1} \\  & ={(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}\cdot {(\frac{3}{2})}^{1-n} \\  & ={(\frac{3}{2})}^{3-n}\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be less than $0.000\,11.$
Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{3}{2})}^{3-n} & <0.000\,11 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡{(\frac{3}{2})}^{3-n} & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,11) \\ (3-n)\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{2}) & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,11) \\ 3-n & <\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,11)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{2})} \\ -n & <\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,11)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{2})}-3 \\ n & >3-\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,11)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{2})}\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get:

$$
3-\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,11)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{2})}≈25.480
$$

Therefore, the $26$th term is the first term of the sequence that is less than $0.000\,11.$

:question/problem: Find $k$, if $u=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{9} \\ \frac{k}{9} \\ -\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{8}{9}\end{bmatrix}$ is a unit vector.
:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate the norm of the vector $x$ in terms of $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖u‖ & =\sqrt{{u}_{1}^{2}+{u}_{2}^{2}+{u}_{3}^{2}+{u}_{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{9})}^{2}+{(\frac{k}{9})}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{3})}^{2}+{(\frac{8}{9})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{81}+\frac{{k}^{2}}{81}+\frac{1}{9}+\frac{64}{81}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{74+{k}^{2}}{81}}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given equation  $‖u‖=1,$ we obtain an equation that we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{74+{k}^{2}}{81}} & =1 \\ \sqrt{74+{k}^{2}} & =9 \\ {(\sqrt{74+{k}^{2}})}^{2} & ={9}^{2} \\ 74+{k}^{2} & =81 \\ {k}^{2} & =7 \\ k & =\pm \sqrt{7}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Find the acute angle between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix},\,\,x=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Round the answer to $2$ decimal places.
:question/worked-solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot {(\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot {\begin{bmatrix}6 & 6 \\ 6 & 9\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 10\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} & -\frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{1}{3} & \frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 10\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$   

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x\cdot {\text{proj}}_{S}x}{‖x‖‖{\text{proj}}_{S}x‖} \\  & =\frac{3\cdot 2+2\cdot 2+1\cdot 2}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{12}{\sqrt{14}\sqrt{12}} \\  & =\frac{12}{2\sqrt{42}} \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{42}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{6}{\sqrt{42}})≈{22.21}^{∘},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

:question/problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x-2y}$ that satisfies $y(0)=0.$
:question/worked-solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{x-2y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{x}\cdot {e}^{-2y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{e}^{x}}{{e}^{2y}} \\ {e}^{2y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{x} \\ \int {e}^{2y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{2y}\,\text{d}y & =\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2y} & ={e}^{x}+{C}_{1} \\ {e}^{2y} & =2{e}^{x}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=2{C}_{1}$ is an arbitrary constant.

Applying the natural logarithm to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2y}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{e}^{x}+C) \\ y & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{e}^{x}+C).\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the condition $y(0)=0$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{e}^{0}+C) & =0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(2+C) & =0 \\ 2+C & =1 \\ C & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x-2y}$ that satisfies the condition $y(0)=0$ is

$$
y=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{e}^{x}-1).
$$

:question/problem: Consider the infinite geometric sequence that has a fourth term equal to $24$ and a seventh term equal to $\frac{3}{8}.$ What is the sum to infinity of the terms of this sequence?
:question/worked-solution:
The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

From the question statement we have ${a}_{4}=24$ and ${a}_{7}=\frac{3}{8}.$ We can find the common ratio using the following formula:

$$
{r}^{n-m}=\frac{{a}_{n}}{{a}_{m}}
$$

Substituting in the known information into the above gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{7-4} & =\frac{(\frac{3}{8})}{24} \\ {r}^{3} & =(\frac{3}{8})(\frac{1}{24}) \\ {r}^{3} & =\frac{1}{64} \\ {r}^{3} & ={(\frac{1}{4})}^{3} \\ r & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the formula

$$
{a}_{n}={a}_{1}{r}^{n-1}
$$

for the $n$th term of the geometric sequence, we can find the first term. Indeed, for $n=4$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{4} & ={a}_{1}(r)^{3} \\ 24 & ={a}_{1}{(\frac{1}{4})}^{3} \\ 24 & ={a}_{1}(\frac{1}{64}) \\ {a}_{1} & =1\,536\end{aligned}
$$

So, using the formula, we find that the sum to infinity is

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{\infty } & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{1\,536}{(1-\frac{1}{4})} \\  & =\frac{1\,536}{(\frac{3}{4})} \\  & =1\,536(\frac{4}{3}) \\  & =2\,048.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Which of the following geometric series converge?

Select all that apply.
:question/worked-solution:
Let's look at each series in turn.

- For the geometric series $1+5+25+125+⋯$ the common ratio is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{5}{1} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the series is divergent because $|r|\ge 1.$

- For the geometric series $\frac{2}{7}+\frac{4}{3}+\frac{56}{9}+\frac{784}{27}+⋯$ the common ratio is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{(\frac{4}{3})}{(\frac{2}{7})} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\cdot \frac{7}{2} \\  & =\frac{14}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the series is divergent because $|r|\ge 1.$

- For the geometric series $\begin{gathered}0.1+0.01+0.001+0.000\,1+⋯\end{gathered}$  the common ratio is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{0.01}{0.1} \\  & =0.1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the series is convergent because $|r|<1.$

In conclusion, only series $\begin{gathered}0.1+0.01+0.001+0.000\,1+⋯\end{gathered}$ converges.

:question/problem:
Consider the negative infinite geometric sequence that has a third term equal to $-1$ and a seventh term equal to $-\frac{1}{4\,096}.$ What is the sum to infinity of the terms of this sequence?

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the fact that $4\,096={8}^{4}.$*
:question/worked-solution:
The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

From the question statement we have ${a}_{3}=-1$ and ${a}_{7}=-\frac{1}{4\,096}.$ We can find the common ratio using the following formula:

$$
{r}^{n-m}=\frac{{a}_{n}}{{a}_{m}}
$$

Substituting in the known information into the above gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{7-3} & =\frac{(-\frac{1}{4\,096})}{(-1)} \\ {r}^{4} & =\frac{1}{4\,096} \\ {r}^{4} & ={(\frac{1}{8})}^{4} \\ r & =\sqrt[4]{{(\frac{1}{8})}^{4}} \\ r & =\frac{1}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we have taken the positive fourth root since we're told that the sequence is negative.

Now, using the formula

$$
{a}_{n}={a}_{1}{r}^{n-1}
$$

for the $n$th term of the geometric sequence, we can find the first term. Indeed, for $n=3$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{3} & ={a}_{1}{r}^{2} \\ -1 & ={a}_{1}{(\frac{1}{8})}^{2} \\ -1 & ={a}_{1}(\frac{1}{64}) \\ {a}_{1} & =-64\end{aligned}
$$

So, using the formula, we find that the sum to infinity is

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{\infty } & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{-64}{(1-\frac{1}{8})} \\  & =-\frac{64}{(\frac{7}{8})} \\  & =-64\cdot \frac{8}{7} \\  & =-\frac{512}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the orthogonal set $U$ below. By adding a new vector $x=[{x}_{1},\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}]^{T},$ extend the set so that it forms an orthogonal basis of ${R}^{3}.$ What is the value of $\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{2}}?$

$$
U={\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ -6\end{bmatrix}}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $U$ as ${u}_{1},\,{u}_{2}.$ To extend the given set to an orthogonal basis of ${R}^{3}$, we need to find a third vector $x=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}$ such that

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot x &=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot x &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}6{x}_{1}+{x}_{3} &=0 \\ {x}_{1}-{x}_{2}-6{x}_{3} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, we consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system above and reduce it to its row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & -6 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{1}{6}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}6 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -\frac{37}{6} & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-\frac{37}{6}{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}6{x}_{1}+{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{6}{x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{6}{x}_{3} \\ -\frac{37}{6}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{3}=6$, we obtain the vector 

$$
x=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -37 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, an orthogonal basis of ${R}^{3}$ is

$$
{\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ -6\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -37 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}}.
$$

Finally, $\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{2}}=\frac{1}{37}.$

Therefore, the range is $f(x)<3.$ Thus, of the given values, only $y=-3$ and $y=2$ are  outputs of $y=f(x).$

:question/problem: For which values of $k$ does the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{16}^{kn+1}}{{4}^{n-1}}$ converge?
:question/worked-solution:
First, we rewrite the series so that it's in the form ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }a{r}^{n},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{16}^{kn+1}}{{4}^{n-1}} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{16}^{kn}\cdot 16}{{4}^{n}\cdot {4}^{-1}} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(16\cdot 4){(\frac{{16}^{k}}{4})}^{n} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }64{(\frac{{16}^{k}}{4})}^{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

We see that this is a geometric series with a common ratio of $r=\frac{{16}^{k}}{4}.$ 

For the series to converge, we require $|r|<1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\frac{{16}^{k}}{4}| & <1 \\ \frac{{16}^{k}}{4} & <1 \\ {16}^{k} & <4.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we could remove the absolute value bars because $\frac{{16}^{k}}{4}$ is always positive.

The equation ${16}^{k}=4$ has the solution $k=\frac{1}{2}.$ Now, since ${16}^{k}$ increases as $k$ increases, the solution to ${16}^{k}<4$ must be $k<\frac{1}{2}.$

:question/problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix},\,{a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},\,\,x=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the distance between $x$ and the subspace $S$ given that the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal.
:question/worked-solution:
Since the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{{a}_{1}}$ and $\text{Span}{{a}_{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{2\cdot 1+2\cdot 1+(-4)\cdot 4}{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{4}^{2}}{a}_{1}=(-\frac{2}{3})\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{2\cdot 2+2\cdot 2+(-4)\cdot (-1)}{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{4}{3}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x \\  & =(-\frac{2}{3})\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}+\frac{4}{3}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}(\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -1 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 4 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}=x.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $x$ coincides with the projection, the distance between $x$ and the subspace $S$ is zero $0.$

:question/problem:
$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 4 \\ 4 & -1\end{bmatrix},\,B=\{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}\}
$$

Consider the subspace $\text{Col}(A)$ and an orthogonal basis $B$ of $\text{Col}(A),$ where $A$ and $B$ are given above. Given that $B$ is derived from $\text{Col}(A)$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $\frac{b}{c}?$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that $\text{Col}(A)$ is the span of the columns of $A.$ 

First, let's denote

$\,$ ${a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}\,$ and $\,{a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 4 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.$ 

We proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows.

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 2**: Next, we find ${v}_{2}$, by using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{2}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{(-3)\cdot 2+4\cdot (-1)+(-1)\cdot 4}{{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{4}^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 4 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}+\frac{2}{3}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{5}{3} \\ \frac{10}{3} \\ \frac{5}{3}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $B=\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\}=\{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{5}{3} \\ \frac{10}{3} \\ \frac{5}{3}\end{bmatrix}\}$ is an orthogonal basis for $\text{Col}(A).$

Finally, $b=\frac{10}{3},$ $c=\frac{5}{3},$ and  

$$
\frac{b}{c}=\frac{(\frac{10}{3})}{(\frac{5}{3})}=2.
$$

:question/problem: A point $P$ has Cartesian coordinates $(-k,k),$ where $k$ is a positive real number. What are the polar coordinates of $P?$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we determine $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-k)^{2}+{k}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2{k}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

For the reference angle, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})| \\  & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{-k}{k})| \\  & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-1)| \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the point $P$ lies in the second quadrant, we subtract the reference angle from $\pi $ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi -\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the polar coordinates of $P$ are $(\sqrt{2}\,k,\frac{3\pi }{4}).$

:question/problem: A point $P$ has Cartesian coordinates $(-\frac{k}{4},\frac{k}{2}),$ where $k$ is a positive real number. What are the polar coordinates of $P?$ Round your answer to the nearest integer where necessary.
:question/worked-solution:
First, we determine $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(-\frac{k}{4})}^{2}+{(\frac{k}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{k}^{2}}{16}+\frac{{k}^{2}}{4}} \\  & =\sqrt{5\cdot \frac{{k}^{2}}{16}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}\,k}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

For the reference angle, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})| \\  & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{(\frac{k}{2})}{(-\frac{k}{4})})| \\  & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-2)| \\  & ≈1.107.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the point $P$ lies in the second quadrant, we subtract the reference angle from $\pi $ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi -1.107 \\  & ≈2.035 \\  & ≈2,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest integer. Therefore, the polar coordinates of $P$ are $(\frac{\sqrt{5}\,k}{4},2).$

:question/problem: The point $A$ has polar coordinates $(r,\frac{3\pi }{4})$ and the point $B$ has polar coordinates $({r}^{2},\frac{4\pi }{3}).$ Find the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ given that the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ are $(-\sqrt{5},\sqrt{5}).$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we use the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ to find $r,$ the distance between $A$ and the origin:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(\sqrt{5})^{2}+(\sqrt{5})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the polar coordinates of $B$ are

$$
((\sqrt{10})^{2},\frac{4\pi }{3})=(10,\frac{4\pi }{3}).
$$

Now, we convert $B$ to Cartesian coordinates. To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =10\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{3}) \\  & =10(-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =10\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{3}) \\  & =10(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =-5\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(-5,-5\sqrt{3}).$

:question/problem: The point $A$ has polar coordinates $(\sqrt{2},\theta )$ and the point $B$ has polar coordinates $(8,\theta +\pi ).$ Find the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ given that the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ are $(-1,-1).$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we use the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ to find its reference angle ${\theta }_{R}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{-1}{-1}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the point $A$ lies in the third quadrant, we have $\theta =\pi +{\theta }_{R}=\frac{5\pi }{4}.$ Consequently, the polar coordinates of $B$ are

$$
(8,\frac{5\pi }{4}+\pi )=(8,\frac{9\pi }{4})=(8,\frac{\pi }{4}).
$$

Now, we convert $B$ to Cartesian coordinates. To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =8\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =8\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(4\sqrt{2},4\sqrt{2}).$

:question/problem:
$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ 6 & -2 \\ -3 & 1\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ -5\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}b \\ c\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of  $3a+\frac{b}{c}?$
:question/worked-solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 6 & -3 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ 6 & -2 \\ -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 6 & -3 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ -5\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}54 & -18 \\ -18 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}12 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}54 & -18 & 12 \\ -18 & 6 & -4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}54 & -18 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{2}{9}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{9}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{9} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
3a+\frac{b}{c}=3\cdot \frac{2}{9}+\frac{(\frac{1}{3})}{1}=1.
$$

:question/problem:
$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 6 & -2 \\ 3 & -1 \\ -6 & 2\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}b \\ c\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $-10a+\frac{6b}{c}?$
:question/worked-solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 6 & 3 & -6 \\ -1 & -2 & -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 6 & -2 \\ 3 & -1 \\ -6 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 6 & 3 & -6 \\ -1 & -2 & -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}90 & -30 \\ -30 & 10\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-27 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}90 & -30 & -27 \\ -30 & 10 & 9\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}90 & -30 & -27 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have  

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{3}{10}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{10}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{10} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
-10a+\frac{6b}{c}=-10\cdot (-\frac{3}{10})+\frac{6\cdot (\frac{1}{3})}{1}=5.
$$

:question/problem:
