A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -4 \\ 1 & -2 \\ -5 & 10\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}b \\ c\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $-2a+\frac{b}{c}?$
:question/worked-solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & -5 \\ -4 & -2 & 10\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -4 \\ 1 & -2 \\ -5 & 10\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & -5 \\ -4 & -2 & 10\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}30 & -60 \\ -60 & 120\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-15 \\ 30\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ -2 & 4 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}+2{x}_{2}.
$$

 Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{2}+2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
-2a+\frac{b}{c}=-2\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})+\frac{2}{1}=3.
$$

:question/problem:
$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}b \\ c \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\,+\,{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $2a-3b-6c?$
:question/worked-solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}12 & -6 & 0 \\ -6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}12 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ -6 & 3 & 0 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:=2{R}_{2}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=(1/6){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=(1/2){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable.  

From the third row, we have

$$
{x}_{3}=1,
$$

and from the first row we obtain

$$
2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=1+\frac{{x}_{2}}{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1+\frac{{x}_{2}}{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
2a-3b-6c=2(\frac{1}{2})-3(1)-6(0)=-2.
$$

:question/problem:
$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -2 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,B={\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c \\ d\end{bmatrix}}
$$

Consider the subspace $V=\text{Col}(A)$ spanned by the columns ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ of the matrix $A$ and an orthogonal basis $B$ of $\text{Col}(A),$ shown above. Given that ${a}_{1}⊥{a}_{2},$ and that $B$ is derived from $V$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$
:question/worked-solution:
Since the first two vectors are already orthogonal, we proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows:

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 2**: We set ${v}_{2}={a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 3**. Next, we find ${v}_{3}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{3} & ={a}_{3}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}\,{a}_{3}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{2}}\,{a}_{3} \\  & ={a}_{3}-\frac{{a}_{3}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}-\frac{{a}_{3}\cdot {v}_{2}}{{v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}}{v}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{3}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{3} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-\frac{4}{4}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-\frac{6}{10}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(5\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-5\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-3\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{5} \\ -\frac{1}{5} \\ \frac{2}{5} \\ \frac{1}{5}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{(-\frac{2}{5})}{(-\frac{1}{5})}=2.
$$

:question/problem:
$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 5 \\ -2 & 0 & 5 \\ 2 & 0 & -5 \\ 1 & -1 & 5\end{bmatrix},\,B={\begin{bmatrix}| \\ \frac{{a}_{1}}{‖{a}_{1}‖} \\ |\end{bmatrix}\,,\begin{bmatrix}| \\ \frac{{a}_{2}}{‖{a}_{2}‖} \\ |\end{bmatrix}\,,\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c \\ d\end{bmatrix}}
$$

Consider the subspace $V=\text{Col}(A)$ spanned by the columns ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ of the matrix $A,$ and an **orthonormal** basis $B$ of $\text{Col}(A),$ shown above. Given that ${a}_{1}⊥{a}_{2},$ and that $B$ is derived from $V$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $|\,a\,|?$
:question/worked-solution:
Since the first two vectors are already orthogonal, we proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process.

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 2**: We set ${v}_{2}={a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 3**. Next, we find ${v}_{3}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{3} & ={a}_{3}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}\,{a}_{3}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{2}}\,{a}_{3} \\  & ={a}_{3}-\frac{{a}_{3}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}-\frac{{a}_{3}\cdot {v}_{2}}{{v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}}{v}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{3}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{3} & =\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 5 \\ -5 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}-(-\frac{10}{10})\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-(\frac{0}{2})\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 5 \\ -5 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-0\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 3 \\ -3 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize ${v}_{3}$ dividing it by $‖{v}_{3}‖=3\sqrt{10}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{3} & =\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 3 \\ -3 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\sqrt{10}}{5} \\ \frac{\sqrt{10}}{10} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{10}}{10} \\ \frac{\sqrt{10}}{5}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $|\,a\,|=\frac{\sqrt{10}}{5}.$

:question/problem:
![](images/7a/7a3c82568cfaf845708a9dcee79a3ac2e0e9d2131776fd1c7daa1c598473f3b3.png)

The polar curve $r=10$ and the ray $\theta =\frac{7\pi }{6}$ intersect at the point $P,$ as shown above. What are the Cartesian coordinates of $P?$
:question/worked-solution:
The polar coordinates of $P$ are $(r,\theta )=(10,\frac{7\pi }{6}).$ We can convert the polar coordinates of $P$ to Cartesian coordinates, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =10\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{6}) \\  & =10\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =-5\sqrt{3} \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =10\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{6}) \\  & =10\cdot (-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are $(-5\sqrt{3},-5).$

:question/problem:
$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 \\ -4 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}b \\ c\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $15a+\frac{b}{c}?$
:question/worked-solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}4 & -2 & -4 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 \\ -4 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & -2 & -4 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}40 & -20 \\ -20 & 10\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}10 & -5 & 1 \\ -10 & 5 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}10 & -5 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{10} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
15a+\frac{b}{c}=15\cdot \frac{1}{10}+\frac{(\frac{1}{2})}{1}=2.
$$

:question/problem:
Let $V=C[0,1]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[0,1],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Normalize the vector $f(t)=t-1.$
:question/worked-solution:
The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨f(t),f(t)⟩}.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),f(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{(t-1)}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\,({t}^{2}-2t+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={(\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-{t}^{2}+t)|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-1+1 \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
‖f(t)‖=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.
$$

To normalize the vector $f(t),$ we divide $f(t)$ by its norm $‖f(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\frac{f(t)}{‖f(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{t-1}{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})} \\  & =\sqrt{3}(t-1)\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to $(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )(1+\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta )?$
:question/worked-solution:
First, use the identity $\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )(1+\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta ) & =(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )(1+\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }) \\  & =(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }) \\  & =\frac{(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we expand the parentheses in the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } & =\frac{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we rewrite the numerator using $1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: $\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{36-{x}^{2}}}\text{d}x\,=$
:question/worked-solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{36-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{36\cdot (1-{x}^{2}/36)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/36}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/6)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

 

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{6})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{6}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{6}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=6\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{36-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{6}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/6)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (6\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{x}{6})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the set ${{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{3}(t)}$ of polynomials from $R[t],$ where

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=1+t+{t}^{2},\,{p}_{2}(t)=1-t,\,{p}_{3}(t)=2+{t}^{2}.
$$

 

If the set is linearly dependent, find the value of $\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{3}}$ from a non-zero solution of ${x}_{1}\cdot {p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}\cdot {p}_{2}(t)+{x}_{3}\cdot {p}_{3}(t)=0.$
:question/worked-solution:
If the set is linearly dependent, then there exist ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}$ not all zero such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t)+{x}_{3}{p}_{3}(t)=0.
$$

Otherwise, if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0,$ the set is linearly independent.

Substituting the given expressions for ${p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t),$ and ${p}_{3}(t)$ into the above equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(1+t+{t}^{2})+{x}_{2}(1-t)+{x}_{3}(2+{t}^{2}) & =0 \\ ({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3})+({x}_{1}-{x}_{2})t+({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}){t}^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation is true for every $t$ if and only if 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} &=0 \\ {x}_{1}-{x}_{2} &=0 \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{3} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, we consider the corresponding augmented matrix and reduce it to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -1 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -1 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-\frac{1}{2}){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd. Hence, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable.

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} &=0 \\ -2{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-{x}_{3}.$ Substitute it into the first equation to get

$$
{x}_{1}+(-{x}_{3})+2{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-{x}_{3}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-{x}_{3} \\ -{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Finally, for any ${x}_{3}\ne 0,$ we obtain 

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{3}}=\frac{-{x}_{3}}{{x}_{3}}=-1.
$$

:question/problem:
Let $V=C[-\pi ,\pi ]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[-\pi ,\pi ],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Calculate the norm of the vector $f(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$
:question/worked-solution:
The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨f(t),f(t)⟩}.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),f(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(f(t))^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\,{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{t}{2}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}{4}){|}_{-\pi }^{\pi } \\  & =(\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi }{4})-(-\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(-2\pi )}{4}) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we made use of the trigonometric identity 

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡t=\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2}.
$$

Finally then,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖f(t)‖ & =\sqrt{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: If $\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta =\frac{5}{3}$ and $\frac{\pi }{2}<\theta <\pi $ then what is the value of $\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ?$
:question/worked-solution:
As $\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta =\frac{5}{3}$ then $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }=\frac{3}{5}.$

Let's sketch our angle $\theta $ in the coordinate plane.

![](images/aa/aaba5af0542d29ef91d4b0e17907a81e32bccc402c48b32c205e7298630b5bc0.png)

We're given that $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{3}{5}$ We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{3}{5}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{3}{5})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{9}{25}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{16}{25}} \\  & =\pm \frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the negative answer since $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ is negative in the second quadrant. So, $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =-\frac{4}{5}.$

Finally, knowing that $\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta },$ and $\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }$ we have:

- $\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta =\frac{(-\frac{4}{5})}{(\frac{3}{5})}=-\frac{4}{3}$

- $\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{(\frac{3}{5})}{(-\frac{4}{5})}=-\frac{3}{4}.$

Finally, we have

$\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta =-\frac{4}{3}-\frac{3}{4}=-\frac{25}{12}.$

We can use the laws of exponents and the algebra of limits to rewrite the given limit, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }{2}^{3x-8} & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }{2}^{3x}\cdot {2}^{-8} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }{({2}^{3})}^{x}\cdot {2}^{-8} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }{8}^{x}\cdot (\frac{1}{256}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{256})\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }{8}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the graph of $y={8}^{x}.$

![](images/85/85319605a7c7b57d4c7ed29b8d409e3169f3331775580b91b70e2be99fef7986.png)

From the graph, we see that the function decreases to zero as $x$ decreases. Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to -\infty }{8}^{x}=0.
$$

So, we conclude that 

$$
(\frac{1}{256})\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }{8}^{x}=(\frac{1}{256})\cdot 0=0
$$

:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true in relation to the function $f(x)={(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}?$

Select all that apply.
:question/worked-solution:
Let's start by recalling the graph of $y={(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}:$

![](images/28/288adf3d1da5cf4bb6e2530318aeb083b69d43639de7704f9df15672be477d0a.png)

Let's go through the statements one by one.

- Statement “Its domain is $-\infty <x<\infty $” is true. The function $f(x)={(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}$ is defined for all input values $x.$

- Statement “It's a decreasing function” is true. For $x\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ falls. Therefore, $y=f(x)$ is a decreasing function.

- Statement “$f(x)\to \infty $ as $x\to \infty $” is false. As $x$ increases, the function value gets smaller and smaller, approaching zero. Therefore $f(x)\to 0$ as $x\to \infty .$

In conclusion, only statements “Its domain is $-\infty <x<\infty $” and “It's a decreasing function” are true.

To compute ${f}^{′}(x),$ we first make the substitution $u=-{x}^{2}$ and then we apply the chain rule, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}{\int }_{-{x}^{2}}^{-4}\frac{1}{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}{\int }_{u}^{-4}\frac{1}{t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

The limit $u$ is located on the lower limit. To apply FTC II, we need the variable to be on the upper limit. Using the properties of the definite integrals, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}{\int }_{u}^{-4}\frac{1}{t}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}(-{\int }_{-4}^{u}\frac{1}{t}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}{\int }_{-4}^{u}\frac{1}{t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by FTC II, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\cdot (-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}{\int }_{-4}^{u}\frac{1}{t}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\cdot (-\frac{1}{u}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-{x}^{2})\cdot (-\frac{1}{u}) \\  & =-2x\cdot (-\frac{1}{-{x}^{2}}) \\  & =-2x\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{2}{x}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Given the functions $f(x),g(x)$ and $h(x)$ below, which of them has a jump discontinuity at $x=0?$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-3x, & x\ne 0 \\ 0, & x=0,\end{aligned} \\ g(x) & ={\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}, & x\ne 0 \\ 2, & x=0,\end{aligned} \\ h(x) & ={\begin{aligned}3, & x<0 \\ \sqrt{x+4}, & x\ge 0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
For $y=f(x),$ let's go through our continuity checklist:

- $f(0)=0$ exists $\,\,✓$

- Let's now check the left and right limits. We see that

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{-}}({x}^{2}-3x)={0}^{2}-3(0)=0, \\ {lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{+}}({x}^{2}-3x)={0}^{2}-3(0)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the overall limit exists and ${lim}_{x\to \,0}f(x)=0.\,\,✓$

- Finally, we check that the value of the limit equals the value of the function:

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,0}f(x)=0=f(0).\,\,✓
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=0.$

Now, for $y=g(x),$ let's go through our continuity checklist:

- $g(0)=2$ exists $\,\,✓$

- Let's now check the left and right limits. We see that

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{-}}g(x) & ={lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{-}}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1})=\frac{1}{{0}^{2}+1}=1, \\ {lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{+}}g(x) & ={lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{+}}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1})=\frac{1}{{0}^{2}+1}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the overall limit exists and ${lim}_{x\to \,0}g(x)=1.$

- Finally, we check that the value of the limit equals the value of the function: 

$$
g(0)=2\ne {lim}_{x\to \,0}g(x).\,\,\times 
$$

So the value of the limit does not equal the value of the function.

Therefore, $g(x)$ has a removable discontinuity at $x=0.$

Finally, for $y=h(x),$ let's go through our continuity checklist:

- $h(0)=\sqrt{0+4}=2$ exists $\,\,✓$

- Let's now check the left and right limits. We see that

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{-}}h(x)={lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{-}}(3)=3
$$

while

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{+}}h(x)={lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{+}}(\sqrt{x+4})=\sqrt{0+4}=2.
$$

So both the left and right limits exist and are finite, but they are not equal.$\,\,\times $

Therefore, $h(x)$ has a jump discontinuity at $x=0.$

:question/problem: If a curve $C$ is given by $y=\frac{{x}^{2}}{ln⁡(x)},$ calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=e.$
:question/worked-solution:
In this case, the expression for $y$ is a quotient $\frac{u(x)}{v(x)}$ with $u(x)={x}^{2}$ and $v(x)=ln⁡x.$ 

Therefore, we apply the quotient rule as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2})^{′}\cdot ln⁡x-{x}^{2}\cdot (ln⁡x)^{′}}{(ln⁡x)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2x\cdot ln⁡(x)-{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{x})}{{(ln⁡(x))}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2x\cdot ln⁡(x)-x}{{ln}^{2}⁡(x)} \\  & =\frac{x(2ln⁡(x)-1)}{{ln}^{2}⁡(x)}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=e$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(e) & =\frac{e(2ln⁡(e)-1)}{{ln}^{2}⁡(e)} \\  & =\frac{e(2-1)}{{1}^{2}} \\  & =e.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $e.$

:question/problem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(2\pi -3x)$ at the point $(\frac{\pi }{2},0).$
:question/worked-solution:
First, the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ is given by ${f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}).$

We will calculate ${f}^{′}(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f=\operatorname{cot}⁡u,\,u=2\pi -3x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=-{csc}^{2}⁡u\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =(-{csc}^{2}⁡u)\cdot (-3) \\  & =3{csc}^{2}⁡(2\pi -3x).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we find

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =3{csc}^{2}⁡(2\pi -\frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & =3{csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =3\cdot {1}^{2} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at the point $(\frac{\pi }{2},0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-0 & =3(x-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\ y & =3x-\frac{3\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: The radius of a circle is increasing. At a particular moment, the rate of increase of the area of the circle is numerically equal to two-thirds of the rate of increase of the circumference. What is the radius of the circle at that moment?
:question/worked-solution:
Let $r$  be the radius, $A$ the area, and $C$ the circumference of the circle. We wish to find $r$ at the moment when $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=\frac{2}{3}\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}.$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the area $A$ and the circumference $C$ of the circle. Since $C=2\pi r$ and $A=\pi {r}^{2},$ the relationship between $A$ and $C$ is

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}=\pi {(\frac{C}{2\pi })}^{2}=\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}C}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{C}{2\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=\frac{2}{3}\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{C}{2\pi } \\ \frac{2}{3} & =\frac{C}{2\pi } \\ C & =\frac{4\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, since $C=2\pi r,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi r & =\frac{4\pi }{3} \\ r & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: The radius of a circle is increasing. At a particular moment, the rate of increase of the area of the circle is numerically equal to one third of the rate of increase of the diameter. Determine the radius of the circle at that moment.
:question/worked-solution:
Let $r$  be the radius, $A$ the area, and $D$ the diameter of the circle. We wish to find $r$ at the moment when $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{3}\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}.$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the area $A$ and the diameter $D$ of the circle. Since $D=2r$ and $A=\pi {r}^{2},$ the relationship between $A$ and $D$ is

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}=\pi {(\frac{D}{2})}^{2}=\frac{\pi {D}^{2}}{4}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\pi {D}^{2}}{4}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}D}(\frac{\pi {D}^{2}}{4}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\pi D}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{3}\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\pi D}{2} \\ \frac{1}{3} & =\frac{\pi D}{2} \\ D & =\frac{2}{3\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, since $D=2r,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2r & =\frac{2}{3\pi } \\ r & =\frac{1}{3\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y={log}_{3}⁡(5x-2)+5$ at the point where $x=\frac{7}{15}.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y={log}_{3}⁡(u)+5,\,u=5x-2.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{uln⁡(3)},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{uln⁡(3)}\cdot 5 \\  & =\frac{1}{(5x-2)ln⁡(3)}\cdot 5 \\  & =\frac{5}{(5x-2)ln⁡(3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope $m$ of the tangent line at the point where $x=\frac{7}{15}$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}m=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{x=7/15} & =\frac{5}{(5x-2)ln⁡(3)}{|}_{x=7/15} \\  & =\frac{5}{(5(\frac{7}{15})-2)ln⁡(3)} \\  & =\frac{5}{\frac{1}{3}ln⁡(3)} \\  & =\frac{15}{ln⁡(3)}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: The distance $d$, in meters, that a car has traveled after $t$ seconds can be modeled by the function $d(t)=\frac{2{t}^{3}+7t}{t+1}.$ What is the instantaneous rate of change of the distance traveled when $t=2$ seconds?
:question/worked-solution:
The instantaneous rate of change of the distance traveled when $t=2$ seconds is equal to ${d}^{′}(2).$ 

First, we take the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{d}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2{t}^{3}+7t}{t+1}) \\  & =\frac{(6{t}^{2}+7)(t+1)-(2{t}^{3}+7t)(1)}{(t+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4{t}^{3}+6{t}^{2}+7}{(t+1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $t=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{d}^{′}(2) & =\frac{4(2)^{3}+6(2)^{2}+7}{((2)+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{32+24+7}{9} \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change of the distance traveled when $t=2$ seconds is $7$ meters per second.

:question/problem: The function $L(s)={s}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡s$ models the surface area of a flower's petal, in squared millimeters, as the flower's stem grows to a length of $s$ centimeters, where $s>1.$ What is the instantaneous rate of change of the surface area as a function of $s?$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we take the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{′}(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}({s}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡s) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}({s}^{2})\operatorname{ln}⁡s+{s}^{2}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\operatorname{ln}⁡s) \\  & =(2s)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡s+{s}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{s}) \\  & =2s\operatorname{ln}⁡s+s \\  & =s(2\operatorname{ln}⁡s+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate change of the surface area is $s(2\operatorname{ln}⁡s+1)$ squared millimeters per centimeter.

:question/problem: The function $P(v)=\frac{2v+50}{v+1}$ models the price at which gas is sold, in dollars, depending on the volume $v$ sold the previous day, in gallons. What is the instantaneous rate of change of the price of gas when $v=5$ gallons?
:question/worked-solution:
The instantaneous rate of change of the price when $v=5$ gallons is equal to ${P}^{′}(5).$

Now, we take the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(v) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}v}(\frac{2v+50}{v+1}) \\  & =\frac{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}v}(2v+50)\cdot (v+1)-(2v+50)\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}v}(v+1)}{(v+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(2)\cdot (v+1)-(2v+50)\cdot (1)}{(v+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2v+2-2v-50}{(v+1)^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{48}{(v+1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $v=5$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(5) & =-\frac{48}{((5)+1)^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{48}{36} \\  & =-\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate change of the price when $v=5$ gallons is $-\frac{4}{3}$ dollars per gallon.

:question/problem:
For the functions $f(x)$ and $g(x),$ you are given the following data:

$$
f(1)=8,\,{f}^{′}(1)=6,\,g(1)=4,\,{g}^{′}(1)=4
$$

Compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{f(x)}{g(x)})$ at $x=1.$
:question/worked-solution:
Using the quotient rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{f(x)}{g(x)})=\frac{{f}^{′}(x)g(x)-f(x){g}^{′}(x)}{(g(x))^{2}}.
$$

At the point where $x=1$, this gives

$$

$$

:question/problem: Given that $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})$ is defined for $x\in (-2\pi ,0),$ find the values of $x$ for which the function is strictly increasing.
:question/worked-solution:
The function is strictly increasing where ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$ Differentiating $f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2}),\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})>0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the domain is $x\in (-2\pi ,0),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-2\pi  & <x<0 \\ -\pi  & <\frac{x}{2}<0.\end{aligned}
$$

We know that cosine is positive in the first and the fourth quadrant. So, this reduces to

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{\pi }{2} & <\frac{x}{2}<0 \\ -\pi  & <x<0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $f(x)$ is strictly increasing on the interval $-\pi <x<0.$

:question/problem: What are the critical points of the function $f(x)=\frac{x+1}{{x}^{2}+3}?$
:question/worked-solution:
A critical point of $f(x)$ is a point $x=c$ in the domain of $f$ such that either ${f}^{′}(c)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(c)$ does not exist.

Differentiating $f(x),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{x+1}{{x}^{2}+3}) \\  & =\frac{(x+1)^{′}\cdot ({x}^{2}+3)-(x+1)\cdot ({x}^{2}+3)^{′}}{({x}^{2}+3)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot ({x}^{2}+3)-(x+1)\cdot (2x)^{′}}{({x}^{2}+3)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}+3-2{x}^{2}-2x}{({x}^{2}+3)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3-2x-{x}^{2}}{({x}^{2}+3)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

- First, we compute the points where ${f}^{′}(c)=0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3-2x-{x}^{2}}{({x}^{2}+3)^{2}} & =0 \\ 3-2x-{x}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+2x-3 & =0 \\ (x+3)(x-1) & =0 \\ x & =-3,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has stationary points at $x=-3$ and $x=1.$

- Second, we note that ${f}^{′}(x)$ exists for all values of $x$ in the domain of $f(x).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, we conclude that the critical points of $f(x)$ are $x=-3$ and $x=1.$

:question/problem:
For the functions $f(x)$ and $g(x),$ you're given the following data:

$$
f(2)=-1,\,{f}^{′}(2)=-2,\,g(2)=-5,\,{g}^{′}(2)=1
$$

If $h(x)=\frac{5f(x)+4}{g(x)+6},$ find the value of ${h}^{′}(2).$
:question/worked-solution:
The quotient rule states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{u}{v})=\frac{v{u}^{′}-u{v}^{′}}{{v}^{2}}.
$$

Let $u=5f(x)+4$ and $v=g(x)+6.$ Differentiating each, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={g}^{′}(x).
$$

Substituting this into the quotient rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(x) & =\frac{v{u}^{′}-u{v}^{′}}{{v}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(g(x)+6)\cdot 5{f}^{′}(x)-(5f(x)+4)\cdot {g}^{′}(x)}{(g(x)+6)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{5{f}^{′}(x)(g(x)+6)-{g}^{′}(x)(5f(x)+4)}{(g(x)+6)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

At $x=2$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(2) & =\frac{5{f}^{′}(2)(g(2)+6)-{g}^{′}(2)(5f(2)+4)}{(g(2)+6)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{5\cdot (-2)\cdot (-5+6)-1\cdot (5\cdot (-1)+4)}{(-5+6)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(-10)\cdot 1-(-1)}{{1}^{2}} \\  & =-9.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Calculate $\int \frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡3x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡3x}\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
We can write the integral as

$$
\int \frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡3x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡3x}\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{sec}⁡3x\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡3x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We then use the fact that $\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡3x}=\operatorname{sec}⁡3x$ to express this as

$$
\int {sec}^{2}⁡3x\,\text{d}x.
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=3x.$ Then $\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int {sec}^{2}⁡3x\,\text{d}x & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡u\cdot \,\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int {sec}^{2}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡3x+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
We can write the integral as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x
$$

We use the fact that $\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}=\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ and $\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}=\operatorname{tan}⁡x$ to express this as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡x{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =(\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-\operatorname{sec}⁡(0)) \\  & =\sqrt{2}-1.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/dc/dcc78643dd44633f778d954de32a955dc5803abf7dc059c30bbbda97bc35413f.png)

A region in the $xy$-plane is bounded by the curve $y=2{cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x,$ the $x$-axis and the lines $x=-\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $x=\pi ,$ as shown above. The area of the region is
:question/worked-solution:
The area of the region is given by

$$
A={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi }(2{cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Recall  ${cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x=1,$ so we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}2{cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x & ={cos}^{2}⁡x+({sin}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x) \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${cos}^{2}⁡x$ term, given by

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x=2{cos}^{2}⁡x-1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡x=\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1).
$$

Hence, the area of the region is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi }({cos}^{2}⁡x+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi }[\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1)+1]\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+3)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+3x)|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi +3\pi )-(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )-\frac{3\pi }{2})] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3\pi +\frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{9\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{9\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\frac{3(\operatorname{sec}⁡x-1)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡x+1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
We are using the identity

$$
{tan}^{2}⁡x+1={sec}^{2}⁡x\,⟹\,{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x-1.
$$

Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\frac{3(\operatorname{sec}⁡x-1)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡x+1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\frac{({sec}^{2}⁡x-1)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\operatorname{sec}⁡x\,{|}_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3} \\  & =3\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-3\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =3\cdot 2-3\cdot \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =6-2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Calculate $\int \frac{x+1}{4x+1}\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we pull out the factor of $4$ from the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x+1}{4x+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{x+1}{4(x+\frac{1}{4})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{x+1}{(x+\frac{1}{4})}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.

$$
\begin{aligned} & x & {x}^{0} \\ -\frac{1}{4} & 1 & 1 \\  & ↓ & -\frac{1}{4} \\  & 1 & \frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x+1}{(x+\frac{1}{4})} & =1+\frac{(\frac{3}{4})}{(x+\frac{1}{4})} \\  & =1+\frac{3}{4(x+\frac{1}{4})} \\  & =1+\frac{3}{4x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x+1}{4x+1}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int (1+\frac{3}{4x+1})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\int \text{d}x+3\int \frac{1}{4x+1}\,\text{d}x] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[x+\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|4x+1|]+C \\  & =\frac{x}{4}+\frac{3}{16}\operatorname{ln}⁡|4x+1|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Calculate $\int \frac{x+2}{2x-3}\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we pull out the factor of $2$ from the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x+2}{2x-3}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{x+2}{2(x-\frac{3}{2})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{x+2}{(x-\frac{3}{2})}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.

$$
\begin{aligned} & x & {x}^{0} \\ \frac{3}{2} & 1 & 2 \\  & ↓ & \frac{3}{2} \\  & 1 & \frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x+2}{(x-\frac{3}{2})} & =1+\frac{(\frac{7}{2})}{(x-\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =1+\frac{7}{2(x-\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =1+\frac{7}{2x-3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x+2}{2x-3}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int (1+\frac{7}{2x-3})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\int \text{d}x+7\int \frac{1}{2x-3}\,\text{d}x] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[x+\frac{7}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-3|]+C \\  & =\frac{x}{2}+\frac{7}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-3|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: $\int \frac{x+1}{3x+2}\,\text{d}x=$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we pull out the factor of $3$ from the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x+1}{3x+2}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{x+1}{3(x+\frac{2}{3})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{x+1}{(x+\frac{2}{3})}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.

$$
\begin{aligned} & x & {x}^{0} \\ -\frac{2}{3} & 1 & 1 \\  & ↓ & -\frac{2}{3} \\  & 1 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x+1}{(x+\frac{2}{3})} & =1+\frac{(\frac{1}{3})}{(x+\frac{2}{3})} \\  & =1+\frac{1}{3(x+\frac{2}{3})} \\  & =1+\frac{1}{3x+2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x+1}{3x+2}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int (1+\frac{1}{3x+2})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\int \text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{3x+2}\,\text{d}x] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[x+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|3x+2|]+C \\  & =\frac{x}{3}+\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{ln}⁡|3x+2|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{4+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{4\cdot (1+{x}^{2}/4)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}/4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{2})}^{2}.$ 

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{2}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{4+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (2\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{2})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: What is the value of ${\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x\,?$
:question/worked-solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $4{x}^{2}=(2x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=2x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $2$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{\text{d}x}{1+(2x)^{2}} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(0) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{-5/2}^{5/2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}}}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-5/2}^{5/2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}}}\, & ={\int }_{-5/2}^{5/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{25\cdot (1-{x}^{2}/25)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-5/2}^{5/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/25}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-5/2}^{5/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/5)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{5})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{5}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{5}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=5\,\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $-\frac{5}{2}$ | $\frac{5}{2}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $-\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-5/2}^{5/2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}}} & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-5/2}^{5/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/5)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (5\,\text{d}u) \\  & ={\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u{|}_{-1/2}^{1/2} \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{1}{2})-\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}+\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{25+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{25\cdot (1+{x}^{2}/25)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{25}\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}/25}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{25}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/5)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{5})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{5}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{5}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=5\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{25+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{25}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/5)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{25}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (5\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{5})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{64+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{2}{64\cdot (1+{x}^{2}/64)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{64}\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}/64}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{32}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/8)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

 

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{8})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{8}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{8}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=8\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{64+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{32}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/8)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{32}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (8\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{8})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4{y}^{3}}{{(1-{y}^{4})}^{5}}\,\text{d}y & =4\int \frac{1}{{(1-{y}^{4})}^{5}}\cdot {y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =4\int \frac{1}{{u}^{5}}\cdot (-\frac{1}{4})\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{4}{4}\int \frac{1}{{u}^{5}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\int \frac{1}{{u}^{5}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-(-\frac{1}{4{u}^{4}})+C \\  & =\frac{1}{4{u}^{4}}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{4{(1-{y}^{4})}^{4}}+C\end{aligned}

:question/problem: Does the sequence ${a}_{n}=\frac{3{(2)}^{n}}{{5}^{n}}$ for $n\ge 1$ converge or diverge? If it converges, what is its limit?
:question/worked-solution:
Suppose we have a geometric sequence with the first term ${a}_{1}$ and common ratio $r.$ Then, we have the following convergence properties:

- if $|r|<1,$ the sequence is convergent and converges to $0$

- if $|r|>1,$ the sequence is divergent

Moreover, we have the following edge cases:

- if $r=1,$ the sequence is convergent and converges to ${a}_{1}$

- if $r=-1,$ the sequence is divergent

First, we rewrite the sequence in the form ${a}_{n}=a\cdot {r}^{n},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =\frac{3{(2)}^{n}}{{5}^{n}} \\  & =3\cdot \frac{{2}^{n}}{{5}^{n}} \\  & =3\cdot {(\frac{2}{5})}^{n}\end{aligned}
$$

We can now see that this is the geometric sequence with $r=\frac{2}{5}.$ 

Since $|r|<1,$ the sequence converges to $0.$

:question/problem: Consider the sequence ${a}_{n}=\frac{{x}^{n+3}}{{3}^{n}\cdot x},$ where $x$ is a positive real number and $n\ge 1.$ What are the values of $x$ for which the sequence converges?
:question/worked-solution:
Suppose we have a geometric sequence with the first term ${a}_{1}$ and common ratio $r.$ Then, we have the following convergence properties:

- if $|r|<1,$ the sequence is convergent and converges to $0$

- if $|r|>1,$ the sequence is divergent

Moreover, we have the following edge cases:

- if $r=1,$ the sequence is convergent and converges to ${a}_{1}$

- if $r=-1,$ the sequence is divergent

First, we rewrite the sequence in the form ${a}_{n}=a\cdot {r}^{n},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =\frac{{x}^{n+3}}{{3}^{n}\cdot x} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{n}\cdot {x}^{3}}{{3}^{n}\cdot x} \\  & ={x}^{2}\cdot {(\frac{x}{3})}^{n}\end{aligned}
$$

 

We see that this is a geometric sequence with the common ratio $r=\frac{x}{3}.$ Since $x$ is positive,  $r$ is also positive. So, the convergence condition is $0<r\le 1.$ 

Therefore, the  sequence converges for 

$$
0<\frac{x}{3}\le 1\,⟹\,0<x\le 3.
$$

:question/problem: Calculate $\int \frac{x}{(9-{x}^{2})^{5}}\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
Let $u=9-{x}^{2}.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2x\,⟹\,(-\frac{1}{2})\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x,
$$

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x}{{(9-{x}^{2})}^{5}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{(9-{x}^{2})}^{5}}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{{u}^{5}}\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{{u}^{5}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{1}{4{u}^{4}})+C \\  & =\frac{1}{8{u}^{4}}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{8(9-{x}^{2})^{4}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The values of functions $h(x)$ and $z(x)$ and their derivatives at $t=2$ are given in the table below.

| $t$ | $h(t)$ | $z(t)$ | ${h}^{′}(t)$ | ${z}^{′}(t)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $2$ | $5$ | $8$ | $-3$ | $4$ |

If $f(t)=\frac{1-h(t)}{z(t)},$ compute ${f}^{′}(2).$
:question/worked-solution:
The quotient rule states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{u}{v})=\frac{{u}^{′}v-u{v}^{′}}{{v}^{2}}.
$$

Let $u=1-h(t)$ and $v=z(t).$ Differentiating each, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=-{h}^{′}(t)\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}={z}^{′}(t).
$$

Substituting this into the quotient rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =\frac{{u}^{′}v-u{v}^{′}}{{v}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(-{h}^{′}(t))\cdot z(t)-(1-h(t))\cdot {z}^{′}(t)}{(z(t))^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-z(t){h}^{′}(t)-{z}^{′}(t)(1-h(t))}{{z}^{2}(t)}.\end{aligned}
$$

At $t=2,$ this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(2) & =\frac{-z(2){h}^{′}(2)-{z}^{′}(2)(1-h(2))}{{z}^{2}(2)} \\  & =\frac{-8\cdot (-3)-4\cdot (1-5)}{{8}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{24+16}{64} \\  & =\frac{5}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: $\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{7+6x-{x}^{2}}}\text{d}x=$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}7+6x-{x}^{2} & =-({x}^{2}-6x-7) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-2\cdot 3x+[{3}^{2}-{3}^{2}]-7) \\  & =-((x-3)^{2}-16) \\  & =16-(x-3)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above in the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{7+6x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{16-(x-3)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{16(1-(x-3)^{2}/16)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{16}\cdot \sqrt{1-(x-3)^{2}/16}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{4\sqrt{1-(x-3)^{2}/16}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-((x-3)/4)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse sine:

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $(\frac{x-3}{4}).$

So, let's perform the substitution

$$
u=\frac{x-3}{4}.
$$

Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=4\,\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{7+6x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-((x-3)/4)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot 4\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{x-3}{4})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: ${\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}2x\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=$
:question/worked-solution:
Let's use integration by parts. We set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=2x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=2 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x) & ⟹\,v=-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into  the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int 2x\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & =-2x\cdot \frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)-\int (-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))\cdot 2\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}2x\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & ={-\frac{2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}|}_{0}^{\pi /6}+\frac{2}{3}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={-\frac{2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}|}_{0}^{\pi /6}+{\frac{2}{9}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)|}_{0}^{\pi /6} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}[\frac{\pi }{6}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{6})-0\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot 0)] \\  & +\frac{2}{9}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{6})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot 0)] \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}[0-0]+\frac{2}{9}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)] \\  & =\frac{2}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: ${\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=$
:question/worked-solution:
Let's use integration by parts. We set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x & ⇒ & {u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) & ⇒ & v=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int x\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =x\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}-\int (\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2})\cdot 1\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & ={\frac{x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}|}_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}-{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{1}{2}x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)|}_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}+\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x){|}_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\frac{\pi }{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{\pi }{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})]+\frac{1}{4}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\frac{\pi }{4}-\frac{\pi }{4}]+\frac{1}{4}[0-0] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[0]+0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate  ${\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /2}x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
Let's use integration by parts. We set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x & ⟹\,v=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int x\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =-x\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\cdot 1\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x{|}_{\pi /6}^{\pi /2}+{\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x{|}_{\pi /6}^{\pi /2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x{|}_{\pi /6}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-[\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\frac{\pi }{6}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})] \\  & +[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})] \\  & =[\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 0-\frac{\pi }{6}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}]+[1-\frac{1}{2}] \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi }{12}+\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
Let's use integration by parts. We set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=2x & ⇒ & {u}^{′}=2 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x) & ⇒ & v=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int 2x\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =2x\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(x)-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\cdot 2\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =2x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x){|}_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}-{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =2x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x){|}_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(x){|}_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =2[\frac{3\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})-\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})] \\  & +2[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})] \\  & =2[-\frac{3\pi }{2}-\frac{\pi }{2}]+2[0-0] \\  & =2(-2\pi )+0 \\  & =-4\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we rewrite the expression inside the square root:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+2)^{2}-25 & =25[\frac{(x+2)^{2}}{25}-1] \\  & =25[{(\frac{x+2}{5})}^{2}-1]\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{75}{|x+2|\sqrt{(x+2)^{2}-25}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{75}{|x+2|\sqrt{25[((x+2)/5)^{2}-1]}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{75}{|x+2|\cdot \sqrt{25}\cdot \sqrt{((x+2)/5)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{75}{|x+2|\cdot 5\cdot \sqrt{((x+2)/5)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{15}{|x+2|\sqrt{((x+2)/5)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\int \frac{1}{|(x+2)/5|\sqrt{((x+2)/5)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse secant:

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}\,u+C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $\frac{x+2}{5}.$

So, let's perform the substitution 

$$
u=\frac{x+2}{5}.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{5}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=5\,\text{d}u.
