:question/problem: The point $U$ has Cartesian coordinates $(1,-\sqrt{3},2).$ What are the spherical polar coordinates of $U?$
:question/worked-solution:
If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

From the above equations, we can express $\rho $, $\theta $, and $ϕ$ in terms of $x$, $y$, and $z$ as follows:

$$
\rho =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{y}{x},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=\frac{z}{\rho }
$$

First, we find $\rho :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-\sqrt{3})^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+3+4} \\  & =\sqrt{8} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, $(x,y)=(1,-\sqrt{3})$ lies in the fourth quadrant. So to find $\theta ,$ we first need to find the reference angle ${\theta }_{R}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{-\sqrt{3}}{1}| \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{3}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we subtract the reference angle from $2\pi $ to get $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =2\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & =2\pi -\frac{\pi }{3} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, for $ϕ$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}ϕ & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{z}{\rho }) \\  & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{2}{2\sqrt{2}}) \\  & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the spherical coordinates of $U$ are $(2\sqrt{2},\frac{5\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{4}).$

:question/problem: The point $S$ has Cartesian coordinates $(7,\sqrt{2},7).$ What are the spherical polar coordinates $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ of $S?$ Express $\theta $ and $ϕ$ in radians rounded to three decimal places.
:question/worked-solution:
If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

From the above equations, we can express $\rho $, $\theta $, and $ϕ$ in terms of $x$, $y$, and $z$ as follows:

$$
\rho =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{y}{x},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=\frac{z}{\rho }
$$

First, we find $\rho :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{7}^{2}+(\sqrt{2})^{2}+{7}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{49+2+49} \\  & =\sqrt{100} \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $(x,y)=(7,\sqrt{2})$ lies in the first quadrant,  we can find $\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{7}) \\  & ≈0.199\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, for $ϕ$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}ϕ & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{z}{\rho }) \\  & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{7}{10}) \\  & ≈0.795.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the spherical coordinates of $S$ are $(10,0.199,0.795).$

:question/problem:
The unit tangent vector to a curve at an arbitrary point is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+16}}\cdot ⟨t,4⟩.
$$

Find the principal normal vector at the point where $t=0.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+16}}\cdot ⟨t,4⟩) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+16}})\cdot ⟨t,4⟩+\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+16}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(⟨t,4⟩) \\  & =-\frac{t}{({t}^{2}+16)\sqrt{{t}^{2}+16}}\cdot ⟨t,4⟩+\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+16}}\cdot ⟨1,0⟩ \\  \\ {T}^{′}(0) & =-\frac{0}{({0}^{2}+16)\sqrt{{0}^{2}+16}}\cdot ⟨0,4⟩+\frac{1}{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+16}}\cdot ⟨1,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{4}⟨1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

  

Next, we find the magnitude of ${T}^{′}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{T}^{′}(0)‖ & =\frac{1}{4}‖⟨1,0⟩‖ \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${T}^{′}(0)$ and obtain the principal normal vector to the curve at the point where $t=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}N(0) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(0)}{‖{T}^{′}(0)‖} \\  & =\frac{\frac{1}{4}⟨1,0⟩}{(\frac{1}{4})} \\  & =⟨1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Note that when we find the scalar product of $T$ and $N$ at the point where $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(0)\cdot N(0) & =\frac{1}{4}⟨0,4⟩\cdot ⟨1,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(0+0) \\  & =0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the unit tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=4\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,i+(t+\frac{4}{t})\,j$ at an arbitrary point where $t\in (0,\infty ).$
:question/worked-solution:
For a curve $r(t)=x(t)i+y(t)j$, the unit tangent vector $T(t)$ at the point $P(x(t),y(t))$ is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+\frac{4}{t})\,j \\  & =\frac{4}{t}\,i+(1-\frac{4}{{t}^{2}})\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{4}{t})}^{2}+{(1-\frac{4}{{t}^{2}})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{16}{{t}^{2}}+{(1-\frac{8}{{t}^{2}}+\frac{16}{{t}^{4}})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{8}{{t}^{2}}+\frac{16}{{t}^{4}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{{t}^{4}}({t}^{4}+8{t}^{2}+16)} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{{t}^{4}}{({t}^{2}+4)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{({t}^{2}+4)}{{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${r}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the unit tangent vector to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}}{({t}^{2}+4)}(\frac{4}{t}\,i+(1-\frac{4}{{t}^{2}})\,j) \\  & =\frac{1}{({t}^{2}+4)}(4t\,i+({t}^{2}-4)\,j)\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the matrix 
$W=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 & 2 \\ -6 & 9 & -2 \\ 8 & -12 & 10\end{bmatrix}.$ 
Find a basis $B$ of  $\text{Col}(W).$
:question/worked-solution:
In order to find a basis of $\text{Col}(W),$ we reduce the matrix $W$ to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 & 2 \\ -6 & 9 & -2 \\ 8 & -12 & 10\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \\ 8 & -12 & 10\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-\frac{1}{2}){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot columns correspond to linearly independent vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent vectors that can be removed. Here, the $1$st and $3$rd columns are pivot columns, while the $2$nd column is a non-pivot column.

Remember that we need to pick the pivot columns from the *original matrix*, not from the reduced one. 

The $1$st and $3$rd columns from the original matrix are ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{3}.$ So, a basis of $\text{Col}(W)$ is $\{{w}_{1},{w}_{3}\},$ that is to say, 

$$
B=\{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -6 \\ 8\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -2 \\ 10\end{bmatrix}\}.
$$

:question/problem:
The matrix $U$ is given below. Let ${u}_{1}$, ${u}_{2}$, and ${u}_{3}$ be the respective columns of $U.$
Determine if $B=\text{{}{u}_{1},{u}_{3}\text{}}$ is a basis of $\text{Col}(U).$ 
If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{3}$, where ${u}_{2}={x}_{1}{u}_{1}+{x}_{3}{u}_{3}.$

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & -3 \\ -4 & 8 & 8\end{bmatrix}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $U$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}U & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & -3 \\ -4 & 8 & 8\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & -4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :=(-\frac{1}{4}){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $3$rd columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(U)$ is ${{u}_{1},{u}_{3}},$ that is to say,

$$
B={\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -4\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 8\end{bmatrix}}.
$$

Now, since the $2$nd column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express ${u}_{2}$ as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

$$
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 8\end{bmatrix}}_{{u}_{2}}=\underbrace{(-2)}_{{x}_{1}}\cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}}_{{u}_{1}}+\underbrace{(0)}_{{x}_{3}}\cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 8\end{bmatrix}}_{{u}_{3}}.
$$

This gives us ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{3}=(-2)\cdot 0=0.$

:question/problem: Find a tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=\operatorname{sec}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,j+t\,k$ at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}.$
:question/worked-solution:
At the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$,  the vector ${r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})$ is tangent to the curve.

Let's calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sec}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{tan}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,k \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,i+{sec}^{2}⁡t\,j+\,k \\ {r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\operatorname{sec}⁡\frac{\pi }{4}\operatorname{tan}⁡\frac{\pi }{4}\,i+{sec}^{2}⁡\frac{\pi }{4}\,j+\,k \\  & =\sqrt{2}\,i+2\,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$  is  $\sqrt{2}\,i+2\,j+\,k.$

:question/problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}-1\,,\,{t}^{3}+1⟩,t\in (-\infty ,0)$ find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $⟨2\,,\,1⟩.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-1)\,,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t\,,\,3{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors  $⟨2\,,\,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $⟨2\,,\,1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨2\,,\,1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨2\,,\,1⟩\cdot ⟨2t\,,\,3{t}^{2}⟩ & =0 \\ 2\cdot 2t+1\cdot 3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ 4t+3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ t(4+3t) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t\in (-\infty ,0)$, the only solution is $t=-\frac{4}{3}$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-\frac{4}{3}) & =⟨{(-\frac{4}{3})}^{2}-1\,,\,{(-\frac{4}{3})}^{3}+1⟩=⟨\frac{7}{9}\,,\,-\frac{37}{27}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $⟨2\,,\,-1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(\frac{7}{9}\,,\,-\frac{37}{27}).$

:question/problem: Calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}$ for the polar curve $r=2,$ given that $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\theta ).$
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\frac{\frac{d}{d\theta }(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{d\theta })}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\theta ).$ Also, since $r=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dx}{d\theta } & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into our formula for the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{d\theta }(-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\theta ))}{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{{csc}^{2}⁡(\theta )}{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{csc}^{3}⁡(\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
A particle $P$ is moving in the $x$-$y$ plane. Its position vector relative to a fixed origin $O$ is given by

$$
r=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the speed of the particle at time $t=\frac{\pi }{2}.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate the velocity vector $v.$ Differentiating the position vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t))⟩ \\  & =⟨-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the velocity when $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we substitute in the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi ),4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )⟩ \\  & =⟨-4(0),4(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

To find the speed at $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ we calculate the magnitude of $v(\frac{\pi }{2}),$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|v(\frac{\pi }{2})| & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The unit tangent vector to a curve at an arbitrary point is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{2}{{t}^{2}+2}\cdot q(t).
$$

Find the principal normal vector at the point where $t=1$, if 

$$
\begin{aligned}q(1)=-i+j+\frac{1}{2}k,\,{q}^{′}(1)=j+k.\end{aligned}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2}{{t}^{2}+2}\cdot q(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2}{{t}^{2}+2})\cdot q(t)+\frac{2}{{t}^{2}+2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(q(t)) \\  & =-\frac{4t}{({t}^{2}+2)^{2}}\cdot q(t)+\frac{2}{{t}^{2}+2}\cdot {q}^{′}(t) \\  \\ {T}^{′}(1) & =-\frac{4(1)}{({1}^{2}+2)^{2}}\cdot q(1)+\frac{2}{{1}^{2}+2}\cdot {q}^{′}(1) \\  & =-\frac{4}{9}(-i+j+\frac{1}{2}k)+\frac{2}{3}(j+k) \\  & =\frac{4}{9}\,i+\frac{2}{9}\,j+\frac{4}{9}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we find the magnitude of ${T}^{′}(1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{T}^{′}(1)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{4}{9})}^{2}+{(\frac{2}{9})}^{2}+{(\frac{4}{9})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{16}{81}+\frac{4}{81}+\frac{16}{81}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{36}{81}} \\  & =\frac{6}{9} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${T}^{′}(1)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve at the point where $t=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}N(1) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(1)}{‖{T}^{′}(1)‖} \\  & =\frac{\frac{4}{9}\,i+\frac{2}{9}\,j+\frac{4}{9}\,k}{(\frac{2}{3})} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\,i+\frac{1}{3}\,j+\frac{2}{3}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Note that when we find the scalar product of $T$ and $N$ at the point where $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(1)\cdot N(1) & =\frac{2}{3}q(1)\cdot (\frac{2}{3}\,i+\frac{1}{3}\,j+\frac{2}{3}\,k) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}(-i+j+\frac{1}{2}k)\cdot (\frac{2}{3}\,i+\frac{1}{3}\,j+\frac{2}{3}\,k) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}(-\frac{2}{3}\,i\cdot \,i+\frac{1}{3}\,j\cdot j+\frac{1}{3}\,k\cdot k) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}(-\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The inverse of the matrix $Y$ is found using row operations, as shown below. What are the row operations corresponding to the blank spaces?

$$
\begin{aligned}[Y\,|\,I\,] & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & -2 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ -1 & -2 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{3}{2} & \frac{1}{2} & 1\end{bmatrix} &  & \underline{\phantom{xxxxxx}} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{1}{3} & -\frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix} &  & \underline{\phantom{xxxxxx}} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & \frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3} \\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{1}{3} & -\frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
We write down $Y$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply the standard Gauss-Jordan method to transform the matrix $Y$ into the identity matrix. We perform the same row operations on both matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}[Y\,|\,I\,] & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & -2 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ -1 & -2 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{3}{2} & \frac{1}{2} & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{2}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{1}{3} & -\frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-\frac{1}{2}){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & \frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3} \\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{1}{3} & -\frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding row operations are

$$
{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1},\,{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1},\,{R}_{2}:=-\frac{2}{3}{R}_{2},\,{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+(-\frac{1}{2}){R}_{2}.
$$

The matrix ${Y}^{-1}$ is given by the right-hand side of our big matrix after all of the transformations have been completed. Therefore, 

$$
{Y}^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{1}{3} & -\frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

:question/problem: Find ${F}^{′}(e)$ if $F(x)={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}^{x}\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.$
:question/worked-solution:
Here, both the lower and upper limits contain a variable. However, to apply FTC II, we need the variable to be on the upper limit only. So, we can split the integral into two integrals, and rewrite them so that in both cases the variable is on the upper limit. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}^{x}\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}^{a}\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{x}\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{a}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{x}\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t,\end{aligned}
$$

where $a$ is any constant number between $\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ and $x.$

The integrand $\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}$ is continuous for all $t,$ so applying FTC II gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-{\int }_{a}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{x}\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{a}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{a}^{x}\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{\text{du}}{\text{d}x}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}({\int }_{a}^{u}\frac{t}{2+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t)+\frac{x}{2+{x}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{x}(\frac{u}{2+{u}^{2}})+\frac{x}{2+{x}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{x}(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{2+(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}})+\frac{x}{2+{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{x}{2+{x}^{2}}-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{2x+x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x))^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the substitution $u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x).$

Finally, we can compute ${F}^{′}(e).$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(e) & =\frac{e}{2+{e}^{2}}-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡e}{2e+e(\operatorname{ln}⁡e)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{e}{2+{e}^{2}}-\frac{1}{2e+e} \\  & =\frac{e}{2+{e}^{2}}-\frac{1}{3e}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The unit tangent vector to a curve at an arbitrary point is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{5}\cdot q(t).
$$

Find the principal normal vector at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ if 

$$
\begin{aligned}q(\frac{\pi }{2})=⟨3,0,-4⟩,\,{q}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=⟨0,3,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\frac{\pi }{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{5}\cdot q(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{5})\cdot q(t)+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{5}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(q(t)) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{5}\cdot q(t)+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{5}\cdot {q}^{′}(t) \\  \\ {T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}{5}\cdot q(\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}{5}\cdot {q}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{q}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨0,3,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{3}{5}⟨0,1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we find the magnitude of ${T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})‖ & =\frac{3}{5}\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}=\frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}N(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})}{‖{T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})‖} \\  & =\frac{\frac{3}{5}⟨0,1,0⟩}{(\frac{3}{5})} \\  & =⟨0,1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Note that when we find the scalar product of $T$ and $N$ at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\frac{\pi }{2})\cdot N(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\frac{1}{5}q(\frac{\pi }{2})\cdot ⟨0,1,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨3,0,-4⟩\cdot ⟨0,1,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(3\cdot 0+0\cdot 1-4\cdot 0) \\  & =0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given the curve $r(t)=t\,i+\frac{1}{t}\,j$, find all of the points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are perpendicular.
:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})\,j \\  & =i-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ [t\,i+\frac{1}{t}\,j]\cdot (i-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,j) & =0 \\ t\cdot 1-\frac{1}{t}\cdot \frac{1}{{t}^{2}} & =0 \\ t-\frac{1}{{t}^{3}} & =0 \\ {t}^{4} & =1 \\ t & =\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $t=\pm 1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1)=1\,i+\frac{1}{1}\,j=\,i+j, \\ r(-1)=(-1)\,i+\frac{1}{(-1)}\,j=-\,i-j,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the points $(1,1)$ and $(-1,-1).$

:question/problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩,t\in [0,\pi )$ find all of the points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are perpendicular.
:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,,\,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors  $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\cdot ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,,\,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t) & =0 \\ -8\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡2t & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t\in [0,\pi )$, the only solutions are $t=0$ and $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡0\,,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡0⟩=⟨0\,,\,3⟩, \\ r(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}\,,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}⟩=⟨1\,,\,0⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the points $(0,3)$ and $(1,0).$

We'll work out the indefinite integral first and then proceed with the definite integral.

First, we note that a denominator of the integrand can be factored as

$$
5{x}^{2}+16x+3=(5x+1)(x+3).
$$

So the integrand can be converted into a sum of partial fractions,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{14}{5{x}^{2}+16x+3} & =\frac{14}{(5x+1)(x+3)}=\frac{A}{(5x+1)}+\frac{B}{(x+3)},\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
14=A(x+3)+B(5x+1).
$$

Plugging in $x=-3,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}14 & =A(-3+3)+B(5(-3)+1) \\ 14 & =-14B \\ B & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, plugging in $x=-\frac{1}{5},$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}14 & =A(-\frac{1}{5}+3)+B(5(-\frac{1}{5})+1) \\ 14 & =\frac{14}{5}A \\ A & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{14}{5{x}^{2}+16x+3}=\frac{5}{5x+1}-\frac{1}{(x+3)}.
$$

Now, we integrate, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{14}{5{x}^{2}+16x+3}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{5}{5x+1}-\frac{1}{x+3})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{5}{5x+1}\,\text{d}x-\int \frac{1}{x+3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|5x+1|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+3|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We can simplify the result using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{14}{5{x}^{2}+16x+3}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|5x+1|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+3|+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{5x+1}{x+3}|+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the definite integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{4}^{11}\frac{14}{5{x}^{2}+16x+3}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{5x+1}{x+3}|{|}_{4}^{11} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{4}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Find the solution to the  following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x-\frac{1}{3}y &=2 \\ \frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{4}y &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
To get rid of fractions, we multiply the first equation by $3$ and the second equation by $4,$ as follows:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x-\frac{1}{3}y &=2 && |\times 3 \\ \frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{4}y &=1 && |\times 4\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}6x-y &=6 \\ 2x-y &=4\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We will use the elimination method to solve the system. Notice that if we multiply the second equation by $-1,$ then we will get a $y$ term that can cancel with the $-y$ term in the first equation:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}6x-y &=6 &&  \\ 2x-y &=4 && |\,\times (-1)\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}6x-y &=6 \\ -2x+y &=-4\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Adding the two equations eliminates the $y$-variable, and allows us to solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}6x-\cancel{y} & =6 \\ -2x+\cancel{y} & =-4 \\ (6x-2x) & =(6-4) \\ 4x & =2 \\ x & =\frac{2}{4} \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $x=\frac{1}{2}$ into the second equation to solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-y & =4 \\ 2(\frac{1}{2})-y & =4 \\ 1-y & =4 \\ y & =1-4 \\ y & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system is $x=\frac{1}{2},\,y=-3.$

:question/problem: Solve for $x$ where $\frac{x-2}{5x}=\frac{3-20x}{5x}+5.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we note that $x=0$ is an excluded solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

We multiply both sides of the equation by $5x,$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-2}{5x} & =\frac{3-20x}{5x}+5 \\ 5x\cdot (\frac{x-2}{5x}) & =5x\cdot (\frac{3-20x}{5x}+5) \\ 5x\cdot \frac{x-2}{5x} & =5x\cdot \frac{3-20x}{5x}+5x\cdot 5 \\ \cancel{5x}\cdot \frac{x-2}{\cancel{5x}} & =\cancel{5x}\cdot \frac{3-20x}{\cancel{5x}}+25x \\ x-2 & =3-20x+25x\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $x,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-2 & =3-20x+25x \\ x-2 & =3+5x \\ 5x-x & =-2-3 \\ 4x & =-5 \\ x & =-\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $x=0$ as a solution. But since $x=-\frac{5}{4}\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $x=-\frac{5}{4}.$

:question/problem: Solve for $a$ where $\frac{a+3}{3a}=\frac{a-1}{a}+2.$
:question/worked-solution:
We note that $a=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

The equation has the denominators $a$ and $3a.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}(a,3a)=3a.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $3a,$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{a+3}{3a} & =\frac{a-1}{a}+2 \\ 3a\cdot (\frac{a+3}{3a}) & =3a\cdot (\frac{a-1}{a}+2) \\ 3a\cdot \frac{a+3}{3a} & =3a\cdot \frac{a-1}{a}+3a\cdot 2 \\ \cancel{3a}\cdot \frac{a+3}{\cancel{3a}} & =3\cancel{a}\cdot \frac{a-1}{\cancel{a}}+6a \\ a+3 & =3(a-1)+6a\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $a,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}a+3 & =3(a-1)+6a \\ a+3 & =9a-3 \\ 9a-a & =3+3 \\ 8a & =6 \\ a & =\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $a=0$ as a solution. But since $a=\frac{3}{4}\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $a=\frac{3}{4}.$

:question/problem: Which value of $m$ satisfies the equation $\frac{2m-3}{3m}+\frac{m+5}{5m}=\frac{m+4}{15m}?$
:question/worked-solution:
We note that $m=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

The equation has the denominators $3m,5m,$ and $15m.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}(3m,5m,15m)=15m.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $15m,$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2m-3}{3m}+\frac{m+5}{5m} & =\frac{m+4}{15m} \\ 15m\cdot (\frac{2m-3}{3m}+\frac{m+5}{5m}) & =15m\cdot (\frac{m+4}{15m}) \\ 15m\cdot (\frac{2m-3}{3m})+15m\cdot (\frac{m+5}{5m}) & =15m\cdot (\frac{m+4}{15m}) \\ 5\cdot 3m\cdot (\frac{2m-3}{3m})+3\cdot 5m\cdot (\frac{m+5}{5m}) & =15m\cdot (\frac{m+4}{15m}) \\ 5\cdot \cancel{3m}\cdot (\frac{2m-3}{\cancel{3m}})+3\cdot \cancel{5m}\cdot (\frac{m+5}{\cancel{5m}}) & =\cancel{15m}\cdot (\frac{m+4}{\cancel{15m}}) \\ 5(2m-3)+3(m+5) & =m+4\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $m,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}5(2m-3)+3(m+5) & =m+4 \\ 10m-15+3m+15 & =m+4 \\ 13m & =m+4 \\ 12m & =4 \\ m & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $m=0$ as a solution. But since $m=\frac{1}{3}\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $m=\frac{1}{3}.$

:question/problem:
The matrix $D$ is given below. Let ${d}_{1}$, ${d}_{2}$, and ${d}_{3}$ be the respective columns of $D.$ Determine if $B=\text{{}{d}_{1},{d}_{2}\text{}}$ is a basis of $\text{Col}(D).$ If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$, where ${d}_{3}={x}_{1}{d}_{1}+{x}_{2}{d}_{2}.$

$$
D=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -1 & -7 & -17\end{bmatrix}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $D$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -1 & -7 & -17\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & -8 & -16\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :=(-\frac{1}{8}){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(D)$ is ${{d}_{1},{d}_{2}},$ that is to say,

$$
B={\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -7\end{bmatrix}}.
$$

Now, since the $3$rd column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express ${d}_{3}$ as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

$$
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -17\end{bmatrix}}_{{d}_{3}}=\underbrace{(3)}_{{x}_{1}}\cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}}_{{d}_{1}}+\underbrace{(2)}_{{x}_{2}}\cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -7\end{bmatrix}}_{{d}_{2}}.
$$

This gives us ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=3\cdot 2=6.$

:question/problem:
The matrix $V$ is given below. Let ${v}_{1}$, ${v}_{2}$,  ${v}_{3}$ and ${v}_{4}$ be the respective columns of $V.$
Determine if $B=\text{{}{v}_{1},{v}_{3}\text{}}$ is a basis of $\text{Col}(V).$ 
If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{3}$, where ${v}_{2}={x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{3}{v}_{3}.$ 

$$
V=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 0 & -6 & -3 \\ 0 & 10 & 20 & 10 \\ 2 & 0 & 4 & 4\end{bmatrix}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $V$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 0 & -6 & -3 \\ 0 & 10 & 20 & 10 \\ 2 & 0 & 4 & 4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=(-\frac{1}{3}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 10 & 20 & 10 \\ 2 & 0 & 4 & 4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 10 & 20 & 10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{10}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st, $2$nd, and $4$th columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(V)$ is $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{4}\}.$ 

Therefore, we conclude that $B=\{{v}_{1},{v}_{3}\}$ is not a basis of $\text{Col}(V).$

:question/problem: Consider the function $f(x)=\frac{2x+1}{x+1}.$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(4).$
:question/worked-solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(4),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(4)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(4))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(4).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(4)=x.$ For $x\ne -1,$ this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(4) & =x \\ f(x) & =4 \\ \frac{2x+1}{x+1} & =4 \\ \frac{2x+1}{x+1}\cdot (x+1) & =4\cdot (x+1) \\ \frac{2x+1}{\cancel{(x+1)}}\cdot \cancel{(x+1)} & =4x+4 \\ 2x+1 & =4x+4 \\ 2x & =-3 \\ x & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(4)=-\frac{3}{2}.$

Now we calculate ${f}^{′}(-\frac{3}{2}),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{2x+1}{x+1} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}} \\ {f}^{′}(-\frac{3}{2}) & =\frac{1}{{(-\frac{3}{2}+1)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{4})} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(4) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(4))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(-\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the largest interval of continuity for the function $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3x-12}{{x}^{2}+1}).$
:question/worked-solution:
Our function is a logarithmic function, so it is continuous over all points in its domain.

To find the domain of $\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3x-12}{{x}^{2}+1}),$ we set the expression under the logarithm to be greater than zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3x-12}{{x}^{2}+1}>0\,⟹\,3x-12>0\,⟹\,x>4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain of $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3x-12}{{x}^{2}+1})$ is $(4,\infty ),$ and it is also continuous on this interval.

:question/problem: Consider the function $f(x)=\sqrt{2x-1}.$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(3).$
:question/worked-solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(3),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(3)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(3))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(3).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(3)=x.$ For $x>\frac{1}{2}$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(3) & =x \\ f(x) & =3 \\ \sqrt{2x-1} & =3 \\ 2x-1 & =9 \\ 2x & =10 \\ x & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate ${f}^{′}(5),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\sqrt{2x-1} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x-1}} \\ {f}^{′}(5) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\cdot 5-1}} \\ {f}^{′}(5) & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(3) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(3))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(5)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{3})} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Given the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}2-\text{i} & 2\text{i}+1 \\ 3\text{i} & -2\end{bmatrix}$, find the result of applying to $A$ the following elementary row operation:

$$
{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-\frac{3\text{i}}{2-\text{i}}){R}_{1}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
Let's apply the row operations to $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\begin{bmatrix}2-\text{i} & 2\text{+}1 \\ 3\text{i} & -2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{3\text{i}}{2-\text{i}}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2-\text{i} & 2\text{i}+1 \\ 3\text{i}+(-\frac{3\text{i}(2-\text{i})}{2-\text{i}}) & -2+(-\frac{3\text{i}(2\text{i}+1)}{2-\text{i}})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2-\text{i} & 2\text{i}+1 \\ 0 & \frac{(-4+2\text{i})+(6-3\text{i})}{2-\text{i}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2-\text{i} & 2\text{i}+1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the result  is 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2-\text{i} & 2\text{i}+1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

:question/problem:
Find the radius and center of the circle whose equation is
${x}^{2}-x+{y}^{2}-4y=-2.$
:question/worked-solution:
To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-x+{y}^{2}-4y & =-2 \\ ({x}^{2}-x)+({y}^{2}-4y) & =-2 \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}x+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2})+({y}^{2}-2\cdot 2y+{2}^{2}) & =-2+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{2}^{2} \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}x+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2})+({y}^{2}-2\cdot 2y+{2}^{2}) & =\frac{9}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can factor the perfect squares and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{(y-2)}^{2} & =\frac{9}{4} \\ {(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{(y-2)}^{2} & ={(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the circle is centered at $(\frac{1}{2},2)$ and its radius is $\frac{3}{2}.$

:question/problem:
Find the radius and center of the circle whose equation is
${x}^{2}+3x+{y}^{2}-y=-\frac{9}{4}.$
:question/worked-solution:
To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+3x+{y}^{2}-y & =-\frac{9}{4} \\ ({x}^{2}+3x)+({y}^{2}-y) & =-\frac{9}{4} \\ ({x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{3}{2}x+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2})+({y}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}y+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}) & =-\frac{9}{4}+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\ ({x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{3}{2}x+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2})+({y}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}y+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}) & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can factor the perfect squares and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x+\frac{3}{2})}^{2}+{(y-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & ={(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\ {(x-(-\frac{3}{2}))}^{2}+{(y-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & ={(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the circle is centered at $(-\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2})$ and its radius is $\frac{1}{2}$

:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}s,$ where $f(x,y,z)=2x-{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}$ and the curve $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2},\,t-1,\,t+1⟩$ for $t\in [0,3]?$
:question/worked-solution:
Since $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2},\,t-1,\,t+1⟩,$ then along the curve we have $x={t}^{2},$ $y=t-1,$ and $z=t+1.$ 

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1)j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)k \\  & =2t\,i+j+k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+2}\end{aligned}
$$

  

Now, since $f(x,y,z)=2x-{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}$, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2({t}^{2})-(t-1)^{2}-(t+1)^{2} \\  & =2{t}^{2}-({t}^{2}-2t+1)-({t}^{2}+2t+1) \\  & =2{t}^{2}-{t}^{2}+2t-1-{t}^{2}-2t-1 \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(-2)\cdot \sqrt{4{t}^{2}+2}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(-2)\cdot \sqrt{2(2{t}^{2}+1)}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(-2)\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{2{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Express $3{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{12})-3{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{12})$ as a single trigonometric ratio.
:question/worked-solution:
Our expression can be factored as follows:

$$
3({cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{12})-{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{12}))
$$

Now, let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x
$$

Substituting $x=\frac{\pi }{12}$ into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{12})-{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{12}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{12}) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}3({cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{12})-{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{12})) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}).\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}y{e}^{x}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the curve $y=5x+2$ for $\,0\le x\le 1?$
:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y=y(t)=5t+2.$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨t,5t+2⟩,\,0\le t\le 1
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5t+2)j \\  & =i+5\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{5}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{26}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=y{e}^{x}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(5t+2){e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(5t+2){e}^{t}\cdot \sqrt{26}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{26}{\int }_{0}^{1}(5t+2){e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}\frac{y}{x}\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is given by $y=\frac{{x}^{2}}{4},$ $\,0\le x\le 4\sqrt{6}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y=y(t)=\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}.$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨t,\,\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}⟩,\,0\le t\le 4\sqrt{6}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(u) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{t}^{2}}{4})j \\  & =i+\frac{t}{2}\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{(\frac{t}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{y}{x}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{(\frac{{t}^{2}}{4})}{t}=\frac{t}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{y}{x}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{4\sqrt{6}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4\sqrt{6}}\frac{t}{4}\cdot \sqrt{1+\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{4\sqrt{6}}t\sqrt{1+\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=1+\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}$, $\text{d}u=\frac{t}{2}\,\text{d}t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{4\sqrt{6}}t\sqrt{1+\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}}\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{25}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{{u}^{3/2}}{3}{|}_{1}^{25} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}({25}^{3/2}-{1}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(125-1) \\  & =\frac{124}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the curve parametrized by $r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{4}.$
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,$ then along the curve we have $x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$  

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if $f(x,y)={y}^{2}$, then we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & ={(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}=4{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}4{sin}^{2}⁡t\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2})\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)\text{d}t \\  & =4{[t-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}{2}]}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =4[(\frac{\pi }{4}-\frac{1}{2})-0] \\  & =\pi -2.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{1}{y-x}$ along the curve $C$ parametrized by $r(t)=⟨t,\,t-4⟩$ for $t\in [0,4].$
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $r(t)=⟨t,\,t-4⟩,$ then along the curve we have $x=t$ and $y=t-4.$     

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-4)j \\  & =i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{1}{y-x}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{t-(4-t)}=-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{4}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}-\frac{1}{4}\cdot \sqrt{2}\,\cdot \,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}{\int }_{0}^{4}\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}t\,{|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\cdot (4-0) \\  & =-\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}({x}^{3}-2{y}^{3})\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the curve parametrized by $r(t)=4{t}^{2}\,i+3{t}^{2}\,j$ for $0\le t\le 1.$
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $r(t)=4{t}^{2}\,i+3{t}^{2}\,j,$ then along the curve we have $x=4{t}^{2}$ and $y=3{t}^{2}.$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{t}^{2})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2})j \\  & =8t\,i+6t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(8t)^{2}+(6t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{64{t}^{2}+36{t}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{100{t}^{2}} \\  & =10|t| \\  & =10t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $|t|=t$ since $t>0$ along the path of $C.$ 

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{3}-2{y}^{3}$, then we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & ={(4{t}^{2})}^{3}-2{(3{t}^{2})}^{3} \\  & ={4}^{3}{t}^{6}-2\cdot {3}^{3}{t}^{6} \\  & =64{t}^{6}-54{t}^{6} \\  & =10{t}^{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{3}-{y}^{3})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}10{t}^{6}\cdot 10t\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =100{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{7}\,\text{d}t \\  & =100\cdot \frac{{t}^{8}}{8}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =100[\frac{{1}^{8}}{8}+\frac{{0}^{8}}{8}] \\  & =100\cdot \frac{1}{8} \\  & =12.5.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$  along the curve $C$ parametrized by $r(t)={t}^{2}\,i-{t}^{2}\,j$ for $0<t<\sqrt{\pi /2}.$
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $r(t)={t}^{2}\,i-{t}^{2}\,j,$ then along the curve we have $x={t}^{2}$ and $y=-{t}^{2}.$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{t}^{2})\,j \\  & =2t\,j-2t\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+(-2t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{8{t}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}|t| \\  & =2\sqrt{2}t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $|t|=t$ because $t>0$ along the path of $C.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi /2}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi /2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{2}\,t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u={t}^{2}$, $\text{d}u=2t\,\text{d}t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi /2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{2}\,t\,\text{d}t & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\,\text{d}u \\  & =\sqrt{2}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡u\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}(1-0) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}\frac{4{y}^{2}}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is given by $y=\frac{1}{x},$ $\,1\le x\le \sqrt[4]{2}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y=y(t)=\frac{1}{t}.$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨t,\,\frac{1}{t}⟩,\,1\le t\le \sqrt[4]{2}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(u) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})j \\  & =i-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{{t}^{4}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{4{y}^{2}}{{x}^{3}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{4{(\frac{1}{t})}^{2}}{{t}^{3}}=\frac{4}{{t}^{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}3{x}^{5}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{\sqrt[4]{2}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\sqrt[4]{2}}\frac{4}{{t}^{5}}\cdot \sqrt{1+\frac{1}{{t}^{4}}}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt[4]{2}}\frac{1}{{t}^{5}}\,\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{{t}^{4}}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=1+\frac{1}{{t}^{4}}$, $\text{d}u=-\frac{4}{{t}^{5}}\,\text{d}t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt[4]{2}}\frac{1}{{t}^{5}}\,\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{{t}^{4}}}\,\text{d}t & =-{\int }_{2}^{3/2}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}{|}_{2}^{3/2} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}(\sqrt{{(\frac{3}{2})}^{3}}-\sqrt{{2}^{3}}) \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}(\frac{3\sqrt{6}}{4}-2\sqrt{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(8\sqrt{2}-3\sqrt{6})\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{5},$ along the curve parametrized by $r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩$ for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].$
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,$ then along the curve we have $x=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ and $y=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$   

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{cos}^{2}+9{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{25{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =5|\operatorname{cos}⁡t| \\  & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $|\operatorname{cos}⁡t|=\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ because $\operatorname{cos}⁡t\ge 0$ when $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{5}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+9{sin}^{2}⁡t}{5} \\  & =\frac{25{sin}^{2}⁡t}{5} \\  & =5{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}5{sin}^{2}⁡t\cdot 5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =25{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

   

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}25{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =25{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =25\cdot {\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =25(\frac{1}{3}-0) \\  & =\frac{25}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions to the equation $\operatorname{sec}⁡x=-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ for ${0}^{∘}\le x<{360}^{∘},$ what is the numerical value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}?$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that $\operatorname{sec}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.$ Therefore, the given equation is equivalent to

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡x=\frac{1}{(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}})}=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.
$$

We find the principal value:

$$
x=\operatorname{arccos}⁡(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})={150}^{∘}
$$

Since ${150}^{∘}$ lies inside the required domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}={150}^{∘}.$

Our first solution lies in the second quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}={30}^{∘}.$ Since $\operatorname{cos}⁡x<0,$ the second solution must lie in the third quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}={30}^{∘}.$

![](images/d6/d61c6dbd94be14f2a455791a584a00f19ab7b52452b3acda984c5b278a5e39ed.png)

Since the second solution ${x}_{2}$ lies in the $3$rd quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={180}^{∘}+{\theta }_{R} \\  & ={180}^{∘}+{30}^{∘} \\  & ={210}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are $x={150}^{∘},{210}^{∘}.$

Finally, 

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=150\cdot 210=31\,500.
$$

:question/problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions to the equation $\operatorname{sec}⁡x=6$ for $0\le x<2\pi ,$ what is the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2},$ rounded to one decimal place?
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that $\operatorname{sec}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.$ Therefore the given equation is equivalent to

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡x=\frac{1}{6}.
$$

First, we find the principal value of $x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{1}{6})=1.403\,348…≈1.403\,3.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $1.403\,3$ lies inside the given domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}=1.403\,3.$

Our first solution lies in the first quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}=1.403\,3.$ Since $\operatorname{cos}⁡x>0,$ the second solution must lie in the fourth quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}=1.403\,3.$

![](images/9b/9b3d60be42ec916f0e62f3a86cb1ce2aa628482c97f68f0df7c6ab533b919102.png)

Since the second solution ${x}_{2}$ lies in the $4$th quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =2\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & =2\pi -1.403\,3 \\  & ≈4.879\,9\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}≈1.403\,3\,\cdot 4.879\,9≈6.8
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral ${\int }_{C}\frac{y+z}{x}\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=t\,i+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\,j+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\,k$
for $1<t<\sqrt{2}.$
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $r(t)=t\,i+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\,j+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\,k,$ then along the curve we have $x=t,$ $y=\frac{{t}^{2}}{2},$ and $z=\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}.$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{t}^{2}}{2})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{t}^{2}}{2})\,k \\  & =i+t\,j+t\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{t}^{2}+{t}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+2{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, if $f(x,y)=\frac{y+z}{x}$, then we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}}{t}=t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{y+z}{x}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}t\sqrt{1+2{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=1+2{t}^{2}$, $\text{d}u=4t\,\text{d}t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}t\sqrt{1+2{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{3}^{5}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{3}^{5}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}\,{|}_{3}^{5} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}({5}^{3/2}-{3}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{5\sqrt{5}-3\sqrt{3}}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions to the equation $\operatorname{sec}⁡x=-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ for $-2\pi <x<0,$ what is the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}?$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that $\operatorname{sec}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.$ Therefore, the given equation is equivalent to

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡x=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.
$$

First, we find the principal value:

$$
x=\operatorname{arccos}⁡(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})=\frac{5\pi }{6}
$$

Note that $x=\frac{5\pi }{6}$ is not in the domain $-2\pi <x<0.$ To get the first solution within the required domain, we subtract $2\pi :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{5\pi }{6}-2\pi =-\frac{7\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Our first solution lies in the second quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{6}.$ Since $\operatorname{cos}⁡x<0,$ the second solution must lie in the third quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{6}.$

![](images/af/afb20de50d2fa92c6550d1e5357b2aaf07311177e3ed82e1a15facccf2c0f0db.png)

A second solution $X$ lies in the $3$rd quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}X & =\pi +{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi +\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

However, this value does not lie in the required domain. To get the solution that's within the given domain, we subtract $2\pi :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =\frac{7\pi }{6}-2\pi =-\frac{5\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the solutions are $x=-\frac{7\pi }{6},-\frac{5\pi }{6}.$

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}{x}_{2}=-\frac{7\pi }{6}\cdot (-\frac{5\pi }{6})=\frac{35{\pi }^{2}}{36}.
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=xy$ along the line segment from $(1,2)$ to $(4,7).$
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(1,2)$ to $(4,7).$

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=i+2\,j$ and $b=4\,i+7j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(i+2\,j)+t[4\,i+7j-(i+2\,j)] \\  & =(i+2\,j)+t(3i+5j) \\  & =(1+3t)\,i+(2+5t)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=1+3t$ and $y=2+5t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+3t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2+5t)j \\  & =3i+5j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{5}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{34}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(1+3t)(2+5t) \\  & =15{t}^{2}+11t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(15{t}^{2}+11t+2)\cdot \sqrt{34}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{34}{\int }_{0}^{1}(15{t}^{2}+11t+2)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{34}{[5{t}^{3}+\frac{11}{2}{t}^{2}+2t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\sqrt{34}(5+\frac{11}{2}+2)-0 \\  & =\frac{25\sqrt{34}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s$ along the line segment from $(1,2,0)$ to $(2,1,3).$
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from$(1,2,0)$ to $(2,1,3).$

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=i+2\,j$ and $b=2\,i+j+3\,k.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(i+2\,j)+t[(2\,i+j+3\,k)-(i+2\,j)] \\  & =(i+2\,j)+t(i-j+3\,k) \\  & =(1+t)\,i+(2-t)\,j+3t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=1+t,$ $y=2-t,$ and $z=3t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-t)j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)k \\  & =i-j+3\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{11}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(1+t)(2-t)^{2} \\  & ={t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}+4)\cdot \sqrt{11}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{11}{\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}+4)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{11}{[\frac{{t}^{4}}{4}-{t}^{3}+4t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\sqrt{11}(\frac{1}{4}-1+4)-0 \\  & =\frac{13\sqrt{11}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}(x+z))\,\text{d}s$ along the line segment from $(-1,2,1)$ to $(1,2,5).$
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(-1,2,1)$ to $(1,2,5).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=-i+2\,j+k$ and $b=i+2\,j+5\,k.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(-i+2\,j+k)+t[(i+2\,j+5\,k)-(-i+2\,j+k)] \\  & =(-i+2\,j+k)+t(2\,i+4\,k) \\  & =(-1+2t)\,i+2\,j+(1+4t)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=-1+2t,$ $y=2,$ and $z=1+4t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-1+2t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2)j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+4t)k \\  & =2\,i+0+4\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{20} \\  & =2\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}(x+z))$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}((-1+2t)+(1+4t))) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi t}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}(x+z))\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi t}{2})\cdot 2\sqrt{5}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =2\sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi t}{2})\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\frac{3\pi t}{2}$, $\text{d}u=\frac{3\pi }{2}\,\text{d}t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi t}{2})\,\text{d}t & =\frac{4\sqrt{5}}{3\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{5}}{3\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡u\,{|}_{0}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{5}}{3\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{5}}{3\pi }(-1-0) \\  & =-\frac{4\sqrt{5}}{3\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}{sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi (y-x)}{8})\,\text{d}s$ along the line segment from $(1,1)$ to $(2,4).$
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(1,1)$ to $(2,4).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=i+j$ and $b=2\,i+4\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(i+j)+t[2\,i+4\,j-(i+j)] \\  & =(i+j)+t(i+3\,j) \\  & =(1+t)\,i+(1+3t)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=1+t$ and $y=1+3t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+3t)j \\  & =1\,i+3\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi (y-x)}{8})$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & ={sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi ((1+3t)-(1+t))}{8}) \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi t}{4}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi (y-x)}{8})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi t}{4})\cdot \sqrt{10}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{10}{\int }_{0}^{1}{sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi t}{4})\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\frac{\pi t}{4},$ $\text{d}u=\frac{\pi }{4}\,\text{d}t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{10}{\int }_{0}^{1}{sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi t}{4})\,\text{d}t & =\frac{4\sqrt{10}}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{sec}^{2}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{10}}{\pi }\operatorname{tan}⁡u\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{10}}{\pi }(\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-\operatorname{tan}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{10}}{\pi }(1-0) \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{10}}{\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-2{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}?$
:question/worked-solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y={sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}$, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}-2{({sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{4}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,(1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,(1-3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-2{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta (1-3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta (1-3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ along the polar curve $r=2\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$
:question/worked-solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$  

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}-(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =4({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}4\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}8\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =4(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi /2)-\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the exact value of $\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{12})}{\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{12})}.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we note that:

$$
\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{12})}{\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{12})}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{12})\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{12})}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{12})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{12})
$$

Now, let's recall the double-angle formula for sine: 

$$
2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x
$$

Substituting $x=\frac{\pi }{12}$ into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{12})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{12}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{12}) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we obtain

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{12})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{12})=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{12})}{\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{12})}=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}(4x+2)\,{e}^{xy}\,\text{d}s$ along the line segment from $(0,1)$ to $(2,3).$
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(0,1)$ to $(2,3).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=j$ and $b=2\,i+3\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =j+t[2\,i+3\,j-j] \\  & =j+t(2\,i+2\,j) \\  & =2t\,i+(1+2t)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=2t$ and $y=1+2t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+2t)j \\  & =2\,i+2\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=(4x+2)\,{e}^{xy}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(4(2t)+2){e}^{2t(1+2t)} \\  & =(8t+2)\,{e}^{2t+4{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{e}^{xy}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(8t+2)\,{e}^{2t+4{t}^{2}}\cdot 2\sqrt{2}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(8t+2)\,{e}^{2t+4{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=2t+4{t}^{2},$ $\text{d}u=(2+8t)\,\text{d}t$ as follows:  

$$
\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(8t+2)\,{e}^{2t+4{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{6}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\,{e}^{u}\,{|}_{0}^{6} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}({e}^{6}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =2\sqrt{2}({e}^{6}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}(2y+3x)\,\text{d}s$, where the curve $C$ is given in polar form by $r=\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$
:question/worked-solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }, \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }$ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }$, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Now, if $f(x,y)=2y+3x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }+3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta +\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡2\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡2\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡2\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(2x+3y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =[-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =(0+3)-(-2+0) \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: $6\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{7})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{7})\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{7})=$

$$
2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{7})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{7})=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{7})=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{7}).

\begin{aligned}6\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{7})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{7})\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{7}) & =3\cdot [2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{7})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{7})]\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{7}) \\  & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{7})\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{7})} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$
