:question/problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=xy$ along the polar curve $r=\sqrt{2}\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$
:question/worked-solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$ 

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\sqrt{2})=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\sqrt{2})}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\cdot (0-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ along the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$
:question/worked-solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y={sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Now, since $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\sqrt{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+({sin}^{2}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{4}⁡\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =|\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta | \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $|\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta |=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ because $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\,⟹\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta >0.$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-0-(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=x\sqrt{{y}^{3}}$ along the polar curve $r=2$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{6}.$
:question/worked-solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{6}.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x\sqrt{{y}^{3}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \sqrt{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{3}} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{sin}^{3/2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\sqrt{{y}^{3}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}4\sqrt{2}{sin}^{3/2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}{sin}^{3/2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta $ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}{sin}^{3/2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}{u}^{3/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =8\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{2}{5}{u}^{5/2}{|}_{0}^{1/2} \\  & =\frac{16\sqrt{2}}{5}({(\frac{1}{2})}^{5/2}-{0}^{5/2}) \\  & =\frac{16\sqrt{2}}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{{2}^{5}}} \\  & =\frac{16\sqrt{2}}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{4\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: What is the general solution to the equation $\sqrt{2}\operatorname{csc}⁡x+2=0?$ Assume that $n$ is an integer.
:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation and isolate $\operatorname{csc}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{2}\operatorname{csc}⁡x+2 & =0 \\ \sqrt{2}\operatorname{csc}⁡x & =-2 \\ \operatorname{csc}⁡x & =-\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.$ Therefore, the given equation is equivalent to

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡x=\frac{1}{-\sqrt{2}}=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.
$$

Now, we find the principal value:

$$
{x}_{1}=\text{arcsin}(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})=-\frac{\pi }{4}
$$

Our first solution lies in the $4$th quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ Since $\operatorname{sin}⁡x<0,$ the second solution must lie in the third quadrant, and it also has ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{4}.$

![](images/87/87b3a90142f4c810433bd2c219382379fc508fa426567708abddb744f39771c2.png)

Since the second solution ${x}_{2}$  lies in the $3$rd quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =\pi +{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi +\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the given equation is

$$
x=-\frac{\pi }{4}+2n\pi ,\,x=\frac{5\pi }{4}+2n\pi .
$$

Writing this as $x=\theta +2n\pi ,$ where $\theta \in [0,2\pi ),$ we get

$$
x=\frac{5\pi }{4}+2n\pi ,\,x=\frac{7\pi }{4}+2n\pi .
$$

:question/problem:
What is the general solution to the equation $\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}+1}?$ Assume that $n$ is an integer.

*Hint: You may use the fact that $\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{8})=1+\sqrt{2}.$*
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that $\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}.$ Therefore, the given equation is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}+1} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =\sqrt{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the principal value:

$$
{x}_{1}=\text{arctan}(\sqrt{2}+1)=\frac{3\pi }{8}
$$

The tangent function has a period of $\pi .$  Hence, the general solution for the given equation is

$$
x=\frac{3\pi }{8}+n\pi .
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s$, where the curve $C$ is given in polar form by $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$
:question/worked-solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ and $y=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={(2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )}^{2}\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =4{cos}^{4}⁡\theta \cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =8{cos}^{5}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}8{cos}^{5}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =16{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}{cos}^{5}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ $\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}16{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}{cos}^{5}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =16{\int }_{1}^{1/2}-{u}^{5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-16\cdot \frac{1}{6}{u}^{6}{|}_{1}^{1/2} \\  & =-\frac{16}{6}({(\frac{1}{2})}^{6}-{1}^{6}) \\  & =-\frac{8}{3}(-\frac{63}{64}) \\  & =\frac{21}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Express $8\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{5})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{5})$ as a single trigonometric ratio.
:question/worked-solution:
First, let's recall the double-angle formula for sine: 

$$
2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x
$$

Substituting $x=\frac{\pi }{5}$ into the above, we get

$$
2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{5})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{5})=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{5})=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{5}).
$$

Therefore,

$$
8\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{5})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{5})=4\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{5})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{5})=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{5}).
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=xy$ along the polar curve $r=6$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$
:question/worked-solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =36\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(6)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{6}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}36\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot 6\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ $\text{d}u=6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =6{\int }_{0}^{3\sqrt{3}}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =6\cdot \frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}{|}_{0}^{3\sqrt{3}} \\  & =3({(3\sqrt{3})}^{2}-{0}^{2}) \\  & =3\cdot 27 \\  & =81\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{arcsin}⁡y$ along the polar curve $r=1$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$
:question/worked-solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{arcsin}⁡y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(1)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\operatorname{arcsin}⁡y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Let's use integration by parts. We denote

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\theta  & ⟹ & {u}^{′}=1, \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & ⟹ & v=\int {v}^{′}\,\text{d}\theta =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting into the formula for the integration by parts, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {|}_{0}^{\pi /3}-{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =(\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi }{6}-0)+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi }{6}+(\frac{1}{2}-1) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi -3}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Find the arc length of the curve $r(t)=⟨t,\,{t}^{2},\,\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3}⟩$
from  $t=0$ to $t=3.$

Find the arc length of the curve $r(t)=⟨2t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,\frac{3{t}^{2}}{2},\,2t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩$
from  $t=0$ to $t=2.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{3{t}^{2}}{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-4t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,3t,\,4t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(-4t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)}^{2}+(3t)^{2}+{(4t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{t}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡2t+9{t}^{2}+16{t}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡2t} \\  & =\sqrt{16{t}^{2}+9{t}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25{t}^{2}} \\  & =5t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $t\ge 0$ for $t\in [0,2].$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{2}‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}5t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={(\frac{5{t}^{2}}{2})|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/e6/e6de928031610e2aaf55e3dd753449f766e7dc028a6618087e7489224a73ea7d.png)

Find the arc length of the curve $r(t)=⟨t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩$
from  $t=0$ to $t=2.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,⟩ \\  & =⟨t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{t}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡t+{t}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{{t}^{2}} \\  & =t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $t\ge 0$ for $t\in [0,2].$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{2}‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={(\frac{{t}^{2}}{2})|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find $∠QPR$ given the points $P(2,4,1),$ $Q(3,4,2)$ and $R(3,3,1).$
:question/worked-solution:
Note that the position vectors of the points $P,$ $Q$ and $R$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}p=⟨2,4,1⟩,\,q=⟨3,4,2⟩,\,r=⟨3,3,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The triangle $△PQR$ is shown (schematically) in the diagram below, where we denote $∠QPR=\theta .$ 

![](images/30/3003f0cb329a8f8ef9bc315c70df4773ac1f0c54843dea1208c68bd0f6227bd1.png)

First, we find the components of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ and $\overset{\to }{PR}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =q-p \\  & =⟨3,4,2⟩-⟨2,4,1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,0,1⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{PR} & =r-p \\  & =⟨3,3,1⟩-⟨2,4,1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,-1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the cosine of the angle between $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ and $\overset{\to }{PR}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot \overset{\to }{PR}}{|\overset{\to }{PQ}||\overset{\to }{PR}|} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot 1+0\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 0}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{1}{2})={60}^{∘}.
$$

:question/problem: Consider the points $A(3t,t,4),$ $B(3t,4t,3)$ and $C(5t,t+1,5).$ Find $∠BAC$ given that $\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot \overset{\to }{AC}=2.$ Round your answer to the nearest degree.
:question/worked-solution:
Note that the position vectors of the points $A,$ $B$ and $C$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}a=⟨3t,\,t,\,4⟩,\,b=⟨3t,\,4t,\,3⟩,\,c=⟨5t,\,t+1,\,5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The triangle $△ABC$ is shown (schematically) in the diagram below, where we denote $∠BAC=\theta .$

![](images/28/285b8343208079181ac6036cf9ca16abc974d59b9262878ed40c0da9af5683d0.png)

First, we find the components of $\overset{\to }{AB}$ and $\overset{\to }{AC}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =⟨3t,\,4t,\,3⟩-⟨3t,\,t,\,4⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,3t,\,-1⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =c-a \\  & =⟨5t,\,t+1,\,5⟩-⟨3t,\,t,\,4⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,1,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot \overset{\to }{AC}=2$, we can solve for $t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot \overset{\to }{AC} & =2 \\ 0\cdot 2t+3t\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 1 & =2 \\ 3t-1 & =2 \\ 3t & =3 \\ t & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨0,3,-1⟩, \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =⟨2,\,1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the cosine of the angle between $\overset{\to }{AB}$ and $\overset{\to }{AC}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot \overset{\to }{AC}}{|\overset{\to }{AB}||\overset{\to }{AC}|} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{10}\cdot \sqrt{6}} \\  & =\frac{2}{2\sqrt{15}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{15}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{15}})≈{75}^{∘}.
$$

:question/problem: Consider the points $A(5,3t+2,2),$ $B(1,3t,2)$ and $C(1,4t,3).$ Find $∠ABC$ given that $\overset{\to }{BA}\cdot \overset{\to }{BC}=4.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
:question/worked-solution:
Note that the position vectors of the points $A,$ $B$ and $C$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}a=⟨5,\,3t+2,\,2⟩,\,b=⟨1,\,3t,\,2⟩,\,c=⟨1,\,4t,\,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The triangle $△ABC$ is shown (schematically) in the diagram below, where we denote $∠ABC=\theta .$

![](images/2c/2c81d48afacc4ac5e81ab501bc713009ea4425451fcf8dbf414672aeadbb1679.png)

First, we find the components of $\overset{\to }{BA}$ and $\overset{\to }{BC}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{BA} & =a-b \\  & =⟨5,\,3t+2,\,2⟩-⟨1,\,3t,\,2⟩ \\  & =⟨4,\,2,\,0⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{BC} & =c-b \\  & =⟨1,\,4t,\,3⟩-⟨1,\,3t,\,2⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,t,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\overset{\to }{BA}\cdot \overset{\to }{BC}=4$, we can solve for $t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{BA}\cdot \overset{\to }{BC} & =4 \\ 4\cdot 0+2\cdot t+0\cdot 1 & =4 \\ 0+2t+0 & =4 \\ 2t & =4 \\ t & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{BA} & =⟨4,2,0⟩, \\ \overset{\to }{BC} & =⟨0,\,2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the cosine of the angle between $\overset{\to }{BA}$ and $\overset{\to }{BC}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{\overset{\to }{BA}\cdot \overset{\to }{BC}}{|\overset{\to }{BA}||\overset{\to }{BC}|} \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{20}\cdot \sqrt{5}} \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{100}} \\  & =\frac{4}{10} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{2}{5})≈{66.42}^{∘}.
$$

:question/problem: Consider the points $A(2t,4,3),$ $B(5t-1,4,3)$ and $C(2t+4,t+5,3).$ Find $∠BAC$ given that $\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot \overset{\to }{AC}=8.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
:question/worked-solution:
Note that the position vectors of the points $A,$ $B$ and $C$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}a=⟨2t,\,4,\,3⟩,\,b=⟨5t-1,\,4,\,3⟩,\,c=⟨2t+4,\,t+5,\,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The triangle $△ABC$ is shown (schematically) in the diagram below, where we denote $∠BAC=\theta .$

![](images/28/285b8343208079181ac6036cf9ca16abc974d59b9262878ed40c0da9af5683d0.png)

First, we find the components of $\overset{\to }{AB}$ and $\overset{\to }{AC}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =⟨5t-1,\,4,\,3⟩-⟨2t,\,4,\,3⟩ \\  & =⟨3t-1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =c-a \\  & =⟨2t+4,\,t+5,\,3⟩-⟨2t,\,4,\,3⟩ \\  & =⟨4,\,t+1,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot \overset{\to }{AC}=8,$ we can solve for $t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot \overset{\to }{AC} & =8 \\ (3t-1)\cdot 4+0\cdot (t+1)+0\cdot 0 & =8 \\ 4(3t-1)+0+0 & =8 \\ 12t-4 & =8 \\ 12t & =12 \\ t & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨2,0,0⟩, \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =⟨4,\,2,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the cosine of the angle between $\overset{\to }{AB}$ and $\overset{\to }{AC}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot \overset{\to }{AC}}{|\overset{\to }{AB}||\overset{\to }{AC}|} \\  & =\frac{8}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{{4}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{8}{\sqrt{4}\cdot \sqrt{20}} \\  & =\frac{8}{\sqrt{80}} \\  & =\frac{8}{4\sqrt{5}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}})≈{26.57}^{∘}.
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/04/0457cb819e6f39ef9c0978e356cff788e1cf5edbef9cbf844a054ab777b70eac.png)

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a the line segment from the point $A(-2,0)$ to the point $B(0,1),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of the line segment from the point $B(0,1)$ to the point $D(1,1).$

Given that ${\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=-\frac{3}{2},$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=(x-2y)\,i+(y-x)\,j,$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$

We're given the value of the second integral, so we only need to work out the first.

The path ${C}_{1}$ is the line segment from $A$ to $B.$  It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =⟨-2,0⟩+t(⟨0,1⟩-⟨-2,0⟩) \\  & =⟨-2+2t,t⟩ \\  & =(-2+2t)i+t\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<1.$ Along this segment, we have $x=-2+2t$ and $y=t.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t)) & =(x-2y)\,i+(y-x)\,j \\  & =((-2+2t)-2t)\,i+(t-(-2+2t))\,j \\  & =-2\,i+(2-t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2+2t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =2\,i+j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =(-2\,i+(2-t)\,j)\cdot (2\,i+j) \\  & =-2-t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t+(-\frac{3}{2}) \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-2-t)\,\text{d}t-\frac{3}{2} \\  & ={[-2t-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1}-\frac{3}{2} \\  & =[-2(1)-\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}-0]-\frac{3}{2} \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}-\frac{3}{2} \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions to the equation $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=-\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}$ for ${0}^{∘}\le x<{360}^{∘},$ what is the numerical value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}?$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x},$ therefore the given equation is equivalent to

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡x=-\frac{3}{2\sqrt{3}}=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.
$$

First, we find the principal value of $x.$ 

$$
x=\text{arcsin}(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})=-{60}^{∘}.
$$

This value is outside the required domain. To get a value inside the range, we add ${360}^{∘}.$

$$
{x}_{1}=x+{360}^{∘}=-{60}^{∘}+{360}^{∘}={300}^{∘}.
$$

So, our first solution is ${x}_{1}={300}^{∘}.$

Our first solution lies in the fourth quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}={60}^{∘}.$ Since $\operatorname{sin}⁡x<0,$ the second solution must lie in the third quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}={60}^{∘}.$

![](images/5f/5fe064cdc2d97e3db894801f6f31a4679881efcf83564e24a1ea2559c15d2085.png)

Since the second solution ${x}_{2}$ lies in the $3$rd quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={180}^{∘}+{\theta }_{R} \\  & ={180}^{∘}+{60}^{∘} \\  & ={240}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are $x={300}^{∘},{240}^{∘}.$

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=300\cdot 240=72\,000.
$$

:question/problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions to the equation $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=-\frac{7}{2}$ for ${0}^{∘}\le x<{360}^{∘},$ what is the numerical value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2},$ rounded to the nearest integer?
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x},$ therefore the given equation is equivalent to

$$

Now, we find the principal value:

$$

This value is outside the required domain. To get a value inside the range, we add ${360}^{∘}.$

$$
{x}_{1}=-{16.602}^{∘}+{360}^{∘}={343.398}^{∘}
$$

So, our first solution is ${x}_{1}={343.398}^{∘}.$

Our first solution lies in the fourth quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}={16.602}^{∘}.$ Since $\operatorname{sin}⁡x<0,$ the second solution must lie in the third quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}={16.602}^{∘}.$

![](images/c8/c86fca87f7f46c0155be358f377550a4adebf1a2040c874d55c00473766745f5.png)

Since the second solution ${x}_{2}$ lies in the $3$rd quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

:question/problem: Find the derivative of  $f(t)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡t\,i+(3{t}^{2}-5t)\,j+\frac{1}{1+t}\,k$ at $t=1.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find ${f}^{′}(t)$ by differentiating each component:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}-5t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{1+t})\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{t}^{2}}\,i+(6t-5)\,j-\frac{1}{(1+t)^{2}}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to compute ${f}^{′}(1)$ we substitute $t=1$ into the expression for ${f}^{′}(t)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1) & =\frac{1}{1+(1)^{2}}\,i+(6(1)-5)\,j-\frac{1}{(1+(1))^{2}}\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,i+\,j-\frac{1}{4}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions to the equation $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=-\frac{12}{5}$ for $0\le x<2\pi ,$ what is the numerical value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2},$ rounded to one decimal place?
:question/worked-solution:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡x=-\frac{5}{12}.
$$

Now, we find the principal value:

$$
x=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(-\frac{5}{12})=-0.429\,775…≈-0.429\,8
$$

This value is outside the required domain. To get a value inside the range, we add $2\pi .$

$$
{x}_{1}=-0.429\,8+2\pi =5.853\,385…≈5.853\,4
$$

Our first solution lies in the fourth quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}=0.429\,8.$ Since $\operatorname{sin}⁡x<0,$ the second solution must lie in the third quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}=0.429\,8.$

![](images/91/912225edc2b860674da7531597fc905a1a9c821eda705dbdcfafdce32385839b.png)

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}≈5.853\,4\cdot 3.571\,4=20.9

rounded to one decimal place.

:question/problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions to the equation $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=\sqrt{2}$ for $-\pi \le x<\pi ,$ what is the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}?$

$$

:question/worked-solution:

$$

$$

First, we have to find the principal value:

$$
x=\text{arcsin}(-\frac{1}{2})=-\frac{\pi }{6}
$$

Since $-\frac{\pi }{6}$ lies inside the given domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{6}.$

Our first solution lies in the fourth quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{6}.$ Since $\operatorname{sin}⁡x<0,$ the second solution must lie in the third quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{6}.$

![](images/85/85b7b73fa793153cfedb2ffdb6825edd0845f93dbb472404862a78476a56fc35.png)

A second solution $X$ lies in the $3$rd quadrant, and we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}X & =\pi +{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi +\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $x=\frac{7\pi }{6}$ is not in the required domain $-2\pi \le x\le 0.$ To get a solution that is inside the required domain, we subtract $2\pi :$

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{7\pi }{6}-2\pi =-\frac{5\pi }{6}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=-\frac{\pi }{6},-\frac{5\pi }{6}.$

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=(-\frac{\pi }{6})(-\frac{5\pi }{6})=\frac{5{\pi }^{2}}{36}.
$$

:question/problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions to the equation $2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{csc}⁡x=\sqrt{3}\operatorname{csc}⁡x-2$ for $-\pi \le x<\pi ,$ what is the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}?$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, isolating $\operatorname{csc}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{csc}⁡x & =\sqrt{3}\operatorname{csc}⁡x-2 \\ \sqrt{3}\operatorname{csc}⁡x & =-2 \\ \operatorname{csc}⁡x & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x},$ therefore the given equation is equivalent to

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡x=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.
$$

Now, we have to find the principal value:

$$
x=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})=-\frac{\pi }{3}
$$

Since $-\frac{\pi }{3}$ lies inside the given domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{3}.$

Our first solution lies in the fourth quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{3}.$ Since $\operatorname{sin}⁡x<0,$ the second solution must lie in the third quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{3}.$

![](images/2e/2e1f1ef6c82e30b5f9a591fca432914562f949a7ed5cabc3c4eb92bfecf899ee.png)

Since the second solution ${x}_{2}$ lies in the $2$nd quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =\pi +{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi +\frac{\pi }{3} \\  & =\frac{4\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $x=\frac{4\pi }{3}$ is not in the required domain $-\pi \le x<\pi .$ To get a solution that is inside the required domain, we subtract $2\pi :$

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{4\pi }{3}-2\pi =-\frac{2\pi }{3}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=-\frac{\pi }{3},-\frac{2\pi }{3}.$

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=(-\frac{\pi }{3})\cdot (-\frac{2\pi }{3})=\frac{2{\pi }^{2}}{9}.
$$

:question/problem: Find the horizontal asymptote of $y=f(x)$ where $f(x)=\frac{4{x}^{2}+5}{2x}.$
:question/worked-solution:
The horizontal asymptote is $y={lim}_{x\to \infty }f(x).$ To find the horizontal asymptote, we apply the usual procedure of dividing the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is $x.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{4{x}^{2}+5}{2x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{4{x}^{2}}{x}+\frac{5}{x})}{(\frac{2x}{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(4x+\frac{5}{x})}{2} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(4x+0)}{2} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }2x \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

 

The limit does not come out to a finite number. Therefore, there is no horizontal asymptote.

:question/problem: What is the parametrization of the curve $r(t)=⟨\frac{t}{2},\,\frac{t}{2},\,t⟩,$ $t\ge 0,$ by its arc length $s?$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{t}{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{t}{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2},\,\frac{1}{2},\,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{4}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the arc length of the curve from $0$ to $t:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}‖{r}^{′}(u)‖\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}\cdot u{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}\,t\end{aligned}
$$

Since $s=\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}\,t$,  we have that $t=\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\,s.$

Therefore, the vector function that parametrizes $r(t)$ by its arc length is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r(\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\,s) \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\,s,\,\frac{1}{2}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\,s,\,\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\,s⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\sqrt{6}\,s}{6},\,\frac{\sqrt{6}\,s}{6},\,\frac{\sqrt{6}\,s}{3}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given the curve  $r(t)=⟨2{e}^{t},\,3{e}^{t},\,6{e}^{t}⟩,$ $t\ge 0,$ for which the arc length $s$ from $r(0)$ to $r(t)$ is given by $s=7({e}^{t}-1),$ find the corresponding unit tangent $T(s),$ parametrized by $s.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, since $s=7({e}^{t}-1)$, we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{s}{7} & ={e}^{t}-1 \\ {e}^{t} & =\frac{s}{7}+1 \\ t & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{s+7}{7}).\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the vector function $R(s)$ that parametrizes $r(t)$ by its arc length is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{s+7}{7})) \\  & =⟨2{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{s+7}{7})},\,3{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{s+7}{7})},\,6{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{s+7}{7})}⟩ \\  & =⟨2\cdot \frac{s+7}{7},\,3\cdot \frac{s+7}{7},\,6\cdot \frac{s+7}{7}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2s+14}{7},\,\frac{3s+21}{7},\,\frac{6s+42}{7}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, since the curve is parametrized by its arc length $s$, the unit tangent can be found as

$$
T(s)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}R(s).
$$

So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}T(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}R(s) \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{2s+14}{7}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{3s+21}{7}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{6s+42}{7})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2}{7},\,\frac{3}{7},\,\frac{6}{7}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: For which values of $k$ does the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{(\frac{64}{{2}^{k}})}^{n}$ converge?
:question/worked-solution:
We see that this is a geometric series with a common ratio of $r=\frac{64}{{2}^{k}}.$ 

For the series to converge, we require $|r|<1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\frac{64}{{2}^{k}}| & <1 \\ \frac{64}{{2}^{k}} & <1 \\ 64 & <{2}^{k} \\ {2}^{k} & >64.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we could remove the absolute value bars because $\frac{64}{{2}^{k}}$ is always positive.

The equation ${2}^{k}=64$ has the solution $k=6.$ Now, since ${2}^{k}$ increases as $k$ increases, the solution to ${2}^{k}>64$ must be $k>6.$

:question/problem:
![](images/a4/a45999ec28d309b3be249304e9b5175f66f2b862cd7f18f2c51b3182333e9a08.png)

Find the area of the finite region bounded between the curve $x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ and the $y$-axis, as shown above.
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the $y$-intercepts of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡y & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡y & =0 \\ y & =\pm \frac{\pi }{2},\pm \frac{3\pi }{2},…\end{aligned}
$$

From the diagram, we see that we want to find the area between the curve $x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ and the $y$-axis from $y=-\frac{\pi }{2}$ to $y=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ To find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}y \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}y \\  & =4\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡y{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =4(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =4(1-0) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-4{y}^{′}+8y=0,\,y(\frac{\pi }{2})={e}^{\pi },\text{ }\text{ }{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=4{e}^{\pi }.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the roots of the characteristic polynomial by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +8 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +4)-4+8 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2}+4 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda -2 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =2\pm 2\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)\end{aligned}
$$

We find the constants $P$ and $Q$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(\frac{\pi }{2})={e}^{\pi }$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-P{e}^{\pi } & ={e}^{\pi } \\ P & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=4{e}^{\pi },$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}=2{e}^{2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+{e}^{2x}(-2P\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+2Q\operatorname{cos}⁡2x).
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=4{e}^{\pi }$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-2P{e}^{\pi }-2Q{e}^{\pi } & =4{e}^{\pi } \\ -2P-2Q & =4 \\ 2-2Q & =4 \\ Q & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $P=-1$ and $Q=-1.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{2x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡2x-\operatorname{sin}⁡2x) \\  & =-{e}^{2x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x).\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x={t}^{3}-1,\,y=3{t}^{6}+2$ where $t$ is a real number. Calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}.$
:question/worked-solution:
To find the first derivative, we will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=3{t}^{2},\,{y}^{′}(t)=18{t}^{5}.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{18{t}^{5}}{3{t}^{2}}=6{t}^{3}.
$$

To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(6{t}^{3})}{3{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{18{t}^{2}}{3{t}^{2}} \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-3.$ Calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}.$
:question/worked-solution:
To find the first derivative, we will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\,{y}^{′}(t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)}=-\operatorname{tan}⁡(2t).
$$

To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(-\operatorname{tan}⁡(2t))}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)} \\  & =-\frac{2{sec}^{2}⁡(2t)}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)} \\  & =-{sec}^{3}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡t+3,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-1.$ Calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}.$
:question/worked-solution:
To find the first derivative, we will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}=2\operatorname{cot}⁡t.
$$

To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(2\operatorname{cot}⁡t)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =-\frac{2{csc}^{2}⁡t}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =-2{csc}^{3}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: A curve has parametric equations $x=\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}-2,\,y={t}^{7}+2.$ Given that $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=7{t}^{2},$ calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}$ at the point where $t=2.$
:question/worked-solution:
To compute $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}},$ we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\frac{dy}{dx}=7{t}^{2},$ and we can calculate $\frac{dx}{dt}$ as follows:

$$
\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}-2)={t}^{4}.
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(7{t}^{2})}{{t}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{14t}{{t}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{14}{{t}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate at $t=2,$ and we get

$$
{\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}|}_{t=2}=\frac{14}{(2)^{3}}=\frac{14}{8}=\frac{7}{4}.
$$

:question/problem: A curve has parametric equations $x={t}^{4}-5,\,y=4{t}^{5}+2.$ Given that $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=5t,$ calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}$ at the point where $t=1.$
:question/worked-solution:
To compute $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}},$ we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\frac{dy}{dx}=5t,$ and we can calculate $\frac{dx}{dt}$ as follows:

$$
\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{d}{dt}({t}^{4}-5)=4{t}^{3}.
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(5t)}{4{t}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{5}{4{t}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate at $t=1,$ and we get

$$
{\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}|}_{t=1}=\frac{5}{4(1)^{3}}=\frac{5}{4}.
$$

:question/problem: $\int 9{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x=$
:question/worked-solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=9{x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int 9{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=3{x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 9{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x\cdot 3{x}^{3}-\int 3{x}^{3}(\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x-\int 3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{x}^{3}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

:question/problem: A curve has parametric equations $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+4,\,y=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t).$ Given that $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=4\operatorname{tan}⁡(3t),$ calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}$ at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{9}.$
:question/worked-solution:
To compute $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}},$ we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\frac{dy}{dx}=4\operatorname{tan}⁡(3t),$ and we can calculate $\frac{dx}{dt}$ as follows:

$$
\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{d}{dt}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+4)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t).
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(4\operatorname{tan}⁡(3t))}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)} \\  & =\frac{12{sec}^{2}⁡(3t)}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)} \\  & =4{sec}^{3}⁡(3t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate at $t=\frac{\pi }{9},$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}{|}_{t=\pi /9} & =4{sec}^{3}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{9}) \\  & =\frac{4}{{cos}^{3}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})} \\  & =\frac{4}{{(\frac{1}{2})}^{3}} \\  & =32.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Calculate $\int \frac{{log}_{3}⁡(2x)}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{3}⁡(2x)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\ {v}^{′}=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{log}_{3}⁡(2x)}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={log}_{3}⁡(2x)\cdot (-\frac{1}{x})-\int (-\frac{1}{x})(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{log}_{3}⁡(2x)}{x}-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\int -\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{log}_{3}⁡(2x)}{x}-\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+C \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3}-\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+C \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)+1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{3}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}.$

:question/problem:
![](images/89/89efc20f1c6527d1bcd501f97ce585fb5a60e9791804f56d61f33653cf1a70d7.png)

The graph above shows the function $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡(3x+C),$ where $C$ is a constant. Given that $-\frac{\pi }{2}<C<\frac{\pi }{2},$ what is the value of $C?$
:question/worked-solution:
The parameter $C$ represents a horizontal shift of the function.

First, we rewrite the function by factoring the horizontal stretch factor, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(3x+C) \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(3(x+\frac{C}{3}))\end{aligned}
$$

The factor $x+\frac{C}{3}$ indicates that the graph of $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡(3(x+\frac{C}{3}))$ is a horizontal translation of $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡(3x).$ Comparing the two graphs below allows us to determine the amount of this shift.

![](images/f8/f8617da98ea9d9fb48b8fef588b624c6961a299233836fe433c1819b697ca0fb.png)

From the diagram, we see that our curve has been obtained by shifting $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡(3x)$ by $0-(-\frac{\pi }{12})=\frac{\pi }{12}$ units to the left. Therefore:

$$
\frac{C}{3}=\frac{\pi }{12}\,⟹\,C=\frac{\pi }{4}
$$

Since $-\frac{\pi }{2}<C<\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $\frac{\pi }{4}$ is in this interval, the value of $C$ is $\frac{\pi }{4}.$

:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{y}{x},\,x\ne 0.
$$

Which of the following is a solution to this equation?

Select all that apply.
:question/worked-solution:
For a function $f(x)$ to be a solution to a differential equation, it must satisfy the equation for all values of $x$ in the equation's domain.

We check each proposed solution by differentiating and substituting it into the original equation. 

- Differentiating $y=\frac{7}{x},$ we get $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{7}{{x}^{2}}.$ Substituting into the original equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{y}{x} \\ -\frac{7}{{x}^{2}} & \overset{?}{=}-\frac{(\frac{7}{x})}{x} \\ -\frac{7}{{x}^{2}} & =-\frac{7}{{x}^{2}}.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

This statement is *true*. Therefore, the function $y=\frac{7}{x}$ *is* a solution to our differential equation.

- Differentiating $y=-\frac{1}{x},$ we get $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.$ Substituting into the original equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{y}{x} \\ \frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & \overset{?}{=}-\frac{(-\frac{1}{x})}{x} \\ \frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

This statement is *true*. Therefore, the function $y=-\frac{1}{x}$ *is* a solution to our differential equation.

- Differentiating $y=\frac{2}{x},$ we get $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}.$ Substituting into the original equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{y}{x} \\ -\frac{2}{{x}^{2}} & \overset{?}{=}-\frac{(\frac{2}{x})}{x} \\ -\frac{2}{{x}^{2}} & =-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

This statement is *true*. Therefore, the function $y=\frac{2}{x}$ *is* a solution to our differential equation.

Therefore, the correct answer is $y=\frac{7}{x}$; $y=-\frac{1}{x}$; $y=\frac{2}{x}$.

:question/problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{e}^{-y}=4{x}^{3}{e}^{-y}$ that satisfies $y(1)=0.$
:question/worked-solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{e}^{-y} & =4{x}^{3}{e}^{-y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4{x}^{3}{e}^{-y}-{e}^{-y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =(4{x}^{3}-1){e}^{-y} \\ {e}^{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4{x}^{3}-1 \\ \int {e}^{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (4{x}^{3}-1)\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int (4{x}^{3}-1)\,\text{d}x \\ {e}^{y} & ={x}^{4}-x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the natural logarithm to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{y}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}-x+C) \\ y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}-x+C)\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the initial condition $y(1)=0$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{4}-1+C) & =0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡C & =0 \\ C & =1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{e}^{-y}=4{x}^{3}{e}^{-y}$ that satisfies the condition $y(1)=0$ is

$$
y=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}-x+1).
$$

:question/problem: Find the degree of the homogeneous function $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{3}-{x}^{3}}\,\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{x}{y}).$
:question/worked-solution:
A function $f(x,y)$ is homogeneous of degree $n$ if it satisfies the property

$$
f(tx,ty)={t}^{n}f(x,y).
$$

So first, we compute $h(tx,ty),$ and then we simplify by writing it as ${t}^{n}f(x,y)$ for some $n$:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty) & =\frac{(tx)^{2}}{(ty)^{3}-(tx)^{3}}\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{tx}{ty}) \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}{x}^{2}}{{t}^{3}{y}^{3}-{t}^{3}{x}^{3}}\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{tx}{ty}) \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}{x}^{2}}{{t}^{3}({y}^{3}-{x}^{3})}\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{tx}{ty}) \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}}{{t}^{3}}\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{3}-{x}^{3}}\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{t}\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{3}-{x}^{3}}\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{t}f(x,y)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
f(tx,ty)=\frac{1}{t}\cdot f(x,y)={t}^{-1}f(x,y)
$$

and so the degree of the homogeneous function $f(x,y)$ is $-1.$

:question/problem:
The position $y(t),$ measured in meters, of a particle oscillating with forced harmonic motion with light damping is governed by the equation

$$
{y}^{″}+4{y}^{′}+8y=8-16t,
$$

where $t>0$ is the time, in seconds. Given that the particle is initially at $y=2\,\text{m}$ with zero velocity, find the position of the particle after $\frac{\pi }{4}$ seconds.
:question/worked-solution:
The general solution to the equation of forced harmonic motion with light damping is the sum of the complementary function and a particular solution.

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
{y}^{″}+4{y}^{′}+8y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +8 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)^{2}+4 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda +2 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-2\pm 2\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
{y}_{c}={e}^{-2t}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2t).
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(t).$

The external force is a linear polynomial. Therefore, we assume that the particular integral is also a linear polynomial, i.e.

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha +\beta t,
$$

where $\alpha ,$ $\beta $ are constants to be determined. 

Substituting ${y}_{p}$ into the differential equation and equating coefficients gives $\alpha =2,$ $\beta =-2.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(t)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=2-2t,
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y={e}^{-2t}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)+2-2t.
$$

Since the particle is initially at $y=2\,\text{m}$ with zero velocity, the initial conditions are $y(0)=2$ and ${y}^{′}(0)=0.$

Solving with these conditions for $P$ and $Q$ gives

$$
P=0,\,Q=1.
$$

So our solution is

$$
y(t)={e}^{-2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+2-2t.
$$

To find the position of the particle after $\frac{\pi }{4}$ seconds, we substitute into the equation $t=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y(\frac{\pi }{4}) & ={e}^{-2(\pi /4)}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})+2-2(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =({e}^{-\pi /2}+2-\frac{\pi }{2})\,\text{m}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $D=x\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x},$ what is $D(y)$ for $y=\frac{1}{x}?$
:question/worked-solution:
The given operator is a second-order differential operator of the form

$$
D(y)={f}_{2}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{f}_{1}(x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{f}_{0}(x)y
$$

with ${f}_{2}=x,{f}_{1}=-1,$ and ${f}_{0}=0.$

To compute $D(y),$ we apply the definition of the operator $D$ to the function $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}D(y) & =D(\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =(x\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x})\frac{1}{x} \\  & =x\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(\frac{1}{x})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})-(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =x\cdot (\frac{2}{{x}^{3}})+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Write the following first-order linear ODE in standard form.

$$
(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{x+y}{x}\,.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
A first order linear ODE is in standard form if it is written as

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)\,,
$$

where $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ do not depend on $y.$

$$

$$

We have

$$
\begin{aligned}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{x+y}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{2}(\frac{x+y}{x}) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x(x+y) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{2}+xy \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,+\underbrace{(-x)}_{P(x)}y & =\underbrace{{x}^{2}}_{Q(x)} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-xy & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the equation is written in standard form with $P(x)=-x$ and $Q(x)={x}^{2}.$

:question/problem: Given a rectangular solid, find the differential $\text{d}V$ for the volume $V$ of the rectangular solid if the lengths of the sides are $a=2,$ $b=5,$ and $c=1.$
:question/worked-solution:
The volume of the rectangular solid is $V=abc.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(a,b,c) & =(\frac{∂V}{∂a})\,\text{d}a+(\frac{∂V}{∂b})\,\text{d}b+(\frac{∂V}{∂c})\,\text{d}c \\  & =bc\,\text{d}a+ac\,\text{d}b+ab\,\text{d}c\end{aligned}
$$

For $a=2,$ $b=5,$ and $c=1,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(2,5,1) & =5\cdot 1\,\text{d}a+2\cdot 1\,\text{d}b+5\cdot 2\,\text{d}c \\  & =5\,\text{d}a+2\,\text{d}b+10\,\text{d}c.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given a rectangular solid, find the differential $\text{d}S$ for the surface area $S$ of the rectangular solid if the base is a square with the side of $a=3$ and the height is $h=7.$
:question/worked-solution:
The surface area of the given rectangular solid is $S=2{a}^{2}+4ah.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}S(a,h) & =(\frac{∂S}{∂a})\,\text{d}a+(\frac{∂S}{∂h})\,\text{d}h \\  & =(4a+4h)\,\text{d}a+4a\,\text{d}h\end{aligned}
$$

For $a=3$ and $h=7,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}S(3,7) & =(4\cdot 3+4\cdot 7)\,\text{d}a+4\cdot 3\,\text{d}h \\  & =40\,\text{d}a+12\,\text{d}h.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Which of the following is a first-order linear ordinary differential equation?
:question/worked-solution:
To determine which of the following differential equations is a first-order linear ordinary differential equation, we attempt to write each option in the standard form.

A first-order linear ODE is in standard form if it is written as

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x).
$$

Let's attempt to write $(\frac{1}{y})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2y+{x}^{2}}{y}$ in the standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\frac{1}{y})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2y+{x}^{2}}{y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y(\frac{2y+{x}^{2}}{y}) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2y+{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2y & ={x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

This differential equation is in standard form with  $P(x)=-2$ and $Q(x)={x}^{2}.$ Since the equation is written in standard form, we conclude that it is a first-order linear ODE.

All of the other equations cannot be written in the standard form, and therefore they are not first-order linear ODEs.

:question/problem: If $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,$ use the differential $\text{d}f$ to estimate the change $Δf$ in the value of $f(x,y)$ from $(2,\frac{\pi }{2})$ to $(1.5,1.5).$
:question/worked-solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}x+x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(2,\frac{\pi }{2}),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(2,\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})\,\text{d}x+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =1\,\text{d}x+0\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(2+Δx,\frac{\pi }{2}+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈1\,Δx+0\,Δy.
$$

Moving from $(2,\frac{\pi }{2})$ to $(1.5,1.5),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =1.5-2=-0.5, \\ Δy & =1.5-\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈1\,Δx+0\,Δy \\  & ≈1\cdot (-0.5)+0\cdot (1.5-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & ≈-0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $f(x,y)$ decreases by approximately $0.5.$

:question/problem: If $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y+\sqrt{y},$ use the differential $\text{d}f$ to estimate the change $Δf$ in the value of $f(x,y)$ from $(0,4)$ to $(-1,5).$
:question/worked-solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =2xy\,\text{d}x+({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}})\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(0,4),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(0,4) & =2\cdot 0\cdot 4\,\text{d}x+({0}^{2}+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{4}})\,\text{d}y \\  & =0\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(0+Δx,4+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈0\,Δx+\frac{1}{4}\,Δy.
$$

Moving from $(0,4)$ to $(-1,5),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =-1-0=-1, \\ Δy & =5-4=1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈0\,Δx+\frac{1}{4}\,Δy \\  & ≈0\cdot (-1)+\frac{1}{4}\cdot (1) \\  & ≈0.25.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $f(x,y)$ increases by approximately $0.25.$

:question/problem: If $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡y,$ use the differential $\text{d}f$ to estimate the change $Δf$ in the value of $f(x,y)$ from $(0.5,1)$ to $(0,2).$
:question/worked-solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =2x\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(0.5,1),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(0.5,1) & =2\cdot 0.5\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =1\,\text{d}x+1\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(0.5+Δx,1+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈1\,Δx+1\,Δy.
$$

Moving from $(0.5,1)$ to $(0,2),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =0-0.5=-0.5, \\ Δy & =2-1=1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈1\,Δx+1\,Δy \\  & ≈1\cdot (-0.5)+1\cdot (1) \\  & ≈0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $f(x,y)$ increases by approximately $0.5.$

:question/problem: If $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y,$ use the differential $\text{d}f$ to estimate the change $Δf$ in the value of $f(x,y)$ from $(0,e)$ to $(1,2).$
:question/worked-solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,\text{d}x+\frac{x}{y}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(0,e),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(0,e) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡e\,\text{d}x+\frac{0}{e}\,\text{d}y \\  & =1\,\text{d}x+0\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(0+Δx,e+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈1\,Δx+0\,Δy.
$$

Moving from $(0,e)$ to $(1,2),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =1-0=1, \\ Δy & =2-e.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈1\,Δx+0\,Δy \\  & ≈1\cdot (1)+0\cdot (2-e) \\  & ≈1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $f(x,y)$ increases by approximately $1.$

:question/problem: If $f(x,y)=xy+x{e}^{y},$ use the differential $\text{d}f$ to estimate the change $Δf$ in the value of $f(x,y)$ from $(2,0)$ to $(1,-0.5).$
:question/worked-solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =(y+{e}^{y})\,\text{d}x+(x+x{e}^{y})\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(2,0),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(2,0) & =(0+{e}^{0})\,\text{d}x+(2+2\cdot {e}^{0})\,\text{d}y \\  & =1\,\text{d}x+4\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(2+Δx,0+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈1\,Δx+4\,Δy.
$$

Moving from $(2,0)$ to $(1,-0.5),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =1-2=-1, \\ Δy & =-0.5-0=-0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈1\,Δx+4\,Δy \\  & ≈1\cdot (-1)+4\cdot (-0.5) \\  & ≈-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $f(x,y)$ decreases by approximately $3.$

:question/problem: If $f(x,y,z)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+y\operatorname{cos}⁡z,$ use the differential $\text{d}f$ to estimate the change $Δf$ in the value of $f(x,y,z)$ from $(1,0,\frac{\pi }{2})$ to $(0,1,1).$
:question/worked-solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂z})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}x+(x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{cos}⁡z)\,\text{d}y-y\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,\text{d}z\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(1,0,\frac{\pi }{2}),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(1,0,\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)\,\text{d}x+(1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))\,\text{d}y-0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})\,\text{d}z \\  & =0\,\text{d}x+1\,\text{d}y+0\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(1+Δx,0+Δy,\frac{\pi }{2}+Δz),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈0\,Δx+1\,Δy+0\,Δz.
$$

Moving from $(1,0,\frac{\pi }{2})$ to $(0,1,1),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =0-1=-1, \\ Δy & =1-0=1 \\ Δz & =1-\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈0\,Δx+1\,Δy+0\,Δz \\  & ≈0\cdot (-1)+1\cdot (1)+0\cdot (1-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & ≈1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $f(x,y,z)$ increases by approximately $1.$

:question/problem: Estimate $\operatorname{cos}⁡(1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(0.12)$ using a differential $\text{d}f$ of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ at the point $(\frac{\pi }{3},0).$
:question/worked-solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(\frac{\pi }{3},0),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\operatorname{sin}⁡0\,\text{d}x+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\operatorname{cos}⁡0\,\text{d}y \\  & =0\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(\frac{\pi }{3}+Δx,0+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈0\,Δx+\frac{1}{2}\,Δy
$$

Note that 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(0.12)=f(1,0.12),
$$

so we want to move to the point $(1,0.12).$

Moving from $(\frac{\pi }{3},0)$ to $(1,0.12),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =1-\frac{\pi }{3}, \\ Δy & =0.12-0=0.12.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈0\cdot (1-\frac{\pi }{3})+\frac{1}{2}\cdot (0.12) \\  & ≈0+0.5\cdot 0.12 \\  & ≈0.06.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that the value of $f$ increases by about $0.06.$ Consequently, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,0.12) & ≈f(\frac{\pi }{3},0)+0.06 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(0.12) & ≈\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+0.06 \\  & ≈0+0.06 \\  & ≈0.06.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Estimate the value of ${e}^{\sqrt{10}-3.2}$ using a differential $\text{d}f$ of the function $f(x,y)={e}^{\sqrt{x}-y}$ at the point $(9,3).$ Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{9}-3}}{2\sqrt{9}}\,\text{d}x-{e}^{\sqrt{9}-3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{{e}^{0}}{6}\,\text{d}x-{e}^{0}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}x-1\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(9+Δx,3+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈\frac{1}{6}\,Δx-1\,Δy
$$

Note that 

$$
{e}^{\sqrt{10}-3.2}=f(10,3.2),
$$

so we want to move to the point $(10,3.2).$

Moving from $(9,3)$ to $(10,3.2),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =10-9=1, \\ Δy & =3.2-3=0.2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈\frac{1}{6}\cdot 1-1\cdot 0.2 \\  & ≈0.167-0.2 \\  & ≈-0.033.\end{aligned}

This means that the value of $f$ decreases by about $0.033.$ Consequently, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(10,3.2) & ≈f(9,3)-0.033 \\ {e}^{\sqrt{10}-3.2} & ≈{e}^{\sqrt{9}-3}-0.033 \\  & ≈1-0.033 \\  & ≈0.967.\end{aligned}

:question/problem: Given that the expression $2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+10\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ can be written as $R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+ϕ)$ with ${0}^{∘}<ϕ<{90}^{∘}$ and $R>0$, what is the value of $ϕ?$
:question/worked-solution:
The sum formula for sine gives

$$
\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+ϕ) & =R(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) \\  & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡x+R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+10\operatorname{cos}⁡x=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+10\operatorname{cos}⁡x=(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ &=2 \\ R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ &=10\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Dividing the second equation by the first, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ} & =\frac{10}{2} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡ϕ & =5 \\ ϕ & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(5).\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that the expression $2\operatorname{sin}⁡x-8\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ can be written as $R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-ϕ)$ with ${0}^{∘}<ϕ<{90}^{∘}$ and $R>0$, what is the value of $ϕ?$
:question/worked-solution:
The difference formula for sine gives

$$
\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-ϕ) & =R(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) \\  & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡x-R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
2\operatorname{sin}⁡x-8\operatorname{cos}⁡x=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
2\operatorname{sin}⁡x-8\operatorname{cos}⁡x=(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡x-(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ &=2 \\ R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ &=8\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Dividing the second equation by the first, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ} & =\frac{8}{2} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡ϕ & =4 \\ ϕ & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(4).\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions to the equation $4=4-\frac{3\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{2}$ for $-2\pi <x<0,$ what is the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}?$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to isolate $\operatorname{cot}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =4-\frac{3\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{2} \\ 0 & =-\frac{3\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{2} \\ \operatorname{cot}⁡x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We can't find an equivalent equation involving tangent, since this would lead to us dividing by $0:$

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{1}{0}=\text{undefined}
$$

However, we can instead find an equivalent equation using the fact that $\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}:$

$$
\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}=0
$$

In this case, we can find the principal solution as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =0 \\ x & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡0 \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\frac{\pi }{2}$ lies outside the given domain, it is not a solution.

To find more solutions, we subtract integer multiples of $\pi $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =-\pi +x=-\pi +\frac{\pi }{2}=-\frac{\pi }{2}, \\ {x}_{2} & =-2\pi +x=-2\pi +\frac{\pi }{2}=-\frac{3\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, our solutions are $x=-\frac{3\pi }{2},-\frac{\pi }{2}.$

Finally, 

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=(-\frac{3\pi }{2})\cdot (-\frac{\pi }{2})=\frac{3{\pi }^{2}}{4}.
$$

:question/problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions to the equation $7\operatorname{cot}⁡x-5=-5-3\operatorname{cot}⁡x$ for $-\pi <x<\pi ,$ what is the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}?$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to isolate $\operatorname{cot}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}7\operatorname{cot}⁡x-5 & =-5-3\operatorname{cot}⁡x \\ 10\operatorname{cot}⁡x & =0 \\ \operatorname{cot}⁡x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We can't find an equivalent equation involving tangent, since this would lead to us dividing by $0:$

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{1}{0}=\text{undefined}
$$

However, we can instead find an equivalent equation using the fact that $\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}:$

$$
\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}=0
$$

In this case, we can find the principal solution as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =0 \\ x & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡0 \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since this value lies inside the desired domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}=\frac{\pi }{2}.$

To find more solutions, we subtract integer multiples of $\pi $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-\pi  \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}-\pi  \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, our solutions are $x=\frac{\pi }{2},-\frac{\pi }{2}.$

Finally, 

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot (-\frac{\pi }{2})=-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{|x+1|\sqrt{(x+1)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{|x+1|\sqrt{(x+1)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse secant:

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $(x+1).$

So, let's perform the substitution 

$$
u=x+1.
$$

Differentiating, we get

\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
