:question/problem: Find the radius of the osculating circle at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ for the curve $r(t)=⟨{cos}^{3}⁡t,{sin}^{3}⁡t⟩.$
:question/worked-solution:
Since we are given only the curve $r(t)$, we will use the cross product formula to find the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t),$ ${r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})$ and $‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({cos}^{3}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({sin}^{3}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,3{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =⟨-3{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}),\,3{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})⟩ \\  & =⟨-3{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2}(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}),3{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2}(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})⟩ \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}⟨-1,\,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖ & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}\cdot \sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{″}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨6\operatorname{cos}⁡t{sin}^{2}⁡t-3{cos}^{3}⁡t,\,6\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t-3{sin}^{3}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =⟨6\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}){sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-3{cos}^{3}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}),\,6\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}){cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-3{sin}^{3}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})⟩ \\  & =⟨6(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}){(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2}-3{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{3},6(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}){(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2}-3{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{3}⟩ \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}⟨1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})$ and ${r}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4})$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})\times {r}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4})⟨-1,\,1,\,0⟩\times (\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4})⟨1,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & ={(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4})}^{2}\cdot \left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \,-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{9}{8}\cdot \left|\begin{aligned}\,-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =-\frac{9}{8}\cdot 2\,k \\  & =-\frac{9}{4}\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})\times {r}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖ & =\frac{9}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of curvature at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\frac{{‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})\times {r}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖}=\frac{{(\frac{3}{2})}^{3}}{\,\frac{9}{4}\,}=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the radius of the osculating circle at the point where $t=4$ for the curve $r(t)=⟨4\sqrt{t-3},t-1⟩.$
:question/worked-solution:
Since we are given only the curve $r(t)$, we will use the cross product formula to find the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t),$ ${r}^{′}(4)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(4)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\sqrt{t-3}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2}{\sqrt{t-3}},1⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(4) & =⟨2,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(4)‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{″}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2}{\sqrt{t-3}}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{\sqrt{(t-3)^{3}}},0⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(4) & =⟨-1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(4)$ and ${r}^{″}(4)$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(4)\times {r}^{″}(4) & =⟨2,1,0⟩\times ⟨-1,0,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(4)\times {r}^{″}(4)‖ & =1\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, the radius of the osculating circle at  $t=4$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(4) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(4){‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(4)\times {r}^{″}(4)‖}=\frac{(\sqrt{5})^{3}}{\,1\,}=5\sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨\text{ }5{t}^{4},\,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨5{t}^{4},\,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int 5{t}^{4}\,\text{d}t,\int (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{5}+{c}_{1},\,\frac{1}{t}+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{5},\,\frac{1}{t}⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{5},\,\frac{1}{t}⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

:question/problem: Find the slope of $f(x)={x}^{2}{sin}^{3}⁡x$ at $x=0.$
:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

This question requires the product rule. Let $u(x)={x}^{2}$ and $v(x)={sin}^{3}⁡x.$ Then

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=2x,\,{v}^{′}(x)=3{sin}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $v.$

Now, applying the product rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & ={u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)+u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x) \\  & =(2x)({sin}^{3}⁡x)+({x}^{2})(3{sin}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =2x{sin}^{3}⁡x+3{x}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope at $x=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x})|}_{x=0} & =2\cdot 0\cdot {sin}^{3}⁡(0)+3\cdot {0}^{2}\cdot {sin}^{2}⁡(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at an arbitrary point, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{4{e}^{4t}+1}}⟨2{e}^{2t},1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ denotes the unit tangent vector.
:question/worked-solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t),
$$

where the principal normal vector $N(t)$ is given by

$$
N(t)=\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find the principal normal $N(t).$ To do this, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2{e}^{2t}}{\sqrt{4{e}^{4t}+1}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{4{e}^{4t}+1}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{4{e}^{2t}}{(4{e}^{4t}+1)^{3/2}},\,-\frac{8{e}^{4t}}{(4{e}^{4t}+1)^{3/2}},\,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{4{e}^{2t}}{(4{e}^{4t}+1)^{3/2}}⟨1,\,-2{e}^{2t},\,0⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{4{e}^{2t}}{(4{e}^{4t}+1)^{3/2}}\sqrt{(1)^{2}+{(-2{e}^{2t})}^{2}+{(0)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4{e}^{2t}}{(4{e}^{4t}+1)^{3/2}}\sqrt{4{e}^{4t}+1} \\  & =\frac{4{e}^{2t}}{4{e}^{4t}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize ${T}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{\frac{4{e}^{2t}}{(4{e}^{4t}+1)^{3/2}}⟨1,-2{e}^{2t},0⟩}{(\frac{4{e}^{2t}}{4{e}^{4t}+1})}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4{e}^{4t}+1}}⟨1,\,-2{e}^{2t},\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{4{e}^{4t}+1}}⟨2{e}^{2t},1,0⟩\times \frac{1}{\sqrt{4{e}^{4t}+1}}⟨1,\,-2{e}^{2t},\,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{4{e}^{4t}+1}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2{e}^{2t} & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2{e}^{2t} & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{4{e}^{4t}+1}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2{e}^{2t} & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}2{e}^{2t} & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}2{e}^{2t} & 1 \\ 1 & -2{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{4{e}^{4t}+1}⟨0+0,-(0-0),-4{e}^{4t}-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{4{e}^{4t}+1}⟨0,0,-(4{e}^{4t}+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/cd/cdce64bf5d02850bbedc2b89af3b2e7447b733831c09d1955e4a9ee97e82d556.png)

The graph above shows $y=k{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}+c.$ Find the value of $k-c.$
:question/worked-solution:
The horizontal asymptote of the curve $y=k{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}+c$ is $y=c.$ In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is $y=2.$ Hence, $c=2.$

We can solve for $k$ by finding a point on the graph and substituting for $x$ and $y.$ The labeled point on the graph is $(0,4),$ so we substitute $x=0$ and $y=4$ into the function and solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}k{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}+c & =y \\ k{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}+2 & =y \\ k{(\frac{1}{2})}^{0}+2 & =4 \\ k+2 & =4 \\ k & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
k-c=2-2=0.
$$

The equation of the curve is $y=2{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}+2.$

Find the area of the closed region between the curve $y=4-{x}^{2}$ and the $x$-axis, shown above.
:question/worked-solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}(4-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{\int }_{-2}^{2}\,\text{d}x-{\int }_{-2}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4x{|}_{-2}^{2}-{\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}|}_{-2}^{2} \\  & =4(2-(-2))-(\frac{8}{3}-(-\frac{8}{3})) \\  & =16-\frac{16}{3} \\  & =\frac{32}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/answer-fields.:answer-field/key: ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
$S={{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product

:question/problem:
Consider the following set of functions:

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=t,\,{f}_{2}(t)={t}^{2},\,{f}_{3}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $C[-\pi ,\pi ]$ of continuous functions over $[-\pi ,\pi ]$ is defined as 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?

*Hint: $⟨{f}_{2},{f}_{3}⟩=0.$*

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement “${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product” is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & =⟨t,{t}^{2}⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }t\cdot {t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{{t}^{4}}{4}{|}_{-\pi }^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{4}}{4}-(\frac{(-\pi )^{4}}{4}) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement “${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product” is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩=⟨t,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's use integration by parts. We denote

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⟹ & {u}^{′}=1, \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡t & ⟹ & v=\int {v}^{′}\,\text{d}t=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t=-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, applying the integration by parts formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =uv{|}_{-\pi }^{\pi }-{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{u}^{′}v\,\text{d}t \\  & =(-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t){|}_{-\pi }^{\pi }-{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(-\pi \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-(-(-\pi )\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(-\pi )))+\operatorname{sin}⁡t{|}_{-\pi }^{\pi } \\  & =\pi +\pi +(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )) \\  & =2\pi \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement “$S={{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product” is false. Since ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is “${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product” only.

${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
$S={{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product

:question/problem:
Consider the following set of functions:

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=t,\,{f}_{2}(t)={t}^{2},\,{f}_{3}(t)=t-\frac{5}{12}{t}^{3}
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $C[-2,2]$ of continuous functions over $[-2,2]$ is defined as 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{-2}^{2}f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?

*Hint: $⟨{f}_{2},{f}_{3}⟩=0.$*

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement “${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product” is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & =⟨t,{t}^{2}⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}t\cdot {t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{{t}^{4}}{4}{|}_{-2}^{2} \\  & =\frac{{2}^{4}}{4}-(\frac{(-2)^{4}}{4}) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement “${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product” is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨t,t-\frac{5}{12}{t}^{3}⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}t\cdot (t-\frac{5}{12}{t}^{3})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}({t}^{2}-\frac{5}{12}{t}^{4})\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-\frac{1}{12}{t}^{5}){|}_{-2}^{2} \\  & =\frac{{2}^{3}}{3}-\frac{1}{12}{2}^{5}-(\frac{(-2)^{3}}{3}-\frac{1}{12}(-2)^{5}) \\  & =\frac{16}{3}-\frac{16}{3} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement “$S={{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product” is true. Since ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t),$ ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t),$ and ${f}_{2}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t),$ the set $S$ is orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is “${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product”; “${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product”; “$S={{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product”.

:question/problem: Find a point that satisfies the mean value theorem for $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}$ on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ are $a=⟨0,2,1⟩$ and $b=⟨1,0,-1⟩,$ respectively.
:question/worked-solution:
The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y,z)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨0,2,1⟩$ and $b=⟨1,0,-1⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,0,-1)-f(0,2,1) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨1,0,-1⟩-⟨0,2,1⟩) \\ 2-(-7) & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,-2,-2⟩ \\ 9 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,-2,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨2x,-4y,2z⟩ \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨2{c}_{1},-4{c}_{2},2{c}_{3}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}9 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,-2,-2⟩ \\ 9 & =⟨2{c}_{1},-4{c}_{2},2{c}_{3}⟩\cdot ⟨1,-2,-2⟩ \\ 9 & =2{c}_{1}+8{c}_{2}-4{c}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-0}{1} & =\frac{y-2}{(-2)}=\frac{z-1}{(-2)} \\ x & =-\frac{y-2}{2}=-\frac{z-1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Parametrizing the line, we get

$$
x=t,\,\,y=2-2t,\,z=1-2t,\,0\le t\le 1.
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
{c}_{1}=t,\,\,{c}_{2}=2-2t,\,{c}_{3}=1-2t.
$$

Substituting the above in the equation $2{c}_{1}+8{c}_{2}-4{c}_{3}=9,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2(t)+8(2-2t)-4(1-2t) & =9 \\ 2t+16-16t-4+8t & =9 \\ -6t & =-3 \\ t & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find the values of ${c}_{1},$ ${c}_{2},$ and ${c}_{3}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}, \\ {c}_{2} & =2-2(\frac{1}{2})=1, \\ {c}_{3} & =1-2(\frac{1}{2})=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the coordinates of $C$ are $(\frac{1}{2},1,0).$

Consider the arc of the curve $x={y}^{3}-9y$ that lies in the fourth quadrant between its $y$-intercepts. What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{3}-9y & =0 \\ y({y}^{2}-9) & =0 \\ y & =0,\pm 3\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $y=-3$ to $y=0.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{3}-9y)=3{y}^{2}-9.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-3}^{0}({y}^{3}-9y)\sqrt{1+(3{y}^{2}-9)^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-3}^{0}({y}^{3}-9y)\sqrt{1+9({y}^{2}-3)^{2}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{0}^{1/4}x{e}^{4x}\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
Let's use integration by parts. We set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x & ⇒ & {u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{4x} & ⇒ & v=\frac{{e}^{4x}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int x\cdot {e}^{4x}\,\text{d}x & =x\cdot \frac{{e}^{4x}}{4}-\int (\frac{{e}^{4x}}{4})\cdot 1\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1/4}x{e}^{4x}\,\text{d}x & ={\frac{1}{4}x{e}^{4x}|}_{0}^{1/4}-\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{1/4}{e}^{4x}\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{1}{4}x{e}^{4x}|}_{0}^{1/4}-{\frac{1}{16}{e}^{4x}|}_{0}^{1/4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\frac{1}{4}{e}^{4(1/4)}-0\cdot {e}^{4\cdot 0}]-\frac{1}{16}[{e}^{4(1/4)}-{e}^{4\cdot 0}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\frac{e}{4}-0]-\frac{1}{16}[e-1] \\  & =\frac{e}{16}-\frac{e}{16}+\frac{1}{16} \\  & =\frac{1}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Let $f$ be a function such that ${f}^{′}(x)=\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ and $f(\frac{\pi }{4})=0.$ Use the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$ to estimate the value of $f(1).$
:question/worked-solution:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(\frac{\pi }{4})+{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})(x-\frac{\pi }{4}).\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $f(\frac{\pi }{4})=0,$ and since ${f}^{′}(x)=\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{sec}⁡x,$ then ${f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})=\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=2.$ So, the tangent line approximation is given by

$$
L(x)=2(x-\frac{\pi }{4}).
$$

Now, we can approximate $f(1)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1) & ≈L(1) \\  & =2(1-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =2-\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=x{y}^{2}$ along the polar curve $r=2$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$
:question/worked-solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =8{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}8{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 2\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =16{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}16{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =16{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{16}{3}{u}^{3}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{16}{3}({1}^{3}-0) \\  & =\frac{16}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Calculate  $\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x+5)\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x+5)\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x+5)\, & ⟹\,v=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x+5)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We, substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int x\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x+5)\,\text{d}x & =x\cdot (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x+5)}{3})-\int (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x+5)}{3})\cdot 1\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x+5)\text{d}x & =-\frac{x\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x+5)}{3}+\frac{1}{3}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x+5)\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{x\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x+5)}{3}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x+5)}{9}+C\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $D={x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{3}}{\text{d}{x}^{3}}+3x\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x},$ what is $D(y)$ for $y=\frac{1}{x}?$
:question/worked-solution:
The given operator is a third-order differential operator of the form

$$
D(y)={f}_{3}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{3}y}{\text{d}{x}^{3}}+{f}_{2}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{f}_{1}(x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{f}_{0}(x)y.
$$

with ${f}_{3}={x}^{2},{f}_{2}=3x,{f}_{1}=-1,$ and ${f}_{0}=0.$

To compute $D(y),$ we apply the definition of the operator $D$ to the function $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}D(y) & =D(\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =({x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{3}}{\text{d}{x}^{3}}+3x\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x})(\frac{1}{x}) \\  & ={x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{3}}{\text{d}{x}^{3}}(\frac{1}{x})+3x\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(\frac{1}{x})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x}) \\  & ={x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})+3x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})-(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & ={x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2}{{x}^{3}})+3x(\frac{2}{{x}^{3}})+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{6}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{6}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find a point that satisfies the mean value theorem for $f(x,y,z)=3{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}$ on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ are $a=⟨0,0,0⟩$ and $b=⟨2,1,3⟩,$ respectively.
:question/worked-solution:
The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y,z)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that $f(x,y,z)=3{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨0,0,0⟩$ and $b=⟨2,1,3⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,1,3)-f(0,0,0) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨2,1,3⟩-⟨0,0,0⟩) \\ -7-0 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,1,3⟩ \\ -7 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,1,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨6x,\,-2y,\,-4z⟩ \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨6{c}_{1},\,-2{c}_{2},\,-4{c}_{3}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-7 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,1,3⟩ \\ -7 & =⟨6{c}_{1},\,-2{c}_{2},\,-4{c}_{3}⟩\cdot ⟨2,1,3⟩ \\ -7 & =12{c}_{1}-2{c}_{2}-12{c}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-0}{2} & =\frac{y-0}{1}=\frac{z-0}{3} \\ \frac{x}{2} & =y=\frac{z}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Parametrizing the line, we get

$$
x=2t,\,y=t,\,z=3t,\,0\le t\le 1.
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
{c}_{1}=2t,\,{c}_{2}=t,\,{c}_{3}=3t.
$$

Substituting the above in the equation $12{c}_{1}-2{c}_{2}-12{c}_{3}=-7,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}12(2t)-2t-12(3t) & =-7 \\ 24t-2t-36t & =-7 \\ -14t & =-7 \\ t & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find the values of ${c}_{1},$ ${c}_{2},$ and ${c}_{3}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =2(\frac{1}{2})=1, \\ {c}_{2} & =\frac{1}{2}, \\ {c}_{3} & =3(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the coordinates of $C$ are $(1,\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2}).$

:question/problem:
Given the transformation
 $T:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x+y \\ 4z-2x \\ z-4x-3y\end{bmatrix},$ find its rank.
:question/worked-solution:
First, the standard matrix of $T$ is given by

$$
T=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 4 \\ -4 & -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Recall that $\text{rank}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Im}(T))=\text{rank}(T).$ 

So, we need to find the rank of the matrix $T.$ We reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 4 \\ -4 & -3 & 1\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+4{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{1}{2}){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $T$ has $3$ pivot columns, we have that 

$$
\text{rank}(T)=\text{rank}(T)=3.
$$

:question/problem:
$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}7 & -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 7 & -2 \\ 2 & -2 & 10\end{bmatrix},\,D=\begin{bmatrix}6 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 12\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first and second columns of the matrix $P?$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=6,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=6,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=12.$ So, the first and second columns of $P$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2}.$ 

Now, we need to find eigenvectors that correspond to ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=6.$ Computing $A-6I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-6I & =\begin{bmatrix}7 & -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 7 & -2 \\ 2 & -2 & 10\end{bmatrix}-6\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & -2 \\ 2 & -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)x=0$ gives two eigenvectors: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$

Notice that eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are not orthogonal. So, we proceed using the Gram-Schmidt process. We set 

$$
{e}_{1}={v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

and we find ${e}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}_{2} & ={v}_{2}-\frac{{v}_{2}\cdot {e}_{1}}{{e}_{1}\cdot {e}_{1}}{e}_{1} \\  & ={v}_{2}+\frac{2}{5}{e}_{1} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\frac{2}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{5} \\ 1 \\ \frac{2}{5}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, dividing ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2}$ by their respective norms, we obtain the first and second columns of $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}_{1}}{‖{e}_{1}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5} \\ 0 \\ \frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\end{bmatrix} \\ \frac{{e}_{2}}{‖{e}_{2}‖} & =\frac{1}{(\frac{\sqrt{30}}{5})}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{5} \\ 1 \\ \frac{2}{5}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\sqrt{30}}{30} \\ \frac{\sqrt{30}}{6} \\ \frac{\sqrt{30}}{15}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
| $f$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ |

| $X=1$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ |
| $X=3$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ |

Compute $P(X=3\,|\,Y=2)$ given that the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ shown in the table above.
:question/worked-solution:
By the multiplication law for conditional probability, the required conditional probability is given by

$$
P(X=3\,|\,Y=2)=\frac{P(X=3,Y=2)}{P(Y=2)}=\frac{f(3,2)}{{f}_{Y}(2)},
$$

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r={e}^{-\theta }\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},$ shown above?
:question/worked-solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={e}^{-\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-{e}^{-\theta }.
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{({e}^{-\theta })}^{2}+{(-{e}^{\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{e}^{-2\theta }+{e}^{-2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{2{e}^{-2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{-\theta }\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta $ for $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$
:question/worked-solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta \operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta \operatorname{cot}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{csc}^{2}⁡\theta +{csc}^{2}⁡\theta {cot}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{csc}^{2}⁡\theta (1+{cot}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{csc}^{4}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}{csc}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-[\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})] \\  & =-(0-1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given the curve $r(t)=\frac{1}{t}\,i+({t}^{2}-3)\,j,$ $t\in (0,\infty ),$ find all points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel.
:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-3)\,j \\  & =-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ \frac{1}{t}\,i+({t}^{2}-3)\,j & =c(-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}i+2t\,j) \\ \frac{1}{t}\,i+({t}^{2}-3)\,j & =-\frac{c}{{t}^{2}}i+2ct\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j$ gives:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{t} &=-\frac{c}{{t}^{2}} \\ {t}^{2}-3 &=2ct\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equation we obtain $-t=c.$ Substituting $c=-t$ into the second equality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-3 & =-2{t}^{2} \\ 3{t}^{2}-3 & =0 \\ 3(t+1)(t-1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t\in (0,\infty )$, the only solution is $t=1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =\frac{1}{1}\,i+({1}^{2}-3)\,j \\  & =\,i-2\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(1,-2).$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}x{y}^{3}\,\text{d}s$, where the curve $C$ is given in polar form by $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$
:question/worked-solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y={sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=x{y}^{3}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot ({sin}^{2}⁡\theta )^{3} \\  & ={sin}^{7}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{y}^{3}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{7}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 1\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{7}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{7}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{8}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot {u}^{8}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}(1-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Let ${J}_{n}(\lambda )$ denote an $n\times n$ Jordan block with $\lambda $ on the main diagonal. Fill in the missing entries in the matrix below.

|  |  | $0$ | $0$ | {{field-6}} |  |
:question/worked-solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=\begin{bmatrix}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In this case, we have $f(x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡x,$ $n=3,$ and $\lambda =\frac{\pi }{4}.$

Since $n=3,$ we need to compute the first $3-1=2$ derivative of $f:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & ={sec}^{2}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =2{sec}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{3}(\pi )) & =\begin{bmatrix}f(\frac{\pi }{4}) & {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & \frac{1}{2!}{f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ 0 & f(\frac{\pi }{4}) & {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ 0 & 0 & f(\frac{\pi }{4})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) & {sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) & \frac{1}{2}\cdot 2{sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ 0 & \operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) & {sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ 0 & 0 & \operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the following boundary value problem (BVP).

$$
{y}^{″}=-1,\,{y}^{′}(-2)=2,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0,\,-2\le x\le 0
$$

The general solution can be written as

$$
y=f(x)+B\cdot g(x)
$$

where $B\in R$ is arbitrary. 

Select functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ that make this statement true.

$\,f(x)=$
{{field-1}} 
$\,g(x)=$
{{field-2}}
:question/worked-solution:
Suppose we have the second-order inhomogeneous boundary value problem (BVP)

$$
{y}^{″}(x)+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=f(x),\,a\le x\le b
$$

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

$$
{\alpha }_{1}y(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}^{′}(a)={\gamma }_{1},\,{\alpha }_{2}y(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}^{′}(b)={\gamma }_{2}
$$

where $P,Q,$ and $f$ are continuous on $[a,b],$ and ${\alpha }_{i}$ and ${\beta }_{i}$ are real constants such that $({\alpha }_{i},{\beta }_{i})\ne (0,0).$ 

If the associated homogeneous BVP has nontrivial solutions, then the inhomogeneous BVP has either no solution or infinitely many solutions. 

To find the solution of an inhomogeneous boundary value problem (BVP):

- First, we find the general solution ${y}_{h}(x)$ of the corresponding homogeneous equation.

- Then, we find a particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ of the inhomogeneous equation.

- Finally, we apply the boundary conditions to determine the arbitrary constants.

However, in this particular case, we can integrate the equation directly. By doing so, we get the general solution

$$
y=-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+Ax+B.
$$

 

Note that the derivative ${y}^{′}$ is

$$
{y}^{′}=-x+A.
$$

Applying the condition ${y}^{′}(-2)=2$ gives

$$
2+A=2\,⇒\,A=0.
$$

So, we have 

$$
y=-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+B.
$$

 

Applying the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-0+A & =0 \\ 0 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

which is automatically satisfied for any $B.$

Therefore, the solution to the boundary value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+B \\  & =(-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})+B(1).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
f(x)=-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2},\,g(x)=1.
$$

 

**Note**: The associated homogeneous BVP

$$
{y}^{″}=0,\,{y}^{′}(-2)=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0,\,-2\le x\le 0
$$

has infinitely many solutions. Therefore, the inhomogeneous BVP has either infinitely many solutions or no solution. Since we have found a solution that contains an arbitrary constant and satisfies both boundary conditions, the BVP has infinitely many solutions.

:question/problem: Given that ${\int }_{-2}^{-1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}$ and ${\int }_{-1}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=2$ then what is ${\int }_{-2}^{1}(5+4f(x))\,\text{d}x?$
:question/worked-solution:
From the adjacent intervals rule, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{-1}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{-1}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-2}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in the known information into the above gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}+2={\int }_{-2}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{5}{2}={\int }_{-2}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we compute the desired integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{1}(5+4f(x))\,\text{d}x & =5{\int }_{-2}^{1}\,\text{d}x+4{\int }_{-2}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =5\cdot x\,{|}_{-2}^{1}+4(\frac{5}{2}) \\  & =5(1-(-2))+10 \\  & =25.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the following system of equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3x+2y &=8 \\ x+y &=-2 \\ x+\frac{1}{2}y &=5.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
:question/worked-solution:
To classify the system, we first try to find its solution. The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 8 \\ 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & \frac{1}{2} & 5\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Using the method of Gaussian elimination, we can reduce this matrix to row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 8 \\ 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & \frac{1}{2} & 5\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & -2 \\ 3 & 2 & 8 \\ 1 & \frac{1}{2} & 5\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 14 \\ 1 & \frac{1}{2} & 5\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 14 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & 7\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-\frac{1}{2}){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 14 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since any numbers $x$ and $y$ are solutions to the third equation $0x+0y=0$, we can remove this equation from the system. So, the corresponding system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y &=-2 \\ -y &=14.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second equation, we get $y=-14.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
x+(-14)=-2\,⟹\,x=12.
$$

 
So,  we conclude that the system is consistent independent.   

As a result, only statement “The system is consistent independent” is true.

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ along the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$
:question/worked-solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y={sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+({sin}^{2}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{4}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\theta ) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\sqrt{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{2\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }{4}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{\pi -0}{4}-\frac{0-0}{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s$, where the curve $C$ is given in polar form by $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,$ for $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le 0.$
:question/worked-solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x={cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, where $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le 0.$ 

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={({cos}^{2}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & ={cos}^{4}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{0}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{0}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{0}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{0}\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{2\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }{4}{|}_{-\pi /4}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(0-(-\frac{\pi }{2})-(-1)) \\  & =\frac{\pi +2}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{3}y$ along the polar curve $r=4$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$
:question/worked-solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{3}y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =(4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{3}4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =256{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(4)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{3}y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}256{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot 4\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =1\,024{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ $\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}1\,024{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =-1\,024{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}/2}{u}^{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-1\,024\cdot \frac{1}{4}{u}^{4}\,{|}_{1}^{\sqrt{2}/2} \\  & =-256((\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})^{4}-{1}^{4}) \\  & =-256(-\frac{3}{4}) \\  & =192\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
$$
\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 3 & 0 \\ 3 & -2\end{bmatrix}}^{A}=\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}{q}_{11} & {q}_{12} \\ {q}_{21} & {q}_{22} \\ {q}_{31} & {q}_{32}\end{bmatrix}}^{Q}\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}{r}_{11} & {r}_{12} \\ 0 & {r}_{22}\end{bmatrix}}^{R}.
$$

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. Given that the columns ${q}_{1},{q}_{2}$ of $Q$ were obtained from the columns of $A$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, find  the value of ${q}_{12}\cdot {r}_{22}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Let ${a}_{1},{a}_{2}$ be the columns of $A.$

First, we find an orthonormal basis of $\text{Col}(A)=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process.

**Step 1**. We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 2**. We find the vector ${v}_{2}$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}\{{v}_{1}\}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}-(-\frac{6}{18})\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we normalize ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\ {q}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute $R:$

$$
\begin{aligned}R & ={Q}^{T}\,A \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 3 & 0 \\ 3 & -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3\sqrt{2} & -\sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 3\sqrt{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following QR factorization of $A:$

$$
\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 3 & 0 \\ 3 & -2\end{bmatrix}}^{A}=\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 & \frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}}^{Q}\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}3\sqrt{2} & -\sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 3\sqrt{2}\end{bmatrix}}^{R}.
$$

Finally, ${q}_{12}\cdot {r}_{22}=(\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}})\cdot (3\sqrt{2})=4.$

:question/problem:
$$
\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}}^{A}=\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}{q}_{11} & {q}_{12} \\ {q}_{21} & {q}_{22} \\ {q}_{31} & {q}_{32}\end{bmatrix}}^{Q}\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}{r}_{11} & {r}_{12} \\ 0 & {r}_{22}\end{bmatrix}}^{R}.
$$

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. Given that the columns ${q}_{1},{q}_{2}$ of $Q$ were obtained from the columns of $A$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, find  the value of ${q}_{22}\cdot {r}_{22}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Let ${a}_{1},{a}_{2}$ be the columns of $A.$

First, we find an orthonormal basis of $\text{Col}(A)=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process.

**Step 1**. We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 2**. We find the vector ${v}_{2}$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}{{v}_{1}}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{3}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we normalize ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ {q}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute $R:$

$$
\begin{aligned}R & ={Q}^{T}\,A \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{3} & \sqrt{3} \\ 0 & \sqrt{6}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following QR factorization of $A:$

$$
\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}}^{A}=\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}}^{Q}\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{3} & \sqrt{3} \\ 0 & \sqrt{6}\end{bmatrix}}^{R}.
$$

Finally, ${q}_{22}\cdot {r}_{22}=(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}})\cdot (\sqrt{6})=-2.$

:question/problem: Consider the arc of the curve $x=\sqrt{y-3}$ that lies between the lines $y=3$ and $y=\frac{15}{4}.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis.
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\sqrt{y-3})=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y-3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}=\frac{1}{4(y-3)}.
$$

Then, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{3}^{15/4}\sqrt{y-3}\cdot \sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4(y-3)}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{3}^{15/4}\sqrt{y-3}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{4y-11}{4(y-3)}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{3}^{15/4}\sqrt{4y-11}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=4y-11.$ Then, $\text{d}y=\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.$

We also need to compute new limits:

| **$y$** | $3$ | $\frac{15}{4}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $4$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =\pi {\int }_{3}^{15/4}\sqrt{4y-11}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot {[\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(\sqrt{{4}^{3}}-\sqrt{{1}^{3}}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(8-1) \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/21/21b55135fd1fbd0c3120b19ee6c4688dea2d8b13ccfe842e95262c87fb0bf6e0.png)

Consider the arc of the curve $y=-{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-4x$ that lies in the fourth quadrant between its $x$-intercepts. What integral gives the area of the surface generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $x$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-4x & =0 \\ -x({x}^{2}-4x+4) & =0 \\ -x(x-2)^{2} & =0 \\ x & =0,2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=2.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-4x)=-3{x}^{2}+8x-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}x\sqrt{1+{(-3{x}^{2}+8x-4)}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=15-3t,$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=14\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=1\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
:question/worked-solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 15-3t & =0 \\ t & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t=5\,\text{s}.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(15-3t) \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(5)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=5\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (15-3t)\text{d}t \\  & =15t-\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(1)=14.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}15(1)-\frac{3}{2}(1)^{2}+C & =14 \\ C & =\frac{3}{2}-1\,⟹\,C=\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{1}{2}+15t-\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(5)=\frac{1}{2}+15(5)-\frac{3}{2}(5)^{2}=38\,\text{m}/\text{s}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/0b/0b69c23833e64df8fa1c938bb87b6cfcf8a67018fb1af73424d26e64e49ee4f5.png)

Consider the arc of the curve $y=2x-{x}^{2}$ that lies in the first quadrant between its $x$-intercepts. What integral gives the area of the surface generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $x$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-{x}^{2} & =0 \\ x(2-x) & =0 \\ x & =0,2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=2.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x-{x}^{2})=2-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}x\sqrt{1+{(2-2x)}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}x\sqrt{1+4-8x+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}x\sqrt{5-8x+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Consider the arc of the curve $x=\sqrt{1-2y}$ that lies between the lines $y=-3$ and $y=0.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis.
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\sqrt{1-2y}) \\  & =\frac{-2}{2\sqrt{1-2y}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-2y}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}=\frac{1}{1-2y}.
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-3}^{0}\sqrt{1-2y}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{1-2y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-3}^{0}\sqrt{1-2y}\sqrt{\frac{2-2y}{1-2y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\pi {\int }_{-3}^{0}\sqrt{1-y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\pi {[-\frac{2}{3}(1-y)^{3/2}]}_{-3}^{0} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\pi (-\frac{2}{3}+\frac{16}{3}) \\  & =\frac{28\sqrt{2}\,\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the unit tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+1}\,p(t)$ at the point corresponding to $t=0$, given that  $p(0)=2\,i+j-k\,$ and $\,{p}^{′}(0)=i-2\,j-2\,k.$
:question/worked-solution:
For a curve $r(t)=x(t)i+y(t)j+z(t)k$, the unit tangent vector $T(t)$ at the point $P(x(t),y(t),z(t))$ is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=0:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+1}\,p(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+1})\cdot p(t)+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+1}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(p(t)) \\  & =-\frac{2t}{{({t}^{2}+1)}^{2}}\,p(t)+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+1}\,{p}^{′}(t) \\ {r}^{′}(0) & =-\frac{2(0)}{{({0}^{2}+1)}^{2}}\,p(0)+\frac{1}{{0}^{2}+1}\,{p}^{′}(0) \\  & =0(2\,i+j-k)+(\,i-2\,j-2k) \\  & =\,i-2\,j-2k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(0):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}‖r(0)‖ & =\sqrt{(1)^{2}+(-2)^{2}+(-2)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${r}^{′}(0):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}T(0) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(0)}{‖{r}^{′}(0)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot (i-2\,j-2\,k) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\,i-\frac{2}{3}\,j-\frac{2}{3}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the unit tangent vector to the curve at the point that corresponds to $t=0$ is  $T(0)=\frac{1}{3}\,i-\frac{2}{3}\,j-\frac{2}{3}\,k.$

:question/problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $k\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=4\,m/s$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}\,m$ and the particle has velocity $v=8\,m/s$ when its displacement is $\pi \,m,$ find the value of $k.$
:question/worked-solution:
![](images/b3/b396b80995e34fe348b3d059737b1eec3d4ce5a9d2e9138a8e7d4ed5c0945dc0.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $k\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int k\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-k\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C.
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=\frac{\pi }{2}\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-k\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =-k\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+C \\ C & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=8-k\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Finally, since $v=8\,m/s$ when $x=\pi \,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8-k\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{1}{2}(8)^{2} & =8-k\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  \\ 32 & =8+k \\ k & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis where $x\ge \frac{1}{2}.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $(4x-2)\,{m/s}^{2},$ and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$
If $P$ has velocity $1\,m/s$ when its displacement is $\frac{1}{2}\,m,$ find the value of $x$ for which $P$ is instantaneously at rest.
:question/worked-solution:
![](images/cd/cdb88c0c679ca9325df42c5c8c4feaea6ce6c0cf02655410158860d7b03d54dc.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $(4x-2)\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-(4x-2).
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-(4x-2).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-4x+2)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-2{x}^{2}+2x+C.
$$

Now, since $v=1\,m/s$ when $x=\frac{1}{2}\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-2{x}^{2}+2x+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(1)^{2} & =-2{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+2(\frac{1}{2})+C \\ C & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}-1 \\ C & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-2{x}^{2}+2x.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x)=0\,m/s.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-2{x}^{2}+2x \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =-2{x}^{2}+2x \\ 2x(1-x) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution of this equation for $x\ge \frac{1}{2}$ is $x=1\,m.$

:question/problem:
The center of the hyperbola $9{x}^{2}-4{y}^{2}-54x=-56$ is$\,\,($
{{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}
$).$
:question/worked-solution:
The equation of a horizontal hyperbola centered at $(h,k)$ is given by

$$
\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

To rewrite the equation of the hyperbola in standard form, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}^{2}-4{y}^{2}-54x & =-56 \\ 9{x}^{2}-54x\,-\,4{y}^{2} & =-56 \\ 9[{x}^{2}-6x]\,-\,4{y}^{2} & =-56 \\ 9[(x-3)^{2}-9]\,-\,4{y}^{2} & =-56 \\ 9(x-3)^{2}-81\,-\,4{y}^{2} & =-56 \\ 9(x-3)^{2}\,-\,4{y}^{2} & =25 \\ \frac{(x-3)^{2}}{{(\frac{5}{3})}^{2}}\,-\,\frac{{y}^{2}}{{(\frac{5}{2})}^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the center of the hyperbola is $(\,3,0\,).$

:question/problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-4y{y}^{′}=6x,\,y(1)=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=0
$$

Use Euler's Method with one step to approximate $y(\frac{5}{4})$ and ${y}^{′}(\frac{5}{4}).$

$y(\frac{5}{4})≈$
{{field-1}},
$\,{y}^{′}(\frac{5}{4})≈$
{{field-2}}
:question/worked-solution:
For a second-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}=f(x,y,{y}^{′}),\,y(a)=c,\,{y}^{′}(a)=d,
$$

we can use Euler's method to approximate a solution by first reducing the second-order ODE to a system of first-order ODEs,

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} &=z,\, && y(a)=c, \\ {z}^{′} &=f(x,y,z)\, && z(a)=d,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

before applying the update rule component-wise to each equation.

To apply Euler’s method, we first isolate ${y}^{″}$ so it can serve as the derivative of a new variable $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-4y{y}^{′} & =6x \\ {x}^{2}{y}^{″} & =6x+4y{y}^{′} \\ {y}^{″} & =\frac{6x+4y{y}^{′}}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute our new variable $z={y}^{′},{z}^{′}={y}^{″}$ in the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{z}^{′}=\frac{6x+4yz}{{x}^{2}}.
$$

Note that the initial value of $z$ is
$z(1)={y}^{′}(1)=0.$
So, the initial value problem reduces to the following system of first-order ODEs:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} &=z,\, && y(1)=0, \\ {z}^{′} &=\frac{6x+4yz}{{x}^{2}},\, && z(1)=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, we can proceed with Euler's method by applying the update rule component-wise.

Since we want to find the values of $y$ and ${y}^{′}=z$ at $x=\frac{5}{4},$ we will use a step size of

$$
Δx=\frac{5}{4}-1=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

First, we place the initial condition data in the table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $0$ |  |  | $0$ |  |  |

Next, we compute both ${y}^{′}$ and ${z}^{′}$ according to the given rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =z=0 \\ {z}^{′} & =\frac{6x+4yz}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{6\cdot 1+4\cdot 0\cdot 0}{{1}^{2}} \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

So, we add these to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $0$ | $0$ |  | $0$ | $6$ |  |

Next, we compute $Δy$ and $Δz$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =0\cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =0 \\ Δz & ={z}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =6\cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{6}{4} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We add these to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $6$ | $\frac{3}{2}$ |

To get the new values of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ in the *next* row, we add $Δx$ to $x,$ $Δy$ to $y,$ and $Δz$ to $z,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=1+\frac{1}{4}=\frac{5}{4} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=0+0=0 \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=0+\frac{3}{2}=\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Adding these values to our table in a new row gives the following:

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $6$ | $\frac{3}{2}$ |
| $\frac{5}{4}$ | $0$ |  |  | $\frac{3}{2}$ |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that
$y(\frac{5}{4})≈0$
and
${y}^{′}(\frac{5}{4})=z(\frac{5}{4})≈\frac{3}{2}.$

:question/problem: Consider a spherical planet with radius $(1.7\times {10}^{7})\,\text{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g=11.8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Which equation best models the velocity $v$ of an object projected radially outward from the planet's surface with an initial velocity of $(7.4\times {10}^{4})\,\text{m/s},$ where $r$ is the distance from the planet's center to the object. Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.
:question/worked-solution:
Let $R$ be the planet's radius and $g$ be the planet's surface gravitational acceleration.

According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the planet is

$$
{F}_{\text{in}}=G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, and $M$ is the planet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-{F}_{\text{in}}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, 

$$
a=-\frac{k}{{r}^{2}},
$$

with constant of proportionality $k=GM>0.$

When at the surface, $r=R,$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-g.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k:$

$$
-g=-\frac{k}{{R}^{2}}\,\,\,⟹\,k=g{R}^{2}
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a=-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}}.
$$

Now, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\frac{dv}{dr}=-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}}
$$

Solving using separation of variables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int v\frac{dv}{dr}\,dr & =\int (-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}})\,dr \\ \int v\,dv & =-g{R}^{2}\int \frac{1}{{r}^{2}}\,dr \\ \frac{{v}^{2}}{2} & =-g{R}^{2}(-\frac{1}{r})+{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{r}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C=2{C}_{1}$ is a constant of integration.

Let ${v}_{0}$ be the initial velocity of the object. Applying the initial condition $v(R)={v}_{0},$ we can solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(R)^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{R}+C \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =2gR+C \\ C & ={v}_{0}^{2}-2gR\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation for the velocity of the object is

$$
{v}^{2}=\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{r}+{v}_{0}^{2}-2gR.
$$

Finally, substituting in the values
$R=(1.7\times {10}^{7}),$
$g=11.8,$ and
${v}_{0}=(7.4\times {10}^{4}),$
we conclude that the equation for the velocity is

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2\cdot 11.8\cdot (1.7\times {10}^{7})^{2}}{r}+(7.4\times {10}^{4})^{2}-2\cdot 11.8\cdot (1.7\times {10}^{7}) \\  & =\frac{23.6\cdot (2.89\times {10}^{14})}{r}+(54.76\times {10}^{8})-(40.12\times {10}^{7}) \\  & =\frac{68.204\times {10}^{14}}{r}+(54.76\times {10}^{8})-(4.012\times {10}^{8}) \\  & =\frac{6.8204\times {10}^{15}}{r}+((54.76-4.012)\times {10}^{8}) \\  & =\frac{6.8204\times {10}^{15}}{r}+(50.748\times {10}^{8}) \\  & =\frac{6.8204\times {10}^{15}}{r}+(5.0748\times {10}^{9}).\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Which of the following gives the unit tangent vector to the curve
 $r(t)=⟨\frac{1}{t},\,t,\,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t⟩$ at an arbitrary point where $t\in (0,\infty )?$
:question/worked-solution:
For a curve $r(t)=⟨x(t),\,y(t),\,z(t)⟩$, the unit tangent vector $T(t)$ at the point $P(x(t),y(t),z(t))$ is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

First, we find the derivative of $r(t):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t),\,\sqrt{2}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},\,1,\,\frac{\sqrt{2}}{t}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})}^{2}+(1)^{2}+{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{{t}^{4}}+1+\frac{2}{{t}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1+{t}^{4}+2{t}^{2}}{{t}^{4}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{(1+{t}^{2})^{2}}{{t}^{4}}} \\  & =\frac{1+{t}^{2}}{{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 Finally, we normalize ${r}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the unit tangent vector to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}}{1+{t}^{2}}⟨-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},\,1,\,\frac{\sqrt{2}}{t}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{t}^{2}}⟨-1,\,{t}^{2},\,\sqrt{2}t⟩\end{aligned}
$$
