$$

First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3})\,⊕\,{J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{4})) & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\begin{bmatrix}{J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3}) & 0 \\ 0 & {J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{4})\end{bmatrix}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3})) & 0 \\ 0 & \operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{4}))\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3}))\,⊕\,\operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{4})).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we compute the function of each Jordan block separately.

- For ${J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3}),$ we have $n=1$ and $\lambda =3.$ since $n=1,$ we don't need any derivatives. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3})) & =\begin{bmatrix}f(\frac{\pi }{3})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{3}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For ${J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{4}),$ we have $n=3$ and $\lambda =2.$ \since $n=3,$ we need to compute the first and second derivatives of $f$ only:

$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{3}(\frac{\pi }{4})) & =\begin{bmatrix}f(\frac{\pi }{4}) & {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & \frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ 0 & f(\frac{\pi }{4}) & {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ 0 & 0 & f(\frac{\pi }{4})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) & {sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) & \frac{1}{2}\cdot 2{sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ 0 & \operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) & {sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ 0 & 0 & \operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Now, using the double-angle formula for cosine and the Pythagorean identity, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t & ={cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡t-(1-{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =2{cos}^{2}⁡t-1.\end{aligned}

:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
7\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-14y=-8\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

Find the general solution to this equation given that the complementary solution is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{2x},$ where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

$y(x)=A{e}^{2x}\,+\,($
{{field-1}}
$)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,+\,($
{{field-2}}
$)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)$
:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation with constant coefficients on the left-hand side, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
7\frac{\text{d}{y}_{c}}{\text{d}x}-14{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{2x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $-8\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).$ So, we assume the particular solution to be 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
7(-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))-14(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))=-8\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
(14\beta -14\alpha )\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+(-14\alpha -14\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)=-8\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}14\beta -14\alpha &=-8\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)) \\ -14\alpha -14\beta &=3\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =\frac{5}{28},\beta =-\frac{11}{28}.$

Therefore,

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\frac{5}{28}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-\frac{11}{28}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{2x}+(\frac{5}{28})\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+(-\frac{11}{28})\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

:question/problem: A coolant reservoir in a manufacturing plant can hold up to $210\,\text{gal}$ of liquid. Initially, it contains $70\,\text{gal}$ of coolant solution with $20\,\text{lb}$ of dissolved corrosion inhibitor. A more concentrated coolant solution with concentration $0.5\,\text{lb/gal}$ flows into the reservoir at a rate of $21\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed solution drains out at a rate of $14\,\text{gal/min}.$ Rounded to one decimal place, find the amount of inhibitor in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow.
:question/worked-solution:
Since $Q$ is the amount of inhibitor in the reservoir at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which inhibitor enters the reservoir minus the rate at which inhibitor leaves the reservoir.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which inhibitor enters the reservoir.

First, note that a solution containing $0.5\,\text{lb/gal}$ of inhibitor enters the reservoir at a rate of $21\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *inhibitor* enters the reservoir is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.5\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (21\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.5\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (21\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =10.5\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which inhibitor exits the reservoir.

To find the rate at which inhibitor leaves the reservoir, we must first determine the volume of solution in the reservoir at time $t.$

The reservoir initially contains $70\,\text{gal}$ of solution; solution enters at $21\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $14\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the reservoir after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=70+21t-14t=7(10+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the reservoir is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of inhibitor in the reservoir, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{7(10+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $14\,\text{gal/min},$ *inhibitor* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(14\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{7(10+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(14\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{7(10+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{14Q}{7(10+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{10+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =10.5-\frac{2Q}{10+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{10+t}\,Q=10.5.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(10+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|10+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(10+t)^{2}} \\  & =(10+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(10+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(10+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{10+t}\,Q) & =(10+t)^{2}\cdot 10.5 \\ (10+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(10+t)Q & =10.5(10+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(10+t)^{2}) & =10.5(10+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(10+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 10.5(10+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(10+t)^{2} & =10.5\cdot \frac{1}{3}(10+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =3.5(10+t)+\frac{C}{(10+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the reservoir initially contains $20\,\text{lb}$ of inhibitor. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=20,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =20 \\ 3.5(10+0)+\frac{C}{(10+0)^{2}} & =20 \\ 35+\frac{C}{(10)^{2}} & =20 \\ \frac{C}{{10}^{2}} & =-15 \\ C & =-15(10)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =3.5(10+t)-\frac{15(10)^{2}}{(10+t)^{2}} \\  & =3.5(10+t)-15{(\frac{10}{10+t})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the reservoir begins to overflow. The reservoir has a capacity of $210\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=210$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =210 \\ 70+21{t}_{o}-14{t}_{o} & =210 \\ 70+7{t}_{o} & =210 \\ 7{t}_{o} & =140 \\ {t}_{o} & =20\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of inhibitor in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(20) & =3.5(10+20)-15{(\frac{10}{10+20})}^{2} \\  & =105-15{(\frac{10}{30})}^{2} \\  & ≈103.3\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: A flavoring tank at a beverage factory can hold up to $150\,\text{gal}$ of liquid. Initially, it contains $75\,\text{gal}$ of flavoring solution with $25\,\text{lb}$ of dissolved flavoring. A more concentrated solution with concentration $\frac{2}{3}\,\text{lb/gal}$ flows into the tank at a rate of $9\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed solution drains out at a rate of $6\,\text{gal/min}.$ Rounded to one decimal place, find the amount of flavoring in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow.
:question/worked-solution:
Since $Q$ is the amount of flavoring in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which flavoring enters the tank minus the rate at which flavoring leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which flavoring enters the tank.

First, note that a solution containing $\frac{2}{3}\,\text{lb/gal}$ of flavoring enters the tank at a rate of $9\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *flavoring* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(\frac{2}{3}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (9\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(\frac{2}{3}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (9\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =6\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which flavoring exits the tank.

To find the rate at which flavoring leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of solution in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $75\,\text{gal}$ of solution; solution enters at $9\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $6\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=75+9t-6t=3(25+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of flavoring in the tank, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{3(25+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $6\,\text{gal/min},$ *flavoring* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(6\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{3(25+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(6\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{3(25+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{6Q}{3(25+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{25+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =6-\frac{2Q}{25+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{25+t}\,Q=6.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(25+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|25+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(25+t)^{2}} \\  & =(25+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(25+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(25+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{25+t}\,Q) & =(25+t)^{2}\cdot 6 \\ (25+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(25+t)Q & =6(25+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(25+t)^{2}) & =6(25+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(25+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 6(25+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(25+t)^{2} & =6\cdot \frac{1}{3}(25+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =2(25+t)+\frac{C}{(25+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the tank initially contains $25\,\text{lb}$ of flavoring. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=25,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =25 \\ 2(25+0)+\frac{C}{(25+0)^{2}} & =25 \\ 50+\frac{C}{(25)^{2}} & =25 \\ \frac{C}{{25}^{2}} & =-25 \\ C & =-25(25)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =2(25+t)-\frac{25(25)^{2}}{(25+t)^{2}} \\  & =2(25+t)-25{(\frac{25}{25+t})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $150\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=150$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =150 \\ 75+9{t}_{o}-6{t}_{o} & =150 \\ 75+3{t}_{o} & =150 \\ 3{t}_{o} & =75 \\ {t}_{o} & =25\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of flavoring in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(25) & =2(25+25)-25{(\frac{25}{25+25})}^{2} \\  & =100-25{(\frac{25}{50})}^{2} \\  & ≈93.8\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: A disinfectant reservoir in a water treatment facility can hold up to $200\,\text{gal}$ of liquid. Initially, it contains $50\,\text{gal}$ of disinfectant solution with $10\,\text{lb}$ of dissolved disinfectant. A more concentrated solution with concentration $0.8\,\text{lb/gal}$ flows into the reservoir at a rate of $15\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed solution drains out at a rate of $10\,\text{gal/min}.$ Rounded to one decimal place, find the amount of disinfectant in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow.
:question/worked-solution:
Since $Q$ is the amount of disinfectant in the reservoir at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which disinfectant enters the reservoir minus the rate at which disinfectant leaves the reservoir.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which disinfectant enters the reservoir.

First, note that a solution containing $0.8\,\text{lb/gal}$ of disinfectant enters the reservoir at a rate of $15\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *disinfectant* enters the reservoir is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.8\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (15\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.8\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (15\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =12\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which disinfectant exits the reservoir.

To find the rate at which disinfectant leaves the reservoir, we must first determine the volume of solution in the reservoir at time $t.$

The reservoir initially contains $50\,\text{gal}$ of solution; solution enters at $15\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $10\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the reservoir after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=50+15t-10t=5(10+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the reservoir is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of disinfectant in the reservoir, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{5(10+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $10\,\text{gal/min},$ *disinfectant* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(10\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{5(10+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(10\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{5(10+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{10Q}{5(10+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{10+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =12-\frac{2Q}{10+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{10+t}\,Q=12.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(10+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|10+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(10+t)^{2}} \\  & =(10+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(10+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(10+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{10+t}\,Q) & =(10+t)^{2}\cdot 12 \\ (10+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(10+t)Q & =12(10+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(10+t)^{2}) & =12(10+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(10+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 12(10+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(10+t)^{2} & =12\cdot \frac{1}{3}(10+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =4(10+t)+\frac{C}{(10+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the reservoir initially contains $10\,\text{lb}$ of disinfectant. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=10,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =10 \\ 4(10+0)+\frac{C}{(10+0)^{2}} & =10 \\ 40+\frac{C}{(10)^{2}} & =10 \\ \frac{C}{{10}^{2}} & =-30 \\ C & =-30(10)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =4(10+t)-\frac{30(10)^{2}}{(10+t)^{2}} \\  & =4(10+t)-30{(\frac{10}{10+t})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the reservoir begins to overflow. The reservoir has a capacity of $200\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=200$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =200 \\ 50+15{t}_{o}-10{t}_{o} & =200 \\ 50+5{t}_{o} & =200 \\ 5{t}_{o} & =150 \\ {t}_{o} & =30\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of disinfectant in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(30) & =4(10+30)-30{(\frac{10}{10+30})}^{2} \\  & =160-30{(\frac{10}{40})}^{2} \\  & ≈158.1\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Find a Cartesian equation of the osculating plane for the curve $r(t)$ at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ given that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ T(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ N(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
:question/worked-solution:
First, notice that the unit tangent and the principal normal at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}⟩=⟨-1,0,0⟩ \\ N(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2},-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2},-\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}⟩=-\frac{1}{5}⟨0,3,4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, the position vector of the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ is

$$
p=r(\frac{\pi }{2})=⟨5\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2},3\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2},4\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}⟩=⟨0,3,4⟩.
$$

Now, we need to find a vector that's perpendicular to the osculating plane. To do that, we use the cross product of the unit tangent $T(\frac{\pi }{2})$ and the principal normal $N(\frac{\pi }{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\frac{\pi }{2})\times N(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨-1,0,0⟩\times (-\frac{1}{5}⟨0,3,4⟩) \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 4\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}⟨0,4,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since we are interested only in the direction of the above vector, let's write our perpendicular vector $n$ as 

$$
n=(-5)\cdot (T(\frac{\pi }{2})\times N(\frac{\pi }{2}))=⟨0,4,-3⟩.
$$

Finally, let $⟨x,y,z⟩$ denote the position vector of a point on the osculating plane. Since the plane is perpendicular to $n$ and passes through the tip of the position vector $p$, its Cartesian equation can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}(⟨x,y,z⟩-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n-p\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨0,4,-3⟩ & =⟨0,3,4⟩\cdot ⟨0,4,-3⟩ \\ 0\cdot x+4\cdot y+(-3)\cdot z & =0 \\ 4y-3z & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
A processing tank initially holds $420\,\text{L}$ of liquid containing $10\,\text{kg}$ of dissolved preservative.
A feed solution containing $0.05\,\text{kg/L}$ of the preservative is pumped into the tank at a rate of $18\,\text{L/min},$ while the completely mixed liquid is drained out at a rate of $12\,\text{L/min}.$
Find, rounded to two decimal places, the amount of preservative in the tank $15$ minutes after pumping begins.
:question/worked-solution:
Let $Q$ be the amount of preservative in the tank at time $t,$ in minutes. Then, the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t.$ This is equal to the rate at which preservative enters the tank minus the rate at which preservative leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which preservative enters the tank.

Note that a feed solution containing $0.05\,\text{kg/L}$ of the preservative enters the tank at a rate of $18\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *preservative* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.05\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (18\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.05\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (18\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0.9\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which preservative exits the tank.

To find the rate at which preservative leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $420\,\text{L}$ of liquid; a solution enters at $18\,\text{L/min}$ and leaves at $12\,\text{L/min}.$
As a result, the volume of liquid in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
420+18t-12t=(420+6t)\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the amount of preservative in the tank, the *concentration* of the mixed solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{420+6t}\,\text{kg/L}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of $12\,\text{L/min},$ *preservative* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(12\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{420+6t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(12\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{420+6t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{12Q}{420+6t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{70+t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0.9-\frac{2Q}{70+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{70+t}Q=0.9.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(70+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|70+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(70+t)^{2}} \\  & =(70+t)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(70+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(70+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{70+t}Q) & =(70+t)^{2}\cdot 0.9 \\ (70+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(70+t)Q & =0.9(70+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(70+t)^{2}) & =0.9(70+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(70+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 0.9(70+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(70+t)^{2} & =0.9\cdot \frac{1}{3}(70+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =0.3(70+t)+\frac{C}{(70+t)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the tank initially contains $10\,\text{kg}$ of preservative. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=10,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =10 \\ 0.3(70+0)+\frac{C}{(70+0)^{2}} & =10 \\ 21+\frac{C}{{70}^{2}} & =10 \\ \frac{C}{{70}^{2}} & =-11 \\ C & =-11(70)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =0.3(70+t)-\frac{11(70)^{2}}{(70+t)^{2}} \\  & =0.3(70+t)-11{(\frac{70}{70+t})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,  the amount of preservative in the tank $15$ minutes after pumping begins is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(15) & =0.3(70+15)-11{(\frac{70}{70+15})}^{2} \\  & =25.5-11{(\frac{70}{85})}^{2} \\  & ≈18.04\,\text{kg},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

:question/problem:
![](images/97/97d661baf511c1e99ee8eed7fbed2ad02d9f96c452ece5b765a3e2cf657c431b.png)

Find the amplitude of the steady-state current for the RL circuit shown above, rounded to two decimal places.

The amplitude of the steady-state current is approximately
{{field-1}} amperes.
:question/worked-solution:
The diagram shows a series RL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $10\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $6\,Ω,$ and an inductor of inductance $1\,\text{H}.$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RL circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=6\,Ω.$

$$
{V}_{R}=6I
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=1\,\text{H}.$

$$
{V}_{L}=1\cdot \frac{dI}{dt}=\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of current $I$ in the circuit is

$$
10\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)=6I+\frac{dI}{dt}
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}+6I=10\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${I}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{I}_{c}}{dt}+6{I}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-6t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $3t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $3t,$ i.e.,

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t), \\ \frac{d{I}_{p}}{dt} & =-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))+6(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =10\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ (-3\alpha +6\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+(6\alpha +3\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) & =10\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-3\alpha +6\beta &=10\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) \\ 6\alpha +3\beta &=0\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{2}{3},$ $\beta =\frac{4}{3}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)={I}_{c}(t)+{I}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-6t}-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-6t}$ is the *transient current*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function ${I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$ is the *steady-state current*. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
I(t)≈{I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current is given by

$$
\sqrt{{(-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}+{(\frac{4}{3})}^{2}}≈1.49\,\text{A},
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

:question/problem:
![](images/3b/3b7ddd9e65fdbd1c8756c4cbf5690640736fb91c5d93bdba941ba62decb0bbf4.png)

Find the amplitude of the steady-state current for the RL circuit shown above, rounded to two decimal places.

The amplitude of the steady-state current is approximately
{{field-1}} amperes.
:question/worked-solution:
The diagram shows a series RL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $4\,Ω,$ and an inductor of inductance $\frac{1}{2}\,\text{H}.$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RL circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=4\,Ω.$

$$
{V}_{R}=4I
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=\frac{1}{2}\,\text{H}.$

$$
{V}_{L}=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of current $I$ in the circuit is

$$
4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)=4I+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{dI}{dt}
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}+8I=8\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${I}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{I}_{c}}{dt}+8{I}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-8t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $2t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $2t,$ i.e.,

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t), \\ \frac{d{I}_{p}}{dt} & =-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))+8(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ (-2\alpha +8\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+(8\alpha +2\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-2\alpha +8\beta &=8\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\ 8\alpha +2\beta &=0\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{4}{17},$ $\beta =\frac{16}{17}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{4}{17}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{16}{17}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)={I}_{c}(t)+{I}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-8t}-\frac{4}{17}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{16}{17}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-8t}$ is the *transient current*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function ${I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{4}{17}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{16}{17}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)$ is the *steady-state current*. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
I(t)≈{I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{4}{17}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{16}{17}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current is given by

$$
\sqrt{{(-\frac{4}{17})}^{2}+{(\frac{16}{17})}^{2}}≈0.97\,\text{A},
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

:question/problem:
A juice-processing tank initially holds $400\,\text{L}$ of liquid containing $4\,\text{kg}$ of dissolved sugar.
A solution containing $0.03\,\text{kg/L}$ of dissolved sugar is pumped into the tank at a rate of $20\,\text{L/min},$ while the completely mixed liquid is drained out at a rate of $30\,\text{L/min}.$ If the amount of sugar $Q(t),$ in kilograms, in the tank $t$ minutes after pumping begins is given by

$$
Q(t)=\alpha \,(1-\frac{t}{40})+\beta {(1-\frac{t}{40})}^{3}
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants, what is the value of $\alpha -\beta ?$
:question/worked-solution:
Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which sugar enters the tank minus the rate at which sugar leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which sugar enter the tank.

First, note that a liquid solution containing $0.03\,\text{kg/L}$ of sugar enters the tank at a rate of $20\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *sugar* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.03\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (20\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.03\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (20\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0.6\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which sugar exit the tank.

To find the rate at which sugar leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $400\,\text{L}$ of liquid; a solution enters at $20\,\text{L/min}$ and leaves at $30\,\text{L/min}.$
As a result, the amount of liquid in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
400+20t-30t=(400-10t)\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the amount of sugar in the tank, the *concentration* of the mixed solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{400-10t}\,\text{kg/L}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of $30\,\text{L/min},$ *sugar* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(30\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{400-10t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(30\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{400-10t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{30Q}{400-10t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{3Q}{40-t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0.6-\frac{3Q}{40-t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{3}{40-t}Q=0.6.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 3/(40-t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{-3\operatorname{ln}⁡|40-t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(40-t)^{-3}} \\  & =(40-t)^{-3}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(40-t)^{-3}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(40-t)^{-3}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{3}{40-t}Q) & =(40-t)^{-3}\cdot 0.6 \\ (40-t)^{-3}\frac{dQ}{dt}+3(40-t)^{-4}Q & =0.6(40-t)^{-3} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(40-t)^{-3}) & =0.6(40-t)^{-3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(40-t)^{-3})\,dt & =\int 0.6(40-t)^{-3}\,dt \\ Q(40-t)^{-3} & =0.6\cdot \frac{1}{2}(40-t)^{-2}+C \\ Q(t) & =0.3(40-t)+C(40-t)^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the tank initially contains $4\,\text{kg}$ of sugar. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=4,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =4 \\ C(40-0)^{3}+0.3(40-0) & =4 \\ C(40)^{3}+12 & =4 \\ C & =-\frac{8}{{40}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =0.3(40-t)-\frac{8}{{40}^{3}}(40-t)^{3} \\  & =0.3\cdot 40\,(\frac{40-t}{40})-8{(\frac{40-t}{40})}^{3} \\  & =12\,(1-\frac{t}{40})-8{(1-\frac{t}{40})}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have $\alpha =12,\beta =-8,$ and

$$
\alpha -\beta =12-(-8)=20.
$$

:question/problem:
A fruit syrup tank initially holds $240\,\text{L}$ of liquid containing $7\,\text{kg}$ of dissolved sweetener.
A solution containing $0.05\,\text{kg/L}$ of dissolved sweetener is pumped into the tank at a rate of $24\,\text{L/min},$ while the completely mixed liquid is drained out at a rate of $32\,\text{L/min}.$ If the amount of sweetener $Q(t),$ in kilograms, in the tank $t$ minutes after pumping begins is given by

$$
Q(t)=\alpha \,(1-\frac{t}{30})+\beta {(1-\frac{t}{30})}^{4}
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants, what is the value of $\alpha -\beta ?$
:question/worked-solution:
Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which sweetener enters the tank minus the rate at which sweetener leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which sweetener enter the tank.

First, note that a solution containing $0.05\,\text{kg/L}$ of sweetener enters the tank at a rate of $24\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *sweetener* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.05\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (24\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.05\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (24\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =1.2\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which sweetener exit the tank.

To find the rate at which sweetener leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $240\,\text{L}$ of liquid; a solution enters at $24\,\text{L/min}$ and leaves at $32\,\text{L/min}.$
As a result, the amount of liquid in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
240+24t-32t=(240-8t)\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the amount of sweetener in the tank, the *concentration* of the mixed solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{240-8t}\,\text{kg/L}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of $32\,\text{L/min},$ *sweetener* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(32\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{240-8t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(32\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{240-8t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{32Q}{240-8t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{4Q}{30-t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =1.2-\frac{4Q}{30-t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{4}{30-t}Q=1.2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 4/(30-t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{-4\operatorname{ln}⁡|30-t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(30-t)^{-4}} \\  & =(30-t)^{-4}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(30-t)^{-4}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(30-t)^{-4}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{4}{30-t}Q) & =(30-t)^{-4}\cdot 1.2 \\ (30-t)^{-4}\frac{dQ}{dt}+4(30-t)^{-5}Q & =1.2(30-t)^{-4} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(30-t)^{-4}) & =1.2(30-t)^{-4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(30-t)^{-4})\,dt & =\int 1.2(30-t)^{-4}\,dt \\ Q(30-t)^{-4} & =1.2\cdot \frac{1}{3}(30-t)^{-3}+C \\ Q(t) & =0.4(30-t)+C(30-t)^{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the tank initially contains $7\,\text{kg}$ of sweetener. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=7,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =7 \\ C(30-0)^{4}+0.4(30-0) & =7 \\ C(30)^{4}+12 & =7 \\ C & =-\frac{5}{{30}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =0.4(30-t)-\frac{5}{{30}^{4}}(30-t)^{4} \\  & =0.4\cdot 30\,(\frac{30-t}{30})-5{(\frac{30-t}{30})}^{4} \\  & =12\,(1-\frac{t}{30})-5{(1-\frac{t}{30})}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have $\alpha =12,\beta =-5,$ and

$$
\alpha -\beta =12-(-5)=17.
$$

:question/problem:
A coolant reservoir initially holds $400\,\text{L}$ of liquid containing $6\,\text{kg}$ of dissolved corrosion inhibitor.
A feed solution containing $0.05\,\text{kg/L}$ of the inhibitor is pumped into the reservoir at a rate of $16\,\text{L/min},$ while the completely mixed liquid is drained out at a rate of $12\,\text{L/min}.$
Find, rounded to two decimal places, the amount of inhibitor in the reservoir $12$ minutes after pumping begins.
:question/worked-solution:
Let $Q$ be the amount of inhibitor in the reservoir at time $t,$ in minutes. Then, the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t.$ This is equal to the rate at which inhibitor enters the tank minus the rate at which inhibitor leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which inhibitor enters the reservoir.

Note that a feed solution containing $0.05\,\text{kg/L}$ of the inhibitor enters the reservoir at a rate of $16\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *inhibitor* enters the reservoir is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.05\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (16\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.05\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (16\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0.8\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which inhibitor exits the reservoir.

To find the rate at which inhibitor leaves the reservoir, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the reservoir at time $t.$

The reservoir initially contains $400\,\text{L}$ of liquid; a solution enters at $16\,\text{L/min}$ and leaves at $12\,\text{L/min}.$
As a result, the volume of liquid in the reservoir after $t$ minutes is 

$$
400+16t-12t=(400+4t)\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the amount of inhibitor in the reservoir, the *concentration* of the mixed solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{400+4t}\,\text{kg/L}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of $12\,\text{L/min},$ *inhibitor* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(12\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{400+4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(12\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{400+4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{12Q}{400+4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{3Q}{100+t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0.8-\frac{3Q}{100+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{3}{100+t}Q=0.8.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 3/(100+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{3\operatorname{ln}⁡|100+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(100+t)^{3}} \\  & =(100+t)^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(100+t)^{3}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(100+t)^{3}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{3}{100+t}Q) & =(100+t)^{3}\cdot 0.8 \\ (100+t)^{3}\frac{dQ}{dt}+3(100+t)^{2}Q & =0.8(100+t)^{3} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(100+t)^{3}) & =0.8(100+t)^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(100+t)^{3})\,dt & =\int 0.8(100+t)^{3}\,dt \\ Q(100+t)^{3} & =0.8\cdot \frac{1}{4}(100+t)^{4}+C \\ Q(t) & =0.2(100+t)+\frac{C}{(100+t)^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the reservoir initially contains $6\,\text{kg}$ of inhibitor. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=6,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =6 \\ 0.2(100+0)+\frac{C}{(100+0)^{3}} & =6 \\ 20+\frac{C}{{100}^{3}} & =6 \\ \frac{C}{{100}^{3}} & =-14 \\ C & =-14(100)^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =0.2(100+t)-\frac{14(100)^{3}}{(100+t)^{3}} \\  & =0.2(100+t)-14{(\frac{100}{100+t})}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,  the amount of inhibitor in the reservoir $12$ minutes after pumping begins is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(12) & =0.2(100+12)-14{(\frac{100}{100+12})}^{3} \\  & =22.4-14{(\frac{25}{28})}^{3} \\  & ≈12.44\,\text{kg},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

:question/problem:
Evaluate the following integral.

${\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x=$ {{field-1}}
:question/worked-solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the second equation from the first, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x-x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x+x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)-\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)]}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))-\frac{1}{12}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{1}{8}(0-0)-\frac{1}{12}(-1-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the following integral.

${\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=$ {{field-1}}
:question/worked-solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the second equation from the first, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x-3x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x+3x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x)).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the following integral.

${\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x=$ {{field-1}}
:question/worked-solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for sine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x+x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x-x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)]}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))-\frac{1}{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}(-1-1)-\frac{1}{4}(0-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The total charge, in coulombs, stored in a device $t$ seconds after charging begins increases at a rate of $\frac{40}{(t+1)^{3}}.$ If, at $t=0$ seconds, the device already stored $7$ coulombs of charge, how much charge will the device store after $1$ second?

After $1$ second, the device stores
{{field-1}} coulombs of charge.
:question/worked-solution:
Let $a(t)=\frac{40}{(t+1)^{3}}$ be the rate at which the amount of charge stored is changing and let $A(T)$ be the amount of charge stored $T$ seconds after charging begins. 

Using our formula for the accumulation of change, we have

$$
A(T)=A(0)+{\int }_{0}^{T}a(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Substituting the known information and carrying out the necessary integration gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A(T) & =A(0)+{\int }_{0}^{T}a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =7+{\int }_{0}^{T}\frac{40}{(t+1)^{3}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =7+(-\frac{20}{(t+1)^{2}}){|}_{0}^{T} \\  & =7+(-\frac{20}{(T+1)^{2}})-(-\frac{20}{{1}^{2}}) \\  & =7-\frac{20}{(T+1)^{2}}+20 \\  & =27-\frac{20}{(T+1)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the amount of charge stored $T=1$ second after charging begins, we substitute in the above:

$$
A(1)=7-\frac{20}{(1+1)^{2}}+20=22.
$$

Thus, after $1$ second, the device stores $22$ coulombs of charge.

Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{10}{9+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{10}{9\cdot (1+{x}^{2}/9)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{10}{9}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}/9}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{10}{9}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{1+(x/3)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

 

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{3})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{3}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=3\,\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $1$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{10}{9+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{10}{9}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{1+(x/3)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{10}{9}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (3\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{10}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{10}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{10}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1)-\frac{10}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(0) \\  & =\frac{10}{3}\cdot \frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))^{2} & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=12{x}^{2} & \,⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int 12{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=4{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 12{x}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))}^{2}(4{x}^{3})-\int (4{x}^{3})(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))}^{2}-8\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x) & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={x}^{2} & \,⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})-\int (\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})(\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 12{x}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))^{2}\,\text{d}x & =4{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))}^{2}-8\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))}^{2}-8(\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9}+D) \\  & =4{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))}^{2}-\frac{8{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{3}+\frac{8{x}^{3}}{9}-8D \\  & ={x}^{3}(4{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))}^{2}-\frac{8}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)+\frac{8}{9})+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-8D.$

Finally, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1/2}^{e/2}12{x}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))^{2}\text{d}x & ={[{x}^{3}(4{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))}^{2}-\frac{8}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)+\frac{8}{9})]}_{1/2}^{e/2} \\  & =[{(\frac{e}{2})}^{3}(4{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot \frac{e}{2}))}^{2}-\frac{8}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot \frac{e}{2})+\frac{8}{9})] \\  & \,-[{(\frac{1}{2})}^{3}(4{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot \frac{1}{2}))}^{2}-\frac{8}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot \frac{1}{2})+\frac{8}{9})] \\  & =[\frac{{e}^{3}}{8}(4{(\operatorname{ln}⁡e)}^{2}-\frac{8}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡e+\frac{8}{9})]-[\frac{1}{8}(4{(\operatorname{ln}⁡1)}^{2}-\frac{8}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡1+\frac{8}{9})] \\  & =[\frac{{e}^{3}}{8}(4-\frac{8}{3}+\frac{8}{9})]-\frac{1}{8}\cdot \frac{8}{9} \\  & =\frac{5{e}^{3}-2}{18}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{1}^{e}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \,\text{d}x=x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}(x)-\int (x)(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =x{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-2\int \operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int \operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \,\text{d}x=x.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x))(x)-\int (x)(\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)-\int \text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)-x+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is a constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =x{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-2(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)-x+D) \\  & =x{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+2x+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-2D.$ 

Finally then, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & ={(x{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+2x)|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =(e{(\operatorname{ln}⁡e)}^{2}-2e\operatorname{ln}⁡(e)+2e)-(1{(\operatorname{ln}⁡1)}^{2}-2\cdot 1\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+2(1)) \\  & =e-2.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Calculate $F(\frac{\pi }{2})$ where $F(x)={\int }_{0}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.$
:question/worked-solution:
Evaluating $F(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we get the following definite integral:

$$
F\,(\frac{\pi }{2})={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t
$$

Then, computing the definite integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(\frac{\pi }{2}) & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡0 \\  & =1-0 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the addition and scalar multiplication properties of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{″}-3{y}^{′}+2y} & =L{6{e}^{-t}} \\ L{{y}^{″}}-3L{{y}^{′}}+2L{y} & =6L{{e}^{-t}}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's introduce $L{y}=Y(s).$

To calculate $L{{y}^{′}}$ and $L{{y}^{″}},$  we use formulas for the Laplace transforms of the derivatives and apply the initial conditions:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{′}} & =sY(s)-y(0)=sY(s) \\ L{{y}^{″}} & ={s}^{2}Y(s)-sy(0)-{y}^{′}(0)={s}^{2}Y(s)-3\end{aligned}
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms, we have the following result:

$$
L{{e}^{-t}}=\frac{1}{s+1}
$$

Therefore, we can solve for $Y(s):$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{″}}-3L{{y}^{′}}+2L{y} & =6L{{e}^{-t}} \\ ({s}^{2}Y(s)-3)-3(sY(s))+2Y(s) & =6(\frac{1}{s+1}) \\ ({s}^{2}-3s+2)Y(s) & =3+\frac{6}{s+1} \\ (s-1)(s-2)Y(s) & =\frac{3s+9}{s+1} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{3(s+3)}{(s+1)(s-1)(s-2)} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{3(s+3)}{({s}^{2}-1)(s-2)}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Find the curvature at an arbitrary point on the curve $r(s)$ parametrized by its arc length $s$, where:

$$
r(s)=⟨\frac{3s+1}{5},\,\frac{3-4s}{5}⟩,\,s\ge 0
$$
:question/worked-solution:
Let $T(s)$ denote the unit tangent to the given curve as a function of the arc length $s.$ Since we are given the curve $r(s)$ parametrized by the arc length $s$, we will use the following formula for the curvature:

$$
κ(s)=‖{T}^{′}(s)‖=‖{r}^{″}(s)‖
$$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(s)$ and ${r}^{″}(s):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(s) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{3s+1}{5}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{3-4s}{5})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{5},\,-\frac{4}{5}⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(s) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{3}{5}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(-\frac{4}{5})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(s) & =‖{r}^{″}(s)‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{(0)}^{2}+{(0)}^{2}} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the parabola shown above?
:question/worked-solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at $(0,0),$ and passes through the point $(6,3).$

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola  that has its vertex at $(0,0)$ are

$$
x=2pt,\,y=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Since the parabola passes through $(6,3),$ we can substitute $x=6$ and $y=3$ into the standard parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}6 &=2pt \\ 3 &=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}6 & =2pt \\ 3 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{3}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =p{(\frac{3}{p})}^{2} \\ 3 & =p\cdot \frac{9}{{p}^{2}} \\ 3 & =\frac{9}{p} \\ p & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x=2(3)t,\,y=(3){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x=6t,\,y=3{t}^{2}.
$$

:question/problem: Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the horizontal parabola given by the Cartesian equation ${y}^{2}=-2x?$
:question/worked-solution:
The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola ${y}^{2}=4px$ that has its vertex at $(0,0)$ are

$$
x=p{t}^{2},\,y=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case ${y}^{2}=4px$ and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4px & =-2x \\ 4p & =-2 \\ p & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x=(-\frac{1}{2}){t}^{2},\,y=2(-\frac{1}{2})t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x=-\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2},\,y=-t.
$$

:question/problem: Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the horizontal parabola given by the Cartesian equation ${y}^{2}=-6x?$
:question/worked-solution:
The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola ${y}^{2}=4px$ that has its vertex at $(0,0)$ are

$$
x=p{t}^{2},\,y=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case ${y}^{2}=4px$ and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4px & =-6x \\ 4p & =-6 \\ p & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x=(-\frac{3}{2}){t}^{2},\,y=2(-\frac{3}{2})t,

:question/problem: What are the coordinates of the vertex of the parabola $(y+6)^{2}=-6(x+8)?$
:question/worked-solution:
The standard equation of a left- or right-opening parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ is

$$
(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h),
$$

where $p$ is constant.

We can rewrite the given equation as 

$$
(y+6)^{2}=4(-\frac{6}{4})(x+8),
$$

which simplifies to

$$
(y+6)^{2}=4(-\frac{3}{2})(x+8).
$$

It is now clear that our equation is of the standard type with $p=-\frac{3}{2}.$ 

Comparing our equation with the standard equation, we can see that we have $h=-8$ and $k=-6.$ Therefore, the coordinates of the vertex of the parabola are $(-8,-6).$

:question/problem: The position $r$ of a particle $P$ at time $t$ is given by $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,\frac{1}{t},\,-1⟩.$ Find the tangential component of the acceleration of $P$ at time $t.$
:question/worked-solution:
The tangential component of acceleration is given by

$$
{a}_{T}=\frac{v\cdot a}{||v||}.
$$

First, we compute the velocity vector by differentiating the position vector, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{t},\,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the acceleration vector by differentiating the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},\,\frac{2}{{t}^{3}},\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute $v\cdot a$ and $||v||:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v\cdot a & =⟨\frac{1}{t},\,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},\,0⟩\cdot ⟨-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},\,\frac{2}{{t}^{3}},\,0⟩ \\  & =-\frac{1}{{t}^{3}}-\frac{2}{{t}^{5}} \\  & =-\frac{{t}^{2}+2}{{t}^{5}} \\ ||v|| & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{t})}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})}^{2}+{(0)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}+\frac{1}{{t}^{4}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{t}^{2}+1}{{t}^{4}}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}}{{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the tangential component of the acceleration, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{T} & =\frac{v\cdot a}{||v||} \\  & =\frac{(-\frac{{t}^{2}+2}{{t}^{5}})}{(\frac{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}}{{t}^{2}})} \\  & =-\frac{{t}^{2}+2}{{t}^{3}\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Determine the horizontal asymptote of $f(x)=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3x+2}.$
:question/worked-solution:
To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to \infty .$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is $x.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{3x+2} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{{x}^{3}}{x})}{(\frac{3x}{x}+\frac{2}{x})} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{(3+\frac{2}{x})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the term $\frac{2}{x}$ becomes very small. Therefore, as $x\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{(3+\frac{2}{x})} \\  & ≈\frac{{x}^{2}}{3+0} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

This is not a constant, which means that $y=f(x)$ does not have a horizontal asymptote.

:question/problem:
$$
\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}}^{A}=\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}{q}_{11} & {q}_{12} \\ {q}_{21} & {q}_{22} \\ {q}_{31} & {q}_{32}\end{bmatrix}}^{Q}\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}{r}_{11} & {r}_{12} \\ 0 & {r}_{22}\end{bmatrix}}^{R}.
$$

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. Given that the columns ${q}_{1},{q}_{2}$ of $Q$ were obtained from the columns of $A$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, find the value of $\frac{{r}_{22}}{{q}_{12}}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Let ${a}_{1},{a}_{2}$ be the columns of $A.$

First, we find an orthonormal basis of $\text{Col}(A)=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process.

**Step 1**. We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 2**. We find the vector ${v}_{2}$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}{{v}_{1}}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-(-\frac{1}{3})\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}+(\frac{1}{3})\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we normalize ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ {q}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{3}{2\sqrt{6}}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute $R:$

$$
\begin{aligned}R & ={Q}^{T}\,A \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{3} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ 0 & \frac{4}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following QR factorization of $A:$

$$
\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}}^{A}=\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}}^{Q}\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{3} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ 0 & \frac{4}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}}^{R}.
$$

Finally, $\frac{{r}_{22}}{{q}_{12}}=\frac{(\frac{4}{\sqrt{6}})}{(\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}})}=2.$

:question/problem:
The function $f(x,y)$ is defined as

Evaluate this function at the point $(\frac{1}{2},1).$
