:question/problem: A dye mixing tank at a textile factory can hold up to $180\,\text{gal}$ of liquid. Initially, it contains $100\,\text{gal}$ of solution with $20\,\text{lb}$ of dissolved dye. A more concentrated dye solution with concentration $0.6\,\text{lb/gal}$ flows into the tank at a rate of $15\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed solution drains out at a rate of $10\,\text{gal/min}.$ Rounded to one decimal place, find the amount of dye in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow.
:question/worked-solution:
Since $Q$ is the amount of dye in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which dye enters the tank minus the rate at which dye leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which dye enters the tank.

First, note that a solution containing $0.6\,\text{lb/gal}$ of dye enters the tank at a rate of $15\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *dye* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.6\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (15\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.6\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (15\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =9\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which dye exits the tank.

To find the rate at which dye leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $100\,\text{gal}$ of liquid; solution enters at $15\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $10\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of liquid in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=100+15t-10t=5(20+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of dye in the tank, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{5(20+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $10\,\text{gal/min},$ *dye* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(10\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{5(20+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(10\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{5(20+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{10Q}{5(20+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{20+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =9-\frac{2Q}{20+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{20+t}\,Q=9.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(20+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|20+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(20+t)^{2}} \\  & =(20+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(20+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(20+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{20+t}\,Q) & =(20+t)^{2}\cdot 9 \\ (20+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(20+t)Q & =9(20+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(20+t)^{2}) & =9(20+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(20+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 9(20+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(20+t)^{2} & =9\cdot \frac{1}{3}(20+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =3(20+t)+\frac{C}{(20+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the tank initially contains $20\,\text{lb}$ of dye. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=20,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =20 \\ 3(20+0)+\frac{C}{(20+0)^{2}} & =20 \\ 60+\frac{C}{(20)^{2}} & =20 \\ \frac{C}{(20)^{2}} & =-40 \\ C & =-40(20)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =3(20+t)-\frac{40(20)^{2}}{(20+t)^{2}} \\  & =3(20+t)-40{(\frac{20}{20+t})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $180\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=180$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =180 \\ 100+15{t}_{o}-10{t}_{o} & =180 \\ 100+5{t}_{o} & =180 \\ 5{t}_{o} & =80 \\ {t}_{o} & =16\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of dye in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(16) & =3(20+16)-40{(\frac{20}{20+16})}^{2} \\  & =108-40{(\frac{20}{36})}^{2} \\  & ≈95.7\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: A saline reservoir for a medical research lab can hold up to $160\,\text{gal}$ of solution. Initially, it contains $100\,\text{gal}$ of saline solution with $25\,\text{lb}$ of dissolved salt. A more concentrated saline solution with concentration $1.0\,\text{lb/gal}$ flows into the reservoir at a rate of $6\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed solution drains out at a rate of $4\,\text{gal/min}.$ Rounded to one decimal place, find the amount of salt in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow.
:question/worked-solution:
Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the reservoir at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which salt enters the reservoir minus the rate at which salt leaves the reservoir.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which salt enters the reservoir.

First, note that a solution containing $1.0\,\text{lb/gal}$ of salt enters the reservoir at a rate of $6\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *salt* enters the reservoir is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(1.0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (6\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(1.0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (6\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =6\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which salt exits the reservoir.

To find the rate at which salt leaves the reservoir, we must first determine the volume of solution in the reservoir at time $t.$

The reservoir initially contains $100\,\text{gal}$ of solution; solution enters at $6\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $4\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the reservoir after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=100+6t-4t=2(50+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the reservoir is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the reservoir, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{2(50+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $4\,\text{gal/min},$ *salt* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(4\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{2(50+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(4\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{2(50+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{4Q}{2(50+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{50+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =6-\frac{2Q}{50+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{50+t}\,Q=6.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(50+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|50+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(50+t)^{2}} \\  & =(50+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(50+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(50+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{50+t}\,Q) & =(50+t)^{2}\cdot 6 \\ (50+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(50+t)Q & =6(50+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(50+t)^{2}) & =6(50+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(50+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 6(50+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(50+t)^{2} & =6\cdot \frac{1}{3}(50+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =2(50+t)+\frac{C}{(50+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the reservoir initially contains $25\,\text{lb}$ of salt. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=25,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =25 \\ 2(50+0)+\frac{C}{(50+0)^{2}} & =25 \\ 100+\frac{C}{(50)^{2}} & =25 \\ \frac{C}{(50)^{2}} & =-75 \\ C & =-75(50)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =2(50+t)-\frac{75(50)^{2}}{(50+t)^{2}} \\  & =2(50+t)-75{(\frac{50}{50+t})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the reservoir begins to overflow. The reservoir has a capacity of $160\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=160$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =160 \\ 100+6{t}_{o}-4{t}_{o} & =160 \\ 100+2{t}_{o} & =160 \\ 2{t}_{o} & =60 \\ {t}_{o} & =30\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of salt in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(30) & =2(50+30)-75{(\frac{50}{50+30})}^{2} \\  & =160-75{(\frac{50}{80})}^{2} \\  & ≈130.7\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the inexact differential equation

$$
xy\,\text{d}x-({x}^{2}+3{y}^{3})\,\text{d}y=0.
$$

It is known that 

$$
\frac{1}{P}(\frac{∂P}{∂y}-\frac{∂Q}{∂x})=\frac{3}{y}
$$

where the functions $P$ and $Q$ are given by 

$$
P(x,y)=xy,\,Q(x,y)=-{x}^{2}-3{y}^{3}.
$$

Use this information to find a suitable integrating factor $I(y)$ and hence find the general solution to the equation.

$\,$ A suitable integrating factor is $I(y)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The general solution is {{field-2}}, where $c$ is a constant.
:question/worked-solution:
For a differential equation of the form

$$
P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y=0,
$$

we have that if

$$
\frac{1}{P}(\frac{∂P}{∂y}-\frac{∂Q}{∂x})=h(y)
$$

where $h(y)$ is independent of $x,$ then an integrating factor for the equation is

$$
I(y)=\operatorname{exp}⁡(-\int h(y)\,\text{d}y)
$$

where $\operatorname{exp}⁡(y)$ denotes the exponential function ${e}^{y}.$

We are given that

$$
\frac{1}{P}(\frac{∂P}{∂y}-\frac{∂Q}{∂x})=\frac{3}{y}.
$$

Since $\frac{3}{y}$ is a function of $y$ only, we can conclude that the integrating factor for the equation is 

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x,y) & ={e}^{-\int 3/y\text{ }\text{d}y} \\  & ={e}^{-3\operatorname{ln}⁡y} \\  & =\frac{1}{{y}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying our equation by the integrating factor, we arrive at the following exact differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{{y}^{3}}(xy\,\text{d}x-({x}^{2}+3{y}^{3})\,\text{d}y) & =0 \\ \underbrace{(\frac{x}{{y}^{2}})}_{\overset{~}{P}}\,\text{d}x+\underbrace{(-1)(\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{3}}+3)}_{\overset{~}{Q}}\,\text{d}y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

For this exact equation, we have

$$
\overset{~}{P}(x,y)=\frac{x}{{y}^{2}},\,\overset{~}{Q}(x,y)=-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{3}}-3.
$$

To solve the equation, let's first integrate $\overset{~}{P}(x,y)$ with respect to $x.$
The result should include an arbitrary function of $y,$ which we'll call $F(y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(x,y) & =\int \overset{~}{P}(x,y)\,\text{d}x+F(y) \\  & =\int \frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+F(y) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2{y}^{2}}+F(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, let's integrate $\overset{~}{Q}(x,y)$ with respect to $y.$
The result should include an arbitrary function of $x,$ which we'll call $G(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(x,y) & =\int \overset{~}{Q}(x,y)\,\text{d}y+G(x) \\  & =\int (-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{3}}-3)\,\text{d}y+G(x) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2{y}^{2}}-3y+G(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing the two solutions, we see that we must have

$$
F(y)=-3y,\,G(x)=0.
$$

Therefore, the general solution $u(x,y)=c$ is

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{2{y}^{2}}-3y=c.
$$

Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =-\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(r) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(-\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot \operatorname{csc}⁡\theta \operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{2}{9}$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{3},$ and solve for $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{9} & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot [\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})] \\ -\frac{2}{9} & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot (\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}) \\ -\frac{2}{9} & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the following initial value problem.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+3y=\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,y(0)=1
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below to find the solution using Laplace transforms. You may make use of the following results:

$$
L\{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t\}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,L\{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t\}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,s>0.
$$

Let $Y(s)=L\{y(t)\}.$ Taking the Laplace transform of both sides of the equation and solving for $Y,$ we have

$$
Y(s)={{field-1}}.
$$

The partial fraction decomposition of $Y$ is

$$
Y(s)={{field-2}}.
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(t)={{field-3}}.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides of the differential equation. Using the linearity property, we have

$$
L\{{y}^{′}\}+3L\{y\}=L\{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\}+L\{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\}.
$$

Using the formula for the transform of a derivative $L\{{y}^{′}\}=sY(s)-y(0)$ and the standard trigonometric transforms

$$
L\{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\}=\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4},\,L\{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4},
$$

we substitute the known values. Note that $y(0)=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(sY(s)-1)+3Y(s) & =\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4}+\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4} \\ (s+3)Y(s)-1 & =\frac{s+2}{{s}^{2}+4}\end{aligned}
$$

We rearrange to solve for $Y(s).$ First, add $1$ to the right-hand side and find a common denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}(s+3)Y(s) & =1+\frac{s+2}{{s}^{2}+4} \\ (s+3)Y(s) & =\frac{{s}^{2}+4}{{s}^{2}+4}+\frac{s+2}{{s}^{2}+4} \\ (s+3)Y(s) & =\frac{{s}^{2}+s+6}{{s}^{2}+4}\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing by $(s+3),$ we obtain

$$
Y(s)=\frac{{s}^{2}+s+6}{(s+3)({s}^{2}+4)}.
$$

Next, we perform a partial fraction decomposition. Since the denominator has a linear factor $(s+3)$ and an irreducible quadratic factor $({s}^{2}+4),$ we write

$$
\frac{{s}^{2}+s+6}{(s+3)({s}^{2}+4)}=\frac{A}{s+3}+\frac{Bs+C}{{s}^{2}+4}.
$$

To find the constants, we clear the denominators:

$$
{s}^{2}+s+6=A({s}^{2}+4)+(Bs+C)(s+3)
$$

- Setting $s=-3,$ we have
 

$$
(-3)^{2}+(-3)+6=A((-3)^{2}+4)+0\,⟹\,12=13A\,⟹\,A=\frac{12}{13}.
$$

- Comparing the coefficients of ${s}^{2},$ we have
  

$$
1=A+B\,⟹\,1=\frac{12}{13}+B\,⟹\,B=\frac{1}{13}.
$$

- Comparing the constant terms, we have
 

$$
6=4A+3C\,⟹\,6=4(\frac{12}{13})+3C\,⟹\,C=\frac{10}{13}.
$$

Thus, the decomposition is

$$
Y(s)=\frac{(\frac{12}{13})}{13(s+3)}+\frac{(\frac{1}{13}s+\frac{10}{13})}{{s}^{2}+4}=\frac{12}{13(s+3)}+\frac{s+10}{13({s}^{2}+4)}.
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s+3}\} & ={e}^{-3t} \\ {L}^{-1}\{\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4}\} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡2t \\ {L}^{-1}\{\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4}\} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking the inverse Laplace transform of $Y(s),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =\frac{12}{13}{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s+3}\}+\frac{1}{13}{L}^{-1}\{\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4}\}+\frac{5}{13}{L}^{-1}\{\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4}\} \\ y(t) & =\frac{12}{13}{e}^{-3t}+\frac{5}{13}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+\frac{1}{13}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{u}{2}) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡v\end{bmatrix}.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{u}{2})$ and $y(u,v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡v.$

First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡v}{2{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{u}{2})} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{u}{2}) \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡v}{2{cos}^{2}⁡(u/2)} & -\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{u}{2}) \\ \,0\, & \,\text{ }\text{ }\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡v}{2{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{u}{2})}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Calculate the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\text{u}=⟨4,1⟩$ and $\text{v}=⟨-6,-\frac{3}{2}⟩.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we construct a matrix where the columns are made up of the components of the corresponding vectors:

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}4 & -6 \\ 1 & -\frac{3}{2}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Then, we find the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(M) & =\begin{vmatrix}4 & -6 \\ 1 & -\frac{3}{2}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =4\cdot (-\frac{3}{2})-(-6)\cdot 1 \\  & =-6+6 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The absolute value of $det(M)$ gives the area $A$ of the parallelogram:

$$
A=|\,0\,|=0
$$

:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=-\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Given that the point $P(-\frac{\pi }{2},0,2)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y}{2}$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=-\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(-\frac{\pi }{2},0).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(-\frac{\pi }{2},0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-\frac{\pi }{2},0) & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡0}{2} \\  & =\frac{(-1)\cdot 1}{2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(-\frac{\pi }{2},0) & ={f}_{y}(-\frac{\pi }{2},0)(y-0) \\ z-2 & =-\frac{1}{2}y \\ z & =-\frac{1}{2}y+2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-\frac{\pi }{2},0,2)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=-\frac{\pi }{2} \\ z &=-\frac{1}{2}y+2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=-\frac{\pi }{2},$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-\frac{1}{2}y+2$ (or $y+2z-4=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,2⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,1,2⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-2j+k \\  & =⟨0,-2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $⟨0,-2,1⟩.$

:question/problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(5,4).$
:question/worked-solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(5,4)$, can be found by computing $∇f(5,4).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(5,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})\text{ }j \\  & =\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\text{ }i-\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\text{ }j \\ ∇f(5,4) & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{(5)^{2}-(4)^{2}}}\text{ }i-\frac{4}{\sqrt{(5)^{2}-(4)^{2}}}\text{ }j \\  & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{9}}i-\frac{4}{\sqrt{9}}j \\  & =\frac{5}{3}i-\frac{4}{3}j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(5,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(5,4)}{‖∇f(5,4)‖} & =\frac{\frac{5}{3}i-\frac{4}{3}j}{\sqrt{{(\frac{5}{3})}^{2}+{(-\frac{4}{3})}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{\frac{5}{3}i-\frac{4}{3}j}{\frac{\sqrt{41}}{3}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{41}}{41}(5i-4j)\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate ${f}_{xyy}(2,2,2)$ given that a function $f(x,y,z)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ and that

$$
{f}_{yx}(x,y,z)=2y\sqrt{\frac{{z}^{3}}{x}}+3{z}^{3}\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xyy}(x,y,z) & ={f}_{yxy}(x,y,z) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{yx}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y\sqrt{\frac{{z}^{3}}{x}}+3{z}^{3}\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}}) \\  & =2\sqrt{\frac{{z}^{3}}{x}}+3{z}^{3}\sqrt{x}(-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{y}^{3}}}) \\  & =2\sqrt{\frac{{z}^{3}}{x}}-\frac{3}{2}{z}^{3}\sqrt{\frac{x}{{y}^{3}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point  $(2,2,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xyy}(2,2,2) & =2\sqrt{\frac{(2)^{3}}{(2)}}-\frac{3}{2}(2)^{3}\sqrt{\frac{(2)}{(2)^{3}}} \\  & =2\cdot 2-3\cdot 2 \\  & =4-6 \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/53/5322f43ff1eeee6e06b3c393cc1b59c9af32bc2e7dba66766607af117954ace1.png)

Find, in amperes, the amplitude of the steady state current for the RCL circuit shown above.

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
:question/worked-solution:
The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $8\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $20\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.1\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $10\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=20\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=20I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.1}=10q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=10\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=10\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
8\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)=20I+10q+10\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(8\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)) & =\frac{d}{dt}(20I+10q+10\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ -8\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & =20\,\frac{dI}{dt}+10\,\frac{dq}{dt}+10\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}+I=-\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${I}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{c}}{d{t}^{2}}+2\,\frac{d{I}_{c}}{dt}+{I}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+Bt{e}^{-t},
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

- Next, we find a particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $t,$ i.e.,

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute this, as well as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d{I}_{p}}{dt} & =-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(t), \\ \frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{p}}{d{t}^{2}} & =-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t))+2(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)) \\ +(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t)) & =-\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ (2\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+(-2\alpha )\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & =-\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2\beta &=0\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)) \\ -2\alpha &=-\frac{4}{5}\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =\frac{2}{5}$ and $\beta =0.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)={I}_{c}(t)+{I}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+Bt{e}^{-t}+\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+Bt{e}^{-t}$ is the *transient current*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function ${I}_{p}(t)=\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)$ is the *steady-state current*. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
I(t)≈{I}_{p}(t)=\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current, in amperes, is given by

$$
\sqrt{{(\frac{2}{5})}^{2}+{0}^{2}}=\frac{2}{5}.
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/70/70072e2a4599c8b1b43ff1782ee270076a384657ab02c7aeec1a3ae87c7674fc.png)

Find, in amperes, the amplitude of the steady state current for the RCL circuit shown above.

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
:question/worked-solution:
The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $13\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $4\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.25\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $1\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=4\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=4I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.25}=4q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=1\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
13\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)=4I+4q+\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(13\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =\frac{d}{dt}(4I+4q+\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ 39\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) & =4\,\frac{dI}{dt}+4\,\frac{dq}{dt}+\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+4\,\frac{dI}{dt}+4I=39\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t).
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${I}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{c}}{d{t}^{2}}+4\,\frac{d{I}_{c}}{dt}+4{I}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-2t}+Bt{e}^{-2t},
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

- Next, we find a particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $3t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $3t,$ i.e.,

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute this, as well as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d{I}_{p}}{dt} & =-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t), \\ \frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{p}}{d{t}^{2}} & =-9\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-9\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-9\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-9\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))+4(-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)) \\ +4(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =39\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ (-5\alpha +12\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+(-12\alpha -5\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & =39\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-5\alpha +12\beta &=39\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)) \\ -12\alpha -5\beta &=0\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{15}{13}$ and $\beta =\frac{36}{13}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{15}{13}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{36}{13}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)={I}_{c}(t)+{I}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-2t}+Bt{e}^{-2t}-\frac{15}{13}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{36}{13}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-2t}+Bt{e}^{-2t}$ is the *transient current*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function ${I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{15}{13}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{36}{13}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$ is the *steady-state current*. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
I(t)≈{I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{15}{13}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{36}{13}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current, in amperes, is given by

$$
\sqrt{{(-\frac{15}{13})}^{2}+{(\frac{36}{13})}^{2}}=3.
$$

:question/problem:
Find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ of the equation 

$$
{x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-3x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3y=9\operatorname{ln}⁡x,\,x>0.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
This Cauchy-Euler equation has non-polynomial forcing, but we are not given two fundamental solutions, so we cannot use variation of parameters.

However, if we make a substitution $x={e}^{t},$ we can transform the Cauchy-Euler equation into a linear ODE with constant coefficients.

Letting $x={e}^{t},$ we note that

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}={e}^{t}=x\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}.
$$

Then, we use the chain rule to compute the first and second derivatives. 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}, \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\underbrace{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x})\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}_{\text{product rule}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\cdot \underbrace{\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}}_{\text{chain rule}}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}-4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+3y=9t.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is a second-order inhomogeneous differential equation with constant coefficients and polynomial forcing. 

Using the usual methods for solving second-order ODEs, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{t}+B{e}^{3t}.
$$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $1.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $1,$ i.e.,

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\alpha t+\beta 
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}t}=\alpha ,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}=0.
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta $ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation for $y(t):$

$$
0-4\alpha +3(\alpha t+\beta )=9t
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
3\alpha t+(3\beta -4\alpha )=9t.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3\alpha &=9\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of }t) \\ 3\beta -4\alpha &=0\, && (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Hence, $\alpha =3$ and $\beta =4,$ and so the particular integral ${y}_{p}(t)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=3t+4.
$$

Now, returning to the variable $x,$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=3\operatorname{ln}⁡x+4.
$$

:question/problem: Find a point that satisfies the mean value theorem for $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ are $a=⟨-1,0,3⟩$ and $b=⟨0,4,0⟩,$ respectively.
:question/worked-solution:
The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y,z)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨-1,0,3⟩$ and $b=⟨0,4,0⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,4,0)-f(-1,0,3) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨0,4,0⟩-⟨-1,0,3⟩) \\ -16-1 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,4,-3⟩ \\ -17 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,4,-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨2x,-2y,0⟩ \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨2{c}_{1},-2{c}_{2},0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-17 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,4,-3⟩ \\ -17 & =⟨2{c}_{1},-2{c}_{2},0⟩\cdot ⟨1,4,-3⟩ \\ -17 & =2{c}_{1}-8{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-(-1)}{1} & =\frac{y-0}{4}=\frac{z-3}{(-3)} \\ x+1 & =\frac{y}{4}=\frac{3-z}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Parametrizing the line, we get

$$
x=t-1,\,y=4t,\,z=3-3t,\,0\le t\le 1.
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
{c}_{1}=t-1,\,{c}_{2}=4t,\,{c}_{3}=3-3t.
$$

Substituting the above in the equation $2{c}_{1}-8{c}_{2}=-17,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2(t-1)-8(4t) & =-17 \\ 2t-2-32t & =-17 \\ -30t & =-15 \\ t & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find the values of ${c}_{1},$ ${c}_{2},$ and ${c}_{3}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}-1=-\frac{1}{2}, \\ {c}_{2} & =4(\frac{1}{2})=2, \\ {c}_{3} & =3-3(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the coordinates of $C$ are $(-\frac{1}{2},2,\frac{3}{2}).$

:question/problem: Express $z=\sqrt{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4})+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}))$ in the form $z=x+\text{i}y.$
:question/worked-solution:
To express the number in Cartesian form, we expand the parentheses and substitute the values of the cosine and sine.

First, we find $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4})$ and $\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,,\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the values and expand the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\sqrt{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4})+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4})) \\  & =\sqrt{2}(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+\text{i}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =-1+\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: The position $x$ of a particle at time $t$ is given by $x(t)=\frac{{t}^{2}}{{t}^{2}+1}.$ Calculate the velocity at time $t.$
:question/worked-solution:
The velocity is the derivative of the position function $x(t)$ with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{t}^{2}}{{t}^{2}+1}) \\  & =\frac{2t({t}^{2}+1)-{t}^{2}(2t)}{({t}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2{t}^{3}+2t-2{t}^{3}}{({t}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2t}{({t}^{2}+1)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The position $s(t)$ of a particle (in miles) at time $t$ hours is given by 

$$
s(t)=\frac{3}{t},\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the speed of the particle when $t=3\,\text{h}.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{3}{t}) \\  & =-\frac{3}{{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

When $t=3,$ the velocity is

$$
v(3)=-\frac{3}{{3}^{2}}=-\frac{1}{3}.
$$

Therefore, the speed is $|-\frac{1}{3}|=\frac{1}{3}\,\text{miles/h}.$

:question/problem:
![](images/92/924444fa2da1709d788d3b3522e86743b46ee1c5a25999bb77731449e621a07d.png)

Consider the arc of the curve $y=1-(x+1)^{2}$ that lies in the second quadrant between its $x$-intercepts. What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $x$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-(x+1)^{2} & =0 \\ (x+1)^{2} & =1 \\ x+1 & =\pm 1 \\ x & =-1\pm 1 \\ x & =-2,0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=-2$ to $x=0.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1-(x+1)^{2})=-2x-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-2}^{0}(1-(x+1)^{2})\sqrt{1+(-2x-2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-2}^{0}(-{x}^{2}-2x)\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+8x+5}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & -12 \\ 3 & 9\end{bmatrix},\,J=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix},\,P=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & a \\ 1 & b\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the matrices above. Given that $A=PJ{P}^{-1}$ is a Jordan canonical decomposition of $A,$ find the value of $3a+6b.$
:question/worked-solution:
From the Jordan matrix $J,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=3.
$$

As a result, we obtain that 

- the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ of the eigenvalue $\lambda =3,$

- the second column of $P$ corresponds to the vector ${v}_{2}$ such that $(A-3I){v}_{2}={v}_{1}.$

Now, computing $A-3I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & -12 \\ 3 & 9\end{bmatrix}-(3)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & -12 \\ 3 & 6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the matrix equation $(A-3I){v}_{2}={v}_{1}$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & -12 & -2 \\ 3 & 6 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-6 & -12 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{3}-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get  

$$
{v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{5}{3} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, $3a+6b=3\cdot (-\frac{5}{3})+6\cdot 1=1.$

:question/problem: Find the equation of the tangent plane to the surface generated by the vector-valued function $r(u,v)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v,\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡v⟩$ at the point where $u=\frac{\pi }{3}$ and $v=\frac{\pi }{2}.$
:question/worked-solution:
We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}(u,v) & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡v)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v,\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′}(u,v) & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡v)⟩ \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,-2\operatorname{sin}⁡v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate these vectors when $u=\frac{\pi }{3}$ and $v=\frac{\pi }{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨-\sqrt{3},\,1,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a normal vector to the surface is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & ={r}_{u}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{2})\times {r}_{v}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -\sqrt{3} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{3} & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{3} & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-2,\,-2\sqrt{3},\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the parameters $u=\frac{\pi }{3}$ and $v=\frac{\pi }{2}$ correspond to the point 

$$
(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))=(1,\sqrt{3},0),
$$

the equation of the tangent plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}n\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨-2,\,-2\sqrt{3},\,0⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-\sqrt{3},\,z⟩ & =0 \\ (-2)\cdot (x-1)-2\sqrt{3}\cdot (y-\sqrt{3})+0\cdot z & =0 \\ -2x-2\sqrt{3\,}y+8 & =0 \\ -x-\sqrt{3}\,y+4 & =0 \\ x+\sqrt{3}\,y & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Compute a normal vector to the parametric surface defined by the equations 

$$
x=2u+v,\,y={u}^{2},\,z={v}^{2}
$$

at the point where $u=1$ and $v=\frac{1}{2}.$
:question/worked-solution:
In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨2u+v,\,{u}^{2},\,{v}^{2}⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}(u,v) & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(2u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}({u}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}({v}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,2u,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′}(u,v) & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(2u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}({u}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}({v}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,2v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate these tangent vectors when $u=1$ and $v=\frac{1}{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}(1,\frac{1}{2}) & =⟨2,\,2(1),\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,2,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′}(1,\frac{1}{2}) & =⟨1,\,0,\,2(\frac{1}{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a normal vector to the surface at the point where $u=1$ and $v=\frac{1}{2}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & ={r}_{u}^{′}(1,\frac{1}{2})\times {r}_{v}^{′}(1,\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,-2,\,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: The geometric series $2+4+8+16+32$ can be expressed using sigma notation as
:question/worked-solution:
First, we must express the given series in the form

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{N}{a}_{1}{r}^{n-1},
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ denotes the first term of the series, $r$ denotes the common ratio, and $N$ denotes the number of terms in the series. In this case, ${a}_{1}=2$ and $N=5.$

To find $r,$ we calculate the ratio of the first two terms in the series:

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{4}{2}=2
$$

Hence, expressing the geometric series given in sigma notation, we obtain:

$$
2+4+8+16+32={\sum }_{n=1}^{5}2\cdot {2}^{n-1}\,\,
$$

Finally, we can simplify the above series using the laws of exponents, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{5}2\cdot {2}^{n-1} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{5}2\cdot {2}^{n}\cdot {2}^{-1} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{5}2\cdot {2}^{-1}\cdot {2}^{n} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{5}2\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot {2}^{n} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{5}{2}^{n}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: What is ${\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?
:question/worked-solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

    

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)={e}^{x},$ the lower bound is $a=0,$ and the upper bound is $b=3.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{3-0}{n}=\frac{3}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(0+i\cdot \frac{3}{n})\,\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(\frac{3i}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{e}^{3i/n}\cdot \frac{3}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: What is ${\int }_{0}^{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?
:question/worked-solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{0}^{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡x,$ the lower bound is $a=0$ and the upper bound is $b=3.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{3-0}{n}=\frac{3}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(0+k\cdot \frac{3}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(\frac{3k}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{3k}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: A particle $P$ is moving along the curve $y=4{x}^{3}+16x$ such that the $x$-coordinate of $P$ is changing at the rate of $-\frac{1}{4}\,\text{cm}/\text{s}.$ Find the rate of change of the $y$-coordinate when $x=3\,\text{cm}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =4{x}^{3}+16x \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{x}^{3}+16x) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{3}+16x) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (12{x}^{2}+16).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{1}{4}\,\text{cm}/\text{s}$ and $x=3$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =(-\frac{1}{4})\cdot (12\cdot (3)^{2}+16)\,\text{cm}/\text{s} \\  & =-31\,\text{cm}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Which of the following shows some of the solution curves of the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{3(x-1)^{2}}{4}?$
:question/worked-solution:
Integrating the equation, we get

$$

$$

We can now plot the solution curves by selecting different values for $C.$ The sketch below shows the solution curves for $C=-2,0,2.$

:question/problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions to the equation $\operatorname{csc}⁡x+3=-1-\operatorname{csc}⁡x$ for ${0}^{∘}\le x<{360}^{∘},$ what is the numerical value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}?$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, isolating $\operatorname{csc}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{csc}⁡x+3 & =-1-\operatorname{csc}⁡x \\ 2\operatorname{csc}⁡x & =-4 \\ \operatorname{csc}⁡x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x},$ therefore the given equation is equivalent to

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡x=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, we find the principal value: 

$$
x=\text{arcsin}(-\frac{1}{2})=-{30}^{∘}
$$

This value is outside the required domain. To get a value inside the range, we add ${360}^{∘}.$ 

$$
{x}_{1}=x+{360}^{∘}=-{30}^{∘}+{360}^{∘}={330}^{∘}.
$$

So,  our first solution is ${x}_{1}={330}^{∘}.$

Our first solution lies in the fourth quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}={30}^{∘}.$ Since $\operatorname{sin}⁡x<0,$ the second solution must lie in the third quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}={30}^{∘}.$

![](images/b3/b3c523e882baf0b3a105e10131091e40de686b4c1483f46e7bdc235e30743a6d.png)

Since the second solution ${x}_{2}$ lies in the $3$rd quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={180}^{∘}+{\theta }_{R} \\  & ={180}^{∘}+{30}^{∘} \\  & ={210}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are $x={210}^{∘},{330}^{∘}.$

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=210\cdot 330=69\,300.
$$

:question/problem:
The position vector $r$ of a particle $P$ (relative to a fixed origin $O$) at time $t$ is given by

$$
r=⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the velocity vector $v$ at time $t=\frac{\pi }{2}.$
:question/worked-solution:
The particle's velocity vector is given by the derivative of its position vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

To find the velocity when $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we substitute into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The velocity vector $v=⟨u,v⟩,$ measured in $\text{m}/\text{s},$ of a particle $P$ at time $t$ seconds is given by

$$
v=⟨-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩.
$$

Find the magnitude of the acceleration of $P$ at time $t=\frac{\pi }{8}.$
:question/worked-solution:
To compute the acceleration vector, we differentiate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨4\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

To find the acceleration at time $t=\frac{\pi }{8},$ we substitute $t=\frac{\pi }{8}$ into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}a(\frac{\pi }{8}) & =⟨4\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{8}),2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{8})⟩ \\  & =⟨4\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}),2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})⟩ \\  & =⟨4\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},2\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨4,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the magnitude of the acceleration, we compute $|a(\frac{\pi }{8})|:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}|a(\frac{\pi }{8})| & =|⟨4,2⟩| \\  & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16+4} \\  & =\sqrt{20} \\  & =2\sqrt{5}\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The velocity vector $v=⟨u,v⟩,$ measured in $\text{m}/\text{s},$ of a particle $P$ at time $t$ seconds is given by

$$
v=⟨{2}^{t-1},\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+1}⟩.
$$

Find the magnitude of the acceleration of $P$ at time $t=1.$
:question/worked-solution:
To compute the acceleration vector, we differentiate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({2}^{t-1}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+1})⟩ \\  & =⟨{2}^{t-1}\operatorname{ln}⁡2,-\frac{2t}{({t}^{2}+1)^{2}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

To find the acceleration at time $t=1,$ we substitute $t=1$ into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}a(1) & =⟨{2}^{1-1}\operatorname{ln}⁡2,-\frac{2(1)}{({1}^{2}+1)^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨{2}^{0}\operatorname{ln}⁡2,-\frac{2}{4}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡2,-\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the magnitude of the acceleration, we compute $|a(1)|:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}|a(1)| & =|⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡2,-\frac{1}{2}⟩| \\  & =\sqrt{(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{ln}^{2}⁡2+\frac{1}{4}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{4{ln}^{2}⁡2+1}{4}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{4{ln}^{2}⁡2+1}}{2}\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The position vector $r$ of a particle $P$ (relative to a fixed origin $O$) at time $t$ is given by

$$
r=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1),2{t}^{4}+3⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the acceleration vector $a$ at time $t=1.$
:question/worked-solution:
To compute the acceleration vector, we need to differentiate the velocity vector. So first, we need to compute the velocity vector, which we can do this by differentiating the position vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{4}+3)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{t+1},8{t}^{3}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to compute the acceleration vector, we differentiate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t+1}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8{t}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{(t+1)^{2}},24{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the acceleration at time $t=1,$ we substitute $t=1$ into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}a(1) & =⟨-\frac{1}{(1+1)^{2}},24({1}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{4},24⟩\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},0⟩\,,\,t\in (0,\infty ).
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $(2,3)$ and has velocity $⟨1,-1⟩$ when $t=1,$ calculate the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$
:question/worked-solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector. 

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},0⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})\text{d}t,\int 0\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{t}+{C}_{1},{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨1,-1⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨\frac{1}{1}+{C}_{1},{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨1,-1⟩ & =⟨1+{C}_{1},{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=-1.$ Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨\frac{1}{t},-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\frac{1}{t},-1⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int \frac{1}{t}\,\text{d}t,\int (-1)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡t+{C}_{3},-t+{C}_{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(1)=⟨2,3⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡1+{C}_{3},-1+{C}_{4}⟩ \\ ⟨2,3⟩ & =⟨{C}_{3},-1+{C}_{4}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{3}=2$ and ${C}_{4}=4.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨2+\operatorname{ln}⁡t,4-t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=1-{y}^{2},$ traversed once along the circle $C$ with equation $(x+3)^{2}+{y}^{2}=1?$
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a circle of radius $1$ centered at $(-3,0).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=1-{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =1-(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({cos}^{2}⁡t)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/62/62f33dab4305a41a0bc180231fef7015361dec4aac63f14c31fd48a39b8fcd68.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}4x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=\frac{2}{y}$ traversed between the points $(2,1)$ and $(\frac{1}{3},6),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parameter $y=t.$*
:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $x=x(y).$ Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have 

$$
x=x(t)=\frac{2}{t}.
$$

 

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨\frac{2}{t},\,t⟩,\,1\le t\le 6
$$

Note that the domain $1\le t\le 6$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2}{t})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =-\frac{2}{{t}^{2}}\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(-\frac{2}{{t}^{2}})}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{4}{{t}^{4}}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{4+{t}^{4}}{{t}^{4}}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{t}^{4}+4}}{{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=4x{y}^{2},$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =4(\frac{2}{t})(t)^{2} \\  & =8t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}4x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{6}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{6}8t\cdot \frac{\sqrt{{t}^{4}+4}}{{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{1}^{6}\frac{\sqrt{{t}^{4}+4}}{t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=x\,{e}^{1-{y}^{2}}$ along the quarter-circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=36,$ traversed from the point $(6,0)$ to the point $(0,6)$ in the first quadrant?
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $6$ centered at $O,$ shown below. 

![](images/c1/c1e3332017b795ed6733a0547e6e449fdba3874f1d1e755118a0687ccaf7448c.png)

The curve $C$ can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨6\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,6\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36{sin}^{2}⁡t+36{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{36({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x\,{e}^{1-{y}^{2}},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{1-(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{1-36{sin}^{2}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{e}^{x+y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{1-36{sin}^{2}⁡t}\cdot 6\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =36{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{1-36{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=x\,\sqrt{9-{y}^{2}}$ along the quarter-circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9,$ traversed from the point $(0,-3)$ to the point $(3,0)$ in the fourth quadrant?
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $3$ centered at $O,$ shown below. 

![](images/b7/b7c2c6f9e50988629007a06213cb3acf0a48f9951f026fb70d5a986b760abdfe.png)

The curve $C$ can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{3\pi }{2}\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+9{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{9({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x\,\sqrt{9-{y}^{2}},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\sqrt{9-(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\sqrt{9-9{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =9{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\,\sqrt{9-{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }9{cos}^{2}⁡t\cdot 3\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =27{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}$ along the quarter-circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4,$ traversed from the point $(-2,0)$ to the point $(0,-2)$ in the third quadrant?
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $2$ centered at $O,$ shown below. 

![](images/1f/1fd6c2df8b8467a46ed36b515842b88656883733376ee732839bab4085ca019c.png)

The curve $C$ can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =2\end{aligned}

Now, since $f(x,y)=2{x}^{2},$ we obtain

Therefore, we can write the integral as

:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\frac{2x}{y}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the ellipse $4{x}^{2}+49{y}^{2}=196,$ traversed once in the counterclockwise direction?
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{7}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $7$ and $2,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨7\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(7\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-7\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{49{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{45{sin}^{2}⁡t+4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{45{sin}^{2}⁡t+4}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{2x}{y},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{2(7\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}=7\operatorname{cot}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{2x}{y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }7\operatorname{cot}⁡t\sqrt{45{sin}^{2}⁡t+4}\,\text{d}t \\  & =7{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cot}⁡t\sqrt{45{sin}^{2}⁡t+4}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}2x\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the ellipse $4{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}=64,$ traversed once in the counterclockwise direction?
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $4$ and $2,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{12{sin}^{2}⁡t+4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{12{sin}^{2}⁡t+4} \\  & =2\sqrt{3{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=2x,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=8\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}2x\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 2\sqrt{3{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =16{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{3{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(3-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the ellipse $12{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}=36,$ traversed once in the counterclockwise direction?
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{(2\sqrt{3})^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $\sqrt{3}$ and $2\sqrt{3},$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{3{sin}^{2}⁡t+12{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡t+3({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡t+3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=3-{x}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3-(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =3-3{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =3(1-{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =3{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(3-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }3{sin}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡t+3}\,\text{d}t \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡t+3}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $r(t)=⟨6\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t),\,{sin}^{2}⁡(5t)⟩,$ calculate $r(\frac{\pi }{3}).$

$$
r(t)=⟨\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{3{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t+3({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t+3}\end{aligned}

:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y)={e}^{x+y},$ traversed along the line segment from $(0,0)$ to $(-3,4)?$
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(0,0)$ to $(-3,4).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=0$ and $b=-3\,i+4\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =0+t\,(b-0) \\  & =t(b) \\  & =t(-3\,i+4\,j) \\  & =-3t\,i+4t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=-3t$ and $y=4t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t)j \\  & =-3\,i+4\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={e}^{x+y}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & ={e}^{-3t+4t} \\  & ={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{t}\cdot 5\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =5{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the line integral ${\int }_{C}(25-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is three-quarters of the ellipse $36{x}^{2}+25{y}^{2}=900,$ shown above?
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{6}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $5$ and $6,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,6\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25{sin}^{2}⁡t+36{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{11{cos}^{2}⁡t+25({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{11{cos}^{2}⁡t+25}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=25-{x}^{2},$ we obtain
