$$

:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{2x+y-z},$ traversed along the line segment from $(3,-2,3)$ to $(5,-1,7)?$
:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(3,-2,3)$ to $(5,-1,7).$

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=3i-2\,j+3k$ and $b=5\,i-j+7\,k.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(3i-2\,j+3k)+t[(5\,i-j+7\,k)-(3i-2\,j+3k)] \\  & =(3i-2\,j+3k)+t(2i+\,j+4k) \\  & =(2t+3)\,i+(t-2)\,j+(4t+3)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=2t+3,y=t-2,$ and $z=4t+3$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t+3)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-2)j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t+3)k \\  & =2i+j+4\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{21}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{2x+y-z}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\sqrt{2(2t+3)+(t-2)-(4t+3)} \\  & =\sqrt{t+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{t+1}\cdot \sqrt{21}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{21}{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\sqrt{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \pi .$
:question/worked-solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\sqrt{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }\,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }{\sqrt{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }}.
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(\sqrt{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta })^{2}+{(-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }{\sqrt{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }})}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )+\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡2\theta }{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{\frac{(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )^{2}+{sin}^{2}⁡2\theta }{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{\frac{2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}\text{ }\,\pi \end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: ${\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}⟨\frac{{csc}^{2}⁡t}{1-\operatorname{cot}⁡t},\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t=$
:question/worked-solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}⟨\frac{{csc}^{2}⁡t}{1-\operatorname{cot}⁡t},\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}\frac{{csc}^{2}⁡t}{1-\operatorname{cot}⁡t}\,\text{d}t,{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\operatorname{cot}⁡t){|}_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4},\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t{|}_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}))-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})),\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4})-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1,\,\sqrt{2}-2⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡2,\,\sqrt{2}-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the first three non-zero terms of the Maclaurin expansion of $\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1+x}{1-4x}).$
:question/worked-solution:
First, using the laws of logarithms, we observe that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1+x}{1-4x}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+x)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-4x).\end{aligned}
$$

For the expansion of $\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+x),$ we recall the standard result

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+x) & =x-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

To obtain the expansion of $\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-4x),$ we replace $x$ with $-4x$ in the standard expansion:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-4x) & =(-4x)-\frac{(-4x)^{2}}{2}+\frac{(-4x)^{3}}{3}-⋯ \\  & =-4x-8{x}^{2}-\frac{64{x}^{3}}{3}-⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, subtracting the expansion for $\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-4x)$ from the expansion for $\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1+x}{1-4x}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+x)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-4x) \\  & =(x-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-⋯)-(-4x-8{x}^{2}-\frac{64{x}^{3}}{3}-⋯) \\  & =(1+4)x+(-\frac{1}{2}+8){x}^{2}+(\frac{1}{3}+\frac{64}{3}){x}^{3}+⋯ \\  & =5x+\frac{15{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{65{x}^{3}}{3}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/ae/ae26451a8f2962ed873fc5eb703197375bc1a02eff2240bd21cebac81ef26205.png)

Consider the arc of the curve $x=y-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}$ that lies to the right of the $y$-axis between its $y$-intercepts. What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2} & =0 \\ 2y-{y}^{2} & =0 \\ y(2-y) & =0 \\ y & =0,2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=2.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(y-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2})=1-y.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(y-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2})\sqrt{1+{(1-y)}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(y-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2})\sqrt{1+(1-2y+{y}^{2})}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(y-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2})\sqrt{2-2y+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/bb/bbdb10a20dd90cd0928e91851662fccaf8d0b03e86c44f58b5311ba805183e8e.png)

Consider the arc of the curve $y={x}^{2}-4x+3$ that lies in the fourth quadrant between its $x$-intercepts. What integral gives the area of the surface generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $x$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-4x+3 & =0 \\ (x-1)(x-3) & =0 \\ x & =1,3\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=1$ to $x=3.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}-4x+3)=2x-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{3}x\sqrt{1+{(2x-4)}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{3}x\sqrt{4{x}^{2}-16x+17}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the first two non-zero terms of the Taylor expansion of $\operatorname{cos}⁡2x$ about $x=\frac{\pi }{4}.$
:question/worked-solution:
We use Taylor's theorem in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}(a)}{3!}(x-a)^{3}+⋯,
$$

with $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x$ and $a=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ 

Computing the required derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x)\,\,\,\, & =\operatorname{cos}⁡2x \\ f(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})=0 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2x \\ {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})=-2 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-4\operatorname{cos}⁡2x \\ {f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})=0 \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡2x \\ {f}^{‴}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})=8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x & =0+(-2)(x-\frac{\pi }{4})+\frac{(0)}{2!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}+\frac{(8)}{3!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{3}+⋯ \\  & =-2(x-\frac{\pi }{4})+\frac{4}{3}{(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{3}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the unit tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=⟨-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩$ at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{3}.$
:question/worked-solution:
For a curve $r(t)=⟨x(t),y(t),z(t)⟩$, the unit tangent vector $T(t)$ at the point $P(x(t),y(t),z(t))$ is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\frac{\pi }{3}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3}) & =⟨\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}),\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}),\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3})‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}+{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}^{2}+(1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{4}+\frac{3}{4}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3})$ and obtain the unit tangent vector to the given curve at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{3}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\frac{\pi }{3}) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3})}{‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3})‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}⟨\frac{3}{2},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},1⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{4},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4},\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at an arbitrary point, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+4{t}^{2}}}⟨1,0,2t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ denotes the unit tangent vector.
:question/worked-solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t),
$$

where the principal normal vector $N(t)$ is given by

$$
N(t)=\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find the principal normal $N(t).$ To do this, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+4{t}^{2}}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2t}{\sqrt{1+4{t}^{2}}})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{4t}{{(1+4{t}^{2})}^{3/2}},\,0,\,\frac{2}{{(1+4{t}^{2})}^{3/2}}⟩ \\  & =\frac{2}{{(1+4{t}^{2})}^{3/2}}⟨-2t,\,0,\,1⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{2}{{(1+4{t}^{2})}^{3/2}}\sqrt{(-2t)^{2}+{(0)}^{2}+{(1)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{(1+4{t}^{2})}^{3/2}}\sqrt{1+4{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{1+4{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize ${T}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{\frac{2}{{(1+4{t}^{2})}^{3/2}}⟨-2t,\,0,\,1⟩}{(\frac{2}{1+4{t}^{2}})}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+4{t}^{2}}}⟨-2t,\,0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+4{t}^{2}}}⟨1,0,2t⟩\times \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+4{t}^{2}}}⟨-2t,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{1+4{t}^{2}}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 2t \\ -2t & 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{1+4{t}^{2}}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 2t \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 2t \\ -2t & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2t & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{1+4{t}^{2}}⟨0-0,-(1+4{t}^{2}),0-0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{1+4{t}^{2}}⟨0,\,-(1+4{t}^{2}),\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,-1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Consider the curve $r(t)=⟨1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡3t,\,3-2\operatorname{sin}⁡3t⟩,$ $t\ge 0,$ for which the arc length $s$ from $r(0)$ to $r(t)$ is given by $s=6t.$ Find $R(s),$ the parametrization of the curve by its arc length $s.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, since $s=6t,$ we have that $t=\frac{s}{6}.$

The vector function that pametrizes the curve $r(t)$ by its arc length $s,$ with $s\ge 0,$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r(\frac{s}{6}) \\  & =⟨1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot \frac{s}{6}),\,3-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot \frac{s}{6})⟩ \\  & =⟨1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{s}{2}),\,3-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{s}{2})⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨\frac{3}{5}{t}^{3/2},\,1,\,\frac{4}{5}{t}^{3/2}⟩,$ $t\ge 0,$ for which the arc length $s$ from $r(0)$ to $r(t)$ is given by $s={t}^{3/2},$ find the corresponding unit tangent $T(s),$ parametrized by $s.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, since $s={t}^{3/2},$ we have that $t={s}^{2/3}.$ 

Therefore, the vector function $R(s)$ that parametrizes $r(t)$ by its arc length is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r({s}^{2/3}) \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{5}{({s}^{2/3})}^{3/2},\,1,\,\frac{4}{5}{({s}^{2/3})}^{3/2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3s}{5},\,1,\,\frac{4s}{5}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, since the curve is parameterized by its arc length $s$, the unit tangent can be found as

$$
T(s)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}R(s).
$$

So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}T(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}R(s) \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{3s}{5}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(1),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{4s}{5})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{5},\,0,\,\frac{4}{5}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨3,0,4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: What is the parametrization of the curve $r(t)=⟨t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3,\,t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,$ $t\ge 0,$ by its arc length $s?$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,0,\,-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(0)}^{2}+{(-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{t}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡t+{t}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{{t}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{{t}^{2}} \\  & =|t| \\  & =t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the arc length of the curve from $0$ to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}‖{r}^{′}(u)‖\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $s=\frac{{t}^{2}}{2},$ we have that $t=\sqrt{2s}.$

Therefore, the vector function that parametrizes $r(t)$ by its arc length is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r(\sqrt{2s}) \\  & =⟨\sqrt{2s}\operatorname{sin}⁡\sqrt{2s}+\operatorname{cos}⁡\sqrt{2s},\,3,\,\sqrt{2s}\operatorname{cos}⁡\sqrt{2s}-\operatorname{sin}⁡\sqrt{2s}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: If $g(u)=⟨\frac{1}{u},\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(u+1),\,1⟩$ and $u(t)=\frac{1}{t}$, then $(g∘u)^{′}(t)=$
:question/worked-solution:
By the chain rule, we have 

$$
(g∘u)^{′}(t)=g′(u(t))u′(t).
$$

Now, let's find the derivatives of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(u) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}(\frac{1}{u}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(u+1)),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{{u}^{2}},\,\frac{1}{u+1},\,0⟩ \\ {u}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})=-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(g∘u)^{′}(t) & =g′(u(t))u′(t) \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{(u(t))^{2}},\,\frac{1}{u(t)+1},\,0⟩\cdot {u}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨-{t}^{2},\,\frac{t}{1+t},\,0⟩\cdot (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}) \\  & =⟨1,-\frac{1}{t+{t}^{2}},0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: At which point on the curve $2{x}^{2}=y+1$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $i+j?$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2} & =y+1 \\ 2{x}^{2}-y & =1\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}-y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=1.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-y)\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-y)\,j \\  & =-i-4x\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $i+j,$ we must have $t\cdot (i+j)=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot (i+j) & =0 \\ (-i-4x\,j)\cdot (i+j) & =0 \\ -1-4x & =0 \\ x & =-\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=-\frac{1}{4}$ into the equation of our curve gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2} & =y+1 \\ 2{(-\frac{1}{4})}^{2} & =y+1 \\ \frac{1}{8} & =y+1 \\ y & =-\frac{7}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the corresponding point is $(-\frac{1}{4},-\frac{7}{8}).$

:question/problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={cos}^{2}⁡t,\,y={sin}^{2}⁡t,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({cos}^{2}⁡t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({sin}^{2}⁡t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+4{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{8{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡t\cdot 2\sqrt{2}\cdot |\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t|\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{3}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=5t+1,\,y={t}^{2},\,t\in [0,3].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=3.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5t+1)=5 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})=2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}{t}^{2}\sqrt{{(5)}^{2}+{(2t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}{t}^{2}\sqrt{25+4{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
$$
\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ -1 & -1\end{bmatrix}}^{A}=\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}{q}_{11} & {q}_{12} \\ {q}_{21} & {q}_{22} \\ {q}_{31} & {q}_{32}\end{bmatrix}}^{Q}\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}{r}_{11} & {r}_{12} \\ 0 & {r}_{22}\end{bmatrix}}^{R}.
$$

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. Given that the columns ${q}_{1},{q}_{2}$ of $Q$ were obtained from the columns of $A$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, find  the value of ${q}_{31}\cdot {r}_{12}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Let ${a}_{1},{a}_{2}$ be the columns of $A.$

First, we find an orthonormal basis of $\text{Col}(A)=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process.

**Step 1**. We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 2**. We find the vector ${v}_{2}$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}\{{v}_{1}\}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-(\frac{4}{2})\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-2\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we normalize ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\ {q}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute $R:$

$$
\begin{aligned}R & ={Q}^{T}\,A \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ -1 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{2} & 2\sqrt{2} \\ 0 & \sqrt{3}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we obtain the following QR factorization of $A:$

$$
\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ -1 & -1\end{bmatrix}}^{A}=\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{bmatrix}}^{Q}\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{2} & 2\sqrt{2} \\ 0 & \sqrt{3}\end{bmatrix}}^{R}.
$$

Finally, ${q}_{31}\cdot {r}_{12}=(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})\cdot (2\sqrt{2})=-2.$

:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}({x}^{3}-2y)\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the curve $y=2-\frac{x}{2}$ for $\,0\le x\le 2?$
:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y=y(t)=2-\frac{t}{2}.$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨t,2-\frac{t}{2}⟩,\,0\le t\le 2
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-\frac{t}{2})j \\  & =i-\frac{1}{2}\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{3}-2y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & ={t}^{3}-2(2-\frac{t}{2})={t}^{3}+t-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}({t}^{3}+t-4)\cdot \frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}({t}^{3}+t-4)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the curve $y=2{e}^{x}$ for $\,0\le x\le 2?$
:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y=y(t)=2{e}^{t}.$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨t,2{e}^{t}⟩,\,0\le t\le 2
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{e}^{t})j \\  & =i+2{e}^{t}\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(2{e}^{t})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+4{e}^{2t}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=y\operatorname{cos}⁡x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{1+4{e}^{2t}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{1+4{e}^{2t}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Which of the following gives the length of the curve $y=\frac{1}{9}{(2{x}^{3}+1)}^{3/2}$ on $[0,3]?$
:question/worked-solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\frac{1}{9}{(2{x}^{3}+1)}^{3/2},$ $a=0,$ and $b=3.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{9}(\frac{3}{2})6{x}^{2}{(2{x}^{3}+1)}^{1/2}={x}^{2}\sqrt{2{x}^{3}+1}
$$

Substituting ${f}^{′}(x)={x}^{2}\sqrt{2{x}^{3}+1}$ into the arc length formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{1+{[{f}^{′}(x)]}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{1+{({x}^{2}\sqrt{2{x}^{3}+1})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}(2{x}^{3}+1)}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{1+2{x}^{7}+{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{2{x}^{7}+{x}^{4}+1}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Consider the portion of the surface $z=x{y}^{2}$ whose projection onto the $xy$-plane is bounded by $y={x}^{2},$ $x=1,$ and the $x$-axis. Find a repeated integral expression for the surface area of this surface.
:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=x{y}^{2},\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le {x}^{2}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/14/1419b067fe92945249655c5d29498aa4d3b0269d79ebd237fd9ed2a713b70b6a.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2})={y}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2})=2xy,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{({y}^{2})}^{2}+(2xy)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{y}^{4}+4{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}\sqrt{1+{y}^{4}+4{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Consider the portion of the surface $z=y{e}^{x}$ whose projection onto the $xy$-plane is bounded by the lines $y=2x,$ $x=1,$ and the $x$-axis. Find a repeated integral expression for the surface area of this surface.
:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=y{e}^{x},\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2x\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/90/903b7f3c6bd9721a974160487ca5099fdf54ce02b61697a7830bb662b26d8953.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y{e}^{x})=y{e}^{x}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{e}^{x})={e}^{x},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(y{e}^{x})^{2}+({e}^{x})^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+({y}^{2}+1){e}^{2x}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2x}\sqrt{1+({y}^{2}+1){e}^{2x}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the maximum value of the function $f(x,y,z)=2x+3y+2z$ on the intersection of the plane $2x-y-z=-1$ and the cylinder ${y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=1.$
:question/worked-solution:
We need to find the maximum value of 

$$
f(x,y,z)=2x+3y+2z
$$

subject to the constraints  

$$
g(x,y,z)=2x-y-z=-1,\,h(x,y,z)={y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=1.
$$

Since $f(x,y,z)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y,z)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) &=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ g(x,y,z) &=-1 \\ h(x,y,z) &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We start by expanding the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x},{f}_{y},{f}_{z}⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x},{g}_{y},{g}_{z}⟩+\mu ⟨{h}_{x},{h}_{y},{h}_{z}⟩ \\ ⟨2,3,2⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2,-1,-1⟩+\mu ⟨0,2y,2z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we have the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}2 &=2\lambda \\ 3 &=-\lambda +2\mu y \\ 2 &=-\lambda +2\mu z\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}\lambda &=1 \\ y &=\frac{2}{\mu } \\ z &=\frac{3}{2\mu }\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\mu $ can't be zero since this leads to a contradiction.

Next, we substitute our expressions for $y$ and $z$ into the second constraint:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =1 \\ \frac{4}{{\mu }^{2}}+\frac{9}{4{\mu }^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{25}{4{\mu }^{2}} & =1 \\ {\mu }^{2} & =\frac{25}{4} \\ \mu  & =\pm \frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, 

$$
y=\pm \frac{4}{5},\,z=\pm \frac{3}{5}.
$$

Finally, we substitute $y$ and $z$ into the first constraint:

- If $y=\frac{4}{5}$ and $z=\frac{3}{5},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-y-z & =-1 \\ 2x-\frac{4}{5}-\frac{3}{5} & =-1 \\ x & =\frac{1}{5}. \\  & \end{aligned}
$$

- If $y=-\frac{4}{5}$ and $z=-\frac{3}{5},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-y-z & =-1 \\ 2x-(-\frac{4}{5})-(-\frac{3}{5}) & =-1 \\ 2x & =-\frac{12}{5} \\ x & =-\frac{6}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(\frac{1}{5},\frac{4}{5},\frac{3}{5}),\,(-\frac{6}{5},-\frac{4}{5},-\frac{3}{5}).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y,z)$ | $(\frac{1}{5},\frac{4}{5},\frac{3}{5})$ | $(-\frac{6}{5},-\frac{4}{5},-\frac{3}{5})$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y,z)$ | $4$ | $-6$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a maximum value at $(\frac{1}{5},\frac{4}{5},\frac{3}{5}),$ and its maximum value is $4.$

:question/problem:
For the transformation $f:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2},$ defined as

$$
f(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy) \\ \frac{y}{x}\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix},
$$

calculate ${f}^{′}(x).$
:question/worked-solution:
Suppose a transformation $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ is defined by 

$$
f:\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{f}_{1}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ {f}_{2}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{m}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))=\frac{1}{x},\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))=\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{y}{x})=-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}},\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{y}{x})=\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{x} & \frac{1}{y} \\ -\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{1}{x}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

:question/problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a force of magnitude $\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{N}$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=4.$
:question/worked-solution:
The work done by a force $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from $x={x}_{1}$ to $x={x}_{2}$ is given by

$$
W={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($J$).

Substituting the given values into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{x}\,{|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =-(\frac{1}{4}-1) \\  & =-(-\frac{3}{4}) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: A particle $P$ of mass $3\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude $\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}\,{m/s}^{2},$ where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing $x,$ and $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the change in kinetic energy of the particle between the times $t=1\,s$ and $t=2\,s.$
:question/worked-solution:
The change in kinetic energy of a particle with mass $m,$ initial velocity ${v}_{0},$ and final velocity ${v}_{1}$ is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($J$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int \frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\frac{1}{6}{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0=\frac{1}{6}({0}^{3})+C\,⟹\,C=0.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{1}{6}{t}^{3}.$ In particular, its inital velocity at time $t=1\,s$ and final velocity at time $t=2\,s$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{0} & =v(1)=\frac{1}{6}({1}^{3})=\frac{1}{6}\,m/s, \\ {v}_{1} & =v(2)=\frac{1}{6}({2}^{3})=\frac{4}{3}\,m/s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change in kinetic energy of the particle between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ\,\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot {(\frac{4}{3})}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot {(\frac{1}{6})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}-\frac{1}{24} \\  & =\frac{21}{8}\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: A particle $P$ of mass $\frac{8}{5}\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude $3t\,{m/s}^{2},$ where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing $x,$ and $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the change in kinetic energy of the particle between the times $t=1\,s$ and $t=2\,s.$
:question/worked-solution:
The change in kinetic energy of a particle with mass $m,$ initial velocity ${v}_{0},$ and final velocity ${v}_{1}$ is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($J$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int 3t\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0=\frac{3}{2}({0}^{2})+C\,⟹\,C=0.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}.$ In particular, its inital velocity at time $t=1\,s$ and final velocity at time $t=2\,s$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{0} & =v(1)=\frac{3}{2}({1}^{2})=\frac{3}{2}\,m/s, \\ {v}_{1} & =v(2)=\frac{3}{2}({2}^{2})=6\,m/s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change in kinetic energy of the particle between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ\,\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{8}{5}\cdot {6}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{8}{5}\cdot {(\frac{3}{2})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{144}{5}-\frac{9}{5} \\  & =27\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
A rectangular plate of mass $\frac{3}{2}\,\text{kg}$ and uniform mass density occupies the region
$D={(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2},$
where $x$ and $y$ are measured in meters.
Find the moment of inertia of the plate about a line perpendicular to $D$ at a distance of $\sqrt{6}\,\text{m}$ from a parallel line passing through its center of mass.
:question/worked-solution:
For a plane lamina of mass $M$ and a line ${l}_{M}$ perpendicular to the lamina passing through its center of mass, the parallel axis theorem states that the moment of inertia of the lamina about a line $l$ parallel to ${l}_{M}$ is given by

$$
{I}_{l}={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M,
$$

where $d$ is the distance between the lines, and ${I}_{M}$ and ${I}_{l}$ are the moments of inertia about the lines ${l}_{M}$ and $l,$ respectively.

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=2\cdot 2=4\,{\text{m}}^{2}.$
Since the plate has a uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{(\frac{3}{2})}{4}=\frac{3}{8}\,\text{kg}/{\text{m}}^{2},
$$

and its center of mass is its centroid:

$$
(\overset{¯}{x},\overset{¯}{y})=(\frac{-1+1}{2},\frac{0+2}{2})=(0,1)
$$

Then, the moment of inertia about the perpendicular line through the center of mass is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{M} & ={∬}_{D}((x-\overset{¯}{x})^{2}+(y-\overset{¯}{y})^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}3{x}^{2}+3(y-1)^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{[3{x}^{2}y+(y-1)^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{-1}^{1}6{x}^{2}+2\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{[2{x}^{3}+2x]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}(2+2-(-2-2)) \\  & =1\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia about a line $\sqrt{6}\,\text{m}$ from the center of mass is

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M \\  & =1+{(\sqrt{6})}^{2}\cdot \frac{3}{2} \\  & =1+9 \\  & =10\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
A rectangular plate occupies the region
$D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 3,\,0\le y\le 2}$
and has mass density function $\lambda (x,y)=2x,$ where $x$ and $y$ are measured in meters.
Given that the center of mass is at $(2,1),$ find the moment of inertia about a line perpendicular to $D$ at a distance of $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}\,\text{m}$ from a parallel line passing through its center of mass.
:question/worked-solution:
For a plane lamina of mass $M$ and a line ${l}_{M}$ perpendicular to the lamina passing through its center of mass, the parallel axis theorem states that the moment of inertia of the lamina about a line $l$ parallel to ${l}_{M}$ is given by

$$
{I}_{l}={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M,
$$

where $d$ is the distance between the lines, and ${I}_{M}$ and ${I}_{l}$ are the moments of inertia about the lines ${l}_{M}$ and $l,$ respectively.

First, we find the mass of the plate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}2x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}2x\,\text{d}x{\int }_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={x}^{2}{|}_{0}^{3}\cdot y{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =9\cdot 2 \\  & =18\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the moment of inertia about the perpendicular line through the center of mass $(2,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{M} & ={∬}_{D}((x-\overset{¯}{x})^{2}+(y-\overset{¯}{y})^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}((x-2)^{2}+(y-1)^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}((x-2)^{2}+(y-1)^{2})2x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}2x(x-2)^{2}+2x(y-1)^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[2x(x-2)^{2}y+\frac{2}{3}x(y-1)^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}4x(x-2)^{2}+\frac{4}{3}x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}4{x}^{3}-16{x}^{2}+16x+\frac{4}{3}x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}4{x}^{3}-16{x}^{2}+\frac{52}{3}x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[{x}^{4}-\frac{16}{3}{x}^{3}+\frac{26}{3}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =81-144+78-0 \\  & =15\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia about a line $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}\,\text{m}$ from the center of mass is

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M \\  & =15+{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3})}^{2}\cdot 18 \\  & =15+4 \\  & =19\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Calculate $\int \frac{10}{|x-6|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-12x+35}}\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we complete the square for the expression inside the square root:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-12x+35 & ={x}^{2}-2\cdot 6x+({6}^{2}-{6}^{2})+35 \\  & =({x}^{2}-12x+36)-36+35 \\  & =(x-6)^{2}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above in the given integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{10}{|x-6|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-12x+35}}\,\text{d}x=10\int \frac{1}{|x-6|\sqrt{(x-6)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse secant:

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}\,u+C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $x-6.$

So, let's perform the substitution 

$$
u=x-6.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{10}{|x-6|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-12x+35}}\,\text{d}x & =10\int \frac{1}{|x-6|\sqrt{(x-6)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =10\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =10\,\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =10\,\text{arcsec}(x-6)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions to the equation $\operatorname{sec}⁡x=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ for $-{360}^{∘}\le x<{0}^{∘},$ what is the numerical value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}?$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that $\operatorname{sec}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.$ Therefore, the given equation is equivalent to

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡x=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.
$$

First, we find the principal value:

$$
x=\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})={30}^{∘}
$$

Note that $x={30}^{∘}$ is not in the domain $-{360}^{∘}\le x<{0}^{∘}.$ To get a solution within the required domain, we subtract ${360}^{∘}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={30}^{∘}-{360}^{∘}=-{330}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Our first solution lies in the first quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}={30}^{∘}.$ Since $\operatorname{cos}⁡x>0,$ the second solution must lie in the fouth quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}={30}^{∘}.$

![](images/8c/8c6e3ae6bdbfb1c66aee719f77225453992fffe6f3c6e3dfdc3f1ff92c59863a.png)

A second solution $X$ lies in the $4$th quadrant, and we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}X & ={360}^{∘}-{\theta }_{R} \\  & ={360}^{∘}-{30}^{∘} \\  & ={330}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $X={330}^{∘}$ is not in the domain $-{360}^{∘}\le x<{0}^{∘}.$ To get a solution within the required dommain, we subtract ${360}^{∘}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={330}^{∘}-{360}^{∘}=-{30}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the solutions are $x=-{30}^{∘},-{330}^{∘}.$

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=-30\cdot (-330)=9\,900
$$

:question/problem:
$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}x(t),\,x(0)=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix},\,x(t)={e}^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{e}^{2t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the initial value problem and its solution given above. What is the tangent vector to the solution curve at the point corresponding to $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡3?$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the $xy$-coordinate plane is called the *phase plane* of the system. A particular solution of an initial value problem is called a *trajectory* (or *orbit*).

First, we compute the point that corresponds to $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡3$ on the given trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(\operatorname{ln}⁡3) & ={e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{e}^{2(\operatorname{ln}⁡3)}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+9\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -36\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3} \\ -36\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the equation of our system, we obtain the tangent vector to the trajectory.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\operatorname{ln}⁡3) & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3} \\ -36\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}(-1)(\frac{2}{3})+0(-36) \\ 0\cdot (\frac{2}{3})+2(-36)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{3} \\ -72\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}x(t),\,x(0)=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix},\,x(t)={e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{e}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the initial value problem and its solution given above. What is the tangent vector to the solution curve at the point corresponding to $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡3?$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the $xy$-coordinate plane is called the *phase plane* of the system. A particular solution of an initial value problem is called a *trajectory* (or *orbit*).

First, we compute the point that corresponds to $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡3$ on the given trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(\operatorname{ln}⁡3) & ={e}^{-2(\operatorname{ln}⁡3)}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+3\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} \\ 6\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the equation of our system, we obtain the tangent vector to the trajectory.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\operatorname{ln}⁡3) & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} \\ 6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2(\frac{1}{3})+0(6) \\ 0(\frac{1}{3})+1(6)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{3} \\ 6\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Consider a spherical planet with radius $(4\times {10}^{7})\,\text{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g=12\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Which equation best models the velocity $v$ of an object projected radially outward from the planet's surface with an initial velocity of $(8\times {10}^{4})\,\text{m/s},$ where $r$ is the distance from the planet's center to the object. Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.
:question/worked-solution:
Let $R$ be the planet's radius and $g$ be the planet's surface gravitational acceleration.

According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the planet is

$$
{F}_{\text{in}}=G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, and $M$ is the planet's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-{F}_{\text{in}}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance,

$$
a=-\frac{k}{{r}^{2}},
$$

with constant of proportionality $k=GM>0.$

When at the surface, $r=R,$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-g.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k:$

$$
-g=-\frac{k}{{R}^{2}}\,\,\,⟹\,k=g{R}^{2}
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a=-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}}.
$$

Now, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\frac{dv}{dr}=-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}}
$$

Solving using separation of variables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int v\frac{dv}{dr}\,dr & =\int (-\frac{g{R}^{2}}{{r}^{2}})\,dr \\ \int v\,dv & =-g{R}^{2}\int \frac{1}{{r}^{2}}\,dr \\ \frac{{v}^{2}}{2} & =-g{R}^{2}(-\frac{1}{r})+{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{r}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C=2{C}_{1}$ is a constant of integration.

Let ${v}_{0}$ be the initial velocity of the object. Applying the initial condition $v(R)={v}_{0},$ we can solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(R)^{2} & =\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{R}+C \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =2gR+C \\ C & ={v}_{0}^{2}-2gR\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation for the velocity of the object is

$$
{v}^{2}=\frac{2g{R}^{2}}{r}+{v}_{0}^{2}-2gR.
$$

Finally, substituting in the values
$R=(4\times {10}^{7}),$
$g=12,$ and
${v}_{0}=(8\times {10}^{4}),$
we conclude that the equation for the velocity is

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2\cdot 12\cdot (4\times {10}^{7})^{2}}{r}+(8\times {10}^{4})^{2}-2\cdot 12\cdot (4\times {10}^{7}) \\  & =\frac{384\times {10}^{14}}{r}+(64\times {10}^{8})-(96\times {10}^{7}) \\  & =\frac{3.84\times {10}^{16}}{r}+(6.4\times {10}^{9})-(0.96\times {10}^{9}) \\  & =\frac{3.84\times {10}^{16}}{r}+((6.4-0.96)\times {10}^{9}) \\  & =\frac{3.84\times {10}^{16}}{r}+(5.44\times {10}^{9}).\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3y=6\operatorname{cosh}⁡3x.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-3{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{3x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{3x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{3x})}^{′}-3(u{e}^{3x}) & =6\operatorname{cosh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+3u{e}^{3x}-3u{e}^{3x} & =6\operatorname{cosh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+\cancel{3u{e}^{3x}}-\cancel{3u{e}^{3x}} & =6\operatorname{cosh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x} & =6\operatorname{cosh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′} & =6{e}^{-3x}\operatorname{cosh}⁡3x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\operatorname{cosh}⁡3x=\frac{{e}^{3x}+{e}^{-3x}}{2}
$$

our equation for $u$ becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =6{e}^{-3x}\operatorname{cosh}⁡3x \\  & =6{e}^{-3x}(\frac{{e}^{3x}+{e}^{-3x}}{2}) \\  & =3{e}^{-3x}({e}^{3x}+{e}^{-3x}) \\  & =3+3{e}^{-6x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =3+3{e}^{-6x} \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int 3+3{e}^{-6x}\,\text{d}x \\ u & =3x-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-6x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{3x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{3x} \\  & =3x{e}^{3x}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+16{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)={y}^{′}(\pi )=0,\,0\le x\le \pi ,\,\lambda \ge 0.
$$

Find the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues and the associated eigenfunctions of this problem.

$\,$ The eigenvalues correspond to the parameter values ${\lambda }_{n}=$ {{field-1}}, where $n\in N.$

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are ${y}_{n}(x)=$ {{field-2}}, where ${B}_{n}\in R.$
:question/worked-solution:
We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(0)={y}^{′}(\pi )=0$ yields $A=0.$ Thus, we have a nontrivial solution, so $\lambda =0$ is a parameter value corresponding to the eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda >0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+16{\lambda }^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm 4\text{i}\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\lambda x),\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\lambda x)
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\lambda x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\lambda x).
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
{y}^{′}=-4A\lambda \operatorname{sin}⁡(4\lambda x)+4B\lambda \operatorname{cos}⁡(4\lambda x).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ yields

$$
-4A\lambda \operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+4B\lambda \operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=0
$$

which gives $B=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\lambda x).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(\pi )=0$ yields

$$
-4A\lambda \operatorname{sin}⁡(4\lambda \pi )=0.
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require 

$$
4\lambda \pi =n\pi 
$$

for $n\in N.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues:

$$
{\lambda }_{n}=\frac{n}{4}.
$$

The corresponding eigenfunctions are 

$$
{y}_{n}(x)={B}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4{\lambda }_{n}x),\,{B}_{n}\in R.
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+2y=f(x)
$$

on $[-1,1]$, where $f$ is $2$-periodic and odd. Which Fourier-series form is appropriate for a particular solution ${y}_{p}?$

$\,$
${y}_{p}(x)=$
{{field-1}}
:question/worked-solution:
Because $f$ is $2$-periodic on $[-1,1]$, we have $L=1$, so Fourier series on this interval use the basis 

$$
cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{1})\,\text{and}\,sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{1}).
$$

Next, since $f$ is odd, its Fourier series contains only sine terms. For a second-order equation with no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an odd function.

Therefore, the appropriate form for ${y}_{p}$ is a sine series:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{1}{2}\,y=f(x)
$$

on $[-2,2]$, where $f$ is $4$-periodic and even. Which Fourier-series form is appropriate for a particular solution ${y}_{p}?$

$\,$
${y}_{p}(x)=$
{{field-1}}
:question/worked-solution:
Because $f$ is $4$-periodic on $[-2,2]$, we have $L=2$, so Fourier series on this interval use the basis

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})\,\text{and}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Next, since $f$ is even, its Fourier series contains only cosine terms. For a second-order equation with no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an even function.

Therefore, the appropriate form for ${y}_{p}$ is a cosine series:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})
$$

:question/problem:
Find an eigenvector of 
$A=\begin{bmatrix}16 & -30 \\ 9 & -17\end{bmatrix}$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2.$
:question/worked-solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-2.$ So, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & -30 \\ 9 & -17\end{bmatrix}-(-2)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}18 & -30 \\ 9 & -15\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}18{x}_{1}-30{x}_{2} &=0 \\ 9{x}_{1}-15{x}_{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}18 & -30 & 0 \\ 9 & -15 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-\frac{1}{2}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}18 & -30 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. 

From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
18{x}_{1}-30{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=\frac{5}{3}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Finally, setting ${x}_{2}=3,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

:question/problem: The first term of a geometric sequence is $\frac{5}{3}$ and the common ratio is $\frac{4}{3}.$ Written in sigma notation, what is the sum of the first $25$ terms?
:question/worked-solution:
First, we must express the series in the form:

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{N}{a}_{1}{r}^{n-1},
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ denotes the first term of the series, $r$ denotes the common ratio, and $N$ denotes the number of terms in the series. In this case, ${a}_{1}=\frac{5}{3},$ $r=\frac{4}{3}$ and $N=25.$

Expressing the geometric series in sigma notation, we obtain:

$$
{S}_{25}={\sum }_{n=1}^{25}\frac{5}{3}\cdot {(\frac{4}{3})}^{n-1}\,\,
$$

Finally, we can simplify the above using the laws of exponents, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{25}\frac{5}{3}\cdot {(\frac{4}{3})}^{n-1} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{25}\frac{5}{3}\cdot {(\frac{4}{3})}^{n}\cdot {(\frac{4}{3})}^{-1} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{25}\frac{5}{3}\cdot {(\frac{4}{3})}^{-1}\cdot {(\frac{4}{3})}^{n} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{25}\frac{5}{3}\cdot \frac{3}{4}\cdot {(\frac{4}{3})}^{n} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{25}\frac{5}{4}{(\frac{4}{3})}^{n}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: The sides (in feet) of a square are increasing. At a particular moment, the rate of increase of the area of the square is numerically equal to four times the rate of increase of the diagonals. What is the length of the diagonals of the square at that moment?
:question/worked-solution:
Let $A$ be the area of the square, and $h$ be the length of the diagonal. The relationship between $A$ and $h$ is

$$
A=\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot h.\end{aligned}
$$

The given information tells us that $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=4\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}$, so replacing $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$ in the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =h\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ 4\cancel{\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}} & =h\cancel{\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}} \\ 4 & =h.\end{aligned}
$$

So at that particular moment, we have that the length of the diagonals of the square is $4\text{ feet}.$

:question/problem: Given that $u=3-2{x}^{2}$, which integral is equivalent to ${\int }_{-1}^{0}{x}^{3}\sqrt{3-2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x?$
:question/worked-solution:
Since $u=3-2{x}^{2}$, then we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-4x\,⟹\,-\frac{\text{d}u}{4}=x\text{d}x.
$$

We also note that ${x}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}(3-u).$ 

Computing our limits of integration, we get

| **$x$** | $-1$ | $0$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **$u$** | $1$ | $3$ |

We can now solve the integral using our new variable $u,$ remembering to use the new limits of integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{0}{x}^{3}\sqrt{3-2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{x}^{2}\sqrt{3-2{x}^{2}}\cdot x\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{2}(3-u)\sqrt{u}\cdot (-\frac{\text{d}u}{4}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{1}^{3}(3-u)\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: $\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=$
:question/worked-solution:
We need to use integration by parts. 

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u={x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({x}^{2})(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})-\int (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2}{3}\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$
