:question/problem:
![](images/aa/aac27058402f89bef73700129a7812b3cf4f971c11975fc1711a46b8d10e61fe.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,x-y+2{z}^{2},\,0⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
:question/worked-solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $y$-component of $F=⟨0,\,x-y+2{z}^{2},\,0⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $y$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the right and left sides. 

![](images/e2/e2d914cf61af684d1f2971ec680acc1a2a53a6a40c85e387728dfea8ebc94730.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the right surface. On this surface, we have $y=2$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 3.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $y=2$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,x-y+2{z}^{2},\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,x-2+2{z}^{2},\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =x+2{z}^{2}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}x+2{z}^{2}-2\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}x+2{z}^{2}-2\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}x+2{z}^{2}-2\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+(2{z}^{2}-2)x]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{2}+2{z}^{2}-2\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}2{z}^{2}-\frac{3}{2}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={[\frac{2}{3}{z}^{3}-\frac{3}{2}z]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =18-\frac{9}{2} \\  & =\frac{27}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the left surface. On this surface, we have $y=0$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 3.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $y=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,x-y+2{z}^{2},\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,x+2{z}^{2},\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩ \\  & =-(x+2{z}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-(x+2{z}^{2})\,\text{d}S \\  & =-{∬}_{D}x+2{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}x+2{z}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+2x{z}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}z \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{2}+2{z}^{2}\,\text{d}z \\  & =-{[\frac{1}{2}z+\frac{2}{3}{z}^{3}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =-(\frac{3}{2}+18) \\  & =-\frac{39}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{27}{2}+(-\frac{39}{2}) \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/e8/e8708a16a0f6db347acf2c1a82a602d2fa8ce60d4bb8369f1414eca3465e4e71.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,0,\,2x+y-2z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
:question/worked-solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $F=⟨0,\,0,\,2x+y-2z⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](images/8e/8ed6ffdeab54bc6888d245ef4f1c050c31e010c67dfa93aea365fc6cb523e382.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=2$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 3.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=2$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,2x+y-2z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,2x+y-4⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =2x+y-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}2x+y-4\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x+y-4\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}2x+y-4\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[{x}^{2}+xy-4x]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}y-3\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}-3y]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =-\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 3.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,0,\,2x+y-2z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,2x+y⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-(2x+y).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-(2x+y)\,\text{d}S \\  & =-{∬}_{D}2x+y\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}2x+y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}{[{x}^{2}+xy]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}1+y\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{[y+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =-\frac{15}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =-\frac{9}{2}+(-\frac{15}{2}) \\  & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the square region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,\frac{1}{4}\le u\le 1,\,\,0\le v\le \frac{5\pi }{12}\},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v).
$$

The image of the top side of $Δ$ under the action of $T$ is a line segment. Which of the following statements are true regarding the image?

Select all that apply.
:question/worked-solution:
To map the entire region $Δ$ onto the $xy$-plane, we consider the transformation of each side. However, in this case, we consider only the top side.

For the top side, we have $v=\frac{5\pi }{12}$ and $\frac{1}{4}\le u\le 1.$ 

Substituting $v=\frac{5\pi }{12}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y) & =T(u,v) \\  & =(u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v) \\  & =(u\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12}),\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12})),\,\frac{1}{4}\le u\le 1.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a parametric equation of the line segment shown below.

![](images/49/49aa7d6ccd4b14b48ede7486f41ab11ac22b593c06d75795fe7819889b2b2f23.png)

 

Note that the line that this segment lies on passes through the origin. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement “The image makes the angle of $0$ with the positive $x$-axis” is false, while statement “The image makes the angle of $\frac{5\pi }{12}$ with the positive $x$-axis” is true. The slope of the line is

$$
k=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12})}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12})}=\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12}).
$$

As a result, our line makes an angle of $\frac{5\pi }{12}$ radians with the positive $x$-axis.

- Statement “The endpoints of the image lie on the circles of radii $\frac{1}{4}$ and $1$ centered at $O.$” is true.

- When $u=\frac{1}{4},$ we obtain the point 
$(\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12}),\,\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12})),$
whose distance to the origin is $\frac{1}{4}.$

- When $u=1,$ we obtain the point 
$(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12}),\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12})),$
whose distance to the origin is $1.$

So, the endpoints of the line segment lie on the circles of radii $\frac{1}{4}$ and $1.$

Therefore, the correct answer is “The image makes the angle of $\frac{5\pi }{12}$ with the positive $x$-axis”; “The endpoints of the image lie on the circles of radii $\frac{1}{4}$ and $1$ centered at $O.$” only.

:question/problem: Find $k$, if $u=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{3}{4} \\ \frac{k}{4}\end{bmatrix}$ is a unit vector.
:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate the norm of the vector $u$ in terms of $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖u‖ & =\sqrt{{u}_{1}^{2}+{u}_{2}^{2}+{u}_{3}^{2}+{u}_{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{4})}^{2}+{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}+{(\frac{k}{4})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{16}+\frac{9}{16}+\frac{{k}^{2}}{16}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{14+{k}^{2}}{16}}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given equation  $‖u‖=1,$ we obtain an equation that we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{14+{k}^{2}}{16}} & =1 \\ \sqrt{14+{k}^{2}} & =4 \\ {(\sqrt{14+{k}^{2}})}^{2} & ={4}^{2} \\ 14+{k}^{2} & =16 \\ {k}^{2} & =2 \\ k & =\pm \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The matrix $F$ is given below. Let ${f}_{1}$, ${f}_{2}$,  ${f}_{3}$ and ${f}_{4}$ be the respective columns of $F.$
Determine if $B=\text{{}{f}_{1},{f}_{2},{f}_{3}\text{}}$ is a basis of $\text{Col}(F).$ 
If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}\cdot {x}_{3}$, where ${f}_{4}={x}_{1}{f}_{1}+{x}_{2}{f}_{2}+{x}_{3}{f}_{3}.$ 

$$
F=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -4 & -24 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & -6 & -1\end{bmatrix}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $F$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -4 & -24 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & -6 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=(-\frac{1}{4}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 6 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & -6 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 6 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 5 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(F)$ is $\{{f}_{1},{f}_{2}\}.$ 

Therefore, we conclude that $B=\{{f}_{1},{f}_{2},{f}_{3}\}$ is not a basis of $\text{Col}(F).$

:question/problem: Given that the random variable $X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{3}{4}),$ calculate $P(X<1).$ Round your final answer to four decimal places.
:question/worked-solution:
An exponential random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda $ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\lambda {e}^{-\lambda x}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that

$$
X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{3}{4}).
$$

So, $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4}{e}^{-3x/4}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate $P(X<1)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<1) & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{4}{e}^{-3x/4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-3x/4}{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-{e}^{-3/4}+{e}^{0} \\  & ≈0.5276\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Given that $X$ is a continuous random variable with the following probability density function, compute $\text{E}[X].$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{x}, & -\sqrt{e}<x<-1 \\ \frac{1}{4}, & -1\le x<1\end{aligned}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ we can calculate the expected value using the following formula:

$$
\text{E}[X]={\int }_{S}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x
$$

 

We compute the expected value of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{-\sqrt{e}}^{1}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-\sqrt{e}}^{-1}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{-1}^{1}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-\sqrt{e}}^{-1}x\cdot (-\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{-1}^{1}x\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{\int }_{-\sqrt{e}}^{-1}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{x}{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-x{|}_{-\sqrt{e}}^{-1}+{\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =1-\sqrt{e}+\frac{1}{8}-\frac{1}{8} \\  & =1-\sqrt{e}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The matrix $A$ and the vector $b$ are given below.
Determine if $b\in \text{Col}(A).$ 
In the affirmative case, find the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}\cdot {x}_{3}$, where ${x}_{1},{x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are real numbers such that $b={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3},$ and ${a}_{1}$, ${a}_{2}$, and ${a}_{3}$ are the respective columns of $A.$

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 & -8 \\ 0 & -1 & 4 \\ 2 & 0 & -4\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
In order to determine whether $b$ lies in $\text{Col}(A),$ we need to check if the equation $Ax=b$ is consistent. So, let's find the row echelon form of the augmented matrix $[A\,|\,b]$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[A\,|\,b] & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 & -8 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & -4 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 & -8 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & -6 & 12 & 6\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-6){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 & -8 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -12 & -6\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}-8{x}_{3} &=-2 \\ -{x}_{2}+4{x}_{3} &=2 \\ -12{x}_{3} &=-6.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the third equation, we get ${x}_{3}=\frac{1}{2}.$ Substituting it into the second equation gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2}+4(\frac{1}{2}) & =2 \\ -{x}_{2}+2 & =2 \\ {x}_{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, from the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3(0)-8(\frac{1}{2}) & =-2 \\ {x}_{1}-4 & =-2 \\ {x}_{1} & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we have a solution, the equation $Ax=b$ is consistent, which implies that $b\in \text{Col}(A).$ 

Moreover, there is exactly one solution, so we have exactly one way to write $b$ as a linear combination of ${a}_{1},$ ${a}_{2},$ and ${a}_{3}:$

$$
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}}_{b}=2\cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}}_{{a}_{1}}+0\cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{{a}_{2}}+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-8 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}}_{{a}_{3}}
$$

Finally, we get ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}\cdot {x}_{3}=2\cdot 0\cdot \frac{1}{2}=0.$

:question/problem:
Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}\frac{z}{y} \\ y \\ xz\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $y,z\ne 0.$*
:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=\frac{z}{y},\,v(x,y,z)=y,\,w(x,y,z)=xz.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =-\frac{z}{{y}^{2}} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =1 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =z & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & -\frac{z}{{y}^{2}} & \frac{1}{y} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ z & 0 & x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =z\begin{vmatrix}-\frac{z}{{y}^{2}} & \frac{1}{y} \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =z(0-\frac{1}{y}) \\  & =-\frac{z}{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{z}{y} & =-u.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-u)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{u}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)),$ given that 

$$
u=x,\,v=2y,\,w=3z.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =2 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(6-0) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that the random variable $X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{1}{5}),$ calculate $P(X\le 2).$ Round your final answer to four decimal places.
:question/worked-solution:
An exponential random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda $ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\lambda {e}^{-\lambda x}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that

$$
X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{1}{5}).
$$

So, $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}{e}^{-x/5}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate $P(X\le 2)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 2) & ={\int }_{0}^{2}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{5}{e}^{-x/5}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{{e}^{-x/5}|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =-{e}^{-2/5}+{e}^{0} \\  & ≈0.3297\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that the random variable $X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{1}{3}),$ calculate $P(2<X<3).$ Round your final answer to four decimal places.
:question/worked-solution:
An exponential random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda $ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\lambda {e}^{-\lambda x}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that

$$
X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{1}{3}).
$$

So, $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-x/3}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}

Therefore, we can calculate $P(2<X<3)$ as follows:

\begin{aligned}P(2<X<3) & ={\int }_{2}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{3}\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-x/3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-x/3}{|}_{2}^{3} \\  & =-{e}^{-1}+{e}^{-2/3} \\  & ≈0.1455\end{aligned}

:question/problem: Given that the random variable $X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{3}{5}),$ calculate $P(X\le 9\,|\,X>4).$
:question/worked-solution:
Given a random variable $X∼Exp(\lambda ),$ and two positive real numbers $s,t,$ the memoryless property of the exponential distribution states that

$$
P(X>s+t\,|\,X>s)=P(X>t)={e}^{-\lambda t}.
$$

We can compute the complementary conditional probability as follows:

$$
P(X\le s+t\,|\,X>s)=1-P(X>s+t\,|\,X>s)=1-{e}^{-\lambda t}
$$

In our case, we have $\lambda =\frac{3}{5},$ $s=4,$ and $s+t=9.$ From this, we can find $t$ as follows:

$$
t=(t+s)-s=9-4=5
$$

Substituting these values into the above formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 9\,|\,X>4) & =1-{e}^{-\lambda t} \\  & =1-{e}^{-(3/5)\cdot (5)} \\  & =1-{e}^{-3}\end{aligned}
$$

To work out ${(-\frac{2}{3})}^{3},$ we multiply $-\frac{2}{3}$ by itself and then multiply the result by $-\frac{2}{3}$ again:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(-\frac{2}{3})}^{3} & =(-\frac{2}{3})\cdot (-\frac{2}{3})\cdot (-\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =-\frac{2\cdot 2\cdot 2}{3\cdot 3\cdot 3} \\  & =-\frac{8}{27}\end{aligned}
$$

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡x & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x} \\ {v}^{′}={x}^{4} & \,⟹\,v=\int {x}^{4}\,dx=\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}{x}^{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{e}u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv{|}_{1}^{e}-{\int }_{1}^{e}v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x(\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}){|}_{1}^{e}-{\int }_{1}^{e}(\frac{{x}^{5}}{5})(\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =[\frac{{e}^{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡(e)}{5}-\frac{{1}^{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)}{5}]-\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{1}^{e}{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡(e)}{5}-\frac{{x}^{5}}{25}{|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{5}}{5}-(\frac{{e}^{5}}{25}-\frac{1}{25}) \\  & =\frac{1}{25}(5{e}^{5}-{e}^{5}+1) \\  & =\frac{1}{25}(4{e}^{5}+1).\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: If $\text{Var}[X]=18,$ calculate $\text{Var}[\frac{1}{3}X+1].$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that for any random variable $X$ and constants $a$ and $b,$ we have

$$
\text{Var}[aX+b]={a}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X].
$$

In our case, $a=\frac{1}{3}$ and $b=1.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\frac{1}{3}X+1] & ={(\frac{1}{3})}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\cdot 18 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
A stick of length $1$ is broken at a point chosen uniformly at random along its length. Let the continuous random variable $X$ denote the distance from the left end of the stick to the break point, and let $Y=Y(X)$ denote the length of the longest piece.

Expressing the integrands in the following equation as polynomials, we have

$\text{E}[Y]={\int }_{0}^{1/2}$
{{field-1}}
$\text{d}x+{\int }_{1/2}^{1}$
{{field-2}}
$\text{d}x.$

Therefore, the expected length of the longer piece is 
{{field-3}}.
:question/worked-solution:
For a continuous random variable $X$ and a function $r(x),$ the rule of the lazy statistician states that 

$$
\text{E}[r(X)]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }r(x)f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In this problem, the break point $X$ is uniformly distributed over the interval $[0,1]$, so the probability density function is

$$
f(x)=1,\,0\le x\le 1.
$$

When the stick is broken at point $X$, it is divided into two pieces: one of length $X$ and the other of length $1-X.$ The longer of the two pieces, $Y,$ is therefore given by

$$
Y=max(X,1-X).
$$

Therefore, we define

$$
r(x)=max(x,1-x).
$$

To evaluate the integral, we express $r(x)$ as an explicit piecewise function. Observe that,

- if $0\le x\le \frac{1}{2}$, then $x\le 1-x$, so the longer piece has length $1-x,$

- if $\frac{1}{2}<x\le 1$, then $x>1-x$, so the longer piece has length $x.$

Therefore,

$$
r(x)=\{\begin{aligned}1-x, & \,0\le x\le \frac{1}{2}, \\ x, & \,\frac{1}{2}<x\le 1.\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & =\text{E}[max(X,1-X)] \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }r(x)f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}(1-x)\cdot 1\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1/2}^{1}x\cdot 1\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}(1-x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1/2}^{1}x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[x-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1/2}+{[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{1/2}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot {(\frac{1}{2})}^{2})+(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot {(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{8})+(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{8}) \\  & =\frac{3}{8}+\frac{3}{8} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the expected length of the longer piece is $\frac{3}{4}.$

For a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ where $n$ is the number of trials, and $p$ is the probability of success on each trial, we have the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x}
$$

Here, we have $X∼B(6,\frac{1}{2}),$ so $X$ has the probability mass function

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{x}){(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}{(\frac{1}{2})}^{6-x}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(2\le X\le 3) & =P(X\in \{2,3\}) \\  & =f(2)+f(3) \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{2}){(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}{(\frac{1}{2})}^{6-2}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{3}){(\frac{1}{2})}^{3}{(\frac{1}{2})}^{6-3} \\  & =15{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}{(\frac{1}{2})}^{4}+20{(\frac{1}{2})}^{3}{(\frac{1}{2})}^{3} \\  & ≈0.547\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

:question/problem: Given that $X∼B(4,\frac{1}{2}),$ compute $P(X=4).$
:question/worked-solution:
For a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ where $n$ is the number of trials, and $p$ is the probability of success on each trial,  we have the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x}
$$

Here, we have $X∼B(4,\frac{1}{2}),$ so $X$ has the probability mass function

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{x}){(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}{(\frac{1}{2})}^{4-x}.
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=4) & =f(4) \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{4}){(\frac{1}{2})}^{4}{(\frac{1}{2})}^{4-4} \\  & =1{(\frac{1}{2})}^{4}{(\frac{1}{2})}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u={y}^{2}-2\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}y}=2y, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}y}={e}^{2y-1}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}y}\,\text{d}y=\int {e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y=\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({y}^{2}-2){e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =({y}^{2}-2)(\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{2})-\int (\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{2})(2y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{({y}^{2}-2){e}^{2y-1}}{2}-\int y\,{e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int y\,{e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=y\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}y}=1 \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}y}={e}^{2y-1}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}y}\,\text{d}y=\int {e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y=\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y\,{e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =(y)(\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{2})-\int (\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{2})(1)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{y\,{e}^{2y-1}}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{y\,{e}^{2y-1}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{4}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is a constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({y}^{2}-2){e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y & =\frac{({y}^{2}-2){e}^{2y-1}}{2}-\int y\,{e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{({y}^{2}-2){e}^{2y-1}}{2}-(\frac{y\,{e}^{2y-1}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{4}+D) \\  & =\frac{({y}^{2}-2){e}^{2y-1}}{2}-\frac{y\,{e}^{2y-1}}{2}+\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{4}-D \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{4}(2{y}^{2}-2y-3)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-D.$ 

Finally then, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}({y}^{2}-2){e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y & ={[\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{4}(2{y}^{2}-2y-3)]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =(\frac{{e}^{2(2)-1}}{4}(2(2)^{2}-2(2)-3))-(\frac{{e}^{2(0)-1}}{4}(2(0)^{2}-2(0)-3)) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3}}{4}(8-4-3)-\frac{1}{4e}(0-0-3) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3}}{4}+\frac{3}{4e} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{4}+3}{4e}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Given that $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda =11$ are the eigenvalues of the matrix
$A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 \\ 3 & 9\end{bmatrix}$,
find two linearly independent eigenvectors of $A.$
:question/worked-solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each of the eigenvalues separately. 

- For $\lambda =0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 \\ 3 & 9\end{bmatrix}-0\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 \\ 3 & 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2} &=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}+9{x}_{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 & 0 \\ 3 & 9 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-\frac{3}{2}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. 
From the first equation, we obtain  ${x}_{1}=-3{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

- For $\lambda =11,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 \\ 3 & 9\end{bmatrix}-11\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 6 \\ 3 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-9{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2} &=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 6 & 0 \\ 3 & -2 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. 
From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=3,$ we get the eigenvector 
${v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$

Therefore, two linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix $A$ are

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

:question/problem:
| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ | $\frac{1}{9}$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ |
| $X=2$ | $\frac{1}{18}$ | $\frac{1}{18}$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ |
| $X=3$ | $\frac{1}{9}$ | $\frac{1}{9}$ | $\frac{1}{18}$ |

Compute $P(Y=0\,|\,X=3)$ given that the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ shown in the table above.
:question/worked-solution:
By the multiplication law for conditional probability, the required probability is given by

$$
P(Y=0\,|\,X=3)=\frac{P(X=3,Y=0)}{P(X=3)}=\frac{f(3,0)}{{f}_{X}(3)},
$$

where $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability mass function of $X$ and $Y,$ and ${f}_{X}(x)$ is the marginal distribution of $X.$

Recall that the marginal distribution for $X$ corresponds to the row totals. Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(3) & =f(3,0)+f(3,1)+f(3,2) \\  & =\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{18} \\  & =\frac{2}{18}+\frac{2}{18}+\frac{1}{18} \\  & =\frac{5}{18}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given table, we have that $f(3,0)=\frac{1}{9}.$ 

Finally, substituting ${f}_{X}(3)=\frac{5}{18}$ and $f(3,0)=\frac{1}{9}$ in our formula above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y=0\,|\,X=3) & =\frac{f(3,0)}{{f}_{X}(3)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{1}{9})}{(\frac{5}{18})} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
A particle of mass $0.4\,\text{kg}$ is attached to a massless spring. An external periodic force $F(t)=-3sin\,(\frac{5}{2}t)\,\text{N}$ is applied to the particle.

The position of the particle is $y(t)$ (measured in meters), and $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle moves with forced harmonic motion without damping and the system experiences resonance, what is the spring constant $k?$

$k=$
{{field-1}}${\text{kg/s}}^{2}$
:question/worked-solution:
The equation of motion for a particle of mass $m$ moving with forced harmonic motion without damping under the action of a spring with spring constant $k$ and external force $F(t)$ is given by

$$
m{y}^{″}=-ky+F(t).
$$

Substituting our values for $m$ and $F(t)$ gives

$$
0.4{y}^{″}=-ky-3sin\,(\frac{5}{2}t).
$$

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{5k}{2}y=-\frac{15}{2}sin\,(\frac{5}{2}t).
$$

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration, and $\omega $ is the system's internal frequency.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=\frac{5k}{2}\,⟹\,k=\frac{2}{5}{\omega }^{2}.
$$

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency of the external periodic force $f(t)=-\frac{15}{2}sin\,(\frac{5}{2}t),$ which is $\frac{5}{2},$ is equal to the frequency of the complementary solution $\omega .$

Therefore,

$$
k=\frac{2}{5}{\omega }^{2}=\frac{2}{5}\cdot {(\frac{5}{2})}^{2}=\frac{5}{2}\,{\text{kg/s}}^{2}.
$$

:question/problem:
A continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function 

$$
f(x)=\frac{5}{2\sqrt{{x}^{7}}},\,x\ge 1.
$$

Calculate $\text{E}[{X}^{2}].$
:question/worked-solution:
For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the expected value of ${X}^{2}$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{2}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We compute the expected value of ${X}^{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{5}{2\sqrt{{x}^{7}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{x}^{-3/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}{x}^{-3/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{(-2{x}^{-1/2})|}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-5{lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}})|}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-5{lim}_{a\to \infty }(\frac{1}{\sqrt{a}}-1) \\  & =-5(0-1) \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Expressed in radians, $\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-1)=${{field-1}}.
:question/worked-solution:
The range of $\theta =\operatorname{arctan}⁡x$ is given by

$$
-\frac{\pi }{2}<\theta <\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Note that the angle $\theta $ spans the first and fourth quadrants.

Since $-1$ is negative, our answer is an angle that lies in the fourth quadrant, where the tangent is negative.

From the special values of the trigonometric functions, we know that 

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{4})=-1.
$$

Since $-\frac{\pi }{4}$ is an angle in the fourth quadrant that lies within the range of $arctan,$ we conclude that

$$
\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-1)=-\frac{\pi }{4}.
$$

:question/problem: For two independent random variables $X$ and $Y,$ we have $\text{Var}[X]=1$ and $\text{Var}[Y]=2.$ Find $\text{Var}[\frac{1}{3}X+\frac{2}{3}Y].$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are independent variables, and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then 

$$
\text{Var}[aX+bY]={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{b}^{2}\text{Var}[Y].
$$

Substituting the given data into the formula above, we obtain 

$$
\text{Var}[\frac{1}{3}X+\frac{2}{3}Y]={(\frac{1}{3})}^{2}\cdot 1+{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2}\cdot 2=1.
$$

:question/problem: For two independent random variables $X$ and $Y,$ we have $\text{Var}[X]=36$ and $\text{Var}[Y]=4.$ Find $\text{Var}[\frac{1}{3}X-\frac{1}{2}Y].$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are independent variables, and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then 

$$
\text{Var}[aX+bY]={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{b}^{2}\text{Var}[Y].
$$

Substituting the given data into the formula above, we obtain 

$$
\text{Var}[\frac{1}{3}X-\frac{1}{2}Y]={(\frac{1}{3})}^{2}\cdot 36+{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}\cdot 4=5.

:question/problem:
The probability mass function of the independent random variables $X$ and $Y$ are given below.
$x$ $-1$ $0$ $1$
$f(x)$ $\frac{1}{3}$ $\frac{1}{3}$ $\frac{1}{3}$

$y$ $1$ $2$
$f(y)$ $\frac{1}{5}$ $\frac{4}{5}$

Find $\text{Var}[\sqrt{3}X-\sqrt{5}Y].$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[aX+bY]={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{b}^{2}\text{Var}[Y].
$$

Also, the variance of $X$ is determined by the formula 

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}.
$$

First, let's find $\text{Var}[X].$ If $X$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{X}$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}x\cdot f(x) \\  & =(-1)(\frac{1}{3})+0(\frac{1}{3})+1(\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x) \\  & =(-1)^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{3})+{0}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{3})+{1}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}-{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, if $Y$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{Y}$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{Y}}y\cdot f(y) \\  & =1(\frac{1}{5})+2(\frac{4}{5}) \\  & =\frac{9}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{Y}}{y}^{2}\cdot f(y) \\  & ={1}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{5})+{2}^{2}\cdot (\frac{4}{5}) \\  & =\frac{17}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =\frac{17}{5}-{(\frac{9}{5})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{4}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\sqrt{3}X-\sqrt{5}Y] & =(\sqrt{3})^{2}\text{Var}[X]+(-\sqrt{5})^{2}\text{Var}[Y] \\  & =3\cdot \frac{2}{3}+5\cdot \frac{4}{25} \\  & =\frac{14}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{0}^{3/2}\frac{3}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3/2}\frac{3}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{0}^{3/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{9\cdot (1-{x}^{2}/9)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\cdot \frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{3/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/9}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/3)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

  

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{3})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{3}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=3\,\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $\frac{3}{2}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3/2}\frac{3}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/3)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (3\,\text{d}u) \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =3\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u{|}_{0}^{1/2} \\  & =3(\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{1}{2})-\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(0)) \\  & =3(\frac{\pi }{6}-0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/c4/c46bf82e7609abe56e9e65ef0e81e21438a67e849d80d560baff5ab0c90bde11.png)

A plate with mass $M$ and uniform mass density occupies the region $D$ enclosed between the curves $y={x}^{2}$ and $y=x+2$, as shown above. Given that the region has an area of $\frac{9}{2},$ find the moment of inertia of the plate about the line $x=2.$
:question/worked-solution:
The moment of inertia of a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ about an axis of rotation $l$ is given by

$$
{I}_{l}={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)[r(x,y)]^{2}\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function of the lamina, and $r(x,y)$ is the distance from the line $l$ to the point $(x,y)$ on $D.$

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 2,\,\,{x}^{2}\le y\le x+2\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/f4/f48cd4e22c083d6c05ba9908a788402b05d839fea710a7328297d9e392e3636e.png)

The distance between a point on $D$ and the line $x=2$ is given by

$$
r(x,y)=|x-2|.
$$

Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{2M}{9}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the line $x=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)[r(x,y)]^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{2M}{9}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{x+2}|x-2{|}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2M}{9}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{x+2}(x-2)^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2M}{9}{\int }_{-1}^{2}(x-2)^{2}[y]_{y={x}^{2}}^{y=x+2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2M}{9}{\int }_{-1}^{2}({x}^{2}-4x+4)(x+2-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2M}{9}{\int }_{-1}^{2}-{x}^{4}+5{x}^{3}-6{x}^{2}-4x+8\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2M}{9}{[-\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}+\frac{5{x}^{4}}{4}-2{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}+8x]}_{-1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2M}{9}[(-\frac{32}{5}+20-16-8+16)-(\frac{1}{5}+\frac{5}{4}+2-2-8)] \\  & =\frac{2M}{9}(\frac{28}{5}-(-\frac{131}{20})) \\  & =\frac{27M}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

If we let $u=5x,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $\pi /20$ | $\pi /10$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\pi /4$ | $\pi /2$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /20}^{\pi /10}5{csc}^{2}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}5{csc}^{2}⁡(u)\cdot \frac{1}{5}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}{csc}^{2}⁡(u)\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡(u){|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-(\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})) \\  & =-(0-1) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Calculate ${\int }_{0}^{\pi /9}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x+\frac{\pi }{3})\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
If we let $u=3x+\frac{\pi }{3},$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\pi /9$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\pi /3$ | $2\pi /3$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /9}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x+\frac{\pi }{3})\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{2\pi /3}\operatorname{sin}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{\pi /3}^{2\pi /3}\operatorname{sin}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡u{|}_{\pi /3}^{2\pi /3} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}(-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The matrix $C$ and the vector $b$ are given below.
Determine if $b\in \text{Col}(C).$ 
In the affirmative case, find the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}\cdot {x}_{3}$, where ${x}_{1},{x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are real numbers such that $b={x}_{1}{c}_{1}+{x}_{2}{c}_{2}+{x}_{3}{c}_{3},$ and ${c}_{1}$, ${c}_{2}$, and ${c}_{3}$ are the respective columns of $C.$

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 & -4 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ -8 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
In order to determine whether $b$ lies in $\text{Col}(C),$ we need to check if the equation $Cx=b$ is consistent. So, let's find the row echelon form of the augmented matrix $[C\,|\,b]$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[C\,|\,b] & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 & -4 & 9 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 & -8 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 & 5\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & ↔{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 & 5 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 & -8 \\ 4 & 1 & -4 & 9\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 & -3 \\ 4 & 1 & -4 & 9\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 & -3 \\ 0 & -7 & -16 & -11\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(\frac{7}{3}){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & -9 & -18\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} &=5 \\ 3{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} &=-3 \\ -9{x}_{3} &=-18.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the third equation, we get ${x}_{3}=2.$ Substituting it into the second equation gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}_{2}+3(2) & =-3 \\ {x}_{2} & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, from the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =5-2{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3} \\  & =5-2(-3)-3(2) \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Since we have a solution, the equation $Cx=b$ is consistent, which implies that $b\in \text{Col}(C).$ 

Moreover, there is exactly one solution, so we have exactly one way to write $b$ as a linear combination of ${c}_{1},$ ${c}_{2},$ and ${c}_{3}:$

$$
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ -8 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}}_{b}=5\cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{{c}_{1}}+(-3)\cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}}_{{c}_{2}}+2\cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}}_{{c}_{3}}
$$

Finally, we get ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}\cdot {x}_{3}=5\cdot (-3)\cdot 2=-30.$

:question/problem: Consider the arc of the curve $y=x-{x}^{4}$ that lies between the lines $x=0$ and $x=1.$ What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${x}_{1}=0$ to ${x}_{2}=1.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x-{x}^{4})=1-4{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(x-{x}^{4})\sqrt{1+{(1-4{x}^{3})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(x-{x}^{4})\sqrt{2-8{x}^{3}+16{x}^{6}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Consider the arc of the curve $x=\sqrt{y}$ that lies between $y=1$ and $y=4.$ What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${y}_{1}=1$ to ${y}_{2}=4.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\sqrt{y})=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{4}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{4}y\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{4}y\sqrt{\frac{4y+1}{y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{y(4y+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the arc of the curve $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ that lies in the first quadrant between its $y$-intercepts (see figure above). What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡y & =0 \\ y & =\pm n\pi ,\,n\in Z\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=\pi .$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }y\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡y}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the arc of the curve $y=2x-{x}^{2}$ that lies in the first quadrant between its $x$-intercepts. What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $x$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-{x}^{2} & =0 \\ x(2-x) & =0 \\ x & =0,2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=2.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x-{x}^{2})=2-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(2x-{x}^{2})\sqrt{1+{(2-2x)}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(2x-{x}^{2})\sqrt{5-8x+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}

:question/problem: Consider the arc of the curve $y=\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}$ that lies between the lines $x=0$ and $x=1.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis.
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${x}_{1}=0$ to ${x}_{2}=1.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}})=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}\,⇒\,{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}=\frac{{x}^{2}}{1-{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{1-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}1\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi x\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2\pi (1-0) \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Consider the arc of the curve $y=\sqrt{x}-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3/2}$ that lies between the lines $x=0$ and $x=3.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis.
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${x}_{1}=0$ to ${x}_{2}=3.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{x}-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3/2})=\frac{1-x}{2\sqrt{x}}\,⇒\,{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}=\frac{1-2x+{x}^{2}}{4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}(\sqrt{x}-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3/2})\sqrt{1+\frac{1-2x+{x}^{2}}{4x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}(\sqrt{x}-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3/2})\sqrt{\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{\sqrt{x}(3-x)}{3}(\frac{x+1}{2\sqrt{x}})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}(3-x)(x+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}(3+2x-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {[3x+{x}^{2}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}\cdot 9 \\  & =3\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Given that $X$ is a continuous random variable with the following probability density function, compute $\text{Var}[X].$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}-\frac{2x}{15},\, & 1\le x\le 4, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ we can calculate the variance using the following formula:

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}
$$

 

First, we compute $\text{E}[X]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{1}^{4}x\cdot (\frac{2}{3}-\frac{2x}{15})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(\frac{2x}{3}-\frac{2{x}^{2}}{15})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{2{x}^{3}}{45})|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =\frac{11}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Then, we compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{1}^{4}{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{2}{3}-\frac{2x}{15})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(\frac{2{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{2{x}^{3}}{15})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{2{x}^{3}}{9}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{30})|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =\frac{11}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the variance is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{11}{2}-{(\frac{11}{5})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{33}{50} \\  & =0.66.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function $f(x)$ stated below. Given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{5}{6},$ compute $\text{Var}[X].$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3x}{2}, & 0<x<1 \\ \frac{1}{{x}^{5}},\, & x\ge 1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ we can calculate the variance using the following formula:

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}
$$

 

We compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}],$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{3x}{2}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{5}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3{x}^{3}}{2}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{3{x}^{4}}{8}|}_{0}^{1}+(-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}){|}_{1}^{\infty } \\  & =\frac{3}{8}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{7}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the variance is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{7}{8}-{(\frac{5}{6})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{13}{72}.\end{aligned}
$$

The continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function $f(x)$ stated below. Given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{17}{24},$ compute $\text{Var}[X].$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.

We compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}],$ as follows:
