:question/problem: If $f(x)=\operatorname{tanh}⁡({x}^{2})$  and $x\ge 0,$ calculate  ${f}^{-1}(x)$ from first-principles.
:question/worked-solution:
Let $y=\operatorname{tanh}⁡{x}^{2}.$ Note that $f(x)$ is a one-to-one function on $x\ge 0.$ We have $y\in [0,1)$ for $x\in [0,\infty ).$ 

To find the inverse function we swap $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
x=\operatorname{tanh}⁡{y}^{2},
$$

where $x\in [0,1)$ and $y\in [0,\infty ).$

Next, we apply the definition of $\operatorname{tanh}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{e}^{2{y}^{2}}-1}{{e}^{2{y}^{2}}+1} \\ x({e}^{2{y}^{2}}+1) & ={e}^{2{y}^{2}}-1 \\ (x-1){e}^{2{y}^{2}} & +(x+1)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Isolating the ${e}^{2{y}^{2}}$ term, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{2{y}^{2}} & =-\frac{x+1}{x-1} \\ {e}^{2{y}^{2}} & =\frac{1+x}{1-x} \\ 2{y}^{2} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1+x}{1-x}) \\ {y}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1+x}{1-x}) \\ y & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1+x}{1-x})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $y\ge 0,$ we select the positive root. Therefore,

$$
y=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1+x}{1-x})}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
{f}^{-1}(x)=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1+x}{1-x})}.
$$

:question/problem:
Find the coefficient of $(x-1)^{2}$ in the second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=\frac{1}{x+2}$ at $x=1.$ Do not round the answer.

The coefficient of $(x-1)^{2}$ is
{{field-1}}.
:question/worked-solution:
The second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=1$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(x) & =f(1)+{f}^{′}(1)(x-1)+\frac{{f}^{″}(1)}{2}(x-1)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The coefficient of $(x-1)^{2}$ in the above Taylor polynomial is

$$
\frac{{f}^{″}(1)}{2}.
$$

To find this coefficient, we start by computing the second derivative ${f}^{″}(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{1}{x+2}=(x+2)^{-1} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-(x+2)^{-2} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =2(x+2)^{-3}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate ${f}^{″}(x)$ at $x=1.$ This gives

$$
{f}^{″}(1)=2(1+2)^{-3}=\frac{2}{27}.
$$

Finally, we determine the coefficient of $(x-1)^{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{f}^{″}(1)}{2}=\frac{(\frac{2}{27})}{2}=\frac{1}{27}\end{aligned}
$$

We use the identity $\operatorname{cot}⁡3x=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡3x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡3x}$ and rewrite the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /18}^{\pi /6}\frac{\operatorname{cot}⁡(3x)}{{sin}^{4}⁡(3x)}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /18}^{\pi /6}\frac{1}{{sin}^{4}⁡(3x)}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡3x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡3x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /18}^{\pi /6}\frac{1}{{sin}^{5}⁡(3x)}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡3x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡3x.$ Then 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3\operatorname{cos}⁡3x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡3x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡3x.$

| $x$ | $\frac{\pi }{18}$ | $\frac{\pi }{6}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $1$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /18}^{\pi /6}\frac{1}{{sin}^{5}⁡(3x)}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡3x\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1/2}^{1}\frac{1}{{u}^{5}}\,\cdot \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1/2}^{1}{u}^{-5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\frac{{u}^{-4}}{-4}){|}_{1/2}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{12}(\frac{1}{{u}^{4}}){|}_{1/2}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{12}(\frac{1}{{1}^{4}}-{(\frac{2}{1})}^{4}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{12}(1-16) \\  & =\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
$$

Which of the following is equivalent to $\operatorname{arsinh}⁡(\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{2t}),$ for $t>0?$
:question/worked-solution:
The definition of $\operatorname{arsinh}⁡x$ is 

$$
\operatorname{arsinh}⁡x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{arsinh}⁡(\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{2t}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{2t}+\sqrt{{(\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{2t})}^{2}+1}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{2t}+\sqrt{\frac{{t}^{4}-2{t}^{2}+1}{4{t}^{2}}+1}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{2t}+\sqrt{\frac{{t}^{4}+2{t}^{2}+1}{4{t}^{2}}}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{2t}+\sqrt{{(\frac{{t}^{2}+1}{2t})}^{2}}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{2t}+|\frac{{t}^{2}+1}{2t}|)\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t>0,$ we have $\frac{{t}^{2}+1}{2t}>0,$ and we can remove the absolute value in the above expression. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{arsinh}⁡(\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{2t}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{2t}+\frac{{t}^{2}+1}{2t}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2{t}^{2}}{2t}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the function $y=({x}^{2}+2x)^{6}\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.$  The derivative of this function is given by

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{({x}^{2}+2x)^{5}}{3\sqrt[3]{{sin}^{2}⁡x}}((ax+36)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+(b{x}^{2}+cx)\operatorname{cos}⁡x)
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$
:question/worked-solution:
Our function can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =({x}^{2}+2x)^{6}\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{sin}⁡x} \\  & =({x}^{2}+2x)^{6}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{1/3}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the product and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+2x)^{6}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{1/3}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+2x)^{6})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{1/3}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =6\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+2x)+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+2x)+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =6\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+2x}\cdot (2x+2)+\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{12(x+1)}{{x}^{2}+2x}+\frac{\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{12(x+1)}{{x}^{2}+2x}+\frac{\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=({x}^{2}+2x)^{6}\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =({x}^{2}+2x)^{6}\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}(\frac{12(x+1)}{{x}^{2}+2x}+\frac{\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{3}) \\  & =({x}^{2}+2x)^{6}\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}(\frac{12(x+1)}{{x}^{2}+2x}+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡x}) \\  & =({x}^{2}+2x)^{6}\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}(\frac{36(x+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+({x}^{2}+2x)\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{3({x}^{2}+2x)\operatorname{sin}⁡x}) \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+2x)^{5}}{3\sqrt[3]{{sin}^{2}⁡x}}((36x+36)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+(1{x}^{2}+2x)\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
a+b+c=36+1+2=39.
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the function $y=\frac{(x+6)^{3}{cos}^{4}⁡x}{(x-1)^{7}}.$  The derivative of this function is given by

$$
{y}^{′}=-\frac{(x+6)^{2}{cos}^{3}⁡x}{(x-1)^{8}}((ax+45)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+(4{x}^{2}+bx+c)\operatorname{sin}⁡x).
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$
:question/worked-solution:
We have the function 

$$
y=\frac{(x+6)^{3}{cos}^{4}⁡x}{(x-1)^{7}}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the product, quotient, and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{(x+6)^{3}{cos}^{4}⁡x}{(x-1)^{7}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((x+6)^{3})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({cos}^{4}⁡x)-\operatorname{ln}⁡((x-1)^{7}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+6)+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-7\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+6)+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-7\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =3\cdot \frac{1}{x+6}+4\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-7\cdot \frac{1}{x-1} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{3}{x+6}-4\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\frac{7}{x-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{3}{x+6}-4\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\frac{7}{x-1})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\frac{(x+6)^{3}{cos}^{4}⁡x}{(x-1)^{7}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{(x+6)^{3}{cos}^{4}⁡x}{(x-1)^{7}}(\frac{3}{x+6}-4\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\frac{7}{x-1}) \\  & =\frac{(x+6)^{3}{cos}^{4}⁡x}{(x-1)^{7}}(\frac{3(x-1)-4\operatorname{tan}⁡x(x+6)(x-1)-7(x+6)}{(x+6)(x-1)}) \\  & =\frac{(x+6)^{3}{cos}^{4}⁡x}{(x-1)^{7}}(\frac{-4x-45-4\operatorname{tan}⁡x({x}^{2}+5x-6)}{(x+6)(x-1)}) \\  & =-\frac{(x+6)^{2}{cos}^{4}⁡x}{(x-1)^{8}}(4x+45+4\operatorname{tan}⁡x({x}^{2}+5x-6)) \\  & =-\frac{(x+6)^{2}{cos}^{3}⁡x}{(x-1)^{8}}((4x+45)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+4\operatorname{tan}⁡x({x}^{2}+5x-6)\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =-\frac{(x+6)^{2}{cos}^{3}⁡x}{(x-1)^{8}}((4x+45)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x(4{x}^{2}+20x-24))\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
a+b+c=4+20+(-24)=0.
$$

Our function can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt[4]{\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{(2{x}^{2}+1)^{8}}} \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{(2{x}^{2}+1)^{8}}]}^{1/4} \\  & =({x}^{2}+4)^{1/4}(2{x}^{2}+1)^{-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the product and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+4)^{1/4}(2{x}^{2}+1)^{-2}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+4)^{1/4})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((2{x}^{2}+1)^{-2}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+4)-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{x}^{2}+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+4)-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{x}^{2}+1)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+4}\cdot (2x)-2\cdot \frac{1}{2{x}^{2}+1}\cdot (4x) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{x}{2({x}^{2}+4)}-\frac{8x}{2{x}^{2}+1} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+4}-\frac{16x}{2{x}^{2}+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{y}{2}(\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+4}-\frac{16x}{2{x}^{2}+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\sqrt[4]{\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{(2{x}^{2}+1)^{8}}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\sqrt[4]{\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{(2{x}^{2}+1)^{8}}}\cdot \frac{1}{2}(\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+4}-\frac{16x}{2{x}^{2}+1}) \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+4)^{1/4}}{2(2{x}^{2}+1)^{2}}(\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+4}-\frac{16x}{2{x}^{2}+1}) \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+4)^{1/4}}{2(2{x}^{2}+1)^{2}}(\frac{x(2{x}^{2}+1)-16x({x}^{2}+4)}{({x}^{2}+4)(2{x}^{2}+1)}) \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+4)^{1/4}}{2(2{x}^{2}+1)^{2}}(\frac{-14{x}^{3}-63x}{({x}^{2}+4)(2{x}^{2}+1)}) \\  & =-\frac{x(14{x}^{2}+63)}{2(2{x}^{2}+1)^{3}\sqrt[4]{({x}^{2}+4)^{3}}}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: The equation $3{z}^{2}-12=9z$ can be written in the form $(z+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $\,p+q,$ and solve the equation.
:question/worked-solution:
First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{z}^{2}-12 & =9z \\ 3{z}^{2}-9z-12 & =0 \\ 3({z}^{2}-3z-4) & =0 \\ {z}^{2}-3z-4 & =0 \\ {z}^{2}-2\cdot z\cdot \frac{3}{2} & =4 \\ {z}^{2}-2\cdot z\cdot \frac{3}{2}+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =-4 \\ [{z}^{2}-2\cdot z\cdot \frac{3}{2}+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}]-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =-4 \\ {(z-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =4 \\ {(z-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-\frac{25}{4} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(z-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =4 \\ {(z-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{25}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=-\frac{3}{2},q=\frac{25}{4}$ and $p+q=\frac{19}{4}.$

Now, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(z-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{25}{4} \\ \sqrt{{(z-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{25}{4}} \\ |z-\frac{3}{2}| & =\frac{5}{2} \\ z-\frac{3}{2} & =\pm \frac{5}{2} \\ z & =\frac{3}{2}\pm \frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{3}{2}+\frac{5}{2}=4 \\ z & =\frac{3}{2}-\frac{5}{2}=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $z=4$ and $z=-1.$

:question/problem:
Given that $y=\sqrt{\frac{{({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)}^{2}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}},$ find ${y}^{′}.$

${y}^{′}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}($
{{field-1}}$+\,\operatorname{tan}⁡x({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8))$
:question/worked-solution:
Our function can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{\frac{{({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)}^{2}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)}^{2}}}{\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}{(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{1/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}{(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{1/2}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)-\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{1/2}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =\frac{1}{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}\cdot (4{x}^{3}+4x)-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{4{x}^{3}+4x}{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}+\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}{2} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{8{x}^{3}+8x}{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}+\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{y}{2}(\frac{8{x}^{3}+8x}{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}+\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\sqrt{\frac{{({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)}^{2}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\sqrt{\frac{{({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)}^{2}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}\cdot \frac{1}{2}(\frac{8{x}^{3}+8x}{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}+\operatorname{tan}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{|{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8|}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}(\frac{8{x}^{3}+8x}{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}+\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8>0\text{ }∀x\in R$, so $|{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8|={x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8$ and we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}(\frac{8{x}^{3}+8x}{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}+\operatorname{tan}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}[\frac{8{x}^{3}+8x}{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}\cdot ({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)+\operatorname{tan}⁡x({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)] \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}(8{x}^{3}+8x+\operatorname{tan}⁡x({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8))\end{aligned}
$$

We have the function 

$$
y=\frac{{6}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{(x-2)^{4}(3-x)^{3}}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient, product, and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{6}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{(x-2)^{4}(3-x)^{3}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({6}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x})-\operatorname{ln}⁡((x-2)^{4}(3-x)^{3}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡6-(\operatorname{ln}⁡((x-2)^{4})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((3-x)^{3})) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡6-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(3-x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡6)-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2))-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3\operatorname{ln}⁡(3-x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =-(\operatorname{ln}⁡6)\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4\cdot \frac{1}{x-2}-3\cdot \frac{-1}{3-x} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =-(\operatorname{ln}⁡6)\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\frac{4}{x-2}+\frac{3}{3-x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(-(\operatorname{ln}⁡6)\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\frac{4}{x-2}+\frac{3}{3-x})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\frac{{6}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{(x-2)^{4}(3-x)^{3}}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{{6}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{(x-2)^{4}(3-x)^{3}}(-(\operatorname{ln}⁡6)\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\frac{4}{x-2}+\frac{3}{3-x}) \\  & =\frac{{6}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{(x-2)^{4}(3-x)^{3}}(\frac{-(\operatorname{ln}⁡6)(x-2)(3-x)\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4(3-x)+3(x-2)}{(x-2)(3-x)}) \\  & =\frac{{6}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{(x-2)^{4}(3-x)^{3}}(\frac{-(\operatorname{ln}⁡6)(x-2)(3-x)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+7x-18}{(x-2)(3-x)}) \\  & =\frac{{6}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}(-\operatorname{ln}⁡6(x-2)(3-x)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+7x-18)}{(x-2)^{5}(3-x)^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: A spherical hot air balloon is inflated. At a particular moment, the rate of increase in the volume of the balloon is numerically equal to nine-halfs the rate of increase in its surface area. What is the radius of the balloon at that moment?
:question/worked-solution:
Let $r$ be the radius of the balloon, $V$ the volume, and $A$ its surface area. We wish to find $r$ at the moment when $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=\frac{9}{2}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the volume $V$ and the surface area $A$ of the sphere. Since $A=4\pi {r}^{2}$ and $V=\frac{4\pi }{3}{r}^{3},$ the relationship between $V$ and $A$ is

$$
V=\frac{4\pi }{3}{r}^{3}=\frac{4\pi }{3}{(\frac{A}{4\pi })}^{3/2}=\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{3(4\pi )^{1/2}}=\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}A}(\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{{A}^{1/2}}{4\sqrt{\pi }}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=\frac{9}{2}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{2}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{{A}^{1/2}}{4\sqrt{\pi }} \\ {A}^{1/2} & =18\sqrt{\pi } \\ A & ={(18\sqrt{\pi })}^{2} \\ A & =324\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, since $A=4\pi {r}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4\pi {r}^{2} & =324\pi  \\ {r}^{2} & =81 \\ r & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/1c/1c16496b13f9ad9fc995cc59dedf1777f25e394ca61dd2ea493d8bd8f69c5e14.png)

Paint dripping onto a floor forms a circular puddle. The radius of the puddle increases at a rate of $10\,\text{in/min}.$ How fast is the area of the puddle increasing at the moment when the radius is $\frac{9}{4\pi }\,\text{in}?$

The area of the puddle is increasing at a rate of
{{field-1}} ${\text{in}}^{2}\text{/min}.$
:question/worked-solution:
In this situation, we want to find $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$ at the moment when $r=\frac{9}{4\pi },$ and we are also told that $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=10.$

To start, let's write down the area formula for the circle and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\pi {r}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\pi r.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=10$ and $r=\frac{9}{4\pi },$ and solve for $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =10\cdot 2\pi (\frac{9}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =45.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the area of the puddle is increasing at a rate of $45\,{\text{in}}^{2}\text{/min}.$

:question/problem: Represent the solution of the inequality $-\frac{a}{4}>-2$ on a number line.
:question/worked-solution:
The variable $a$ is being *divided* by $4.$ To isolate $a$ and remove the negative sign, we *multiply* by $-4.$ 

Remember, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{a}{4}\,\, & >\,\,-2 \\ (-4)\cdot (-\frac{a}{4})\,\, & <\,\,(-4)\cdot (-2) \\ (-4)\cdot (-\frac{a}{4})\,\, & <\,\,8\end{aligned}
$$

Since two negative numbers multiply to give a positive number, we first cancel the negatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-4)\cdot (-\frac{a}{4}) & <8 \\ (\cancel{-}4)\cdot (\cancel{-}\frac{a}{4}) & <8 \\ 4\cdot \frac{a}{4} & <8\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $4$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot \frac{a}{4} & <8 \\ \frac{4a}{4} & <8 \\ \frac{\cancel{4}a}{\cancel{4}} & <8 \\ a & <8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $a<8.$ The solution can be expressed on a number line, as shown below.

:question/problem: The equation $-4{x}^{2}-6x+10=0$ can be written in the form $4(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $p,$ and solve the equation.
:question/worked-solution:
First, we multiply the equation by $-1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)\cdot (-4{x}^{2}-6x+10) & =(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 4{x}^{2}+6x-10 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now we move the constant term to the right-hand side and complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}+6x-10 & =0 \\ 4{x}^{2}+6x & =10 \\ 4{x}^{2}+6x & =10 \\ 4({x}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}x) & =10 \\ 4[{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{3}{4}x+{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}] & =10 \\ 4[{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-\frac{9}{16}] & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-4\cdot \frac{9}{16} & =10 \\ 4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-\frac{9}{4} & =10 \\ 4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =10+\frac{9}{4} \\ 4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =\frac{49}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{3}{4}.$ We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =\frac{49}{4} \\ {(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =\frac{49}{16} \\ \sqrt{{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{49}{16}} \\ |x+\frac{3}{4}| & =\frac{7}{4} \\ x+\frac{3}{4} & =\pm \frac{7}{4} \\ x & =-\frac{3}{4}\pm \frac{7}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-\frac{3}{4}-\frac{7}{4}=-\frac{10}{4}=-\frac{5}{2} \\ x & =-\frac{3}{4}+\frac{7}{4}=1\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are $x=-\frac{5}{2}$ and $x=1.$

:question/problem:
Consider the function $y=\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{3}(x-3)^{8}}.$ The derivative of this function is given by

$$
{y}^{′}=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}(x-3)^{3}(a{x}^{2}+bx+c).
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$
:question/worked-solution:
Our function can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{3}(x-3)^{8}} \\  & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{3}}\cdot \sqrt{(x-3)^{8}} \\  & =({x}^{2}+1)^{3/2}(x-3)^{8/2} \\  & =({x}^{2}+1)^{3/2}(x-3)^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the product and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+1)^{3/2}(x-3)^{4}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+1)^{3/2})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((x-3)^{4}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-3)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\cdot 2x+4\cdot \frac{1}{x-3} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{3x}{{x}^{2}+1}+\frac{4}{x-3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{3x}{{x}^{2}+1}+\frac{4}{x-3})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{3}(x-3)^{8}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{3}(x-3)^{8}}(\frac{3x}{{x}^{2}+1}+\frac{4}{x-3}) \\  & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{3}(x-3)^{8}}(\frac{3x(x-3)+4({x}^{2}+1)}{({x}^{2}+1)(x-3)}) \\  & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{3}(x-3)^{8}}(\frac{7{x}^{2}-9x+4}{({x}^{2}+1)(x-3)}) \\  & =({x}^{2}+1)^{3/2}(x-3)^{4}(\frac{7{x}^{2}-9x+4}{({x}^{2}+1)(x-3)}) \\  & =({x}^{2}+1)^{1/2}(x-3)^{3}(7{x}^{2}-9x+4) \\  & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}(x-3)^{3}(7{x}^{2}-9x+4)\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore,

$$
a+b+c=7+(-9)+4=2.
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the function $y=\frac{(x+3)^{6}(x+8)^{5}}{{sin}^{8}⁡x}.$ The derivative of this function is given by

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{(x+3)^{5}(x+8)^{4}}{{sin}^{8}⁡x}(ax+63-8({x}^{2}+bx+c)\operatorname{cot}⁡x).
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$
:question/worked-solution:
We have the function 

$$
y=\frac{(x+3)^{6}(x+8)^{5}}{{sin}^{8}⁡x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the product, quotient, and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{(x+3)^{6}(x+8)^{5}}{{sin}^{8}⁡x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((x+3)^{6})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((x+8)^{5})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({sin}^{8}⁡x) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =6\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+3)+5\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+8)-8\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+3)+5\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+8)-8\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =6\cdot \frac{1}{x+3}+5\cdot \frac{1}{x+8}-8\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{6}{x+3}+\frac{5}{x+8}-8\operatorname{cot}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{6}{x+3}+\frac{5}{x+8}-8\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\frac{(x+3)^{6}(x+8)^{5}}{{sin}^{8}⁡x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{(x+3)^{6}(x+8)^{5}}{{sin}^{8}⁡x}(\frac{6}{x+3}+\frac{5}{x+8}-8\operatorname{cot}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{(x+3)^{6}(x+8)^{5}}{{sin}^{8}⁡x}(\frac{6(x+8)+5(x+3)-8\operatorname{cot}⁡x(x+3)(x+8)}{(x+3)(x+8)}) \\  & =\frac{(x+3)^{6}(x+8)^{5}}{{sin}^{8}⁡x}(\frac{6x+48+5x+15-8\operatorname{cot}⁡x({x}^{2}+11x+24)}{(x+3)(x+8)}) \\  & =\frac{(x+3)^{6}(x+8)^{5}}{{sin}^{8}⁡x}(\frac{11x+63-8\operatorname{cot}⁡x({x}^{2}+11x+24)}{(x+3)(x+8)}) \\  & =\frac{(x+3)^{5}(x+8)^{4}}{{sin}^{8}⁡x}(11x+63-8\operatorname{cot}⁡x({x}^{2}+11x+24))\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
a+b+c=11+11+24=46.
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the function $y=\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{4}+2x}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}}.$ The derivative of this function is given by

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{a{x}^{5}+3{x}^{4}+b{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+c}{({x}^{2}+2x+2)^{3/2}\sqrt{{x}^{4}+2x}}.
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$
:question/worked-solution:
Our function can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{4}+2x}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{x}^{4}+2x}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+2x+2}} \\  & =\frac{({x}^{4}+2x)^{1/2}}{({x}^{2}+2x+2)^{1/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{({x}^{4}+2x)^{1/2}}{({x}^{2}+2x+2)^{1/2}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{4}+2x)^{1/2})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+2x+2)^{1/2}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}+2x)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+2x+2)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}+2x)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+2x+2)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{4}+2x}\cdot (4{x}^{3}+2)-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}\cdot (2x+2) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{2{x}^{3}+1}{{x}^{4}+2x}-\frac{x+1}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{2{x}^{3}+1}{{x}^{4}+2x}-\frac{x+1}{{x}^{2}+2x+2})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{4}+2x}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{4}+2x}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}}(\frac{2{x}^{3}+1}{{x}^{4}+2x}-\frac{x+1}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}) \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{4}+2x}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}}(\frac{(2{x}^{3}+1)({x}^{2}+2x+2)-(x+1)({x}^{4}+2x)}{({x}^{4}+2x)({x}^{2}+2x+2)}) \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{4}+2x}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}}(\frac{2{x}^{5}+4{x}^{4}+4{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}+2x+2-({x}^{5}+{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+2x)}{({x}^{4}+2x)({x}^{2}+2x+2)}) \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{4}+2x}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}}(\frac{{x}^{5}+3{x}^{4}+4{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+2}{({x}^{4}+2x)({x}^{2}+2x+2)}) \\  & =\frac{1{x}^{5}+3{x}^{4}+4{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+2}{({x}^{2}+2x+2)^{3/2}\sqrt{{x}^{4}+2x}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
a+b+c=1+4+2=7.
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the function $y=\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}}}{{e}^{2-4x}}.$ The derivative of this function is given by

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}-1}}{{e}^{2-4x}}((x+2)^{2}+g(x)).
$$

Find the function $g(x).$
:question/worked-solution:
We have the function 

$$
y=\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}}}{{e}^{2-4x}}.
$$

First, we find the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}}}{{e}^{2-4x}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((x+1)^{{x}^{2}})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2-4x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & ={x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-(2-4x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-2+4x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{x+1}+4 \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{x+1}+4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{x+1}+4)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}}}{{e}^{2-4x}}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}}}{{e}^{2-4x}}(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{x+1}+4) \\  & =\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}}}{{e}^{2-4x}}(\frac{2x(x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+{x}^{2}+4(x+1)}{x+1}) \\  & =\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}-1}}{{e}^{2-4x}}(2x(x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+{x}^{2}+4(x+1)) \\  & =\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}-1}}{{e}^{2-4x}}(2x(x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+{x}^{2}+4x+4) \\  & =\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}-1}}{{e}^{2-4x}}(2x(x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+(x+2)^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
g(x)=2x(x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1).
$$

:question/problem: Factor ${x}^{2}-x+\frac{1}{4}.$
:question/worked-solution:
The "square of a difference" formula states that

$$
{x}^{2}-2ax+{a}^{2}=(x-a)^{2}.
$$

We will use this formula to factor the given trinomial. Our trinomial is

$$
{x}^{2}-x+\frac{1}{4}.
$$

First, we write the constant term as a perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-x+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we factor a $2$ out of the linear term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}x+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the trinomial using the square of difference formula with $a=\frac{1}{2}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given the plots of $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ above, find ${h}^{′}(1)$ where $h(x)=\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}.$

${h}^{′}(1)=$
{{field-1}}
:question/worked-solution:
The quotient rule for derivatives gives

$$
{h}^{′}(x)=\frac{{f}^{′}(x)\cdot g(x)-f(x)\cdot {g}^{′}(x)}{(g(x))^{2}}.
$$

As a result, we have that

$$
{h}^{′}(1)=\frac{{f}^{′}(1)\cdot g(1)-f(1)\cdot {g}^{′}(1)}{(g(1))^{2}}.
$$

From the graphs above, we obtain that $f(1)=2$ and $g(1)=1.$

Additionally:

- The slope of $f(x)$ on $x\in (-1,3)$ equals $-\frac{1}{2}.$ So, ${f}^{′}(1)=-\frac{1}{2}.$

- The slope of $g(x)$ on $x\in (0,3)$ equals $-1.$ So, ${g}^{′}(1)=-1.$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(1) & =\frac{{f}^{′}(1)\cdot g(1)-f(1)\cdot {g}^{′}(1)}{(g(1))^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(-\frac{1}{2})\cdot 1-2\cdot (-1)}{(1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\frac{3}{2}}{1} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Solve the inequality $\frac{2y-8}{3}\le \frac{8-2y}{4}.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we clear the rational expressions by multiplying both sides of the inequality by the lowest common positive multiple of the denominators:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2y-8}{3} & \le \frac{8-2y}{4} \\ 12\cdot (\frac{2y-8}{3}) & \le 12\cdot (\frac{8-2y}{4}) \\ 4\cdot (2y-8) & \le 3\cdot (8-2y) \\ 8y-32 & \le 24-6y\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}8y-32 & \le 24-6y \\ 8y-32+6y & \le 24-6y+6y \\ 14y-32 & \le 24 \\ 14y-32+32 & \le 24+32 \\ 14y & \le 56 \\ \frac{14y}{14} & \le \frac{56}{14} \\ y & \le 4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $y\le 4.$

:question/problem:

Consider the initial value problem above. By applying the Laplace transform $L$ to both sides of each equation in our system, we get a system with variables ${X}_{1}(s)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}$ and ${X}_{2}(s)=L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}.$ In terms of the parameter $s,$ the solution of the new system is

$\,{X}_{2}(s)=$ {{field-2}}.

First, we find the Laplace transforms of both sides of each equation in our system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}L\{{x}_{1}^{′}(t)\} &=L\{-{x}_{1}(t)\} \\ L\{{x}_{2}^{′}(t)\} &=L\{4{x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t)\}\end{aligned}\right.\,\,
$$

Using the derivative property of the Laplace transform, we obtain the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}sL\{{x}_{1}(t)\}-{x}_{1}(0) &=-L\{{x}_{1}(t)\} \\ sL\{{x}_{2}(t)\}-{x}_{2}(0) &=4L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}+2L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

which can be simplified to the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)+1 &=-{X}_{1}(s) \\ s{X}_{2}(s)-3 &=4{X}_{1}(s)+2{X}_{2}(s)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where ${X}_{1}(s)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}$ and ${X}_{2}(s)=L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}.$

Now, solving the first equation for ${X}_{1}(s),$ we get

$$
s{X}_{1}(s)+1=-{X}_{1}(s)\,⟹\,{X}_{1}(s)=-\frac{1}{s+1}.
$$

$$
s{X}_{2}(s)-3=4(-\frac{1}{s+1})+2{X}_{2}(s)\,⟹\,{X}_{2}(s)=\frac{3s-1}{(s+1)(s-2)}.
$$

:question/problem:
Find the values of the constants $a$ and $b$ that make the function $f(x)$ below continuous at $x=-1$ and $x=2.$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}-5, & x\le -1 \\ 2ax+3b, & -1<x\le 2 \\ 4, & x>2\end{aligned}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
At $x=-1,$ the left-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {(-1)}^{-}}f(x) & =f(-1) \\  & =-5,\end{aligned}
$$

and the right-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {(-1)}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {(-1)}^{+}}(2ax+3b) \\  & =2a(-1)+3b \\  & =-2a+3b.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=-1,$ we require that

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1)^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to (-1)^{+}}f(x) \\ -5 & =-2a+3b \\ 2a-3b & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, at $x=2,$ the left-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}(2ax+3b) \\  & =2a(2)+3b \\  & =4a+3b,\end{aligned}
$$

and the right-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}4=4.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=2,$ we require that

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x) \\ 4a+3b & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's solve the following system of equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2a-3b &=5 \\ 4a+3b &=4.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Adding both equations we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}6a & =9 \\ a & =\frac{9}{6} \\ a & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can replace $a$ by $\frac{3}{2}$ into the first equation. Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2(\frac{3}{2})-3b & =5 \\ 3-3b & =5 \\ -3b & =2 \\ b & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=-1$ and $x=2$ for $a=\frac{3}{2}$ and $b=-\frac{2}{3}.$

Let $X$ represent the height of a randomly selected tree. Then we have $X∼N(\mu ,{8}^{2}),$ and we want to find $P(X>50).$

:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=f(x),$ where the $6$-periodic forcing function is given by 

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below regarding the resonant component of a particular solution of the equation.

The natural frequency of the system matches the frequency of the {{field-1}} harmonic of the forcing function. 

Consequently, the particular solution contains a resonant term of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}={{field-2}}.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}}=\frac{2\pi }{3}.
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $6$-periodic function $(L=3)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{3}.
$$

For $n=2$, we have ${\omega }_{2}=\frac{2\pi }{3}.$ Since ${\omega }_{2}=\omega ,$ the $n=2$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=2$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{2}(x)=-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{y}_{{p}_{2}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}))+x(-\frac{2\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+\frac{2\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})) \\ \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{y}_{{p}_{2}}^{″} & =-\frac{4\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+\frac{4\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})-\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{2}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{2}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}):$

$$
\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,[-\frac{4\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+\frac{4\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})-\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}{y}_{{p}_{2}}]+\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}{y}_{{p}_{2}}=-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-\frac{4\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+\frac{4\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})=-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{4\pi }{3}A &=-\frac{3}{4} \\ \frac{4\pi }{3}B &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}A &=\frac{9}{16\pi } \\ B &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}=\frac{9x}{16\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}).
$$

The definition of $\operatorname{tanh}⁡x$ is

$$
\operatorname{tanh}⁡x=\frac{{e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}.
$$

Substituting the above definition into the equation $8\operatorname{tanh}⁡x=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}8(\frac{{e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}) & =1 \\ 8({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}) & ={e}^{x}+{e}^{-x} \\ 8{e}^{x}-8{e}^{-x} & ={e}^{x}+{e}^{-x} \\ 7{e}^{x} & =9{e}^{-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we multiply both sides of the equation by ${e}^{x}$ and solve the equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}\cdot 7{e}^{x} & ={e}^{x}\cdot 9{e}^{-x} \\ {e}^{2x} & =\frac{9}{7} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2x}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{9}{7}) \\ 2x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{9}{7}) \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{9}{7})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only real solution is

$$
x=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{9}{7}).
$$

:question/problem: Find the real solutions to the equation $5\operatorname{cosh}⁡x-\operatorname{sinh}⁡x=5.$
:question/worked-solution:
The definitions of $\operatorname{cosh}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{sinh}⁡x$ are

$$
\operatorname{cosh}⁡x=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}),\,\operatorname{sinh}⁡x=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}).
$$

Substituting the above definitions into the equation  $5\operatorname{cosh}⁡x-\operatorname{sinh}⁡x=5,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5\cdot (\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}))-\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}) & =5 \\ \frac{5}{2}{e}^{x}+\frac{5}{2}{e}^{-x}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-x} & =5 \\ 2{e}^{x}+3{e}^{-x} & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we multiply both sides of the equation by ${e}^{x},$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}\cdot (2{e}^{x}+3{e}^{-x}) & ={e}^{x}\cdot 5 \\ 2{e}^{2x}+3 & =5{e}^{x} \\ 2{e}^{2x}-5{e}^{x}+3 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This is a quadratic equation in ${e}^{x}$ that we can factor as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(2{e}^{x}-3)({e}^{x}-1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

By the zero-product property, we have to solve two equations:

$$
2{e}^{x}-3=0,\,{e}^{x}-1=0
$$

Solving the two equations above for $x,$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{e}^{x}-3 & =0 &  & \, & {e}^{x}-1 & =0 \\ {e}^{x} & =\frac{3}{2} &  & \, & {e}^{x} & =1 \\ {e}^{x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{2}) &  & \, & x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡1=0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=0$ and $x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{2})$ are the real solutions to the equation.

:question/problem:
$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) &=3{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) &=-2{x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t),\end{aligned}\right.\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the initial value problem above. By applying the Laplace transform $L$ to both sides of each equation in our system, we get a system with variables ${X}_{1}(s)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}$ and ${X}_{2}(s)=L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}.$ In terms of the parameter $s,$ the solution of the new system is

${X}_{1}(s)=$ {{field-1}},
$\,{X}_{2}(s)=$ {{field-2}}.
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the Laplace transforms of both sides of each equation in our system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}L\{{x}_{1}^{′}(t)\} &=L\{3{x}_{1}(t)\} \\ L\{{x}_{2}^{′}(t)\} &=L\{-2{x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t)\}\end{aligned}\right.\,\,
$$

Using the derivative property of the Laplace transform, we obtain the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}sL\{{x}_{1}(t)\}-{x}_{1}(0) &=3L\{{x}_{1}(t)\} \\ sL\{{x}_{2}(t)\}-{x}_{2}(0) &=-2L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}+L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

which can be simplified to the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)-4 &=3{X}_{1}(s) \\ s{X}_{2}(s)+2 &=-2{X}_{1}(s)+{X}_{2}(s)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where ${X}_{1}(s)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}$ and ${X}_{2}(s)=L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}.$

Now, solving the first equation for ${X}_{1}(s),$ we get

$$
s{X}_{1}(s)-4=3{X}_{1}(s)\,⟹\,{X}_{1}(s)=\frac{4}{s-3}.
$$

Substituting this in the second equation and solving for ${X}_{2}(s),$ we have

$$
s{X}_{2}(s)+2=-2(\frac{4}{s-3})+{X}_{2}(s)\,⟹\,{X}_{2}(s)=\frac{-2s-2}{(s-1)(s-3)}.
$$

:question/problem:
The continuous random variable $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{3}{{x}^{4}},\,x>1
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{3}{2},$ compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}+2X-1].$

*Hint: You may assume that $\text{E}[aX+bY]=a\text{E}[X]+b\text{E}[Y]$ for any random variables $X$ and $Y$ and constants $a$ and $b.$*
:question/worked-solution:
First, we simplify using the hint and the properties of expected value:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}+2X-1] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]+2\text{E}[X]-\text{E}[1] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]+2\text{E}[X]-1\end{aligned}
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We already know $\text{E}[X].$ So, we compute the second raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{S}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{3}{{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(-\frac{3}{x})|}_{1}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(3-\frac{3}{a}) \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\text{E}[X]=\frac{3}{2}$ and $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]=3$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}+2X-1] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]+2\text{E}[X]-1 \\  & =3+2\cdot \frac{3}{2}-1 \\  & =3+3-1 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Find the solution $(x,y)$ to this system using the method of substitution.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3x+3y &=2 \\ 3x+y &=-5\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The solution is $($ {{field-1}} $, $ {{field-2}} $)$
:question/worked-solution:
We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. 

Using the second equation, we can isolate $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+y & =-5 \\ y & =-5-3x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $y=-5-3x$ into the first equation and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+3y & =2 \\ 3x+3(-5-3x) & =2 \\ 3x-15-9x & =2 \\ -6x-15 & =2 \\ -6x & =17 \\ x & =-\frac{17}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $x=-\frac{17}{6}$ into $y=-5-3x,$ we can then find the value of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-5-3(-\frac{17}{6}) \\ y & =\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=-\frac{17}{6},\,y=\frac{7}{2}.$

:question/problem:
Find the solution $(x,y)$ to this system using the method of substitution.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-3x+4y &=8 \\ -2x+y &=6\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The solution is $($ {{field-1}} $, $ {{field-2}} $)$
:question/worked-solution:
We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. 

Using the second equation, we can isolate $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x+y & =6 \\ y & =6+2x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $y=6+2x$ into the first equation and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-3x+4y & =8 \\ -3x+4(6+2x) & =8 \\ -3x+24+8x & =8 \\ 5x+24 & =8 \\ 5x & =-16 \\ x & =-\frac{16}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $x=-\frac{16}{5}$ into $y=6+2x,$ we can then find the value of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =6+2(-\frac{16}{5}) \\ y & =-\frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=-\frac{16}{5},\,y=-\frac{2}{5}.$

:question/problem:
Find the solution $(x,y)$ to this system using the method of substitution.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}5x-2y &=5 \\ 2x+y &=-1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The solution is $($ {{field-1}} $, $ {{field-2}} $)$
:question/worked-solution:
We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. 

Using the second equation, we can isolate $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+y & =-1 \\ y & =-1-2x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $y=-1-2x$ into the first equation and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}5x-2y & =5 \\ 5x-2(-1-2x) & =5 \\ 5x+2+4x & =5 \\ 9x+2 & =5 \\ 9x & =3 \\ x & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $x=\frac{1}{3}$ into $y=-1-2x,$ we can then find the value of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-1-2(\frac{1}{3}) \\ y & =-\frac{5}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=\frac{1}{3},\,y=-\frac{5}{3}.$

:question/problem:
Find the solution $(x,y)$ to this system using the method of substitution.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x+2y &=12 \\ -2x+y &=5\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The solution is $($ {{field-1}} $, $ {{field-2}} $)$
:question/worked-solution:
We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. 

Using the second equation, we can isolate $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x+y & =5 \\ y & =5+2x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $y=5+2x$ into the first equation and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+2y & =12 \\ 2x+2(5+2x) & =12 \\ 2x+10+4x & =12 \\ 6x+10 & =12 \\ 6x & =2 \\ x & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $x=\frac{1}{3}$ into $y=5+2x,$ we can then find the value of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =5+2(\frac{1}{3}) \\ y & =\frac{17}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=\frac{1}{3},\,y=\frac{17}{3}.$

:question/problem: Evaluate ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{x+2}{x+1})}^{2x+2}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Notice that as $x\to \infty ,$ 

- the expression inside the parentheses approaches $1,$ while

- the exponent approaches $\infty .$

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{x+2}{x+1})}^{2x+2}={1}^{\infty },
$$

which is an indeterminate form.

Instead, let's recall the following special limit:

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}=e
$$

We rewrite the given limit as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{x+2}{x+1})}^{2x+2} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{(x+1)+1}{x+1})}^{2x+2} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{x+1})}^{2(x+1)}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $x+1=n.$ Therefore, since $n\to \infty $ as $x\to \infty ,$ we rewrite the limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{x+2}{x+1})}^{2x+2} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{x+1})}^{2(x+1)} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{2n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{[{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{2} \\  & ={[{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{2} \\  & ={e}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/9e/9ea7b23d8dd14a0ed092152592800022400ee73e7b371146f5e972900f2c2f29.png)

A community organizer wants to install a border around a walkway made up of a rectangle and two semicircles, as shown in the diagram. She has only $120\,m$ of border material. The organizer wishes to maximize the area of the **rectangle**. Find $x+2r$ where $x$ and $2r$ are the dimensions of the rectangle that has the greatest area. Do not round the answer.

$x+2r=$
{{field-1}}
$\text{m}$
:question/worked-solution:
First, let $r$ be the radius of the semicircles (the same for both semicircles) and let $x$ be the length of the other side of the rectangle. We want to maximize the area

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =2rx.\end{aligned}
$$

We know that the perimeter is fixed at $120\text{ m},$ so we also have the constraint condition

$$
120=\pi r+\pi r+2x=2\pi r+2x.
$$

Now, by making $x$ the subject of the constraint equation, we find that 

$$
\begin{aligned}120 & =2\pi r+2x \\ 2x & =120-2\pi r \\ x & =60-\pi r.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging the above into our expression for $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =2r(60-\pi r) \\  & =120r-2\pi {r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to maximize $A,$ so we need to differentiate $A$ and set the derivative equal to zero. The derivative is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(r) & =120-4\pi r.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting ${A}^{′}(r)=0$ and solving for $r$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(r) & =0 \\ 120-4\pi r & =0 \\ 4\pi r & =120 \\ r & =\frac{30}{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we confirm that $r=\frac{30}{\pi }$ is a maximum using the second derivative test. The second derivative gives

$$
{A}^{″}(r)=-4\pi \,⟹\,{A}^{″}(\frac{30}{\pi })=-4\pi <0.
$$

Since ${A}^{″}(\frac{30}{\pi })$ is negative, we conclude that $r=\frac{30}{\pi }$ is indeed a maximum of $A(r).$

Finally, when $r=\frac{30}{\pi }$, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =60-\pi (\frac{30}{\pi }) \\  & =60-30 \\  & =30.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the dimensions of the rectangle with the largest area are $x=30$ and $2r=\frac{60}{\pi },$ and we conclude that

$$
x+2r=30+\frac{60}{\pi }=\frac{30\pi +60}{\pi }.
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/ab/ab0416aeff61e4916acc1765a7931da0a41a64ba9d0ac4c05a322de6a1ed431b.png)

A box whose depth $z$ is equal to half of its height $y$ has a manufacturing cost that depends on two materials. The material for the top and bottom costs $$4$ per square meter, and the material for the lateral faces costs $$1$ per square meter. The box must have a volume of $36\,{m}^{3}.$

What is the value of $z$ for the box that has the smallest production cost? Do not round the answer.

$z=$
{{field-1}} units
:question/worked-solution:
**Step 1**: We need to find the value of $z$ such that the manufacturing cost

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =4\cdot 2xz+1\cdot 2xy+1\cdot 2yz \\  & =8xz+2xy+2yz\end{aligned}
$$

is the smallest possible value.

**Step 2**: The volume must be $36\,{m}^{3}.$ So, we have the constraint equation

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =x\cdot z\cdot y \\ 36 & =xz(2z) \\ 36 & =2x{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: We make $x$ the subject of the constraint equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x{z}^{2} & =36 \\ x & =\frac{18}{{z}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute the above into our expression for $C,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =8xz+2xy+2yz \\  & =8\,(\frac{18}{{z}^{2}})\,z+2\,(\frac{18}{{z}^{2}})\,(2z)+2(2z)z \\  & =\frac{144}{z}+\frac{72}{z}+4{z}^{2} \\  & =4{z}^{2}+\frac{216}{z}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: We solve the equation ${C}^{′}(z)=0.$ Taking the derivative, we have

$$
{C}^{′}(z)=8z-\frac{216}{{z}^{2}},
$$

and solving for the stationary points, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ 8z-\frac{216}{{z}^{2}} & =0 \\ 8{z}^{3} & =216 \\ {z}^{3} & =27 \\ z & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 5**: We confirm that $z=3$ is a minimum using the second derivative test. The second derivative is

$$
{C}^{″}(z)=8+\frac{432}{{z}^{3}}\,⟹\,{C}^{″}(3)=8+16=24>0.
$$

Since ${C}^{″}(3)$ is positive, we conclude that $z=3$ is indeed a minimum of $C(z).$

Therefore, the production cost is the smallest when $z=3$ units.

:question/problem:
![](images/b0/b024db5e134e25212b44cef850118a6823148b01f782c67dccc42f12b82e3854.png)

A piece of cardboard measures $8\,cm\times 6\,cm.$ A tray of height $y\,\text{cm}$ is formed by cutting a $y\times y\,{\text{cm}}^{2}$ square from each of the corners and folding up the sides, as shown in the diagram. Determine the height of the box that gives the maximum possible volume. Round your answer to two decimal places.
:question/worked-solution:
**Step 1**: We need to find the values of $x,y,$ and $z$ such that the volume

$$
V=xyz
$$

is the greatest possible value.

**Step 2**: Notice that the width $x$ and the depth $z$ of the tray are given by

$$
x=8-2y,\,z=6-2y.
$$

 

Since $x>0$ and $z>0,$ we must have that $8-2y>0$ and $6-2y>0$, hence $y<3.$ Therefore, the range of validity for $y$ is $0<y<3.$

**Step 3**: Substituting the above into the expression for $V,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =xyz \\  & =(8-2y)(y)(6-2y) \\  & =4{y}^{3}-28{y}^{2}+48y.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: We solve the equation ${V}^{′}(y)=0.$ Taking the first derivative, we have

$$
{V}^{′}(y)=12{y}^{2}-56y+48,
$$

and solving for the stationary points, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}^{′}(y) & =0 \\ 12{y}^{2}-56y+48 & =0 \\ 3{y}^{2}-14y+12 & =0 \\ y & =\frac{7\pm \sqrt{13}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We discard $\frac{7+\sqrt{13}}{3}$ since we already know that $0<y<3.$

**Step 5**: We confirm that $\frac{7-\sqrt{13}}{3}$ is a maximum using the second derivative test. The second derivative is

$$
{V}^{″}(y)=24y-56.
$$

Since ${V}^{″}(\frac{7-\sqrt{13}}{3})$ is negative, we conclude that $\frac{7-\sqrt{13}}{3}$ is indeed a maximum of $V(y).$

Therefore, the stationary point $y=\frac{7-\sqrt{13}}{3}≈1.13$ gives the maximum possible volume.

A box whose width $x$ is $2$ times its depth $z$ has a manufacturing cost that depends on two materials. The material for the top and bottom costs $$5$ per square foot, and the material for the lateral faces costs $$2$ per square foot. The box must have a volume of $180\,{ft}^{3}.$

What is the value of $z$ for the box that has the smallest production cost? Do not round the answer.

$z=$
{{field-1}} units
:question/worked-solution:
**Step 1**: We need to find the value of $z$ such that the manufacturing cost

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =5\cdot 2xz+2\cdot 2xy+2\cdot 2yz \\  & =10xz+4xy+4yz\end{aligned}
$$

is the smallest possible value.

**Step 2**: The volume must be $180\,{ft}^{3}.$ So, we have the constraint equation

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =x\cdot z\cdot y \\ 180 & =2{z}^{2}y.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: We make $y$ the subject of the constraint equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{z}^{2}y & =180 \\ y & =\frac{90}{{z}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute the above into our expression for $C,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =10xz+4xy+4yz \\  & =10(2z)z+4(2z)(\frac{90}{{z}^{2}})+4\,(\frac{90}{{z}^{2}})\,z \\  & =20{z}^{2}+\frac{720}{z}+\frac{360}{z} \\  & =20{z}^{2}+\frac{1080}{z}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: We solve the equation ${C}^{′}(z)=0.$ Taking the derivative, we have

$$
{C}^{′}(z)=40z-\frac{1080}{{z}^{2}},
$$

and solving for the stationary points, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ 40z-\frac{1080}{{z}^{2}} & =0 \\ 40{z}^{3} & =1080 \\ {z}^{3} & =27 \\ z & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 5**: We confirm that $z=3$ is a minimum using the second derivative test. The second derivative is

$$
{C}^{″}(z)=40+\frac{2160}{{z}^{3}}\,⟹\,{C}^{″}(3)=40+80=120>0.
$$

Since ${C}^{″}(3)$ is positive, we conclude that $z=3$ is indeed a minimum of $C(z).$

Therefore, the production cost is the smallest when $z=3$ units.

:question/problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3y=6\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-3{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{3x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{3x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{3x})}^{′}-3(u{e}^{3x}) & =6\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+3u{e}^{3x}-3u{e}^{3x} & =6\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+\cancel{3u{e}^{3x}}-\cancel{3u{e}^{3x}} & =6\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x} & =6\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′} & =6{e}^{-3x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x=\frac{{e}^{3x}-{e}^{-3x}}{2}
$$

our equation for $u$ becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =6{e}^{-3x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\  & =6{e}^{-3x}(\frac{{e}^{3x}-{e}^{-3x}}{2}) \\  & =3{e}^{-3x}({e}^{3x}-{e}^{-3x}) \\  & =3-3{e}^{-6x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =3-3{e}^{-6x} \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int 3-3{e}^{-6x}\,\text{d}x \\ u & =3x+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-6x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{3x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{3x} \\  & =3x{e}^{3x}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider a box with width $x,$ height $y,$ and depth $z,$ as shown above. The depth of the box is four times its height. Given that the box's volume is $800$ cubic units, what is the smallest possible surface area ${S}_{\text{min}}$ of the box? Do not round the answer.

${S}_{\text{min}}=$
{{field-1}} square units
:question/worked-solution:
**Step 1**: We need to find the value of $y$ such that the surface area

$$
S=2xz+2xy+2yz
$$

is the smallest possible value.

**Step 2**: The volume is $800$ cubic units. So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =x\cdot y\cdot z \\ 800 & =xyz.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the fact that $z=4y,$ we get the constraint equation

$$
800=4x{y}^{2}.
$$

**Step 3**: We make $x$ the subject of the constraint equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}4x{y}^{2} & =800 \\ x & =\frac{200}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute the above into our expression for $S,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2xz+2xy+2yz \\  & =2x(4y)+2xy+2y(4y) \\  & =8xy+2xy+8{y}^{2} \\  & =10xy+8{y}^{2} \\  & =10(\frac{200}{{y}^{2}})y+8{y}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2000}{y}+8{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: We solve the equation ${S}^{′}(y)=0.$ Taking the derivative, we have

$$
{S}^{′}(y)=16y-\frac{2000}{{y}^{2}},
$$

and solving for the stationary points, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(y) & =0 \\ 16y-\frac{2000}{{y}^{2}} & =0 \\ 16{y}^{3} & =2000 \\ {y}^{3} & =125 \\ y & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 5**: We confirm that $y=5$ is a minimum using the second derivative test. The second derivative is

$$
{S}^{″}(y)=16+\frac{4000}{{y}^{3}}\,⟹\,{S}^{″}(5)=16+32=48>0.
$$

Since ${S}^{″}(5)$ is positive, we conclude that $y=5$ is indeed a minimum.

Now, the smallest surface area ${S}_{\text{min}}$ that the box can have is

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{\text{min}}=S(5) & =8(5)^{2}+\frac{2000}{5} \\  & =600\,\text{square units}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Ralf is investigating the effect of a substance on some bacteria. In the beginning, there were $3\,000$ bacteria. After introducing the substance, Ralf noticed that the number of bacteria reduces by $\frac{1}{4}$ every minute.

The function $y(t)$ models the number of bacteria after $t$ minutes and is given by

$$
y(t)=3\,000\cdot {(\text{___})}^{t}.
$$

What number is missing?
:question/worked-solution:
If the number of alive bacteria reduces by $\frac{1}{4}$ every minute, then $\frac{3}{4}$ of the bacteria remains every minute. So the decay factor is $\frac{3}{4}.$

The formula for exponential decay (in terms of a decay factor $b$) is

$$
y=a{b}^{t}.
$$

In our case, we have the following:

- $a=3\,000$ is the initial number of bacteria.

- $b=\frac{3}{4}$ is the decay factor.

- $t=$ the time, in minutes.

Therefore, the correct expression for $y(t)$ is

$$
y(t)=3\,000\cdot {(\frac{3}{4})}^{t}.
$$

So the missing number is $\frac{3}{4}.$

Consider a box with width $x,$ height $y,$ and depth $z,$ as shown above. The depth of the box is one-third its width. Given that the box's volume is $288$ cubic units, what is the smallest possible surface area ${S}_{\text{min}}$ of the box? Do not round the answer.

${S}_{\text{min}}=$
{{field-1}} square units
:question/worked-solution:
**Step 1**: We need to find the value of $x$ such that the surface area

$$
S=2xz+2xy+2yz
$$

is the smallest possible value.

**Step 2**: The volume is $288$ cubic units. So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =x\cdot y\cdot z \\ 288 & =xyz.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the fact that $z=\frac{x}{3},$ we get the constraint equation

$$
288=xy(\frac{x}{3})=\frac{{x}^{2}y}{3}.
$$

**Step 3**: We make $y$ the subject of the constraint equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}y}{3} & =288 \\ {x}^{2}y & =864 \\ y & =\frac{864}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute the above into our expression for $S,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2xz+2xy+2yz \\  & =2x(\frac{x}{3})+2x(\frac{864}{{x}^{2}})+2(\frac{864}{{x}^{2}})(\frac{x}{3}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{x}^{2}+\frac{1728}{x}+\frac{576}{x} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{x}^{2}+\frac{2304}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: We solve the equation ${S}^{′}(x)=0.$ Taking the derivative, we have

$$
{S}^{′}(x)=\frac{4}{3}x-\frac{2304}{{x}^{2}},
$$

and solving for the stationary points, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ \frac{4}{3}x-\frac{2304}{{x}^{2}} & =0 \\ \frac{4}{3}x & =\frac{2304}{{x}^{2}} \\ \frac{4}{3}{x}^{3} & =2304 \\ {x}^{3} & =1728 \\ x & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 5**: We confirm that $x=12$ is a minimum using the second derivative test. The second derivative is

$$
{S}^{″}(x)=\frac{4}{3}+\frac{4608}{{x}^{3}}\,⟹\,{S}^{″}(12)=\frac{4}{3}+\frac{8}{3}=4>0.
$$

Since ${S}^{″}(12)$ is positive, we conclude that $x=12$ is indeed a minimum.

Now, the smallest surface area ${S}_{\text{min}}$ that the box can have is

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{\text{min}}=S(12) & =\frac{2}{3}(12)^{2}+\frac{2304}{12} \\  & =96+192 \\  & =288\,\text{square units}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Suppose that $f(x)$ is defined as

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}-x}{{x}^{2}-1}, & x<1 \\ \frac{1}{x+1}, & x\ge 1.\end{aligned}
$$

On which of the following intervals can the extreme value theorem be applied to the function?

I. $[-5,1)$

II. $[0,5]$

III. $[5,10]$
:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the extreme value theorem is only applicable to closed intervals on which the function is continuous.

So, let's check whether the function is continuous on each of the intervals.

- The interval $[-5,1)$ is not closed, so the extreme value theorem is not applicable.

- Now, consider $[0,5].$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to 1}(\frac{{x}^{2}-x}{{x}^{2}-1}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}(\frac{x(x-1)}{(x-1)(x+1)}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{x}{x+1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}, \\ {lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to 1}(\frac{1}{x+1})=\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the limits from the left and from the right of $x=1$ are the same. Hence, $f(x)$ is continuous on the interval $[0,5],$ and the extreme value theorem is applicable on this interval.

- Finally, consider $[5,10].$ In this interval $f(x)=\frac{1}{x+1}$ and so $f(x)$ is continuous on $[5,10].$ Therefore, the extreme value theorem is applicable on this interval.

In conclusion, the correct answer is "II and III only".

:question/problem: Evaluate ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{3x+1}{3x})}^{6x}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Notice that as $x\to \infty ,$ 

- the expression inside the parentheses approaches $1,$ while

- the exponent approaches $\infty .$

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{3x+1}{3x})}^{6x}={1}^{\infty },
$$

which is an indeterminate form.

Instead, let's recall the following special limit:

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}=e
$$

We rewrite the given limit as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{3x+1}{3x})}^{6x} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{3x})}^{2(3x)}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $3x=n.$ Therefore, since $n\to \infty $ as $x\to \infty ,$ we rewrite the limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{3x+1}{3x})}^{6x} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{3x})}^{2(3x)} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{2n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{[{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{2} \\  & ={[{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{2} \\  & ={e}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+5y=f(x),\,y(0)=0,\,y(1)=6
$$

where $f(x)$ is $4$-periodic and even. Select the missing part in the solution of the BVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ of the differential equation.

*Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function $f(x)$ is chosen such that the particular solution ${y}_{p}$ satisfies ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}(1)=0.$*

$$
y(x)∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$
:question/worked-solution:
We write the solution as $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}$, where ${y}_{c}$ solves the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, solve the homogeneous equation ${y}^{″}+5y=0.$ Its general solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}x).
$$

Now, we use the hint. Since ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}(1)=0$, we have

$$
y(0)={y}_{c}(0)\,\text{and}\,y(1)={y}_{c}(1).
$$

Next, we apply the boundary conditions.

- Use $y(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 0 & =A(1)+B(0)+0 \\ A & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{c}(x)=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}x).$

- Use $y(1)=6$ with $A=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})+{y}_{p}(1) \\ 6 & =B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})+0 \\ B & =\frac{6}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)∼\frac{6}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}x)+{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

:question/problem: The price of a new bicycle is $$625.$ If the bicycle loses $\frac{1}{5}$ of its value every year, what will be its value after $4$ years?
:question/worked-solution:
Since the value of the bicycle reduces by $\frac{1}{5}$ per year, $\frac{4}{5}$ of its value remains every year. 

Let's calculate the value of the bicycle after every year:

- After $1$ year, the bicycle will be worth $625\cdot (\frac{4}{5})$ dollars.

- After $2$ years, the bicycle will be worth $625\cdot {(\frac{4}{5})}^{2}$ dollars.

- After $3$ years, the bicycle will be worth $625\cdot {(\frac{4}{5})}^{3}$ dollars.

- After $4$ years, the bicycle will be worth $625\cdot {(\frac{4}{5})}^{4}$ dollars.

Evaluating the last expression, we get

$$
625\cdot {(\frac{4}{5})}^{4}=256.
$$

So after $4$ years, the bicycle will be worth $$256.$

By the end of $2020,$ the number of reservations per night decreased to $75\cdot {(\frac{3}{4})}^{9}.$ What does the factor $75$ mean in this context?

- $t=9$ is the time, in months, since March $2020.$

Since $a=75,$ this indicates that there were $75$ reservations initially.

:question/problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-4y=16\operatorname{sinh}⁡4x.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-4{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{4x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{4x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{4x})}^{′}-4(u{e}^{4x}) & =16\operatorname{sinh}⁡4x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{4x}+4u{e}^{4x}-4u{e}^{4x} & =16\operatorname{sinh}⁡4x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{4x}+\cancel{4u{e}^{4x}}-\cancel{4u{e}^{4x}} & =16\operatorname{sinh}⁡4x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{4x} & =16\operatorname{sinh}⁡4x \\ {u}^{′} & =16{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡4x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\operatorname{sinh}⁡4x=\frac{{e}^{4x}-{e}^{-4x}}{2}
$$

our equation for $u$ becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =16{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡4x \\  & =16{e}^{-4x}(\frac{{e}^{4x}-{e}^{-4x}}{2}) \\  & =8{e}^{-4x}({e}^{4x}-{e}^{-4x}) \\  & =8-8{e}^{-8x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =8-8{e}^{-8x} \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int 8-8{e}^{-8x}\,\text{d}x \\ u & =8x+{e}^{-8x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{4x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{4x} \\  & =8x{e}^{4x}+{e}^{-4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{2x-1}{2x-2})}^{x-1}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Notice that as $x\to \infty ,$ 

- the expression inside the parentheses approaches $1,$ while

- the exponent approaches $\infty .$

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{2x-1}{2x-2})}^{x-1}={1}^{\infty },
$$

which is an indeterminate form.

Instead, let's recall the following special limit:

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}=e
$$

We rewrite the given limit as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{2x-1}{2x-2})}^{x-1} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{(2x-2)+1}{2x-2})}^{x-1} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{2x-2})}^{x-1} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{2(x-1)})}^{x-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $2(x-1)=n$ Then, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}2(x-1) & =n \\ x-1 & =\frac{n}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $n\to \infty $ as $x\to \infty ,$ we rewrite the limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{2x-1}{2x-2})}^{x-1} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{2(x-1)})}^{x-1} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n/2} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{[{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{1/2} \\  & ={[{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{1/2} \\  & ={e}^{1/2} \\  & =\sqrt{e}\end{aligned}
$$

A piece of cardboard measures $15\,in\times 8\,in.$ A tray of height $y\,\text{in}$ is formed by cutting a $y\times y\,{\text{in}}^{2}$ square from each of the corners and folding up the sides, as shown in the diagram. Determine the height of the box that gives the maximum possible volume.
:question/worked-solution:
**Step 1**: We need to find the values of $x,y,$ and $z$ such that the volume

$$
V=xyz
$$

is the greatest possible value.

**Step 2**: Notice that the width $x$ and the depth $z$ of the tray are given by

$$
x=15-2y,\,z=8-2y.
$$

 

Since $x>0$ and $z>0,$ we must have that $15-2y>0$ and $8-2y>0$, hence $y<4.$ Therefore, the range of validity for $y$ is $0<y<4.$

**Step 3**: Substituting the above into the expression for $V,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =xyz \\  & =(15-2y)(y)(8-2y) \\  & =4{y}^{3}-46{y}^{2}+120y.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: We solve the equation ${V}^{′}(y)=0.$ Taking the first derivative, we have

$$
{V}^{′}(y)=12{y}^{2}-92y+120,
$$

and solving for the stationary points, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}^{′}(y) & =0 \\ 12{y}^{2}-92y+120 & =0 \\ 3{y}^{2}-23y+30 & =0 \\ (3y-5)(y-6) & =0 \\ y & =\frac{5}{3},\,6.\end{aligned}
$$

We discard $6$ since we already know that $0<y<4.$

**Step 5**: We confirm that $\frac{5}{3}$ is a maximum using the second derivative test. The second derivative is

$$
{V}^{″}(y)=24y-92.
$$

Since ${V}^{″}(\frac{5}{3})$ is negative, we conclude that $\frac{5}{3}$ is indeed a maximum of $V(y).$

Therefore, the stationary point $y=\frac{5}{3}$ gives the maximum possible volume.

:question/problem: A five gallons water bottle is leaking its content. The number of gallons of water left inside the bottle after $t$ minutes is given by the formula $W(t)=5\cdot {(\frac{1}{5})}^{t}.$ How many gallons of water will be inside the bottle after $3$ minutes?
:question/worked-solution:
To get the number of gallons of water inside the bottle after $3$ minutes, we evaluate the function at $t=3.$ Substituting $t=3$ into the function $W(t)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}W(3) & =5\cdot {(\frac{1}{5})}^{3} \\  & =5\cdot (\frac{{1}^{3}}{{5}^{3}}) \\  & =5\cdot \frac{1}{125} \\  & =\frac{5}{125} \\  & =0.04.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, after $3$ minutes, there will be $0.04$ gallons of water inside the bottle.

A farmer wants to fence a field that is made up of a rectangle and two semicircles, as shown in the diagram. He has only $200\,m$ of fencing. What is the length $2x$ of the side of the field that covers the greatest area?
:question/worked-solution:
First,  let $r$ the radius of the upper semicircle (top) and $x$ the radius of the lateral semicircle (right), hence the dimensions of the rectangle are $2r$ and $2x.$ We want to maximize the area

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =(2r)(2x)+\frac{\pi {r}^{2}}{2}+\frac{\pi {x}^{2}}{2} \\  & =4rx+\frac{\pi {r}^{2}}{2}+\frac{\pi {x}^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We know that the perimeter is fixed at $200$ units, so we also have the constraint condition

$$
200=\pi r+\pi x+2x+2r\,.
$$

Now, by making $x$ the subject of the constraint equation, we find that 

$$
\begin{aligned}200 & =\pi r+\pi x+2x+2r \\ x(\pi +2) & =200-r(\pi +2) \\ x & =\frac{200}{\pi +2}-r\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging the above into our expression for $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =4rx+\frac{\pi {r}^{2}}{2}+\frac{\pi {x}^{2}}{2} \\  & =4r(\frac{200}{\pi +2}-r)+\frac{\pi {r}^{2}}{2}+\frac{\pi }{2}{(\frac{200}{\pi +2}-r)}^{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to maximize $A,$ so we need to differentiate $A$ and set the derivative equal to zero. The derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(r) & =4(\frac{200}{\pi +2}-r)+4r(-1)+\pi r+\pi (\frac{200}{\pi +2}-r)(-1) \\  & =\frac{800}{\pi +2}-4r-4r+\pi r-\frac{200\pi }{\pi +2}+\pi r \\  & =-8r+2\pi r+\frac{800-200\pi }{\pi +2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting ${A}^{′}(r)=0$ and solving for $r$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(r) & =0 \\ -8r+2\pi r+\frac{800-200\pi }{\pi +2} & =0 \\ 2r(\pi -4) & =-\frac{800-200\pi }{\pi +2} \\ 2r(\pi -4) & =\frac{200\pi -800}{\pi +2} \\ r & =\frac{100\pi -400}{(\pi +2)(\pi -4)} \\ r & =\frac{100(\pi -4)}{(\pi +2)(\pi -4)} \\ r & =\frac{100}{\pi +2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we confirm that $r=\frac{100}{\pi +2}$ is a maximum using the second derivative test. The second derivative gives

$$
{A}^{″}(r)=-8+2\pi \,⟹\,{A}^{″}(\frac{100}{\pi +2})=-8+2\pi <0.
$$

Since ${A}^{″}(\frac{100}{\pi +2})$ is negative, we conclude that $r=\frac{100}{\pi +2}$ is indeed a maximum of $A(r).$

Finally, when $r=\frac{100}{\pi +2}$, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{200}{\pi +2}-\frac{100}{\pi +2} \\  & =\frac{100}{\pi +2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the length of the side of the field with the largest area is $2x=\frac{200}{\pi +2}.$
