Evaluate the line integral
${\int }_{C}2 x y^{6}\,\text{d}s,$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=\frac{1}{y}$ from $(1,1)$ to $(\frac{1}{2},2),$ as shown above.
:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $x=x(y),$ Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have

$$
x=x(t)=\frac{1}{t}.
$$

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨\frac{1}{t},\,t⟩,\,1\le t\le 2
$$

Note that the domain $1\le t\le 2$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =- \frac{1}{t^{2}}\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(- \frac{1}{t^{2}})^2+1^2} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{t^{4}}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{1 + \frac{1}{t^{4}}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=2 x y^{6},$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2 \left(\frac{1}{t}\right) t^{6} \\  & =2 t^{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}2 x y^{6}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\left(2 t^{5}\right)\cdot\left(\sqrt{1 + \frac{1}{t^{4}}}\right)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}2 t^{3} \sqrt{t^{4} + 1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve this using the substitution $u=t^{4} + 1,$ $\text{d}u=4 t^{3}\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}2 t^{3} \sqrt{t^{4} + 1}\,\text{d}t & =2{\int }_{2}^{17}\sqrt{u}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{17}\frac{\sqrt{u}}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\left[\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{2}{3}u^{3/2}\right]_{2}^{17} \\  & =\left[\frac{u^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right]_{2}^{17} \\  & =\left(\left(\frac{\left(17\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right)\right)-\left(\left(\frac{\left(2\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right)\right) \\  & =\left(\left(\frac{17 \sqrt{17}}{3}\right)\right)-\left(\left(\frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{3}\right)\right) \\  & =- \frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{3} + \frac{17 \sqrt{17}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral

where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=e^{\frac{y}{2}}$ from $(1,0)$ to $(\sqrt{2},\ln{\left(2 \right)}).$
:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $x=x(y),$ Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have

$$
x=x(t)=e^{\frac{t}{2}}.
$$

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨e^{\frac{t}{2}},\,t⟩,\,0\le t\le \ln{\left(2 \right)}
$$

Note that the domain $0\le t\le \ln{\left(2 \right)}$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(e^{\frac{t}{2}})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{e^{\frac{t}{2}}}{2}\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(\frac{e^{\frac{t}{2}}}{2})^2+1^2} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{e^{t}}{4}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{e^{t}}{4} + 1}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=2 x^{6} e^{- 2 y},$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2 \left(e^{\frac{t}{2}}\right)^{6} e^{- 2 t} \\  & =2 e^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}2 x^{6} e^{- 2 y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}\left(2 e^{t}\right)\cdot\left(\sqrt{\frac{e^{t}}{4} + 1}\right)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}\sqrt{e^{t} + 4} e^{t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve this using the substitution $u=e^{t} + 4,$ $\text{d}u=e^{t}\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}\sqrt{e^{t} + 4} e^{t}\,\text{d}t & =1{\int }_{5}^{6}\sqrt{u}\cdot\left(1\right)\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{5}^{6}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\left[1\cdot\frac{2}{3}u^{3/2}\right]_{5}^{6} \\  & =\left[\frac{2 u^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right]_{5}^{6} \\  & =\left(\left(\frac{2 \left(6\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right)\right)-\left(\left(\frac{2 \left(5\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right)\right) \\  & =\left(\left(4 \sqrt{6}\right)\right)-\left(\left(\frac{10 \sqrt{5}}{3}\right)\right) \\  & =- \frac{10 \sqrt{5}}{3} + 4 \sqrt{6}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral

where $C$ is the section of the curve $y^2=6x$ from $(\frac{7}{6},\sqrt{7})$ to $(\frac{8}{3},4).$
:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve can be expressed in the form $x=x(y),$ as follows:

$$
y^2=6x\,⟹\,x=\frac{y^{2}}{6}.
$$

Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have

$$
x=x(t)=\frac{t^{2}}{6}.
$$

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨\frac{t^{2}}{6},\,t⟩,\,\sqrt{7}\le t\le 4
$$

Note that the domain $\sqrt{7}\le t\le 4$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{t^{2}}{6})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{t}{3}\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(\frac{t}{3})^2+1^2} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{t^{2}}{9}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{t^{2}}{9} + 1}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=\frac{6 x}{y},$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{6 \left(\frac{t^{2}}{6}\right)}{t} \\  & =t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{6 x}{y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\sqrt{7}}^{4}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\sqrt{7}}^{4}\left(t\right)\cdot\left(\sqrt{\frac{t^{2}}{9} + 1}\right)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\sqrt{7}}^{4}\frac{t \sqrt{t^{2} + 9}}{3}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve this using the substitution $u=t^{2} + 9,$ $\text{d}u=2 t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\sqrt{7}}^{4}\frac{t \sqrt{t^{2} + 9}}{3}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{16}^{25}\sqrt{u}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{16}^{25}\frac{\sqrt{u}}{6}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\left[\frac{1}{6}\cdot\frac{2}{3}u^{3/2}\right]_{16}^{25} \\  & =\left[\frac{u^{\frac{3}{2}}}{9}\right]_{16}^{25} \\  & =\left(\left(\frac{\left(25\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{9}\right)\right)-\left(\left(\frac{\left(16\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{9}\right)\right) \\  & =\left(\left(\frac{125}{9}\right)\right)-\left(\left(\frac{64}{9}\right)\right) \\  & =\frac{61}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

x=x(t)=2 \sqrt{t}.
$$

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨2 \sqrt{t},\,t⟩,\,1\le t\le 5
$$

Note that the domain $1\le t\le 5$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2 \sqrt{t})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}})^2+1^2} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{t}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{1 + \frac{1}{t}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=8 x y,$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =8 \left(2 \sqrt{t}\right) t \\  & =16 t^{\frac{3}{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}8 x y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{5}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{5}\left(16 t^{\frac{3}{2}}\right)\cdot\left(\sqrt{1 + \frac{1}{t}}\right)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{5}16 t \sqrt{t + 1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve this using the substitution $u=4 t + 4,$ $\text{d}u=4\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{5}16 t \sqrt{t + 1}\,\text{d}t & =8{\int }_{8}^{24}\frac{u-4}{4}\cdot\sqrt{u}\cdot\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{8}^{24}\frac{u^{\frac{3}{2}}}{2} - 2 \sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\left[\frac{1}{2}\cdot\left(\frac{2}{5}u^{5/2}-(4)\cdot\frac{2}{3}u^{3/2}\right)\right]_{8}^{24} \\  & =\left[\frac{u^{\frac{5}{2}}}{5} - \frac{4 u^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right]_{8}^{24} \\  & =\left(\left(\frac{\left(24\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}}{5}\right)+\left(- \frac{4 \left(24\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right)\right)-\left(\left(\frac{\left(8\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}}{5}\right)+\left(- \frac{4 \left(8\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right)\right) \\  & =\left(\left(\frac{1152 \sqrt{6}}{5}\right)+\left(- 64 \sqrt{6}\right)\right)-\left(\left(\frac{128 \sqrt{2}}{5}\right)+\left(- \frac{64 \sqrt{2}}{3}\right)\right) \\  & =- \frac{64 \sqrt{2}}{15} + \frac{832 \sqrt{6}}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $X$ are shown above. Find the conditional expected value $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=1].$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]$ is a function of $x.$ 

The conditional density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3x+{y}^{2}}{8})}{(\frac{3x+1}{8})} \\  & =\frac{3(x+{y}^{2})}{3x+1},\end{aligned}
$$

 

where $0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$

Now, substituting $x=1$ into the expression for ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x),$ we get

$$
{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,1)=\frac{3(1+{y}^{2})}{3\cdot 1+1}=\frac{3(1+{y}^{2})}{4}.
$$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,1)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\cdot \frac{3(1+{y}^{2})}{4}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{\int }_{0}^{1}(y+{y}^{3})\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}[(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{4})-0] \\  & =\frac{9}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
For the function of two variables 
$f(x,y)=\sqrt{x+y+4},$
the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)=2+ax+\frac{1}{4}y-\frac{1}{64}{x}^{2}+bxy+c{y}^{2}.
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$
:question/worked-solution:
If the function $f(x,y)$ is twice differentiable at $(x,y)=(0,0),$ then the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈\overbrace{f(0,0)+{f}_{x}(0,0)\cdot x+{f}_{y}(0,0)\cdot y}^{\text{Linear approximation}} \\  & \,\,+\underbrace{\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(0,0)\cdot {x}^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(0,0)\cdot xy+{f}_{yy}(0,0)\cdot {y}^{2})}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial.

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y+4}}, & \,{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y+4}} \\ {f}_{x}(0,0) & =\frac{1}{4}, & \,{f}_{y}(0,0) & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y) & =-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{(x+y+4)^{3}}}, & \,{f}_{xx}(0,0) & =-\frac{1}{32} \\ {f}_{xy}(x,y) & =-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{(x+y+4)^{3}}}, & \,{f}_{xy}(0,0) & =-\frac{1}{32} \\ {f}_{yy}(x,y) & =-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{(x+y+4)^{3}}}, & \,{f}_{yy}(0,0) & =-\frac{1}{32}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈2+\frac{1}{4}\cdot x+\frac{1}{4}\cdot y+\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{1}{32}\cdot {x}^{2}+2(-\frac{1}{32})\cdot xy+(-\frac{1}{32})\cdot {y}^{2}) \\  & =2+\frac{1}{4}x+\frac{1}{4}y-\frac{1}{64}{x}^{2}+(-\frac{1}{32})xy+(-\frac{1}{64}){y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=\frac{1}{4}+(-\frac{1}{32})+(-\frac{1}{64})=\frac{13}{64}.
$$

:question/problem: The slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\sqrt{4x+1}$ at the point where $x=0$ is{{field-1}}.
:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=4x+1.$ Then $y=\sqrt{u}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}},
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot 4 \\  & =\frac{4}{2\sqrt{4x+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=0} & ={(\frac{4}{2\sqrt{4x+1}})|}_{x=0} \\  & =\frac{4}{2\sqrt{4(0)+1}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=- x - 3 y$ along the curve $C$ parametrized by $r(t)=⟨\frac{16 t^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3},\,2 t^{2} - 4 t⟩$ for $t\in [0,2].$
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\text{d}s=\int_a^b f(r(t))\,\|r^{\prime}(t)\|\,\text{d}t.
$$

Since $r(t)=⟨\frac{16 t^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3},\,2 t^{2} - 4 t⟩,$ then along the curve we have $x=\frac{16 t^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}$ and $y=2 t^{2} - 4 t.$

\begin{aligned}\int_C - \frac{3}{- x + y}\,\text{d}s&=\int_{-2}^{2}f(r(t))\|r^{\prime}(t)\|\,\text{d}t \\ &=\int_{-2}^{2}(- \frac{1}{2})\cdot (3 \sqrt{2})\,\text{d}t \\ &=(3 \sqrt{2})\int_{-2}^{2}- \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}t \\ &=\int_{-2}^{2}- \frac{3 \sqrt{2}}{2}\,\text{d}t \\ &=(- \frac{3 \sqrt{2}}{2})\left[t\right]_{-2}^{2} \\ &=\left[(- \frac{3 \sqrt{2} t}{2})\right]_{-2}^{2} \\ &=\left((- \frac{3 \sqrt{2} (2)}{2})\right)-\left((- \frac{3 \sqrt{2} (-2)}{2})\right) \\ &=\left((- 3 \sqrt{2})\right)-\left((3 \sqrt{2})\right) \\ &=- 6 \sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=x^{2} + y^{2} - 2$ along the curve $C$ parametrized by $r(t)=⟨2 t \sin{\left(t \right)} + 2 \cos{\left(t \right)},\,- 2 t \cos{\left(t \right)} + 2 \sin{\left(t \right)}⟩$ for $t\in [0,\pi].$
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\text{d}s=\int_a^b f(r(t))\,\|r^{\prime}(t)\|\,\text{d}t.
$$

Since $r(t)=⟨2 t \sin{\left(t \right)} + 2 \cos{\left(t \right)},\,- 2 t \cos{\left(t \right)} + 2 \sin{\left(t \right)}⟩,$ then along the curve we have $x=2 t \sin{\left(t \right)} + 2 \cos{\left(t \right)}$ and $y=- 2 t \cos{\left(t \right)} + 2 \sin{\left(t \right)}.$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t)$ and $\|r^{\prime}(t)\|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t)&=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}j \\ &=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2 t \sin{\left(t \right)} + 2 \cos{\left(t \right)})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(- 2 t \cos{\left(t \right)} + 2 \sin{\left(t \right)})j \\ &=(2)(-\sin t+\sin t+t\cos t)i+(2)(\cos t-\cos t+t\sin t)j \\ &=(2 t \cos{\left(t \right)})i+(2 t \sin{\left(t \right)})j \\ \|r^{\prime}(t)\|&=\sqrt{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})^2+(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})^2} \\ &=\sqrt{(2 t \cos{\left(t \right)})^2+(2 t \sin{\left(t \right)})^2} \\ &=\sqrt{4t^2(\cos^2t+\sin^2t)} \\ &=2|t| \\ &=2 t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $|t|=t$ since $t\geq0$ along the path of $C.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=x^{2} + y^{2} - 2$, then we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t))&=(1)\left((2 t \sin{\left(t \right)} + 2 \cos{\left(t \right)})^2+(- 2 t \cos{\left(t \right)} + 2 \sin{\left(t \right)})^2\right)+(-2) \\ &=(4)\left(\cos^2t+2t\sin t\cos t+t^2\sin^2t+\sin^2t-2t\sin t\cos t+t^2\cos^2t\right)+(-2) \\ &=(4)(1+t^2)+(-2) \\ &=4 t^{2} + 2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C x^{2} + y^{2} - 2\,\text{d}s&=\int_{0}^{\pi}f(r(t))\|r^{\prime}(t)\|\,\text{d}t \\ &=\int_{0}^{\pi}(4 t^{2} + 2)\cdot (2 t)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\int_{0}^{\pi}8 t^{3} + 4 t\,\text{d}t \\ &=\left[(2 t^{2})+(2 t^{4})\right]_{0}^{\pi} \\ &=\left((2 (\pi)^{2})+(2 (\pi)^{4})\right)-\left((2 (0)^{2})+(2 (0)^{4})\right) \\ &=\left((2 \pi^{2})+(2 \pi^{4})\right)-\left((0)+(0)\right) \\ &=2 \pi^{2} \left(1 + \pi^{2}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Find the general nonzero real solution to the differential equation

$$
(x-6)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y={(x-6)}^{2}{y}^{3/4}.
$$

Work on an interval where $x-6>0$. Choose constants and intervals on which all displayed real expressions are defined. Take $y>0$.

{{selection}}
:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-6)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y={(x-6)}^{2}{y}^{3/4} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{y}{(x-6)} & =(x-6){y}^{3/4}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)={(x-6)}^{-1},\,q(x)=(x-6),\,n=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

Now, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{3/4},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-3/4}\frac{dy}{dx}+{(x-6)}^{-1}{y}^{1/4}=(x-6).\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{1/4}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4}{y}^{-3/4}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-3/4}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=4\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
4\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+{(x-6)}^{-1}z=(x-6)
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{4}{(x-6)}^{-1}z=\frac{(x-6)}{4}
$$

The above equation is now in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x),
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{1}{4\cdot (x-6)},\,Q(x)=\frac{(x-6)}{4}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (\frac{1}{4\cdot (x-6)})\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{(1/4)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-6)} \\  & ={(x-6)}^{1/4}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={(x-6)}^{1/4}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x-6)}^{1/4}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{4}{(x-6)}^{-1}z) & ={(x-6)}^{1/4}\cdot (\frac{(x-6)}{4}) \\ {(x-6)}^{1/4}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{4}{(x-6)}^{-3/4}z & =\frac{{(x-6)}^{5/4}}{4} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{(x-6)}^{1/4}) & =\frac{{(x-6)}^{5/4}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{(x-6)}^{1/4})\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{{(x-6)}^{5/4}}{4}\,\text{d}x \\ z{(x-6)}^{1/4} & =\frac{1}{9}{(x-6)}^{9/4}+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{{(x-6)}^{9/4}+C}{9{(x-6)}^{1/4}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=9{C}_{1}.$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{1/4}.$ This results in

$$
{y}^{1/4}=\frac{{(x-6)}^{9/4}+C}{9{(x-6)}^{1/4}}\,⇒\,y={(\frac{{(x-6)}^{9/4}+C}{9{(x-6)}^{1/4}})}^{4}\,.
$$

These are the nonzero real solutions on the specified intervals; exclude denominator zeros and restrict constants and intervals to the real branches used above. Since $z=y^{1/4}>0$, retain only intervals where the displayed expression for $z$ is positive.

![](images/19/197557b866b4a4a1c2c151c29cc529e12a5048b941223fe8e2eb4a7c4959223e.png)

The diagonals of a square increase in length at a rate of $1.5\text{ mm/min}.$ At what rate is the area of the square changing when the diagonals are $4\,\text{mm}$ long?
:question/worked-solution:
Let $A$ be the area of the square, and $h$ be the length of the diagonal. The relationship between $A$ and $h$ is

$$
A=\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot h.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that each diagonal of the square is increasing at a rate of $1.5\,\text{mm/min},$ so we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}=1.5.
$$

Also, when the diagonals are $4\,\text{mm},$ we have $h=4.$ Substituting this information into the above expression for $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=1.5\cdot 4=6{\text{ mm}}^{2}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the square increases at $6\,{\text{mm}}^{2}/\text{min}.$

:question/problem:
![](images/89/8946fc7f3b9a087304d893d69196f8462913974aab552b05a442a7460a619bef.png)

Water leaking onto a floor forms a circular pool. The radius of the pool increases at a rate of $6\,\text{cm/min}.$ How fast is the area of the pool increasing at the moment when the radius is $\frac{2}{\pi }\,\text{cm}?$
:question/worked-solution:
In this situation, we want to find $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$ at the moment when $r=\frac{2}{\pi },$ and we are also told that  $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=6.$

To start, let's write down the area formula for the circle and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\pi {r}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\pi r.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=6$ and $r=\frac{2}{\pi },$ and solve for $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =6\cdot 2\pi (\frac{2}{\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the area of the pool is increasing at a rate of $24{\text{ cm}}^{2}\text{/min}.$

:question/problem: Rewrite $-8{z}^{2}-12z-\frac{7}{2}$ by completing the square.
:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the leading coefficient is $-8$. So, we take out a factor of $-8$ from the entire expression:

$$
-8({z}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}z+\frac{7}{16})
$$

Let's now complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
{z}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}z+\frac{7}{16}
$$

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with $2$ as a factor:

$$
{z}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{3}{4}\cdot z+\frac{7}{16}
$$

Then, we *add* and *then subtract* ${(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}$, writing the constant term $\frac{7}{16}$ last:

$$
\underbrace{{z}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{3}{4}\cdot z+{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}}-{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}+\frac{7}{16}
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
{(z+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}+\frac{7}{16}
$$

Evaluating the last two terms, we get

$$
{(z+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-\frac{1}{8}.
$$

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}-8({z}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}z+\frac{7}{16}) & =-8({(z+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-\frac{1}{8}) \\  & =-8{(z+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}+(-8)\cdot (-\frac{1}{8}) \\  & =-8{(z+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}+1\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\operatorname{cot}⁡{20}^{∘}=\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{9})$

II. $\operatorname{cot}⁡{50}^{∘}=\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{18})$

III. $\operatorname{cot}⁡{80}^{∘}=\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{9})$
:question/worked-solution:
Let's examine the statements one by one.

- Statement I is true. Converting ${20}^{∘}$ from degrees to radians, we get 

$$
{20}^{∘}=20\cdot \frac{\pi }{180}=\frac{\pi }{9}\,\text{radians}.
$$

- Statement II is true. Converting ${50}^{∘}$ from degrees to radians, we get 

$$
{50}^{∘}=50\cdot \frac{\pi }{180}=\frac{5\pi }{18}\,\text{radians}.
$$

- Statement III is false. Converting ${80}^{∘}$ from degrees to radians, we get 

$$
{80}^{∘}=80\cdot \frac{\pi }{180}=\frac{4\pi }{9}\,\text{radians}.
$$

The statement is false because $\frac{4\pi }{9}\ne \frac{2\pi }{9}.$

So, the correct answer is 'I and II only'.

A laser technician is reducing the diagonals of a square aperture at a rate of $2.4\text{ mm}\text{/s}.$ At what rate is the area of the aperture decreasing when the diagonals are $12.5\,\text{mm}$ long each?

*Hint*: Assume that the rate of decrease is positive.

The area is decreasing at a rate of
{{field-1}} ${\text{mm}}^{2}\text{/s}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Let $h$ and $A$ be the length of the diagonals and the area of the square, respectively. Using the Pythagorean theorem, it can be shown that the relationship between $A$ and $h$ is

$$
A=\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}.
$$

We want to find

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot h.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $h$ decreases at a rate of $2.4\,\text{mm/s},$ so

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-2.4.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we want to compute the rate of change of the area when the diagonal has length $h=12.5.$ Substituting this information into our expression for $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t},$ we get

$$

$$

We conclude that the area of the square aperture is decreasing at a rate of $30{\text{ mm}}^{2}\text{/s}.$

:question/problem:
A spotlight $S$ is on the ground $6\,\text{m}$ away from a wall and a $1.5\,\text{m}$ tall robot is moving towards the wall at a rate of $0.6\,\text{m/s}.$ To **one decimal place**, how fast is the height of the shadow on the wall decreasing when the robot is $2.5\,\text{m}$ from the spotlight?

The shadow decreases at a speed of approximately 

{{field-1}} $\text{m/s}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Let's draw a figure according to the given data.

![](images/e9/e91c4e08aa785de1fe500c2f43e0981501ee597bb7bb042827154842ec06ad0c.png)

In the figure, $x$ is the robot’s distance from the wall, while $y$ is the length of the shadow. Both $x$ and $y$ change with time. In particular, we know that the robot’s velocity is

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-0.6\,\text{m/s}.
$$

Notice that the robot’s velocity is *negative* because it is moving *toward* the wall, and therefore the distance between it and the wall *decreases* with time.

Since we want to calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we need to find a relation between $x$ and $y.$ Since the two triangles are similar, the ratios between the corresponding sides are equal, and we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{(6-x)+x} & =\frac{1.5}{6-x} \\ \frac{y}{6} & =\frac{1.5}{6-x} \\ y & =\frac{9}{6-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We differentiate both sides with respect to $t$ using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{9}{6-x}) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{9}{(6-x)^{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=6-2.5=3.5\,\text{m}$ and $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-0.6\,\text{m/s}$ into the above expression gives, to one decimal place

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{9}{{2.5}^{2}}\cdot (-0.6) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & ≈-0.9\,\text{m/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the shadow decreases at a speed of approximately  $0.9\,\text{m/s}.$

Let $r$ be the radius of the hailstone, $V$ the volume, and $A$ its surface area. We wish to find $r$ at the moment when

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=3\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the volume $V$ and the surface area $A$ of the sphere. Since $A=4\pi {r}^{2}$ and $V=\frac{4\pi }{3}{r}^{3},$ the relationship between $V$ and $A$ is

$$
V=\frac{4\pi }{3}{r}^{3}=\frac{4\pi }{3}{(\frac{A}{4\pi })}^{3/2}=\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{3(4\pi )^{1/2}}=\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}A}(\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{{A}^{1/2}}{4\sqrt{\pi }}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=3\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}3\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{{A}^{1/2}}{4\sqrt{\pi }} \\ {A}^{1/2} & =12\sqrt{\pi } \\ A & =(12\sqrt{\pi })^{2} \\ A & =144\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, since $A=4\pi {r}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4\pi {r}^{2} & =144\pi  \\ {r}^{2} & =36 \\ r & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/34/34a41e39a36d3e073ef2ca4144bd346b340efa22a9da7d3e8a9df48d32d900b3.png)

A square opening in a testing chamber is being reduced, causing the area of the opening to decrease at a rate of $49{\text{ mm}}^{2}\text{/s}.$ At what rate are the diagonals decreasing when each diagonal measures $35\,\text{mm}?$

*Hint*: Assume that the rate of decrease is positive.

The diagonal is decreasing at a rate of
{{field-1}} $\text{mm/s}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Let $A$ be the area of the square opening, and $h$ be the length of its diagonal. The relationship between $A$ and $h$ is

$$
A=\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}.
$$

We want to find

$$
\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.
$$

Differentiating the relationship between $A$ and $h$ with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot h \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{h}\cdot \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the area of the square is decreasing at a rate of $49{\text{ mm}}^{2}\text{/s},$ so

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=-49.
$$

Also, we want to compute the rate of change of the diagonals when the diagonal has length $h=35.$ Substituting this information into our expression for $\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{35}\cdot (-49) \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{49}{35} \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-1.4\text{ mm/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the diagonal of the opening is decreasing at a rate of 
$1.4\text{ mm/s}.$

:question/problem:
A bright lantern $L$ is on the ground $18\,\text{ft}$ away from a wall and a $6\,\text{ft}$ tall actor is moving towards the wall at a rate of $3\,\text{ft/s}.$ To **one decimal place**, how fast is the height of the shadow on the wall decreasing when the actor is $8\,\text{ft}$ from the lantern?

The shadow decreases at a speed of approximately 

{{field-1}} $\text{ft/s}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Let's draw a figure according to the given data.

![](images/0a/0a47e801db651c027415a7943e5327bd378c1a08e533dc69673ab4304c8cc7b4.png)

In the figure, $x$ is the actor’s distance from the wall, while $y$ is the length of the shadow. Both $x$ and $y$ change with time. In particular, we know that the actor’s velocity is

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-3\,\text{ft/s}.
$$

Notice that the actor’s velocity is *negative* because it is moving *toward* the wall, and therefore the distance between it and the wall *decreases* with time.

Since we want to calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we need to find a relation between $x$ and $y.$ Since the two triangles are similar, the ratios between the corresponding sides are equal, and we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{(18-x)+x} & =\frac{6}{18-x} \\ \frac{y}{18} & =\frac{6}{18-x} \\ y & =\frac{108}{18-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We differentiate both sides with respect to $t$ using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{108}{18-x}) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{108}{(18-x)^{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=18-8=10\,\text{ft}$ and $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-3\,\text{ft/s}$ into the above expression gives, to one decimal place

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{108}{{8}^{2}}\cdot (-3) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & ≈-5.1\,\text{ft/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the shadow decreases at a speed of approximately  $5.1\,\text{ft/s}.$

:question/problem: Suppose that $f(x)=\frac{x}{8}$ and $g(x)=kx.$ If $g$ is the inverse of $f,$ then $k=$
:question/worked-solution:
If $g$ is the inverse of $f,$ then we must have:

$$
g(f(x))=x
$$

To find $g(f(x)),$ we write down the function $g$ and replace every occurrence of $x$ with $f(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(x) & =kx \\ g(f(x)) & =kf(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $f(x)=\frac{x}{8}$ into the right-hand side of our expression and simplify, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(f(x)) & =kf(x) \\  & =k(\frac{x}{8}) \\  & =\frac{k}{8}x\end{aligned}
$$

However, we also know that $g(f(x))=x.$ Equating the expression above with $x$ and solving for $k$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{k}{8}x & =x \\ \frac{k}{8}\cancel{x} & =\cancel{x} \\ \frac{k}{8} & =1 \\ k & =8\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/8b/8b4196d82bf27236e6c28651a01678c60c41bc851afbb7aad2e754578ba330e9.png)

Jacob is a carpenter. He wishes to reduce the size of a wooden square while maintaining its shape. The lengths of the diagonals of the square decrease at a rate of $2\text{ cm}\text{/h}.$ At what rate, in squared centimeters per hour, is the area of ​​the square decreasing when the length of the diagonal is $45\,\text{cm}?$
:question/worked-solution:
Let $h$ and $A$ be the length of the diagonals and the area of the square, respectively. Using the Pythagorean theorem, it can be shown that the relationship between $A$ and $h$ is

$$
A=\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}.
$$

We want to find

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot h.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $h$ decreases at a rate of $2\,\text{cm/h},$ so

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we want to compute the rate of change of the area when the diagonal has length $h=45.$ Substituting this information into our expression for $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-2\cdot 45=-90\,{\text{cm}}^{2}\text{/h}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the area of the square is decreasing at a rate of $90\,{\text{cm}}^{2}\text{/h}.$

:question/problem:
![](images/bc/bc7e248783ccf6b1eda95a1c2c80300e48d8cdb48f39ea07296ed3bf51bfaa29.png)

A small, circular puddle evaporates on a floor. If the puddle’s area is decreasing at a rate of $32\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{2}/\text{min},$ calculate the rate of change of its circumference at the moment when the radius is $8\,\text{cm}.$ Do not round the answer.

The circumference of the puddle is decreasing at a rate of 
{{field-1}} $\text{cm}/\text{min}.$
:question/worked-solution:
In this situation, we want to find $\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}$ at the moment when $r=8,$ and we are also told that  $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=-32\pi .$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the area $A$ and the circumference $C$ of the circle. Since $C=2\pi r$ and $A=\pi {r}^{2},$ the relationship between $A$ and $C$ is

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}=\pi {(\frac{C}{2\pi })}^{2}=\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}C}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{C}{2\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

When $r=8\,\text{cm},$ $C=2\pi (8)=16\pi \text{ cm}.$ Hence, substituting $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=-32\pi $ and $C=16\pi ,$ and solving for $\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-32\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{16\pi }{2\pi } \\ -32\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot 8 \\ \frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t} & =-4\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the circumference is decreasing at a rate of $4\pi \text{ cm}\text{/min}.$

:question/problem: Rewrite $-2{x}^{2}-6x+4$ by completing the square.
:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the leading coefficient is $-2$. So, we take out a factor of $-2$ from the entire expression:

$$
-2({x}^{2}+3x-2)
$$

Let's now complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
{x}^{2}+3x-2
$$

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with $2$ as a factor:

$$
{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{3}{2}x-2
$$

Then, we *add* and *then subtract* ${(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}$, writing the constant term $2$ last:

$$
\underbrace{{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{3}{2}x+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}}-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-2
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
{(x+\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-2
$$

Evaluating the last two terms, we get

$$
{(x+\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-\frac{17}{4}
$$

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2({x}^{2}+3x-2) & =-2({(x+\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-\frac{17}{4}) \\  & =-2{(x+\frac{3}{2})}^{2}+(-2)\cdot (-\frac{17}{4}) \\  & =-2{(x+\frac{3}{2})}^{2}+\frac{17}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given the function $f(x,y)=- 5 x^{2} + 5 x y^{2} + 2 y^{2}$, find the equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(- \frac{3}{2},\frac{5}{2}).$
:question/worked-solution:
The equation of the tangent line to the level curve $f(x,y)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(- \frac{3}{2},\frac{5}{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(- 5 x^{2} + 5 x y^{2} + 2 y^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(- 5 x^{2} + 5 x y^{2} + 2 y^{2})\,j \\  & =(- 10 x + 5 y^{2})\,i+(10 x y + 4 y)\,j \\ ∇f(- \frac{3}{2},\frac{5}{2}) & =(- 10 (- \frac{3}{2}) + 5 (\frac{5}{2})^{2})\,i+(10 (- \frac{3}{2}) (\frac{5}{2}) + 4 (\frac{5}{2}))\,j \\  & =(\frac{185}{4})\,i+(- \frac{55}{2})\,j \\  & =⟨\frac{185}{4},- \frac{55}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the Cartesian equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(- \frac{3}{2},\frac{5}{2})\cdot ⟨x-(- \frac{3}{2}),\,y-(\frac{5}{2})⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨\frac{185}{4},- \frac{55}{2}⟩\cdot ⟨x + \frac{3}{2},\,y - \frac{5}{2}⟩ & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

${\text{in}}^{2}/\text{s}.$

Let $x,y,z$ be the dimensions of the solid, and let $S$ be its surface area. We are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =12\,\text{in}, \\ y & =7\,\text{in}, \\ z & =5\,\text{in}, \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =3\,\text{in}\text{/s}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =2\,\text{in}\text{/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t}.$

We want to find the rate of change of $S$ knowing the rate of change of $x$ and $y.$ So, we start with the formula for the surface area of the rectangular prism:

$$
S=2xz+2xy+2yz
$$

Since $z=5\,\text{in}$ is not changing, we get

$$
S=10x+2xy+10y.
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(10x+2xy+10y) \\ \frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =(10+2x)(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})+(10+2y)(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}).\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug in the known values into the above expression. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =(10+2\cdot 12)(2)+(10+2\cdot 7)(3) \\  & =(34)(2)+(24)(3) \\  & =68+72 \\  & =140\,{\text{in}}^{2}\text{/s}.\end{aligned}

Therefore, the surface area of the rectangular prism is increasing at a rate of $140\,{\text{in}}^{2}/\text{s}.$

A rectangular block of ice is melting in a narrow channel that keeps its length fixed at $12\,\text{in}.$ Its width is decreasing by $1\,\text{in}\text{/h},$ while its height is decreasing by $0.4\,\text{in}\text{/h}.$ How fast is its volume decreasing when its dimensions are $5\,\text{in}$ in width and $4\,\text{in}$ in height? Assume that the volume's rate of decrease is positive.

The volume is decreasing at a rate of
{{field-1}}
${\text{in}}^{3}/\text{h}.$
:question/worked-solution:
We define the following variables:

- let $L,$ $W,$ and $H$ be the length, width, and height of the ice block, respectively, and

- let $V$ be the volume of the ice block.

Note that $H,$ $W,$ and $V$ change with time, while $L$ is constant. 

We are given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L=12\text{ in},\, & W=5\text{ in}, \\ H=4\text{ in},\, & \frac{\text{d}W}{\text{d}t}=-1\text{ in/h}, \\ \frac{\text{d}H}{\text{d}t}=-0.4\text{ in/h}\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.$

The relation between the three time-dependent variables, $V,$ $W$ and $H,$ is given by the formula for the volume of ice block:

$$
V=LWH
$$

We differentiate both sides of $V=LWH$ with respect to $t,$ treating $L$ as a constant, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}V & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(LWH) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =L\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(WH) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =L[W(\frac{\text{d}H}{\text{d}t})+H(\frac{\text{d}W}{\text{d}t})] \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =L\cdot W(\frac{\text{d}H}{\text{d}t})+L\cdot H(\frac{\text{d}W}{\text{d}t}).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can plug in the known values and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =(12)(5)(-0.4)+(12)(4)(-1) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =-24+(-48) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =-72.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of ice is decreasing at a rate of $72\,{\text{in}}^{3}\text{/h}.$

$$

$$

Also, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-0.5\text{ feet}\text{/min}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =1\text{ feet}\text{/min}, \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =-10{\text{ feet}}^{3}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}$ when $x=2\,\text{feet},$ $y=1\,\text{feet},$ and $z=3\,\text{feet}.$

We start with the formula for the volume of the rectangular prism:

$$
V=xyz
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x\cdot y\cdot z) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =xy(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})+xz(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})+yz(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\end{aligned}

:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the polynomial $f(x)=4{x}^{2}-25?$

I. $x=\frac{5}{2}$ is a root of $f(x)$

II. $(2x-5)$ is a factor of $f(x)$

III. $(2x-5)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder
:question/worked-solution:
The factor theorem states that $(ax-b)$ is a factor of the polynomial $p(x)$ if and only if the root $x=\frac{b}{a}$ is also root of $p(x).$ 

Here, we are considering $(2x-5).$ The root of this expression can be found by setting the expression equal to $0$ and solving:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-5 & =0 \\ 2x & =5 \\ x & =\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now check each of the statements, in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, $x=\frac{5}{2}$ is a root of $f(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{5}{2}) & =4{(\frac{5}{2})}^{2}-25 \\  & =4(\frac{25}{4})-25 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. According to the factor theorem, since $x=\frac{5}{2}$ is a root of $f(x),$ then $(2x-5)$ is a factor of $f(x).$

- Statement III is true. Since $(2x-5)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ then $(2x-5)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

:question/problem: $2\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{{e}^{4}})=$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we rewrite $\frac{1}{{e}^{4}}$ as a power of $e$ (the base of the natural logarithm) as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{{e}^{4}}={e}^{-4}
$$

Therefore, we have:

$$
2\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{{e}^{4}})=2\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-4})
$$

The natural logarithm reverses the action of the exponent. The principle is:

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x})=x
$$

In our case, we have $x=-4.$ Therefore:

$$
2\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-4})=2\cdot (-4)=-8
$$

$$

$$
S=2xz+2xy+2yz
$$

Since $z=6\,\text{cm}$ is not changing, we get

$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$

:question/problem:
Consider the finite region $R$ in the $xyz$-space, given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,1\le x\le 2,\,\frac{1}{x}\le y\le \frac{2}{x},\,\frac{1}{xy}\le z\le \frac{2}{xy}\}.
$$

By performing the change of variables

$$
u=x,\,v=xy,\,w=xyz,
$$

the triple integral

$$
{∭}_{R}\,{e}^{xyz}\,dV
$$

can be written in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w$ as
:question/worked-solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To find the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$ 

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=x,\,v=xy,\,w=xyz
$$

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is 

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y,z) \\ v(x,y,z) \\ w(x,y,z)\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the required integral, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v,w)\,:\,1\le u\le 2,\,1\le v\le 2,\,1\le w\le 2\}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ y & x & 0 \\ yz & xz & xy\end{aligned}| \\  & =xy|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ y & x\end{aligned}| \\  & =xy(x-0) \\  & ={x}^{2}y \\  & =uv\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}=\frac{1}{uv}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{e}^{xyz}\,dV & ={∭}_{Δ}{e}^{w}\cdot |\frac{1}{uv}|\,\,dw\,dv\,du \\  & ={∭}_{Δ}\frac{{e}^{w}}{uv}\,\,dw\,dv\,du \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{{e}^{w}}{uv}\,dw\,dv\,du\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate the gamma function at multiples of one-half, we use the following recursive formula:

$$
Γ(z+1)=zΓ(z),\,Γ(\frac{1}{2})=\sqrt{\pi }
$$

So, we have the following:

$$
Γ(\frac{3}{2})=\frac{1}{2}Γ(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\pi },
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ(\frac{7}{2}) & =\frac{5}{2}\,Γ(\frac{5}{2}) \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{3}{2}\,Γ(\frac{3}{2}) \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\pi } \\  & =\frac{15}{8}\sqrt{\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{4}{\sqrt{\pi }}\,Γ(\frac{7}{2})+\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi }}\,Γ(\frac{3}{2})=\frac{4}{\sqrt{\pi }}\cdot \frac{15}{8}\sqrt{\pi }+\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi }}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\pi }=8.
$$

Since $f(x)$ is $\text{continuous}$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ the corresponding Fourier series converges to 

$$
f(\frac{\pi }{2})=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

 

Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =2{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}) \\ \frac{\pi }{2} & =2{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2n-1}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡((2n-1)\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})-2{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2n}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(2n\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}) \\ \frac{\pi }{2} & =2{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2n-1}\cdot (-1)^{n+1}-2{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2n}\cdot 0 \\ \frac{\pi }{4} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{2n-1} \\ {\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{2n-1} & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/00/0060643c716e8f9c6d0420c419ba1d6efd7c3dc986279feb4ceae9f860dfb313.png)

The length of the rectangular prism shown above is increasing, while the $4\,\text{in}$ width and the $6\,\text{in}$ height don't change. What is the rate of change of the length of the rectangular prism if the volume is increasing at a rate of $72\,{\text{in}}^{3}/\text{min}?$
:question/worked-solution:
Let $x,y,z$ be the dimensions of the rectangular prism, let $V$ be its volume. We are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =4\,\text{in}, \\ z & =6\,\text{in}.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=72\,{\text{in}}^{3}/\text{min}.
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}$ when $y=4\,\text{in}$ and $z=6\,\text{in}.$

We start with the formula for the volume of the rectangular prism:

$$
V=xyz
$$

Substituting the known values, we get

$$
V=x(4)(6)=24x.
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(24x) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =24(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}).\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug in the known value into the above expression. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}72 & =24(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =3\,\text{in}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the length of the rectangular prism is increasing at a rate of $3\,\text{in}/\text{min}.$

$$
Γ(\frac{5}{2})=\frac{3}{2}Γ(\frac{3}{2})=\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}Γ(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\pi }=\frac{3}{4}\sqrt{\pi },

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ(\frac{7}{2})=\frac{5}{2}Γ(\frac{5}{2})=\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{3}{4}\sqrt{\pi }=\frac{15}{8}\sqrt{\pi }\end{aligned}

Therefore,

:question/problem: $-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{{e}^{5}})=$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we rewrite $\frac{1}{{e}^{5}}$ as a power of $e$ (the base of the natural logarithm) as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{{e}^{5}}={e}^{-5}
$$

Therefore, we have:

$$
-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{{e}^{5}})=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-5})
$$

The natural logarithm reverses the action of the exponent. The principle is:

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x})=x
$$

In our case, we have $x=-5.$ Therefore:

$$
-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-5})=-\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-5)=\frac{5}{2}
$$

:question/problem:
Use the change of variables 

$$
u=2x+y,\,v=3x+2z,\,w=z
$$

to evaluate the triple integral

$$
{∭}_{R}\frac{12}{1+(3x+2z)^{2}}\,dV,
$$

where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,\frac{1}{\pi }\le 2x+y\le \frac{2}{\pi },\,\,0\le 3x+2z\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 2\}.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=2x+y,\,v=3x+2z,\,w=z
$$

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y,z) \\ v(x,y,z) \\ w(x,y,z)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v,w)\,:\,\frac{1}{\pi }\le u\le \frac{2}{\pi },\,0\le v\le 1,\,0\le w\le 2\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =1(-1)^{3+3}|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =0-3 \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{3}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\frac{12}{1+(3x+2z)^{2}}\,dV & ={∭}_{Δ}\frac{12}{1+{v}^{2}}\cdot |-\frac{1}{3}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & ={∭}_{Δ}\frac{4}{(1+{v}^{2})}\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & ={\int }_{1/\pi }^{2/\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{4}{(1+{v}^{2})}\,dw\,dv\,du \\  & ={\int }_{1/\pi }^{2/\pi }\,du\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{4}{(1+{v}^{2})}\,dv\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}dw \\  & =[u]_{1/\pi }^{2/\pi }\cdot {[4\operatorname{arctan}⁡v]}_{v=0}^{v=1}\cdot [w]_{w=0}^{w=2} \\  & =(\frac{2}{\pi }-\frac{1}{\pi })\cdot (4\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}-0)\cdot (2-0) \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
For which of the following polynomials is $(5x+4)$ a factor?

I. $f(x)=5{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}$

II. $g(x)=15{x}^{2}+25x+4$

III. $h(x)=4{x}^{3}+5{x}^{2}$
:question/worked-solution:
According to the factor theorem, $(ax-b)$ is a factor of the polynomial $p(x)$ if and only if the root $x=\frac{b}{a}$ is also root of $p(x).$ 

Here, we are considering $(5x+4).$ The root of this expression can be found by setting the expression equal to $0$ and solving:

$$
\begin{aligned}5x+4 & =0 \\ 5x & =-4 \\ x & =-\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

According to the factor theorem, then, $(5x+4)$ is a factor of $p(x)$ if $x=-\frac{4}{5}$ is a root of $p(x).$

Now we will check if $x=-\frac{4}{5}$ is a root of the polynomials $f,$ $g$ and $h.$

- Evaluating $x=-\frac{4}{5}$ at $f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-\frac{4}{5}) & =5{(-\frac{4}{5})}^{3}+4{(-\frac{4}{5})}^{2} \\  & =5(-\frac{64}{125})+4(\frac{16}{25}) \\  & =-\frac{64}{25}+\frac{64}{25} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, by the factor theorem, we conclude that $(5x+4)$ is indeed a factor of $f(x).$

- Now, evaluating $x=-\frac{4}{5}$ at $g(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-\frac{4}{5}) & =15{(-\frac{4}{5})}^{2}+25(-\frac{4}{5})+4 \\  & =15(\frac{16}{25})-20+4 \\  & =\frac{48}{5}-16 \\  & =-\frac{32}{5}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, by the factor theorem, $(5x+4)$ is not a factor of $g(x).$

- Finally, evaluating $x=-\frac{4}{5}$ at $h(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}h(-\frac{4}{5}) & =4{(-\frac{4}{5})}^{3}+5{(-\frac{4}{5})}^{2} \\  & =4(-\frac{64}{125})+5(\frac{16}{25}) \\  & =-\frac{256}{125}+\frac{16}{5} \\  & =\frac{144}{125}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, by the factor theorem, $(5x+4)$ is not a factor of $g(x).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =10\,\text{cm}, \\ y & =4\,\text{cm}, \\ z & =1\,\text{cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =2\,\text{cm}\text{/min}, \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =32\,{\text{cm}}^{3}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}$ when $x=10\,\text{cm},$ $y=4\,\text{cm}$ and $z=1\,\text{cm}.$

We start with the formula for the volume of the rectangular prism:

$$
V=xyz
$$

Since $z$ is not changing and $z=1,$ we get

$$
V=xy.
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(xy) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =x(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})+y(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}).\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug in the known values into the above expression. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}32 & =10(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})+4(2) \\ 32 & =10(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})+8 \\ 24 & =10(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =2.4\,\text{cm}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the width of the solid is increasing at a rate of $2.4\,\text{cm}/\text{min}$ at the moment when $x=10\,\text{cm},$ $y=4\,\text{cm}$ and $z=1\,\text{cm}.$

:question/problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+25{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,y(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(2)=0,\,0\le x\le 2,\,\lambda \ge 0.
$$

Find the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues and the associated eigenfunctions of this problem.

$\,$ The eigenvalues correspond to the parameter values ${\lambda }_{n}=$ {{field-1}}, where $n\in N.$

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are ${y}_{n}(x)=$ {{field-2}}, where ${B}_{n}\in R.$
:question/worked-solution:
We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions $y(0)=0$ and ${y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ does not correspond to an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda >0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+25{\lambda }^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm 5\text{i}\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\lambda x),\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\lambda x)
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\lambda x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\lambda x).
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(0)=0$ yields

$$
A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)=0
$$

which gives $A=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\lambda x).
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
{y}^{′}=5B\lambda \operatorname{cos}⁡(5\lambda x).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields

$$
5B\lambda \operatorname{cos}⁡(10\lambda )=0.
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require 

$$
10\lambda =\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi =\frac{(2n+1)\pi }{2}
$$

for $n\in N.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues:

$$
{\lambda }_{n}=\frac{(2n+1)\pi }{20}.
$$

The corresponding eigenfunctions are 

$$
{y}_{n}(x)={B}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5{\lambda }_{n}x),\,{B}_{n}\in R.
$$

:question/problem: Two groups of high school students are competing in a math contest. Group $A$ consists of $5$ girls and $3$ boys, while Group $B$ consists of $2$ girls and $4$ boys. For the first challenge, one group is randomly selected, and one student is randomly selected from that group. If the selected student is a girl, what is the probability that she is from Group $B?$
:question/worked-solution:
Let $B$ be the event that Group $B$ is selected, and let $G$ be the event that a randomly selected student is a girl. Then, we require $P(B|G),$ which we can compute using Bayes' theorem.

$$
P(B|G)=\frac{P(G|B)P(B)}{P(G)}=\frac{P(G|B)P(B)}{P(G|B)P(B)+P(G|{B}^{′})P({B}^{′})}
$$

Note that ${B}^{′}$ is the event that Group A is selected.

From the problem statement, we have the following:

- Since Group $A$ consists of $5$ girls and $3$ boys and Group $B$ consists of $2$ girls and $4$ boys, we have

$$
P(G|B)=\frac{2}{6}=\frac{1}{3},\,P(G|{B}^{′})=\frac{5}{8}.
$$

- Since the group is selected at random, we have

$$
P(B)=P({B}^{′})=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, using Bayes' theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(B|G) & =\frac{P(G|B)P(B)}{P(G|B)P(B)+P(G|{B}^{′})P({B}^{′})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{2})}{(\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{2}+\frac{5}{8}\cdot \frac{1}{2})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{1}{6})}{(\frac{1}{6}+\frac{5}{16})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{1}{6})}{(\frac{23}{48})} \\  & =\frac{8}{23}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: In what unit direction does the function $f(x,y,z)=\ln (x^{4}y^{1}z^{3})$ decrease most rapidly at the point $(3,3,3)$?
:question/worked-solution:
At a given point, a function $f(x,y,z)$ decreases most rapidly in the direction opposite to that of its gradient.

So, we compute $∇f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at the point $(3,3,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\ln (x^{4}y^{1}z^{3})),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(\ln (x^{4}y^{1}z^{3})),\,\frac{∂}{∂z}(\ln (x^{4}y^{1}z^{3}))⟩ \\ & =⟨\frac{1}{x^{4}y^{1}z^{3}}\cdot 4x^{3}y^{1}z^{3},\,\frac{1}{x^{4}y^{1}z^{3}}\cdot x^{4}y^{0}z^{3},\,\frac{1}{x^{4}y^{1}z^{3}}\cdot 3x^{4}y^{1}z^{2}⟩ \\ & =⟨\frac{4}{x},\,\frac{1}{y},\,\frac{3}{z}⟩ \\ ∇f(3,3,3) & =⟨\frac{4}{3},\,\frac{1}{3},\,\frac{3}{3}⟩ \\ & =⟨\frac{4}{3},\,\frac{1}{3},\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding unit direction is

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =-\frac{∇f(3,3,3)}{‖∇f(3,3,3)‖} \\ & =\frac{-1}{\sqrt{(\frac{4}{3})^{2}+(\frac{1}{3})^{2}+(1)^{2}}}⟨\frac{4}{3},\,\frac{1}{3},\,1⟩ \\ & =⟨-\frac{2 \sqrt{26}}{13},\,-\frac{\sqrt{26}}{26},\,-\frac{3 \sqrt{26}}{26}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function decreases most rapidly in the unit direction of $⟨-\frac{2 \sqrt{26}}{13},\,-\frac{\sqrt{26}}{26},\,-\frac{3 \sqrt{26}}{26}⟩.$

:question/problem: In what unit direction does the function $f(x,y,z)=\ln (x^{5}y^{2}z^{2})$ increase most rapidly at the point $(3,2,2)$?
:question/worked-solution:
At a given point, a function $f(x,y,z)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient.

So, we compute $∇f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at the point $(3,2,2):$

$$

$$

The corresponding unit direction is

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{∇f(3,2,2)}{‖∇f(3,2,2)‖} \\ & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{(\frac{5}{3})^{2}+(1)^{2}+(1)^{2}}}⟨\frac{5}{3},\,1,\,1⟩ \\ & =⟨\frac{5 \sqrt{43}}{43},\,\frac{3 \sqrt{43}}{43},\,\frac{3 \sqrt{43}}{43}⟩\end{aligned}

Therefore, the function increases most rapidly in the unit direction of $⟨\frac{5 \sqrt{43}}{43},\,\frac{3 \sqrt{43}}{43},\,\frac{3 \sqrt{43}}{43}⟩.$

:question/problem:
![](images/ce/ce513880934a99b289c22f734e8a455c3534bddd911968cd06b7fe88f65441aa.png)

A hot air balloon $B$ is flying horizontally to the observer $O$ at a constant height of $300\,\text{m}$ above the ground. The angle of elevation $\theta $ made by the balloon and an observer is increasing at a rate of $0.05$ radians per second. What is the speed of the balloon when $\theta =\frac{\pi }{6}?$
:question/worked-solution:
![](images/81/813a4a253bdac3c44fe66da2728ad01bf3f1db2e0612093ce8f6a81b60e50161.png)

In the figure, $y$ is the altitude of the hot air balloon, and $x$ is the horizontal distance between the balloon and the observer. The quantity $y=300\,\text{m}$ does not change with time because the hot air balloon stays at a constant altitude.

We wish to calculate $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $x$ and $y.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ,$ the sides $x$ and $y$ are the adjacent and opposite, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{x} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{300}{x} \\ x & =300\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(300\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-300{csc}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given information, we have $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}=0.05$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{6}.$ Substituting these values into the above, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-300{csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})(0.05) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-300(2)^{2}(0.05) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-60.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the speed of the hot air balloon is $60\,\text{m/s}.$

We will write the equation of the line in the slope-intercept form 

$$
y=mx+b.
$$

As we found previously, the slope is $m=-\frac{1}{3}.$

Substituting $m=-\frac{1}{3}$ into the slope-intercept form above, we get

$$
y=-\frac{1}{3}x+b.
$$

We now need to find the $y$-intercept $b.$ We can find this by substituting the coordinates of a point on the line. Any point will do, so let's substitute $(4,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{1}{3}x+b \\ 1 & =-(\frac{1}{3})(4)+b \\ 1 & =-\frac{4}{3}+b \\ 1+\frac{4}{3} & =b \\ b & =\frac{7}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the line is 

$$
y=-\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{7}{3}.
$$

$$

:question/problem:
![](images/77/7732722fc875e8cf13482394990baa0b5f8306a8151fca934491bb12dd181d9e.png)

A  $10\,\text{cm}$ tall funnel containing water is being drained at a constant rate of  $10\,{\text{cm}}^{3}\text{/s}.$ The mouth of the funnel is $12\,\text{cm}$ in diameter. How fast is the water level dropping when there is $15\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}$ of water remaining in the funnel?
:question/worked-solution:
First, let's consider the dimensions of the funnel. Let's call $H=10\,\text{cm}$ the height of the funnel, and $R=\frac{12}{2}=6\,\text{cm}$ its radius at the top. These quantities are fixed and do not change with time.

Now, let's consider the water level. We call $h$ the water level's height and $r$ the radius of the cone formed by the water. Both of these quantities, and the water volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-10\,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{s},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}$ when $v=15\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}.$

We need to find a relation between $h$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $v.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $r$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$

Note that the cones formed by the funnel and the water must be similar. Therefore, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{r}{h} & =\frac{R}{H} \\ \frac{r}{h} & =\frac{6}{10} \\ r & =\frac{3h}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {(\frac{3h}{5})}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{3}{25}\pi {h}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we have an equation relating $v$ and $h,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{3}{25}\pi {h}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{9}{25}\pi {h}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the rate at which the level of water in the funnel is changing when $v=15\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}.$ We can compute the value of $h$ at this moment as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}15\pi  & =\frac{3}{25}\pi {h}^{3} \\ {h}^{3} & =125 \\ h & =5\,\text{cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we plug in the known values into the formula for $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-10 & =\frac{9}{25}\pi ({5}^{2})\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ -10 & =9\pi \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{10}{9\pi }\,\text{cm}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the water level is decreasing at a rate of $\frac{10}{9\pi }\,\text{cm}/\text{s}.$

:question/problem:
The height of a cone is increasing at a rate of $4\,\text{in}/\text{s}.$ The diameter of the cone is always $4$ times its height. Find the rate of the cone's volume increase when height is $\frac{1}{2}\,\text{in}.$ Do not round the answer.

The volume is increasing at a rate of
{{field-1}} ${\text{in}}^{3}/\text{s}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Let's call $h$ the height of the cone and $r$ the radius of its base. Both of these quantities, as well as the volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}=4\,\text{in}\text{/s},
$$

and we need to find $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ when $h=\frac{1}{2}\,\text{in}.$

We need to find a relation between $v$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $h.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $r$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$

We're told that the diameter is $4$ times the height. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =4h \\ 2r & =4h \\ r & =2h.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {(2h)}^{2}\cdot h=\frac{4}{3}\pi {h}^{3}.
$$

Now that we have an equation relating just $v$ and $h,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {h}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =4\pi {h}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting the known values, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =4\pi {(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}(4) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =4\pi \,{\text{in}}^{3}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the cone's volume is increasing at a rate of $4\pi \,{\text{in}}^{3}/\text{s}.$

:question/problem: The equation of the normal line to the curve $y=\frac{3}{{x}^{3}}$ at the point $(1,3)$ is given by $x+py=q$ where $p$ and $q$ are constants. Find the value of $p-q.$
:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=\frac{3}{{x}^{3}}.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{3}{{x}^{3}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{-3}) \\  & =-9{x}^{-4} \\  & =-\frac{9}{{x}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(1)=-\frac{9}{(1)^{4}}=-9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=\frac{1}{9}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(3) & =\frac{1}{9}(x-1) \\ 9y-27 & =x-1 \\ x-9y & =-26.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p-q=-9-(-26)=17.$

$$

$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $r$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$

We're told that the diameter is one third of the height. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\frac{1}{3}h \\ 2r & =\frac{1}{3}h \\ r & =\frac{1}{6}h.\end{aligned}

$$

The height of an ice cream cone is $12\,\text{cm}$ and the radius at the top of the cone is $2\,\text{cm}.$ Ice cream is leaking from a small hole at the bottom at a rate of $2\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{min}.$ If the ice cream level is $6\,\text{cm}$ at a particular moment, how fast is the ice cream level decreasing at that moment?
:question/worked-solution:
First, let's consider the dimensions of the cone. Let's call $H=12\,\text{cm}$ the height of the cone, and $R=2\,\text{cm}$ its radius at the top. These quantities are fixed and do not change with time.

Now, let's consider the ice cream level. We call $h$ the height of the ice cream in the cone and $r$ the radius of the ice cream top surface. Both of these quantities, and the ice cream volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-2\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{min},
$$

and we want to find the rate of change of the ice cream level $\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}$ when $h=6\,\text{cm}.$

We need to find a relation between $v$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $h.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of the ice cream:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $r$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$

Note that the cone and the ice cream part of the cone must be similar. Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{r}{h} & =\frac{R}{H} \\ \frac{r}{h} & =\frac{2}{12} \\ r & =\frac{h}{6}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {(\frac{h}{6})}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{1}{108}\pi {h}^{3}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we have an equation relating $v$ and $h,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{108}\pi {h}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{36}\pi {h}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the rate of change of the ice cream level in the cone when $h=6\,\text{cm}.$ We can compute the value of $h$ at this moment as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2\pi  & =\frac{1}{36}\pi ({6}^{2})\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-2\,\text{cm/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the height of the ice cream is decreasing at a rate of $2\,\text{cm/min}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{x} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{900} \\ y & =900\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(900\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =900{sec}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}

:question/worked-solution:
First, let's consider the dimensions of the cup. Let's call $H=6\,\text{cm}$ the height of the cup, and $R=2\,\text{cm}$ its radius at the top. These quantities are fixed and do not change with time.

Now, let's consider the water level. We call $h$ the water level's height and $r$ the radius of the cone formed by the water. Both of these quantities, and the water volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-2\,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{s},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ when $h=3\,\text{cm}.$

We need to find a relation between $h$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $v.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $r$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$

Note that the cones formed by the cup and the water must be similar. Therefore, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{r}{h} & =\frac{R}{H} \\ \frac{r}{h} & =\frac{2}{6} \\ r & =\frac{h}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {(\frac{h}{3})}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{1}{27}\pi {h}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we have an equation relating $v$ and $h,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{27}\pi {h}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{9}\pi {h}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we plug in the known values, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & =\frac{1}{9}\pi ({3}^{2})\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ -2 & =\pi \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{2}{\pi }\,\text{cm}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the water level is decreasing at a rate of $\frac{2}{\pi }\,\text{cm/s}.$

$$

A potato $P$ is fired from a cannon $C$ at an angle of $\frac{\pi }{6}$ radians from the horizontal. The horizontal distance the projectile travels increases at a rate of $18\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$ If the angle of elevation does not change, what is the speed of the potato?
:question/worked-solution:
![](images/8b/8b5af04f58fe65b46adaae47d97b857d1e8765122a811179cf25ba22733e6415.png)

Let $x$ be the horizontal distance from the potato to the cannon and $z$ be the actual distance between them, as shown above.

We want to find $\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}.$ To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $x$ and $z.$ Relative to the angle $\theta =\frac{\pi }{6},$ the sides $x$ and $z$ are the adjacent and hypotenuse, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) & =\frac{x}{z} \\ \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & =\frac{x}{z} \\ z & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(z) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}x) \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We know that $\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}=18\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}=\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\cdot 18=12\sqrt{3}.
$$

Therefore, the speed of the potato is $12\sqrt{3}\,\text{m/s}.$

A car $C$ drives toward a $108\,\text{m}$ high building $B$ following a straight path. The angle of elevation $\theta $ made by the car and the top of the building $T$ is increasing at a rate of $\frac{\pi }{36}$ radians per second. What is the speed of the car when $\theta =\frac{\pi }{3}?$
:question/worked-solution:
![](images/f2/f28ca3385d2179984c29d27a06926806e445c1dbab2cfa5f9fd6857149b632bb.png)

  

In the figure, $x$ is the distance between the car and the building, and $y$ is the building's height. The quantity $y=108$ meters does not change with time because the building's height is fixed.

We wish to calculate $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$
To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $x$ and $y.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ,$ the sides $x$ and $y$ are the adjacent and opposite, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x}{y} \\ \operatorname{cot}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x}{108} \\ x & =108\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(108\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =(-108{csc}^{2}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given information, we have $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}=\frac{\pi }{36}$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{3}.$ Substituting these values into the above, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =(-108{csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}))\frac{\pi }{36} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-108{(\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3})}^{2}\frac{\pi }{36} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-3\pi (\frac{4}{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-4\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the speed of the car is $4\pi \,\text{m/s}.$

:question/problem:
