A lifeguard $L$ is watching a weather balloon $W$ rise vertically from a point $S$ on the beach. The point $S$ is $10\,\text{m}$ away from the lifeguard. If the balloon is rising at a constant speed of $1\,\text{m/s},$ determine the rate at which the angle of elevation $\theta $ formed by the lifeguard and the balloon is increasing at the moment when $\theta =\frac{\pi }{6}.$ Do not round the answer.

The angle of elevation is increasing at a rate of
{{field-1}}
$\text{rad/s}.$
:question/worked-solution:
![](images/b4/b4b48ffa8202e15042190b98b8fc11bb02bc06547abcfbfba87b1433e5161d9b.png)

  

In the figure, $x$ is the horizontal distance between the lifeguard and the point on the beach directly beneath the balloon, and $y$ is the balloon's height. The quantity $x=10\,\text{m}$ does not change with time because the lifeguard does not move.

We wish to calculate $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}$ when $\theta =\frac{\pi }{6}.$
To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $x$ and $y.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ,$ the sides $x$ and $y$ are the adjacent and opposite, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{x} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{10} \\ y & =10\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(10\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =10{sec}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given information, we have $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=1$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{6}.$ Substituting these values into the above, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =10{sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})\cdot \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ 1 & =10{(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}})}^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ 1 & =10\cdot \frac{4}{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ 1 & =\frac{40}{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} & =\frac{3}{40}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the angle of elevation is increasing at a rate of $\frac{3}{40}\,\text{rad/s}.$

:question/problem: Find the gradient of the product $f(x,y,z)g(x,y,z),$ given that $f(x,y,z)=x^{2} y^{3} z - x y z^{3}$ and $g(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{x y z}.$
:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y,z)$ and $g(x,y,z)$ is given by

$$
∇[fg]=g∇f+f∇g.
$$

Now, we calculate the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x^{2} y^{3} z - x y z^{3})=2 x y^{3} z - y z^{3} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x^{2} y^{3} z - x y z^{3})=3 x^{2} y^{2} z - x z^{3} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(x^{2} y^{3} z - x y z^{3})=x^{2} y^{3} - 3 x y z^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}j+\frac{∂f}{∂z}k=(2 x y^{3} z - y z^{3})\,i+(3 x^{2} y^{2} z - x z^{3})\,j+(x^{2} y^{3} - 3 x y z^{2})\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the partial derivatives of $g(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{x y z})=- \frac{1}{x^{2} y z} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{x y z})=- \frac{1}{x y^{2} z} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{1}{x y z})=- \frac{1}{x y z^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}i+\frac{∂g}{∂y}j+\frac{∂g}{∂z}k=(- \frac{1}{x^{2} y z})\,i+(- \frac{1}{x y^{2} z})\,j+(- \frac{1}{x y z^{2}})\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Using the product rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y,z)g(x,y,z)] & =g(x,y,z)∇f(x,y,z)+f(x,y,z)∇g(x,y,z) \\  & =(\frac{1}{x y z})((2 x y^{3} z - y z^{3})\,i+(3 x^{2} y^{2} z - x z^{3})\,j+(x^{2} y^{3} - 3 x y z^{2})\,k)+(x^{2} y^{3} z - x y z^{3})((- \frac{1}{x^{2} y z})\,i+(- \frac{1}{x y^{2} z})\,j+(- \frac{1}{x y z^{2}})\,k) \\  & =(\frac{1}{x y z})(2 x y^{3} z - y z^{3})i+(\frac{1}{x y z})(3 x^{2} y^{2} z - x z^{3})j+(\frac{1}{x y z})(x^{2} y^{3} - 3 x y z^{2})k+(x^{2} y^{3} z - x y z^{3})(- \frac{1}{x^{2} y z})i+(x^{2} y^{3} z - x y z^{3})(- \frac{1}{x y^{2} z})j+(x^{2} y^{3} z - x y z^{3})(- \frac{1}{x y z^{2}})k \\  & =(2 y^{2} - \frac{z^{2}}{x})i+(3 x y - \frac{z^{2}}{y})j+(\frac{x y^{2}}{z} - 3 z)k+(- y^{2} + \frac{z^{2}}{x})i+(- x y + \frac{z^{2}}{y})j+(- \frac{x y^{2}}{z} + z)k \\  & =(y^{2})\,i+(2 x y)\,j+(- 2 z)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=f(x),$ where the $4$-periodic forcing function is given by 

$$
f(x)∼2+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below regarding the resonant component of a particular solution of the equation.

The natural frequency of the system matches the frequency of the {{field-1}} harmonic of the forcing function. 

Consequently, the particular solution contains a resonant term of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{3}}={{field-2}}.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}}=\frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $4$-periodic function $(L=2)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{2}.
$$

For $n=3$, we have ${\omega }_{3}=\frac{3\pi }{2}.$ Since ${\omega }_{3}=\omega ,$ the $n=3$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=3$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{3}(x)=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2}).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{3}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{3}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2}))+x(-\frac{3\pi }{2}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+\frac{3\pi }{2}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})) \\ {y}_{{p}_{3}}^{″} & =-3\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+3\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})-\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2}))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{3}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{3}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2}):$

$$
[-3\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+3\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})-\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{3}}]+\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{3}}=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-3\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})+3\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2})=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-3\pi A=0 \\ 3\pi B=\frac{1}{9}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}A=0 \\ B=\frac{1}{27\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{3}}=\frac{x}{27\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi x}{2}).
$$

:question/problem:
Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{″}-10y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $4$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼10+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{5(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

*Hint: You may assume that all the cosine coefficients in the Fourier series of the particular solution are equal to zero.*

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-2}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})
$$
:question/worked-solution:
We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{″}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation and have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})-10(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}))=10+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{5(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
-10\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}(-\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{4}-10)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})=10+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{5(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, equating the free terms and sine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-10\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=10 \\ {b}_{n}(-\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{4}-10)=\frac{5(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=-1 \\ {b}_{n}=\frac{20(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+40)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼-1+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{20(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+40)}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

:question/problem:
$$

If $f(x)=\frac{\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(x)}{\sqrt{x}},$ calculate ${f}^{′}(x).$

${f}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}($ 
{{field-1}} $-\frac{\operatorname{arcoth}⁡x}{2x})$
:question/worked-solution:
In this case, the expression for $f(x)$ is a quotient $\frac{u(x)}{v(x)}$ with $u(x)=\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(x)$ and $v(x)=\sqrt{x}.$

Therefore, we apply the product rule as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{{[v(x)]}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{(\operatorname{arcoth}⁡x)}^{′}\cdot \sqrt{x}-\operatorname{arcoth}⁡x\cdot {(\sqrt{x})}^{′}}{{(\sqrt{x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{(\operatorname{arcoth}⁡x)}^{′}\cdot \sqrt{x}}{x}-\frac{\operatorname{arcoth}⁡x\cdot {(\sqrt{x})}^{′}}{x} \\  & =(\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}})\cdot \frac{\sqrt{x}}{x}-\frac{\operatorname{arcoth}⁡x}{x}\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \\  & =(\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}})\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}-\frac{\operatorname{arcoth}⁡x}{2x}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}(\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}-\frac{\operatorname{arcoth}⁡x}{2x}).\end{aligned}
$$

First, we differentiate $x=\frac{3}{5y-2}$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{3}{5y-2}) \\  & =3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}((5y-2)^{-1}) \\  & =-3(5y-2)^{-2}\cdot 5 \\  & =-\frac{15}{(5y-2)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, taking the reciprocal of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y},$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{15}(5y-2)^{2}.
$$

:question/problem: The slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\sqrt{3{x}^{2}+2x}$ at the point where $x=-1$ is{{field-1}}.
:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=3{x}^{2}+2x.$ Then $y=\sqrt{u}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}},
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6x+2.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot (6x+2) \\  & =\frac{6x+2}{2\sqrt{3{x}^{2}+2x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=-1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=-1} & ={(\frac{6x+2}{2\sqrt{3{x}^{2}+2x}})|}_{x=-1} \\  & =\frac{6(-1)+2}{2\sqrt{3(-1)^{2}+2(-1)}} \\  & =\frac{-4}{2\sqrt{1}} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
$$

If $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\operatorname{arsech}⁡x,$ calculate ${f}^{′}(x).$

${f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\operatorname{arsech}⁡x}{x}\,-$ 
{{field-1}}
:question/worked-solution:
In this case, the expression for $f(x)$ is a product $u(x)\cdot v(x)$ with $u(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ and $v(x)=\operatorname{arsech}⁡x.$

Therefore, we apply the product rule as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)+u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x) \\  & ={(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{′}\cdot \operatorname{arsech}⁡x+\operatorname{ln}⁡x\cdot {(\operatorname{arsech}⁡x)}^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\cdot \operatorname{arsech}⁡x\,+\,\operatorname{ln}⁡x\cdot (-\frac{1}{x\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{arsech}⁡x}{x}-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: In an online poker tournament, the maximum loss is $10$ dollars, and the maximum win is $8$ dollars. Assuming that a player's earnings are uniformly distributed between $-10$ and $8,$ what is the probability that a randomly chosen player loses between $2$ and $8$ dollars?
:question/worked-solution:
Let $X$ represent the earnings of a randomly chosen player. From the problem statement, we know that $X∼U[-10,8],$ and we wish to compute $P(-8\le X\le -2).$

In general, if $X∼U[a,b],$ then $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{b-a}, & a\le x\le b \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

So, for our random variable $X∼U[-10,8],$ we have the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{18}, & -10\le x\le 8 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-8\le X\le -2) & ={\int }_{-8}^{-2}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-8}^{-2}\frac{1}{18}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{x}{18}|}_{-8}^{-2} \\  & =-\frac{2}{18}-(-\frac{8}{18}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
$$

If $f(x)=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{arcoth}⁡x},$ then ${f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{arcoth}⁡x}+g(x).$ What is $g(x)?$
:question/worked-solution:
In this case, the expression for $f(x)$ is a quotient $\frac{u(x)}{v(x)}$ with $u(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $v(x)=\operatorname{arcoth}⁡x.$

Therefore, we apply the quotient rule as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{′}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot (\operatorname{arcoth}⁡x)^{′}}{{arcoth}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{′}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡x}{{arcoth}^{2}⁡x}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot (\operatorname{arcoth}⁡x)^{′}}{{arcoth}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{′}}{\operatorname{arcoth}⁡x}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot (\operatorname{arcoth}⁡x)^{′}}{{arcoth}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{arcoth}⁡x}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{arcoth}^{2}⁡x}\cdot (\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{arcoth}⁡x}+\underbrace{(-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{(1-{x}^{2}){arcoth}^{2}⁡x})}_{g(x)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x)=-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{(1-{x}^{2}){arcoth}^{2}⁡x}.$

Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{″}-5y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $4$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼5+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
:question/worked-solution:
We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{″}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation and have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})-5(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}))=5+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
-5\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}(-\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{4}-5)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})=5+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, equating the free terms and sine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-5\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=5 \\ {b}_{n}(-\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{4}-5)=\frac{2(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=-1 \\ {b}_{n}=-\frac{8(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+20)}\end{aligned}

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼-1+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,-\frac{8(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+20)}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).

What is the least distance between the curve $y=\sqrt{x+1}$ and the point $(2,0)?$
:question/worked-solution:
Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(2,0)$ and a general point $P(x,y)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-2)^{2}+(y-0)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{x+1}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-2)^{2}+(y)^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+(\sqrt{x+1})^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+x+1 \\  & ={x}^{2}-4x+4+x+1 \\  & ={x}^{2}-3x+5.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=2x-3 & =0 \\ 2x & =3 \\ x & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(x)=2>0.$ Therefore, $x=\frac{3}{2}$ is a minimum of $S.$

Since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=\frac{3}{2}$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S(\frac{3}{2})}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S(\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-3(\frac{3}{2})+5} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{11}{4}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{11}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x+3{x}^{\sqrt{5}}+7) \\  & =4(\frac{1}{x})+(\sqrt{5}\,{x}^{\sqrt{5}-1}) \\  & =\frac{4}{x}+\sqrt{5}\,{x}^{\sqrt{5}-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{4}\,\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{1}{x} \\  & =\frac{1}{4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Suppose ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{14}$ is an I.I.D random sample with ${X}_{i}∼N(\theta ,{1}^{2}),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown mean. For a particular sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{14},$ you're given that 

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{14}{x}_{i}=26.8,\,{\sum }_{i=1}^{14}{x}_{i}^{2}=264.8.
$$

Given that the log-likelihood function of the sample is

$$
l(\theta )=-7\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )+a+b\theta +c{\theta }^{2},
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$

*Hint: The probability density function for a normal random variable with mean $\theta $ and standard deviation $1$ is given by* 

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i};\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=14$ independent normal random variables with unknown mean $\theta $ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=1,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x,\theta )=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Next, we write down the log-density function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡f(x,\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{(x-\theta )^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{n}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\frac{({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}}{2} \\  & =-\frac{n}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{1}{2}({\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}-2\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+n{\theta }^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

We are told that ${\sum }_{i=1}^{14}{x}_{i}=26.8,$ ${\sum }_{i=1}^{14}{x}_{i}^{2}=264.8,$ and $n=14.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =-\frac{14}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{1}{2}(264.8-2\theta \cdot 26.8+14{\theta }^{2}) \\  & =-7\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )+(-132.4)+26.8\theta +(-7){\theta }^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b+c=(-132.4)+26.8+(-7)=-112.6.
$$

What is the least distance between the curve $y=\sqrt{x}+1$ and the point $(1,1)?$
:question/worked-solution:
Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(1,1)$ and a general point $P(x,y)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{x}+1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2} \\  & =(x-1)^{2}+(\sqrt{x}+1-1)^{2} \\  & =(x-1)^{2}+(\sqrt{x})^{2} \\  & =(x-1)^{2}+x \\  & ={x}^{2}-2x+1+x \\  & ={x}^{2}-x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=2x-1 & =0 \\ 2x & =1 \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(x)=2>0.$ Therefore, $x=\frac{1}{2}$ is a minimum of $S.$

Since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=\frac{1}{2}$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S(\frac{1}{2})}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S(\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-(\frac{1}{2})+1} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${sin}^{2}$ term: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .

We can rearrange the above formula as

$$
\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .
$$

Letting $\theta =\frac{x}{2},$ we have

$$

$$

Suppose ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},{X}_{3}$ is an I.I.D random sample with ${X}_{i}∼N(\theta ,{1}^{2}),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown mean. The log-likelihood function of the sample $2.5,\,0.2,\,-1.1$ is

$$

$$

What is the value of $a+b+c?$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i};\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=3$ independent normal random variables with unknown mean $\theta $ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=1,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x,\theta )=\frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-\frac{1}{2}{(\frac{x-\theta }{\sigma })}^{2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Next, we write down the log-density function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡f(x,\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{(x-\theta )^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{n}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\frac{({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}}{2} \\  & =-\frac{n}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{1}{2}({\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}-2\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+n{\theta }^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

For our sample, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} \\  & =2.5+0.2+(-1.1) \\  & =1.6 \\ C & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2} \\  & =(2.5)^{2}+(0.2)^{2}+(-1.1)^{2} \\  & =7.5\end{aligned}
$$

and $n=3.$ Therefore,  

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =-\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{1}{2}(7.5-2\theta \cdot (1.6)+3{\theta }^{2}) \\  & =-1.5\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )+(-3.75)+(1.6)\theta +(-1.5){\theta }^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b+c=-3.75+(1.6)+(-1.5)=-3.65.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡f(x,\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{(x-\theta )^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{- 4 r \sin{\left(\theta \right)} + 8 r \cos{\left(\theta \right)}}{3 r^{2} \sin^{2}{\left(\theta \right)} - 4 r^{2} \sin{\left(\theta \right)} \cos{\left(\theta \right)} + 4 r^{2} \cos^{2}{\left(\theta \right)}}, \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{6 r \sin{\left(\theta \right)} - 4 r \cos{\left(\theta \right)}}{3 r^{2} \sin^{2}{\left(\theta \right)} - 4 r^{2} \sin{\left(\theta \right)} \cos{\left(\theta \right)} + 4 r^{2} \cos^{2}{\left(\theta \right)}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂\theta} & =(\frac{- 4 r \sin{\left(\theta \right)} + 8 r \cos{\left(\theta \right)}}{3 r^{2} \sin^{2}{\left(\theta \right)} - 4 r^{2} \sin{\left(\theta \right)} \cos{\left(\theta \right)} + 4 r^{2} \cos^{2}{\left(\theta \right)}})(- r \sin{\left(\theta \right)})+(\frac{6 r \sin{\left(\theta \right)} - 4 r \cos{\left(\theta \right)}}{3 r^{2} \sin^{2}{\left(\theta \right)} - 4 r^{2} \sin{\left(\theta \right)} \cos{\left(\theta \right)} + 4 r^{2} \cos^{2}{\left(\theta \right)}})(r \cos{\left(\theta \right)}) \\  & =(\frac{4 r^{2} \sin^{2}{\left(\theta \right)}}{3 r^{2} \sin^{2}{\left(\theta \right)} - 4 r^{2} \sin{\left(\theta \right)} \cos{\left(\theta \right)} + 4 r^{2} \cos^{2}{\left(\theta \right)}} - \frac{8 r^{2} \sin{\left(\theta \right)} \cos{\left(\theta \right)}}{3 r^{2} \sin^{2}{\left(\theta \right)} - 4 r^{2} \sin{\left(\theta \right)} \cos{\left(\theta \right)} + 4 r^{2} \cos^{2}{\left(\theta \right)}})+(\frac{6 r^{2} \sin{\left(\theta \right)} \cos{\left(\theta \right)}}{3 r^{2} \sin^{2}{\left(\theta \right)} - 4 r^{2} \sin{\left(\theta \right)} \cos{\left(\theta \right)} + 4 r^{2} \cos^{2}{\left(\theta \right)}} - \frac{4 r^{2} \cos^{2}{\left(\theta \right)}}{3 r^{2} \sin^{2}{\left(\theta \right)} - 4 r^{2} \sin{\left(\theta \right)} \cos{\left(\theta \right)} + 4 r^{2} \cos^{2}{\left(\theta \right)}}) \\  & =\frac{4 \sin^{2}{\left(\theta \right)} - 2 \sin{\left(\theta \right)} \cos{\left(\theta \right)} - 4 \cos^{2}{\left(\theta \right)}}{3 \sin^{2}{\left(\theta \right)} - 4 \sin{\left(\theta \right)} \cos{\left(\theta \right)} + 4 \cos^{2}{\left(\theta \right)}}\end{aligned}

The joint CDF of two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
F(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<1\,\text{or}\,y<0 \\ \frac{xy-y}{x}, & x\ge 1,\,0\le y\le 1 \\ {F}_{X}(x), & x\ge 1,\,y>1.\end{aligned}
$$

Find ${F}_{Y}(y),$ the marginal CDF of $Y,$ for $0\le y\le 1.$
:question/worked-solution:
The marginal CDF of $Y$ is given by

$$
{F}_{Y}(y)=F(\infty ,y)={lim}_{x\to \infty }F(x,y).
$$

Therefore, for $0\le y\le 1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }(\frac{xy-y}{x}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }(\frac{y(x-1)}{x}) \\  & =y{lim}_{x\to \infty }(1-\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =y{lim}_{x\to \infty }(1-0) \\  & =y.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider all non-critical points of the transformation $T:(u,v)\to (x(u,v),y(u,v)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y)\to (u(x,y),v(x,y))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}xy \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{y}\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T$ in terms of $u$ and $v.$
:question/worked-solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have $u(x,y)=xy$ and $v(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}.$ 

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =y & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =x \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =\frac{2x}{y} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}y & x \\ \frac{2x}{y} & -\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}| \\  & =y\cdot (-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}})-x\cdot \frac{2x}{y} \\  & =\frac{-3{x}^{2}}{y} \\  & =-3\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{y} \\  & =-3v.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3v}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The joint CDF of two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
F(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-2)({y}^{2}-1)}{x{y}^{2}}, & x\ge 2,\,y\ge 1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the joint PDF $f(x,y)$ for $x\ge 2,\,y\ge 1.$
:question/worked-solution:
Since the partial derivatives of $F(x,y)$ are defined, the joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{{∂}^{2}}{∂x∂y}F(x,y).
$$

For $x\ge 2$ and $y\ge 1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\frac{{∂}^{2}}{∂x∂y}F(x,y) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{(x-2)({y}^{2}-1)}{x{y}^{2}})) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x-2}{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(1-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}})) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x-2}{x}\cdot \frac{2}{{y}^{3}}) \\  & =\frac{2}{{y}^{3}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(1-\frac{2}{x}) \\  & =\frac{2}{{y}^{3}}\cdot \frac{2}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{{x}^{2}{y}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Otherwise, $f(x,y)=0.$

Therefore, we have

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{{x}^{2}{y}^{3}}, & x\ge 2,\,y\ge 1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y={sin}^{2}⁡t,\,t\in [0,\pi ].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
:question/worked-solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\pi .$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({sin}^{2}⁡t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t(1+{cos}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\cdot |2\operatorname{sin}⁡t|\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{3}⁡t\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The joint CDF of two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
F(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<0\,\text{or}\,y<0 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡y}{2\pi }, & 0\le x\le 2,\,y\ge 0 \\ {F}_{Y}(y), & x>2,\,y\ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Find ${F}_{X}(x),$ the marginal CDF of $X,$ for $0\le x\le 2.$
:question/worked-solution:
The marginal CDF of $X$ is given by

$$
{F}_{X}(x)=F(x,\infty )={lim}_{y\to \infty }F(x,y).
$$

Therefore, for $0\le x\le 2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{X}(x) & ={lim}_{y\to \infty }(\frac{{x}^{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡y}{2\pi }) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2\pi }\cdot {lim}_{y\to \infty }\operatorname{arctan}⁡y \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The marginal CDFs of two continuous independent random variables $X$ and $Y$ are given below. 

$$
{F}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{2+x}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,\,{F}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}1-{e}^{-2y}, & y\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Find the expression for the joint CDF when $x\ge 0$ and $y\ge 0.$
:question/worked-solution:
If $X$ and $Y$ are independent continuous random variables with marginal CDFs ${F}_{X}(x)$ and ${F}_{Y}(y),$ respectively, then the corresponding joint CDF of $F(x,y)$ is given by

$$
F(x,y)={F}_{X}(x)\cdot {F}_{Y}(y).
$$

Therefore, for $x\ge 0$ and $y\ge 0,$ the joint CDF for our random variables is 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y) & ={F}_{X}(x)\cdot {F}_{Y}(y) \\  & =(\frac{x}{2+x})(1-{e}^{-2y}) \\  & =\frac{x}{2+x}(1-{e}^{-2y}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for the joint CDF is

$$
F(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{2+x}(1-{e}^{-2y}), & x\ge 0,\,y\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using $\theta ={\theta }^{′}+{180}^{∘},$ we get $\theta ={45}^{∘}+{180}^{∘}={225}^{∘}.$

The difference of cubes formula is given by

$$
{a}^{3}-{b}^{3}=(a-b)({a}^{2}+ab+{b}^{2}).
$$

Notice that we can write our expression as a difference of cubes, as follows:

$$
\frac{{u}^{3}}{8}-1={(\frac{u}{2})}^{3}-{1}^{3}
$$

Now, we factor our expression using the difference of cubes formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{u}^{3}}{8}-1 & ={(\frac{u}{2})}^{3}-{1}^{3} \\  & =(\frac{u}{2}-1)({(\frac{u}{2})}^{2}+\frac{u}{2}\cdot 1+{(1)}^{2}) \\  & =(\frac{u}{2}-1)(\frac{{u}^{2}}{4}+\frac{u}{2}+1)\end{aligned}
$$

The difference of cubes formula is given by

$$
{a}^{3}-{b}^{3}=(a-b)({a}^{2}+ab+{b}^{2}).
$$

Notice that we can write our expression as a difference of cubes, as follows:

$$
\frac{8}{{w}^{3}}-\frac{1}{{z}^{9}}={(\frac{2}{w})}^{3}-{(\frac{1}{{z}^{3}})}^{3}
$$

Now, we factor our expression using the difference of cubes formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{8}{{w}^{3}}-\frac{1}{{z}^{9}} & ={(\frac{2}{w})}^{3}-{(\frac{1}{{z}^{3}})}^{3} \\  & =(\frac{2}{w}-\frac{1}{{z}^{3}})({(\frac{2}{w})}^{2}+\frac{2}{w}\cdot \frac{1}{{z}^{3}}+{(\frac{1}{{z}^{3}})}^{2}) \\  & =(\frac{2}{w}-\frac{1}{{z}^{3}})(\frac{4}{{w}^{2}}+\frac{2}{w{z}^{3}}+\frac{1}{({z}^{3})^{2}}) \\  & =(\frac{2}{w}-\frac{1}{{z}^{3}})(\frac{4}{{w}^{2}}+\frac{2}{w{z}^{3}}+\frac{1}{{z}^{6}})\end{aligned}

:question/problem:
The joint CDF of two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
F(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<0\,\text{or}\,y<1 \\ \frac{4{x}^{2}({y}^{2}-1)}{3{y}^{2}}, & 0\le x\le 1,\,1\le y\le 2 \\ {F}_{X}(x), & 0\le x\le 1,\,y>2 \\ {F}_{Y}(y), & x>1,\,1\le y\le 2 \\ 1, & x>1,\,y>2.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${F}_{X}$ and ${F}_{Y}$ are the marginal CDFs of $X$ and $Y,$ respectively. Find the joint PDF $f(x,y)$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $1\le y\le 2.$
:question/worked-solution:
Since the partial derivatives of $F(x,y)$ are defined, the joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ is determined by

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{{∂}^{2}}{∂x∂y}F(x,y).
$$

For $0\le x\le 1$ and $1\le y\le 2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\frac{{∂}^{2}}{∂x∂y}F(x,y) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{4{x}^{2}({y}^{2}-1)}{3{y}^{2}})) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{4}{3}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(1-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}})) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{4}{3}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{2}{{y}^{3}}) \\  & =\frac{8}{3{y}^{3}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{8}{3{y}^{3}}\cdot 2x \\  & =\frac{16x}{3{y}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Otherwise, $f(x,y)=0.$
Therefore, we have

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{16x}{3{y}^{3}}, & 0\le x\le 1,\,1\le y\le 2 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The joint CDF of two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
F(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-1)(y-1)}{xy}, & x\ge 1,\,y\ge 1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the joint PDF $f(x,y)$ for $x\ge 1$ and $y\ge 1.$
:question/worked-solution:
Since the partial derivatives of $F(x,y)$ are defined, the joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{{∂}^{2}}{∂x∂y}F(x,y).
$$

For $x\ge 1$ and $y\ge 1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\frac{{∂}^{2}}{∂x∂y}F(x,y) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{(x-1)(y-1)}{xy})) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x-1}{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(1-\frac{1}{y})) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x-1}{x}\cdot \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(1-\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Otherwise, $f(x,y)=0.$

Therefore, we have

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}, & x\ge 1,\,y\ge 1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=4t\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{t}{\pi }),\,y=t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,t\in (0,\infty ).
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=\pi $ on the curve. Determine the point at which the normal to the curve at $C$ crosses the $x$-axis.
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=\pi $ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =4\pi \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{\pi }{\pi })=4\pi (0)=0, \\ y & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi =-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to determine the equation of the normal at the point $(0,-\pi ).$ For this, we need to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{t}{\pi })+4,\,{y}^{′}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{t}{\pi })+4}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=\pi ,$ the slope $m$ of the tangent line is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=\pi } & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi }{4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{\pi }{\pi })+4} \\  & =\frac{-1}{4\cdot 0+4}=-\,\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope ${m}_{n}$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m$:

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{\,(-\frac{1}{4})\,}=4
$$

To calculate the equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(0,-\pi )$ and the slope ${m}_{n}=4.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(-\pi ) & =4(x-0) \\ y & =4x-\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

The normal intersects the $x$-axis when $y=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4x-\pi  & =0 \\ 4x & =\pi  \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $(\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ is the $x$-intercept.

:question/problem: $6\operatorname{sec}⁡{60}^{∘}+3\operatorname{csc}⁡{30}^{∘}+\operatorname{cot}⁡{30}^{∘}=${{field-1}}
:question/worked-solution:
Remember that $sec$  is the reciprocal of $cos,$  $csc$ is the reciprocal of $sin$  and $cot$  is the reciprocal of $tan.$
So, we have

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡{60}^{∘}=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡{60}^{∘}},\,\operatorname{csc}⁡{30}^{∘}=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡{30}^{∘}},\,\operatorname{cot}⁡{30}^{∘}=\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡{30}^{∘}}.
$$

The angle ${60}^{∘}$ and ${30}^{∘}$ are special, and its trigonometric ratios have the values

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡{60}^{∘}=\frac{1}{2},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡{30}^{∘}=\frac{1}{2},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡{30}^{∘}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}6\operatorname{sec}⁡{60}^{∘}+3\operatorname{csc}⁡{30}^{∘}+\operatorname{cot}⁡{30}^{∘} &= 6(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡{60}^{∘}})+3(\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡{30}^{∘}})+\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡{30}^{∘}} \\ &= \frac{6}{\operatorname{cos}⁡{60}^{∘}}+\frac{3}{\operatorname{sin}⁡{30}^{∘}}+\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡{30}^{∘}} \\ &= \frac{6}{(\frac{1}{2})}+\frac{3}{(\frac{1}{2})}+\frac{1}{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})} \\ &= 12+6+\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}} \\ &= 18+\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}} \\ &= 18+\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}} \\ &= 18+\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x={e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t),\,y={e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t),\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Determine the values of $t$ at which the tangent to the curve is vertical. Do not round the answers.

In **ascending order**, the tangent to the curve is vertical at $t=$
{{field-1}}
and $t=$
{{field-2}}.
:question/worked-solution:
The slope $m$ of a tangent line to a curve defined parametrically is given by

$$
m=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

The tangent line is vertical if ${x}^{′}(t)=0$ while ${y}^{′}(t)\ne 0.$

So, we first find the derivatives of $x$ and $y:$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)={e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)),\,{y}^{′}(t)={e}^{t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))
$$

Solving ${x}^{′}(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)) & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & =0 \\ 0 & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)} & =1 \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡(t)=1 \\ t & =\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{5\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we note that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & ={e}^{\frac{\pi }{4}}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})]=\sqrt{2}{e}^{\frac{\pi }{4}}\ne 0, \\ {y}^{′}(\frac{5\pi }{4}) & ={e}^{\frac{5\pi }{4}}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{4})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{4})]=-\sqrt{2}{e}^{\frac{5\pi }{4}}\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the tangent to the curve is vertical at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ and $t=\frac{5\pi }{4}.$

:question/problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
We break up the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Evaluating the first of these integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =2{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{1}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(2\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2x){|}_{a}^{0}) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\operatorname{arctan}⁡0-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2a)) \\  & =0-(-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand is an **even** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{2}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}+\frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=\sqrt{t+1},\,y={t}^{3}+4,\,-1<t<\infty .
$$

Calculate the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=1.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting $t=1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\sqrt{1+1}=\sqrt{2}, \\ y & =(1)^{3}+4=5.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent at the point $(\sqrt{2},5).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t+1}},\,{y}^{′}(t)=3{t}^{2}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{3{t}^{2}}{(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t+1}})} \\  & =6{t}^{2}\sqrt{(t+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=1} & =6\cdot {1}^{2}\sqrt{1+1} \\  & =6\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(\sqrt{2},5)$ and the slope $m=6\sqrt{2}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-5 & =6\sqrt{2}(x-\sqrt{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the point(s) of the intersection of the elliptic cone ${x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=8{z}^{2}$ and the line $\frac{x}{4}=\frac{y}{2}=z-1.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we write the equation of our line in parametric form:

$$
\frac{x}{4}=\frac{y}{2}=z-1=t\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}x=4t \\ y=2t \\ z=t+1,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Substituting the above expressions for $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ into the equation of the elliptic cone, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2} & =8{z}^{2} \\ (4t)^{2}+4(2t)^{2} & =8(t+1)^{2} \\ 16{t}^{2}+16{t}^{2} & =8(t+1)^{2} \\ 32{t}^{2} & =8(t+1)^{2} \\ 4{t}^{2} & =(t+1)^{2} \\ 4{t}^{2} & ={t}^{2}+2t+1 \\ 3{t}^{2}-2t-1 & =0 \\ (3t+1)(t-1) & =0 \\ t & =-\frac{1}{3},1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute our solutions back into the equations of the line.

- For $t=-\frac{1}{3},$ we have

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=4(-\frac{1}{3})=-\frac{4}{3} \\ y=2(-\frac{1}{3})=-\frac{2}{3} \\ z=-\frac{1}{3}+1=\frac{2}{3},\end{aligned}
$$

so the first point is $(-\frac{4}{3},-\frac{2}{3},\frac{2}{3}).$

- For $t=1,$ we have

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=4(1)=4 \\ y=2(1)=2 \\ z=1+1=2,\end{aligned}
$$

so the second point is $(4,2,2).$

Therefore, the points of intersection are $(-\frac{4}{3},-\frac{2}{3},\frac{2}{3})$ and $(4,2,2).$

:question/problem:
For the elliptic paraboloid $\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{3}=z+4$, the section in the plane $\sqrt{3}x-2y=4$ is a parabola. 
Find the vertex of the projection of this parabola onto $yz$-plane.
:question/worked-solution:
Since we want to find the projection onto the $yz$-plane, we need to eliminate the variable $x.$ First, we solve for $x$ in the equation of the plane, as follows:

$$
\sqrt{3}x-2y=4\,⟹\,x=\frac{2(y+2)}{\sqrt{3}}
$$

Substituting the expression for $x$ into the equation of the paraboloid, we obtain: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{(\frac{2(y+2)}{\sqrt{3}})}^{2}}{2}+\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{3} & =z+4 \\ \frac{4(y+2)^{2}}{3\cdot 2}+\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{3} & =z+4 \\ \frac{2(y+2)^{2}}{3}+\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{3} & =z+4 \\ \frac{3(y+2)^{2}}{3} & =z+4 \\ (y+2)^{2} & =z+4 \\ z & =(y+2)^{2}-4\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the vertex of the projection onto $yz$-plane is $(-2,-4).$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the triple integral

$$
{∭}_{R}xyz\,\text{d}V
$$

where $R$ is the type III region given by 

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le z\le 2,\,0\le x\le \sqrt{4-2z},\,0\le y\le x\}.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
Writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}xyz\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-2x}}{\int }_{0}^{x}xyz\,dy\,dx\,dz.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y$, treating $x$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-2x}}{\int }_{0}^{x}xyz\,dy\,dx\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-2x}}[{\int }_{0}^{x}xyz\,dy]dx\,dz \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-2x}}xz{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=x}dx\,dz \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-2x}}xz(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})\,dx\,dz \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-2x}}{x}^{3}z\,dx\,dz\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x$, treating $z$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-2x}}{x}^{3}z\,dx\,dz & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}z[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-2z}}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}z{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}]}_{x=0}^{x=\sqrt{4-2z}}\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{4}(4-2z)^{2}z\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}4z-4{z}^{2}+{z}^{3}\,\text{d}z\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}4z-4{z}^{2}+{z}^{3}\,\text{d}z & =\frac{1}{2}{[2{z}^{2}-\frac{4}{3}{z}^{3}+\frac{1}{4}{z}^{4}]}_{z=0}^{z=2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(8-\frac{32}{3}+4)-0 \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/31/31d4236bf58cd579c49c7259c32a2a9171e07c771b4c34040ac92896809f695f.png)

The region enclosed by the curves $x=\frac{2}{y}$ and $x=3-y$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=-2.$ Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?
:question/worked-solution:
First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{y} & =3-y \\ 2 & =3y-{y}^{2} \\ {y}^{2}-3y+2 & =0 \\ (y-1)(y-2) & =0 \\ y & =1,2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, our limits of integration are from $y=1$ to $y=2.$

Now, let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](images/b7/b73c341f4d09b1df7bea162bc7dbe10d0ee60920c847f9c24210386a3d139e61.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x=\frac{2}{y},$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $x=3-y.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $x=3-y.$

![](images/c8/c8c8e766c66e47a54f316f54893d603b245acec8f529da3a5033d2bba547a319.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}[\,(3-y)-(-2)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{[5-y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x=\frac{2}{y}.$

![](images/1b/1b31331f1c0da353bee6fe29d10e9e58dd531cbc8152cbce214d1adea771b032.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{[\,(\frac{2}{y})-(-2)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{[\frac{2}{y}+2]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{[5-y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y-\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{[\frac{2}{y}+2]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({[5-y]}^{2}-{[\frac{2}{y}+2]}^{2})\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

The angle ${45}^{∘}$ is special, and its trigonometric ratios have the values

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡{45}^{∘}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡{45}^{∘}=1,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡{45}^{∘}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.
$$

Also, note that ${sin}^{2}⁡{45}^{∘}$ means $(\operatorname{sin}⁡{45}^{∘})^{2},$ ${cos}^{2}⁡{45}^{∘}$ means $(\operatorname{cos}⁡{45}^{∘})^{2}$ and  ${tan}^{2}⁡{45}^{∘}$ means $(\operatorname{tan}⁡{45}^{∘})^{2}.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}5{cos}^{2}⁡{45}^{∘}+3{sin}^{2}⁡{45}^{∘}-7{tan}^{2}⁡{45}^{∘} &= 5(\operatorname{cos}⁡{45}^{∘})^{2}+3(\operatorname{sin}⁡{45}^{∘})^{2}-7(\operatorname{tan}⁡{45}^{∘})^{2} \\ &= 5{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2}+3{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2}-7(1)^{2} \\ &= 8{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2}-7 \\ &= 8(\frac{2}{4})-7 \\ &= 4-7 \\ &= -3.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
| $f$ | $Y=4$ | $Y=8$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $\frac{1}{16}$ | $\frac{3}{16}$ |
| $X=1$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |

Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. Find $\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=4]$ given that the random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ shown in the table above and the corresponding conditional expected value is ${\mu }_{X|4}=\frac{4}{5}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the conditional variance of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=y] & =\text{E}[(X-{\mu }_{X|y})^{2}\,|\,Y=y] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=y]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2} \\  & =[{\sum }_{x}{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In order to find ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y),$ let's first find the marginal distribution of $Y,$ corresponding to the column totals: 

| $f$ | $Y=4$ | $Y=8$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $\frac{1}{16}$ | $\frac{3}{16}$ |
| $X=1$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |
| ${f}_{Y}(y)$ | $\frac{5}{16}$ | $\frac{11}{16}$ |

The conditional probability mass function of $X$ given that $Y=y$ is

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)}.
$$

Therefore, dividing each joint probability by the corresponding column total, we obtain the conditional probability mass function of $X$ given that $Y=y:$

| ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)$ | $Y=4$ | $Y=8$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $\frac{1}{5}$ | $\frac{3}{11}$ |
| $X=1$ | $\frac{4}{5}$ | $\frac{8}{11}$ |
|  | $1$ | $1$ |

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=4] & =[{\sum }_{x}{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,4)]-{\mu }_{X|4}^{2} \\  & =[{0}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{5}+{1}^{2}\cdot \frac{4}{5}]-{(\frac{4}{5})}^{2} \\  & =0+\frac{4}{5}-\frac{16}{25} \\  & =\frac{4}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0<t<2\pi .
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=\frac{\pi }{6}$ on the curve. Determine the coordinates of the point at which the normal to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis. Do not round the answers.

The normal to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis at $(${{field-1}},
{{field-2}}$).$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=\frac{\pi }{6}$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})=3\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ y & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we're looking to determine the equation of the normal at the point $(\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$ For this, we need to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cot}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{6},$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t\,=\,\frac{\pi }{6}} & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}(\sqrt{3}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope ${m}_{n}$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m:$

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})}=\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}}=\sqrt{3}
$$

To calculate the equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{1}{2})$ and the slope ${m}_{n}=\sqrt{3}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-\frac{1}{2} & =\sqrt{3}(x-\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\ y-\frac{1}{2} & =\sqrt{3}x-\frac{3(3)}{2} \\ y & =\sqrt{3}x-\frac{9}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\ y & =\sqrt{3}x-4.\end{aligned}
$$

The normal crosses the $y$-axis when $x=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the normal to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis at  $(0,\,-4).$

:question/problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x={t}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}t+\frac{3}{2},\,y={t}^{3}+7{t}^{2}+8t,\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=-1$ on the curve. Determine the coordinates of the point at which the tangent to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis. Do not round the answers.

The tangent to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis at $(${{field-1}},
{{field-2}}$).$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=-1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =(-1)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(-1)+\frac{3}{2}=1-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{3}{2}=2 \\ y & =(-1)^{3}+7(-1)^{2}+8(-1)=-1+7-8=-2\end{aligned}
$$

So, we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point $(2,-2).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2t+\frac{1}{2},\,{y}^{′}(t)=3{t}^{2}+14t+8
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{3{t}^{2}+14t+8}{2t+\frac{1}{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=-1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t\,=\,-1} & =\frac{3(-1)^{2}+14(-1)+8}{2(-1)+\frac{1}{2}} \\  & =\frac{-3}{(-\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(2,-2)$ and the slope $m=2.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(-2) & =2(x-2) \\ y+2 & =2x-4 \\ y & =2x-4-2 \\ y & =2x-6.\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent crosses the $y$-axis when $x=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2(0)-6 \\ y & =0-6 \\ y & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the tangent to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis at  $(0,\,-6).$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{1}^{2}x\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
Let $u={x}^{2}-1.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,x\text{d}x=\frac{\text{d}u}{2}.
$$

Computing our limits of integration, we get

| **$x$** | $1$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **$u$** | $0$ | $3$ |

We can now solve the integral using our new variable $u,$ remembering to use the new limits of integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}x\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{(\frac{2{u}^{3/2}}{3})|}_{0}^{3} \\  & ={\frac{{u}^{3/2}}{3}|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{{3}^{3/2}}{3}-\frac{{0}^{3/2}}{3} \\  & =\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The Taylor series for the function $f(x)$ about $x=0$ is given by

$$
f(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-1)^{n}\sqrt{n}{(\frac{x}{6})}^{n}.
$$

The series converges to $f(x)$ for $|x|<R,$ where $R$ is the radius of convergence of the Taylor series. Calculate the radius of convergence of the series expansion of ${f}^{′}(x),$ the derivative of $f(x),$ about $x=0.$

The radius of convergence of the series expansion of ${f}^{′}(x)$ is
{{field-1}}.
:question/worked-solution:
The radius of convergence for the Taylor series of ${f}^{′}(x)$ is the same as the Taylor series of $f(x).$ So, to find the radius of convergence of ${f}^{′}(x),$ we need to compute $R.$

To calculate $R,$ we can use the ratio test. Computing the limit of the absolute value of the ratio of two consecutive terms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{(-1)^{n+1}\sqrt{n+1}{(\frac{x}{6})}^{n+1}}{(-1)^{n}\sqrt{n}{(\frac{x}{6})}^{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{\sqrt{n+1}}{\sqrt{n}}||\frac{x}{6}| \\  & =\frac{|x|}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The series converges when $L<1.$ So, it converges when

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{|x|}{6} & <1 \\ |x| & <6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of convergence of the series expansion of ${f}^{′}(x)$ is $R=6.$

:question/problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=4\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,y=2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,0<t<\infty .
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=e$ on the curve. Find the equation of the normal to the curve at $C.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=e$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡e=4, \\ y & =2e\operatorname{ln}⁡e=2e\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point $(4,2e).$ For this, we need to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\frac{4}{t},\,{y}^{′}(t)=2\operatorname{ln}⁡t+2
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡t+2}{(\frac{4}{t})} \\  & =\frac{t\operatorname{ln}⁡t+t}{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=e,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=e} & =\frac{e\operatorname{ln}⁡e+e}{2} \\  & =\frac{e+e}{2}=e\,.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope ${m}_{n}$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m$:

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{\,e\,}
$$

To calculate the equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(4,2e)$ and the slope ${m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{\,e\,}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-2e & =(-\frac{1}{\,e\,})(x-4) \\ y-2e & =-\frac{1}{\,e\,}x+\frac{4}{\,e\,} \\ y & =-\frac{1}{\,e\,}x+\frac{2{e}^{2}+4}{\,e\,}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the equation of the midline for a transformed sine function with a minimum value of $- \frac{83}{6}$ and a maximum value of $- \frac{22}{3}.$
:question/worked-solution:
A sinusoidal graph's midline (or vertical shift) is the horizontal line that divides it vertically in half. 

The equation of the midline is given by

$$
y=\frac{{y}_{\text{min}}+{y}_{\text{max}}}{2},
$$

where ${y}_{\text{min}}$ and ${y}_{\text{max}}$ are the minimum and maximum values of the function. The midline equals the average of the maximum and minimum values. 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{y}_{\text{min}}+{y}_{\text{max}}}{2} & =\frac{- \frac{83}{6}+(- \frac{22}{3})}{2} \\  & =\frac{\frac{-83}{6}+(\frac{-44}{6})}{2} \\  & =\frac{- \frac{127}{6}}{2} \\  & =- \frac{127}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the midline is $y=- \frac{127}{12}.$

:question/problem: Given that ${a}_{1}=-\frac{5}{2}$ and $\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}=-\frac{1}{10}$ for all integers $n\ge 1,$ find the value of ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given series is geometric series because the ratio of any two consecutive terms is constant.

The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

We're told that the first term is

$$
{a}_{1}=-\frac{5}{2}.
$$

The common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}=-\frac{1}{10}.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{-\frac{5}{2}}{(1-(-\frac{1}{10}))} \\  & =\frac{-\frac{5}{2}}{(\frac{11}{10})} \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{10}{11} \\  & =-\frac{25}{11}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/8c/8ce8a8061ec087c39ce93d73d0566832f33c4e6ce5c2f5185170c9372a0d88fa.png)

Consider the finite region above bounded by $y=2x+2$ and $y=\sqrt{4x+4},$ as shown above. Calculate the volume of the solid generated when this region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x\text{-axis.}$
:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=2x+2$ and $g(x)=\sqrt{4x+4}.$

First, we determine the limits of integration. To do that, we find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =g(x) \\ 2x+2 & =\sqrt{4x+4} \\ 2(x+1) & =\sqrt{4x+4} \\ 4(x+1)^{2} & =4x+4 \\ {x}^{2}+2x+1 & =x+1 \\ {x}^{2}+x & =0 \\ x(x+1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the limits of integration are from $x=-1$ to $x=0.$

Let's draw our vertical arrow through the region to determine the inner function and the outer function. The arrow should be pointing *away* from the axis of rotation.

![](images/0a/0a6bdcc071500ac8dd40143c3219a14c80fc73d543d7307cb2c880a22db793a3.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner function $y=f(x)=2x+2,$ and

- *leaves* through the outer function $y=g(x)=\sqrt{4x+4}.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{a}^{b}([\text{outer}]^{2}-[\text{inner}]^{2})\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{0}({[\sqrt{4x+4}]}^{2}-{[2x+2]}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{0}[4x+4-(2(x+1))^{2}]\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{0}[4(x+1)-4({x}^{2}+2x+1)]\text{d}x \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{-1}^{0}[x+1-({x}^{2}+2x+1)]\text{d}x \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{-1}^{0}(-{x}^{2}-x)\text{d}x \\  & =4\pi {(-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})|}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =4\pi (0-(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2})) \\  & =4\pi (\frac{1}{6}) \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/98/98bc6f2ea4d71368226f0f784d629e98949e07005bc08158206de35a87bea520.png)

Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r=3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ for $\frac{3\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 2\pi ,$ as shown above.
:question/worked-solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{3\pi }{2}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=2\pi $, this gives 

$$

$$

:question/problem:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2+y-x}{3}, & 0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{5-2x}{6}, & 0\le x\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $X$ are shown above. Find the conditional expected value $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=1].$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]$ is a function of $x.$ 

The conditional density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{2+y-x}{3})}{(\frac{5-2x}{6})} \\  & =\frac{2(2+y-x)}{5-2x},\end{aligned}
$$

 

where $0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$

Now, substituting $x=1$ into the expression for ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x),$ we get

$$
{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,1)=\frac{2(2+y-1)}{5-2\cdot 1}=\frac{2(1+y)}{3}.
$$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,1)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\cdot \frac{2(1+y)}{3}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}(y+{y}^{2})\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}[(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3})-0] \\  & =\frac{5}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the matrix $Q$ given below?

Select all that apply.

$$
Q=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4 \sqrt{2}}{3} & -1 & \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{3} & \frac{3}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ - \frac{8 \sqrt{2}}{3} & 2 & - \sqrt{2}\end{bmatrix}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
Remember that a square matrix is singular if its determinant is equal to $0.$

Using the formula, we take the alternating sum of the entries in the top row of the matrix, multiplied by their respective minors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(Q) & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{4 \sqrt{2}}{3} & -1 & \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{3} & \frac{3}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ - \frac{8 \sqrt{2}}{3} & 2 & - \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{4 \sqrt{2}}{3}|\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ 2 & - \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}|+1|\begin{aligned}\frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{3} & \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ - \frac{8 \sqrt{2}}{3} & - \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}|+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}|\begin{aligned}\frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{3} & \frac{3}{2} \\ - \frac{8 \sqrt{2}}{3} & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{4 \sqrt{2}}{3}(- \frac{3 \sqrt{2}}{2}- \sqrt{2})+1(- \frac{4}{3}+\frac{8}{3})+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\frac{4 \sqrt{2}}{3}+4 \sqrt{2}) \\  & =\frac{4 \sqrt{2}}{3}\cdot (- \frac{5 \sqrt{2}}{2})+1\cdot \frac{4}{3}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \frac{16 \sqrt{2}}{3} \\  & =- \frac{20}{3}+\frac{4}{3}+\frac{16}{3} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Since $det(Q)=0$, the matrix is singular. 

Therefore, only statements “$Q$ is a singular matrix” and $det(Q)=0$ are true.

:question/problem:
Consider the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y + 2x + 4 &=0 \\ 4y - 4x + 9 &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

This system of equations has {{field-1}}.
:question/worked-solution:
Let's start by solving the system using elimination.

First, rearrange each equation to put the variable terms on the left and the constant on the right:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2x + y &= -4 \\
-4x + 4y &= -9
\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that if we multiply the first equation by $2$, then we will get a $4x$ term that can cancel with the $-4x$ term in the second equation:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x + y &=-4 && \mid \cdot (2) \\ -4x + 4y &=-9\end{aligned}\right.
$$

When we add the two equations, the $x$ terms cancel, and we can solve for $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
4x + 2y &= -8 \\
-4x + 4y &= -9 \\
6y &= (-8 - 9) \\
6y &= -17 \\
y &= - \frac{17}{6}
\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the first equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2x + (1)(- \frac{17}{6}) &= -4 \\
2x &= - \frac{7}{6} \\
x &= - \frac{7}{12}
\end{aligned}
$$

The system has *a single solution*, $(- \frac{7}{12},- \frac{17}{6})$.

:question/problem: A heated metal body cools in a room at ${18}^{∘}\text{C}.$ Its temperature is ${60}^{∘}\text{C}$ after $3$ minutes and ${39}^{∘}\text{C}$ after $7$ minutes. The temperature $T(t)$, in degrees Celsius, obeys Newton's law of cooling, with $t$ measured in minutes since cooling began. To the nearest minute, how long after cooling began does the body reach ${25}^{∘}\text{C}$?
:question/worked-solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-18),\qquad k>0.
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-18} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-18} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-18| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-18>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-18 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-18 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-18 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =18+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

Apply the two observed conditions $T(3)=60$ and $T(7)=39$:

$$
\begin{aligned}60 & =18+Ke^{-3k} \\ 42 & =Ke^{-3k} \\ 39 & =18+Ke^{-7k} \\ 21 & =Ke^{-7k}\end{aligned}
$$

Divide the excess temperatures to eliminate $K$, then take natural logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{21}{42} & =\frac{Ke^{-7k}}{Ke^{-3k}} \\ \frac{1}{2} & =e^{-4k} \\ \ln(\frac{1}{2}) & =-4k \\ k & =\frac{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Now substitute this rate into $T(3)=60$ to determine the constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}42 & =Ke^{-3(\frac{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}{4})} \\ K & =42e^{3(\frac{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}{4})} \\ K & =42\left(\frac{42}{21}\right)^{\frac{3}{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution satisfying both observations is

$$
T(t)=18+42\left(\frac{42}{21}\right)^{\frac{3}{4}}e^{-(\frac{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}{4})t}.
$$

Substituting the two observation times confirms the model:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(3) & =18+(42\left(\frac{42}{21}\right)^{\frac{3}{4}})e^{-(\frac{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}{4})\cdot 3}=60 \\ T(7) & =18+(42\left(\frac{42}{21}\right)^{\frac{3}{4}})e^{-(\frac{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}{4})\cdot 7}=39\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the body reaches ${25}^{∘}\text{C}.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T({t}_{1}) & =25 \\ 18+Ke^{-k{t}_{1}} & =25 \\ Ke^{-k{t}_{1}} & =7 \\ e^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{7}{K} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\ln\left(\frac{7}{K}\right) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\ln\left(\frac{7}{K}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute the values of $K$ and $k$ to obtain the time measured since cooling began:

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{\frac{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}{4}}\ln\left(\frac{7}{42\left(\frac{42}{21}\right)^{\frac{3}{4}}}\right) \\ {t}_{1} & =3+4\frac{\ln(\frac{1}{6})}{\ln(\frac{1}{2})}≈13\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$
