First, let's recall the quotient rule for natural logarithms:

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡(a)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(b)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{a}{b})
$$

If we factor the given expression and use the quotient rule for logarithms, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}6\operatorname{ln}⁡(68)-6\operatorname{ln}⁡(17) & =6(\operatorname{ln}⁡(68)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(17)) \\  & =6\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{68}{17}) \\  & =6\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

$$
6\operatorname{ln}⁡(68)-6\operatorname{ln}⁡(17)=6\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)
$$

The sum of cubes formula is given by

$$
{a}^{3}+{b}^{3}=(a+b)({a}^{2}-ab+{b}^{2}).
$$

Notice that we can write our expression as a sum of cubes, as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{27}+{z}^{3}={(\frac{1}{3})}^{3}+{z}^{3}
$$

Now, we factor our expression using the sum of cubes formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{27}+{z}^{3} & ={(\frac{1}{3})}^{3}+{z}^{3} \\  & =(\frac{1}{3}+z)({(\frac{1}{3})}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}\cdot z+{z}^{2}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{3}+z)(\frac{1}{9}-\frac{z}{3}+{z}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: $\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{z}^{6}}{13})=$
:question/worked-solution:
The laws of logarithms are:

- ${log}_{n}⁡(a)+{log}_{n}⁡(b)={log}_{n}⁡(ab)$ - the product rule

- ${log}_{n}⁡(a)-{log}_{n}⁡(b)={log}_{n}⁡(\frac{a}{b})$ - the quotient rule

- ${log}_{n}⁡({c}^{m})=m{log}_{n}⁡(c)$ - the power rule

Using the quotient quotient and then the power rule for logarithms, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{z}^{6}}{13}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{6})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(13) \\  & =6\operatorname{ln}⁡(z)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(13).\end{aligned}
$$

The difference of cubes formula is given by

$$
{a}^{3}-{b}^{3}=(a-b)({a}^{2}+ab+{b}^{2}).
$$

Notice that all of the terms have a common factor of $8.$ To simplify the computation, we can factor out the $8,$ as follows:

$$
\frac{8}{{t}^{6}}-1000=8(\frac{1}{{t}^{6}}-125)
$$

The expression in parentheses can be written as a difference of cubes:

$$
8(\frac{1}{{t}^{6}}-125)=8({(\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})}^{3}-{5}^{3})
$$

Now, we factor the expression in parentheses using the difference of cubes formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{8}{{t}^{6}}-1000 & =8({(\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})}^{3}-{5}^{3}) \\  & =8(\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}-5)({(\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})}^{2}+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\cdot 5+{5}^{2}) \\  & =8(\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}-5)(\frac{1}{{t}^{4}}+\frac{5}{{t}^{2}}+25)\end{aligned}
$$

The laws of logarithms are:

- ${log}_{n}⁡(a)+{log}_{n}⁡(b)={log}_{n}⁡(ab)$ - the product rule

- ${log}_{n}⁡(a)-{log}_{n}⁡(b)={log}_{n}⁡(\frac{a}{b})$ - the quotient rule

- ${log}_{n}⁡({c}^{m})=m{log}_{n}⁡(c)$ - the power rule

Note that ${log}_{5}⁡({x}^{2}{y}^{3})$ can be rewritten using the product and power rules as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{5}⁡({x}^{2}{y}^{3}) & ={log}_{5}⁡({x}^{2})+{log}_{5}⁡({y}^{3}) \\  & =2{log}_{5}⁡(x)+3{log}_{5}⁡(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since ${log}_{5}⁡(x)=3$ and ${log}_{5}⁡(y)=2$, we conclude that

$$
2{log}_{5}⁡(x)+3{log}_{5}⁡(y)=2\cdot 3+3\cdot 2=12.
$$

Hence

$$
{log}_{5}⁡({x}^{2}{y}^{3})=12.
$$

The laws of logarithms are:

- ${log}_{n}⁡({c}^{m})=m{log}_{n}⁡(c)$ - the power rule

Using the quotient rule and then the product rule for logarithms, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{3}⁡(\frac{5x}{27}) & ={log}_{3}⁡(5x)-{log}_{3}⁡(27) \\  & ={log}_{3}⁡(5)+{log}_{3}⁡(x)-{log}_{3}⁡({3}^{3}) \\  & ={log}_{3}⁡(5)+{log}_{3}⁡(x)-3.\end{aligned}
$$

The laws of logarithms are:

Note that ${log}_{2}⁡(x{y}^{3})$ can be rewritten using the product and power rules as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{2}⁡(x{y}^{3}) & ={log}_{2}⁡(x)+{log}_{2}⁡({y}^{3}) \\  & ={log}_{2}⁡(x)+3{log}_{2}⁡(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since ${log}_{2}⁡(x)=k$ and ${log}_{2}⁡(y)=4,$ we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{2}⁡(x)+3{log}_{2}⁡(y) & =k+3\cdot 4 \\  & =k+12.\end{aligned}

Therefore,

:question/problem:
Suppose ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},{X}_{3},{X}_{4},{X}_{5}$ is an I.I.D random sample with ${X}_{i}∼N(\theta ,{1}^{2}),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown mean. The log-likelihood function of the sample $0.7,\,0.6,\,-0.5,\,1.7,\,-1.1$ is

$$
l(\theta )=-2.5\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )+a+b\theta +c{\theta }^{2}
$$

What is the value of $a+b+c?$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i};\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=5$ independent normal random variables with unknown mean $\theta $ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=1,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x,\theta )=\frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-\frac{1}{2}{(\frac{x-\theta }{\sigma })}^{2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Next, we write down the log-density function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡f(x,\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{(x-\theta )^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{n}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\frac{({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}}{2} \\  & =-\frac{n}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{1}{2}({\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}-2\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+n{\theta }^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

For our sample, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} \\  & =0.7+0.6+(-0.5)+1.7+(-1.1) \\  & =1.4 \\ C & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2} \\  & =(0.7)^{2}+(0.6)^{2}+(-0.5)^{2}+(1.7)^{2}+(-1.1)^{2} \\  & =5.2\end{aligned}
$$

and $n=5.$ Therefore,  

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =-\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{1}{2}(5.2-2\theta \cdot (1.4)+5{\theta }^{2}) \\  & =-2.5\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )+(-2.6)+(1.4)\theta +(-2.5){\theta }^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b+c=-2.6+(1.4)+(-2.5)=-3.7.
$$

:question/problem: Consider the equation $2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5x}{2})+3=0$ for $0\le x<2\pi .$ If the solutions ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3},{x}_{4}$ and ${x}_{5}$ are written in ascending order, what is the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{3}?$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5x}{2})+3 & =0 \\ 2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5x}{2}) & =-3 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5x}{2}) & =-\frac{3}{2\sqrt{3}} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5x}{2}) & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We will find the general solution to the equation, and then generate all of the solutions in the required domain.

The general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5x}{2} & =\frac{5\pi }{6}+2n\pi , & \, & \, & \frac{5x}{2} & =\frac{7\pi }{6}+2n\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the two equations above for $x$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}5x & =\frac{5\pi }{3}+4n\pi  & \, & \, & 5x & =\frac{7\pi }{3}+4n\pi  \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{3}+\frac{4n\pi }{5} & \, & \, & x & =\frac{7\pi }{15}+\frac{4n\pi }{5} \\ x & =\frac{(12n+5)\pi }{15} & \, & \, & x & =\frac{(12n+7)\pi }{15}\end{aligned}
$$

We set $n=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…,$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain $0\le x<2\pi .$

- Setting $n=0$ gives $x=\frac{\pi }{3}$ and $x=\frac{7\pi }{15}$

- Setting $n=1$ gives $x=\frac{17\pi }{15}$  and $x=\frac{19\pi }{15}.$

- Setting $n=2$ gives $x=\frac{29\pi }{15}$  and $x=\frac{31\pi }{15}.$ We reject the solution $\frac{31\pi }{15}$ since it lies outside the domain of interest.

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain $0\le x<2\pi .$ So, the solutions ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3},{x}_{4},{x}_{5}$ (written in ascending order) are

$$
x=\frac{\pi }{3},\,\frac{7\pi }{15},\,\frac{17\pi }{15},\,\frac{19\pi }{15},\,\frac{29\pi }{15}.
$$

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{3}=\frac{\pi }{3}\cdot \frac{17\pi }{15}=\frac{17{\pi }^{2}}{45}.
$$

The laws of logarithms are:

- ${log}_{n}⁡(a)+{log}_{n}⁡(b)={log}_{n}⁡(ab)$ - the product rule

- ${log}_{n}⁡(a)-{log}_{n}⁡(b)={log}_{n}⁡(\frac{a}{b})$ - the quotient rule

- ${log}_{n}⁡({c}^{m})=m{log}_{n}⁡(c)$ - the power rule

Using the quotient rule for logarithms, we get:

$$
{log}_{3}⁡(\frac{{x}^{2}{y}^{3}}{\sqrt{z}})={log}_{3}⁡({x}^{2}{y}^{3})-{log}_{3}⁡(\sqrt{z})
$$

Now, using the product rule for logarithms, we obtain

$$
{log}_{3}⁡({x}^{2}{y}^{3})-{log}_{3}⁡(\sqrt{z})={log}_{3}⁡({x}^{2})+{log}_{3}⁡({y}^{3})-{log}_{3}⁡(\sqrt{z}).
$$

Finally, using the power rule for logarithms, we have

$$
{log}_{3}⁡({x}^{2})+{log}_{3}⁡({y}^{3})-{log}_{3}⁡(\sqrt{z})=2{log}_{3}⁡(x)+3{log}_{3}⁡(y)-\frac{1}{2}{log}_{3}⁡(z).
$$

Therefore

$$
{log}_{3}⁡(\frac{{x}^{2}{y}^{3}}{\sqrt{z}})=2{log}_{3}⁡(x)+3{log}_{3}⁡(y)-\frac{1}{2}{log}_{3}⁡(z).
$$

The first three terms are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}=\frac{x}{4},\,{a}_{2}=x,\,{a}_{3}=64.\end{aligned}
$$

The common ratio of the first two terms is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{x}{(\frac{x}{4})}=x\cdot \frac{4}{x}=4.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, the common ratio of the second and third terms is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}}=\frac{64}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, by equating the values for $r$ and solving for $x,$ we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =\frac{64}{x} \\ 4x & =64 \\ x & =\frac{64}{4} \\ x & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/5e/5e11606627f4b91c977670cf9f919aff8b659cb5b4776cf3d04bb561b50b79fb.png)

Suppose that $F$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ defined over the region $D$ above. Given that 

$$
{∮}_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=- \frac{17}{2},\,{∮}_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=- \frac{19}{3},\,{∮}_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r=\frac{23}{3},
$$

where ${C}_{1},$ ${C}_{2},$ and ${C}_{3}$ are oriented clockwise, calculate the value of ${∮}_{∂D}F\cdot \text{d}r.$
:question/worked-solution:

:question/problem: Find the exact solution of the equation ${3}^{x}=5.$
:question/worked-solution:
We take ${log}_{3}$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{x} & =5 \\ {log}_{3}⁡({3}^{x}) & ={log}_{3}⁡(5)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that ${log}_{b}⁡({b}^{c})=c$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
x={log}_{3}⁡(5)
$$

Previously, we found that the slope of the tangent line at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{3}$ is

$$
m=-\sqrt{3}.
$$

The equation of the tangent is

$$
y-{y}_{0}=m(x-{x}_{0}),
$$

where $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ are the coordinates of the point on the curve that correspond to $\theta =\frac{\pi }{3}.$ Let's work these out. 

In part 1, we found that

$\,$ $x(\theta )=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,$ and $\,y(\theta )=6{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .$

As a result, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{0} & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ) \\  & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}) \\  & =3\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}, \\ {y}_{0} & =6{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =6{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =6{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})=(\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{9}{2}).$

$$

$$

:question/problem: The waiting time for one customer to be served at a cafeteria varies continuously, independently, and at a constant average rate of one person served every $4$  minutes. Determine the probability that the next person is served at least $2$ minutes after the previous one. Round your answer to $4$ decimal places.
:question/worked-solution:
Since the waiting time for one customer to be served at the cafeteria varies continuously, independently, and at a constant average rate, we can model the time until serving the next person as an exponential distribution.

An exponential random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda $ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\lambda {e}^{-\lambda x}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ be the time needed to serve the next person. The time needed to serve the next person can be modeled as an exponential random variable. Since one person is served every $4$ minutes on average, the rate is $\lambda =\frac{1}{4},$ and we can write 

$$
X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{1}{4}).
$$

 In this case, $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-x/4}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability that the next person will be served at least $2$ minutes after the previous one is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 2) & ={\int }_{2}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{\infty }\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-x/4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-x/4}{|}_{2}^{\infty } \\  & =-{e}^{-\infty }+{e}^{-2/4} \\  & =0+{e}^{-1/2} \\  & ={e}^{-1/2} \\  & ≈0.6065.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
A customer support team resolves tickets continuously in time, independently, and at a constant average rate of $1$ ticket every $5$ minutes. If a ticket has been open for $20$ minutes already, what is the probability that it will remain unresolved for at least another $10$ minutes? Round your final answer to **three decimal places.**

The required probability is
{{field-1}}.
:question/worked-solution:
Since the customer support team resolves tickets continuously in time, independently, and at a constant average rate, we can model the time until the next ticket is resolved using an exponential distribution.

Let $X$ be the ticket resolving time, in minutes. Since the team resolves $1$ ticket every $5$ minutes on average, the rate is $\lambda =\frac{1}{5}$ tickets per minute, and we can write 

$$
X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{1}{5}).
$$

Recall that exponential random variables have the memoryless property. So, given two positive real numbers $s,t,$ we have that

$$
P(X>s+t\,|\,X>s)=P(X>t)={e}^{-\lambda t}.
$$

In our case, we have $\lambda =\frac{1}{5},$ $s=20,$ and $t=10.$ 

Substituting these values into the above formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>20+10\,|\,X>20) & =P(X>10) \\  & ={e}^{-\lambda t} \\  & ={e}^{-(1/5)\cdot (10)} \\  & ={e}^{-2} \\  & ≈0.135.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: On a busy waterway, barges pass by a particular point continuously, independently, and at a constant average rate of one every $10$ minutes. Determine the probability that the next barge will pass between $5$ and $7$ minutes after the previous one. Round your answer to four decimal places.
:question/worked-solution:
Since barges pass continuously, independently, and at a constant average rate, we can model the time between two successive barges using an exponential distribution.

An exponential random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda $ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\lambda {e}^{-\lambda x}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ be the amount of time between two successive barges. Since a barge passes every $10$ minutes, the rate is $\lambda =\frac{1}{10}$ barges per minute.

The time interval between two successive barges can be modeled as an exponential random variable with rate $\lambda =\frac{1}{10},$ and we can write 

$$
X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{1}{10}).
$$

So, $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{10}{e}^{-x/10}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability that the next barge will pass between $5$ and $7$ minutes after the previous one is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(5<X<7) & ={\int }_{5}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{5}^{7}\frac{1}{10}{e}^{-x/10}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-x/10}{|}_{5}^{7} \\  & =-{e}^{-7/10}+{e}^{-5/10} \\  & ≈0.1099\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
While riding on a road, a cyclist encounters potholes continuously in time, independently, and at a constant average rate of $4$ potholes per hour. If the cyclist has not encountered any potholes in the past $30$ minutes, what is the probability that he will encounter a pothole in the next $10$ minutes? Round your final answer to **three decimal places.**

The required probability is
{{field-1}}.
:question/worked-solution:
Since the cyclist encounters potholes continuously in time, independently, and at a constant average rate, we can model the time until the next pothole as an exponential distribution.

Let $X$ be the time, in minutes, until the cyclist encounters the next pothole. Since the cyclist encounters, on average, $4$ potholes per hour (or $1$ pothole every $15$ minutes), the rate is $\lambda =\frac{1}{15}$ potholes per minute, and we can write 

$$
X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{1}{15}).
$$

Recall that exponential random variables have the memoryless property. Therefore, given two positive real numbers $s,t,$ we have that

$$
P(X>s+t\,|\,X>s)=P(X>t)={e}^{-\lambda t}.
$$

We can compute the complementary conditional probability as follows:

$$
P(X\le s+t\,|\,X>s)=1-P(X>s+t\,|\,X>s)=1-{e}^{-\lambda t}
$$

In our case, we have $\lambda =\frac{1}{15},$ $s=30,$ and $t=10.$ 

Substituting these values into the above formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 30+10\,|\,X>30) & =P(X\le 10) \\  & =1-{e}^{-\lambda t} \\  & =1-{e}^{-(1/15)\cdot (10)} \\  & =1-{e}^{-2/3} \\  & ≈0.487.\end{aligned}

$$

Hence, our limits of integration are from $y=-1$ to $y=2.$

$$

$$

$(r,\theta )=(${{field-1}}$,$

:question/worked-solution:
To determine the polar coordinates of the intersection points, we will solve the following system of equations for $r$ and $\theta :$  

$$
\{\begin{aligned}r=2-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ r=-7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

We begin by setting the equations equal to each other and solve for $\theta .$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =-7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 2 & =-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =-\frac{1}{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation in the interval $[0,2\pi ),$ we obtain ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{2\pi }{3}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{4\pi }{3}.$

Therefore, the $\theta $-coordinate of the point that we're interested in is $\theta =\frac{4\pi }{3},$ since it lies in the third quadrant.

Now, we use the equation $r=-7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ to find the $r$-coordinate of our point:

$$
r=-7\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{3})=\frac{7}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the polar coordinates of the desired intersection point are

$\,$ $(r,\theta )=(\frac{7}{2},\text{ }\frac{4\pi }{3}).$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{8}{7}xy, & 0\le y\le 1,\,y\le x\le 2 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{7}y(4-{y}^{2}), & 0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $Y$ are shown above. Find the conditional variance $\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=\frac{1}{2}]$ given that the corresponding expected value is ${\mu }_{X|\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{7}{5}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the conditional variance of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=y] & =\text{E}[(X-{\mu }_{X|y})^{2}\,|\,Y=y] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=y]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where 

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ is a function of $y.$ 

The conditional density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{\frac{8}{7}xy}{\frac{4}{7}y(4-{y}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{2x}{4-{y}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le y\le 1,\,y\le x\le 2.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=0.$

Now, substituting $y=\frac{1}{2}$ into the expression for ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y),$ we get

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,\frac{1}{2})=\frac{2x}{(4-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2})}=\frac{2x}{(\frac{15}{4})}=\frac{8}{15}x.
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=\frac{1}{2}] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{8}{15}x\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{8}{15}{\int }_{1/2}^{2}{x}^{3}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{8}{15}{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}]}_{1/2}^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{15}\cdot \frac{1}{4}[{x}^{4}]_{1/2}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{15}(16-\frac{1}{16}) \\  & =\frac{2}{15}\cdot \frac{255}{16} \\  & =\frac{17}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=\frac{1}{2}] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=\frac{1}{2}]-{\mu }_{X|\frac{1}{2}}^{2} \\  & =\frac{17}{8}-{(\frac{7}{5})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{17}{8}-\frac{49}{25} \\  & =\frac{33}{200}.\end{aligned}
$$

To determine the polar coordinates of the intersection points, we will solve the following system of equations for $r$ and $\theta :$  

$$
\{\begin{aligned}r=3-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ r=4+3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

We begin by setting the equations equal to each other and solve for $\theta .$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =4+3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 5\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =-1 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =-\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation in the interval $[{0}^{∘},{360}^{∘}),$ we obtain ${\theta }_{1}≈{191.5}^{∘}$ and ${\theta }_{2}≈348.5,$ rounded to $1$ decimal place. 

Now, we use the equation $r=4+3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ to find the $r$-coordinates of the intersection points: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1} & =4+3\operatorname{sin}⁡{\theta }_{1}=4+3\cdot (-\frac{1}{5})=\frac{17}{5}=3.4 \\ {r}_{2} & =4+3\operatorname{cos}⁡{\theta }_{2}=4+3\cdot (-\frac{1}{5})=\frac{17}{5}=3.4\end{aligned}

$\,$ $(r,\theta )≈(3.4,{191.5}^{∘})\,$ and $\,(r,\theta )≈(3.4,{348.5}^{∘}).$

Let $X$ and $Y$ be continuous random variables. 
Find the conditional variance $\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=4]$ given that the conditional probability density function ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,4)$ is shown above and the corresponding expected value is ${\mu }_{Y|4}=\frac{8}{5}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the conditional variance of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=x] & =\text{E}[(Y-{\mu }_{Y|x})^{2}\,|\,X=x] \\  & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\,|\,X=x]-{\mu }_{Y|x}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where 

$$
\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\,|\,X=x]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }{y}^{2}\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\,|\,X=4] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }{y}^{2}\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,4)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }{y}^{2}\cdot \frac{8}{3{y}^{11/3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{8}{3{y}^{5/3}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{8}{3}{y}^{-5/3}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{8}{3}\cdot (-\frac{3}{2})\cdot {y}^{-2/3}]}_{1}^{\infty } \\  & ={[-\frac{4}{{y}^{2/3}}]}_{1}^{\infty } \\  & =0-(-4) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=4] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\,|\,X=4]-{\mu }_{Y|4}^{2} \\  & =4-{(\frac{8}{5})}^{2} \\  & =4-\frac{64}{25} \\  & =\frac{36}{25}.\end{aligned}

The region enclosed by the curves $x={y}^{2}+2$ and $y=x-4$ for $y\in [-1,2]$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=-2.$ Find the volume $V$ of the resulting solid. Do not round the answer.

$V=$
{{field-1}}
:question/worked-solution:
First, since we are rotating about a vertical axis, we need to solve the equation of our second curve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =x-4\,⟹\,x=y+4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](images/7e/7e08a30f9ef1f8ce748ba0fcac73f1e93d994e4fd3a3d3d1367568c89c29f4d0.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x={y}^{2}+2,$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $x=y+4.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $x=y+4.$

![](images/26/262546bf3f1d1c9025d23b9fb134c9de7b5299c7b6383563531dffa62244163d.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}{[\,(y+4)-(-2)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}{[y+6]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x={y}^{2}+2.$

![](images/ce/cefab13ca3d09fcf596e7906384c2efd1718c289783792f1b0ff950632c823ad.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}{[\,({y}^{2}+2)-(-2)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}{[{y}^{2}+4]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of our solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}({[y+6]}^{2}-{[{y}^{2}+4]}^{2})\,\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}({y}^{2}+12y+36-({y}^{4}+8{y}^{2}+16))\,\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}(12y+20-{y}^{4}-7{y}^{2})\,\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {(6{y}^{2}+20y-\frac{{y}^{5}}{5}-\frac{7{y}^{3}}{3})|}_{-1}^{2} \\  & =\pi [\,(6\cdot {2}^{2}+20\cdot 2-\frac{{2}^{5}}{5}-\frac{7\cdot {2}^{3}}{3})\,-\,(6-20+\frac{1}{5}+\frac{7}{3})\,] \\  & =\pi (\frac{584}{15}-(-\frac{172}{15})) \\  & =\frac{252\pi }{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $Y$ are shown above. Find the conditional variance $\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=1]$ given that the corresponding expected value is ${\mu }_{X|1}=\frac{8}{15}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the conditional variance of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=y] & =\text{E}[(X-{\mu }_{X|y})^{2}\,|\,Y=y] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=y]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where 

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ is a function of $y.$ 

The conditional density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{2(x+2y)}{3})}{(\frac{1+4y}{3})} \\  & =\frac{2(x+2y)}{1+4y},\end{aligned}
$$

 

where $0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=0.$ 

Now, substituting $y=1$ into the expression for ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y),$ we get

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)=\frac{2(x+2\cdot 1)}{1+4\cdot 1}=\frac{2x+4}{5}.
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}(\frac{2x+4}{5})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{2}+\frac{4{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{4}{3})-0] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\frac{11}{6}] \\  & =\frac{11}{30}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=1] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=1]-{\mu }_{X|1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{11}{30}-{(\frac{8}{15})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{37}{450}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=3{e}^{-4x-6}+6$ at the point where $x=- \frac{7}{4}.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=3{e}^{u}+6,\,u=-4x-6.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=3{e}^{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-4.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =3{e}^{u}\cdot (-4) \\  & =-12{e}^{u} \\  & =-12{e}^{-4x-6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=- \frac{7}{4}$, we have to evaluate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{x=- \frac{7}{4}} & =-12{e}^{-4x-6}{|}_{x=- \frac{7}{4}} \\ & =-12{e}^{(-4)(- \frac{7}{4})-6} \\ & =- 12 e.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, the $y$-value of the point on the curve where $x=x_1=- \frac{7}{4}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}y_1 & =(3{e}^{-4x-6}+6){|}_{x=- \frac{7}{4}} \\ & =3{e}^{(-4)(- \frac{7}{4})-6}+6 \\ & =6 + 3 e.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at that point:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-y_1 & =m(x-x_1) \\ y-(6 + 3 e) & =(- 12 e)(x-(- \frac{7}{4})) \\ y-(6 + 3 e) & =- 12 e x-(21 e) \\ y & =- 12 e x - 18 e + 6.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=-2{e}^{-3x+2}+3$ at the point where $x=\frac{1}{3}.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=-2{e}^{u}+3,\,u=-3x+2.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=-2{e}^{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =-2{e}^{u}\cdot (-3) \\  & =6{e}^{u} \\  & =6{e}^{-3x+2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=\frac{1}{3}$, we have to evaluate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{x=\frac{1}{3}} & =6{e}^{-3x+2}{|}_{x=\frac{1}{3}} \\ & =6{e}^{(-3)(\frac{1}{3})+2} \\ & =6 e.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, the $y$-value of the point on the curve where $x=x_1=\frac{1}{3}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}y_1 & =(-2{e}^{-3x+2}+3){|}_{x=\frac{1}{3}} \\ & =-2{e}^{(-3)(\frac{1}{3})+2}+3 \\ & =3 - 2 e.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at that point:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-y_1 & =m(x-x_1) \\ y-(3 - 2 e) & =(6 e)(x-(\frac{1}{3})) \\ y-(3 - 2 e) & =6 e x-(2 e) \\ y & =6 e x - 4 e + 3.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=5{e}^{6x-4}+1$ at the point where $x=\frac{5}{6}.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{x=\frac{5}{6}} & =30{e}^{6x-4}{|}_{x=\frac{5}{6}} \\ & =30{e}^{(6)(\frac{5}{6})-4} \\ & =30 e.\end{aligned}

Also, the $y$-value of the point on the curve where $x=x_1=\frac{5}{6}$ is

$$

$$

:question/problem:
Consider the following data sets:

$$
x=\{2,\,1,\,-1\},\,y=\{15,\,12,\,9\}
$$

You're given that $\overset{―}{x}=\frac{2}{3},$ $\overset{―}{y}=12,$ ${\sigma }_{x}≈1.247,$ and ${\sigma }_{y}≈2.449.$ Calculate the corresponding linear correlation coefficient. Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
:question/worked-solution:
The (population) linear correlation coefficient of the data sets $x=\{{x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}\}$ and $y=\{{y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n}\}$ is given by 

$$
\rho (x,y)=\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}}
$$

where $\text{Cov}(x,y)$ is the covariance, and ${\sigma }_{x}$ and ${\sigma }_{y}$ are the standard deviations of the data sets.

First, we need to compute the covariance:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[(2-\frac{2}{3})(15-12)+(1-\frac{2}{3})(12-12)+(-1-\frac{2}{3})(9-12)] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[(\frac{4}{3})(3)+(\frac{1}{3})(0)+(-\frac{5}{3})(-3)] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[4+0+5] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot 9 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the formula. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}} \\  & ≈\frac{3}{1.247\cdot 2.449} \\  & ≈0.98\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

:question/problem:
Evaluate the following integral.

${\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x=$ {{field-1}}
:question/worked-solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the second equation from the first, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-4x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+4x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)]}_{0}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{9\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))-\frac{1}{10}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{15\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(1-0)-\frac{1}{10}(-1-0) \\  & =\frac{4}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}xy\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{1}xy\cdot \frac{x+y}{3}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{2}+\frac{x{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{x}{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{6}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the covariance and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{2}{3}-(\frac{11}{9})(\frac{5}{9}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{81}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & ≈\frac{(-\frac{1}{81})}{(0.5329)\cdot (0.2833)} \\  & ≈-0.08,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

:question/problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{1}^{e}({log}_{2}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=({log}_{2}⁡x)^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2{log}_{2}⁡x}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \,\text{d}x=x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({log}_{2}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={({log}_{2}⁡x)}^{2}(x)-\int (x)(\frac{2{log}_{2}⁡x}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =x{({log}_{2}⁡x)}^{2}-\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int {log}_{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate  $\int {log}_{2}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{2}⁡x\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \,\text{d}x=x.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {log}_{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({log}_{2}⁡x)(x)-\int (x)(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =x{log}_{2}⁡x-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int \,\text{d}x \\  & =x{log}_{2}⁡x-\frac{x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({log}_{2}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =x{({log}_{2}⁡x)}^{2}-\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(x{log}_{2}⁡x-\frac{x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+D) \\  & =x{({log}_{2}⁡x)}^{2}-\frac{2x{log}_{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+\frac{2x}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}+C \\  & =\frac{x{ln}^{2}⁡x}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}-\frac{2x\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}+\frac{2x}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}+C \\  & =\frac{x}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}({ln}^{2}⁡x-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+2)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-\frac{2D}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{2}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$

Finally then, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}({log}_{2}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & ={[\frac{x}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}({ln}^{2}⁡x-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+2)]}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{e}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}({ln}^{2}⁡e-2\operatorname{ln}⁡e+2)-\frac{1}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}({ln}^{2}⁡1-2\operatorname{ln}⁡1+2) \\  & =\frac{e}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}-\frac{2}{{ln}^{2}⁡2} \\  & =\frac{e-2}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Find where the tangent to the curve $y=\frac{2}{x}+x$ at the point  $(2,3)$ intersects the $x$-axis.

The tangent intersects the $x$-axis at
$($
{{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}} $).$
:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=\frac{2}{x}+x.$ Let's first calculate the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2}{x}+x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2}{x})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{-1})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) \\  & =-2{x}^{-2}+1 \\  & =-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at our point is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={f}^{′}(2) \\  & =-\frac{2}{{2}^{2}}+1 \\  & =-\frac{2}{4}+1 \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}+1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the tangent is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-3 & =\frac{1}{2}(x-2) \\ y & =\frac{1}{2}x-1+3 \\ y & =\frac{1}{2}x+2.\end{aligned}
$$

To find where the tangent line intercepts the $x$-axis, we set $y=0$ and solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}x+2 & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}x & =-2 \\ x & =-2\cdot 2 \\ x & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point of intersection is $(-4,0).$

:question/problem: $\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=$
:question/worked-solution:
We need to use integration by parts. 

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u={x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({x}^{2})(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2})(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}-\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: A $500\,\text{L}$-capacity water tank initially holds $320\,\text{L}$ of water containing $20\,\text{kg}$ of a dissolved contaminant. Clean water begins to flow into the tank at a rate of $9\,\text{L/min},$ while the completely mixed water flows out at a rate of $5\,\text{L/min}.$ Find, rounded to two decimal places, the amount of contaminant in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow.
:question/worked-solution:
Let $Q$ be the amount of contaminant in the tank at time $t.$ Then, the derivative

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which contaminant enters the tank minus the rate at which contaminant leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg/min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which contaminant enters the tank.

First, note that clean water (i.e., water containing $0\,\text{kg/L}$ of contaminant) enters the tank at a rate of $9\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *contaminant* enters the tank is

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (9\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which contaminant exits the tank.

To find the rate at which contaminant leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of water in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $320\,\text{L}$ of water; clean water enters at $9\,\text{L/min},$ and mixed water leaves at $5\,\text{L/min}.$
As a result, the amount of water in the tank after $t$ minutes is

$$
V(t)=320+9t-5t=(320+4t)\,\text{L}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of contaminant in the tank, the *concentration* of the water at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{320+4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed water leaves at a rate of $5\,\text{L/min},$ *contaminant* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(5\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{320+4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =\frac{5Q}{320+4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{5Q}{4(80+t)}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0-\frac{5Q}{4(80+t)},\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}=-\frac{5}{4(80+t)}\,Q.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{5}{4(80+t)} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\,dQ & =-\frac{5}{4}\int \frac{1}{80+t}\,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-\frac{5}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|80+t|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus,

$$
Q(t)=\frac{A}{(80+t)^{5/4}}.
$$

Using the initial condition $Q(0)=20,$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{A}{{80}^{5/4}} & =20 \\ A & =20(80)^{5/4}.\end{aligned}
$$

So,

$$
Q(t)=20{(\frac{80}{80+t})}^{5/4}.
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. Since the tank has a capacity of $500\,\text{L},$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =500 \\ 320+4{t}_{o} & =500 \\ 4{t}_{o} & =180 \\ {t}_{o} & =45\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the amount of contaminant in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(45)7 & =20{(\frac{80}{80+45})}^{5/4} \\  & =20{(\frac{80}{125})}^{5/4} \\  & ≈11.45\,\text{kg},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

:question/problem:
$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{1}{2}, & \,1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

The joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ for the continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is shown above. Given that 

$$
\text{E}[X]=\frac{3}{4}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2,\,\text{E}[Y]=\frac{7}{12},\,\text{SD}[X]≈0.2898,\,\text{SD}[Y]≈0.2764,
$$

 
find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}xy\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{1}xy\cdot (\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{2{y}^{2}}{x}+\frac{1}{2}xy)\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{[\frac{2}{3x}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{4}x{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(\frac{2}{3x}+\frac{1}{4}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\frac{1}{8}{x}^{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =(\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡2+\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{8}) \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{3}+\frac{3}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the covariance and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{3}+\frac{3}{8})-(\frac{3}{4}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2)(\frac{7}{12}) \\  & =(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{3}-\frac{7\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{12})+(\frac{3}{8}-\frac{7}{16}) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{12}-\frac{1}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & ≈\frac{(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{12}-\frac{1}{16})}{(0.2898)\cdot (0.2764)} \\  & ≈-0.06,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-5x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+5x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)).\end{aligned}

Substituting this into the integral gives

Find the area $A$ of the shaded region that lies between the polar curves $r=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $r=\frac{3}{2},$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.

\,{\theta }_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{3},\,\text{ and }\,{\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{3}.

:question/problem:
Evaluate the following integral.

First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-4x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+4x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)).\end{aligned}

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)]}_{0}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{9\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))+\frac{1}{10}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{15\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(1-0)+\frac{1}{10}(-1-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

The joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ for the continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is shown above. Given that

find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician and integration by parts, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}xy\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}xy\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)}{2}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}xy\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[xy\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y)+y\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)]_{x=0}^{x=\pi /2}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[\frac{\pi }{2}y\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-y)+y\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-y)-y\operatorname{cos}⁡(-y)]\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(\frac{\pi }{2}y\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\operatorname{sin}⁡y-y\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[(\frac{\pi }{2}-1)(y\operatorname{sin}⁡y+\operatorname{cos}⁡y)+\operatorname{sin}⁡y-y\operatorname{cos}⁡y]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[(\frac{\pi }{2}-1)\frac{\pi }{2}+1-(\frac{\pi }{2}-1)] \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}-4\pi +8}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the covariance and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}-4\pi +8}{8}-(\frac{\pi }{4})(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}-8\pi +16}{16} \\  & ={(\frac{\pi }{4}-1)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & ≈\frac{{(\frac{\pi }{4}-1)}^{2}}{(0.4332)\cdot (0.4332)} \\  & ≈0.25,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

:question/problem: Which of the following gives the total area enclosed by the graph of the polar curve $r=1+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )}{3}$ for $\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi ?$
:question/worked-solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=1+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )}{3}$, ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{2}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{(1+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )}{3})}^{2}\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

:question/problem:
A vat initially holds $500\,\text{L}$ of a sugar-water solution containing $15\,\text{kg}$ of dissolved sugar.
Pure water is pumped into the vat at a rate of $14\,\text{L/min},$ while the completely mixed sugar-water solution leaves the vat at a rate of $10\,\text{L/min}.$
Find, rounded to two decimal places, the amount of sugar in the vat $14$ minutes after the water pumping begins.
:question/worked-solution:
Let $Q$ be the amount of sugar in the vat at time $t.$ Then, the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which sugar enters the vat minus the rate at which sugar leaves the vat.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which sugar enters the vat.

Note that pure water (i.e., water containing $0\,\text{kg/L}$ of sugar) enters the vat at a rate of $14\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *sugar* enters the vat is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (14\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (14\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which sugar exits the vat.

To find the rate at which sugar leaves the vat, we first determine the volume of solution in the vat at time $t.$

The vat initially contains $500\,\text{L}$ of solution; water enters at $14\,\text{L/min}$ and drains out at $10\,\text{L/min}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the vat after $t$ minutes is 

$$
500+14t-10t=(500+4t)\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the amount of sugar in the vat, the *concentration* of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{500+4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed sugar-water solution leaves at a rate of $10\,\text{L/min},$ *sugar* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(10\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{500+4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(10\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{500+4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{10Q}{500+4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{5Q}{2(125+t)}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0-\frac{5Q}{2(125+t)}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}=-\frac{5}{2(125+t)}\,Q.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{5}{2(125+t)} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\int (-\frac{5}{2(125+t)})\,dt \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \,dQ & =-\frac{5}{2}\int \frac{1}{125+t}\,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|125+t|+C \\ |Q| & ={e}^{-\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|125+t|+C} \\ Q(t) & =\frac{A}{(125+t)^{5/2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $A=\pm {e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the vat initially contains $15\,\text{kg}$ of sugar. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=15,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =15 \\ \frac{A}{(125+0)^{5/2}} & =15 \\ A & =15\cdot {125}^{5/2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
Q(t)=15{(\frac{125}{125+t})}^{5/2}
$$

Finally, the amount of sugar in the vat $14$ minutes after the water is first pumped in is

$$
Q(12)=15{(\frac{125}{139})}^{5/2}≈11.50\,\text{kg},
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

:question/problem: If $f(x)=A\cdot {(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}$ and $f(4)=2,$ then $A=${{field-1}}.
:question/worked-solution:
We substitute $x=4$ and $f(x)=2$ into the expression for $f(x)$ and solve for $A,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =A\cdot {(\frac{1}{3})}^{4} \\ 2 & =A\cdot (\frac{{1}^{4}}{{3}^{4}}) \\ 2 & =A\cdot \frac{1}{81} \\ 2\cdot 81 & =A \\ 162 & =A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $A=162.$

:question/problem:
$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{12}(xy+1), & \,{y}^{2}\le x\le 1,\,-1\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

The joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ for the continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is shown above. Given that 

$$
\text{E}[X]=\frac{3}{5},\,\text{E}[Y]=\frac{1}{7},\,\text{SD}[X]≈0.2619,\,\text{SD}[Y]≈0.4238,
$$

 
find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}xy\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}[{\int }_{{y}^{2}}^{1}xy\cdot \frac{9}{12}(xy+1)\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{9}{12}{\int }_{-1}^{1}[{\int }_{{y}^{2}}^{1}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}+xy)\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{9}{12}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}y]}_{x={y}^{2}}^{x=1}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{9}{12}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(\frac{1}{3}{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}y-\frac{1}{3}{y}^{8}-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{5})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{9}{12}{[\frac{1}{9}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{4}{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{27}{y}^{9}-\frac{1}{12}{y}^{6}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{9}{12}[\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{27}-\frac{1}{12}-(-\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{27}-\frac{1}{12})] \\  & =\frac{9}{12}(\frac{2}{9}-\frac{2}{27}) \\  & =\frac{1}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the covariance and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}-(\frac{3}{5})(\frac{1}{7}) \\  & =\frac{8}{315}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & ≈\frac{(\frac{8}{315})}{(0.2619)\cdot (0.4238)} \\  & ≈0.23,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2} & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=18{x}^{2} & \,⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int 18{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=6{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 18{x}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}(6{x}^{3})-\int (6{x}^{3})(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =6{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-12\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡x & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={x}^{2} & \,⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})-\int (\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})(\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 18{x}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =6{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-12\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =6{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-12(\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9}+D) \\  & =6{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-4{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\frac{4{x}^{3}}{3}-12D \\  & ={x}^{3}(6{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-4\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\frac{4}{3})+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-12D.$

Finally, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}18{x}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\text{d}x & ={[{x}^{3}(6{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-4\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\frac{4}{3})]}_{1}^{e} \\  & =[{e}^{3}(6{(\operatorname{ln}⁡e)}^{2}-4\operatorname{ln}⁡e+\frac{4}{3})]-[{1}^{3}(6{(\operatorname{ln}⁡1)}^{2}-4\operatorname{ln}⁡1+\frac{4}{3})] \\  & =[{e}^{3}(6-4+\frac{4}{3})]-\frac{4}{3} \\  & =\frac{10{e}^{3}-4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$
