:question/problem: Calculate the integral $\int (3{x}^{2}+2){e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
We need to use integration by parts.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=3{x}^{2}+2\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6x \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={e}^{3x}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int {e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{e}^{3x}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (3{x}^{2}+2){e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(3{x}^{2}+2)(\frac{{e}^{3x}}{3})-\int (\frac{{e}^{3x}}{3})(6x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{(3{x}^{2}+2){e}^{3x}}{3}-\frac{6}{3}\int x{e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{(3{x}^{2}+2){e}^{3x}}{3}-2\int x{e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int x{e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1 \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={e}^{3x}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int {e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{e}^{3x}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x(\frac{{e}^{3x}}{3})-\int (\frac{{e}^{3x}}{3})(1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{x{e}^{3x}}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{x{e}^{3x}}{3}-\frac{{e}^{3x}}{9}+D \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3x}}{9}(3x-1)+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (3{x}^{2}+2){e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{(3{x}^{2}+2){e}^{3x}}{3}-2(\frac{{e}^{3x}}{9}(3x-1)+D) \\  & =\frac{(3{x}^{2}+2){e}^{3x}}{3}-\frac{2{e}^{3x}}{9}(3x-1)-2D \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3x}}{9}(3(3{x}^{2}+2)-2(3x-1))-2D \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3x}}{9}(9{x}^{2}-6x+8)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-2D.$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{0}^{1}4({z}^{2}+1){e}^{2z}\,\text{d}z.$
:question/worked-solution:
We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u={z}^{2}+1\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}z}=2z, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}z}=4{e}^{2z}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}z}\,\text{d}z=4\int {e}^{2z}\,\text{d}z=2{e}^{2z}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4({z}^{2}+1){e}^{2z}\,\text{d}z & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}z}\,\text{d}z \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}z}\,\text{d}z \\  & =({z}^{2}+1)(2{e}^{2z})-\int (2{e}^{2z})(2z)\,\text{d}z \\  & =2({z}^{2}+1){e}^{2z}-4\int z{e}^{2z}\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int z{e}^{2z}\text{d}z.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=z\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}z}=1 \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}z}={e}^{2z}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}z}\,\text{d}z=\int {e}^{2z}\,\text{d}z=\frac{{e}^{2z}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int z{e}^{2z}\,\text{d}z & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}z}\,\text{d}z \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}z}\,\text{d}z \\  & =(z)(\frac{{e}^{2z}}{2})-\int (\frac{{e}^{2z}}{2})(1)\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{z{e}^{2z}}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{2z}\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{z{e}^{2z}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{2z}}{4}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is a constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4({z}^{2}+1){e}^{2z}\,\text{d}z & =2({z}^{2}+1){e}^{2z}-4\int z{e}^{2z}\,\text{d}z \\  & =2({z}^{2}+1){e}^{2z}-4(\frac{z{e}^{2z}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{2z}}{4}+D) \\  & =2({z}^{2}+1){e}^{2z}-2z{e}^{2z}+{e}^{2z}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-4D.$ 

Finally, then, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}4({z}^{2}+1){e}^{2z}\,\text{d}z & =(2({z}^{2}+1){e}^{2z}-2z{e}^{2z}+{e}^{2z}){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(2({1}^{2}+1){(e)}^{2}-2(1)^{2}{e}^{2}+{e}^{2})-(2(0+1){e}^{0}-2\cdot 0\cdot {e}^{0}+{e}^{0}) \\  & =3{e}^{2}-3\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/3d/3da35964a3877c7a0b3fce7e4f8c2db2d320f1d69f720541afa5dd1428447b73.png)

Find the area $A$ of the shaded region that lies between the polar curves $r=2-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ and $r=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the values of $\theta $ for which the two curves intersect:

$$
\begin{aligned}2-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =2 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us two solutions for $\theta \in [-\pi ,\pi ]:$

$$
\theta =\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{5\pi }{6}
$$

To determine which is the inner function and which is the outer, let's draw an arrow from the origin that passes through the shaded region.

![](images/dd/dd265c911aa4fc5713b0e53cea2ee751e84cd7c54b2b2aefb83bfae8d1f7d92f.png)

The arrow

- *enters* the region through the inner function $r=2-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and

- *leaves* through the outer function $r=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

To find the area, we use the formula

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}([\text{outer}]^{2}-[\text{inner}]^{2})\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where

$\,$ ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{6},\,$ and $\,{\theta }_{2}=\frac{5\pi }{6}.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /6}^{5\pi /6}((2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}-(2-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /6}^{5\pi /6}(4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -(4-8\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /6}^{5\pi /6}(8\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -4)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -4\theta )\,{|}_{\pi /6}^{5\pi /6} \\  & =-2(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\theta )\,{|}_{\pi /6}^{5\pi /6} \\  & =-2(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6})+\frac{5\pi }{6})+2(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})+\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =-2(-\sqrt{3}+\frac{5\pi }{6})+2(\sqrt{3}+\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =4\sqrt{3}-\frac{4\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=3{x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6x \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula for integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(3{x}^{2})(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2})(6x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}-3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we use integration by parts to evaluate $\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) & \,⟹\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\text{d}x=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2})-\int (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2})\cdot 1\,dx \\  & =-\frac{x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,dx \\  & =-\frac{x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{4}+D\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =\frac{3{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}-3\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}-3(-\frac{x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{4}+D) \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{3x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{4}+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-3D.$ Finally then, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & ={[\frac{3{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{3x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{4}]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{3{(\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )}{2}+\frac{3(\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )}{2}-\frac{3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )}{4}-(\frac{3(0)^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)}{2}+\frac{3(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)}{2}-\frac{3\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)}{4}) \\  & =0+\frac{3\pi (-1)}{4}-0-0 \\  & =-\frac{3\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: If $k=\frac{21-3k}{4},$ then $k=${{field-1}}.
:question/worked-solution:
First, we clear the rational expression by multiplying the equation through by $4$:

$$
\begin{aligned}k & =\frac{21-3k}{4} \\ \frac{21-3k}{4} & =k \\ 4(\frac{21-3k}{4}) & =4\cdot k \\ \cancel{4}(\frac{21-3k}{\cancel{4}}) & =4k \\ 21-3k & =4k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we solve the remaining equation using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}21-3k & =4k \\ 21-3k+3k & =4k+3k \\ 21 & =7k \\ \frac{21}{7} & =\frac{7k}{7} \\ 3 & =\frac{\cancel{7}k}{\cancel{7}} \\ 3 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $k=3.$

Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(2,2)$ and a general point $P(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-2)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{|x-1|}+2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-2)^{2}+(y-2)^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+{(\sqrt{|x-1|}+2-2)}^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+|x-1|.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x\ge 1,$ we have $|x-1|=x-1,$ so

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-2)^{2}+x-1 \\  & ={x}^{2}-4x+4+x-1 \\  & ={x}^{2}-3x+3.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=2x-3 & =0 \\ 2x & =3 \\ x & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(x)=2>0.$ Therefore, $x=\frac{3}{2}$ is a minimum of $S.$

Since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=\frac{3}{2}$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S\,(\frac{3}{2})}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S\,(\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-3(\frac{3}{2})+3} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{4}-\frac{9}{2}+3} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the following integral.

${\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=$ {{field-1}}
:question/worked-solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x-3x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x+3x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi }\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+\frac{1}{16}\operatorname{sin}⁡(8x)]}_{\pi /4}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))+\frac{1}{16}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(8\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(0-1)+\frac{1}{16}(0-0) \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{8({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}{\pi }, & \,x\ge 0,\,y\ge 0,\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

The joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ for the continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is shown above. Given that 

$$
\text{E}[X]=\frac{8}{5\pi },\,\text{E}[Y]=\frac{8}{5\pi },\,\text{SD}[X]≈0.2719,\,\text{SD}[Y]≈0.2719,
$$

 
find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}xy\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}xy\cdot \frac{8({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}{\pi }\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{8}{\pi }\text{ }{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}({x}^{3}y+x{y}^{3})\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{8}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}y+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{8}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}[\frac{1}{4}{(1-{y}^{2})}^{2}y+\frac{1}{2}(1-{y}^{2}){y}^{3}]\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}[(1-2{y}^{2}+{y}^{4})y+2(1-{y}^{2}){y}^{3}]\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}(y-{y}^{5})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }{[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{6}{y}^{6}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the covariance and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{2}{3\pi }-(\frac{8}{5\pi })(\frac{8}{5\pi }) \\  & =\frac{50\pi -192}{75{\pi }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & ≈\frac{(\frac{50\pi -192}{75{\pi }^{2}})}{(0.2719)\cdot (0.2719)} \\  & ≈-0.64,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

:question/problem:
Evaluate the following integral.

${\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x=$ {{field-1}}
:question/worked-solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x-x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x+x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)+\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)]}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))+\frac{1}{12}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{1}{8}(0-0)+\frac{1}{12}(-1-0) \\  & =-\frac{1}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/af/af57b718e46c7ce0c99f4ec49a3e6903e31996ee5373556357f972deb604f6f0.png)

Find the area $A$ of the shaded region that lies between the polar curves $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the values of $\theta $ for which the two curves intersect:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us two solutions for $\theta \in [-\pi ,\pi ]:$

$$
\theta =-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}
$$

To determine which is the inner function and which is the outer, let's draw an arrow from the origin that passes through the shaded region.

![](images/47/47d82588a97e539328dd60a48e07e78d30b020ca1da7a0bf9c091148c18b5d73.png)

The arrow

- *enters* the region through the inner function $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ and

- *leaves* through the outer function $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

To find the area, we use the formula

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}([\text{outer}]^{2}-[\text{inner}]^{2})\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where

$$
\,{\theta }_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{2},\,\text{ and }\,{\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}((2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}-(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}3{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\frac{3}{2}+\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{3}{2}\theta +\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )){|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}((\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}+\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi ))-(\frac{3}{2}\cdot (-\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi ))) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: $\int 4{x}^{2}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2})}^{2}\,\,\text{d}x=$
:question/worked-solution:
We need to use integration by parts.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u={(\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2})}^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\cdot 2x=\frac{4\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2}}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=4{x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int 4{x}^{2}\,\,\text{d}x=\frac{4{x}^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4{x}^{2}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2})}^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2})}^{2}(\frac{4{x}^{3}}{3})-\int (\frac{4{x}^{3}}{3})(\frac{4\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2}}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{4{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2})}^{2}}{3}-\frac{16}{3}\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}))(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})-\int (\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})(\frac{2}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})}{3}-\frac{2}{3}\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})}{3}-\frac{2{x}^{3}}{9}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4{x}^{2}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2})}^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{4{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2})}^{2}}{3}-\frac{16}{3}(\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})}{3}-\frac{2{x}^{3}}{9}+D) \\  & =\frac{4{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2})}^{2}}{3}-\frac{16{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})}{9}+\frac{32{x}^{3}}{27}-\frac{16D}{3} \\  & =\frac{4{x}^{3}}{27}(9{(\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2})}^{2}-12\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2}+8)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

Where, $C=-\frac{16D}{3}.$

:question/problem:
![](images/97/9798487c945153400cf573ab87361d316c21a9040c1e17adf16051843bc9acd3.png)

Find the area of the shaded region that lies between the polar curves $r=\sqrt{3}-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ as shown above.
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the values of $\theta $ for which the two curves intersect:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\sqrt{3} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us two solutions for $\theta \in [-\pi ,\pi ]:$

$$
\theta =-\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\pi }{6}
$$

To determine which is the inner function and which is the outer, let's draw an arrow from the origin that passes through the shaded region.

![](images/33/336b0f0bb8c1d5bba38d2fa5b40a09fb9c76fb4cdd7db21d04ceb14c0816aa52.png)

The arrow

- *enters* the region through the inner function $r=\sqrt{3}-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ and

- *leaves* through the outer function $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

To find the area, we use the formula

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}([\text{outer}]^{2}-[\text{inner}]^{2})\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where

$\,$ ${\theta }_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{6},\,$ and $\,{\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{6}.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}((\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}-(\sqrt{3}-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -(3-2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}(-3+2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[-3\theta {|}_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}+2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta ){|}_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[-3(\frac{\pi }{6}+\frac{\pi }{6})+2\sqrt{3}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{6}))] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[-\pi +2\sqrt{3}(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2})] \\  & =\sqrt{3}-\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
A tank initially holds $450\,\text{gal}$ of a sugar-water solution containing $18\,\text{lb}$ of sugar.
Fresh water is poured into the tank at a rate of $15\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed sugar solution leaves the tank at a rate of $10\,\text{gal/min}.$
Find an equation for the amount of sugar $Q(t),$ in pounds, in the tank $t$ minutes after the fresh water is first added.
:question/worked-solution:
Since $Q$ is the amount of sugar in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which sugar enters the tank minus the rate at which sugar leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which sugar enters the tank.

First, note that fresh water (i.e., a solution containing $0\,\text{lb/gal}$ of sugar) enters the tank at a rate of $15\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *sugar* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (15\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (15\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which sugar exits the tank.

Now, to find the rate at which sugar leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of solution in the tank at time $t.$

- The tank initially contains $450\,\text{gal}$ of solution.

- Fresh water enters the tank at a rate of $15\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $15t\,\text{gal}$ have entered the tank.

- The completely mixed solution leaves the tank at a rate of $10\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $10t\,\text{gal}$ have left the tank.

As a result, the volume of solution in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
450+15t-10t=(450+5t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Then, since $Q$ is the amount of sugar in the tank, the *concentration* of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{450+5t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $10\,\text{gal/min},$ *sugar* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(10\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{450+5t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(10\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{450+5t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{10Q}{450+5t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{90+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\ \frac{dQ}{dt} & =0-\frac{2Q}{90+t} \\ \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{2}{90+t}\,Q.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{2}{90+t} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\int (-\frac{2}{90+t})\,dt \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \,dQ & =-2\int \frac{1}{90+t}\,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|90+t|+C \\ |Q| & ={e}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|90+t|+C} \\ Q(t) & =\frac{A}{(90+t)^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $A=\pm {e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the tank initially contains $18\,\text{lb}$ of sugar. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=18,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =18 \\ \frac{A}{(90+0)^{2}} & =18 \\ A & =18\cdot {90}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
Q(t)=18{(\frac{90}{90+t})}^{2}
$$

:question/problem: Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r=2-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ for $\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi .$
:question/worked-solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=2-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{2}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(2-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(4-8\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }-2{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(-1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }-2(-\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi })) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+2\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }) \\  & =3\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =3(\pi -\frac{\pi }{2})+4(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{2}+4\cdot (-1)-\frac{1}{2}(0) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{2}-4 \\  & =\frac{3\pi -8}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Calculate $\frac{2}{3}L+2A$, where
$L=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & -3 & -9 \\ 18 & -3 & 0\end{bmatrix}$
and
$A=\begin{bmatrix}- \frac{3}{2} & 3 & - \frac{3}{2} \\ -3 & 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}$
$\frac{2}{3}L+2A=$
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}$-9$
{{field-3}}$2${{field-4}}
:question/worked-solution:
We multiply each entry of $L$ by $\frac{2}{3}$ and each entry of $A$ by $2,$ and then add the resulting matrices, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}L+2A & =\frac{2}{3}\begin{bmatrix}-3 & -3 & -9 \\ 18 & -3 & 0\end{bmatrix}+2\begin{bmatrix}- \frac{3}{2} & 3 & - \frac{3}{2} \\ -3 & 2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3}\cdot (-3) & \frac{2}{3}\cdot (-3) & \frac{2}{3}\cdot (-9) \\ \frac{2}{3}\cdot 18 & \frac{2}{3}\cdot (-3) & \frac{2}{3}\cdot 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot (- \frac{3}{2}) & 2\cdot 3 & 2\cdot (- \frac{3}{2}) \\ 2\cdot (-3) & 2\cdot 2 & 2\cdot 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -2 & -6 \\ 12 & -2 & 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 6 & -3 \\ -6 & 4 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2-3 & -2+6 & -6-3 \\ 12-6 & -2+4 & 0+2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 4 & -9 \\ 6 & 2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

First, note that the index $n$ starts from $3.$ However, it is still a geometric series because it is in the form $\sum a{r}^{n}.$ 

In this case, the first term is ${a}_{3},$ and so the sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of this geometric series is given by

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{3}}{1-r},\,|r|<1.
$$

For the first few terms, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{3} & =\frac{4}{9}{(\frac{3}{4})}^{3}=\frac{4}{9}(\frac{27}{64})=\frac{3}{16} \\ {a}_{4} & =\frac{4}{9}{(\frac{3}{4})}^{4}=\frac{4}{9}(\frac{81}{256})=\frac{9}{64}\end{aligned}
$$

The common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{4}}{{a}_{3}}=\frac{(\frac{9}{64})}{(\frac{3}{16})}=\frac{9}{64}\cdot \frac{16}{3}=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=3}^{\infty }\frac{4}{9}{(\frac{3}{4})}^{n} & =\frac{{a}_{3}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{16})}{(1-\frac{3}{4})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{16})}{(\frac{1}{4})} \\  & =\frac{3}{16}\cdot 4 \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I=\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that 

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2{e}^{-2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(-2{e}^{-2x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2{e}^{-2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(-2{e}^{-2x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2I.\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2J \\ I & ={e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2(-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2I) \\ I & ={e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-4I \\ 5I & ={e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-2x}}{5}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =(\frac{{e}^{-2x}}{5}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x)){|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =(\frac{{e}^{-2\pi /2}}{5}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})))-(\frac{{e}^{-2(0)}}{5}(\operatorname{sin}⁡0-2\operatorname{cos}⁡0)) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-\pi }}{5}+\frac{2}{5} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}({e}^{-\pi }+2)\end{aligned}
$$

Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I=\int \frac{{ln}^{4}⁡x}{6x}\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={ln}^{4}⁡x & \,⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{4{ln}^{3}⁡x}{x}, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{6x} & \,⇒\,v=\int \frac{1}{6x}\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int \frac{{ln}^{4}⁡x}{6x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({ln}^{4}⁡x)(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{6})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{6})(\frac{4{ln}^{3}⁡x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{5}⁡x}{6}-4\int \frac{{ln}^{4}⁡x}{6x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{5}⁡x}{6}-4I.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $I.$ We can ignore the constant of integration in this case, because it is insignificant for further evaluation of the definite integral.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\frac{{ln}^{5}⁡x}{6}-4I \\ 5I & =\frac{{ln}^{5}⁡x}{6} \\ I & =\frac{{ln}^{5}⁡x}{30}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}\frac{{ln}^{4}⁡x}{6x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{30}({ln}^{5}⁡x)\,{|}_{1}^{{e}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{30}({ln}^{5}⁡({e}^{3})-{ln}^{5}⁡(1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{30}((3\operatorname{ln}⁡e)^{5}-{0}^{5}) \\  & =\frac{1}{30}({3}^{5}-0) \\  & =\frac{81}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I=\int \frac{{ln}^{4}⁡x}{3x}\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={ln}^{4}⁡x & \,⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{4{ln}^{3}⁡x}{x}, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3x} & \,⇒\,v=\int \frac{1}{3x}\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int \frac{{ln}^{4}⁡x}{3x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({ln}^{4}⁡x)(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{3})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{3})(\frac{4{ln}^{3}⁡x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{5}⁡x}{3}-4\int \frac{{ln}^{4}⁡x}{3x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{5}⁡x}{3}-4I.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $I.$ We can ignore the constant of integration in this case, because it is insignificant for further evaluation of the definite integral.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\frac{{ln}^{5}⁡x}{3}-4I \\ 5I & =\frac{{ln}^{5}⁡x}{3} \\ I & =\frac{{ln}^{5}⁡x}{15}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{5}}\frac{{ln}^{4}⁡x}{3x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{15}({ln}^{5}⁡x)\,{|}_{1}^{{e}^{5}} \\  & =\frac{1}{15}({ln}^{5}⁡({e}^{5})-{ln}^{5}⁡(1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{15}((5\operatorname{ln}⁡e)^{5}-{0}^{5}) \\  & =\frac{1}{15}({5}^{5}-0) \\  & =\frac{625}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Calculate $\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})-\int (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3})(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{1}{3}I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}J \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}(\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{1}{3}I) \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{9}-\frac{1}{9}I \\ \frac{10}{9}I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{9} \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))}{10}+C\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}2y\operatorname{cos}⁡x, & \,0\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the expected value of $Y.$
:question/worked-solution:
The marginal density function for $Y$ when $0\le y\le 1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2y[\operatorname{sin}⁡x]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =2y(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =2y(1-0) \\  & =2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for ${f}_{X}(x)$ is given by

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}2y, & 0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the  expected value of $Y$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\cdot 2y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{2}{3}-0) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1.
$$

The first term is 

$$
{a}_{1}=\frac{9}{4}{(-\frac{1}{3})}^{2(1)}=\frac{9}{4}{(-\frac{1}{3})}^{2}
$$

 

and the second term is 

$$
{a}_{2}=\frac{9}{4}{(-\frac{1}{3})}^{2(2)}=\frac{9}{4}{(-\frac{1}{3})}^{4}.
$$

Therefore, the common ratio is 

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{\frac{9}{4}{(-\frac{1}{3})}^{4}}{\frac{9}{4}{(-\frac{1}{3})}^{2}}={(-\frac{1}{3})}^{2}=\frac{1}{9}.
$$

 

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{9}{4}{(-\frac{1}{3})}^{2n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{\frac{9}{4}(\frac{1}{9})}{(1-\frac{1}{9})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{1}{4})}{(\frac{8}{9})} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{9}{8} \\  & =\frac{9}{32}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}48y(x-y),\, & 0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le \frac{x}{2}, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{4}{5},$ $\text{E}[Y]=\frac{1}{4},$ and $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]=\frac{2}{3},$ find the covariance matrix for $X$ and $Y.$
:question/worked-solution:
For two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ the covariance matrix $Σ$ is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}].
$$

Recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, we find $\text{Var}[X].$ Using the given results, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}-{(\frac{4}{5})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{75}.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we compute $\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}{y}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}48{y}^{3}(x-y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}(x{y}^{3}-{y}^{4})\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{4}x{y}^{4}-\frac{1}{5}{y}^{5}]}_{y=0}^{y=x/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{64}{x}^{5}-\frac{1}{160}{x}^{5})\text{d}x \\  & =48\cdot \frac{3}{320}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{5}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{9}{20}{[\frac{1}{6}{x}^{6}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{3}{40}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{40}-{(\frac{1}{4})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{80}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ By the rule of the lazy statistician, we find $\text{E}[XY]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}xy\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}48x{y}^{2}(x-y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}-x{y}^{3})\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}-\frac{1}{4}x{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=x/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{24}{x}^{5}-\frac{1}{64}{x}^{5})\text{d}x \\  & =48\cdot \frac{5}{192}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{5}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{4}{[\frac{1}{6}{x}^{6}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{5}{24}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{5}{24}-(\frac{4}{5})\cdot (\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{120}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the covariance matrix is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{75} & \frac{1}{120} \\ \frac{1}{120} & \frac{1}{80}\end{aligned}].
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.$
:question/worked-solution:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2})(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2})-\int (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2})(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{1}{2}I.\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}J \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{1}{2}I) \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{4}-\frac{1}{4}I \\ \frac{5}{4}I & =\frac{2{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{4} \\ I & =\frac{1}{5}{e}^{-x}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =(\frac{1}{5}{e}^{-x}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))){|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =(\frac{1}{5}{e}^{-\pi /2}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})))-(\frac{1}{5}{e}^{-0}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(0))-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(0)))) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-\pi /2}}{5}+\frac{1}{5} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-\pi /2}+1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Given that

{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+4)}^{4}=A{x}^{8}+B{x}^{6}+C{x}^{4}+128{x}^{2}+256

The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2},\, & -1\le x\le 1,\,\,-1\le y\le 2, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

If $\text{E}[X]=0$ and $\text{E}[Y]=\frac{5}{4},$ find the covariance matrix for $X$ and $Y.$
:question/worked-solution:
For two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ the covariance matrix $Σ$ is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}].
$$

Recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}.
$$

We compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{2}(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2})\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{4}\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{2}\cdot {[\frac{1}{5}{x}^{5}]}_{-1}^{1}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{-1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{5}-{(0)}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we compute $\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{y}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{y}^{2}(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2})\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{4}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{4}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{-1}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {[\frac{1}{5}{y}^{5}]}_{-1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{33}{5} \\  & =\frac{11}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =\frac{11}{5}-{(\frac{5}{4})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{51}{80}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the covariance of $X$ and $Y.$ The joint support of $X$ and $Y$ is given by the rectangle

$$
S=[-1,1]\times [-1,2].
$$

Moreover, we can write

$$
f(x,y)=g(x)\cdot h(y),
$$

where $g(x)=\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}$ and $h(y)=\frac{{y}^{2}}{3}.$

Hence, $X$ and $Y$ are independent, and consequently $\text{Cov}[X,Y]=0.$

Therefore, the covariance matrix is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{51}{80}\end{aligned}].
$$

:question/problem:
The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{16}({x}^{2}-y),\, & 0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le {x}^{2}, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{5}{3},$ $\text{E}[Y]=\frac{20}{21},$ and $\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]=\frac{40}{27},$ find the covariance matrix for $X$ and $Y.$
:question/worked-solution:
For two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ the covariance matrix $Σ$ is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}].
$$

Recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, we find $\text{Var}[X].$
We compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}\frac{5}{16}{x}^{2}({x}^{2}-y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}({x}^{4}-y{x}^{2})\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}{[y{x}^{4}-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}{x}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y={x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{6})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{32}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{6}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{32}{[\frac{1}{7}{x}^{7}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{20}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{20}{7}-{(\frac{5}{3})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{63}.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we compute $\text{Var}[Y].$ Using the given results, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =\frac{40}{27}-{(\frac{20}{21})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{760}{1\,323}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ By the rule of the lazy statistician, we find $\text{E}[XY]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}xy\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}\frac{5}{16}xy({x}^{2}-y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}({x}^{3}y-x{y}^{2})\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}x]}_{y=0}^{y={x}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{5}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{1}{6}{x}^{7})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{96}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{7}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{96}{[\frac{1}{8}{x}^{8}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{5}{3}-(\frac{5}{3})\cdot (\frac{20}{21}) \\  & =\frac{5}{63}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the covariance matrix is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{63} & \frac{5}{63} \\ \frac{5}{63} & \frac{760}{1\,323}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, note that the index $n$ starts from $3.$ However, it is still a geometric series because it is in the form $\sum a{r}^{n}.$ 

In this case, the first term is ${a}_{3},$ and so the sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of this geometric series is given by

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{3}}{1-r},\,|r|<1.
$$

For the first few terms, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{3} & =\frac{25}{27}{(\frac{3}{5})}^{3}=\frac{25}{27}(\frac{27}{125})=\frac{1}{5} \\ {a}_{4} & =\frac{25}{27}{(\frac{3}{5})}^{4}=\frac{25}{27}(\frac{81}{625})=\frac{3}{25}\end{aligned}

:question/problem: Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=\theta +{e}^{\theta }$ for $-\pi \le \theta \le \pi ?$
:question/worked-solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\theta +{e}^{\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=1+{e}^{\theta }.
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\sqrt{(\theta +{e}^{\theta })^{2}+(1+{e}^{\theta })^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\sqrt{{\theta }^{2}+2\theta {e}^{\theta }+{e}^{2\theta }+1+2{e}^{\theta }+{e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\sqrt{{\theta }^{2}+2{e}^{\theta }(\theta +1)+2{e}^{2\theta }+1}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the given series is a geometric series because it is in the form $\sum a{r}^{n}.$ 

The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

The first term is

$$
{a}_{1}=10{(\frac{1}{2})}^{1}=5.
$$

 

The common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{10{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}}{10{(\frac{1}{2})}^{1}}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }10{(\frac{1}{2})}^{n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{5}{(1-\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =\frac{5}{(\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =5\cdot \frac{2}{1} \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}x{y}^{3},\, & 0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le 2, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

If $\text{E}[X]=\frac{2}{3}$ and $\text{E}[Y]=\frac{8}{5},$ find the covariance matrix for $X$ and $Y.$
:question/worked-solution:
For two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ the covariance matrix $Σ$ is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}].
$$

Recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}.
$$

We compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}(\frac{1}{2}x{y}^{3})\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{3}\cdot {[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}]}_{0}^{1}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot {[\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot 4 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{18}.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we compute $\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}(\frac{1}{2}x{y}^{3})\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{5}{\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{5}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{5}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot {[\frac{1}{6}{y}^{6}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{32}{3} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}-{(\frac{8}{5})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{75}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the covariance of $X$ and $Y.$ The joint support of $X$ and $Y$ is given by the rectangle

$$
S=[0,1]\times [0,2].
$$

Moreover, we can write

$$
f(x,y)=g(x)\cdot h(y),
$$

where $g(x)=2x$ and $h(y)=\frac{{y}^{3}}{4}.$

Hence, $X$ and $Y$ are independent, and consequently $\text{Cov}[X,Y]=0.$

Therefore, the covariance matrix is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{18} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{8}{75}\end{aligned}].
$$

:question/problem:
In a factory, the average amount of sugar in a cookie is $15$ grams. However, $10%$ of cookies contain no more than $14$ grams of sugar. Assuming that the amount of sugar in each cookie is normally distributed, find the standard deviation of the amount of sugar in a cookie, rounded to $2$ decimal places.

*Hint: A table of values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p$ is given below, where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $p$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.10\,$ | $\,0.15\,$ | $\,0.20\,$ | $\,0.25\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\,-2.3263\,$ | $\,-1.8808\,$ | $\,-1.6449\,$ | $\,-1.2816\,$ | $\,-1.0364\,$ | $\,-0.8416\,$ | $\,-0.6745\,$ |
:question/worked-solution:
Let $X$ represent the amount (in grams) of sugar in a cookie. Then we have $X∼N(15,{\sigma }^{2}),$ and we want to find the standard deviation $\sigma .$ 

We know that $P(X\le 14)=0.10.$ Converting $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 14) & =0.10 \\ P(Z\le \frac{14-15}{\sigma }) & =0.10 \\ Φ(-\frac{1}{\sigma }) & =0.10 \\ -\frac{1}{\sigma } & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.10).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, 

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(0.10)=-1.2816.
$$

Finally then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sigma } & =-1.2816 \\ \frac{1}{\sigma } & =1.2816 \\ \sigma  & =\frac{1}{1.2816} \\  & ≈0.78.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:

Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. Find $\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=4]$ given that the random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ shown in the table above and the corresponding conditional expected value is ${\mu }_{X|4}=\frac{3}{2}.$

Recall that the conditional variance of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=y] & =\text{E}[(X-{\mu }_{X|y})^{2}\,|\,Y=y] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=y]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2} \\  & =[{\sum }_{x}{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In order to find ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y),$ let's first find the marginal distribution of $Y,$ corresponding to the column totals:

| ${f}_{Y}(y)$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |

The conditional probability mass function of $X$ given that $Y=y$ is

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)}.
$$

Therefore, dividing each joint probability by the corresponding column total, we obtain the conditional probability mass function of $X$ given that $Y=y:$

| ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |

|  | $1$ | $1$ |

:question/problem: Calculate $\int \frac{{ln}^{8}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x$ using integration by parts.
:question/worked-solution:
First, we let

$$
I=\int \frac{{ln}^{8}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={ln}^{8}⁡x & \,⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{8{ln}^{7}⁡x}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x} & \,⇒\,v=\int \frac{1}{x}\text{d}x=\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int \frac{{ln}^{8}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={ln}^{8}⁡x(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)(\frac{8{ln}^{7}⁡x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={ln}^{9}⁡x-8\int \frac{{ln}^{8}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={ln}^{9}⁡x-8I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $I,$ remembering to add a constant of integration $C$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={ln}^{9}⁡x-8I \\ 9I & ={ln}^{9}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{ln}^{9}⁡x}{9}+C\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: A golden eagle is moving in a straight line with a velocity of $v(t)=\frac{{2}^{t}}{12}\,\text{m/s},$ where $t$ is the time in seconds. Find the average velocity of the golden eagle on the interval $[2,6].$
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the average value of the velocity on $[{t}_{1},{t}_{2}],$ we use the average value formula

$$
{v}_{\text{avg}}=\frac{1}{{t}_{2}-{t}_{1}}{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}v(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{1}{6-2}\,{\int }_{2}^{6}(\frac{{2}^{t}}{12})\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{4\cdot 12\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡2}({2}^{t}){|}_{2}^{6} \\  & =\frac{1}{48\operatorname{ln}⁡2}({2}^{6}-{2}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{60}{48\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\  & =\frac{5}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the average velocity is $\frac{5}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\,\text{m/s}.$

:question/problem:
Consider the polar curve $r=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ).$ Given that 

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ),\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta ),
$$

and ${y}^{′}(\frac{3\pi }{2})=0,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. ${x}^{′}(\frac{3\pi }{2})=0$

II. ${lim}_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\infty $

III. The curve has a vertical tangent at $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{2}$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the following results.*

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta )\to {0}^{-}\,\text{as}\,\theta \to {(\frac{3\pi }{2})}^{-} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta )\to {0}^{+}\,\text{as}\,\theta \to {(\frac{3\pi }{2})}^{+}\end{aligned}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
For a given polar curve, there is a vertical tangent at $\theta ={\theta }_{0}$ if

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}{{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}
$$

is infinite. This means that

$$
{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})\ne 0\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})=0.
$$

However, if the curve is continuous at ${\theta }_{0}$ yet the derivative takes the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}$ at this point, we say that the curve has a vertical tangent at this point if

$$
{lim}_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\pm \infty \,\text{and}\,{lim}_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\pm \infty .
$$

In this case, we're told that ${y}^{′}(\frac{3\pi }{2})=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Substituting $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{2}$ into the expression for ${x}^{′}(\theta ),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\frac{3\pi }{2}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{3\pi }{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot \frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi ) \\  & =-1+1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Computing the limit as $\theta \to {(\frac{3\pi }{2})}^{-}$ using L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={lim}_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta )}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta )}) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}(\frac{(\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta ))^{′}}{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ))^{′}}) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}(\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta )}{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta )}) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}(\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta )}{-2(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta ))}).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the limit in the numerator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ) & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot \frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi ) \\  & =4\cdot 1 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the first hint, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={lim}_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}(\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta )}{-2(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta )}) \\  & =\frac{4}{-2\cdot {0}^{-}} \\  & =\frac{4}{{0}^{+}} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Using the calculations from part II, and the second hint, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={lim}_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{+}}(\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta )}{-2(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta )}) \\  & =\frac{4}{-2\cdot {0}^{+}} \\  & =\frac{4}{{0}^{-}} \\  & =-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Since the limits of our derivative are both infinite, there is a vertical tangent to the curve at $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{2}.$

![](images/f9/f9a4fc8fa61dac84d3dbc4bc48f86e2b702f7854b1fd1d3b3e5f4303fe7769a7.png)

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

:question/problem:
Consider the polar curve $r={tan}^{2}⁡\theta $ for $\theta \in (-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}).$ Given that 

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta ),\,{y}^{′}(\theta )={tan}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sec}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +2),\,
$$

and ${x}^{′}(0)=0,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. ${y}^{′}(0)=0$

II. ${lim}_{\theta \to {0}^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\infty $

III. The curve has a vertical tangent at $\theta =0$
:question/worked-solution:
For a given polar curve, there is a vertical tangent at $\theta ={\theta }_{0}$ if

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}{{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}
$$

is infinite. This means that

$$
{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})\ne 0\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})=0.
$$

However, if the curve is continuous at ${\theta }_{0}$ yet the derivative takes the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}$ at this point, we say that the curve has a vertical tangent at this point if

$$
{lim}_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\pm \infty \,\text{and}\,{lim}_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\pm \infty .
$$

In this case, we're told that ${x}^{′}(0)=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Substituting $\theta =0$ into the expression for ${y}^{′}(\theta ),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & ={tan}^{2}⁡(0)\operatorname{sec}⁡(0)({cos}^{2}⁡(0)+2) \\  & =0\cdot 1\cdot ({1}^{2}+2) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Computing the limit as $\theta \to {0}^{+},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to {0}^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={lim}_{\theta \to {0}^{+}}\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to {0}^{+}}(\frac{{tan}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sec}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +2)}{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta )}) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to {0}^{+}}(\frac{{tan}^{\cancel{2}}⁡\theta \operatorname{sec}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +2)}{\cancel{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta )}) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to {0}^{+}}(\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \operatorname{sec}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +2)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡(0)\operatorname{sec}⁡(0)({cos}^{2}⁡(0)+2)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+\operatorname{sec}⁡(0)} \\  & =\frac{0\cdot 1\cdot ({1}^{2}+2)}{1+1} \\  & =\frac{0}{2} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since the right limit of our derivative is not infinite, the curve does *not* have a vertical tangent at $\theta =0.$ In fact, it is a horizontal tangent.

![](images/49/498b937eba18870a36ee6f09bb99cf7dde38eb95c4cc2aa6edcb46080d0fcf04.png)

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

:question/problem:
Compute the values of $\theta \in [0,\pi )$ for which the polar curve $r=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ has a horizontal tangent, given that

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ),\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).
$$

In **ascending order**, the polar curve has horizontal tangents at

${\theta }_{1}=$ 
{{field-1}}$\,$ and $\,{\theta }_{2}=$ 
{{field-2}}.
:question/worked-solution:
We have a horizontal tangent when

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}=0,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{y}^{′}(\theta )=0\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}(\theta )\ne 0.
$$

To find the horizontal tangents, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Compute the derivatives ${y}^{′}(\theta )$ and ${x}^{′}(\theta ).$

We're given that

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ),\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).
$$

**Step 2**: Find the values of $\theta $ where ${y}^{′}(\theta )=0.$

By writing down and solving the equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ) & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ) & =0 \\ 2\theta  & =\pi n \\ \theta  & =\frac{\pi }{2}n,\end{aligned}
$$

where $n$ is any integer. However, among the solutions above, only two belong to the required domain, namely

$$
{\theta }_{1}=0,\,{\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

**Step 3**: Check to see whether any candidates have ${x}^{′}(\theta )=0.$

We substitute our candidate solutions into ${x}^{′}(\theta )$ and check that ${x}^{′}(\theta )\ne 0.$ If ${x}^{′}(\theta )=0,$ further investigation is necessary.

- Substituting ${\theta }_{1}=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(0) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot 0) \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(0) \\  & =3 \\  & \ne 0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ is a valid solution.

- Substituting ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ) \\  & =-3 \\  & \ne 0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}$ is also a valid solution.

Therefore, in ascending order, our curve has horizontal tangents at ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}.$

:question/problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the parabola defined by the parametric equations

$$
x+1=2{t}^{2},\,y+3=4t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$
:question/worked-solution:
First, let's make $t$ the subject of the parametric equations. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & =\frac{x+1}{2},\,t=\frac{y+3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring both sides of the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & ={(\frac{y+3}{4})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{(y+3)^{2}}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now eliminate the parameter $t$ by substituting the above into the equation ${t}^{2}=\frac{x+1}{2}$ and rearranging to find the Cartesian equation of the parabola, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(y+3)^{2}}{16} & =\frac{x+1}{2} \\ (y+3)^{2} & =16\cdot (\frac{x+1}{2}) \\ (y+3)^{2} & =8(x+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${(\frac{1}{3})}^{2x}$ is always positive and $-(0.52)^{4x-3}$ is always negative, we always have

$$
{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2x}>-(0.52)^{4x-3}.
$$

This means that the given inequality is satisfied by all real values of $x.$

Therefore,

$$
-\infty <x<\infty 
$$

:question/problem:
Which of the three sequences below are geometric sequences?

I. $\frac{1}{3},\,-\frac{4}{3},\,-\frac{16}{3},\,…$

II. $-5,\,-20,\,80,\,…$

III. $f(n+1)=4f(n)-4,\,f(1)=2,\,n\ge 1$
:question/worked-solution:
A sequence is geometric if there is a common ratio between its terms. Let's check each sequence in turn.

- Sequence I is not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{(-\frac{4}{3})}{(\frac{1}{3})}=-4 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{(-\frac{16}{3})}{(-\frac{4}{3})}=4\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence II is not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{-20}{-5}=4 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{80}{-20}=-4\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence III is not a geometric sequence. To see this, we can calculate the first $3$ terms of the sequence and then compute the ratios of consecutive terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1) & =2 \\ f(2) & =4\cdot 2-4=4 \\ f(3) & =4\cdot 4-4=12\end{aligned}
$$

So, the first two pairs of consecutive terms have different ratios:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{f(2)}{f(1)} & =\frac{4}{2}=2 \\ \frac{f(3)}{f(2)} & =\frac{12}{4}=3\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, none of the given is a geometric sequence.

:question/problem:
Compute the value of $\theta \in [0,\frac{\pi }{2})$ for which the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ has a vertical tangent, given that

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )+\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ),\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ).
$$

The polar curve has a vertical tangent at $\theta =$
{{field-1}}.
:question/worked-solution:
We have a vertical tangent when

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}
$$

is infinite. This means that

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=0\,\text{and}\,{y}^{′}(\theta )\ne 0.
$$

To find the vertical tangents, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Compute the derivatives ${y}^{′}(\theta )$ and ${x}^{′}(\theta ).$ 

We're given that

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )+\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ),\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ).
$$

**Step 2**: Find the values of $\theta $ where ${x}^{′}(\theta )=0.$

By writing down and solving the equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )+\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ) & =0 \\ \sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ) \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡(2\theta ) & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ 2\theta  & =-\frac{\pi }{6}+\pi n \\ \theta  & =-\frac{\pi }{12}+\frac{\pi }{2}n,\end{aligned}
$$

where $n$ is any integer. However, among the solutions above, only one belongs to the required domain, namely

$$
{\theta }_{1}=\frac{5\pi }{12}.
$$

**Step 3**: Check to see whether our candidate has ${y}^{′}(\theta )=0.$ 

We substitute our candidate solution into ${y}^{′}(\theta )$ and check that ${y}^{′}(\theta )\ne 0.$ If ${y}^{′}(\theta )=0,$ further investigation is necessary.

- Substituting ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{5\pi }{12},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\frac{5\pi }{12}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(\frac{5\pi }{12}))-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(\frac{5\pi }{12})) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6})-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\sqrt{3}(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{3}{2} \\  & =2 \\  & \ne 0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

We have a horizontal tangent when

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}=0,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{y}^{′}(\theta )=0\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}(\theta )\ne 0.
$$

To find the horizontal tangents, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Compute the derivatives ${y}^{′}(\theta )$ and ${x}^{′}(\theta ).$ 

We're given that

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

**Step 2**: Find the values of $\theta $ where ${y}^{′}(\theta )=0.$

By writing down and solving the equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ \theta  & =\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi n,\end{aligned}
$$

where $n$ is any integer. However, among the solutions above, only one belongs to the required domain, namely

$$
{\theta }_{1}=\frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

**Step 3**: Check to see whether our candidate has ${x}^{′}(\theta )=0.$ 

We substitute our candidate solution into ${x}^{′}(\theta )$ and check that ${x}^{′}(\theta )\ne 0.$ If ${x}^{′}(\theta )=0,$ further investigation is necessary.

- Substituting ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{3\pi }{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\frac{3\pi }{2}) & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & =-2(-1) \\  & =2 \\  & \ne 0.\,✓\end{aligned}
